title: 15 Responsible Engineering
text:
Teams can still fail after assembling assessment frameworks, fairness metrics, explainability mechanisms, efficiency analyses, and governance infrastructure. A team may retrofit fairness after benchmark success, trust aggregate accuracy, or treat compliance evidence as paperwork rather than system behavior, drawing on intuitions from traditional software engineering where bugs are local and testing is deterministic.

Fallacy: Responsibility can be addressed after the system achieves technical objectives.
Teams assume fairness constraints can be retrofitted once models demonstrate strong benchmark performance. In production, early architectural decisions constrain what interventions remain feasible. Amazon’s recruiting tool, abandoned after remediation failed (section 15.2.1), is the case in point. Integrating fairness constraints early can be less costly than retrofitting them after data contracts, monitoring, and release gates are fixed.


Pitfall: Relying on aggregate metrics to assess fairness.
Engineers assume high overall accuracy indicates the system works well for all users. The flaw of averages (section 15.3.2) shows why this intuition fails, because aggregate metrics can conceal large subgroup disparities. The credit-service analysis in section 15.3.2.1 showed a 30 percentage-point TPR gap, with qualified minority applicants rejected at 4× the majority-group rate. These disparities can persist undetected when standard monitoring tracks only aggregates. Production systems require disaggregated evaluation with application-specific thresholds, such as the 5-percentage-point TPR threshold used for the credit service.


Fallacy: Removing sensitive attributes from training data eliminates bias.
Teams remove gender, race, and protected attributes expecting this ensures fairness. Other features can act as proxy variables when they correlate with sensitive characteristics. ZIP codes, purchase patterns, browsing history, college names, and language choices can carry indirect demographic signal. Amazon’s recruiting tool kept encoding sex through college and organization names after explicit gender terms were removed (section 15.2.1), and the care-management algorithm (war story 15.1) reproduced racial disparity through its cost target, a proxy that no attribute filter would remove. Removing protected attributes does not by itself establish fairness.


Pitfall: Treating documentation as sufficient accountability.
Teams invest effort in model cards, then consider responsibility requirements satisfied. Documentation provides transparency (section 15.3.3.2) but not enforcement. A model card specifying “not validated for high-stakes decisions” has no effect when the system is repurposed for loan approvals without technical restrictions. Accountability requires operational integration: monitoring dashboards, documented subgroup-disparity alert thresholds, incident response procedures, and access controls preventing deployment beyond validated use cases.


Fallacy: Responsible AI is primarily a legal compliance issue.
Teams treat responsibility as external oversight rather than engineering practice. Engineering decisions made months before legal review constrain the solution space more than any compliance assessment. Architecture selection determines what fairness interventions are feasible, while data pipeline design establishes whether disaggregated evaluation is even possible. As section 15.2.5 establishes, systems designed with responsibility as an engineering objective enable efficient validation; systems where responsibility is added at late-stage review face redesign or deployment with documented risks.


Pitfall: Measuring the environmental impact of training but not inference.
Public discourse focuses on training-run carbon, and engineers often follow this framing when assessing environmental responsibility. The illustrative TCO analysis in section 15.4.2 shows why this focus is incomplete: under its unbatched service-demand assumptions for the DLRM ranking service (table 10), the inference-to-training cost ratio is about 40:1, and inference emits about 63× as much CO2 as training. A model trained periodically but served millions of times daily can have a lifecycle footprint dominated by inference rather than training. These values are scenario-dependent, but they show why lifecycle accounting must include both terms.


Fallacy: Model weights are exempt from data governance and deletion requests.
Teams often assume that once training data has been compiled into model weights, the data is gone and compliance obligations cannot reach the artifact. In reality, models can memorize training data, and membership inference attacks can reveal whether a sensitive record appeared in the training set (Shokri et al. 2017). Unlike a database delete, a neural network diffuses each training point’s statistical influence across its parameters through gradient updates, so verifiably purging that influence forces systems trade-offs. Exact retraining from scratch on a cleaned dataset provides a reference for removing the excluded records’ contribution, but it re-expends the training budget (potentially thousands of accelerator-hours) and its carbon emissions. It also does not erase other copies or facts inferable from retained data. Machine unlearning, introduced with audit infrastructure (section 15.5.5), aims to bound that cost, but verifying that an intervention removes statistical influence without degrading model utility remains an open systems challenge. Engineering teams must track data-to-model lineage and evaluate retraining, machine unlearning, or compensating controls with legal and privacy specialists whenever an erasure request affects deployed artifacts.

Across these failures, the recurring mistake is to treat responsibility as something added after the system is built rather than as a system property. Measurable constraints, continuous monitoring, and enforceable governance carry responsibility through the full lifecycle.

Self-Check: Question

A deployed automated lending model achieves an impressive 88% overall accuracy on its global test set. However, a disaggregated audit reveals that qualified minority applicants experience a 60% True Positive Rate compared to 90% for majority applicants (a 30 percentage-point gap) and face \(4\times\) higher false rejection rates. Which engineering pitfall does this scenario illustrate?

Relying on aggregate metrics to assess fairness, which conceals severe subgroup disparities behind strong overall averages (the Flaw of Averages).
Treating documentation as sufficient accountability, assuming a model card automatically prevents operational misuse.
The belief that model weights are exempt from data governance and right-to-erasure regulations.
Assuming that edge deployment power budgets scale linearly with dataset sample size.

A team removes race and gender columns from their training dataset, asserting that “the model cannot discriminate on features it cannot see.” Drawing on the Amazon recruiting and Optum healthcare cases, explain why this naive attribute removal creates false confidence, and identify the specific engineering analyses required.
True or False: Because a model card explicitly specifies that a vision model is “not validated for high-stakes medical or security screening,” publishing the model card guarantees operational compliance without requiring technical access controls or deployment release gates.
True or False: For a high-traffic production ML service, measuring and reporting only the electricity consumed during model training runs provides an accurate accounting of the system’s long-term environmental carbon footprint.

See Answers →

title: 15 Responsible Engineering
text:
Responsible engineering is ML systems engineering done completely, not a separate discipline. The chapter traced a path from failure diagnosis through prevention to enforcement, beginning with the responsibility gap (the distance between technical performance and responsible outcomes) and demonstrating how proxy variables, feedback loops, and distribution shift can harm users while conventional metrics remain acceptable. The engineering response follows the model’s lifecycle. Specification fixes targets, populations, and oversight before training forecloses them. Fairness metrics make disparities measurable. Explanation and documentation are selected for applicable stakeholder and regulatory requirements. Monitoring infrastructure can surface silent failures and connect signals to response.
Translating responsibility concerns into measurable properties makes them tractable. A justified, application-specific bound on disparity is testable; “be fair” is not. This translation extends beyond fairness: in the chapter’s illustrative TCO scenario, a 20 percent accelerator-service-demand reduction saves $304K and is modeled to avoid 19 t of CO2 under the stated assumptions. Documentation becomes model cards with explicit intended use and known limitations. Governance becomes access control, lineage tracking, and audit infrastructure that makes compliance evidence available rather than merely aspirational. Across these cases, abstract ethical obligations become concrete engineering requirements that can be specified, tested, monitored, and enforced.
Every row of the chapter map (table 1) now carries a measured machine cost. Specification needs labeled evaluation data in proportion to how rare each named population is, and mitigation needs a second network head. Exact attribution needs explanation compute that grows exponentially with feature count, and keeping feedback in check needs randomized exploration traffic. The DLRM service consumes accelerator-hours and tonnes of CO2, and governance consumes log bytes, privacy noise, and retraining hours. These practices share one principle: a responsibility property can be enforced only at a lifecycle stage that still has the freedom to change it. Measurement can gate only the populations that specification named, documentation can record only what measurement produced, and governance can prove only what the pipeline retained. A system that defers fairness, efficiency, transparency, or governance to a late review is therefore incomplete in the same sense as a system shipped without a latency budget; the requirement exists, but nothing in the architecture can meet it. The chapter’s quantitative tools fit in one table (table 12), and each turns a responsibility requirement into a number a team can compute before launch and monitor after it.



Table 12: Key Equations: The chapter’s responsibility quantities in the notation of the sections that derive them. Each converts a requirement (a fairness criterion, an evaluation budget, an explanation path, a feedback horizon, a carbon footprint, or an audit trail) into a value that can be computed before launch and monitored after it.










Quantity
Formula
Where Derived




Alignment gap
\(\text{Gap} = \mathbb{E}[\text{Proxy}] - \mathbb{E}[\text{True}]\) for metrics on a common scale
equation 1


Demographic parity
\(\Pr(\PredictedDecision=1 \mid \ProtectedGroupMembership=\text{A}) = \Pr(\PredictedDecision=1 \mid \ProtectedGroupMembership=\text{B})\), gated on the difference
section 15.3.2.1


Equal opportunity
\(\Pr(\PredictedDecision=1 \mid \TrueOutcome=1, \ProtectedGroupMembership=\text{A}) = \Pr(\PredictedDecision=1 \mid \TrueOutcome=1, \ProtectedGroupMembership=\text{B})\)
section 15.3.2.1


Equalized odds
Equal opportunity for both \(\TrueOutcomeLevel\in \{0,1\}\), so true and false positive rates both match
section 15.3.2.1


Slice sample size
Worst-case margin \(1.96\sqrt{0.25/\SubgroupSampleSize}\); random collection \(\RandomSampleCollectionSize\) = per-group target divided by the group’s share
section 15.3.1


Exact attribution cost
\(\mathcal{O}(2^{\AttributionFeatureCount})\) model evaluations per explained decision
section 15.3.3.1


Bias feedback
\(\GroupDisparity(\FeedbackIntervalCount) \approx \GroupDisparity(0) \cdot \BiasFeedbackFactor^\FeedbackIntervalCount\)
section 15.3.4


Operational carbon
\(\text{Energy}_{\text{hardware}} \times \text{PUE} \times \text{Carbon Intensity}\)
section 15.4.3


Audit log volume
Recorded events per unit time, times bytes per event, times the retention window
section 15.5.5







Key Takeaways: Reliable for whom?

Aggregate correctness hides harm: A model can look accurate in aggregate while one subgroup’s error rate is 43.1× another subgroup’s rate, as in the Face++ Gender Shades audit. Responsible evaluation therefore starts with disaggregated and intersectional slices, not aggregate accuracy alone.
Responsibility becomes testable through thresholds: “Be fair” is not testable, but bounded disparity, documented intended use, and explainability requirements are. Translating values into measurable constraints lets teams review trade-offs among fairness, accuracy, latency, and cost.
Efficiency is a social constraint: An efficient model can reduce energy and cost and broaden who can deploy it. In the chapter’s illustrative scenario, the inference-to-training cost ratio is 40:1, making per-query optimization responsible engineering.
Monitoring must watch outcomes: Bias and privacy failures can continue with green uptime dashboards because harmful predictions look operationally normal. Production monitoring must track subgroup outcomes, data lineage, feedback loops, and incident paths with the same rigor as latency regressions.
Governance has to be built in: Model cards, datasheets, access controls, erasure workflows, human-review paths, and audit trails are technical infrastructure, not optional policy overlays. Regulations such as GDPR require capabilities that should be designed into the pipeline; later remediation may remain possible but can be narrower and costlier once the system is serving decisions.



A system that does exactly what it was told is dangerous precisely because the telling is never complete. Every objective a model is given is a specification with gaps, and an optimizer is a machine for finding them. It can reproduce the bias latent in its data, chase the proxy instead of the goal, and call the result success because nothing in the objective said otherwise. Responsible engineering is the discipline of writing back in what the specification left out. Constraints and monitoring reduce the risk that optimization amplifies harms encoded in the data. The constraint is the same kind the rest of the book imposed in latency and memory, except that here it protects people the objective never named. A model that is fast and accurate while wrong about whom it serves has not failed less than one that crashes, only more quietly.

What’s Next: From local targets to the whole systemResponsibility was the last constraint this book added, and it behaves like the ones before it. A disparity bound, a carbon budget, or a lineage requirement can be met only if every upstream stage preserved the freedom to meet it, exactly as a latency budget can. Every constraint so far has been taught one layer at a time, yet the costliest failures arise where layers interact, when each component meets its own target and the system still misses its goal. Conclusion returns to the voice-assistant request that opened the book, follows it across every layer the chapters built, and gathers their quantitative principles, from the iron law (principle \(\ref{pri-iron-law}\)) onward, into one framework for reasoning across the whole stack.

title: 15 Responsible Engineering
text:
Self-Check: Answer

An AI recruiting tool meets its latency SLA, maintains 99.9% availability, and achieves 87% aggregate accuracy, yet it systematically downgrades resumes containing the word “women’s” or graduates of women’s colleges. Applying the systems-engineering verification-versus-validation framing, which diagnosis correctly explains this outcome?

The system failed verification because any discriminatory outcome is by definition a low-level coding defect in the model implementation.
The failure is primarily an operational reliability defect that responsible engineering addresses only after serving infrastructure destabilizes.
The root cause is insufficient model capacity, which can be resolved by scaling up model parameters without altering the optimization objective.
The system passed verification by meeting its stated technical requirements, but failed validation because the specification itself did not capture the organization’s true goal of fair hiring.

Answer: The correct answer is D. In systems engineering, verification asks whether the system was built correctly against stated specifications, while validation asks whether the right system was built to meet true needs. The tool met all monitored technical targets (passing verification) but optimized a flawed objective that reproduced historical hiring bias (failing validation). The low-level defect claim is incorrect because the code executed without error on the objective it was assigned. The operational reliability option conflates service uptime with specification correctness. The model capacity explanation is flawed because a larger model would simply fit and reproduce the biased historical patterns more faithfully.
Learning Objective: Classify an ML deployment failure using the systems-engineering verification-versus-validation framework.
A team argues that a one-time ethics sign-off before deployment is sufficient because their model passes all latency and aggregate accuracy checks. Using the MLOps control-loop analogy, explain why responsible engineering must instead operate as a continuous control loop, and identify one specific production metric that a one-time pre-launch review cannot capture.
Answer: MLOps functions as a continuous control loop for operational reliability because data distributions drift over time; responsible engineering is the corresponding control loop for safety because outcome quality degrades as downstream user populations, proxies, and deployment environments evolve. A one-time sign-off cannot detect post-deployment subgroup-level error rate disparities (such as a widening true-positive-rate gap between demographic slices) that emerge as input distributions shift while overall latency and availability dashboards remain green.
Learning Objective: Explain why responsible engineering requires a continuous production control loop analogous to MLOps rather than a static pre-deployment review.
True or False: Because ML systems are constructed from modular software components, a fairness defect originating from biased training data can be isolated and patched within a single function without altering data pipelines, training objectives, or shared representations.
Answer: False. Unlike traditional software where defects can often be isolated within a specific function or module, ML systems exhibit tight data-dependent coupling. Data flows through shared representations (such as embeddings and learned feature weights), meaning a biased training signal propagates across multiple downstream predictions. Remediating such a failure requires architectural interventions across the D·A·M axes—including data curation, constrained optimization objectives, and disaggregated outcome monitoring.
Learning Objective: Distinguish localized software bugs from data-coupled ML specification failures across shared representations.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

In an audited commercial healthcare algorithm (Optum), predicting future healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs resulted in Black patients receiving lower risk scores despite having more chronic conditions than White patients with identical scores. What systems mechanism explains why this proxy failed?

The model suffered from severe overfitting due to an excessive number of gradient descent epochs on a small training dataset.
The proxy variable inherited historical systemic disparities in healthcare spending, so predicting costs faithfully reproduced unequal access to care rather than actual medical need.
The failure was caused by real-time concept drift that occurred after deployment when hospital billing codes suddenly changed.
The algorithm used an unconstrained loss function that optimized inference latency at the expense of regression calibration.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Because less money is spent on Black patients than on White patients with the same level of illness due to systemic barriers, using healthcare cost as a proxy for medical need meant the model learned to predict spending disparities rather than actual health need. Correcting the target from cost to chronic condition count raised the proportion of Black patients identified for high-risk care management from 17.7% to 46.5%. The overfitting distractor is incorrect because the model generalized its cost-prediction task accurately. The concept drift distractor misattributes the failure to post-deployment environmental change rather than training-target proxy bias. The latency optimization choice conflates infrastructure performance tuning with loss function specification.
Learning Objective: Analyze how proxy variables inherit and amplify systemic disparities in training targets.
A hospital sepsis prediction model begins recommending aggressive treatments for low-risk patients after an EHR update alters how vital signs are logged. System health checks, latency, and prediction confidence remain normal. Explain why this constitutes a silent failure, and identify two monitoring signals that would support investigation without assuming either proves the cause.
Answer: This is a silent failure because harmful recommendations occur while the monitored service properties remain normal. The logging change motivates investigation of input semantics and distributions; it does not establish covariate shift, which additionally requires the label relationship to remain stable. Two complementary signals are: (1) input-feature distribution drift detection using divergence metrics such as Jensen-Shannon divergence (\(\mathcal{D}_{\text{JS}}(P_t \parallel P_0)\)) on vital-sign feature distributions, and (2) disaggregated clinical outcome tracking with mature labels, coverage, and comparable cohorts. Input divergence can warn of change without proving quality loss; outcome evidence can establish a quality change, while matched-input replay and pipeline inspection test the suspected logging defect.
Learning Objective: Analyze silent distribution-shift failures in production ML and identify statistical and outcome-based monitoring signals.
A content recommendation service reports that optimizing a ranker for short-term user clicks increased click-through rate by 20%, but long-term user satisfaction dropped by 5% and 30-day retention declined. Which systems-engineering concept best explains this divergence, and what is the appropriate mitigation?

The alignment gap governed by Goodhart’s Law, where optimizing an observable proxy metric degrades the unobserved true objective; mitigated by maintaining counterfactual holdouts and multi-objective optimization with explicit satisfaction constraints.
Model capacity collapse, where the embedding table runs out of capacity for rare items; mitigated by increasing embedding dimension and memory bandwidth.
Hardware-level numerical underflow in attention layers; mitigated by upgrading from FP16 to FP32 mixed precision across serving clusters.
Training-serving skew in network protocol buffers; mitigated by implementing automated schema validation in feature pipelines.

Answer: The correct answer is A. When a measurable proxy (clicks) becomes the optimization target, Goodhart’s Law dictates that it ceases to be a reliable measure of the true underlying goal (user satisfaction), creating a signed alignment gap \((\text{Gap} = \mathbb{E}[\text{Proxy}] - \mathbb{E}[\text{True}])\). The appropriate mitigation combines multi-objective optimization with safety constraints and randomized counterfactual holdouts that track true long-term satisfaction. The capacity collapse option misattributes a loss-function specification failure to memory constraints. The numerical underflow option confuses mathematical representation limits with metric misalignment. The schema validation option addresses data pipeline serialization rather than proxy divergence.
Learning Objective: Apply Goodhart’s Law and alignment gap mechanics to diagnose metric divergence in recommendation systems.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

An engineering team is evaluating a facial verification model. To estimate the error rate of a minority demographic group representing 1% of the population with a margin of error of \(\pm 1\) percentage point at 95% confidence, they require 10,000 labeled evaluation samples from that group. Under uniform random sampling from the natural population distribution, how many total images must the team collect and label in expectation?

About 10,000 total images, because evaluating subgroup accuracy requires only that the total test set contains 10,000 images.
About 100,000 total images, because statistical confidence intervals scale with the square root of the overall dataset size.
About 1,000,000 total images in expectation, because a 1% subgroup yields only 1 target image per 100 randomly sampled images, imposing a \(100\times\) multiplier.
About 10,000,000 total images, because the binomial confidence interval width expands exponentially for minority subgroups.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Dividing the required subgroup sample size (\(10{,}000\)) by the subgroup prevalence (\(0.01\)) yields an expected total collection size of \(D_{\text{eval,total}} = 10{,}000 / 0.01 = 1{,}000{,}000\) images—a \(100\times\) data collection multiplier. This demonstrates why relying on natural random distributions for fairness evaluation is prohibitively expensive and why intentional stratified data engineering is required. The 10,000 total images choice confuses subgroup sample requirements with overall dataset size, yielding only ~100 minority samples. The 100,000 total images choice underestimates the collection requirement by a factor of 10. The 10,000,000 total images choice applies an incorrect \(1{,}000\times\) scaling factor.
Learning Objective: Calculate the expected data collection multiplier required for minority subgroup evaluation under random versus stratified sampling.
A team plans to write their model card six months after launch so that it accurately reflects observed production behavior. Explain why this timing constitutes a guard-rail failure, and describe one concrete scope-creep risk that a pre-deployment model card with automated deployment gates prevents.
Answer: A model card functions as an operational guard rail only when written before deployment to explicitly define intended use, validated populations, and excluded use cases that automated release gates can enforce. Writing the card after deployment turns it into a passive historical record that fails to constrain ongoing misuse. A concrete scope-creep risk prevented by pre-deployment gating is when a lightweight vision model validated only for consumer photo organization is repurposed without re-validation for high-stakes security screening or medical diagnostics.
Learning Objective: Explain how pre-deployment model cards operate as enforced guard rails to prevent deployment scope creep.
A loan approval classifier is evaluated on a fully labeled sample whose repayment outcomes are observed independently of its approval predictions. Group A (Majority): 4,500 True Positives, 500 False Negatives (TPR = 90%), 1,000 False Positives, 4,000 True Negatives (FPR = 20%). Group B (Minority): 600 True Positives, 400 False Negatives (TPR = 60%), 200 False Positives, 800 True Negatives (FPR = 20%). Which statement accurately diagnoses the fairness metrics for this system?

Demographic parity is satisfied because both groups share an identical False Positive Rate of 20%.
Equalized odds is satisfied because matching False Positive Rates compensate for differences in True Positive Rates.
Equal opportunity is violated due to the 30 percentage-point TPR gap, and equalized odds is also violated because equalized odds strictly requires parity in both TPR and FPR.
Calibration is the only metric affected, because True Positive Rate disparities impact accuracy but do not constitute algorithmic bias.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Equal opportunity requires equal True Positive Rates among qualified applicants (\(P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=1, A=a) = P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=1, A=b)\)); the 30 percentage-point gap (90% vs. 60%) directly violates it. Equalized odds requires equality in both TPR and FPR (\(P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=y, A=a) = P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=y, A=b)\) for \(y \in \{0,1\}\)); matching FPRs (20% vs. 20%) cannot satisfy the criterion when TPRs differ. Demographic parity requires equal overall approval rates regardless of true qualifications, which is not measured by FPR. The calibration-only option incorrectly dismisses severe true-positive-rate disparities as benign accuracy differences.
Learning Objective: Analyze equal-opportunity and equalized-odds violations directly from group confusion matrices.
For the credit service, closing the 30 percentage-point TPR gap for Group B via threshold adjustment adds \(\$225\) in margin on newly approved loans that are repaid but creates \(\$300\) in losses on newly approved loans that default, per Group B applicant, whose baseline utility is \(\$150\) per applicant. Using the chapter’s two-sided accounting, calculate the net utility change per applicant and explain what deliverable engineers owe stakeholders.
Answer: The net change is \(\FiniteChange\text{Utility} = \$225 - \$300 = -\$75\) per Group B applicant, a 50% within-group utility loss relative to that group’s \(\$150\) baseline. Rather than treating threshold adjustment as an automatic fix or imposing a value judgment, engineers owe stakeholders the explicit Pareto frontier along with all economic and base-rate assumptions, showing the exact trade-offs between fairness metrics and utility.
Learning Objective: Calculate two-sided utility changes under fairness threshold adjustments and justify presenting Pareto frontiers to stakeholders.
After mitigation, the credit service ships with a 3 percentage-point TPR gap under a 5-point release gate, and the next quarterly audit measures 3.3 points. Using the bias feedback model, estimate the fitted feedback factor and the retraining cycle in which the projected gap first exceeds the gate. Why does the projection motivate changing what the loop observes rather than only shortening the audit interval?
Answer: The fitted factor is \(3.3/3.0 = 1.10\) per quarter. The projected gap \(3.0 \times 1.10^{\FeedbackIntervalCount}\) first exceeds 5 points when \(\FeedbackIntervalCount > \ln(5/3)/\ln 1.10 \approx 5.4\), so on the sixth quarterly cycle, at about 5.3 points. Two audits do not validate future dynamics, so the factor must be refitted at every audit. Denied applicants generate no repayment labels, so each retraining learns from a population the previous model selected. Approving a small randomized sample of marginal applicants restores the censored outcomes and can bring the factor below one, so the gap decays instead of growing; a shorter audit interval only detects the breach sooner.
Learning Objective: Apply the bias feedback model to project when a launch-time fairness gap breaches its gate and identify the loop change that stabilizes it.
A team is designing a fairness and robustness testing suite for the credit service. Explain why subgroup representation and labeled sample sufficiency must be checked before interpreting subgroup error rates. How do invariance tests and boundary/stress tests complement those rates, and when can the team compare candidate configurations on a fairness-accuracy Pareto frontier?
Answer: Representation and labeled sample checks establish whether each subgroup rate has enough relevant evidence and acceptable uncertainty. Insufficient evidence cannot support a parity claim. Invariance tests probe decision stability under defensible, semantically irrelevant substitutions; they do not alone establish a causal account of discrimination. Boundary and stress tests probe sparse or corrupted input regimes. Once candidate configurations have comparable evaluation evidence, stakeholders can review their measured fairness-accuracy trade-offs. The chapter presents complementary testing regimes, not a mandatory unique order between invariance and stress testing.
Learning Objective: Explain the evidence dependencies and complementary roles of subgroup, invariance, stress, and trade-off evaluations.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A team optimizes an inference model using INT8 quantization and structured pruning, reducing dedicated accelerator compute by \(4\times\) while preserving accuracy. According to the chapter, why is this efficiency improvement classified as a responsible engineering intervention rather than a pure performance optimization?

Because quantization mathematically guarantees that disparate impact across all protected demographic groups drops to zero.
Because reducing model parameters eliminates the need for data governance and audit logging in production pipelines.
Because efficiency optimizations are relevant only for one-time training runs, where carbon emissions are legally regulated.
Because it can lower lifecycle energy and cost and broaden hardware access when the actual runtime reduces measured service demand at the required quality and the deployment converts that gain into savings.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Supported kernels and representations must reduce measured service demand for the required traffic and predictive quality, including consequential subgroup slices. Lower demand can permit fewer provisioned devices or more accessible hardware, but dollar savings depend on billing and provisioning. Lifecycle energy and emissions must include added training or preprocessing, idle power, facility overhead, and the grid boundary. Compression does not guarantee demographic parity or remove governance duties. Recurring inference can dominate at sufficient traffic; measured lifecycle accounting determines whether it does in this deployment.
Learning Objective: Explain the conditions under which efficiency optimizations improve energy, cost, and hardware accessibility.
A wearable device has an inference power budget of 500 mW. Under the chapter’s assumed active-power profiles (KWS DS-CNN: 50 mW; MobileNetV2: 1.2 W), which statement about the resource screen is correct?

MobileNetV2 passes, because its power overage can always be removed by offloading inference to the cloud.
The DS-CNN passes with a 10\(\times\) power margin and MobileNetV2 exceeds the budget by 2.4\(\times\); passing the screen still does not establish that the DS-CNN suits the intended task.
Both pass, because duty cycling makes any active power draw acceptable on a wearable.
Neither passes, because no ML model can run within a sub-watt budget.

Answer: The correct answer is B. The DS-CNN’s assumed 50 mW is one-tenth of the 500 mW budget, while MobileNetV2’s 1.2 W exceeds it by 2.4\(\times\) before sustained thermals are considered. Offloading changes the system design and its latency, privacy, and connectivity assumptions, so it does not make MobileNetV2 fit this budget. Duty cycling lowers average draw but not the active power the budget bounds. Passing the screen does not establish suitability, since the DS-CNN is the keyword-spotting lighthouse and its inputs and outputs must match the intended application.
Learning Objective: Apply an edge power budget to screen candidate models while separating resource fit from task suitability.
In the chapter’s illustrative three-year TCO model of the DLRM ranking service (Training: ~2%, Operations: ~25%, Inference: ~73%), assume one intervention halves total training cost, while another reduces total inference cost by 20% under unchanged traffic and quality. Which intervention saves more dollars, and by what approximate ratio? Why would halving only the final training run time not establish the first saving?
Answer: Using the rounded shares, the inference intervention saves 20% of 73%, or approximately 14.6% of total TCO. Halving all training cost saves 50% of 2%, or approximately 1.0% of TCO, so the ratio is about 14.6:1. Halving only final-run time does not halve data preparation, hyperparameter search, or every retraining cost. The comparison assumes that the interventions actually reduce the stated billed costs; lower service demand on an unchanged provisioned fleet need not reduce the bill. These scenario shares establish where savings have more leverage here, not a universal optimization priority.
Learning Objective: Compare the financial leverage of training versus inference optimizations using a lifecycle TCO breakdown.
True or False: For an identical serving workload, relocating an inference deployment from a carbon-intensive fossil-fuel grid region to a region powered predominantly by low-carbon renewable energy can reduce operational carbon emissions more than a modest algorithmic efficiency improvement.
Answer: True. Operational carbon emissions are computed as \(\text{Carbon} = \text{Energy (kWh)} \times \text{PUE} \times \text{Carbon Intensity (kg CO}_2\text{e/kWh})\). Because regional grid carbon intensity varies widely (e.g., from over \(0.6\text{ kg/kWh}\) in fossil-heavy grids to under \(0.05\text{ kg/kWh}\) in renewable-dominated regions—more than a \(10\times\) difference), shifting workloads to cleaner regions or using carbon-aware scheduling can reduce emissions by factors that far exceed a typical 10% to 20% algorithmic speedup.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the carbon reduction impact of grid-carbon-intensity region selection versus algorithmic efficiency.
In data-center environmental accounting, the metric defined as the ratio of total facility energy to the energy consumed specifically by computing equipment is known as ____ (abbreviated PUE).
Answer: The correct answer is power usage effectiveness (or Power Usage Effectiveness). Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) measures data center infrastructure energy efficiency by dividing total facility power (including cooling, lighting, and power distribution) by IT equipment power; an ideal PUE is 1.0, with modern hyperscale facilities typically achieving 1.1 to 1.2.
Learning Objective: Explain the definition and operational significance of power usage effectiveness (PUE) in ML data center carbon accounting.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

In 2023, Ireland’s Data Protection Commission found that Meta had processed user data for behavioral advertising without a valid legal basis and in violation of transparency and fairness requirements, an infraction involving no data breach or server compromise. Which systems-engineering principle does this case demonstrate?

Security encryption at rest and in transit is sufficient to guarantee total regulatory compliance across all data privacy laws.
Data governance is an enforceable technical constraint across the data lifecycle, requiring infrastructure to verify lawful basis, purpose limitation, and consent rather than relying on policy assertions.
Regulatory compliance applies only to static tabular data lakes and exempts real-time streaming feature stores.
Publishing a public datasheet for a dataset eliminates all downstream corporate liability for unlawful processing.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Data governance requires demonstrable, technically enforceable controls across the entire data engineering lifecycle: establishing a lawful basis for processing, verifying purpose limitation in feature pipelines, tracking consent, and enforcing retention limits. Meeting encryption standards (security) does not satisfy lawful processing or transparency obligations (governance). The static lake exemption is incorrect because governance binds all storage and streaming tiers. The datasheet liability claim is false because documentation does not substitute for lawful processing and technical compliance.
Learning Objective: Explain why data governance requires enforceable technical infrastructure across the ML pipeline rather than standalone security or policy documents.
A voice assistant receives an erasure request. Explain how retained lineage helps identify derived artifacts, why database deletion alone may be insufficient, and why identifying an artifact does not automatically require deleting it.
Answer: Source audio can feed features, caches, training snapshots, and model artifacts, so deleting one database record does not establish removal of every in-scope copy or training contribution. Retained lineage identifies candidate dependencies for scope review. The team determines applicable duties, exceptions, and retention boundaries, then executes and verifies appropriate deletion, restriction, retraining, or validated unlearning. Lineage supplies evidence for that decision; it does not establish that every linked artifact is covered or that automation alone proves completion.
Learning Objective: Explain how lineage supports scoped erasure workflows and why database deletion alone may be insufficient.
A smart-home voice assistant (such as the Lighthouse KWS system) is designed with an always-listening microphone. Which combination of architectural choices best embodies privacy-by-design for this deployment?

Stream continuous raw ambient audio to a centralized cloud cluster where access is protected exclusively by role-based access control (RBAC).
Store all raw acoustic recordings permanently on local edge flash memory so that future model versions can be trained without cloud connectivity.
Perform wake-word detection locally, bound the audio window released after a trigger and test false wakes and egress controls, apply retention/deletion policies, and use training-capable clients with appropriately accounted differential privacy for federated model improvements.
Rely on third-party cloud data warehouses to handle all privacy filtering after raw audio ingestion has completed.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Local detection and bounded buffers reduce routine audio exposure, but false wakes can still release ambient speech. Testing must cover false-activation rates, pre-trigger audio, and buffer and egress controls. Retention policies must cover in-scope copies. Federated training requires capable clients, and model updates can leak information; differential privacy supplies a bound only under the declared mechanism, neighboring-dataset relation, and accounting assumptions. RBAC alone does not minimize continuously uploaded audio, permanent local retention preserves an exposure surface, and filtering after ingestion does not avoid the initial collection.
Learning Objective: Design privacy-by-design architectures for always-listening edge ML systems using data minimization and on-device processing.
A team plans to ingest raw audio, transform it into features, and only then configure feature-store RBAC and encryption. It will add lineage and inference logging after deployment. Explain which safeguards must exist before the corresponding data handling begins, and how retained lineage supports a later erasure request.
Answer: The team must establish lawful processing authority and appropriate access and encryption controls before handling the covered raw audio or features. Provenance must be captured at ingestion, and lineage must be captured as transformations and training create artifacts. Privacy-preserving training needs its clipping, noise, sampling, and accounting controls in place before the protected training or release. Decision logging must operate when inference decisions occur. A later erasure request uses retained lineage to identify candidate derived artifacts, determine applicable scope and exceptions, and execute the appropriate deletion, restriction, retraining, or unlearning workflow. These are dependencies between safeguards and the actions they protect, not a unique order in which all governance work must occur.
Learning Objective: Explain when governance safeguards must operate and how lineage supports scoped erasure workflows.
An empirical privacy attack in which an adversary analyzes model output probabilities to determine whether a specific individual’s record was part of the model’s training dataset is known as a ____.
Answer: The correct answer is membership inference attack (or membership inference). In a membership inference attack, the adversary exploits the fact that machine learning models often exhibit higher confidence and lower loss on samples seen during training compared to unseen test samples, allowing them to infer individual participation in private training datasets.
Learning Objective: Analyze the mechanism and vulnerability surface of membership inference attacks in ML privacy auditing.
A European financial institution deploys an automated machine learning system to make sole decisions on credit applications. Under the EU AI Act (high-risk classification) and GDPR Article 22, which set of architectural capabilities must the engineering team build into the system from inception?

Post-hoc saliency map visualization tools only, because EU regulations apply strict requirements exclusively to generative foundation models.
A manual spreadsheet of training dataset URLs and an annual retrospective fairness report submitted after year-end financial audits.
An unconstrained deep neural network optimized for accuracy, since high aggregate predictive power automatically satisfies legal safety criteria.
Automated risk management, training data provenance logging, explainable adverse-action factor generation, and an operational workflow supporting substantive human review and user contestability.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Covered high-risk systems under the EU AI Act and solely automated decision pipelines under GDPR Article 22 require technical infrastructure for risk management, dataset provenance and lineage logging, explainability (providing meaningful information about the automated logic), and substantive human oversight with the ability for affected individuals to contest decisions. Saliency maps alone do not satisfy comprehensive risk-management or adverse-action requirements. The retrospective spreadsheet option fails the requirement for continuous, built-in audit trails. The unconstrained optimization option ignores the explicit legal mandate that high accuracy does not exempt systems from governance, transparency, and human oversight controls.
Learning Objective: Analyze how EU AI Act and GDPR Article 22 mandates translate into technical architecture requirements for automated decision systems.
A randomized algorithm \(\mathcal{M}\) satisfies \((\epsilon, \delta)\)-____ if for any two neighboring datasets \(D, D'\) differing by at most one record, the probability of any output set \(\mathcal{S}\) satisfies \(\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{M}(D) \in \mathcal{S}] \le e^\epsilon \cdot \mathbb{P}[\mathcal{M}(D') \in \mathcal{S}] + \delta\), providing a mathematical upper bound on privacy loss.
Answer: The correct answer is differential privacy (or differential-privacy). The stated inequality bounds the change in the output distribution under the declared neighboring-dataset relation. Epsilon controls the multiplicative bound, and delta is additive slack in that inequality. The bound comes from the mechanism and valid accounting of its releases, not from an empirical privacy attack.
Learning Objective: Explain the mathematical definition and core parameters of \((\epsilon, \delta)\)-differential privacy.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A deployed automated lending model achieves an impressive 88% overall accuracy on its global test set. However, a disaggregated audit reveals that qualified minority applicants experience a 60% True Positive Rate compared to 90% for majority applicants (a 30 percentage-point gap) and face \(4\times\) higher false rejection rates. Which engineering pitfall does this scenario illustrate?

Relying on aggregate metrics to assess fairness, which conceals severe subgroup disparities behind strong overall averages (the Flaw of Averages).
Treating documentation as sufficient accountability, assuming a model card automatically prevents operational misuse.
The belief that model weights are exempt from data governance and right-to-erasure regulations.
Assuming that edge deployment power budgets scale linearly with dataset sample size.

Answer: The correct answer is A. The Flaw of Averages demonstrates that aggregate accuracy is a weighted average across all samples that masks severe performance degradation in minority subgroups. A model can boast 88% aggregate accuracy while rejecting qualified minority applicants at \(4\times\) the majority rate (\(40\%\) vs. \(10\%\) False Negative Rate). The documentation-as-accountability choice addresses written model cards versus active deployment gates, not metric aggregation. The model-weights governance choice refers to post-training compliance, not metric illusions. The edge power budget choice confuses physical hardware limits with statistical evaluation metrics.
Learning Objective: Identify the pitfall of relying on aggregate metrics to assess system fairness.
A team removes race and gender columns from their training dataset, asserting that “the model cannot discriminate on features it cannot see.” Drawing on the Amazon recruiting and Optum healthcare cases, explain why this naive attribute removal creates false confidence, and identify the specific engineering analyses required.
Answer: Naive attribute removal fails because non-sensitive features act as proxy variables that reconstruct protected attributes through statistical correlations: Amazon’s tool penalized terms such as ‘women’s’ and women’s colleges without a gender label, and Optum’s algorithm used healthcare spending as a proxy for need, under-enrolling Black patients because of unequal historical access to care. Eliminating protected attributes creates false confidence while preserving discriminatory patterns. Engineers must instead conduct proxy and causal correlation analyses, perform disaggregated subgroup evaluations across demographic slices, implement constrained optimization objectives (such as equal opportunity constraints), and monitor per-group production outcomes continuously.
Learning Objective: Explain why proxy variables defeat naive attribute removal and specify the necessary statistical and monitoring countermeasures.
True or False: Because a model card explicitly specifies that a vision model is “not validated for high-stakes medical or security screening,” publishing the model card guarantees operational compliance without requiring technical access controls or deployment release gates.
Answer: False. This illustrates the pitfall of treating documentation as sufficient accountability. A model card provides transparency but has no technical enforcement mechanism. When downstream teams repurpose an artifact, documentation alone cannot prevent scope creep. True accountability requires operationalizing model card constraints through technical deployment gates, RBAC permissions, monitoring alerts, and automated policy enforcement that actively block unvalidated deployments.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why documentation without operational enforcement fails to prevent deployment scope creep.
True or False: For a high-traffic production ML service, measuring and reporting only the electricity consumed during model training runs provides an accurate accounting of the system’s long-term environmental carbon footprint.
Answer: False. Training-only accounting omits recurring inference and provisioned serving equipment. The chapter’s illustrative service-demand scenario has an inference-to-training dollar-cost ratio of about 40:1, and its separate accelerator-carbon accounting also shows inference dominance under the stated power and traffic assumptions. The 73% inference and 2% training shares describe dollar TCO, not carbon shares. Responsible carbon accounting measures lifecycle energy and applies the relevant grid and facility boundaries, including idle energy and other omitted impacts; the dominant term depends on the deployment.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why training-only carbon accounting fails to capture lifecycle environmental impacts in production ML.

title: 13 Model Serving
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter: Part 1 · Part 2












Architecture stack focus for this chapter.
Why does serving change the optimization priorities that made training successful?
Training and serving pursue opposing operating objectives. Training maximizes aggregate throughput across large, scheduled batches and long runs, whereas serving must answer individual, heterogeneous requests under strict latency deadlines. Training amortizes hardware initialization and weight streaming across millions of examples; serving pays its full fixed cost on every query, and small inefficiencies accumulate into machine time that must be provisioned. A system handling one billion requests a day recovers more than eleven days of machine time every day from a single millisecond saved per request. Each request also runs inside a fixed end-to-end latency budget, in which network ingress, serialization, preprocessing, queueing, and postprocessing all spend time the model cannot use. When those stages consume most of the budget, kernel optimizations barely reach the user, and a prediction that arrives after the client has timed out has no value however accurate it is. Serving is therefore a capacity problem under uncontrolled traffic as much as a latency problem. Arrival rates swing between daily peaks and troughs, so capacity provisioned for the average collapses at the peak, while capacity provisioned for the peak sits idle and costly the rest of the day. The question a serving system answers is not whether the model computes correct outputs in isolation but whether it sustains reliable, low-latency execution under production variability. In D·A·M terms, serving is where the trained algorithm meets unpredictable live data inside the machine’s latency budget, and all three constraints bind on every request.

Learning Objectives

Explain serving inversion from training throughput to per-request latency, headroom, and tail behavior
Decompose request latency across serialization, preprocessing, inference, queuing, postprocessing, and network overhead
Apply queueing laws and simple queue models to plan capacity and admission control against percentile latency targets
Select batching windows and inference runtimes that trade formation delay and precision for throughput within a latency budget
Diagnose cold-start delays from weight transfer, runtime initialization, graph compilation, and warmup during model loading
Evaluate LLM serving bottlenecks using token latency, KV-cache memory, and continuous batching constraints
Calculate cost per inference from precision, hardware utilization, replica count, and runtime throughput



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



The benchmarks of Benchmarking measured models under a load generator that decided when each request arrived, whereas production serving faces live clients that no scheduler controls. When a user uploads a photograph and waits for its label, or a chat interface sends a prompt and waits for the first word of the reply, the request arrives stochastically and must return within a service-level objective (SLO) of tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Moving from offline training to live traffic therefore triggers the serving inversion, a reversal of engineering priorities: offline training packs large batches to amortize weight transfers from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and maximize work completed per hour, whereas online serving is judged by whether each individual request completes before its deadline while live traffic tests the operating envelope continuously.
That priority shift restructures the balance of terms across both levels of the iron law of ML systems. Shrinking a task from a large training batch to small batches or individual inputs (\(\BatchSize=1\)) slashes the Data factor (\(\text{Samples/Task}\) in equation 1.2) and inflates the Machine factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)). The same shift appears across the unpacked terms of equation 1.3 (\(\Time = \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency\)). For weight-dominated operations, small batches reduce arithmetic intensity and can shift execution from compute-bound matrix multiplications toward memory-bandwidth-bound transfers (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)). Simultaneously, the latency term \(\Latency\) expands beyond microsecond accelerator kernel launches to include network transit, request serialization, and host orchestration, often becoming the binding constraint on end-to-end response time.


↩︎ The multiplicative, additive, and pipelined formulations of the iron law of ML systems are established in Iron Law of ML Systems.
The inversion reshapes each D·A·M layer at once. In the data layer, the constraint shifts from total dataset volume to the arrival rate, payload freshness, and variable sequence dimensions of live queries. In the algorithm layer, execution becomes strictly forward-only: backpropagation state and optimizer memory vanish from the accelerator, even as dynamic input shapes introduce runtime execution variability into previously static operator graphs. In the machine layer, the operating target shifts from maximum hardware utilization to headroom. Whereas offline training treats an idle accelerator as wasted capital, online serving treats near-saturation as an operational hazard, because stochastic request arrivals make queue lengths and waiting times diverge nonlinearly as utilization approaches 100 percent. Maintaining adequate headroom preserves the spare capacity needed to absorb transient traffic spikes without violating tail-latency percentiles, so serving optimizes completed requests under a strict latency deadline rather than steady-state hardware occupancy.
Meeting that latency deadline governs how engineering teams partition the end-to-end serving stack. Every stage between the network socket and the response draws on the same single allowance, so any millisecond consumed by unoptimized feature retrieval, host serialization, or queueing delays directly subtracts from the execution time available to the neural network itself. Consequently, the central engineering task in model serving is deciding which operations must remain on the synchronous request path, which tasks can be offloaded to asynchronous background pipelines, and how much headroom the system must reserve before tail-latency guarantees collapse under load. Three conditions therefore separate serving from the forward pass that a benchmark times: a per-request deadline, arrivals that no scheduler controls, and a stack in which the model is one stage among several.

Definition 13.1: Model serving
Model serving is the operational phase that provides model predictions to end-users or downstream systems under latency, throughput, availability, and cost constraints.

Significance: Online serving turns training’s priority on sustained hardware efficiency (\(\EfficiencyHw\)) into a request-latency constraint (\(\EndToEndRequestLatency\)), requiring a stack designed around the percentile named by its SLO.
Distinction: Unlike model training, which commonly processes scheduled batches, serving may handle stochastic online requests, synchronized streams, or offline batches.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that serving is “just the forward pass.” In reality, it is a systems problem: model execution is only one component of a stack that may include request routing, load balancing, and data transformation.



The SLO1 turns those three conditions into a single time budget across the end-to-end request pipeline (figure 1). Host-side ingress and input preprocessing (network termination, payload deserialization, and tokenization or feature transformation), neural network evaluation on the accelerator, and output postprocessing with safety validation all draw from that allowance. Any of the three stages can become the binding latency bottleneck, and section 13.3.1 shows that host preprocessing alone can take longer than the forward pass.
1 SLOs in ML serving: An SLO is the internal target, as distinct from the contractual SLA. For ML serving, task quality and inference latency can both contribute to SLOs, creating multidimensional targets where improving one dimension (for example, deploying a larger model for accuracy) can violate another (latency).
↩︎ SLOs, service level agreements (SLAs), and the tail-latency percentiles they constrain are established in Latency and tail latency.







Figure 1: The Inference Pipeline: ML serving systems transform raw inputs into final outputs through sequential stages: preprocessing, neural network computation, and postprocessing. The neural network represents just one component; preprocessing and postprocessing make end-to-end latency depend on more than neural-network execution.



Two services carry the chapter, one per half, and each lighthouse arrives in the regime it represents. The first half follows a ResNet-50 image-classification service on one accelerator node. ResNet-50 is the book’s compute-bound lighthouse. Each forward pass performs about 8.2 GFLOP of arithmetic on 102.2 MB of FP32 weights, so a large training batch keeps the matrix units busy. A served request arrives alone, however, and at batch one the same forward pass spends most of its time on weight traffic and kernel launches rather than arithmetic. Recovering the efficiency that training enjoyed without breaking the deadline is the first half’s problem, and the reference request profile introduced with the latency budget carries the service through queuing, batching, runtime selection, and replica startup. Large language model (LLM) serving then follows a GPT-2 XL chat service, the bandwidth-bound lighthouse whose decoding step Autoregressive decoding traced. Each generated token streams all 3 GB of its FP16 weights from memory, about 0.9 ms on the book’s reference H100, so memory bandwidth sets token latency and the memory each conversation holds sets concurrency. Llama 3 8B, a larger member of the same transformer family, extends that case where the per-conversation cache grows large enough to bound how many requests share the accelerator. DLRM, the capacity-bound lighthouse, appears once as a contrast in which embedding lookups rather than arithmetic dominate a request, and MobileNetV2 appears where the target device cannot hold ResNet-50 at all.

The first four sections in table 1 follow a single ResNet-50 replica from its internal request path through single-request latency, multi-request queuing, and batching; the remaining five change the runtime engine, host-to-device execution path, replica startup, output modality, and fleet economics. Before a team designs any of those layers, however, two placement decisions fix the operating regime: a temporal choice of whether predictions are computed ahead of time or on demand, and a spatial choice of where the model physically runs.


A nightly job that precomputes product recommendations for existing users can pack thousands of items into each accelerator batch, whereas a live content-moderation API must score an uploaded image within milliseconds of arrival. Deciding whether to generate predictions before or during a user request sets the trade-off between offline hardware efficiency and online responsiveness (Google 2024). It determines whether an accelerator runs in an unconstrained throughput regime or under the strict tail-latency deadlines of an interactive serving loop.

Google. 2024. Static Vs. Dynamic Inference. Google Machine Learning Crash Course.


Static inference (also called offline or batch inference) precomputes predictions for anticipated inputs and stores them in a retrieval store. Moving model execution entirely out of the user request path alters the underlying hardware constraints. Because batch jobs have no millisecond-level deadlines, accelerators can use large batches (\(\BatchSize\gg 1\)) selected for throughput within memory limits. Reusing weights across samples raises arithmetic intensity for weight-dominated operations. A batch-size sweep identifies where throughput stops improving. When a client issues a request (for example, a user opening nightly generated recommendation rankings), the serving system performs a low-latency key-value lookup rather than executing a forward pass on an accelerator. The primary operational constraint shifts from accelerator latency to storage capacity and data freshness. Precomputing predictions across an entire input domain scales combinatorially (\(\mathcal{O}(\RecommenderUserCount\times \RecommenderItemCount)\) for \(\RecommenderUserCount\) users and \(\RecommenderItemCount\) items in recommendation systems), and stale predictions persist until the next batch refresh.



Dynamic inference (also called online or real-time inference) evaluates inputs on demand as requests arrive. On-demand execution accommodates arbitrary, previously unseen inputs within the model schema and immediately reflects newly deployed model weights without requiring precomputation. However, executing the model directly within the user request path subjects inference to the strict end-to-end latency budget set by its SLO. Because user requests arrive stochastically, the serving runtime cannot delay execution indefinitely to accumulate large batches. Serving requests individually or in small batches (\(\BatchSize=1\) to \(\BatchSize=4\)) can expose weight traffic or launch overhead that larger batches amortize. When these costs bind execution, the device completes fewer queries per unit time, increasing provisioned cost per query. This tension between interactive response time and hardware efficiency can make dynamic serving more expensive per query than offline batching (example 13.1).

Example 13.1: The cost of latencyLatency constraints directly dictate infrastructure costs. The figures below come from the ResNet-50 reference profile that section 13.5.1 later sweeps across batch sizes. Consider a GPU server renting for $4/hour.
Scenario A (low latency): Batch size 1.

Latency: 3.5 ms.
Throughput: 283 req/s.
Cost per million queries: $3.92.

Scenario B (high throughput): Batch size 8.

Latency: 3.8 ms, barely above batch one, because the fixed launch cost dominates both.
Throughput: 2,129 req/s.
Cost per million queries: $0.52.

Systems insight: Serving one image at a time saves only the difference between 3.8 ms and 3.5 ms of latency, yet multiplies the hardware cost per million queries by 7.5×. Engineers must quantify whether that speedup generates enough business value to justify the 7.5× cost increase.


Consider two contrasting deployment scenarios for a ResNet-50 image classifier. A static batch approach suits a photo management application that preclassifies every image in a user library overnight. Classifying 10,000 photos one at a time, at 3.5 ms per batch-one forward pass on the reference H100, would take 35 s. At the 89,500 images/s that MLPerf Inference (Reddi et al. 2019) measured for a compiled INT8 engine at large batch on the same accelerator, the same library takes 0.11 s, about 320× faster. Clients then experience instantaneous retrieval upon browsing. Conversely, a dynamic online approach suits a content moderation service that must evaluate user-uploaded media in real time, where each image traverses the complete preprocessing, accelerator execution, and postprocessing pipeline within a 100 ms service-level objective.
These two modes optimize for different operating regimes. Static inference maximizes accelerator utilization and amortizes memory transfers across large, offline batches, trading persistent storage capacity for zero serving latency at query time. Dynamic inference minimizes tail latency under stochastic, concurrent traffic, accepting lower compute efficiency and higher marginal cost per query to evaluate arbitrary, unpredictable inputs. Production architectures frequently combine both paradigms in a tiered design. Static precomputation populates key-value caches with predictions for high-frequency queries, such as catalog items or viral media, while dynamic serving clusters evaluate the long tail of novel or personalized requests. Deciding when predictions are computed resolves only the temporal dimension of serving, however. Equally binding is the spatial dimension, where the model physically executes, because physical placement dictates memory hierarchy limits, network boundaries, and the hardware budget available to the serving stack.




A cloud server can pool accelerators behind an HTTP endpoint at the cost of a network round trip and multi-second cold starts, whereas a hearing aid or industrial sensor microcontroller cannot afford a network hop or an operating system at all. Although “serving” often implies a networked server processing API requests, the four deployment paradigms (Cloud, Edge, Mobile, and TinyML) and the physical constraints that give rise to them—the light barrier, the power wall, and the memory wall—shape the serving stack into different forms. Serving spans a continuum. At the cloud end, centralized networked microservices pool accelerators to optimize throughput and cost per query, at the expense of network round-trip overhead and cold-start latency. Further along, application-embedded edge serving runs models inside client processes via direct function calls, which eliminates network latency and preserves privacy at the expense of strict device memory and power limits. At the far end, bare-metal firmware execution runs on microcontrollers. Those hardware limits do not disappear at serving time; serving adds latency SLOs and cost pressure on top of limits that training could absorb through patience. The same model may therefore require different serving strategies depending on where it runs.


↩︎ The light barrier, power wall, and memory wall that give rise to the four deployment paradigms are established in Physical Constraints on Deployment.
The three architectures differ in what binds. Networked serving runs the model as a standalone service behind HTTP or gRPC, so network transfer and serialization join model execution as candidate bottlenecks. Data-center accelerators support batching and concurrency, but a new replica’s cold start can stretch from seconds to minutes because container startup, model loading, and warmup sit outside the steady-state request path. Application-embedded serving runs the model inside the user’s application process on a phone or embedded board, behind a function call rather than a network interface. With no shared server to batch for, optimization targets energy and responsiveness (the shape that benchmarking calls SingleStream), and a passively cooled envelope of a few watts throttles sustained inference once the chassis heats. Bare-metal serving compiles the model into microcontroller firmware, often without an operating system or a dynamic allocator, so weights execute in place from flash memory and activations fit a preallocated tensor arena of a few hundred kilobytes of SRAM. Batching is impossible on a single sensor stream.


↩︎ The MLPerf SingleStream, MultiStream, Server, and Offline scenarios are established in MLPerf execution scenarios.
Embedded execution enables zero-copy inference. When data moves through a system, each copy consumes CPU cycles and memory bandwidth. In cloud serving, separate physical memory spaces force repeated transfers. A camera frame passes from a network socket buffer to user space, through a preprocessing buffer into page-locked host DRAM, and across PCIe into accelerator memory. A mobile pipeline can eliminate these intermediate copies when its camera, image signal processor (ISP), CPU, and NPU exchange shared buffer descriptors in unified system memory. In unified-memory system-on-chip (SoC) architectures, such as Apple A- and M-series processors or Qualcomm Snapdragon, all compute engines share a single physical DRAM pool. When software passes buffer handles rather than duplicating bytes, inference latency drops and memory bus power decreases, although format conversions may still require CPU or ISP intervention.
The deployment tiers differ first in their operating envelopes (latency targets, memory, and power), which Physical Constraints on Deployment derived and tabulated for each paradigm. What serving adds is the model each tier can actually run. Applying those envelopes to one image-classification workload, table 2 shows why cloud and mobile can adapt ResNet-50 while TinyML must substitute MobileNetV2. The cloud column runs the model through TensorRT, NVIDIA’s ahead-of-time inference compiler,2 and the mobile column through the TensorFlow Lite runtime. The chapter uses these engines as given until section 13.6 examines what such runtimes do to a model.
2 TensorRT: TensorRT builds its engine ahead of time for one microarchitecture (such as Hopper or Blackwell) (NVIDIA 2024a). That target-specific build phase allows the compiler to generate fused kernels, select microarchitecture-specific Tensor Core execution paths, and optimize memory layouts (such as NC/32HW32). The resulting nonportable engine reduces per-request execution latency and minimizes the accelerator count needed to satisfy a target throughput.
