Systems Perspective 13.1: ResNet-50 across the serving spectrumSystems insight: It is tempting to read table 2 as one model deployed three ways. That reading is misleading: the cloud and mobile tiers share the ResNet-50 graph but use different precision and runtimes, while the TinyML tier cannot run ResNet-50 at all and substitutes an architecture designed for its constraints. Treating these as one model hides the work that makes each deployment possible.


Whichever tier hosts it, a networked deployment runs the model inside a server process, and each such replica must turn an irregular stream of requests into work its accelerator can execute efficiently. That conversion is the job of the inference server’s internal architecture.

Self-Check: Question

When transitioning a deep learning model from training to an online serving environment, how does the system constraint in the D·A·M (Data-Algorithm-Machine) taxonomy fundamentally shift regarding machine utilization and algorithm state?

Machine utilization must be maximized at 100% to amortize capital costs, while the algorithm continues parameter backpropagation during request serving.
Machine capacity must maintain operational headroom below saturation to prevent tail-latency queueing collapse, while the algorithm’s weights remain fixed for a deployed version.
Machine allocation switches from accelerators to general-purpose CPUs exclusively, while the algorithm dynamically modifies its architecture per incoming user payload.
Machine throughput replaces latency as the primary operational constraint, while data volume shifts from live request streams to historical offline batches.

True or False: In online model serving, the latency term (\(L_{\text{lat}}\)) in the iron law of ML systems must encompass external factors such as network round-trip time, request serialization, and system orchestration, rather than solely the accelerator kernel execution time.
Explain why achieving high average throughput during offline benchmarking does not guarantee that an online serving system will satisfy its tail-latency Service-Level Objective (SLO) during production traffic spikes.
An e-commerce platform evaluates precomputing product recommendations offline (static inference) versus computing them on demand when a user visits the homepage (dynamic inference). Which trade-off correctly characterizes static inference compared to dynamic inference?

Static inference eliminates database storage costs but increases real-time p99 latency by executing large batched matrix multiplications during user page loads.
Static inference guarantees real-time contextual adaptation to intra-session user clicks but requires dedicated high-end GPUs on the critical request path.
Static inference trades storage capacity and potential prediction staleness for retrieval latency that avoids per-request model execution, whereas dynamic inference provides fresh predictions from live context at the expense of computational latency and variable serving capacity.
Static inference requires running unbatched single-sample inferences across microcontrollers, whereas dynamic inference processes large offline shards across cloud clusters.

Why does bare-metal TinyML serving on microcontrollers (e.g., ARM Cortex-M) preclude the use of standard cloud serving frameworks (like Triton or vLLM), and what architectural adaptations are required?

See Answers →






Inside each replica, user requests arrive in irregular bursts—milliseconds apart one moment and silent for seconds the next—whereas accelerator compute engines demand steady streams of uniform, dense batches to saturate memory bandwidth and arithmetic units. Reconciling these two incompatible rhythms at the system boundary requires a serving architecture that decouples network ingress from execution scheduling, absorbing arrival bursts and packing irregular inputs into dense batches without violating latency SLOs.


If a web server invoked the accelerator synchronously every time a socket read completed, slow client uploads would stall the GPU and concurrent connections would contend for device memory. An inference server3 (such as NVIDIA Triton or TensorFlow Serving) avoids this by acting as a specialized runtime scheduler that manages concurrency, device memory, and data movement between host CPUs and accelerator devices. Rather than running the model directly on the network thread, the server pipelines incoming requests through dedicated subsystems that isolate client network handling from accelerator compute. Every request traverses a six-stage runtime pipeline (figure 2) from network ingress and request-buffering queues through the dynamic batcher to the inference runner and hardware accelerator.
3 Inference server: Google’s TensorFlow Serving (Olston et al. 2017) helped establish the separation of model logic from serving infrastructure; NVIDIA’s Triton (NVIDIA 2024b) extends this pattern across multiple model frameworks and backends. The critical design insight is that a scheduler and dynamic batcher turn irregular single-request traffic into accelerator-friendly execution, improving utilization when latency budgets allow batching. Exact utilization gains depend on model, hardware, arrival rate, and the configured batching window.
Olston, Christopher, Noah Fiedel, Kiril Gorovoy, Jeremiah Harmsen, Li Lao, Fangwei Li, Vinu Rajashekhar, Sukriti Ramesh, and Jordan Soyke. 2017. “TensorFlow-Serving: Flexible, High-Performance ML Serving.” CoRR abs/1712.06139. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1712.06139.

NVIDIA. 2024b. NVIDIA Triton Inference Server.






Figure 2: Inference Server Anatomy: A modern inference server decouples network handling from accelerator execution through a staged pipeline. Each stage isolates a concern, from absorbing bursty traffic to forming efficient batches, so the hardware accelerator stays busy despite irregular arrival patterns.



Across the stages in figure 2, the server handles concurrency management, request transformation, model lifecycle management, and execution scheduling. At network ingress, the server manages concurrency through asynchronous event loops (such as epoll or kqueue) and worker thread pools that handle thousands of concurrent client TCP connections without stalling accelerator execution pipelines. Decoupling network I/O from compute ensures that slow client transfers or network stalls do not starve the accelerator of ready work.
Once a payload arrives, the server transforms requests into tensors, decoding serialized network bytes into contiguous, aligned memory buffers that match the tensor layout required by the underlying execution engine. For example, four-dimensional vision tensors typically adopt NCHW4 or NHWC formats. On modern accelerators, matrix multiplication units (such as Tensor Cores) load 8- or 16-element channel vectors using coalesced memory transactions that favor channels-last (NHWC) layout. If the execution kernel requires a different physical layout, the server must materialize that layout. Calling torch.permute merely creates a view with reordered strides; an explicit memory copy or transpose kernel must physically reorder the data in memory. Because such materialization performs zero arithmetic (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\approx 0\) FLOP/byte), memory traffic and launch overhead dominate its cost. A device-local conversion consumes device memory bandwidth, whereas conversions across the host-device boundary consume PCIe bandwidth.
4 NCHW and NHWC (tensor memory layouts): These acronyms encode the dimension order of 4D image tensors: N (batch), C (channels), H (height), and W (width). In a contiguous NCHW tensor, each channel plane is contiguous; in NHWC, channels for one spatial position are adjacent. Optimized kernels may favor either layout, and a semantic mismatch can scramble values even when the element count is correct. Serving code should therefore make both dimension meaning and any physical-layout conversion explicit.For those tensors to execute without startup stalls, the server also manages the model’s local lifecycle. The runtime establishes the CUDA context before allocating device memory (VRAM) and streaming weights onto the accelerator. It also pins host memory buffers for direct memory access (DMA) transfers and executes representative warmup passes to trigger deferred compilation and memory allocation before admitting live client traffic. While enterprise model registries, canary rollouts, and rollback policies belong to cluster-level operations (ML Operations), the serving engine governs local state, validating that active model instances are warmed, resident in accelerator memory, and ready for dispatch.
Between request buffering and the warmed model sits the execution scheduler, which coordinates accelerator dispatch by implementing dynamic batching (section 13.5). For weight-dominated inference at batch size \(\BatchSize=1\), streaming parameters from HBM can limit execution before the arithmetic units reach peak throughput. Grouping \(\BatchSize\) requests into a concurrent batch amortizes the byte transfers of reading model weights across all \(\BatchSize\) inputs, increasing the arithmetic intensity (\(\ArithmeticIntensity= \Operations/\DataVolume\)).
To balance individual request latency against batch compute efficiency, the scheduler tunes queue residency using a batching window (or timeout threshold). Setting the batching window to zero removes deliberate batch formation delay, but requests can still wait for an available worker. An immediately dispatched small batch may also expose too little work to use the accelerator efficiently. Conversely, setting a bounded window (such as 2 to 5 ms) allows the scheduler to buffer arriving requests until either the queue reaches a target batch size or the timeout expires. The window bounds deliberate formation delay; waiting for a busy worker is a separate resource-queue delay. Batching trades that formation time for greater weight reuse and potentially higher service capacity, while total latency includes both waits and execution. Before a request ever reaches those internal queues, however, it must cross the network boundary into the API gateway.



At that network boundary, a request’s wire representation can cost more CPU time than the model itself spends on the accelerator. As device kernels undergo aggressive compilation (via TensorRT, TorchDynamo, or custom kernels), forward-pass execution often drops below a single millisecond, leaving payload ingestion, transport, and deserialization as a major share of end-to-end latency (quantified stage by stage in section 13.3.2.1). Two interface choices, the wire serialization format and the network transport protocol, determine whether that host ingress path stays in microseconds or consumes the latency budget before inference begins.


Machine learning payloads differ from conventional web API payloads. They consist of multi-dimensional arrays of floating-point numbers (such as image tensors, dense embedding vectors, or token sequence logits). While text-based JSON is ubiquitous in web services, serializing dense numerical arrays into text incurs severe CPU and memory penalties. Serialization overhead manifests because JSON parsers must scan every byte sequentially, validate syntax, allocate heap nodes, and invoke string-to-float conversion routines (such as strtod). Each 32-bit float expands from 4 raw bytes into 7 to 15 ASCII characters including punctuation. Furthermore, raw binary data (such as compressed JPEG or raw image bytes) requires Base64 encoding to travel within JSON strings, imposing a 33 percent size inflation before parsing begins.


↩︎ Clipper’s decomposition of serving latency, in which serialization rivals model execution, is established in End-to-end vs. component latency.
5 Protocol Buffers (Protobuf): Protobuf uses a predefined schema (from a .proto file) to encode structured data into a compact binary format (Protocol Buffers Authors 2026). Because the schema carries field names and types, the wire payload need not repeat them as JSON does. Its wire format is still not identical to a C++ object’s in-memory layout, so it requires a parsing step and does not provide the same direct zero-copy access pattern that FlatBuffers targets.
Protocol Buffers Authors. 2026. Overview: Protocol Buffers.
6 FlatBuffers: The “flat” in the name describes the design: the binary buffer can serve as the serialized representation and the data structure being read, avoiding a separate parsing or unpacking phase for supported access patterns (FlatBuffers Authors 2026). For ML inference, this can enable zero-copy access to tensor metadata, because the serving system reads tensor shapes and offsets directly from the buffer rather than allocating a second object representation.
FlatBuffers Authors. 2026. FlatBuffers Documentation.
Binary serialization formats, such as Protocol Buffers5 and FlatBuffers,6 bypass this text conversion cost. Float arrays transmit directly as packed IEEE 754 byte streams with zero ASCII conversion and zero Base64 framing. Furthermore, FlatBuffers organizes serialized records with internal relative offsets, enabling zero-copy deserialization. The serving application reads tensor dimensions, data types, and byte offsets directly out of the network receive buffer without allocating an intermediate object graph on the heap.



Transport protocol selection governs connection life cycles and socket multiplexing. Conventional REST APIs typically deploy HTTP/1.1 with JSON payloads. HTTP/1.1 clients commonly use multiple persistent TCP connections for concurrency. Establishing each connection incurs handshake and, for HTTPS, TLS costs, but keep-alive reuse amortizes setup across requests. HTTP/1.1 also suffers from request-level head-of-line blocking, because responses on a single connection must return in request order. While REST APIs can adopt HTTP/2 or binary encodings, the combination of HTTP/1.1 and JSON creates significant socket overhead and CPU parsing contention when serving high-throughput tensor workloads.
In contrast, gRPC (gRPC Remote Procedure Call)7 pairs HTTP/2 transport with Protocol Buffers serialization. HTTP/2 establishes a single long-lived TCP connection and multiplexes hundreds of concurrent request and response streams simultaneously using binary framing. This architecture multiplexes concurrent streams over a persistent connection and removes HTTP-level response-order blocking (a lost TCP packet can still stall every stream on the connection, which HTTP/3 addresses by moving to QUIC). Protobuf, meanwhile, enforces strongly typed contracts and serializes binary tensor payloads efficiently. Consequently, gRPC is the standard protocol for internal microservice communication in model serving clusters, where low latency, compact wire payloads, and bidirectional token streaming are primary design criteria. Even a modest embedding payload shows the gap in wire footprint and host parsing time.
7 gRPC (gRPC remote procedure call): The gRPC framework pairs HTTP/2 transport with an interface definition language and message format, most commonly Protocol Buffers (gRPC Authors 2026). The size and latency benefit over REST/JSON depends on payload shape, client/server implementation, and whether serialization is a meaningful share of the end-to-end latency budget.
gRPC Authors. 2026. Introduction to gRPC.

Napkin Math 13.1: JSON vs. Protobuf serializationConsider a request payload containing 1,000 floating point numbers (for example, an embedding vector).

JSON: Uses ~9 KB on the wire. Requires ~50 μs to parse.
Protobuf: Uses ~4 KB on the wire. Requires ~5 μs to parse.

Math: Switching one request to the binary payload saves 50 μs − 5 μs = 45 μs of parse time. For this illustrative system processing 10,000 requests per second, the savings compound to 10,000 \(\times\) 45 μs = 0.45 s of CPU time reclaimed every wall-clock second, which is 45 percent of one core freed from serialization overhead alone.
Systems insight: This 10× scenario gain makes gRPC/Protobuf, FlatBuffers, or another binary protocol a strong candidate for high-throughput internal microservices when serialization is a visible part of the latency budget.


Architectural selection is governed by system constraints. REST over HTTP/1.1 remains practical for public-facing edge gateways where broad client compatibility and human-readable debugging take precedence over raw wire efficiency. Within cluster boundaries, gRPC over HTTP/2 with binary serialization can reduce overhead when high query volume or tensor serialization consumes a significant share of the host CPU budget; its streaming support also suits incremental token responses.




When traffic exceeds what a single machine can handle, adding model replicas does not prevent tail-latency spikes if requests still land on a replica that is mid-batch or still loading weights into GPU memory. Cloud and data center deployments therefore place a load balancer between clients and model servers to route around busy or unready replicas. A serving load balancer protects the fleet by coupling request distribution with readiness checks and traffic shifting. It routes incoming requests across replicas using policies such as round-robin or least-connections, so that traffic steers around slow or saturated workers before queues build. It also backs that routing with health monitoring that inspects both process liveness and model initialization state, confirming that weights are loaded and warmup passes are complete before a replica receives live queries. The same routing control also supports progressive rollouts, shifting traffic gradually between model versions rather than cutting over abruptly.


↪ Shadow, canary, and blue-green release strategies that build on this traffic shifting are developed in Model deployment.
On a single machine running several model instances, such as several Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) Runtime sessions, the serving framework and the operating system queue requests without a separate balancer. A dedicated balancer becomes necessary once replicas span machines, and its distribution algorithms belong to that distributed setting. This chapter therefore plans capacity one node at a time. The unit of capacity is the sustained model throughput of one node. The queueing analysis in section 13.4 determines the utilization at which that node can no longer meet its latency target and a second replica must be added behind the balancer. Protocol selection, process architecture, and the balancer in front of the replicas establish the structural skeleton of a serving deployment. Evaluating actual operational performance requires tracing how latency accumulates as one request traverses each stage of a replica’s runtime pipeline.

When a single HTTP request carrying a \(224{\times}224\) JPEG image arrives at an inference server, the clock starts on the client’s deadline as soon as the first byte enters the network stack and stops only when the classification payload departs. Between those two boundaries, the request must be decoded on the host, copied across the interconnect, evaluated on the accelerator, and formatted into a response, with every stage drawing from the same millisecond allowance.


A vision service that completes thousands of classifications per second still fails its users if individual requests take two seconds to return and miss their interactive deadlines. For dynamic inference systems, the serving inversion established in section 13.1 therefore imposes a strict latency budget across the entire request path (Gujarati et al. 2020).
8 Tail latency: Unlike averages, percentile latencies reveal the performance impact of system outliers common in ML serving, such as model cache misses or garbage collection pauses. These rare, high-latency requests can disproportionately harm user satisfaction and business outcomes. Because the magnitude is workload-specific, services validate percentile targets (p95, p99) against their own users and SLOs.Relevant metrics expand from aggregate throughput and mean latency to the latency distribution. Mean and p50 describe the center, while p95 and p99 expose the slow tail. If mean latency is 50 ms but p99 is two seconds, the p99 threshold is 40× the mean, so about 1 percent of requests are at or beyond two seconds. Whether that tail matters depends on the service and its users, which is why percentile targets should come from the SLO rather than convention.8 Managing these percentile constraints requires decomposing the total allowed response time into a latency budget that allocates time across each processing phase, the serial accounting that the latency budget principle (\(\ref{pri-latency-budget}\)) states formally.

Definition 13.2: Latency budget
Latency budget is the time allocated to request stages under an end-to-end deadline; the SLO also specifies the required completion quantile.

Significance: It acts as a zero-sum constraint system where any milliseconds consumed by serialization or network overhead directly reduce the latency budget (\(\EndToEndRequestLatency\)) available for model inference.
Distinction: The budget allocates time across stages, while the latency SLO of Latency and tail latency couples the deadline (for example, \(<50\text{ ms}\)) with a completion quantile (\(\text{p99}\) or \(\text{p99.9}\)). A service-level indicator (SLI) is the measured quantity used to evaluate that objective. Tail latency spikes can stem from queueing, batch formation, cache state, interference, or data movement.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that the “model” has the entire budget. In the illustrative breakdown in table 3, the remainder is consumed by host preprocessing and data movement (JPEG decode, resize, normalization, and PCIe transfer), while upstream network and serialization overheads (table 5) consume further margin.






Inference is one slice of the latency budget; preprocessing rivals it.
Every serving request traverses three sequential phases that share this latency budget. Preprocessing converts raw input such as image bytes or text strings into model-ready tensors, inference executes the model computation over those tensors, and postprocessing turns the resulting device outputs into user-facing responses. Accelerating model execution alone yields diminishing returns when host-side preprocessing and response formatting consume the majority of the latency budget, an immediate manifestation of Amdahl’s law. As hardware compilers compress accelerator kernel runtimes into sub-millisecond durations, host-device coordination and memory transfers emerge as the primary latency bottlenecks.



An engineer who measures only total request duration in a vision service sees a single millisecond number that lumps together CPU-bound JPEG decompression, host-to-device PCIe transfers, accelerator kernel execution, and response formatting. It is then easy to spend weeks optimizing GPU kernels that account for less than half of total response time. Timing each pipeline boundary independently isolates the actual bottleneck before optimization begins.

Barroso, Patterson, and colleagues identified a gap in how computer systems handle latency across time scales (Barroso et al. 2017). Nanosecond-scale stalls (such as cache misses) are hidden by hardware instruction-level parallelism, while millisecond-scale delays (such as disk I/O or network RPCs) are hidden by operating system thread context switching. Operations in the microsecond range (1–100 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)) fall into the gap between these two mechanisms. They are too long to spin-wait on a CPU core without wasting compute cycles and power, yet too short for the operating system to context-switch to another thread without paying scheduling overheads that exceed the wait time itself.

Barroso, Luiz, Mike Marty, David Patterson, and Parthasarathy Ranganathan. 2017. “Attack of the Killer Microseconds.” Communications of the ACM 60 (4): 48–54. https://doi.org/10.1145/3015146.
Serving infrastructure operates directly in this killer microseconds regime. Using the representative ranges in table 5, serialization at 50–500 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\), dispatch at 10–50 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\), and data copy at 100–500 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) are each individually small. For the 3.5 ms reference forward pass, however, these named microsecond-scale overheads collectively add about 5 percent to 30 percent of the latency budget before network and queuing delays are counted. No single overhead justifies optimization in isolation, yet together they determine whether the system meets its SLO.
Reducing this compound overhead requires changing the architecture across the software-hardware interface. When microsecond delays accumulate across serialization, kernel dispatch, and memory copies, isolated optimizations to individual functions yield negligible improvements. Instead, high-performance serving runtimes remove the boundaries themselves. They use zero-copy memory buffers between networking and execution runtimes, maintain persistent CUDA streams to bypass driver dispatch latencies, and migrate preprocessing kernels directly onto the accelerator to avoid intermediate host-device transfers. Eliminating those fixed boundary taxes leaves the portion of preprocessing and execution that scales with the dimensions of the input payload itself.




Doubling an image’s side length from \(224{\times}224\) to \(448{\times}448\) quadruples the pixel count that the host must decode and that the convolutional layers must process, making input resolution a primary serving control as well as a model property. Model architectures are often evaluated at fixed resolutions, but the serving runtime must ingest variable client inputs and rescale them before kernel execution. In convolution-dominated vision networks, floating-point operations scale quadratically with spatial dimensions (\(\mathcal{O}(\ImageHeight \cdot \ImageWidth)\)), whereas static costs (such as weight streaming from accelerator memory and kernel launch overheads) remain invariant. Varying input resolution therefore shifts the operational arithmetic intensity across the roofline boundary. Compute-bound stages slow down quadratically as pixel count expands, whereas memory-bound stages scale with activation memory footprint.

Different deployment contexts choose resolution according to which constraint binds first. A mobile application may accept \(224{\times}224\) inputs because latency and battery life outweigh marginal accuracy gains, whereas medical-imaging workloads often step up to \(512{\times}512\) or higher because diagnostic detail justifies the extra compute. Between those fixed choices, a perception pipeline may run a wide field at low resolution and reserve high-resolution crops for fine-grained recognition. A public API that receives arbitrary user uploads can either normalize every image to a single input size or route each request to one of several validated resolution profiles.



Adaptive resolution lets production systems select resolution dynamically based on content. One approach runs a lightweight classifier at \(128{\times}128\) to categorize content type, then selects task-appropriate resolution with documents at \(512{\times}512\), landscapes at \(224{\times}224\), and faces at \(384{\times}384\). In this illustrative scenario, the policy provides 1.4× throughput improvement with 99.2 percent accuracy retention vs. fixed high resolution. This pattern trades preprocessing cost from running the lightweight classifier for inference savings on the main model. While resolution sets the cost of the stages before the model, the stage after it is usually far cheaper, though it still crosses the device boundary and spends host CPU time and therefore belongs on the same budget.




When a model finishes a forward pass, its raw output logits sit in accelerator memory that client applications cannot read directly; copying thousands of unreduced floats across the PCIe bus and formatting strings on the CPU can stall the worker thread between batches. Postprocessing turns those device tensors into structured application responses across the physical boundary between the accelerator and the host CPU. How the serving engine splits computation across that boundary determines whether the final stage finishes in microseconds or blocks the pipeline.


Classification models emit unnormalized logits across the label space, and turning those raw scores into application-ready predictions requires a chain of reduction, filtering, and calibration steps. When only the single most likely label matters, argmax selection extracts the index of the highest logit, whereas applications that present ranked alternatives use top-\(\TopClassCount\) extraction to keep the \(\TopClassCount\) largest scores alongside their class indices. Before returning those candidates, probability calibration (such as temperature scaling) rescales raw logits so that output confidences reflect empirical accuracy, allowing thresholding to discard predictions that fall below a required certainty cutoff.
Executing reduction operations on the accelerator can reduce host-device transfer volume when the saved transfer cost outweighs the device execution and launch overhead. Performing softmax, argmax, or top-\(\TopClassCount\) selection in device memory prunes the payload before it crosses the PCIe bus. In ResNet-50 classification, for example, running top-\(\TopClassCount\) on the GPU reduces the transfer payload from 1,000 float32 logits (4,000 bytes) to five values and five integer indices. For ResNet-50 image classification, listing 1 traces this execution path from GPU tensor operations to host CPU label lookup and response formatting.

# Extract top-5 predictions for multi-class response
# topk returns (values, indices) sorted by probability
top5_probs, top5_indices = probs.topk(5)  # GPU operation
top5_probs = top5_probs.squeeze(0).tolist()
top5_indices = top5_indices.squeeze(0).tolist()

# Map class indices to human-readable labels
# imagenet_labels: list of 1000 class names from synset mapping
labels = [imagenet_labels[i] for i in top5_indices]  # CPU lookup

# Format response with predictions and metadata for API contract
response = {
    "predictions": [
        {"label": label, "confidence": float(prob)}
        for label, prob in zip(labels, top5_probs)
    ],
    "model_version": "resnet50-v2.1",  # Client-side version tracking
    "inference_time_ms": 5.2,  # Observability for latency monitoring
}



In listing 1, total postprocessing time is approximately 0.1 ms, negligible compared with preprocessing and inference. The GPU handles the normalization and top-5 reduction, so the subsequent .tolist() call transfers only tens of bytes across PCIe. However, .tolist() forces a synchronous device-to-host copy, blocking the host thread until the GPU stream finishes. In high-throughput pipelined servers, such synchronization barriers must be scheduled carefully to avoid stalling the CPU thread while it feeds subsequent requests. Fitting a calibration mapping is an offline task; applying a simple fitted mapping online is usually inexpensive, but it is valuable only when downstream decisions require confidence scores whose empirical meaning has been validated.



Production systems package predictions to satisfy application-level API contracts. These contracts govern JSON serialization schemas, floating-point formatting, error codes, and fallback defaults when thresholding rejects all candidates. In Python-based runtimes, repetitive JSON serialization and string allocation can consume unexpected host CPU cycles under heavy concurrency, turning a microsecond-scale formatting step into a CPU bottleneck. High-throughput servers address this by delegating serialization to native C++ runtimes or binary protocols like Protocol Buffers. Response metadata, including model version and inference execution time, completes the payload to enable downstream observability. Characterizing postprocessing closes the individual request’s latency budget, though analyzing these stages strictly in isolation assumes sequential evaluation, where each transaction completes its entire lifecycle before subsequent work begins.




Executing each request in lockstep isolation leaves specialized accelerators heavily underutilized. Because network termination, payload preprocessing, neural network evaluation, and response serialization bind on distinct physical subsystems (host network interfaces, CPU cores, PCIe interconnects, and accelerator matrix units), strict serial processing forces the accelerator into idle bubbles while the host prepares incoming tensors. The central systems objective is to maximize the accelerator’s duty cycle, the proportion of wall-clock time spent actively executing arithmetic kernels, without violating request tail-latency deadlines. Serving runtimes achieve this through request pipelining, overlapping asynchronous host preprocessing of forthcoming queries with concurrent accelerator execution on previously staged batches.


↩︎ Asynchronous host-accelerator transfer and double buffering mechanisms are established in Transfer optimization.


Figure 4 sequences execution across CPU preprocessing and GPU inference to demonstrate how request pipelining recovers lost compute capacity. In serial execution (A), each request must complete its entire lifecycle (Network \(\rightarrow\) CPU Preprocessing \(\rightarrow\) GPU Inference \(\rightarrow\) Postprocessing) before the next request begins, leaving the GPU idle for more than 50 percent of wall-clock time. Pipelining concurrent requests (B) overlaps CPU preprocessing of upcoming requests with active GPU inference on earlier inputs, eliminating the idle bubbles and maximizing accelerator duty cycle.






Figure 4: Request Pipelining: Pipelining hides latency by overlapping independent operations across different hardware resources. In pipelined execution (B), the CPU processes the next request’s data while the GPU executes the current request’s inference. This can increase accelerator duty cycle and throughput without changing the model.



Pipelining relies on non-blocking hardware queues and asynchronous execution streams. Instead of blocking until a GPU kernel completes, the host CPU thread enqueues memory transfers and kernel launches into an accelerator stream and immediately begins preprocessing the next incoming request. The accelerator’s DMA engine and compute cores execute those queued operations independently, overlapping host preprocessing with device execution.



System efficiency here measures accelerator duty cycle rather than the fraction of peak arithmetic throughput or bandwidth achieved. In equation 2, compute time is the union of useful kernel-active intervals on each resource, summed across resources; overlapping kernels on one GPU are not counted twice. \[\text{System Efficiency} = \frac{\sum \KernelActiveTime}{\text{Wall Clock Time} \times \text{Resource Count}} \tag{2}\]
The reference ResNet-50 request spends 4.5 ms preprocessing on a host CPU core and 3.5 ms on the accelerator, so a serial system keeps the accelerator busy only 41 percent of the time. With at least two requests in flight in a sustained stream, the accelerator works on one request while the host prepares the next, and duty cycle rises to 78 percent after pipeline fill. It cannot reach 100 percent with one preprocessing worker, because the host stage is the slower of the two; a second worker removes that cap. A finite pair still pays pipeline fill and drain time, and stochastic service must retain enough capacity headroom to meet its tail-latency objective. If the CPU is too slow to feed the GPU, the system becomes CPU-bound, and further model optimization provides zero throughput gain. This is the Amdahl ceiling of section 13.3.2 seen from the throughput side. Hardware upgrades tighten it, because accelerator compute throughput has grown far faster than CPU single-thread performance across successive generations. A system that was compute-bound on an older accelerator may become CPU-bound after a hardware upgrade, not because preprocessing got slower but because the model got dramatically faster while the CPU did not.

An inference service that responds in a few milliseconds at moderate load can suffer sudden, tenfold latency spikes when traffic climbs toward capacity, even though no hardware has failed and the model’s execution time has not changed. Because requests arrive in irregular bursts and contend for shared accelerator queues, host-to-device PCIe links, and memory buses, queuing theory governs how waiting times grow and why latency explodes nonlinearly as utilization approaches capacity.


Before deciding how many accelerators to provision, an engineer must know how many requests will sit inside the server at the same time. Underestimating that in-flight population exhausts host request buffers, worker threads, and device activation memory under load. Given an expected arrival rate and mean response time, Little’s Law determines this average concurrency directly from throughput, while queuing models predict how response times climb as utilization nears saturation.


↪ The derivation of Little’s Law from conservation of requests is collected for reference in Little's Law.

Systems Perspective 13.3: Notation alert: L vs. latencyClassical queueing texts write Little’s law with single letters for the in-system count and the time in system. This book writes \(\RequestConcurrency\) for the count and \(\RequestTimeInSystem\) for the time, because the classical count letter would collide with the loss \(\LossFunction\) and with the iron law’s fixed-latency term \(\Latency\). In queuing theory, \(\RequestTimeInSystem\) denotes the response time or time in system per request; queue-only waiting time is \(\QueueWaitTime\). Here, \(\RequestConcurrency\) denotes the average in-system request count, \(\ArrivalRate\) the arrival rate, \(\ServiceRate\) the service rate of a server that handles one request at a time, and \(\ServingUtilization=\ArrivalRate/\ServiceRate\) the serving utilization. The subscripts distinguish queueing notation from the degradation equation’s \(\FittedSensitivity\) sensitivity parameter and keep serving utilization from occupying bare \(\Glyph{\rho}\). Section 13.5.2 adds the few symbols that batching needs.


Formulated by John D. C. Little (Little 1961), Little’s law establishes an exact relationship among three macroscopic metrics in any stable queuing system: \[\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem \tag{3}\] where \(\RequestConcurrency\) is the average number of requests residing in the system, \(\ArrivalRate\) is the arrival rate (requests per second), and \(\RequestTimeInSystem\) is the average time each request spends from arrival to completion.

Little, John D. C. 1961. “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: \(L = \lambda W\).” Operations Research 9 (3): 383–87. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383.
Little’s law holds regardless of the arrival distribution, service-time distribution, or scheduling discipline; it requires only that the system is stable and that requests are neither created nor destroyed internally. For an inference service targeting 1000 QPS with a mean response time of 50 ms, Little’s law dictates the average in-flight request population that host memory buffers and worker threads must sustain.

Napkin Math 13.2: Little's Law capacity sizingProblem: How many requests are in the system on average at 1,000 QPS?
Math: Little’s Law gives \(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \RequestTimeInSystem\), so average population equals throughput multiplied by mean time in system.
Given:

Arrival rate \((\ArrivalRate)\), equal to throughput in a stable system: 1,000 QPS.
Mean time in system \((\RequestTimeInSystem)\): 50 ms (0.05 s).

Math: \(\RequestConcurrency\) = 1,000 QPS \(\times\) 0.05 s = 50 concurrent requests on average
Systems insight: The system holds 50 requests on average across batch and queue state. That population is a memory and concurrency requirement, not a limit on the accelerator. A server whose GPU executes at most 32 requests per batch can still sustain this load, because the requests not currently executing wait in host memory. Service rate, queueing behavior, and the tail distribution, not the population itself, determine whether the load is feasible.


Because equation 3 binds these three variables, constraining any two dictates the third. If an inference service averages 10 ms per request \((\RequestTimeInSystem = 0.01 \text{ s})\) and holds 50 concurrent requests on average \((\RequestConcurrency = 50)\), the sustainable arrival rate must be \(\ArrivalRate = \RequestConcurrency / \RequestTimeInSystem = 5000\) requests per second. Conversely, if host memory limits concurrency to an average of 10 requests while average time in system remains 10 ms, the system cannot exceed a throughput of 1,000 requests per second without dropping traffic.



Little’s Law describes average system inventory under steady-state conditions, but it does not reveal how latency behaves as traffic approaches system capacity. The M/M/1 queuing model (in Kendall’s notation: Markovian, that is Poisson, arrivals; Markovian, that is exponential, service times; and one server) quantifies the headroom required to prevent latency collapse (Harchol-Balter 2013).9 For a system with Poisson arrivals10 and exponential service times, equation 4 gives the average time in system: \[\RequestTimeInSystem = \frac{1}{\ServiceRate- \ArrivalRate} = \frac{\text{service time}}{1 - \ServingUtilization} \tag{4}\] where \(\ArrivalRate\) is the arrival rate, \(\ServiceRate\) is the service rate (requests per second the server can handle), and \(\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate/\ServiceRate\) is the utilization (the fraction of time the server is busy).
9 M/M/1 queue: Queuing theory originated with Agner Krarup Erlang’s 1909 analysis of the Copenhagen Telephone Exchange, where call arrivals were modeled as memoryless (Poisson).10 Poisson process: Named after French mathematician Simeon Denis Poisson (1781–1840), this stochastic model describes events occurring continuously and independently at a constant average rate, so counts in disjoint intervals are independent.11 Kendall notation: Kendall’s A/S/c (arrival/service/servers) shorthand (Kendall 1953) is the one already used for \(\KendallMarkovianCode/\KendallMarkovianCode/1\), where “M” signifies a Markovian (memoryless) process; the “D” in M/D/1 denotes deterministic service. Neither model replaces measurement of a production workload’s arrival process, service-time variance, or tail behavior.
Kendall, David G. 1953. “Stochastic Processes Occurring in the Theory of Queues and Their Analysis by the Method of the Imbedded Markov Chain.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 24 (3): 338–54. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177728975.
Because the denominator contains \(1 - \ServingUtilization\), latency grows nonlinearly as utilization approaches unity, and small incremental increases in traffic near saturation trigger severe backpressure and queuing delays. The standard M/M/1 formulation assumes exponentially distributed service times. For compiled neural networks processing fixed-size batches and static tensor dimensions, execution times are nearly constant, making an M/D/1 queue a tighter model of mean queuing delay. The analysis here retains the M/M/1 model because it yields closed-form solutions and predicts greater mean queueing delay than M/D/1 under matched arrival rate and mean service time. In production environments, variable input lengths, dynamic batch formation, CPU preprocessing, and key-value cache lookups introduce runtime variance that quickly breaks deterministic assumptions.11 Under this model, average time in system multiplies rapidly as utilization approaches 100 percent (table 7).

At 50 percent utilization, time in system is 2× service time; at 90 percent, it reaches 10×. Plotted against the serving utilization \(\ServingUtilization\), the fraction of time the server is busy, the same \(\KendallMarkovianCode/\KendallMarkovianCode/1\) model shows why the knee matters (figure 5). Latency stays nearly flat at low utilization and then climbs without bound as the server approaches 100 percent busy, because each new arrival is increasingly likely to find work already waiting. The 99th percentile curve rises even faster in absolute terms, staying a fixed multiple above the mean that section 13.4.3 derives next. ↪ Why long-tailed latency distributions make high percentiles, rather than the mean, govern what users experience is collected for reference in Distributions and the long tail.














Figure 5: The Tail Latency Explosion: Request latency vs. serving utilization \(\ServingUtilization\). Mean latency (blue) and the p99 approximation (red) both grow nonlinearly as utilization approaches saturation; the 70 percent marker is an illustrative planning knee rather than a model-derived breakpoint. In an \(\KendallMarkovianCode/\KendallMarkovianCode/1\) queue, the 99th percentile latency scales as \(-\ln(0.01) \approx 4.6\times\) mean latency, illustrating why tail delays compound violently near saturation.






A serving cluster running at 70 percent utilization can report a comfortable mean latency while its slowest 1 percent of requests wait more than four times as long in the queue. Because averages hide this tail contention, production SLOs specify percentile targets (p95, p99) that bound experience for the slowest requests (Dean and Barroso 2013).
The M/M/1 model that produced the mean in equation 4 also yields the full latency distribution, and the tail follows from it. Total request latency (queue wait plus service) is exponentially distributed with cumulative distribution function \(\ResponseTimeDistributionFunction(\RequestResponseTime) = 1 - e^{-\RequestResponseTime/ \RequestTimeInSystem}\), where \(\RequestTimeInSystem = \frac{\text{service time}}{1 - \ServingUtilization}\) is that mean response time. To derive the 99th percentile latency (p99), we solve for the time \(\RequestResponseTime_{99}\) where 99 percent of requests have completed (\(\ResponseTimeDistributionFunction(\RequestResponseTime_{99}) = 0.99\)): \[1 - e^{-\RequestResponseTime_{99}/\RequestTimeInSystem} = 0.99 \implies e^{-\RequestResponseTime_{99}/\RequestTimeInSystem} = 0.01 \implies -\frac{\RequestResponseTime_{99}}{\RequestTimeInSystem} = \ln(0.01) = -\ln(100) \approx -4.605\] Solving for \(\RequestResponseTime_{99}\) and substituting the mean latency \(\RequestTimeInSystem\) yields the governing expression for tail latency: \[\TailRequestLatency\approx \frac{\text{service time}}{1 - \ServingUtilization} \cdot \ln\left(\frac{1}{1 - 0.99}\right) \approx \frac{4.6 \cdot \text{service time}}{1 - \ServingUtilization} \tag{5}\]
At 70 percent utilization, average latency is only 3.3 times service time, while p99 latency reaches 15.3 times service time \((4.6/0.3 \approx 15.3)\). Evaluating a serving cluster by average latency therefore conceals severe tail degradation. Before exploring software mitigations like hedging, systems engineers must first provision sufficient accelerator capacity to satisfy tail-latency SLOs under peak load. For a ResNet-50 deployment, the M/M/1 tail-response-time model turns provisioning into a short sequence of steps.

Napkin Math 13.3: ResNet-50 capacity planningConsider designing a ResNet-50 serving system with these requirements:

Queue-plus-GPU p99 subbudget: 50 ms
Peak expected traffic: 5,000 QPS
GPU service time (batch one, the chapter’s reference ResNet-50 profile): 3.5 ms

Step 0: Define the modeled request boundary. The worker model covers waiting for the GPU and the GPU forward pass only. This scenario allocates 50 ms to that portion of the request and separately assumes a combined 18 ms upper bound for network transit, serialization, preprocessing, transfer, and postprocessing. The end-to-end deadline must accommodate both allowances. A 50 ms end-to-end deadline would instead require subtracting the outside-worker allowance before applying the queue model; the arithmetic below would no longer apply. An outside-stage mean or p99 cannot substitute for the stipulated combined upper bound.
Step 1: Find safe utilization. From equation 5, \(\TailRequestLatency\approx\) 4.6 \(\times\) service time / \((1 - \ServingUtilization)\). Setting \(\TailRequestLatency\leq\) 50 ms with 3.5 ms service time gives \(\ServingUtilization \leq 1 - (4.6 \times 3.5\,\mathrm{ms})/50\,\mathrm{ms} = 0.68\) (68 percent maximum utilization). This is an M/M/1 p99 estimate under the stated arrival and service assumptions; a load test must validate the tail.
Step 2: Calculate required service rate. \(\RequiredServiceRate = 5,000\,\mathrm{QPS} / 0.68 = 7402.9\,\mathrm{req}/\mathrm{s}\)
Step 3: Determine GPU count. In this M/M/1 model, the single-GPU rate is 283 req/s.
GPUs needed = 7402.9 req/s / 283 req/s = 26.1 → 27 GPUs
This single-GPU rate is the batch-1 service rate. Each request holds the GPU for the full service time, which keeps the M/M/1 model closed-form. Dynamic batching (section 13.5) amortizes fixed overhead across requests and raises the per-GPU rate several-fold, so a batched deployment may need fewer GPUs after its own latency distribution is validated. Section 13.10.2 compares the two regimes.
Step 4: Add headroom for variance. This scenario adds 30 percent headroom for traffic spikes and variance: final count = 27 \(\times\) 1.3 = 35.1, rounded up to 36.
Step 5: Verify fault tolerance. The 30 percent headroom addresses traffic variance, but production systems also need fault tolerance. With 36 GPUs, losing one leaves 35 GPUs handling 5,000 QPS. The postfailure utilization is 5,000 QPS / (283 req/s \(\times\) 35) = \(50.4\%\).
This remains well below the 68 percent safe utilization threshold, confirming N+1 redundancy is satisfied. For stricter fault tolerance requirements, N+2 redundancy (tolerating two simultaneous failures) would require 29 GPUs under the same safe-utilization threshold, or about 38 GPUs if the 30 percent headroom must remain after two simultaneous failures.
Result: Under the batch-1 M/M/1 assumptions, 36 H100 GPUs supply the modeled queue-plus-GPU capacity for 5,000 QPS within the 50 ms p99 subbudget, including one failed replica. End-to-end acceptance still requires validating the tail under load and the separately reserved outside-worker allowance.


The queuing analysis explains the capacity planning approach detailed in section 13.10.2 and connects directly to the MLPerf Server scenario. The Server scenario (Server) is defined as Poisson arrivals scored by throughput against a tail-latency target. A Server result is therefore valid only when the run satisfies its percentile-latency constraint; otherwise, the target QPS must be reduced and the run repeated.



A capacity plan built on stationary Poisson arrivals holds only while traffic stays near the planned rate. Production traffic instead arrives in bursty, uncoordinated surges driven by user behavior, scheduled jobs, and daily cycles. When a surge pushes arrivals past the reserved headroom, accelerator service times cannot shrink to absorb the excess, so queries pile up in host and device queues and clients begin timing out.

Example 13.3: The 'Black Friday' traffic spikeScenario: An e-commerce recommendation serving system experiences a 10× traffic surge (10,000 QPS) during Black Friday sales events.
Diagnosis: A fleet sized for normal traffic now receives more requests per second than it can complete. Utilization pins at 100 percent, and every second of the surge adds the excess arrivals to a queue that the servers cannot drain, so waiting time grows for as long as the surge lasts. In this scenario, latency reaches 10 s and clients time out. Section 13.4.2 showed why the queue starts growing sharply well before utilization reaches 100 percent.
Systems lesson: High average throughput does not prevent queueing collapse under traffic surges. Depending on the service, preserving a tail-latency objective may require load shedding, graceful degradation, or autoscaling before utilization reaches the workload’s queueing knee.


Eliminating all sources of latency variability is often impractical. Production systems instead use techniques that tolerate variability while still meeting SLOs (Dean and Barroso 2013; Dean 2012). For one serving node, the first distinction is between an isolated straggler and overload. Racing an isolated slow request can reduce its latency when spare capacity exists. When the node is overloaded, however, racing requests injects duplicate work and deepens the queue, so the system must instead protect the latency of admitted requests through graceful degradation or admission control. Graceful degradation returns lower-fidelity results to preserve throughput: classification pipelines fall back to cached approximations, generative models truncate decoding lengths, and model ensembles evaluate only a subset of members. Dynamically reducing active ensemble members shortens the service time \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) of each batch of \(\BatchSize\) requests. That increases the effective service rate \(\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) = \BatchSize/\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) and lowers utilization \(\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate / \EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize)\) toward a workload-appropriate operating point with more headroom, as illustrated by figure 5. The system trades a controlled accuracy reduction for SLO survival instead of an uncontrolled latency collapse. Admission control enforces an even stricter boundary. When the ingress queue exceeds a designated threshold, the server immediately rejects excess queries with HTTP 503 status codes rather than admitting work doomed to violate its latency deadline.

Dean, Jeffrey. 2012. Achieving Rapid Response Times in Large Online Services. Berkeley AMPLab Cloud Seminar.
Setting this rejection threshold requires comparing how long the arriving request can afford to wait against how long the work already ahead of it will take to drain. Consider a warmed, isolated worker that serves requests sequentially in first-in-first-out (FIFO) order, without batching or preemption, and assume known upper bounds on each request’s service time and on every remaining stage outside the worker, including the response path. An arriving request has already spent some of its end-to-end latency allowance on network ingress and preprocessing, and it must still reserve enough time for its own execution on the worker and for the remaining outside-worker stages after the worker finishes. Subtracting the time already spent, the remaining outside-worker bound, and the arriving request’s own service bound from the end-to-end deadline leaves the request’s waiting allowance, the maximum time it can sit in the queue and still finish on time. If those non-queue stages already exceed the deadline, the waiting allowance is negative and the request cannot meet its target even on an idle worker. Otherwise, the request must wait for the worker’s outstanding-work bound, which is the remaining service bound of the request currently executing plus the service bounds of all requests already waiting in the queue. Admission passes the deadline screen only when that outstanding-work bound fits within the waiting allowance. A simple limit on queue length approximates this comparison only when service costs are nearly uniform across requests. When they are, a practical starting point bounds the ingress queue at two or three requests per worker, the backlog a worker clears within two or three further service times, and the deadline screen and measured tails then tighten or relax that bound.
When the queued backlog exceeds the full model’s waiting allowance, the server can still check whether a smaller, faster fallback model that is already resident and warmed would finish in time. Switching the arriving request to a faster model does not shorten the backlog already queued ahead of it, because those earlier requests still have to finish first. Instead, it shrinks the service time that the arriving request must reserve for its own execution, which transfers that saved millisecond budget into a larger waiting allowance. If the existing backlog fits inside that expanded waiting allowance and the fallback model’s prediction quality meets the application’s minimum requirement, the server can admit the request on the fallback path. If neither acceptable model fits, rejection avoids spending accelerator time on a result that would arrive too late. Rejection reduces availability, while fallback can reduce prediction fidelity. Both outcomes must be counted alongside latency so that shedding difficult requests does not make the service appear successful merely by shrinking its measurement population.
The deadline screen is a deterministic bound only under the stated service, isolation, and scheduling assumptions. Mean service time or a per-stage p99 cannot replace those upper bounds. Variable input lengths, batch formation, and shared memory-bus contention require empirical calibration against the joint request-latency distribution. Completed-request tails must be reported together with rejection rates and fallback quality over offered traffic. Adaptive admission control can tighten the admissible backlog as measured tail latency approaches the SLO, but neither a fixed queue count nor the simplified screen certifies a production p99 target.



Once traffic outgrows a single node’s safe utilization knee, no single-machine tuning can prevent queue build-up. Higher aggregate volume requires horizontal replication, placing identical model replicas behind a load balancer so that each holds a complete model copy and serves disjoint queries without inter-node synchronization. (Model parallelism, which shards one large model across accelerators linked by a fabric such as NVLink, solves a different problem: fitting a model that exceeds one device’s memory or latency budget.) The \(\KendallMarkovianCode/\KendallMarkovianCode/\QueueServerCount\) queuing model extends the single-server analysis to \(\QueueServerCount\) parallel workers. Pooling requests in one shared queue absorbs arrival bursts better than isolated single-server queues, provided dispatch is balanced (least-loaded routing, for example) and each replica keeps its own headroom.


Dean and Barroso’s analysis reveals why tail latency becomes critical as systems scale beyond single machines (Dean and Barroso 2013). When requests fan out to \(\FanoutBackendCount\) parallel backends (querying an ensemble of models, searching sharded embedding indices, or parallelizing pipeline stages), the overall user request completes only when the slowest sub-task finishes. If sub-task completion events are independent and each has a 99 percent probability of finishing within latency threshold \(\LatencySlo\), the probability that all \(\FanoutBackendCount\) backends finish within \(\LatencySlo\) is \((0.99)^\FanoutBackendCount\). For a fan-out of \(\FanoutBackendCount= 10\), only \(0.99^{10} \approx 90.4\%\) of requests meet the target; at \(\FanoutBackendCount= 100\), that probability drops to \(0.99^{100} \approx 36.6\%\), meaning nearly two-thirds of user requests experience a tail delay. This “tail at scale” effect makes controlling single-node tail variance essential for overall system performance.

Dean, Jeffrey, and Luiz André Barroso. 2013. “The Tail at Scale.” Communications of the ACM 56 (2): 74–80. https://doi.org/10.1145/2408776.2408794.
12 Hedging: The term is borrowed from finance, where an offsetting position reduces risk; here, the redundant request insures against a slow server. The insurance is not free. For ML systems, the losing hedged request may still occupy accelerator time if inference has already launched, because ordinary GPU kernels are not cheaply canceled mid-execution. Thus, a hedging policy must budget duplicate work as well as the latency benefit.Hedging and tied requests limit the damage from a straggler replica. Under hedging, a request that has not completed within the expected time is duplicated to another server, and the client keeps whichever response arrives first.12 With a stable latency distribution, a threshold at the historical 95th percentile duplicates about 5 percent of requests; correlated slowdowns raise that fraction and can make hedging amplify overload instead of reducing the tail. Tied requests instead enter several server queues at once and cancel the other copies when one server begins processing, which avoids waiting to detect a slow response. Both techniques create duplicate work. Cancellation before dispatch prevents a losing copy from consuming accelerator time, whereas cancellation after dispatch only discards its result, so either needs spare capacity and an explicit duplicate-work budget. Canary requests apply the same idea to fan-out, sending the request first to one or two servers and committing to the full fan-out only if they answer within the expected time.
Replicas or streams on one machine can also race requests, but sharing an accelerator or memory bus can correlate their slowdowns and exhaust the same headroom. The local admission decision remains the foundation; fleet coordination is an extension of it. Retries across a fleet obey the same duplicate-work constraint, because load balancers that retry rejected requests at other overloaded replicas amplify the overload. Replicas should therefore share load information and shed the same fraction of requests rather than each rejecting independently. Production frameworks may use shortest-job-first or deadline-aware scheduling rather than FIFO, changing which queued work lies ahead of an arrival and requiring a corresponding admission analysis (Harchol-Balter 2013).

Checkpoint 13.2: Queuing and SLO headroom
Latency SLOs are not enforced by fast inference alone; they are enforced by headroom.

Little’s Law: at a fixed stable throughput, can you use \(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \RequestTimeInSystem\) to explain why a higher average in-system population implies a higher mean response time, even if per-request compute time is unchanged?
Utilization cliff: can you explain why latency grows nonlinearly as utilization \(\ServingUtilization\) approaches one, and why production systems target a conservative \(\ServingUtilization\) rather than “100 percent busy”?
Queue behavior: use the mean and p99 curves in figure 5 to explain nonlinear latency growth near saturation. Why is the marked 70 percent knee an illustrative planning choice rather than a model-derived breakpoint?
Capacity planning: can you explain why a throughput number is only “real” if requests still meet the percentile latency SLO under load?
Admission decision: for the isolated FIFO worker, how does increasing the arriving request’s service bound change its waiting allowance? If a faster fallback fits behind the outstanding work, what quality and availability conditions distinguish admitting it from rejecting the request? Why would substituting measured mean times invalidate the deterministic bound?
Headroom estimate: a stable service handles 2,000 requests per second and measures a 10 ms mean response time. Use \(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \RequestTimeInSystem\) to estimate its average in-flight population. Why does this result alone not establish compliance with a 50 ms p99 SLO?



Headroom keeps the queue stable by leaving capacity idle, and adding replicas creates headroom by adding accelerators. The other way to keep utilization below the knee is to raise each replica’s service rate, and for an accelerator that executes one request at a time the largest lever is to execute several at once.

Consider the reference ResNet-50 classifier on an H100 GPU operating at batch size one. Each forward pass reads the model’s weights from high-bandwidth memory to serve a single image and issues a long sequence of small kernels whose fixed launch cost is paid once per image, leaving neither weight traffic nor launch overhead shared across inputs. Processing requests continuously at 280 images/s, each pass spends 99 percent of its time on those fixed costs. Processing 32 images at once delivers 7,000 images/s, a 25× throughput improvement on identical hardware, because one kernel sequence and one weight read now serve thirty-two inputs. The fixed-cost share must not be confused with serving utilization. A single worker processing batch 1 at 280 requests/s is 100 percent busy in queueing terms (\(\ServingUtilization = 1.0\)) with zero spare serving capacity, yet nearly all of its time goes to work that a larger batch would share. Batching13 is the primary lever for improving serving economics, but its operational constraints differ sharply between training and serving (Crankshaw et al. 2017). Training batches maximize throughput by grouping hundreds or thousands of samples together with no constraint on individual sample latency. Serving batches must balance accelerator saturation against individual request deadlines, ensuring that no early-arriving input waits excessively for a batch to form. An inference server resolves this tension through dynamic batching, adjusting batch size at runtime to match incoming request arrivals.
13 Batch: From Old French bache (a quantity baked at one time), entering computing in the 1950s for jobs processed together without human interaction. The ML serving usage preserves the original trade-off: grouping requests amortizes fixed costs (kernel launch, weight movement) across multiple inputs, but an online request may wait for a batch to form.

Definition 13.3: Dynamic batching
Dynamic batching is the ML serving optimization that trades latency for throughput under stochastic arrival patterns.

Significance: By buffering requests into a batching window, the scheduler amortizes fixed overheads \((\Latency)\) across multiple inputs, pushing the system away from the bandwidth-bound regime \((\Bandwidth)\) toward the compute-bound regime \((\PeakRate)\).
Distinction: Unlike fixed-size serving batches, dynamic batching adjusts the realized batch size at inference time according to arriving traffic, a timeout, and a maximum-batch limit.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that batching “always helps.” In reality, there is a latency-throughput Pareto frontier: if the batching window is too large, the increased queuing delay may violate the system’s SLO before the throughput gains are realized.





A single request often leaves an accelerator’s compute units idle because its operations expose too little parallel work to hide kernel launch overhead or reuse weights streamed from memory (though large spatial inputs or smaller edge accelerators may already saturate at batch one). For workloads that underuse the device at small batches, increasing the batch size improves hardware efficiency (Shen et al. 2019) by amortizing fixed costs across multiple requests and running inputs in parallel across the batch dimension.

Shen, Haichen, Lequn Chen, Yuchen Jin, Liangyu Zhao, Bingyu Kong, Matthai Philipose, Arvind Krishnamurthy, and Ravi Sundaram. 2019. “Nexus: A GPU Cluster Engine for Accelerating DNN-Based Video Analysis.” Proceedings of the 27th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 322–37. https://doi.org/10.1145/3341301.3359658.
Two fixed costs dominate at small batch sizes. Kernel launch overhead is the time for the CPU to prepare and submit work to the GPU. The number of launches depends on graph lowering and fusion rather than the layer count. For each launch, the CPU must assemble kernel parameters, copy them to GPU-accessible memory, and signal the GPU to begin execution. The cost per kernel does not depend on batch size. The reference ResNet-50 profile issues 174 kernels at 15 μs of host time each, 2.6 ms per forward pass. At batch size 1, this overhead far exceeds the actual compute time; at batch size 32, the same overhead is amortized across thirty-two images. Weight loading reads model parameters from GPU memory (VRAM) to the compute units. In a weight-streaming approximation, batch size 1 reads the weights for one image; batch size 32 reuses that weight stream across thirty-two images, increasing weight-only operational intensity by 32\(\times\). Activation traffic, caches, and workspace determine the executed operation’s full intensity.


↩︎ Per-kernel launch overhead, and why fusion and graph execution attack it, are established in The dispatch overhead law.
Larger batches improve hardware efficiency but inflate per-request latency. The engineering objective is to identify the operating point that maximizes sustainable throughput while satisfying the request deadline. For the reference ResNet-50 profile quantified in table 8 below, serving batch size 8 with a 10 ms batching window requires a mean formation-plus-inference budget of approximately 8.8 ms. An arriving request waits on average half the window (5 ms, as derived in section 13.5.4.1) and requires 3.8 ms of inference. If the service must meet a 20 ms SLO, the remaining 11.2 ms provides headroom for worker backlog and auxiliary pipeline stages, while delivering 7.5× higher service throughput than batch 1 on identical hardware. On this accelerator the batching window, not the computation, is most of the batch-8 budget. Batch size cannot grow indefinitely, and figure 6 shows why by modeling this relationship across batch sizes on a logarithmic axis. To isolate the planning knee under worst-case scheduling conditions, the figure assumes a strictly serialized single worker that waits out the full batching window before executing each batch, without pipelined overlap (\(\text{Latency} = \BatchingWindow + \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\)). Under this unpipelined assumption, batch-1 throughput is 74 requests/s rather than the 280 images/s sustained when inference runs back to back. Throughput rises almost in proportion to batch size while the fixed overhead dominates each batch, because each added image costs only 33 μs of device time. The planning knee sits where the batch’s total per-image work equals the fixed part of its latency, the window plus the fixed cost, near batch 410. There latency is approximately twice that of batch one and throughput is half its ceiling. Beyond it, each doubling of the batch roughly doubles latency while throughput gains less and less. In this model throughput never declines; it saturates, so latency, not throughput, sets the largest useful batch.
