Key Takeaways: Inverting every training priority

Serving is latency economics: Training rewards throughput over long runs, but serving spends a fixed per-request budget across serialization, preprocessing, queuing, inference, postprocessing, and the network. Optimizing only model latency misses the stages users actually wait on.
Utilization turns into waiting: In the chapter’s M/M/1 approximation, average time in system rises from 5\(\times\) service time at 80 percent utilization to 10\(\times\) at 90 percent. Headroom keeps modest traffic surges from becoming SLO failures.
Fast models expose the rest of the pipeline: Once inference is fast, image decode, tokenization, and other preprocessing can dominate total latency. The binding optimization becomes the request path, not the neural network kernel.
Batching follows traffic, not habit: Poisson-modeled web arrivals can use dynamic batching, synchronized sensors need aligned batches, and single-stream mobile workloads may have little batching opportunity. A useful window converts available latency slack into throughput without violating the SLO.
Skew breaks accuracy without errors: Resize methods, color-channel order, normalization constants, or feature definitions that differ between training and serving can change the model’s effective input distribution. Shared transformations, parity tests, and production-slice monitoring reduce this risk.
Runtime choices become infrastructure cost: Precision, graph compilation, kernel fusion, and serving runtime translate directly into replica count and cost per inference. Quantization and specialized runtimes can materially reduce required serving capacity when they preserve accuracy and fit the target hardware.
LLM serving is memory management: Decode often reads weights from VRAM for every generated token, so token latency is bandwidth-bound unless batching changes the constraint. KV-cache layout, PagedAttention, continuous batching, precision, and runtime choice determine both concurrency and cost per token.



Training is judged by useful work completed; an online service is judged by whether requests meet their latency objective. Each stage draws on the same latency envelope: serialization, preprocessing, the queue, the model, and the response. Data determines input size and arrival shape, the algorithm determines compute and state, and the machine determines service rate and movement costs. Queueing couples all three nonlinearly, so a system within budget at moderate traffic can breach it after a small surge. Serving engineering therefore allocates the budget across the request path, preserves headroom for variability and failure, and verifies that the required fraction of requests finishes before the deadline, which is the latency budget principle (\(\ref{pri-latency-budget}\)) in operational form.

What’s Next: From fast to still correctThis chapter evaluates the request path under a specified workload: latency within budget, headroom preserved, and useful throughput converted into cost. Those performance checks do not establish whether the answers are still right. Training-serving skew showed that a service can stay fast and error-free while its predictions change, and drift produces the same silence when the world moves rather than the pipeline. ML Operations widens the unit of concern from request-path performance to the model’s operating lifetime. Monitoring tracks prediction quality alongside system health, feature stores and model registries keep serving aligned with training, and staged rollout with rollback lets a replacement model reach users without turning a bad release into an outage.

title: 13 Model Serving
text:
Self-Check: Answer

When transitioning a deep learning model from training to an online serving environment, how does the system constraint in the D·A·M (Data-Algorithm-Machine) taxonomy fundamentally shift regarding machine utilization and algorithm state?

Machine utilization must be maximized at 100% to amortize capital costs, while the algorithm continues parameter backpropagation during request serving.
Machine capacity must maintain operational headroom below saturation to prevent tail-latency queueing collapse, while the algorithm’s weights remain fixed for a deployed version.
Machine allocation switches from accelerators to general-purpose CPUs exclusively, while the algorithm dynamically modifies its architecture per incoming user payload.
Machine throughput replaces latency as the primary operational constraint, while data volume shifts from live request streams to historical offline batches.

Answer: The correct answer is B. In online serving, the machine-side priority shifts from maximizing average utilization to preserving headroom, because queueing delay grows nonlinearly as utilization approaches saturation and can break tail-latency SLOs. At the same time, a deployed serving path runs forward-only inference on fixed model weights rather than updating them with backpropagation. The 100 percent utilization view fits training better than latency-sensitive serving, and serving does not imply abandoning accelerators or making throughput the primary constraint.
Learning Objective: Analyze the fundamental architectural and operational shifts in the D·A·M taxonomy when transitioning machine learning models from offline training to online serving.
True or False: In online model serving, the latency term (\(L_{\text{lat}}\)) in the iron law of ML systems must encompass external factors such as network round-trip time, request serialization, and system orchestration, rather than solely the accelerator kernel execution time.
Answer: True. In an operational online serving system, user-perceived response time includes client-server network transport, ingress routing, payload serialization/deserialization, queue waiting time, and CPU preprocessing/postprocessing in addition to accelerator forward-pass execution. Consequently, optimizing only the raw accelerator kernel latency often yields diminishing returns if orchestration and transport overheads dominate the latency envelope.
Learning Objective: Evaluate how end-to-end serving latency budgets extend beyond isolated accelerator kernel execution times.
Explain why achieving high average throughput during offline benchmarking does not guarantee that an online serving system will satisfy its tail-latency Service-Level Objective (SLO) during production traffic spikes.
Answer: A high offline throughput number shows what the model and runtime can sustain under the benchmarked conditions, but it does not by itself prove that live requests will meet a tail-latency SLO. In production, arrival timing, queueing, preprocessing, and network overhead all vary over time; a system that looks strong in a saturated or controlled benchmark can still miss p99 targets when bursts consume its headroom. The practical implication is that serving capacity must be validated under representative traffic and percentile-latency measurements, not inferred from throughput alone.
Learning Objective: Explain why steady-state throughput benchmarks fail to predict tail-latency degradation under stochastic online arrival workloads.
An e-commerce platform evaluates precomputing product recommendations offline (static inference) versus computing them on demand when a user visits the homepage (dynamic inference). Which trade-off correctly characterizes static inference compared to dynamic inference?

Static inference eliminates database storage costs but increases real-time p99 latency by executing large batched matrix multiplications during user page loads.
Static inference guarantees real-time contextual adaptation to intra-session user clicks but requires dedicated high-end GPUs on the critical request path.
Static inference trades storage capacity and potential prediction staleness for retrieval latency that avoids per-request model execution, whereas dynamic inference provides fresh predictions from live context at the expense of computational latency and variable serving capacity.
Static inference requires running unbatched single-sample inferences across microcontrollers, whereas dynamic inference processes large offline shards across cloud clusters.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Catastrophic forgetting in the weights caused by static batching; the solution is retraining the model with dynamic dropout.

Answer: The correct answer is A. The matched-input rerun shows the weights are not the root cause by themselves; the problem is that training and serving are producing different tensors from the same image. That is training-serving skew caused by inconsistent preprocessing. The fix is to make preprocessing shared or parity-verified across environments, whether through a common implementation or an exported graph when the required operations are supported. Numerical differences can matter in some pipelines, but the evidence here points specifically to preprocessing mismatch rather than thermal behavior or weight changes.
Learning Objective: Analyze the root causes of training-serving skew and design unified preprocessing pipelines to maintain inference accuracy.
Why does simply copying model weights into GPU HBM upon container startup fail to prevent latency spikes on the very first incoming user requests, and how does executing a ‘warmup pass’ resolve this issue?
Answer: Having weights resident in GPU memory is not enough because first requests may still trigger lazy allocator growth, kernel compilation or selection, graph capture, and other runtime setup on the execution path. A warmup pass sends representative dummy inputs through the model before the server is marked ready, so those deferred costs are paid during initialization instead of by live users. The practical effect is reduced first-request latency spikes, though only for the shapes and paths the warmup actually exercises.
Learning Objective: Explain the systems mechanisms behind cold-start latency spikes and justify the use of synthetic warmup passes.
**Sequence the stages of an illustrative serial cold-start initialization workflow when autoscaling an inference server pod from an idle state to serving live production traffic:


Initialize device context or runtime state needed before host-to-device copies, then transfer model weights from host staging memory to GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) over PCIe
Fetch model checkpoint artifacts and configuration from remote object storage (e.g., S3) to local NVMe SSD cache
Initialize remaining execution-engine state, allocate memory pools, and run synthetic dummy warmup passes
Container initialization, environment bootstrap, and runtime dependency loading
Register pod as healthy with load balancer gateway to begin receiving live traffic
Memory-map (mmap) or deserialize model weights from local SSD into host memory, with explicit pinned staging buffers if the transfer path uses them**

Answer: The correct order is: (4) Container initialization, environment bootstrap, and runtime dependency loading, (2) Fetch model checkpoint artifacts and configuration from remote object storage to local NVMe SSD cache, (6) Memory-map or deserialize model weights from local SSD into host memory, with explicit pinned staging buffers if used, (1) Initialize device context or runtime state needed before host-to-device copies, then transfer model weights to GPU HBM over PCIe, (3) Initialize remaining execution-engine state, allocate memory pools, and run synthetic dummy warmup passes, (5) Register pod as healthy with the load balancer gateway. This is an illustrative serial workflow because later stages depend on earlier artifacts and memory state: the model must exist locally before it can be mapped, host-visible weights must exist before transfer, and warmup must happen before the pod is declared ready. Other implementations may overlap parts of the pipeline, but admitting traffic before warmup would push initialization cost onto live requests.
Learning Objective: Design the end-to-end cold-start and initialization lifecycle for autoscaling inference infrastructure.

True or False: In multi-model serving on a shared GPU, Volta-era NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) provides hard physical hardware partitioning of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) channels and compute cores, completely preventing memory out-of-memory (OOM) faults caused by co-located tenant models.
Answer: False. Volta-era MPS gives clients separate GPU address spaces and contexts, but they still share the same underlying compute and memory hardware. That is not MIG-style physical partitioning, and a fatal GPU fault can still affect other clients on the affected GPU even though one tenant’s OOM does not guarantee every colocated client will crash.
Learning Objective: Compare GPU multi-tenant isolation mechanisms (MPS vs. MIG) regarding memory safety and compute partitioning.
A multi-model serving platform hosts 50 distinct fine-tuned vision models on a single GPU node with 24 GB of VRAM. Each model requires 2 GB of memory, exceeding total VRAM capacity. Traffic to individual models is sporadic. What loading and memory management architecture enables serving all 50 models while minimizing request latency?

Redeploy the cluster on 50 dedicated GPU nodes running continuous batching 24/7.
Quantize all models to 1-bit weights to fit all 50 models into GPU L2 cache simultaneously.
Maintain a tiered memory cache (storing active models in GPU VRAM and inactive models in host pinned DRAM), using asynchronous PCIe DMA transfers to swap weights into VRAM on demand with an LRU eviction policy.
Compress all models into a single shared zip archive on remote S3 and download the entire archive over HTTP on each incoming request.

Answer: The correct answer is C. When model demand is sparse and total VRAM is too small, a tiered design keeps active models resident on the GPU while staging less active ones in host memory for faster reload than remote storage. On-demand swaps still pay transfer time bounded below by bytes moved over available bandwidth, plus runtime overheads, so this design reduces but does not eliminate latency. The approach also assumes host cache capacity and enough GPU workspace for the active model. Provisioning 50 dedicated GPUs wastes capacity for sporadic traffic, and re-downloading from object storage per request would be far slower.
Learning Objective: Design a tiered memory caching and dynamic model swapping architecture for multi-model serving under GPU memory constraints.
Why can loading model weights from modern safetensors format provide faster startup times than some legacy PyTorch checkpoint paths?

safetensors files compress weights using gzip, reducing disk storage by \(10\times\).
safetensors files store raw tensor buffers in a simple deterministic layout that supports memory mapping (mmap) without Python object deserialization or arbitrary code execution.
safetensors files compile PyTorch code directly into binary x86 machine instructions on disk.
safetensors files automatically quantize FP32 weights into 4-bit integers during read operations.

Answer: The correct answer is B. safetensors stores tensor data in a simple tensor-oriented format, so loaders can avoid the heavy Python object reconstruction associated with general pickle-based checkpoints and can use memory mapping efficiently. That can reduce cold-start overhead, though the exact gain still depends on storage speed, paging behavior, and the rest of runtime initialization. Gzip compression, compiling Python into machine code, and automatic on-read quantization are not what explains the startup benefit here.
Learning Objective: Compare tensor-oriented checkpoint formats with pickle-based checkpoints in terms of loading overhead, memory mapping, and security.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

In Large Language Model (LLM) serving, how do the computational and hardware characteristics of the Prefill phase fundamentally differ from the Decode phase?

Prefill processes tokens autoregressively one by one and is memory-bandwidth bound, whereas Decode processes all output tokens simultaneously and is compute-bound.
Prefill processes all prompt tokens concurrently in parallel matrix multiplications and is often more compute-intensive, whereas Decode generates one token per step autoregressively and at low batch sizes is often memory-bandwidth bound due to repeated weight and KV-state movement.
Prefill operates exclusively on host CPU DRAM, whereas Decode runs on GPU Tensor Cores.
Prefill latency scales quadratically with batch size, whereas Decode latency is strictly independent of sequence length and KV-cache size.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Prefill handles the whole prompt together, so it uses larger parallel matrix operations and typically has higher arithmetic intensity than decode. Decode then generates output step by step, and at low batch sizes often becomes limited by repeatedly moving model weights and KV state through memory rather than by raw compute. The autoregressive behavior belongs to decode, not prefill. Both phases usually run on the accelerator, and TTFT includes more than just the prefill kernel time in a full serving path.
Learning Objective: Compare the typical computational bottlenecks and hardware behavior of LLM prefill versus decode in serving.
**Order the step-by-step execution cycle of Speculative Decoding for accelerating LLM inference:


Target model runs a single parallel forward pass over the draft candidate tokens to compute verification logits
Draft model (a lightweight autoregressive model) generates \(K\) candidate tokens sequentially
Engine appends the accepted tokens to the KV cache and advances the generation context
Verification logic compares the draft tokens with the target model’s verification results and accepts a prefix of them**

Answer: The correct order is: (2) Draft model (a lightweight autoregressive model) generates \(K\) candidate tokens sequentially, (1) Target model runs a single parallel forward pass over the draft candidate tokens to compute verification logits, (4) Verification logic compares the draft tokens with the target model’s verification results and accepts a prefix of them, (3) Engine appends the accepted tokens to the KV cache and advances the generation context. The sequence matters because the target model cannot verify tokens before the draft proposes them, and the engine should not advance the live context until verification decides which proposed tokens are accepted. Swapping verification and context advancement would commit unverified state and break correctness.
Learning Objective: Sequence the high-level workflow of speculative decoding from draft generation through verification and context update.

True or False: Speculative decoding speeds up serving regardless of draft-model quality, because the target model always verifies multiple tokens in parallel.
Answer: False. Speculative decoding helps only when the draft model is cheap enough and its proposed tokens are accepted often enough to offset the extra draft-and-verify work. If acceptance is low, the system can spend more time running two models than it saves through parallel verification.
Learning Objective: Evaluate how draft-model cost and acceptance rate determine whether speculative decoding improves LLM serving performance.
In a multi-turn conversational AI system with extensive system prompts (e.g., 2,000 tokens of instructions and few-shot examples shared across thousands of user sessions), what serving optimization eliminates redundant prefill compute across requests?

Linear Attention Approximation, which drops system prompt tokens entirely from the attention window.
Static Graph Compilation, which hardcodes user inputs directly into the weight tensors.
Prefix Caching (e.g., RadixAttention), which stores the KV-cache states of common prompt prefixes in memory and reuses them across queries matching the prefix.
Speculative Quantization, which quantizes prompt tokens into 1-bit binary representations during the decode phase.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Prefix caching stores KV states for a compatible shared prefix so later requests with that same prefix can reuse the prefill result instead of recomputing it. This can cut TTFT substantially for the cached portion, though any uncached suffix still has to be processed normally. Dropping prompt tokens changes model behavior, static graph compilation does not reuse dynamic KV state, and 1-bit prompt quantization is not the mechanism described here.
Learning Objective: Apply prefix caching to reduce repeated prefill work for shared prompt prefixes in conversational serving.
Contrast traditional request-level dynamic batching with iteration-level continuous batching (as introduced in Orca and vLLM) for Large Language Model (LLM) serving. Why is request-level batching severely inefficient for autoregressive generation?
Answer: In request-level batching, batch membership stays fixed while requests decode, so short generations that finish early cannot immediately free their slots for unrelated waiting work. In continuous batching, the scheduler can admit or remove sequences at iteration boundaries, which uses capacity more efficiently when output lengths vary. For example, if one reply ends after 20 tokens while another runs for 500, a fixed request-level batch leaves part of the batch underused until the long sequence advances far enough. The practical consequence is lower throughput and longer waits for queued requests unless the runtime can reschedule state across iterations.
Learning Objective: Compare request-level dynamic batching with iteration-level continuous batching for autoregressive LLM serving and explain why variable output lengths make fixed batch membership inefficient.
True or False: PagedAttention resolves the primary memory waste in LLM KV-caching by allocating key and value states in non-contiguous, fixed-size physical memory blocks managed via a virtual page table, eliminating both internal fragmentation from over-allocation and external memory fragmentation.
Answer: False. PagedAttention removes the need for one large contiguous KV-cache allocation and greatly reduces external fragmentation, but it does not eliminate internal waste entirely: each sequence can still leave one partially filled final block. Its benefit is reducing fragmentation enough to raise usable concurrency, not making memory waste literally zero.
Learning Objective: Explain how PagedAttention reduces KV-cache fragmentation and identify the remaining source of memory waste.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A team evaluates deploying a small classification model with an average arrival rate of 5 QPS and a 200 ms latency SLA. Measurements at 5 QPS show that both a single CPU server instance and a single GPU server instance meet the matched quality target and the p99 latency target of 200 ms. The CPU instance costs $0.20/hour and sustains up to 20 QPS under the target latency; the GPU instance costs $2.00/hour and sustains up to 200 QPS under the target latency. Which deployment option is more cost-effective for this specific workload, and why?

The GPU server is more cost-effective because its 10x greater SLO-qualified peak throughput more than offsets its 10x higher hourly cost, making it the lower-cost choice even at 5 QPS.
The GPU server is more cost-effective because GPUs always have lower total cost of ownership regardless of arrival traffic.
The CPU server is more cost-effective because at 5 QPS, it already meets the SLA with adequate headroom at $0.20/hour, whereas the GPU server would use only 2.5% of its SLO-qualified capacity and cost about \(10\times\) more per served query at that traffic level.
Neither option is viable because 5 QPS requires at least a 10-node cluster for high availability.

Answer: The correct answer is C. The measured requirement is simply 5 QPS at under 200 ms, and the CPU instance already satisfies that at 25% of its proven SLO-qualified capacity. At this traffic level, cost per served query is about $0.20 divided by \(5 \times 3600\), which is approximately $0.0000111 for the CPU, versus $2.00 divided by \(5 \times 3600\), which is approximately $0.000111 for the GPU, so the GPU is about \(10\times\) more expensive here. Comparing only peak throughput misses the idle-capacity waste of the GPU at such low load.
Learning Objective: Evaluate CPU-versus-GPU serving cost effectiveness using SLO-qualified capacity, utilization, and cost per served query.
In capacity planning for a mission-critical model serving cluster with a peak expected traffic of \(\lambda_{\text{peak}} = 1\text{,}000\text{ QPS}\) and an individual replica capacity of \(R = 100\text{ QPS}\) at its target latency SLO, why would a capacity engineer provision 16 to 20 replicas (\(1.6\times\text{--}2.0\times\) headroom multiplier) rather than exactly 10 replicas?
Answer: Ten replicas cover only the forecast peak under the measured per-replica SLO-qualified capacity, leaving essentially no reserve for failures, burstiness, uneven load distribution, or slow scale-out. Provisioning 16 to 20 replicas is an illustrative way to preserve headroom so the system can keep meeting its latency target when real conditions deviate from the forecast. For example, if one zone loses capacity or traffic spikes above the expected peak, the extra replicas absorb the shock instead of pushing every remaining node immediately to its limit. The practical consequence is that capacity planning is a resilience decision, not just a division problem.
Learning Objective: Justify why mission-critical serving clusters provision reserve capacity beyond forecast peak demand.
True or False: For an 8-billion-parameter LLM with 32 layers, 8 KV heads, and head dimension 128, deployed in FP16 precision with a 16 GB weight footprint on an 80 GB GPU, serving long-context requests with batch size \(B = 8\) and context length \(S = 32\text{,}768\) tokens causes the KV cache to exceed the static weight footprint of the model itself.
Answer: True. For this specific architecture, each token per sequence needs \(2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072\) bytes, which is \(128\ \text{KiB}\), to store both Keys and Values in FP16. At \(B = 8\) and \(S = 32{,}768\), the KV-cache payload is \(131{,}072 \times 32{,}768 \times 8 = 34{,}359{,}738{,}368\) bytes, which is \(32\ \text{GiB}\) or about \(34.36\ \text{GB}\) in decimal units. That exceeds the 16 GB weight footprint, showing how long contexts can make dynamic KV memory dominate static weights.
Learning Objective: Compare dynamic KV-cache growth against static model weights for a specified LLM architecture, batch size, and context length.
An engineer serves an 8-billion parameter LLM on a GPU with 2 TB/s of High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) bandwidth. Assume the model weights are 16 GB in FP16, the decode step effectively streams those 16 GB of weights from HBM each token at batch size \(B = 1\), and ignore KV-cache traffic and compute time. What is the theoretical hardware-bandwidth lower bound on Time Per Output Token (TPOT)?

\(8.0\text{ ms}\) (\(\text{TPOT} = 16\text{ GB} / 2\text{,}000\text{ GB/s}\))
\(0.8\text{ ms}\) (\(\text{TPOT} = 1.6\text{ GB} / 2\text{,}000\text{ GB/s}\))
\(80.0\text{ ms}\) (\(\text{TPOT} = 160\text{ GB} / 2\text{,}000\text{ GB/s}\))
\(0.08\text{ ms}\) (\(\text{TPOT} = 16\text{ MB} / 2\text{,}000\text{ GB/s}\))

Answer: The correct answer is A. Under the stated assumption that one decode step streams 16 GB of weights from HBM and the device provides an idealized 2 TB/s = 2,000 GB/s of bandwidth, the transfer-time floor is \(16\text{ GB} / 2{,}000\text{ GB/s} = 0.008\text{ s} = 8.0\text{ ms}\). That makes 8 ms a lower bound from weight movement alone in this simplified case. The smaller and larger numbers come from unit or arithmetic mistakes, and the setup intentionally ignores KV-cache traffic, compute, and other overheads.
Learning Objective: Calculate a bandwidth-only lower bound on LLM decode TPOT from model size and HBM bandwidth.
When LLM decode at small batch sizes is dominated by moving model weights rather than by arithmetic throughput, why can INT4 weight-only quantization (e.g., AWQ or GPTQ) reduce Time Per Output Token (TPOT), and what limits the gain even if INT4 compute kernels provide no higher FLOP/s than FP16 Tensor Cores?
Answer: At small batch sizes, decode is often dominated by moving model weights rather than by raw arithmetic throughput. Weight-only INT4 quantization cuts the raw weight payload by about \(4\times\) relative to FP16, so the memory system has fewer bytes to fetch each decode step even if the math units themselves are not any faster. For an 8B model, that can mean reading something closer to 4 GB of quantized weights instead of 16 GB of FP16 weights per step, excluding metadata and dequantization overhead. The practical consequence is lower TPOT when weight traffic is the bottleneck, although the realized gain is usually less than \(4\times\) once KV traffic, dequantization, launch overhead, and kernel details are included.
Learning Objective: Explain why weight-only quantization can speed up memory-bound LLM decode even without increasing raw compute throughput.
Calculate the total memory footprint (in bytes) required to store the KV cache for a batch of \(B = 16\) requests, each with an active context length of \(S = 2\text{,}048\) tokens, for a model with \(L = 32\) transformer layers, \(H_{\text{kv}} = 8\) key-value attention heads (Grouped-Query Attention), head dimension \(D_{\text{head}} = 128\), stored in FP16 precision (\(P = 2\text{ bytes}\)).
Answer: The KV-cache payload is \(\text{Memory} = 2 \times L \times H_{\text{kv}} \times D_{\text{head}} \times P \times S \times B\) bytes, where the factor of 2 accounts for both Keys and Values. Substituting gives \(2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 \times 2048 \times 16 = 4{,}294{,}967{,}296\) bytes. That is exactly \(4\ \text{GiB}\), or about \(4.295\ \text{GB}\) in decimal units. This is the KV-cache payload only; allocator overhead and runtime workspace would add more memory in a real serving system.
Learning Objective: Calculate KV-cache payload requirements for transformer serving from batch size, context length, and model architecture.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A team attempts to maximize hardware cost efficiency by targeting 95% steady-state utilization \(\rho\) across their production serving queue. Why is this strategy a dangerous engineering pitfall?

High utilization permanently erases model weights from GPU memory registers.
In stochastic serving systems, queue waiting times grow asymptotically toward infinity as utilization approaches 100%, causing minor traffic fluctuations to trigger massive tail-latency spikes and widespread SLO breaches.
Running above 90% utilization forces the operating system to switch from 64-bit to 32-bit execution mode.
Modern GPUs automatically shut down power when utilization exceeds 80% for more than 10 seconds.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Here \(\rho\) means arrival rate divided by service capacity in the serving queue, not a coarse GPU busy counter. In queueing models, waiting time grows sharply as \(\rho\) approaches 1, so a system run near 95% has very little headroom for burstiness or service-time variation. That makes p99 latency fragile even if average load looks efficient. The other answers invent hardware or OS behaviors unrelated to the chapter’s queueing argument.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why operating a serving queue near saturation creates tail-latency risk even when average utilization looks cost-efficient.
True or False: Evaluating an online serving system using mean (average) latency is sufficient for capacity planning, because if the average latency is well below the SLA target, user-facing requests are guaranteed to experience good performance.
Answer: False. Average latency conceals extreme tail outliers (p95, p99, p99.9) where requests experience severe queueing delays. In modern microservice architectures where a user query fans out to dozens of downstream models in parallel, the slowest component determines overall user latency, meaning a low average latency can co-exist with a large fraction of users experiencing SLA violations.
Learning Objective: Justify why tail-latency metrics (p99/p99.9) must be used over mean latency for evaluating online serving systems.
Why is the assumption that ‘cold-start latency only affects the very first request’ a critical fallacy in autoscaling serverless or Kubernetes-based serving environments with bursty traffic?
Answer: During a burst, new replicas may spend time loading weights, initializing runtimes, or warming caches before they can accept traffic, so cold start reduces usable capacity exactly when demand is rising. Requests usually are not sent to replicas that are still unready, but they still suffer indirectly by waiting longer on the already-live replicas or in upstream queues. For example, if traffic doubles before new GPU pods finish becoming ready, p99 latency can spike across many users even though no request is intentionally routed to an uninitialized instance. The practical consequence is that cold start is a fleet-level capacity problem, not just a first-request problem.
Learning Objective: Analyze how cold-start delays amplify tail latency during autoscaling events by withholding new capacity during bursts.
An engineering team increases the dynamic batch size on their vision model serving nodes from 8 to 64. Offline peak throughput doubles, and production traces show batch-formation wait time grew sharply after the change. User-facing p99 latency violations then increase by 40%. What fallacy explains this outcome?

Model weights become corrupted when executed with batch sizes greater than 16.
GPU Tensor Cores disable INT8 acceleration when batch size exceeds 32.
High batch sizes reduce arithmetic intensity on the GPU Roofline model.
The fallacy that larger serving batches always improve throughput without affecting latency; early-arriving requests can spend too much of the latency budget waiting in the batcher before execution.

Answer: The correct answer is D. The added trace detail matters: if batch-formation wait rose sharply, the doubled offline throughput did not come for free in the online path. Larger batches can improve hardware efficiency, but they also make early arrivals wait longer before execution, and that extra waiting can dominate p99 latency even when the per-batch compute is efficient. The corruption, universal Tensor Core cutoff, and reduced-arithmetic-intensity explanations do not match the serving mechanism described here.
Learning Objective: Evaluate how batch-formation delay can turn an offline throughput win into an online p99 latency regression.
Describe the pitfall of ‘Calibrating quantization ranges with unrepresentative data,’ and explain how it can lead to silent production failure despite passing offline validation checks.
Answer: PTQ calibration chooses quantization ranges from the activation statistics seen in the calibration set. If that data is cleaner or from a different domain than production traffic, the resulting scales may clip important live activations or represent them too coarsely, degrading prediction quality without causing crashes or latency alarms. The failure can stay hidden if offline validation used similarly unrepresentative data, because both calibration and evaluation would miss the same production patterns. The practical consequence is that quantized models need calibration and quality checks on data that matches the real serving distribution as closely as possible.
Learning Objective: Explain how unrepresentative calibration and evaluation data can hide quantization-induced production accuracy failures.

← Back to Questions

title: 12 Benchmarking
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter: Part 1 · Part 2












Architecture stack focus for this chapter.
How can ML systems be compared fairly when hardware, models, data, and deployment all interact?
Every optimization claim must eventually face deployment-representative conditions, and many do not survive the encounter. Each decision targets one dimension (latency, accuracy, throughput, or energy), but an ML system is the product of all these dimensions simultaneously: a pruned model may run faster on one accelerator yet slower on another, while a larger batch size improves accelerator utilization at the cost of violating a latency service-level agreement. Similarly, an edge device may advertise peak throughput that thermal throttling sharply reduces within minutes of sustained load, and a speedup measured on a warm, idle machine with synthetic inputs can vanish or reverse once real requests, cold caches, and competing jobs share the hardware. The challenge is not whether a local metric improves but whether the combined system improves under conditions that actually matter. Benchmarking makes such comparisons systematic rather than anecdotal. It requires defining what to measure, at what granularity (a single kernel, a full model, an end-to-end pipeline), and under which conditions (batch size, input distribution, thermal state, concurrent load). Without this structure, teams compare numbers that were never measured on the same terms, and decisions that looked sound in a spreadsheet collapse under production workloads. Choosing hardware, a model, or a deployment configuration on such numbers can commit an organization to millions of dollars of infrastructure that delivers a fraction of the capacity it was bought to provide. Benchmarking validates each optimization, bringing claims into contact with evidence and quantifying the gap between promise and delivery. In D·A·M terms, benchmarking holds co-design to account by revealing whether Data, Algorithm, and Machine were matched or merely assembled.

Learning Objectives

Explain the benchmark–production gap and benchmarking as D·A·M validation that tests whether optimization claims hold under representative conditions
Design a benchmark that turns an optimization claim into a test by fixing its task, data, model, metrics, harness, and run rules
Select micro, macro, or end-to-end granularity based on the engineering decision being tested, and compare a roofline prediction with a measurement
Compare training and inference benchmarks using standardized run rules, time to quality, throughput, and latency percentiles
Measure energy per inference and average power with matched measurement boundaries, windows, and duty cycles
Determine whether a measured difference exceeds noise using repeated runs, paired tests, and confidence intervals
Evaluate model and data quality with confidence calibration, robustness, representativeness, and slice-level metrics, and diagnose benchmark–production gaps caused by drift, thermal throttling, and dynamic load



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



A model quantized to INT8 may benchmark 2\(\times\) faster on a synthetic workload and show no improvement under real traffic with variable input sizes and concurrent requests. A pruned model may hold its accuracy on the test set and fail on the edge cases the benchmark never covered. Every engineering claim about speed, size, or energy is a number measured somewhere: on a warm accelerator or a cold one, at a batch of 256 or a batch of one, on curated test images or on whatever a camera returns at night. The benchmark–production gap is the difference between how a machine learning system performs under the conditions a measurement fixed and how it performs under the conditions it meets in deployment. Benchmarking is the engineering discipline that measures this gap before a deployment pays for it, and that narrows it by making the measured conditions match the deployed ones.
Hardware Acceleration ended on predictions. Its roofline placed ResNet-50’s layers against an accelerator’s compute and bandwidth ceilings, and at INT8 the doubled ridge point moved some of those layers off the compute roof. Before it, Model Compression produced an INT8 artifact a quarter of the FP32 size, and Data Selection reached target accuracy on fewer examples. Each is a favorable local number, computed for one stage in isolation, and the stages interact once they run together on a real machine under real load. Benchmarking measures which of those numbers survive. It comes before serving and operations because every later decision, from how many accelerators to provision to when to roll a model back, rests on measurements made the way this chapter prescribes.

Definition 12.1: Machine learning benchmarking
Machine learning benchmarking is the empirical measurement of ML workloads under specified conditions, used to test claims about components, models, or end-to-end systems against representative evidence rather than peak specifications alone.

Significance: The gap between peak and sustained performance can be large. An H100 delivers 989 TFLOP/s of dense FP16 arithmetic at peak, yet ResNet-50 training at about 5,000 images/s per accelerator, the rate NVIDIA’s 64-accelerator H100 system logged in MLPerf Training v3.1 (MLCommons 2023), sustains about 123 TFLOP/s of model arithmetic. That is a model FLOPs utilization (MFU, achieved model FLOP/s divided by the hardware’s peak FLOP/s) of about 12.4 percent. Memory-bound layers, the input pipeline, and launch and synchronization overhead account for the difference. Benchmarking quantifies the actual \(\EfficiencyHw\) gap for a workload; vendor spec sheets do not.
Distinction: ML benchmarking spans multiple scopes. Micro-benchmarks isolate operations such as matrix multiplication, model-level benchmarks evaluate complete training or inference workloads, and end-to-end benchmarks include surrounding work such as data loading, preprocessing, optimization, checkpoint I/O, or serving infrastructure. The scope must match the engineering claim.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that benchmark numbers are stable references. Both the workload (new model architectures) and the hardware (new GPU generations) evolve, so a result that leads a benchmark under one version often becomes the baseline under a later version. Year-over-year comparisons are therefore meaningful only when the benchmark version is held constant.




MLCommons. 2023. MLPerf Training V3.1 Results.
The iron law predicts how long a workload should take, and a benchmark measures how long it does; the difference between the two is the benchmark–production gap made quantitative. For bandwidth-bound workloads, the gap between peak and sustained performance follows from the memory wall. Compute-bound workloads can approach peak, yet ResNet-50’s training step shows how much of a nominally compute-bound workload still falls outside the arithmetic. Every later section that quotes a peak number is measured against this gap.


↩︎ The iron law, whose utilization term \(\EfficiencyHw\) benchmarks measure against peak, is established in Iron Law of ML Systems.

Systems Perspective 12.1: The fallacy of peak performanceA long-standing computer architecture quip calls peak performance “the performance the manufacturer guarantees you will not exceed.” For ML systems, the gap can be wide because of the memory wall. A bandwidth-bound model leaves much of the advertised FLOP/s unreachable no matter how fast the arithmetic units run. Standardized benchmarks like MLPerf require systems to run specified models and data, revealing sustained performance at a documented operating point rather than a universal rate for every workload.


ML benchmarking operates across three interdependent dimensions that map directly to the components of any deployed system. System benchmarking measures whether the hardware delivers promised performance under realistic workloads or whether memory bandwidth saturation and software dispatch overhead erode the gains. Model benchmarking measures whether optimization techniques preserve model quality across the full input distribution, not just on curated test sets. Data benchmarking measures whether the model generalizes to real-world data with all its noise, bias, and distributional shift. Each dimension can independently reveal problems invisible to the others, and a system that passes all three provides far stronger deployment confidence than one evaluated along any single axis. The three dimensions do not receive equal space. System benchmarking carries most of the chapter, because its measurement problems (how a benchmark is built, at what granularity it measures, which standardized suite it follows, and how it measures training, inference, and power) also shape how models and data are evaluated. Model and data evaluation follow once that machinery is in place, and the summary asks whether all three survive live traffic.

Systems Perspective 12.2: Benchmarks as moving targetsIn traditional systems (for example, SPEC CPU), the benchmark is a rigid specification. A sorting algorithm is correct if it sorts the list. Correctness is absolute and unchanging. In ML systems, the benchmark is a soft specification: correctness is defined by a finite set of examples (ImageNet), and the world moves. A model that scores highly on ImageNet can still underperform on user photos taken years after the benchmark was created.
In computer architecture, engineers design for the benchmark because the benchmark represents the workload. In ML engineering, designing solely for the benchmark is overfitting. Robustness comes from acknowledging that the benchmark is only a proxy for a shifting reality.


Three lighthouse workloads carry the chapter, each chosen because it sits in a home regime and arrives with claims from the preceding chapters. ResNet-50, the book’s compute-bound lighthouse, carries the measurement and training half. It is the MLPerf Training reference workload, with a published quality target (75.9 percent top-1 on ImageNet) and a published per-accelerator throughput, and its INT8 profile is the one Model Compression modeled and Hardware Acceleration placed on the roofline. MobileNetV2, compute-bound in its efficient regime, carries the deployment half. It runs on one edge board in a labeled composite scenario, a wildlife camera trap whose low-power host CPU and attached INT8 accelerator must classify each frame within its deadline on battery power. The measurements made on that board recur from the harness through the energy budget. Keyword spotting (KWS), the power-bound lighthouse, carries the power section, where the question is the energy a wake-word detector spends listening rather than how fast it answers. Each stage of that pipeline arrives with a favorable number from its own chapter, such as a smaller model file or a faster kernel. The benchmarking question is which of those local numbers still hold once the stages run together on the target device, and three principles guide how the chapter answers it.
First, benchmarks are proxies, not truth. Every benchmark measures specific conditions that may not match the target deployment. A system can achieve high sample throughput in Offline mode (bulk throughput with all inputs available) and much lower queries per second (QPS) in Server mode (latency-constrained requests arriving over time). The critical question is always what the benchmark does not measure.
Second, Goodhart’s Law governs benchmark rankings.1 “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” Teams that optimize for benchmark rankings often produce systems that excel in evaluation but fail in production. Benchmark-specific optimizations frequently degrade characteristics that matter for deployment: robustness, calibration, and efficiency.

In ML, the same failure mode recurs structurally: BLEU rewards n-gram overlap (Papineni et al. 2002), ImageNet rewards performance on a fixed visual distribution (Deng et al. 2009; Recht et al. 2019), and benchmark leaderboards can incentivize test-set-specific tuning.

Third, end-to-end beats component metrics. A component speedup is diluted by every stage of the request it does not touch, and the dilution follows Amdahl’s law; section 12.3 quantifies it on a vision pipeline. These principles reappear throughout the methodology and return as misconceptions in section 12.10.
Two terms recur from here on. A service-level objective (SLO) is the target a deployed service commits to meet for a measured quantity, such as answering 99 percent of requests within a stated time; section 12.6.2.1 defines it formally. The 99th-percentile latency (p99) is the response time that 99 percent of requests meet or beat, so it describes the slowest 1 percent of requests rather than the typical one.
The chapter builds the measurement before it applies it (table 2). Benchmark carpentry turns a claim into a test that fixes the task, data, model, metrics, harness, and run rules. Granularity decides how much of the system a test spans, from one kernel to the whole request path, and it is where the roofline’s prediction for ResNet-50 meets a measurement. Benchmark suites standardize those choices across organizations. The training and inference sections apply them to ResNet-50 and to MobileNetV2 on its edge board, and power measurement adds the joules, with keyword spotting as the case. Best practices supply the statistics that decide whether a measured difference is real, and model and data evaluation test the two dimensions that a hardware result cannot certify. The fallacies and the summary close by asking whether the evidence survives production traffic.

Knowing what to measure is only half of the problem. Measuring incorrectly, with the wrong workload, a biased baseline, or an uncontrolled variable, produces numbers that look precise and mislead the decision they inform. The history of computing benchmarks2 is full of technically sound metrics applied with flawed methodology, from compiler-gamed Whetstone scores to throughput claims that predict nothing about sustained workloads (section 12.4.1). The defense is construction. A benchmark must be built so that it measures what its claim says, and that construction is where the chapter begins.

Just as an elevation measurement is meaningless without a calibrated reference, an ML throughput number is meaningless without controlled workloads, thermal state, and precision settings.

A claim that ResNet-50 runs faster at INT8 than at FP32 can reverse depending on whether timing starts at a JPEG on storage or at a preprocessed tensor in accelerator memory, or whether the quantized weights drop accuracy below the target floor. Benchmark carpentry is the craft of building a benchmark that measures what its claim says. It fixes the task, data, model, metrics, harness, system specification, and run rules so that the number the benchmark produces answers the engineering question and no other. A synthetic matrix-multiplication loop, a ResNet-50 training run over ImageNet, and a full serving pipeline all need these specifications, and changing one component changes what the next can measure. The components follow the D·A·M taxonomy. The problem definition fixes the input representation (Data). The dataset and task objective bound the feasible models (Algorithm). The target hardware’s memory, energy envelope, and deadlines bound how the model may execute (Machine).
Evaluating an ML system requires coupling statistical task metrics with physical efficiency metrics. Quantization and pruning reduce parameter footprint and memory bus traffic, but they alter numerical representations and risk degrading task accuracy. A benchmark that records execution latency without statistical accuracy (such as area under the ROC curve (AUC) or classification error) rewards aggressive approximations that produce invalid outputs. Conversely, reporting accuracy without latency or memory consumption conceals whether the model satisfies the target system’s physical constraints.
The measurement harness and run rules provide the experimental controls that make these evaluations reproducible. The protocol follows the question being tested. A controlled steady-state experiment can use warm-up iterations, fixed processor clocks, and pinned host memory to isolate execution differences. A deployment benchmark instead retains the relevant dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) policy, cold starts, and competing workloads, documenting their effects. Recording tail latency distributions (p95, p99) alongside the mean exposes delays hidden by averages. Each component is built here on the claim the chapter inherited, that ResNet-50 runs faster at INT8 than at FP32, and MLPerf Tiny’s anomaly-detection benchmark at the end shows every component fixed at once on a small embedded model.


Every benchmark begins as a claim. The claim from the preceding chapters, that ResNet-50 at INT8 runs faster than at FP32 without unacceptable accuracy loss, is not yet testable, because it names neither the inputs, the output, nor the conditions under which faster must hold. Fixing those boundaries is the first act of carpentry. Without an explicit task specification, hardware and software optimizations cannot be evaluated on equivalent terms: altering an input resolution, a numerical datatype, or a latency deadline changes how much work the machine does. For ResNet-50 the input is a decoded \(224{\times}224\) RGB image and the output is one of a thousand ImageNet class labels. Whether the task is natural language processing (Hirschberg and Manning 2015) or computer vision (Everingham et al. 2009; Lin et al. 2014), a complete problem definition establishes three specifications: an input specification, an output specification, and a performance specification.

The input and output specifications fix the data each run must move and define the exact scope of timed execution. The input specification fixes tensor dimensions, batching behavior, numerical representations (such as FP16 or INT8), and ingestion rates. For the ResNet-50 claim, it decides whether timing starts at a JPEG on storage or at a preprocessed tensor already in accelerator memory, a choice that can change the measured time more than the precision change being tested. Conversely, the output specification defines the termination boundary of the computation. Benchmarks frequently introduce measurement bias by timing only accelerator forward passes while ignoring the CPU post-processing required to turn raw tensor outputs into usable decisions. A robust output specification defines whether the system emits raw logits, intermediate embeddings, or final class labels, accounting for any downstream thresholding or reduction kernels that consume host memory bandwidth.
The performance specification defines the operational envelope that governs whether an optimization is viable. Unconstrained throughput numbers are meaningless if statistical accuracy degrades below acceptable thresholds, and high average throughput cannot rescue a system that violates a latency service-level agreement (SLA). For the ResNet-50 claim, the performance specification couples a quality floor (MLPerf Training requires 75.9 percent top-1, and an INT8 deployment might permit at most one percentage point of loss against FP32) with hardware execution limits. These are a tail-latency ceiling, sustained throughput matching the arrival rate of images, and a resident memory footprint that leaves room for activations at the chosen batch size. By defining these three boundaries up front, the benchmark ensures that the later stages, from dataset construction to measurement harness configuration, evaluate system optimizations against the true operational constraints of deployment.



Fixing ResNet-50’s quality floor at 75.9 percent top-1 accuracy means nothing until the evaluation dataset itself is fixed, because a team that tests its INT8 model on a private slice of easy daytime photographs can claim no accuracy loss while a team testing on all 50,000 ImageNet validation images sees a regression. Standardized datasets enforce identical evaluation conditions across competing approaches, preventing teams from cherry-picking private slices that obscure comparative weaknesses. In computer vision, ImageNet (Deng et al. 2024, 2009), COCO (Lin et al. 2014), and CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky 2009) establish reference tasks across classification and detection. In natural language processing, SQuAD3 (Rajpurkar et al. 2016), GLUE4 (Wang et al. 2018), and WikiText (Merity 2016; Merity et al. 2016) fulfill equivalent roles by standardizing comprehension, classification, and language modeling across diverse textual domains.

Even a standardized dataset is the first place a benchmark can lose contact with deployment reality. ImageNet’s validation set fixes ResNet-50’s quality target, but its curated, centered photographs are not the frames a camera trap returns at dusk, a gap that section 12.9.2 returns to. A benchmark dataset must be representative enough to expose deployment failures and hard enough to separate models, so that the model architecture and metrics chosen next are tested against meaningful inputs.



Even on the same ImageNet validation split, two ResNet-50 benchmarks cannot be compared if one team alters layer widths or swaps the runtime while the other changes the accelerator. In systems benchmarking, the model defines the execution workload because its computational graph sets arithmetic intensity, memory footprint, and communication topology. Selecting and fixing the benchmark model determines whether measured performance variations reflect architectural efficiency, software runtime optimizations, or raw accelerator capacity. Evaluating an architectural modification requires holding the runtime and hardware target constant. Conversely, evaluating hardware platforms or software execution engines requires standardizing on a fixed, representative model graph so that throughput differences isolate execution efficiency rather than mathematical changes to the workload.
Baseline models establish the empirical reference point for a target domain. Rather than toy algorithms, systems benchmarks rely on canonical workloads whose computational profiles and memory access patterns are well-characterized. In vision, ResNet-50 plays this role, which is why the chapter’s claim is stated on it. In language processing, BERT5 serves as a standard baseline because its multi-head self-attention and dense feed-forward blocks exercise both compute-bound matrix multiplications and memory-bandwidth-bound reduction operations. However, a baseline specification cannot stop at the mathematical graph. Two implementations of the identical architecture across different frameworks or runtimes often behave differently at runtime. Differences in kernel fusion (such as fusing normalization and activation functions directly into general matrix multiply (GEMM) output epilogues to avoid round-trips to high-bandwidth memory (HBM)), kernel launch overhead, and memory allocator behavior can exceed the performance impact of minor architectural variations. A comparison that isolates hardware must control the runtime implementation alongside the mathematical model. A runtime comparison instead names that implementation as the intervention and documents both stacks.
5 BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers): BERT-Large (340M parameters) is a language-processing workload in MLPerf Inference. The benchmark fixes the task, data, quality target, and applicable execution scenarios so systems can be compared on the same workload. BERT latency still depends on sequence length, batching, and implementation.A benchmark must select the operational regime relevant to its engineering question. In training, memory capacity and interconnect bandwidth can be binding constraints, because storing forward activations, backward gradients, and optimizer states across multiple accelerators limits batch size and demands high-bandwidth collective communication. Training benchmarks therefore measure time-to-accuracy under fixed convergence criteria rather than raw iteration speed alone. In inference, backward passes and optimizer states disappear. Evaluation instead emphasizes the serving objective, such as tail latency under SLAs, while low-batch autoregressive decode often faces bandwidth pressure. Transitioning a model to production frequently requires precision reduction, quantizing FP32 or BF16 weights and activations to INT8 or FP8. Moving eligible tensors from a 16-bit to an 8-bit format halves their raw storage and can reduce traffic or raise supported arithmetic throughput. Whole-model gains depend on the execution path, and validation must establish whether numerical error stays within the quality target. A development-to-deployment comparison may need both regimes because efficient training does not establish serving feasibility; a deployment decision for a fixed pretrained model can focus on inference.
Evaluation metrics6 translate raw model behavior into numbers that can be compared, ranked, and used to make engineering decisions. The difficulty lies in choosing the right numbers. A metric that captures accuracy but ignores latency may declare the winner to be a model too slow for production; one that rewards throughput but ignores energy may optimize for a deployment budget that does not exist. The metrics in table 3 expose physical trade-offs governed by the accelerator architecture. Throughput measures aggregate processing capacity, whereas latency measures individual request completion time. These two objectives conflict directly at the hardware boundary. Maximizing throughput requires aggregating requests into larger batches to amortize weight-loading memory bandwidth across multiple inputs, raising arithmetic intensity on tensor units. That batching mechanism inflates per-sample latency, because individual requests wait in arrival queues while a batch forms, and larger matrix operations take longer to complete. Furthermore, arithmetic mean latency masks tail behavior. Queuing jitter, memory allocation stalls, and accelerator thermal throttling cause execution times to diverge; a system with a 10 ms mean latency can still suffer a 500 ms p99 latency that violates service-level agreements. Benchmarks must therefore report distribution percentiles (p50, p95, p99) rather than averages. Compound metrics such as samples/second/watt compress multiple dimensions into a single scalar, simplifying high-level comparisons but obscuring where bottlenecks reside. Reporting atomic metrics (latency distributions, throughput, and power draw) alongside compound figures isolates which physical constraint limits the system.

Task-specific metrics evaluate the algorithmic dimension, quantifying whether the model solves the statistical problem. Classification workloads evaluate accuracy (the fraction of correct predictions), precision, recall, and the F1 score (Sokolova and Lapalme 2009). Precision and recall isolate true positive rates from false alarms, which is essential when class distributions are imbalanced. Continuous estimation tasks rely on Mean Squared Error (MSE) or Mean Absolute Error (MAE), while sequence generation uses specialized scoring rules such as BLEU7 to measure modified n-gram precision against human reference translations (Papineni et al. 2002).
Task metrics evaluate algorithmic quality in isolation, but deployment viability depends on physical machine constraints. Model capacity, measured in parameter count and memory footprint, determines whether weights fit into on-chip SRAM or accelerator memory, or whether they spill across high-latency interconnects. Per-inference execution latency dictates whether a system meets real-time deadlines, while energy consumption per inference (measured in joules or millijoules) bounds thermal dissipation and battery life.
Benchmarks must also account for measurement sensitivity across software runtimes. As established in Model Training, different frameworks handle loss computation, kernel fusion, and gradient accumulation differently, altering reported benchmark numbers. Subtle implementation differences shift measured accuracy and latency enough to invert benchmark rankings when candidate models differ by narrow margins. Examples include whether batch normalization is configured to use stored running statistics or current mini-batch statistics during evaluation, and how reduction kernels reorder non-associative floating-point additions. Controlling how the runtime is driven and how those metrics are timed is the job of the benchmark harness.



When host software initiates an inference or training step on an accelerator, the framework runtime enqueues commands onto a work queue (such as a CUDA stream or hardware command buffer) and returns control to the CPU in microseconds. A naive timer wrapping that host-level call measures queue dispatch rather than device execution. Avoiding such measurement traps is the job of the benchmark harness, the software and instrumentation scaffold that feeds inputs to the system under test, coordinates execution across the asynchronous host-accelerator boundary, collects timing and power traces, and enforces reproducibility. A rigorous harness inserts explicit device synchronization barriers (such as torch.cuda.synchronize()) or queries on-device timestamp events (such as torch.cuda.Event), ensuring that recorded timings cover the declared device-work interval rather than host enqueue overhead.
The timer endpoints determine which work enters the result. Figure 1 separates the host call, the synchronized host interval, and the device-event interval for one inference.






Figure 1: Timing Across an Asynchronous Boundary: The host call returns after enqueueing work, before the accelerator completes it. A synchronized host timer spans enqueueing through completion; device events measure elapsed time between their positions on the stream. The timing boundaries determine whether transfers and other queued work are included.



These intervals answer different questions. Earlier device work must finish before the host timer starts. A synchronized host interval then measures elapsed completion time under the stated synchronization boundary, whereas events measure the interval between their positions in the accelerator stream. A report must state those boundaries before comparing two implementations; neither method includes work that falls outside them.
Harness architecture must align with the operational regime of the deployment target. In server environments, the harness generates concurrent request traffic using an open-loop load generator, often parameterizing inter-arrival times with a Poisson distribution.8 An open-loop harness issues requests according to an independent arrival schedule regardless of server responsiveness. This decoupling exposes queuing delays and tail latency (such as p99 response times) when arrival bursts saturate available compute.
8 Poisson distribution: Named after Siméon Denis Poisson, who formalized it in 1837 while modeling wrongful conviction rates in French courts. The distribution models independent events at a constant average rate \((\ArrivalRate)\) and is a common baseline for server request arrivals. Real ML serving traffic often violates its assumptions through burstiness, correlation, and time-varying rates. A Poisson harness can therefore misestimate tail latency unless traces or stress cases cover those production patterns.In contrast, a naive benchmarking client often employs a closed-loop pattern: sending a request, blocking until the response arrives, and only then issuing the next request. This design introduces the severe measurement distortion known as coordinated omission. Consider a server that experiences a transient 500 ms garbage collection pause or memory reallocation stall. In an open-loop production environment, independent users continue submitting queries, causing dozens of requests to accumulate in the server’s ingress queue; once the pause ends, every queued query suffers inflated tail latency. In a closed-loop benchmark, however, the client blocks idly during the entire 500 ms pause, sending zero traffic while the server is struggling. The benchmark records a single slow query and zero queue backlog. By coordinating request generation with server responsiveness, the closed-loop harness artificially paces traffic, systematically erasing the very queue collapse and p99 latency spikes it was constructed to measure.
The missing requests are the source of the distortion. Figure 2 aligns the two arrival policies against one server pause so that the change in offered work remains visible.






Figure 2: A Pause Under Two Arrival Policies: Each green interval runs from a request arrival to its response. Independent arrivals continue through the same server pause, while one closed-loop client waits for a response before sending again. The resulting workloads differ, so the closed-loop sample omits delays that the independent stream would experience. The timeline is schematic.



A closed-loop result is valid for a population whose clients wait in this way. It does not by itself estimate latency for an independent arrival stream, because it reduces the offered load precisely when the server slows. The harness must therefore reproduce the deployment arrival policy or report why a different policy answers the intended question.
Offline batch processing eliminates arrival scheduling entirely; the harness pre-stages large input batches in memory to saturate accelerator execution units, maximize memory bandwidth utilization, and measure peak sustained throughput.
In embedded and edge deployments, workloads are neither stochastic network streams nor unconstrained batch queues. Instead, inputs arrive sequentially from physical sensors (such as an audio analog-to-digital converter or an image sensor) governed by fixed hardware sampling clocks. The harness must inject these sensor streams through direct memory access into limited on-chip SRAM buffers, verifying that each inference completes within the inter-sample arrival deadline to prevent buffer overflow. Furthermore, edge harnesses must integrate physical instrumentation, such as shunt resistors or external power analyzers, to sample voltage and current across active execution cycles and low-power sleep states, capturing the true energy consumed per inference.
Reproducibility requires specifying which runtime and environmental conditions are controlled and which are part of the workload. Warm-up matters at every scale, from a single kernel to a whole run, because modern accelerators and runtime frameworks have substantial cold-start transients. Initial inference passes trigger on-demand memory allocations, dynamic just-in-time (JIT) compilation, driver initialization, and weight transfers from secondary storage into accelerator memory. For steady-state measurements, the harness executes unmeasured warm-up iterations until caches populate, memory allocators stabilize, and the intended thermal operating state is reached. Controlled experiments may fix clocks and remove competing processes; deployment tests retain and report the relevant DVFS policy and contention. Cold-start measurements time initialization separately instead of discarding it. Finally, telemetry logging must minimize the probe effect by recording execution timestamps and performance counters into non-blocking, pre-allocated memory buffers. The remaining instrumentation overhead should be checked against a minimally instrumented run.



Even a well-instrumented harness produces an uninterpretable number if the report omits the machine and the rules under which the harness ran. A throughput figure reported without accelerator model, memory bandwidth, or operating clocks conceals whether an observed speedup stems from algorithmic efficiency or upgraded silicon, and a result reported without its seed policy conceals whether it is reproducible at all, because the stochastic processes catalogued in section 12.4.2 mean that two runs on identical hardware can produce different numbers. System specifications record the computational environment, the physical hardware and software stack that establishes the Machine (\(\text{M}\)) boundaries of the system, while run rules govern how the benchmark executes on it. Because every execution metric reflects the interaction between an algorithm’s arithmetic intensity and a machine’s peak arithmetic throughput, memory bandwidth, and interconnect latency, a protocol must either fix seeds and data order when isolating system effects or require repeated runs and quality thresholds when stochastic variation is part of the workload. Reference suites may distribute containerized environments that encapsulate dependencies and configurations, while experimental logs retain training metrics, checkpoints, and any mid-run adjustments. Together, these records turn a one-time measurement into evidence another team can inspect and, when access permits, reproduce.



Once the harness and run rules produce a number, such as a 2 ms inference latency or a 10,000 images/s throughput figure, a single metric still rarely reveals whether an optimization will succeed in deployment.  Turning raw benchmark numbers into an engineering decision requires checking both the experimental intervention and the execution state. First, state what changes and what remains comparable. ResNet-50 versus MobileNet can be a valid architecture comparison at matched task and quality requirements; FP32 versus INT8 can be a valid precision comparison on a supported execution path. Hold the other relevant conditions fixed or report their changes, including batch size, hardware, runtime, input distribution, and service targets. Second, distinguish steady-state execution from initialization, using the harness’s warm-up protocol (section 12.2.4). A single run conflates cold-start overhead (kernel compilation, page faults, and cache warming) with sustained throughput, while a prolonged stress test may instead capture the thermal throttling examined for edge devices in section 12.6.4. Report cold-start and steady-state results according to the deployment question, and record variation across repeated trials. Whether a measured difference exceeds that variation is a statistical question, answered with the interval and paired-test rules of section 12.8.1.

Systems Perspective 12.3: Interpreting a benchmark claimA vendor claims “Our system achieves 10,000 inferences/second on ResNet-50.” Taken alone, the number cannot support deployment planning because the conditions that determine its meaning are unstated.
Four unstated conditions determine what the claim means:

Batch size: Large batches amortize weight transfers and maximize compute utilization but inflate queuing delay; batch 1 minimizes latency but leaves execution units underutilized.
Precision: INT8 execution exploits higher-throughput integer pipelines and cuts memory traffic, but requires quantization-range calibration that can compromise numerical fidelity.
Measurement boundary: The measurement window must state whether it isolates pure accelerator kernel execution or includes host-to-device transfers, JPEG decoding, and tensor format conversions.
Accuracy: The claim must state whether the optimized model retains baseline validation accuracy (such as 76.1 percent Top-1 on ImageNet) or trades task quality for raw execution speed.

Example: “10,000 inferences/second on ResNet-50 at batch size 32, INT8 precision, 76 percent Top-1 accuracy, including JPEG decoding, on NVIDIA H100 at 700 W thermal design power (TDP).”
Systems insight: A throughput figure lacking batch size, precision, measurement scope, and accuracy targets is a marketing metric rather than an engineering specification.


A claim whose workload boundary, precision, and excluded costs cannot be reconstructed should be rejected. Marketing phrases compress such omissions into a few words, usually reporting the most favorable operating point without saying so. Table 5 translates common ones into the technical caveats behind each.

Which metric governs viability depends on the deployment. In safety-critical applications such as medical imaging or autonomous driving, a 1 percent accuracy gain justifies substantial computational cost. In interactive search or speech transcription, tail latency within a tight service-level agreement dominates, so a minor accuracy gain is irrelevant if it breaches the latency budget. Systems evaluation must also guard against benchmark overfitting, in which an optimization targets the idiosyncratic computational patterns of a standardized suite at the expense of production workloads. For example, aggressive kernel fusion or operator tiling tuned exclusively for fixed sequence lengths in a benchmark harness can degrade throughput when deployed against dynamic, variable-length user requests. Robust interpretation requires validating performance across diverse input distributions, perturbed batch sizes, and representative operational duty cycles.

Checkpoint 12.1: Decoding vendor benchmark claims
When evaluating hardware or software based on vendor-reported benchmarks, check whether the claim identifies the workload, measurement boundary, and operating conditions.

Measured quantity: Does the latency number include preprocessing and postprocessing, not just model execution?
Precision boundary: Can the precision behind a throughput claim, such as INT4 versus INT8 or FP16, be identified?
Workload boundary: Are the model, batch size, and input distribution used to produce the comparison explicitly named?
Excluded costs: Are memory transfers, model loading, initialization, sustained thermal behavior, and power accounted for at the claimed performance level?
Claimed vs. achieved: Given a 1,000 TFLOP/s peak claim and a benchmark that sustains 350 TFLOP/s, estimate the MFU and state whether that utilization ratio alone identifies the bottleneck.

Each stage fixes boundary conditions for the next. The problem definition dictates the acoustic sampling rate and input representation (Data). The dataset properties and task objective determine feasible model architectures (Algorithm). The microcontroller’s hardware limits (SRAM capacity, energy envelope, and real-time latency deadlines) dictate INT8 quantization and memory-efficient kernel compilation (Machine). Here every choice constrains the next, so a benchmark that measures only classification accuracy or only raw inference latency misses cross-stage interactions, where an engineering decision at any stage narrows the feasible design space downstream.
