Its problem definition fixes the same three specifications that the ResNet-50 claim needed. The input is single-channel audio streamed at 16 kHz in fixed one-second windows, which sets a rigid ingestion rate and memory buffer requirement before feature extraction begins. The output is a binary “Normal” or “Anomaly” flag, including any thresholding that turns a reconstruction error into that decision. The performance specification couples a quality metric, area under the ROC curve (AUC), with execution limits. These are a per-inference latency that keeps pace with the one-second input windows, sustained throughput matching the arrival rate, and a resident footprint that avoids out-of-memory faults on the microcontroller.
At the dataset selection stage (the second chevron), the benchmark pipeline ingests representative audio waveform samples of normal machine operation alongside anomalous conditions before spectrogram feature extraction. Domain-specific collections cover different audio tasks: ToyADMOS9 (Koizumi et al. 2019) supports controlled anomaly-detection research, while Google Speech Commands (Warden 2018) supports keyword recognition. This interdependence between statistical quality and hardware constraints is evident in anomaly detection. In industrial monitoring, extreme class imbalance renders raw accuracy deceptive. If anomalies constitute only 0.1 percent of operating samples, a trivial model that constantly predicts normal operation achieves 99.9 percent accuracy while failing to detect any faults. The benchmark must instead report AUC, which scores how well the model ranks anomalous samples above normal ones across every decision threshold, alongside physical resource metrics.
This multi-metric evaluation approach governs the anomaly detection pipeline, which balances four simultaneous constraints. The model has 270K parameters, and its stored representation and runtime buffers must fit the embedded SRAM budget. Processing takes 10.4 ms per inference, which maintains real-time sampling. Detection accuracy is 0.86 AUC. Energy consumption is 516 µJ per inference, within the target battery budget. Evaluating across all four axes prevents declaring a model superior when its accuracy gain stems from an architecture too large to fit in memory or too power-hungry to survive sustained deployment.

For the fully connected autoencoder (FC-AE) on the ARM mbed OS target, each certifies something different. Parameter count and per-inference latency certify computational resources, the AUC certifies task effectiveness, and energy per inference certifies operational efficiency.
On a microcontroller, each metric governs a different failure: energy per inference sets battery life on untethered devices, model size decides whether weights fit in fast on-chip SRAM or spill into off-chip DRAM, and latency determines whether streaming audio is processed without dropped frames. The metrics trade against one another: reducing model size below 270K parameters can reduce memory traffic and execution time on a supported path, but risks degrading the 0.86 AUC detection accuracy. Whether these measurements constitute a passing benchmark depends on the operational envelope; the benchmark specification standardizes the evaluation protocol, but application requirements dictate the acceptance thresholds.
The reference flow fixes the task, data, model, and measurement boundary, but it measures one model on one device at one scope. Before choosing that scope, a benchmark should pass three methodological checks.

Checkpoint 12.2: Benchmarking methodology
Three practices distinguish rigorous benchmarks from misleading ones:

Representative data: Compare the benchmark input distribution against the production distribution.
Warm-up: State whether the goal is steady-state or cold-start performance, and which initialization work is timed or discarded.
Isolation: Document the machine, runtime, and competing workloads; explain which controls isolate the intervention and which conditions represent deployment.



A benchmark that passes those checks has still made a second choice, often implicitly. It decides how much of the system it measures. A single kernel, the whole model, and the request path around the model each answer a different question, and each fails in a different way.

A kernel that runs 3\(\times\) faster in isolation may deliver no end-to-end speedup if the data pipeline cannot keep the accelerator fed. In an illustrative request, a 3× inference speedup applied to a 10 ms model stage inside a 50 ms request yields only about a 1.2× end-to-end improvement, or less if the optimization increases memory pressure. The dilution makes the measurement boundary a design choice. Carpentry specifies how a measurement is built, while benchmarking granularity specifies what physical boundary it measures. System validation spans multiple architectural scales, from individual tensor operations to complete production pipelines, with each granularity diagnosing distinct bottlenecks:

Micro benchmarks isolate individual components: kernel execution time, memory bandwidth utilization, and single-layer numerical behavior. These diagnose where low-level hardware inefficiencies occur.
Macro benchmarks evaluate composed model subsystems: full model training convergence, inference pipeline throughput, and dataset accuracy metrics. These reveal what architectural trade-offs exist across layer compositions.
End-to-end benchmarks measure complete operational pipelines: client request-to-response latency including preprocessing, training time-to-accuracy including storage I/O, and model robustness on production data distributions. These show whether the combined system satisfies real-world service-level objectives.




Component speedup rarely survives as end-to-end benchmark speedup.
Optimization techniques operate across distinct granularities: kernel fusion targets micro-level execution, structured pruning alters macro-level parameter structures, and data curation determines end-to-end generalization. System validation must align with these respective boundaries. An isolated micro-benchmark may show substantial kernel speedup, yet a macro-benchmark can reveal that increased activation memory footprints force smaller batch sizes that degrade overall throughput. Similarly, an end-to-end benchmark exposes storage or host deserialization stalls that remain invisible at the accelerator kernel level.

An application benchmark then adds the supporting host compute around the model (AI Task), and the end-to-end benchmark adds the non-AI compute nodes the request also traverses. While end-to-end metrics govern service-level agreements, optimizing an accelerator pipeline requires isolating the specific mathematical operations that consume execution time and energy. Micro-benchmarks serve this diagnostic role by evaluating individual tensor operations in isolation, measuring the accelerator’s hardware primitives directly. When profiling a slow inference service, macro-benchmarks report aggregate latency violations, but only micro-benchmarks reveal whether execution time is dominated by matrix multiplications, self-attention projections, memory copies across the host-accelerator interconnect, or elementwise activation kernels.

Tensor operations constitute the primary target of micro-benchmarking because matrix multiplications and convolutions dominate the arithmetic budget of deep neural networks. Highly optimized runtime libraries such as cuDNN10 (Chetlur et al. 2014) provide hand-tuned kernel implementations tailored to specific microarchitectures. Micro-benchmarks also evaluate standalone activation functions (such as ReLU, Sigmoid, and GELU) and structural submodules (such as multi-head attention projections or transformer feed-forward blocks) across standardized input shapes. Benchmark suites such as Baidu’s DeepBench (Baidu Research 2016) formalized this methodology by evaluating raw GEMM, convolution, and collective communication primitives across diverse hardware platforms, isolating silicon-level execution efficiency from higher-level framework dispatch overhead.
Measuring isolated kernels requires rigorous experimental control. Without disciplined measurement protocols, dynamic hardware frequency scaling, asynchronous execution queues, and cache state introduce transient artifacts that distort kernel runtime.

Systems Perspective 12.4: Micro-benchmarking rules
Five rules keep a micro-benchmark measuring the kernel rather than a hardware artifact:

The warm-up rule: Do not measure cold-start iterations as steady-state performance. Modern hardware uses DVFS (dynamic voltage and frequency scaling) and dynamic frequency boosting; caches, kernels, and clocks need warm-up before the measured loop represents sustained behavior.
The variance rule: Report the coefficient of variation (CV) \((\text{CV} = \RepeatedRunStandardDeviation/ \RepeatedRunMean)\), where \(\RepeatedRunStandardDeviation\) and \(\RepeatedRunMean\) are the standard deviation and mean across repeated runs. Investigate values above the protocol’s workload-specific tolerance; common causes include background OS jitter, thermal throttling, and memory contention, and 5 percent is not a universal cutoff.
The “speed of light” (SOL) check: Compare the achieved throughput against the roofline. If a kernel achieves 10 TFLOP/s on an H100 (peak ~989 TFLOP/s FP16, or ~1,979 TFLOP/s FP8 dense), the diagnostic step is to identify the cause of low utilization (often kernel launch latency from too many small kernels) before optimizing the code itself.
The cache-state rule: Set cache state to match the claim. Flush or exceed the L2 cache when measuring cold dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) bandwidth; preserve a warmed cache when measuring steady-state reuse. Otherwise a nominal DRAM result may instead reflect cache bandwidth (~5 TB/s–10 TB/s) rather than DRAM bandwidth (~1 TB/s–2 TB/s).
The synchronization barrier rule: Accelerator kernel launches are asynchronous on the host CPU. Timing GPU operations using CPU clocks without an explicit device barrier (such as torch.cuda.synchronize()) measures host enqueue latency rather than kernel execution; always place synchronization barriers immediately before and after the timed region, or use GPU-side timestamp events (cudaEventRecord).



The roofline model11 of Performance Bounds, which plots the bound of the arithmetic intensity law (principle \(\ref{pri-arithmetic-intensity}\)), is a prediction, and a benchmark is the measurement that tests it. The roofline bounds where a kernel can sit; a benchmark determines where it does sit, and the gap between the two is the diagnostic. A kernel far below its predicted ceiling is losing time to something the model omits (launch overhead, poor coalescing, synchronization), which is exactly what profiling looks for. Making the prediction requires the workload’s arithmetic intensity at a named memory interface and the target’s matching compute and bandwidth limits. For an NVIDIA H100 with 989 TFLOP/s of dense FP16 Tensor Core performance (FP32 is 67 TFLOP/s)12 and 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth, the ridge point (peak compute divided by peak bandwidth, the intensity at which the two ceilings meet) falls at 295 FLOP/byte. Below it, bandwidth sets the lower ceiling; above it, compute does (Hardware ridge points derives the threshold).
11 Roofline model: Williams et al. (2009) introduced the Berkeley model, named for the visual shape of its performance ceiling. Its ridge point (peak FLOP/s divided by peak bandwidth) separates bandwidth-limited from compute-limited ceilings, suggesting which interventions to test against measured execution.

The H100 advertises 989 TFLOP/s of dense FP16 Tensor Core arithmetic, but real workloads achieve different fractions of peak depending on arithmetic intensity, memory access patterns, precision, and runtime overhead. Reporting peak FLOP/s without utilization context is the most common benchmarking distortion.

A profiler translates these measurement rules into physical diagnostics by decomposing kernel execution time into the three governing terms of the iron law: data movement, compute throughput, and latency overhead. Comparing the measured utilization of each resource against hardware limits reveals which term dominates the trace.

Systems Perspective 12.5: Measuring the iron law terms
Moving from theory to trace means mapping the iron law equation onto a profiler timeline (like Nsight Systems or PyTorch Profiler).
Measuring the data term \(\left(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}\right)\)

Signal: Look for the “Memory Throughput” or “DRAM Bandwidth” line.
Formula: \(\AchievedKernelBandwidth = \frac{\DataVolume}{\KernelExecutionTime}\).
Diagnosis: If \(\AchievedKernelBandwidth \approx \PeakMemoryBandwidth\) (for example, close to the H100’s 3.35 TB/s peak), bandwidth pressure is a strong candidate bottleneck. Test whether reducing traffic or increasing bandwidth improves time; a high bandwidth reading alone does not establish that changing compute (\(\Operations\)) has no effect.

Measuring achieved compute throughput \((\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\)

Signal: Distinguish “SM Active,” the fraction of time the GPU’s Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), its parallel execution cores, have work resident, from executed-operation throughput. A busy multiprocessor does not imply high useful-model FLOP/s.
Formula: \(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw = \frac{\Operations}{\KernelExecutionTime}\), reported in TFLOP/s.
Diagnosis: If \(\EfficiencyHw \ll 1\) AND \(\AchievedKernelBandwidth \ll \PeakMemoryBandwidth\), neither quoted peak is being approached. Kernels too small to amortize launch latency or too few threads to occupy the SMs are candidate explanations, but low aggregate rates alone do not exclude dependency stalls or an inefficient memory-access path. Separate inter-kernel gaps from in-kernel stalls, then inspect the corresponding dispatch, dependency, occupancy, or memory-access evidence before selecting an optimization.

Measuring the latency term \((\Latency)\)

Signal: Look for gaps (empty space) between colored kernel bars on the timeline.
Formula: \(\text{Kernel gap fraction} = \frac{\InterKernelGapTime}{\KernelExecutionTime+ \InterKernelGapTime}\).
Diagnosis: A “Sawtooth” pattern (Compute, Gap, Compute, Gap) suggests exposed waiting; correlate CPU dispatch, dependencies, and transfers before attributing it to software overhead. If dispatch dominates, candidates include kernel fusion, covered in Kernel fusion on the accelerator, or the CUDA Graphs of Graph capture and JIT compilation. They capture a repeated sequence of GPU launches so the runtime can replay it with less CPU dispatch overhead.



Profilers supply the measurements this mapping needs. A framework profiler such as the PyTorch Profiler isolates the dominant layer on the step timeline. A kernel profiler such as NVIDIA Nsight Compute explains it from on-chip performance counters, the top-down method developed on a training step in Identifying Bottlenecks. Counter collection and kernel replay perturb timing, so diagnostic traces are compared against a minimally instrumented run. The benchmarking use is narrower, confirming or refuting a prediction.


↩︎ The feeding problem, the wall-clock time an accelerator loses waiting on input I/O, is established in The feeding problem.
These granular measurements enable precise kernel optimization, but they cannot reveal how components interact when assembled into complete models. Macro-benchmarks address this gap.



A convolution kernel that hits 80 percent of the roofline in a micro-benchmark can still stall when chained into a 50-layer network. Macro-benchmarks determine whether operator-level gains persist when layers are composed into a complete model. Composing layers introduces physical interactions that isolated benchmarks cannot observe, because intermediate activation tensors expand peak memory footprint, sequential kernel launches expose CPU driver dispatch overhead, and memory access streams from preceding operations evict shared cache lines before downstream kernels can reuse them.
Evaluating composed model architectures and runtime configurations under standardized workloads exposes trade-offs across those interactions, including generalization accuracy on unseen validation data, dynamic memory allocation across batch sizes and context lengths, and aggregate throughput across varied request arrival patterns. An architecture that achieves higher accuracy may require an activation footprint that forces a smaller batch size under device memory constraints, collapsing the computational throughput that justified its adoption. ResNet-50’s training step tests the roofline’s prediction at exactly this granularity, because the prediction is made layer by layer and the measurement is made on the composed model.

Napkin Math 12.1: ResNet-50 on the roofline: Predicted versus measuredProblem: The roofline predicts the fastest an H100 can train ResNet-50, and MLPerf measures how fast it does. How large is the gap, and what does it say about where the time goes?
Prediction: One training image costs about 24.6 GFLOP, three times the 8.2 GFLOP forward pass, because the backward pass computes gradients with respect to both activations and weights. At training batch sizes, the convolution layers reuse each weight across hundreds of images and sit above the 295 FLOP/byte ridge, so the roofline places the step on the compute roof. Dividing the 989 TFLOP/s peak by the work per image gives a ceiling of about 40,200 images/s.
Measurement: In MLPerf Training v3.1, NVIDIA’s 64-accelerator H100 system trained ResNet-50 at about 5,000 images/s per accelerator, which delivers about 123 TFLOP/s of model arithmetic, 12.4 percent of peak.
Diagnosis: The measurement sits 8.0× below the prediction. The roofline did not err; it bounded the convolutions and omitted the rest of the step. Normalization and elementwise layers have intensities far below the ridge and run on the bandwidth slope, the host must decode and augment thousands of JPEG images every second, and every step pays launch and synchronization overhead. The prediction cannot say which of these dominates. A profiler attributes the gap among them (perspective 12.5), and Identifying Bottlenecks works that attribution for a training step.
Systems insight: A prediction and a measurement together locate a bottleneck; either alone does not. The roofline says ResNet-50 could train 8.0× faster on this accelerator, and the measurement says something other than arithmetic is setting its pace.


The claim the chapter inherited, that ResNet-50 runs faster at INT8 than at FP32, needs a different macro-benchmark from this training one. An inference run under MLPerf Inference rules settles it directly, because the ResNet-50 Offline scenario on ImageNet (Deng et al. 2024), run at INT8 and at the higher-precision baseline on the same accelerator across fixed batch sizes with each required to hold the reference top-1 accuracy within the benchmark’s quality gate, reports both throughputs and latencies under one set of rules. Natural language macro-benchmarks apply the same model-level discipline to sequence-to-sequence translation and autoregressive generation, pairing output quality with token generation rate across defined context lengths.

Industry-standard suites make these model-level comparisons reproducible across platforms. The MLPerf suite spans data centers, edge appliances, mobile devices, and microcontrollers (section 12.6.3), while EEMBC’s MLMark quantifies inference throughput and energy under strict embedded memory budgets and AI-Benchmark (Ignatov and Timofte 2024) evaluates mobile systems-on-chip across heterogeneous compute units. The chapter’s own deployment measurement moves to MobileNetV2 on the camera-trap board, where even a composed-model benchmark is not yet enough because timing only the model omits the host preprocessing, storage, and transfer stages that surround it in an end-to-end pipeline.



In a computer vision service, decoding a compressed JPEG image, resizing, cropping, and normalizing colors on the host CPU can take several times longer than running the model itself on a modern accelerator, leaving high-throughput tensor cores idle while they wait for host memory transfers. Macro-benchmarks that start at a pre-staged tensor never see that stall. End-to-end benchmarks encompass the entire production pipeline, capturing every stage required to ingest raw data, generate model predictions, and deliver results to downstream clients. Across workloads, the primary bottleneck frequently sits in these surrounding stages, where natural language pipelines can be paced by host-CPU subword tokenization and dynamic sequence padding, while object detection pipelines can stall on sequential postprocessing such as non-maximum suppression (NMS) and bounding-box coordinate transformations when those steps remain outside the accelerated graph.
Distributed infrastructure components introduce further performance constraints beyond the compute fabric. Remote storage systems bound training throughput when reading large multimodal datasets, and network interface card (NIC) saturation in distributed clusters throttles collective communication. End-to-end benchmarks must measure pipeline throughput under realistic network latencies, concurrent query arrival patterns, and actual storage I/O constraints to ensure reproducible evaluation of the deployment as an integrated system.
Public benchmark suites rarely measure storage, networking, and compute within a single unified protocol. While MLPerf Training and Inference evaluate end-to-end scenarios more closely than isolated operator tests, their closed divisions deliberately standardize input data loading to isolate accelerator performance from storage and network variability. Consequently, production end-to-end benchmarking remains primarily an internal engineering practice, evaluated through distributed tracing and production telemetry on live query distributions, where the first diagnostic step is separating model execution time from the rest of the request.



When Clipper’s designers profiled serving pipelines for lightweight models, CPU-side JSON deserialization and interprocess data copying took more wall-clock time than the accelerator’s model execution (Crankshaw et al. 2017). Reporting model latency alone would have hidden the largest cost in the request path, a serialization bottleneck that The serialization bottleneck develops for serving systems. Measured at the request, the critical distinction is therefore between component latency (time spent in model computation) and end-to-end latency (total time from request arrival to response delivery). Because serialization, network hops, and queue wait time can dominate total request time, benchmarks that report only model inference time obscure what the user experiences and overstate the return on model-only optimizations.

These component-level contributions explain why optimizing any single stage yields diminishing returns on end-to-end performance, an optimization ceiling formalized by Amdahl’s Law (principle \(\ref{pri-amdahl}\)). The bound itself appears as equation 11.1, where hardware acceleration states it for an accelerated path; the notebook below applies it to a measured pipeline.

Napkin Math 12.2: Amdahl's Law: Optimization ceilingProblem: A vision pipeline spends 8 ms on preprocessing (JPEG decode, resize, normalize) and 10 ms on inference. If inference alone is optimized by 5×, how much does end-to-end latency actually improve?
Math: Assume fixed work, sequential stages, and unchanged preprocessing, with no queueing feedback. Optimizing inference from 10 ms to 2 ms reduces total latency from 18 ms to only 10 ms, a 1.8× improvement rather than 5×. Amdahl’s Law formalizes this ceiling: if inference, the part being accelerated, is fraction \(\ParallelFraction\) of total latency, then even infinitely fast inference yields at most \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) speedup, because the preprocessing fraction \(1-\ParallelFraction\) remains. With preprocessing at 44.4 percent of total latency, the remaining fraction \(1-\ParallelFraction\) is 0.444, which yields a maximum achievable speedup \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) of 2.25×, regardless of model optimization.
Systems insight: Aggressive model optimization yields disappointing end-to-end results whenever the nonmodel fraction dominates. Any component speedup quoted in isolation shrinks once the untouched stages are measured alongside it, and the shortfall grows as those stages take a larger share of the pipeline. Comprehensive benchmarks must either include preprocessing in measurements or state explicitly that reported speedups apply only to the inference component.


A latency report that supports a deployment decision therefore states which components it includes, the load it was measured under, and whether each figure is a component or an end-to-end number. Choosing that boundary is the trade-off between isolating a component bottleneck and measuring what the user experiences.



Choosing a measurement boundary means deciding which question the benchmark must answer, because an engineer tuning a convolution kernel needs micro-level isolation free of network jitter, an architect comparing ResNet-50 and MobileNetV2 needs macro-level model composition, and a release engineer certifying an SLO needs the full end-to-end request path. Selecting a single granularity level is rarely sufficient because benchmarking presents an inherent trade-off between diagnostic isolation and production fidelity. Along the descending diagonal in figure 5, evaluation regimes trade diagnostic power for operational realism. Micro-benchmarks (the red point at the top left) isolate kernel-level memory bandwidth and warp occupancy at the expense of end-to-end context. Macro-benchmarks (the blue center point) capture composed model topologies. End-to-end benchmarks (the green point at the bottom right) encompass live production traffic but obscure the root causes of latency spikes. This trade-off maps directly onto the D·A·M taxonomy. Micro-benchmarks assess the physical capability of the Machine (\(\text{M}\)) executing a primitive Algorithm (\(\text{A}\)). Macro-benchmarks evaluate how the Algorithm (\(\text{A}\)) orchestrates tensor data flow across composed layers on the Machine (\(\text{M}\)). End-to-end benchmarks evaluate how raw Data (\(\text{D}\)) ingestion from external storage and network infrastructure interacts with both Algorithm and Machine under production load. Systematic performance engineering requires evaluating all three tiers to ensure local kernel optimizations translate into global system speedups.
Carpentry and granularity let one team build a trustworthy measurement. Comparing that measurement with another team’s, or with a vendor’s, requires that both were built the same way, and that agreement is what standardized benchmark suites provide.

Without that shared measurement protocol, a team evaluating five candidate system-on-chip (SoC) designs for the camera trap’s next board faces incompatible claims. Vendor A reports 8 TOPS at INT8; Vendor B reports 15 TOPS at INT4; Vendor C reports inference latency on a proprietary model; Vendor D cites MLPerf scores from two generations ago; Vendor E provides only peak throughput at maximum batch size. None of these figures can be directly compared because each vendor isolates a favorable metric under idiosyncratic conditions, obscuring true operating trade-offs. Standardized benchmark suites resolve this fragmentation by enforcing uniform measurement harnesses and evaluation rules across every submission.
Each generation of benchmark suites arose to close a gap of exactly this kind, when the metrics of the day stopped predicting what users experienced. Their history explains the rules modern suites enforce.


Three shifts mark that history: from isolated kernels to representative application suites, from single-metric throughput to multi-objective energy profiles, and from generic compute metrics to domain-specific execution constraints. The earliest computing benchmarks were open to benchmark gaming. Whetstone (Curnow and Wichmann 1976) used a synthetic mix of scientific operations, while LINPACK (Dongarra et al. 1979) measured dense linear-system solving. Because both relied on predictable computational loops, compiler and hardware vendors could optimize for the benchmark kernels (unrolling synthetic loops, or tailoring cache tiling to exact matrix dimensions) without improving general application performance. SPEC CPU (1989) addressed this by evaluating complete, portable software suites that stressed integer branching, irregular memory hierarchies, and floating-point pipelines (Dixit 1993). The same vulnerability applies to ML, since model-specific kernel tuning can overfit a single workload. Model compression claims therefore require validation on representative tasks such as ResNet-50 and BERT across the full software runtime.

Energy benchmarking also exposes algorithmic efficiency. Compression and efficient architectures such as MobileNet (Howard et al. 2017; Sandler et al. 2018) save energy by reducing operations and off-chip traffic. Traffic reduction is a primary lever, because a DRAM read costs orders of magnitude more energy than an arithmetic operation (Where precision saves energy).
As specialized accelerators emerged, generic benchmarks failed to capture domain-specific execution constraints. Data center training clusters optimize aggregate throughput within rack-level power envelopes, mobile AI operates within thermal limits (typically under 5 watts), and embedded microcontrollers function within milliwatt budgets. These budgets decide whether a benchmark prioritizes samples per second or joules per inference. Application requirements add functional constraints such as calibration for clinical models, hard tail-latency cutoffs for trading systems, and bounded worst-case latency for autonomous vehicles.
Because ML workloads couple tensor execution units, memory bandwidth, and communication fabrics, no single metric or workload can characterize a system. MLPerf therefore splits into distinct deployment suites. MLPerf Training evaluates multi-node scaling and high-bandwidth interconnects under time-to-quality targets (Mattson et al. 2020). MLPerf Inference measures throughput and latency percentiles under SLAs across server and client systems (Reddi et al. 2019). MLPerf Tiny tests ultra-low-power microcontrollers operating with tight memory constraints (Banbury et al. 2021). The cross-cutting MLPerf Power track measures useful work per watt across each environment. Three lessons from benchmark history (representative workloads, multi-objective evaluation, and integrated system measurement) converge on a requirement unique to machine learning: managing statistical approximation. Traditional computing benchmarks specify correctness checks, which may require exact outputs or permit stated numerical tolerances. In ML systems, low-level engineering choices routinely alter numerical output: aggressive weight quantization, kernel pruning, or reduced-precision accumulators trade accuracy for execution speed and lower memory bandwidth pressure. Consequently, an ML benchmark cannot evaluate execution time in isolation; output accuracy serves as an inviolable operational constraint.
Evaluating an ML system therefore means testing the coupled Data, Algorithm, and Machine (D·A·M) choices together rather than measuring raw compute throughput. A suite earns trust by solving three problems. It must produce valid measurements despite run-to-run noise, finite test sets, unrepresentative workloads, and misaligned metrics. It must then isolate what the hardware-software stack contributes, which is the job of a system benchmark and its roofline diagnostic. Finally, it must make results comparable across organizations, which is the job of community standardization.
ML systems combine several sources of measurement variability that classical software benchmarks were not designed to evaluate together. These fluctuations originate at both the machine and algorithmic layers. On the machine side, sustained execution pushes accelerators against thermal and power envelopes, triggering dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) that throttles processor clocks mid-run. Host operating-system activity (thread scheduling jitter, memory paging, and PCIe bus contention during batch staging) further introduces latency variance across runs. On the algorithmic side, floating-point addition is non-associative, so reduction orders that change across parallel execution threads shift results slightly. Mini-batch shuffling, pseudo-random augmentations, stochastic dropout masks, and weight initialization also perturb the trajectory that stochastic gradient descent takes across a non-convex loss surface.
Distinguishing a genuine systems optimization from background measurement noise requires isolating these overlapping sources of variance with repeated runs, paired comparisons, and confidence intervals. Those statistical controls apply to every benchmark in the chapter, so section 12.8.1 collects them in one place, including how large a test set must be before it can resolve a one-point accuracy difference.
Beyond run-to-run variance, benchmark validity depends on workload representativeness. Synthetic microbenchmarks generate uniform, statically sized tensors directly in accelerator HBM. By executing continuous, compute-bound GEMM operations in an isolated loop, microbenchmarks measure theoretical peak arithmetic throughput. However, they conceal the memory hierarchies and scheduling bottlenecks that dominate production deployments. Synthetic workloads bypass host-to-device PCIe data transfers, input decoding pipelines, dynamic memory allocation churn, and GPU cache evictions. In contrast, trace-based benchmarking replays timestamped request logs recorded from live serving clusters. Production traces capture Poisson and bursty request arrival distributions, variable sequence lengths, and concurrent query streams. Replaying live traces forces the serving infrastructure to manage dynamic batching (grouping requests that arrive within a short time window into one batch), key-value (KV) cache allocation under memory pressure, and queuing delays, stress-testing the system under operational conditions that synthetic steady-state loops obscure.

A representative workload can still mislead if the evaluation metric fails to reflect deployment constraints. When an engineering team optimizes a single algorithmic figure of merit (such as an offline BLEU score, top-1 classification accuracy, or token perplexity) in isolation from system SLOs, the metric ceases to measure genuine operational fitness. This divergence is the chapter’s second principle, Goodhart’s Law, operating inside a single team’s choice of metric, and once the proxy becomes the sole optimization target it stops reporting overall system health. In neural machine translation, an offline accuracy optimization can break the serving deadline outright.

Example 12.1: Goodhart's Law in actionScenario: An engineering team optimizes a neural machine translation model for offline BLEU score, increasing the beam search size (the number of candidate partial translations kept at each decoding step) from 1 to 10.
Diagnosis: The larger beam search achieves a 0.5-point BLEU gain on paper but increases candidate evaluations by 10×, increasing inference latency from 50 ms to 200 ms (4× slowdown), exceeding the serving deadline.
Systems lesson: Optimizing offline accuracy without latency constraints invites Goodhart’s Law failures. Production benchmarks must enforce strict SLOs for serving latency (e.g., latency < 100 ms).


The translation example shows an algorithmic change (a tenfold wider beam) multiplying computational load and memory traffic for a marginal quality gain while violating a hardware latency deadline. Fixed benchmarks also assess execution under an unvarying input distribution, which conceals how systems degrade under production distribution shifts. Model and data evaluation must test those distribution limits. System comparisons address a separate question by isolating infrastructure execution efficiency from model architecture and dataset variation. Standardized suites like MLPerf establish reference workloads, datasets, quality targets, and permitted implementation changes, enabling reproducible comparisons of hardware-software execution efficiency within a specified benchmark version and division.



Hardware specifications advertise peak arithmetic rates that application workloads do not sustain—the gap between an H100’s dense FP16 peak and the model arithmetic ResNet-50 training actually achieves (section 12.1). System benchmarks expose that gap by running standardized ML workloads across hardware architectures, memory systems, and interconnects rather than relying on spec-sheet peaks alone.
The underlying hardware, whether CPUs, GPUs, Tensor Processing Units (TPUs),14 and application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs),15 determines ML-system speed, efficiency, and scale. System benchmarks provide standardized methods for comparing hardware across AI workloads by computational throughput, memory bandwidth, power efficiency, operator coverage, and scaling (Reddi et al. 2019; Mattson et al. 2020).

For practitioners, they enable informed hardware selection by providing comparative data across configurations. Definition 12.2: Machine learning system benchmarks
Machine learning system benchmarks are standardized evaluation protocols that hold the workload and quality target constant while varying the hardware-software stack, measuring \(\EfficiencyHw = \SustainedComputeRate/ \PeakRate\) (the measured sustained rate \(\SustainedComputeRate\) over the peak rate) and \(\Latency\) to isolate infrastructure efficiency from algorithmic improvements.

Significance: The same ResNet-50 model can report the same ImageNet Top-1 accuracy while delivering very different throughput across hardware stacks, precision formats, batch sizes, and compiler configurations. Only a system benchmark exposes that gap.
Distinction: Unlike algorithmic benchmarks (which vary the Data and Algorithm factors, \(\text{Samples/Task}\) and \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\), to improve convergence or accuracy), system benchmarks hold the algorithm and quality target fixed and vary the implementation (kernel libraries, quantization formats, batch sizes, and hardware generations). They measure how efficiently the hardware-software stack executes the workload, lowering the iron law’s realized Machine factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) across compute (\(\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\)), data movement (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)), and fixed latency (\(\Latency\)).
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that a system benchmark result generalizes across workloads. An accelerator that achieves high utilization on ResNet-50 (a compute-friendly vision workload) may achieve much lower utilization on a recommendation system, whose embedding lookups are bound by memory capacity and bandwidth rather than arithmetic. System benchmarks are workload-specific; no single metric characterizes a hardware platform.



System benchmarks evaluate performance across scales, ranging from single-chip configurations to large distributed systems and covering both training and inference. The ImageNet challenge shows why separating the hardware’s contribution from the model’s is hard to do after the fact. Between 2010 and 2014, top-5 error (the blue line in figure 6) fell from 28.2 percent to 7.3 percent, with the steepest single drop at AlexNet’s arrival in 2012. Over the same years, GPU-accelerated entries (the green bars) rose from zero to over 100 (Krizhevsky et al. 2012; Russakovsky et al. 2015; Gray 2015). These paired series plot contemporaneous empirical trends, not a causal attribution of how much accuracy gain stemmed from hardware throughput versus algorithmic design, training schedules, or dataset expansion. A system benchmark avoids that ambiguity by construction: it fixes the model and quality target so that any change in the result belongs to the hardware-software stack.

While section 12.9.1 evaluates model compression against task accuracy baselines, system benchmarking isolates the execution efficiency of the hardware-software stack under a fixed model. Modern accelerators rarely sustain theoretical peak throughput because physical execution depends on the coupling between tensor shapes and memory hierarchies. ResNet-50 training, which the roofline places on the compute roof, sustains about 12.4 percent of an H100’s peak (notebook 12.1). Parameter-heavy transformer decodes and activation-heavy convolutional passes stress entirely different levels of the memory subsystem, causing achievable throughput to diverge across precision formats.
Measuring sustained utilization rather than peak capability establishes two critical scope boundaries. First, energy consumption scales with execution efficiency, because performance per watt varies widely across hardware platforms, and an underutilized accelerator draws substantial static power for minimal computational output. Second, multi-accelerator execution introduces communication boundaries. While multi-node cluster scaling involves network-topology effects beyond this book’s single-node scope, intra-node benchmarking must account for interconnect bandwidth, memory sharing across accelerators, and gradient synchronization over NVLink or PCIe.



Without shared measurement boundaries, utilization numbers cannot be compared. If one benchmark includes host-side preprocessing and PCIe transfers while another measures only device kernel execution, or if one power meter reads only the accelerator voltage rail while another includes host processors and chassis fans, the resulting figures reflect incompatible boundaries rather than architectural efficiency. No single vendor can resolve this discrepancy, because each has a commercial incentive to draw the boundary around its own hardware strengths. Formal standards bodies move too slowly for hardware and model structures that change every year, so consortia such as MLCommons maintain living benchmark suites. These pair open-source reference implementations with compliance rules so that numbers from different laboratories describe comparable workloads under the same version, division, quality target, and scenario.
Standardizing system benchmarks requires formalizing the D·A·M taxonomy so that evaluations isolate the Machine without confounding changes to the Algorithm or Data. The MLPerf Training benchmark enforces this separation by measuring time-to-train to a specified quality target rather than raw floating-point throughput or epoch duration (Mattson et al. 2020). High TFLOP/s from aggressive low-precision scaling helps only if faster steps outweigh any extra work needed to reach the target, and a run that misses the target is invalid. MLPerf splits submissions into two divisions. In the closed division, every submitter must run the reference model and reach the same quality target, so differences in time-to-train belong to the system. The open division permits model and algorithm changes, so its results compare whole solutions rather than machines. Within the closed division, the rules constrain the workload while permitting specified tunable hyperparameters and approved numerical formats. Quality and compliance checks establish which hardware, compiler, and training-configuration improvements constitute valid submissions.
The MLPerf Inference benchmark applies this discipline to production deployment constraints (Reddi et al. 2019). An accelerator cannot simply report peak throughput under infinite batching if interactive serving requires guaranteed responsiveness. The benchmark therefore fixes how queries arrive, through execution scenarios matched to physical operating regimes: one query at a time for a single interactive user, randomly arriving queries under a tail-latency bound for a shared service, and all inputs supplied upfront for bulk throughput. By standardizing these execution boundaries, community benchmarks account for queueing delays and host-to-device PCIe transfers, making the tested load and timing boundary explicit when interpreting a throughput claim.


The same hardware can report dramatically different benchmark numbers depending on how requests arrive, which explains why vendor claims often fail to predict production performance. Classic MLPerf Inference defines four execution scenarios that characterize distinct traffic patterns, each requiring different optimization strategies (Reddi et al. 2019). Current client and generative-AI benchmark variants also include interactive measurements for latency-sensitive large language model (LLM) workloads, where time to first token and time per output token, the two measured quantities defined in section 12.6.2.2, become central (MLCommons 2026b).


SingleStream processes one request at a time, measuring latency for sequential inference. This scenario models mobile and embedded applications where a single user interacts with the device: a smartphone camera app classifying images, a voice assistant processing speech, or a wearable detecting gestures. The key metric is a tail percentile of per-query latency (the 90th percentile in MLPerf’s rules), and inter-request batching is unavailable because the next query arrives after the previous one completes. Optimization focuses on preprocessing efficiency and power consumption rather than throughput.



MultiStream processes multiple synchronized input streams simultaneously, modeling scenarios like autonomous vehicles with multiple cameras that must be processed together for spatial fusion. The application motivation is synchronized processing, but the benchmark rule is version-specific: current MultiStream rules issue a group of samples per query, wait for its completion before the next query, and report a specified latency percentile. Earlier versions used fixed arrival intervals. Grouped-query latency helps assess multi-input execution; it does not establish a hard-deadline guarantee for a vehicle planning loop.



Server generates requests following a Poisson distribution, simulating cloud API traffic where requests arrive independently and unpredictably. This scenario models web services handling millions of queries from different users. Unlike SingleStream’s guaranteed sequential arrival, Server traffic creates queuing dynamics where multiple requests compete for resources. The key metrics are throughput (queries per second) and the workload’s tail-latency bound, typically set at the 99th percentile, and dynamic batching can improve efficiency by grouping requests that arrive within a time window. Optimization balances throughput against latency SLOs.



Offline provides all inputs upfront, measuring maximum throughput when latency constraints are removed. This scenario models batch processing pipelines: overnight data processing, scientific computing, or precomputing recommendations. With no per-query latency requirement, systems can tune batch size for sustained throughput within memory and execution limits. The key metric is pure throughput (samples per second), and optimization focuses entirely on hardware efficiency. Training and inference fail in opposite ways on the same accelerator. A training run stalls when synchronizing gradients across accelerators saturates the interconnect; a serving deployment violates its SLO when request bursts build a queue. The two regimes also measure different resources. Training iteratively refines parameters over billions of samples and must hold parameters, gradients, optimizer state, and the activations retained for the backward pass, a footprint that can far exceed the weights alone (table 1 gives ResNet-50’s). Its figure of merit is wall-clock time to a target accuracy. Inference evaluates fixed parameters against arriving queries, discards the backward graph and optimizer state, and is judged by latency percentiles and throughput under bursty load. A training result and an inference result on the same accelerator therefore measure different resources and cannot stand in for each other, which is why MLPerf maintains separate Training and Inference suites (Mattson et al. 2020; Reddi et al. 2019). This chapter measures training on ResNet-50 and serving on MobileNetV2 (section 12.6).

↩︎ The training memory budget of weights, gradients, optimizer state, and retained activations is established in Reducing optimizer memory.

Because training couples per-step computation with gradient communication and multi-gigabyte state, a team that purchases a larger GPU cluster expecting proportional training-speed gains can discover after procurement that interconnect stalls and memory bottlenecks swallow much of the speedup. Training benchmarks exist to catch that gap before capital is committed. They span six dimensions (table 12), anchored by three, namely convergence metrics that measure learning progress, throughput metrics that measure computational efficiency, and scalability metrics that measure distributed performance.

Definition 12.3: ML training benchmarks
ML training benchmarks are machine learning system benchmarks that measure the time to reach a target quality metric (for example, a specified validation accuracy or loss threshold) on a fixed dataset and model, quantifying the rate of convergence per unit of resource.

Significance: Training benchmarks reveal large gaps invisible to hardware specs. Holding the model and quality target fixed, the time to convergence can vary widely across hardware-software stacks because training performance depends on the full pipeline: data loading \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\), compute utilization \((\EfficiencyHw)\), gradient synchronization \((\Bandwidth, \Latency)\), and fault recovery overhead. A peak FLOP/s spec sheet captures none of these interactions.
Distinction: Unlike inference benchmarks, which measure per-query latency and throughput under load, training benchmarks measure time-to-accuracy across the full optimization loop: data loading, forward pass, backward pass, gradient synchronization, and optimizer step. As scale increases, communication \((\Bandwidth)\) can displace compute \((\PeakRate)\) as the binding constraint; profiling establishes the transition for a particular workload.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that training benchmarks measure “how fast the GPU runs.” At large scale, interconnect bandwidth \((\Bandwidth)\) for gradient synchronization and fault tolerance overhead (checkpoint I/O, straggler mitigation) often dominate the benchmark result more than peak FLOP/s.



Because training represents the largest capital expenditure in many ML organizations, only time-to-accuracy measurement reveals whether added accelerators and faster kernels deliver proportional value rather than dissipating into scaling inefficiencies, input stalls, or communication overhead. After examining how standardized suites track these system-wide gains, this section defines and works the core training metrics (time-to-accuracy, scaling efficiency, utilization, energy, and checkpoint overhead) at the scale of one machine with one to eight accelerators.


MLPerf Training (Mattson et al. 2020; MLCommons 2024c) provides the standardized framework for this time-to-quality measurement. The longitudinal scaling curves in figure 7 track cumulative relative performance gains across nine model workloads between 2018 and 2024 against the orange Moore’s Law baseline. Every workload curve outpaces cumulative transistor scaling (which reaches 6.6\(\times\) by mid-2024), led by Mask R-CNN climbing to 48.8\(\times\) and ResNet reaching 34\(\times\) as distributed scaling and compiler optimizations compound hardware improvements (Tschand et al. 2024). This trajectory documents improvements in the full hardware-software system beyond transistor scaling alone; the plotted results do not isolate the contribution of competitive pressure from other causes.

The gap between the 6.6\(\times\) transistor baseline and the 34\(\times\) to 48.8\(\times\) workload curves in figure 7 came from exposing and removing bottlenecks that raw silicon TFLOP/s never show, including slow data loading, underutilized accelerators, excessive memory overhead, and communication stalls that erode scaling efficiency. Advertised hardware capability becomes a training speedup only to the extent that an end-to-end training benchmark verifies it under realistic conditions.
Training benchmarks therefore serve four interconnected functions. First, they enable hardware and software optimization by providing vendor-neutral comparisons across accelerator architectures and frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch) on standardized tasks, guiding hardware selection for data centers and cloud environments. Software optimizations including mixed-precision training16 and memory-efficient data loading are similarly quantified. Second, they evaluate scalability, because adding GPUs should reduce training time proportionally, yet communication overhead, synchronization latency, and memory bottlenecks limit scaling efficiency in practice. Training benchmarks quantify these losses, revealing whether infrastructure investments deliver proportional returns. Third, they provide cost and energy accountability, because with a single large-scale training run consuming energy on the scale of the GPT-3 estimate in section 12.5.2.4, benchmarks that track cost per training run and power consumption per unit of progress help organizations balance computational power with sustainability goals. Finally, standardized evaluation criteria, controlled randomness, submission rules, and audits make comparisons more reproducible and constrain implementation-specific shortcuts. Serving all four functions requires a matched set of training metrics, anchored by time to quality and backed by diagnostic measures of scaling, utilization, energy, and fault recovery.
16 Mixed-precision training: Uses lower precision for most arithmetic while preserving higher-precision accumulation where needed (Micikevicius et al. 2018). The benchmarking consequence: mixed-precision and full-precision runs are not directly comparable because reduced memory traffic and larger feasible batch sizes can change convergence dynamics. MLPerf addresses this by fixing the accuracy target, making time-to-accuracy the comparable quantity regardless of precision strategy.
Micikevicius, Paulius, Sharan Narang, Jonah Alben, Gregory Diamos, Erich Elsen, David Garcia, Boris Ginsburg, et al. 2018. “Mixed Precision Training.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).



No single counter captures all four functions of a training benchmark. A complete evaluation pairs an outcome metric, the wall-clock time required to reach a verified quality target, with diagnostic metrics that explain what paced or interrupted the run, namely sample throughput, multi-accelerator scaling efficiency, compute and memory utilization, total energy, and checkpoint overhead.


A training cluster that processes twice as many images per second by doubling the minibatch or dropping precision has not sped up training if the run requires twice as many epochs to converge—or never reaches the quality floor at all. That is why the primary metric for evaluating training efficiency is the time required to reach a predefined accuracy threshold. Training time \((\TrainingTime)\) measures how long a model takes to converge to an acceptable performance level, reflecting the overall computational efficiency of the system. Let \(\text{Accuracy}_{\text{val}}(\TimeInstant)\) be the model’s validation accuracy at training time \(\TimeInstant\), and let the target accuracy be the benchmark-specific threshold (for example, 75.9 percent top-1 accuracy for ResNet-50 on ImageNet in MLPerf). Equation 1 formally defines this metric, keeping the benchmark focused on how quickly a system achieves meaningful results: \[\TrainingTime= \inf \big\{\TimeInstant\geq 0 : \text{Accuracy}_{\text{val}}(\TimeInstant) \geq \text{target accuracy} \big\} \tag{1}\]
A run that never reaches the target has no finite time-to-accuracy, preventing raw training speed from rewarding a system that fails the benchmark’s quality criterion.
Throughput,17 often expressed as the number of training samples processed per second, provides an additional measure of system performance. Let \(\ProcessedSampleCount\) be the total number of training samples processed and \(\TrainingTime\) the training time from equation 1. Equation 2 makes the rate explicit by dividing processed samples by training time: \[\text{Throughput} = \frac{\ProcessedSampleCount}{\TrainingTime} \tag{2}\]
17 Throughput: Originating in manufacturing to measure units produced per unit time, the term entered computing in the 1960s batch-processing era. The manufacturing origin carries a systems lesson: throughput and latency are inherently opposed, because batching increases throughput (more units per hour) at the cost of individual item wait time. In ML serving, this manifests as the batch-size trade-off: larger batches improve GPU utilization but increase per-request latency.
MLCommons. 2024c. MLPerf Training Benchmark.
Throughput alone cannot certify system capability. A platform may sustain high sample rates using aggressive low-precision formats or enormous minibatches, yet fail to reach target accuracy because of gradient divergence or poor generalization. In MLPerf Training, for instance, a ResNet-50 benchmark on ImageNet is valid only if the model achieves the required 75.9 percent top-1 validation accuracy (Mattson et al. 2020; MLCommons 2024c). Evaluating throughput strictly as the rate of progress toward convergence ensures that reported gains reflect genuine learning productivity rather than wasted arithmetic cycles.



Scalability measures how effectively training performance improves as resources are added. Ideally, doubling GPU count should halve training time. In practice, communication overhead, memory bandwidth limits, and parallelization inefficiencies constrain scaling well below linear.

Napkin Math 12.3: Scaling efficiency calculationProblem: A team trains an image classifier on a fixed dataset. Single-GPU training takes 24 hours. With 8 GPUs, training takes 4 hours. Is this good scaling? Where did the efficiency go?
Step 1: Define scaling efficiency. For strong scaling (fixed problem size, more processors), let \(\Time(1)\) be the training time on a single GPU, and \(\Time(\AcceleratorCount)\) the training time on \(\AcceleratorCount\) GPUs. Equation 3 defines efficiency: \[\text{Eff}_{\text{scaling}}(\AcceleratorCount) = \frac{\Time(1)}{\AcceleratorCount \times \Time(\AcceleratorCount)} \times 100\% \tag{3}\]
Step 2: Calculate efficiency. \(\text{Eff}_{\text{scaling}}(8) = \frac{24\,\text{hours}}{8 \times 4\,\text{hours}} \times 100\%\) = 24/32 = 75 percent
With perfect scaling, 8 GPUs would complete in 3 hours (24 hours/8 GPUs). The actual 4 hours represents 75 percent efficiency.
Step 3: Investigate the efficiency loss. The two elapsed times establish the “missing” 25 percent, but do not attribute it. Table 11 lists illustrative contributions and profiling signals for gradient synchronization, memory copy, load imbalance, and batch-size effects. Strong-scaling comparisons hold total work fixed; time-to-quality comparisons must also account for any change in steps to convergence.
In multi-accelerator data-parallel training (such as 2, 4, or 8 GPUs connected over PCIe or NVLink within a host), each accelerator computes gradients on its own local slice of the minibatch. The AllReduce collective of Data parallelism must sum these gradients so every worker receives the identical global gradient average before the next step. Gradient tensors have one entry per trained parameter, but their byte payload equals weight storage only when their representations match. Moving them across interconnects adds communication whose cost depends on topology, the collective algorithm, and overlap. With fixed total work and ideal partitioning, compute time per step shrinks (\(\IronLawComputeTime \propto 1/\AcceleratorCount\)), while communication may shrink more slowly or grow. Exposed synchronization then occupies a larger fraction of the step; traces determine how much of the observed scaling loss it explains.

Parallelism strategies (data, model, and pipeline parallelism) and the synchronization each requires are developed in Data parallelism; within one machine of two to eight accelerators, data parallelism is the common case. A benchmark’s job is narrower: to report how much of the added capacity a configuration converts into speedup without degrading convergence. That conversion is scaling efficiency. While strong scaling evaluates whether adding processors reduces training time on a fixed total workload, weak scaling scales the problem size proportionally with processor count to keep the per-device workload constant. It measures whether the system can train larger models or ingest larger datasets within a fixed time budget without communication bottlenecks dominating.



Training efficiency depends on learning speed, cluster scalability, and how effectively the hardware resources are used. Compute utilization requires an explicit numerator. Model FLOPs utilization (MFU), the metric of definition \(\ref{dfn-training-model-flops-utilization-mfu}\), compares the useful model operation rate with the matching hardware peak; activity counters instead report whether units are busy. MFU contrasts with hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU), which counts all executed operations including activation recomputation; recomputation adds executed FLOPs without adding useful model FLOPs for the same step. Comparing them separates useful model work from work expended to relieve memory capacity limits. Low utilization may indicate bottlenecks in data movement, memory access, or inefficient workload scheduling.
For instance, when training ResNet-50 on a dataset too large to fit entirely in host memory, retrieving batches from storage and decoding and augmenting thousands of JPEG images per second on the host can limit throughput even when the accelerators have compute to spare, the crossing from compute-bound to input-bound that Data pipeline traces. If storage retrieval or host preprocessing cannot keep up, the accelerators wait; profiling I/O and compute utilization isolates that stall so prefetching, caching, and parallel input processing can restore sustained throughput.
Memory bandwidth is another limiting factor, as deep learning models require frequent access to large volumes of data during training. If memory bandwidth saturates, increasing compute power alone will not improve training speed. Benchmarks assess how well models use available memory, ensuring that data transfer rates between storage, main memory, and processing units do not become performance bottlenecks.



Training GPT-3 was estimated to consume 1,287 MWh of electricity (Patterson et al. 2021). At that scale, energy efficiency metrics quantify the power usage of training workloads so teams can identify systems that reach target accuracy without wasted energy. Fewer iterations reduce energy only when their total energy cost is lower; a more expensive step can offset the reduced count, so suites such as MLPerf Training measure total energy over the complete run to the same quality target. The same power accounting governs inference, where precision is one potential energy lever; section 12.7 works through why INT8 quantization cuts per-inference energy by attacking both memory traffic and arithmetic cost.
Cost considerations extend beyond electricity usage to include hardware expenses, cloud computing costs, and infrastructure maintenance. Training benchmarks provide insights into the cost-effectiveness of different hardware and software configurations by measuring training time in relation to resource expenditure. Organizations can use these benchmarks to balance performance and budget constraints when selecting training infrastructure.



Training workloads often run for extended periods, sometimes spanning days or weeks, making fault tolerance an essential consideration. A resilient system must handle unexpected failures (hardware malfunctions, network disruptions, and memory errors) without compromising accuracy convergence.
Production systems checkpoint for fault tolerance, periodically saving progress so a failure does not restart the run. On a single host, a benchmark records the save interval, the state written, and the pause each save exposes to training. Model weights and optimizer states consume storage bandwidth, and any pause extends wall-clock time to the quality target. Asynchronous saving can overlap I/O with computation, but its staging buffers and competing storage traffic remain part of the measured workload. Cluster recovery and parallel file systems extend this problem beyond the local machine; the local benchmarking lesson is to include the intended saving behavior in sustained performance measurements. MLPerf Training primarily measures time-to-quality under standardized workloads and does not benchmark failure recovery directly.
Training runs are also where reproducibility is hardest, because stochastic processes interact with hardware-specific behavior over many hours. What a training report must preserve to make its result reproducible, the full run envelope rather than the random seed alone, is collected with the other statistical controls in section 12.8.2.




A single time-to-accuracy score tells an engineering team whether a run met its deadline, but not why an eight-GPU configuration lost a quarter of its ideal speedup or whether buying faster interconnects would fix it. Each metric category in table 12 isolates a different way hardware investment can fail to become convergence, turning a headline runtime into an actionable diagnosis.

The measured completion times establish a speedup and a resource-efficiency cost, but they do not identify which overhead caused the difference. A procurement decision therefore uses the time-to-quality result first, then the utilization and communication measurements to decide whether additional hardware or a different execution configuration would address the limiting resource.
