Exporting an optimized model from a training framework produces an intermediate graph representation, not an executable binary. Compilers and runtime engines such as TensorRT, Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA), OpenVINO, and TVM own the final translation step: compiling a pruned, quantized, or fused graph into machine instructions tailored to the target accelerator. In D·A·M terms, algorithmic compression remains theoretical until the graph maps to kernels that physically exploit the target machine’s memory hierarchy and execution units.
The compilation pass verifies whether nominal compression yields physical speedup. Pruning that leaves zeros in dense tensors still streams and multiplies those entries with a dense kernel. Compact sparse formats need matching kernels, such as a supported 2:4 path, while structured channel removal can produce smaller tensors for ordinary dense kernels. Quantization lowers bitwidth, but a weight-only path may unpack operands into floating-point registers before arithmetic. That unpacking adds instructions; its cost must be compared with the packed weight traffic saved.
The result can be the runtime dequantization trap. If an accelerator provides native INT8 matrix-multiplication kernels but lacks an INT8 implementation for an adjacent operation (such as LayerNorm, GeLU, or an attention softmax reduction), the runtime encounters a type boundary. An unfused execution path may allocate a temporary buffer, launch a dequantization kernel to recover floating-point values (\(\QuantizerInput= \QuantizationScale(\QuantizedIntegerCode - \QuantizationZeroPoint)\), equation 4), execute the unsupported operator, and launch another kernel to re-quantize its output. The floating-point format and opportunities to fuse conversion depend on the runtime. These intermediate format conversions incur extra kernel launches, introduce synchronization barriers, and add temporary floating-point traffic that can make the quantized model slower than the FP16 baseline. A fused weight-only path instead unpacks values within the consuming kernel, the fusion of section 10.4.1, and retains a net memory-traffic benefit.
Low-precision kernels also require specialized tensor layouts, such as tiled or interleaved memory channels, to ensure coalesced loads into shared memory or register files. When an unsupported operator sequence blocks the fusions of section 10.4.1, the memory-bandwidth bottleneck remains intact. Whether integrated into a framework or supplied separately, the compiler and runtime determine which graph-level opportunities become an efficient machine execution plan. Whether that plan delivers the savings computed in the earlier sections is a question only measurement on the target hardware can answer.

Shrinking a model’s weights by \(4\times\) with INT8 quantization rarely cuts end-to-end latency by \(4\times\), because cache residency, memory bus contention, and kernel launch overhead absorb much of the theoretical gain. Every saving computed so far in this chapter is a paper bound, and only a measurement on the target device turns a bound into a result. Profiling on the deployment hardware identifies which resource binds each layer, fixes an honest baseline, and separates model execution time from runtime and pipeline overhead.


Compressing the layers with the most parameters or FLOPs can leave wall-clock latency barely changed when low-intensity operators, such as layer normalization or elementwise activations, contribute almost no FLOPs yet consume a large share of execution time by streaming whole activation tensors across memory. The top-down profiling method of Identifying Bottlenecks tells compression where to act, and two of its measurements decide the technique. Static footprint (weight tensors and persistent buffers) decides whether parameters fit in fast memory or device DRAM without spilling across PCIe, while dynamic allocation (activation tensors and KV caches) sets peak residency and so bounds batch size and serving concurrency. Alongside memory residency, each operator’s arithmetic intensity (\(\ArithmeticIntensity= \Operations/\DataVolume\)) shows whether removing FLOPs or removing bytes will actually shorten it.
A profile of a Vision Transformer (ViT) on an edge accelerator illustrates this operational heterogeneity. Per token and layer, the multilayer perceptron (MLP) block costs about \(8\HiddenDimension^2\) multiply-accumulates against \(4\HiddenDimension^2\) for the query, key, value, and output projections. In a ViT-Base-sized model the MLP blocks therefore carry nearly two-thirds of FLOPs and the projections just under one-third, with the attention score and weighting products adding only a few percent at standard image resolution. Layer normalization inverts the picture, contributing almost no FLOPs yet claiming a visible share of wall-clock latency, because it streams whole activation tensors with little arithmetic per byte. The camera pipeline’s MobileNetV2 splits the same way in convolutional form. Its \(1{\times}1\) expansion and projection layers carry most of the multiply-accumulates (Sandler et al. 2018), while its depthwise layers, like layer normalization, do little arithmetic per byte moved and take a larger share of time than of work. Profiling isolates the governing physical bottleneck for each component, which calls for targeted optimizations rather than uniform compression. Structured pruning of MLP hidden units relieves the compute-dominant blocks. Kernel fusion eliminates intermediate global memory round-trips for memory-bound normalization layers. INT8 quantization shrinks the static footprint that the MLP and projection weights dominate.

Sandler, Mark, Andrew Howard, Menglong Zhu, Andrey Zhmoginov, and Liang-Chieh Chen. 2018. “MobileNetV2: Inverted Residuals and Linear Bottlenecks.” 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 4510–20. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2018.00474.


Non-model work dominates latency, so compression caps speedup at 1.25\(\times\).

Translating layer-level profiling metrics into end-to-end system speedup requires accounting for the complete serving pipeline. In production serving systems, model execution frequently represents only a fraction of total latency, with the remainder consumed by image decoding, tokenization, RPC deserialization, or network transfer. Optimizing the model in isolation encounters an Amdahl ceiling whenever non-model stages dominate the latency budget, a ceiling that End-to-end vs. component latency measures end to end.

Systems Perspective 10.4: FLOPs reduction is not proportional speedupReducing a model’s FLOPs by 50 percent does not guarantee 50 percent latency reduction. Memory-bound operations see little benefit from arithmetic reduction because data movement, not multiplication, sets their time. Amdahl’s law (principle \(\ref{pri-amdahl}\)) applies at the system level. If model inference accounts for only 20 percent of end-to-end latency (with the remaining 80 percent spent on data loading, preprocessing, and postprocessing), then even perfect model optimization yields at most 1.25× overall speedup. Tokenization and network transfer can occupy the non-model fraction in language-model serving; image decoding, resizing, and normalization can do the same in vision pipelines. Profile the complete path on target hardware before estimating optimization benefits.


Complementing latency and throughput profiles, layer-wise sensitivity analysis quantifies how individual layers tolerate perturbation. In deep networks, different layers tolerate different amounts of precision reduction or weight removal. Profiling accuracy degradation while systematically perturbing one layer at a time, with quantization noise or weight removal, identifies which components require high-precision representations and which can absorb aggressive 4-bit quantization or structured pruning without compromising task accuracy. Once opportunity and sensitivity profiles have guided a compression pass, the resulting candidate must be evaluated across both statistical quality and physical execution metrics.



Judging a compressed model by a single scalar metric, such as top-1 accuracy or parameter count, can approve a candidate whose batch-one latency barely budges under kernel-launch overhead or whose confidence calibration drifts past safety limits on rare subgroups. Evaluating compression requires balancing statistical quality against physical execution costs across the Data, Algorithm, and Machine (D·A·M) axes. Quality baselines must capture aggregate accuracy, confidence calibration (verifying that predicted probabilities reflect empirical correctness), and performance across underrepresented input slices. Simultaneously, efficiency baselines must record peak memory residency, latency distributions (including p99 tail latency), memory bus saturation, and per-inference energy.

Converting weights to INT8 shrinks the artifact by 4× (from 102.2 MB to 25.6 MB), but the speed gain depends on how the model is served. At batch one, a compiled INT8 engine is only 1.3× faster than its FP32 counterpart (0.30 ms against 0.38 ms), because launch overhead, per-kernel floors, and the weight read form most of a single image’s time and shrink little with precision. At large batch the arithmetic dominates, and INT8 throughput of 89,470 img/s, as MLPerf Inference measured it, is 5.9× the modeled FP32 rate, a ratio between a measured rate and a modeled one from different software stacks. Energy per image follows throughput only if the board draws its full 700 W in both precisions; the 5.9× energy figure is that assumption, not a separate measurement. The runtime comparison in Inference Runtime Selection derives both latency figures from the same engine profile. While aggregate top-1 accuracy drops by only 0.3 percentage points (from 76.1 percent to 75.8 percent), confidence-calibration error (the gap between predicted probability and observed accuracy, distinct from the range calibration of quantization) increases from 2.1 percent to 3.4 percent. Post-quantization probability distributions drift, which can compromise safety-critical confidence thresholds even when top-1 classification accuracy appears preserved. Production deployment decisions require corresponding quality, latency, and energy measurements using a supported execution path on target hardware.
Suppose the application requires at least 75.5 percent top-1 accuracy and no more than 3.0 percent confidence-calibration error, measured with the same validation data and calibration metric as the profile. The INT8 candidate passes the accuracy limit but fails the calibration limit. Its modeled resource savings therefore do not justify acceptance. Retain the baseline for comparison, try confidence recalibration or a less aggressive quantization configuration, and repeat the quality checks before validating resource gains on the target runtime.



The INT8 candidate fails the calibration limit despite holding accuracy.
A deployment profile shows whether a compressed model meets its limits but not why it misses one. Explaining a failure such as the calibration miss above requires looking inside the model, at where clipping, rounding, and pruning masks have changed its internal values.



An exported model can fail a quality or latency gate, as the ResNet-50 candidate did when its confidence calibration drifted to 3.4 percent. Summary metrics cannot tell whether the culprit is a single activation channel saturating its clipping bounds, a pruning mask erasing an active feature detector, or an unsupported operator falling back to floating point. Diagnostic inspection looks inside the compressed graph to verify numerical integrity after framework APIs calibrate the model and hardware optimization libraries lower it to the execution substrate (section 10.5.4). While system-scale validation and artifact monitoring belong to downstream deployment infrastructure, the immediate diagnostic task is verifying that quantization clipping, pruning masks, or sparsity patterns have not perturbed internal feature distributions beyond acceptable task error tolerances.
Quantization error histograms show whether error is broadly distributed or concentrated in outliers. Activation visualizations help detect clipping, overflow, and saturation. In a grid of first-layer convolutional filters, the top rows show distinct edge, color, and frequency detectors, while the bottom row shows uniform-looking filters that appear redundant at a glance but require measured activation tracing before they can be pruned safely (figure 31). Framework observers and debuggers can expose quantization ranges and tensor error, while compiler or runtime inspectors can show the graph and kernels that the exported model actually executes.

Appearance alone does not establish inactivity; pruning requires measured activation or importance evidence in addition to low weight variance.



Sparsity diagnostics identify candidate layers for sparse execution. The layer-wise schematic in figure 32 spans convolutional, fully connected, and transformer layer types and is not a measurement from one model or pruning run. Its rows illustrate how a pruning policy might distribute zeros unevenly across architectural blocks. A real diagnostic would pair each layer’s density with its storage format and target-kernel profile to determine whether those zeros reduce memory traffic or execution time. Graph viewers and sparsity inspection tools help locate the affected tensors; profiling establishes the deployment benefit.






Figure 32: Illustrative Layer-Wise Sparsity Distribution: This schematic combines several layer types to illustrate non-uniform parameter removal. Darker tiles indicate more zero-valued weights; their shade establishes neither task redundancy nor a runtime benefit.



The diagnostic value is the nonuniformity, not the exact shade of any one cell. Greater sparsity in later layers shows where the policy removed weights; it does not establish that those representations were redundant. Compare task quality after removing weights from a candidate layer and after recovery training, including performance on important input slices. Early-layer sparsity warrants the same checks because damaging feature extraction can propagate through subsequent layers. Only those comparisons can establish whether the observed removal pattern preserves required behavior. Each density also has a machine reading, because a layer whose zeros never cross the storage and execution break-even of section 10.4.2.2 saves neither bytes nor time, however dark its tile.

Checkpoint 10.5: From compression claim to deployment evidence
A compressed artifact must pass the same application requirements as its baseline.

Footprint and feasibility: distinguish raw weight size from peak runtime memory, including activations, caches, metadata, and workspace.
Modeled and measured gains: identify which claims in the ResNet-50 profile require target-hardware measurements, and explain why fewer FLOPs or bytes alone cannot establish latency.
Quality and operating limits: specify the accuracy, confidence calibration, tail-latency, sustained-power, and energy checks needed before accepting a candidate.



Profiling, six-metric deployment scorecards, and layer-wise diagnostic plots turn compression from a paper-FLOP exercise into a verifiable engineering discipline, while the experimental design and statistical rigor that make benchmark comparisons reproducible across systems are developed in Benchmarking. Even with those measurement tools in place, however, recurring traps across pruning, quantization, and hardware lowering can still turn a promising checkpoint into a latency regression or a silent quality failure, and the fallacies that follow collect the most common ones.

A team deploying GPT-2 XL on a phone might find that an uncalibrated 4-bit quantization cuts weight memory by 4\(\times\) while generation quality collapses. Conversely, a vision team might achieve 70 percent weight sparsity through unstructured pruning only to find inference latency increases because commodity GPU kernels cannot execute irregular sparse indexing. Model compression presents numerous counterintuitive traps where theoretical parameter or FLOP reductions fail to produce wall-clock speedups. The following fallacies and pitfalls examine where standard engineering assumptions break down across the model-runtime interface.

Fallacy: Optimization techniques can be applied independently without considering their interactions.
Engineers assume optimization strategies compose additively: 50 percent pruning plus 4× quantization yields combined benefits. In reality, techniques interact nonlinearly and compound losses. In a representative BERT-style compression scenario, pruning to 70 percent sparsity may preserve most task performance, but applying INT8 quantization afterward can lose more accuracy than QAT on the pruned model. Knowledge distillation from heavily pruned teachers can also transfer degenerate attention patterns that reduce student accuracy compared with distilling from dense teachers. As section 10.5.3 demonstrates, successful optimization requires coordinated application where techniques are sequenced together.


Pitfall: Assuming theoretical metrics or compression ratios translate directly into proportional deployment speedup.
Teams frequently reduce FLOPs or parameter counts substantially without realizing proportional latency gains on physical hardware. In one representative trace, a pruned model with 40 percent fewer parameters achieves only a 12 percent latency reduction because irregular sparsity prevents efficient execution. Similarly, reducing a transformer from 440 MB to 110 MB through INT8 quantization yields a 4× raw weight-payload reduction, yet format conversion and scalar fallback on hardware without a native low-precision datapath erode the latency gain. In the chapter’s illustrative composed pipeline combining 50 percent structured pruning and INT8 quantization, the realized speedup reaches only 1.5× against an 8× paper target. Measure wall-clock latency on the target execution units rather than extrapolating from nominal compression ratios.


Fallacy: Aggressive quantization maintains model performance with minimal accuracy loss.
Engineers assume quantization error scales uniformly with bit width. In practice, precision reduction can show threshold effects, and the threshold depends on the model, layer, quantizer, calibration, and training method. The ResNet and BERT values in this chapter are illustrative rather than universal degradation bands. Even operations such as LayerNorm and Softmax can be implemented with integer approximations, so they do not universally require FP16; whether a low-precision implementation preserves task quality must be measured. As section 10.3.3 demonstrates, mixed-precision approaches can retain higher precision where uniform quantization fails.


Pitfall: Defaulting to FP32 everywhere to avoid quantization risk.
FP32 uses twice the raw storage and bandwidth of BF16, but lower-precision execution does not automatically preserve convergence or accuracy. Mixed-precision training often retains FP32 accumulators or master weights and may require loss scaling, while inference precision must be validated per model and operator. The right question is what lowest precision preserves quality on the evaluation distribution and maps efficiently to the target hardware.


Fallacy: Post-training optimization is always enough.
Teams often begin with post-training quantization (PTQ) because it avoids retraining, and move to quantization-aware training (QAT) only when the PTQ artifact misses its thresholds. Post-training pruning and post-hoc distillation can likewise underperform training-aware schedules at aggressive sparsity or bit width. As detailed in section 10.3.3, the production threshold, not a presumption that either path is universally superior, governs the decision.


Fallacy: Sparse matrix representations always save memory and accelerate inference.
Sparse formats introduce coordinate metadata that erodes storage savings at moderate densities, as the 16-bit case of section 10.4.2.2 showed; 32-bit indices make the penalty larger. To represent \(\NonzeroCount\) nonzero values across \(\SparseMatrixRowCount\) rows, a coordinate list (COO) stores explicit coordinate tuples (row_idx, col_idx, value). For 32-bit floats and 32-bit integer indices, each nonzero element consumes 12 bytes (\(3\times\) a dense 4-byte FP32 entry), requiring greater than 66.7 percent sparsity just to break even on memory footprint. Compressed sparse row (CSR) eliminates redundant row coordinates by storing three arrays: values (\(\NonzeroCount \times 4\text{ B}\)), col_indices (\(\NonzeroCount \times 4\text{ B}\)), and row_pointers (\((\SparseMatrixRowCount+1) \times 4\text{ B}\)). Each nonzero entry costs 8 bytes (\(2\times\) a dense FP32 entry), requiring over 50 percent sparsity before the sparse structure consumes less memory than the original dense tensor; below 50 percent sparsity, CSR metadata expands the model’s memory footprint.
Execution faces similar break-even constraints. Converting tensors to sparse storage as soon as pruning creates zeros degrades latency if metadata decoding, irregular gather operations, and poor cache locality outweigh the saved arithmetic. No universal sparsity threshold exists, because tensor dimensions, sparse format, runtime kernel, batch size, and hardware architecture jointly govern whether sparse execution outperforms dense execution. Specialized formats such as 2:4 structured sparsity eliminate index arrays in favor of fixed 2-bit multiplexer metadata, providing an accelerator datapath that nearly halves weight traffic with minimal indexing overhead (section 10.2.1.3). Production workflows must therefore measure realized density and commit to a sparse representation only after verifying that the operational break-even threshold has been crossed on target hardware.

Model compression fits a trained model inside a deployment budget by working three tiers of one stack, the descent the chapter map laid out at the start (table 2). Structural optimization changes what the model computes, precision changes how each value is stored, and hardware implementation decides how efficiently the remaining operations execute. The running cases showed each tier where it matters most. The camera pipeline’s MobileNetV2 spends its frame budget on arithmetic, so channel pruning, distillation from a ResNet-50 teacher, and an INT8 path onto the phone’s integer accelerator are its levers. GPT-2 XL decoding spends its token on bytes, so INT4 weights raise its token rate by 3.1× on the same phone, and only when dequantization is fused into the matrix multiplication. The tiers can compound, but their gains do not multiply automatically. Pruning, distillation, and quantization together produce the illustrative pipeline’s 16× footprint reduction from 440 MB to 28 MB; metadata, unsupported operators, and hardware mapping determine the realized deployment gain. A parameter reduction approaches the same latency reduction only when the affected work is on the critical path and the runtime can exploit the new representation. Profile on target hardware, not paper metrics.
Data selection and model compression divide the efficiency work along the D·A·M axes. Data selection acts on the Data axis and lowers the cost of producing a model by spending compute only on examples that carry signal. Compression acts where Algorithm meets Machine and lowers the cost of running the model by reshaping its structure and numerics for the target. Whether those deployment savings become real speedups still depends on the hardware and runtime that execute the compressed model. The need for them does not fade, because the bitter lesson keeps growing the models that win benchmarks while the envelopes of phones and microcontrollers stay fixed.

Key Takeaways: From benchmark winner to production model

Compression spends surplus capacity: Production models trade unused parameters, precision, and capacity for latency, memory, power, or cost limits the deployment cannot violate. The target is an artifact that meets the deployment objective and all required quality and resource constraints.
Savings multiply only when aligned: Structural pruning, distillation, quantization, and architecture changes can compound raw footprint reductions, as the modeled BERT mobile pipeline’s 16× ratio illustrates. The gain becomes real only when task quality holds and the resulting operators match the target runtime and accelerator.
Precision is a deployment decision: Where the target runtime supports it, INT8 post-training quantization is a useful first experiment because it reduces raw FP32 weight payload by 4\(\times\) without retraining. QAT, distillation, or mixed precision become candidates when range calibration or layer sensitivity exposes unacceptable error.
Hardware decides what a saving is worth: Unstructured sparsity and theoretical FLOP cuts do not imply latency gains unless kernels and memory layouts can exploit them. The chapter’s hypothetical 8× paper target vs. 1.5× realized outcome illustrates why target-hardware profiling is mandatory.
End-to-end latency caps model wins: Compression reduces end-to-end latency only when it accelerates the critical path; capacity or energy savings can remain valuable elsewhere. When inference is 20 percent of total request latency, Amdahl’s law (principle \(\ref{pri-amdahl}\)) caps even perfect model acceleration at 1.25×, so preprocessing, dispatch, and data movement may be the true optimization target.



The techniques in this chapter differ in almost every detail, yet one rule runs beneath all of them. Each obtains a smaller, faster, or cooler model by giving up something else. Pruning gives up capacity, quantization gives up numerical precision, and distillation consumes training compute. Where the model holds no surplus to give up, task quality degrades instead. Apart from removing genuinely avoidable work, such as an unfused intermediate round-trip, compression does not make the work disappear; it moves cost or risk from one part of the system to another, and the hardware decides how much each move saves. A technique that helps on a phone can therefore be worthless on a data-center GPU. This is the conservation-of-complexity heuristic at the level of a single model. A production artifact is a model whose structure, representation, and execution path have been engineered together until they fit the silicon and application constraints that govern deployment.

What’s Next: From math to physicsThese optimization techniques compress the model’s logic, reducing the work the algorithm asks the machine to perform. Whether less work becomes less time depends on the silicon that executes it, and this chapter repeatedly ran into the memory wall, the regime where fetching a weight costs more than computing with it. Hardware Acceleration starts from that wall and from the ResNet-50 INT8 profile that closed this chapter. It explains how GPUs, TPUs, and NPUs organize tensor units, systolic arrays, and tiered SRAM/HBM hierarchies to keep arithmetic fed, which is what decides whether a quantized or sparse representation actually runs faster.

A ____ is the memory, time, and energy that a target device grants to each result a model produces, and model compression is the work of bringing a trained model’s demands inside it.
Answer: deployment budget. Memory capacity bounds the bytes of weights and activations that can stay resident, a frame rate or token rate bounds the milliseconds available for each result, and a battery or thermal envelope bounds the joules each result may consume. A trained model’s demands were set by the accelerators it trained on, not by the device it must run on.
Learning Objective: Define the deployment budget and name the three resources it bounds.
Across the deployment contexts analyzed in the chapter, which platform most clearly makes model compression a feasibility requirement rather than mainly a throughput or cost optimization?

TinyML microcontrollers, where SRAM and storage budgets are so small that some models cannot be placed at all without compression or redesign
Cloud inference clusters, where only cloud systems face hard capacity limits and all smaller devices can compensate in software
Autonomous edge servers, where continuous thermal throttling is preferred over changing the model
Mobile smartphones, where unified memory architecture eliminates meaningful capacity constraints for large neural networks

Answer: The correct answer is A. TinyML devices can have only hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM plus separate flash or storage limits, so a model may simply not fit unless its weights and working set are reduced enough. Capacity limits also matter on mobile and cloud systems, but the chapter uses microcontrollers to illustrate the clearest hard feasibility boundary. Claims that only cloud has hard limits or that phone memory is effectively unconstrained contradict the section’s deployment-budget comparison.
Learning Objective: Compare deployment contexts to identify where compression is most directly required for basic model feasibility
A mobile video-conferencing feature requires \(30\text{ FPS}\) background segmentation, but baseline FP32 MobileNetV2 runs at only \(8\text{ FPS}\). Applying INT8 quantization accelerates the model to \(35\text{ FPS}\) with a minor \(0.4\%\) drop in mIoU, satisfying the shipping requirement. Which region of the chapter’s compression-accuracy Pareto frontier best describes this outcome?

Region 1 (little or no quality loss), because achieving 35 FPS proves that INT8 quantization incurs zero loss in segmentation boundary fidelity
Region 3 (steep quality loss), because any reduction in numerical precision destabilizes temporal consistency in video processing
An unfeasible operating point outside the Pareto frontier, because 35 FPS exceeds the maximum display refresh rate
Region 2 (a moderate trade), because a modest, acceptable drop in segmentation accuracy unlocks a 4.4× frame rate increase that satisfies the 30 FPS real-time shipping threshold

Answer: The correct answer is D. Region 2 (a moderate trade) represents the practical operational sweet spot where an engineer trades a small, tolerable accuracy concession for a massive efficiency gain (\(8\text{ FPS} \to 35\text{ FPS}\)) that moves the application across a hard production requirement (\(30\text{ FPS}\)). Placing it in region 1 (little or no quality loss) overlooks that INT8 rounding introduces real numerical quantization error, while placing it in region 3 (steep quality loss) confuses a successful deployment trade-off with catastrophic accuracy failure.
Learning Objective: Classify real-world deployment trade-offs into the three characteristic regions of the compression-accuracy Pareto frontier

Structured pruning removes more total weight parameters than unstructured pruning at any given nominal sparsity percentage
Structured pruning removes entire contiguous channels or filters, allowing smaller dense kernels to execute efficiently, whereas unstructured sparsity needs sparse storage, metadata, and irregular activation access

Order the stages of finding a winning lottery ticket in a neural network according to the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH): (1) Reset surviving weights to their original initialization values (\(W_0\)), (2) Train the dense unpruned network to convergence, (3) Retrain the sparse subnetwork to convergence, (4) Prune the lowest-magnitude weights to create a sparse mask.
Answer: The correct order is: (2) Train the dense unpruned network to convergence, (4) Prune the lowest-magnitude weights to create a sparse mask, (1) Reset surviving weights to their original initialization values (\(W_0\)), (3) Retrain the sparse subnetwork to convergence. First, dense training allows gradient descent to differentiate parameter importance. Second, magnitude pruning isolates the most critical connections to form a binary mask. Third, resetting surviving parameters to their exact initial values (\(W_0\)) isolates the subnetwork’s topological initialization. Finally, retraining the sparse subnetwork validates whether it can match or exceed the original dense model’s accuracy.
Learning Objective: Design an experimental procedure that sequences the iterative steps used to evaluate winning lottery tickets under the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
A team must compress a large transformer model for deployment across a fleet of commodity GPUs that lack dedicated sparse-matrix acceleration kernels. Which structural optimization technique is the strongest candidate for producing a smaller model that still executes efficiently on this hardware?

Unstructured magnitude pruning, because sparse matrix multiplication routines run with zero memory overhead on all standard GPUs
Extreme binary weight quantization, because 1-bit representations eliminate all memory traffic without degrading language model perplexity
Knowledge distillation, because it transfers teacher behavior into a compact dense student architecture that runs well on standard dense GPU kernels
Low-rank factorization without fine-tuning, because mathematical decomposition guarantees zero loss in representation capacity

Answer: The correct answer is C. Distillation trains a new compact dense student, so the deployed model can use ordinary dense kernels that commodity GPUs already execute efficiently. That makes it a strong candidate when sparse acceleration support is absent. Unstructured pruning still depends on sparse formats and kernels, low-rank factorization is an approximation rather than a zero-loss guarantee, and the section does not claim pruning can never remove layers or that binary quantization is broadly safe for this setting.
Learning Objective: Evaluate distillation as a structural optimization candidate when deployment hardware favors dense execution
A square weight matrix of size \(4096 \times 4096\) in a transformer layer is decomposed using low-rank factorization at rank \(r = 128\). Calculate the theoretical reduction factor in both parameter count and multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, and explain what trade-off this structural approximation introduces.
Answer: The original matrix contains \(4096 \times 4096 = 16{,}777{,}216\) parameters (\(16.78\text{M}\) MACs per vector product). Factoring into two matrices of dimensions \(4096 \times 128\) and \(128 \times 4096\) requires \(2 \times (4096 \times 128) = 1{,}048{,}576\) parameters (\(1.05\text{M}\) MACs). This yields an exact theoretical reduction factor of \(\frac{4096^2}{2 \times 4096 \times 128} = \frac{4096}{256} = 16\times\) for both parameter storage and arithmetic operations. The trade-off is that factorization restricts the layer’s representational capacity to a low-dimensional subspace of rank 128, which can degrade model expressiveness and task accuracy unless recovered through subsequent fine-tuning, while introducing the runtime overhead of launching two consecutive matrix multiplication kernels.
Learning Objective: Calculate parameter and arithmetic reduction factors for low-rank matrix factorization and evaluate the resulting rank-capacity trade-off
An engineering organization is deciding between running a custom Neural Architecture Search (NAS) from scratch versus adopting an established NAS-discovered family (such as MobileNetV3 or EfficientNet). Which circumstance most strongly justifies investing in custom NAS?

Novel or custom hardware accelerators with unique memory hierarchies or massive production deployment scale where small per-inference efficiency gains amortize large one-time search costs
Standard GPU clusters running established vision benchmarks where off-the-shelf architectures like MobileNetV3 already fit latency budgets
Rapid prototyping projects with a total engineering timeline under one week and fewer than 10 available GPUs
Small-scale enterprise applications processing fewer than 1,000 queries per day on cloud instances

Answer: The correct answer is A. Custom Neural Architecture Search (NAS) incurs substantial compute expenditure (historically hundreds to thousands of GPU-days), making it justifiable primarily when targeting novel hardware accelerators whose physical constraints are not served by existing architectures, or when extreme deployment scale (billions of daily inferences) allows modest per-query latency and energy gains to rapidly amortize the upfront search cost. For standard hardware, existing NAS-designed architectures (e.g., EfficientNet, MobileNetV3) provide proven efficiency out of the box without incurring search expenses. Fast prototyping and low-volume applications cannot justify the substantial time and compute cost required by NAS.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the economic and architectural conditions that justify custom Neural Architecture Search versus adopting established efficient architectures
Compare one-shot pruning with an iterative schedule that removes 10 percentage points of the original weights in each of 8 rounds with recovery between rounds. Explain why staged recovery can help, and what controlled comparison is needed before concluding that the iterative schedule is better.
Answer: Iterative pruning removes capacity in stages, giving the surviving weights chances to recover after each cut, so it is often a strong candidate when high sparsity is the goal. For example, eight rounds of removing \(10\) percentage points of the original weights each can reach \(80\%\) total sparsity while interleaving recovery. But the chapter does not claim this always beats one-shot pruning at the same final target: the outcome depends on the recovery budget, architecture, and pruning procedure. The practical implication is to compare schedules fairly at matched recovery effort instead of assuming staged pruning is universally superior.
Learning Objective: Compare one-shot and iterative pruning while recognizing that recovery quality depends on schedule and recovery budget, not a universal rule

According to the chapter’s Horowitz energy constants, an INT8 integer addition consumes roughly \(0.03\text{ pJ}\) compared to \(0.90\text{ pJ}\) for an FP32 addition—a \(30\times\) energy reduction despite only a \(4\times\) reduction in bit-width. What explains this operation-level energy dividend?

INT8 arithmetic eliminates the need for registers and ALU logic on the silicon die
INT8 quantization automatically prunes zero-valued parameters before they reach the execution units
The 8-bit integer adder circuit requires significantly fewer logic gates, capacitance, and switching energy per operation than a 32-bit floating-point adder with exponent alignment and normalization logic
Floating-point operations require continuous synchronization with host CPU DRAM on every instruction

Answer: The correct answer is C. The \(30\times\) arithmetic energy disparity (\(0.03\text{ pJ}\) for INT8 add vs. \(0.9\text{ pJ}\) for FP32 add based on Horowitz constants) stems directly from silicon circuit complexity: an 8-bit integer addition requires a compact adder circuit with minimal logic gates and switching capacitance, whereas a 32-bit floating-point adder requires extensive barrel shifters for exponent alignment, mantissa addition, normalization, and rounding logic. Quantization does not eliminate ALU circuitry or prune parameters, nor does FP32 require host CPU synchronization.
Learning Objective: Explain the circuit-level physical mechanisms responsible for the energy efficiency advantage of INT8 arithmetic over FP32
In affine (asymmetric) quantization, the integer parameter ____ shifts the quantized grid so that real-valued zero maps exactly to an integer representation, ensuring that zero-padded tensor regions introduce no numerical bias.
Answer: zero-point. The zero-point (or zero point, \(Z\)) provides an integer offset that ensures the real floating-point value \(0.0\) is mapped precisely to an integer without rounding error, which is crucial for preserving exact zero representations in padded convolutional feature maps and ReLU activations.
Learning Objective: Calculate the zero-point parameter in affine asymmetric quantization to preserve exact zero representations
Order the stages of a standard post-training quantization workflow with static activation calibration: (1) quantize the finalized weights and export the deployment artifact, (2) run representative floating-point calibration inputs through the model and collect activation statistics, (3) choose activation clipping bounds from the collected statistics, (4) derive activation scales and zero-points from those chosen bounds.
Answer: The correct order is: (2) run representative floating-point calibration inputs through the model and collect activation statistics, (3) choose activation clipping bounds from the collected statistics, (4) derive activation scales and zero-points from those chosen bounds, (1) quantize the finalized weights and export the deployment artifact. Calibration data must be observed before clipping bounds can be chosen, and those bounds must be fixed before scales and zero-points can be derived. Export belongs last because the deployment artifact should reflect the completed quantization parameters rather than precede them. Swapping calibration with export would freeze an artifact before the activation ranges needed to define it were established.
Learning Objective: Sequence the main stages of static-calibrated post-training quantization from calibration through export
Compare two validation settings for low-bit quantization: (1) candidate INT4 weight-only quantization for autoregressive decoding when profiling shows weight traffic dominates, and (2) candidate low-bit quantization for large-batch training of the same model. Explain why these two settings require different validation conditions before concluding the quantization is worthwhile.
Answer: In low-batch autoregressive decoding, each generated token can be dominated by streaming dense model weights, so cutting weight bytes from FP16 toward INT4 can substantially reduce weight traffic and improve latency when the runtime has a matching kernel. The ideal bound is set by the weight-byte reduction, not an automatic \(4\times\) end-to-end speedup, because KV-cache traffic, activations, and dequantization overhead remain. Large-batch training is different: it is not automatically accelerated by weight-only INT4, because training is often compute-heavy and also requires a low-precision training recipe, supported execution units, and numerical validation rather than just compressing stored weights.
Learning Objective: Contrast why weight-only low-bit quantization is most compelling for weight-bandwidth-bound decoding rather than automatically for training
During post-training quantization of a convolutional network, activation profiling reveals that values are heavily concentrated near zero with a small set of extreme positive outliers. Which calibration strategy best preserves numerical resolution for the bulk of typical activations?

Max-absolute-value calibration, because extending the quantization grid to include extreme outliers guarantees zero clipping error across all layers
Uncalibrated uniform quantization, because activation distributions in neural networks always follow a perfectly uniform probability density
Static symmetric quantization with range [-128, +127] mapped unconditionally to [-1.0, +1.0] across every layer
Percentile or KL-divergence (entropy) calibration, which can clip extreme tails so more integer levels represent the dense bulk of activations

Answer: The correct answer is D. When a tensor has a dense bulk near zero plus a rare outlier tail, percentile or KL-based calibration can trade some clipping of that tail for better resolution where most values actually lie. A percentile method such as keeping \(99.9\%\) of values clips the remaining tail by design. That trade can improve typical representation quality, but it is not harmless by definition because rare outliers may still matter for task accuracy. Max calibration instead spends range on those extremes and can waste bins on mostly empty space.
Learning Objective: Compare calibration strategies for long-tailed activation distributions by analyzing the trade-off between clipping and resolution
A team quantizing a deep convolutional network finds that per-channel (filter-wise) quantization achieves significantly higher accuracy than per-tensor (layer-wise) quantization at the same INT8 bit-width. Which mechanism explains this accuracy advantage?

Per-channel quantization eliminates the need to compute or store scale factors and zero-points
Individual convolutional filters within a layer often exhibit drastically different weight magnitude ranges; per-channel quantization assigns an independent scale factor to each filter, preventing wide-range filters from degrading the precision of narrow-range filters
Per-tensor quantization can only be executed on CPUs, whereas per-channel quantization is restricted to edge microcontrollers
Per-channel quantization automatically converts float operations into sparse matrix multiplications

Answer: The correct answer is B. In deep convolutional neural networks, different filters within the same layer specialize in distinct feature patterns, often resulting in weight distributions with variances that differ by orders of magnitude. Under per-tensor (layer-wise) quantization, a single clipping range must encompass all filters, forcing narrow-distribution filters into a tiny subset of quantization bins. Per-channel (per-filter) quantization assigns an independent scale factor \(S_c\) and zero-point \(Z_c\) to each output channel, giving narrow-range filters finer numerical resolution when their ranges differ. This can explain the measured quality advantage, but scale metadata, kernel support, and the calibration policy still determine the deployment trade-off.
Learning Objective: Explain why per-channel quantization granularity preserves accuracy in convolutional networks compared to per-tensor quantization

A paper estimate predicts an \(8\times\) speedup for a compressed model under ideal assumptions, but the implementation measured on an unmodified GPU delivers only \(1.5\times\). Which statement best defines the role of hardware implementation in explaining this gap?

It aligns computation graphs, memory access layouts, operator scheduling, and sparsity patterns with physical accelerator architectures so that theoretical compression can translate into measured wall-clock speedup
It reduces the volume of training data needed to fine-tune compressed neural networks
It eliminates all memory-bound operations by converting every neural network layer into a compute-bound GEMM
It automates the hyperparameter tuning of learning rates and batch sizes during pretraining

Answer: The correct answer is A. Hardware implementation is the layer that determines whether compressed representations map to efficient kernels, memory layouts, and execution paths on the target accelerator. A paper target such as \(8\times\) can collapse to a much smaller measured gain when sparse patterns, metadata, unsupported kernels, or layout issues block efficient execution. The section’s example is illustrative rather than a guaranteed multiplication of pruning and INT8 effects, so the right lesson is to explain the measured gap, not to assume the paper ratio must appear in practice.

Operator fusion of Conv-BatchNorm-ReLU sequences produces substantial execution speedup on modern GPUs even though the fused kernel preserves the intended layer function. Which mechanism explains this latency reduction?

Fusion reduces the total number of weight parameters stored in the convolutional layer
Fusion retrains the network to use lower numerical precision during the forward pass
Fusion skips zero-valued activation elements by converting dense tensors to sparse matrices
Fusion executes convolution, batch normalization, and ReLU inside a single GPU kernel, keeping intermediate activations on chip and cutting intermediate-tensor traffic and launch overhead

Answer: The correct answer is D. Fusion helps by avoiding extra writes and rereads of intermediate activations and by reducing separate kernel launches. In the chapter’s idealized Conv-BN-ReLU accounting, the intermediate-tensor stream falls from six transfers to two, but that count excludes weights, auxiliary inputs, cache effects, and spills. The idea that fusion preserves exactly the same arithmetic is too strong: some patterns such as batch-normalization folding change the operation sequence while preserving the intended function within numerical tolerance.

A compressed neural network achieves a \(50\%\) reduction in total floating-point operations (FLOPs), yet on the deployment accelerator, end-to-end inference latency decreases by only \(10\%\). Explain two distinct hardware and architectural mechanisms that cause this discrepancy.
Answer: First, Amdahl’s Law at the pipeline level limits overall speedup: if model execution accounts for only a fraction of the end-to-end request pipeline (with data ingestion, preprocessing, tokenization, and postprocessing consuming the remainder), accelerating model arithmetic yields a diminished system-level improvement. Second, within the model itself, many non-compute-intensive layers (such as LayerNorm, Softmax, residual additions, and activation functions) are memory-bandwidth bound or latency-bound rather than compute-bound; cutting FLOPs in the compute-heavy layers leaves memory-bound execution time largely unchanged, capping measured speedup.
Learning Objective: Explain why theoretical FLOP reductions fail to produce proportional latency gains using Amdahl’s law and memory-bound layer analysis

To skip them, the runtime needs a compact sparse representation and a matching kernel, but that path adds metadata handling, irregular activation accesses, and possible load imbalance. Whether sparse execution wins depends on format, shape, batch size, and hardware; there is no universal sparsity percentage that guarantees proportional speedup.
Learning Objective: Reject the misconception that unstructured sparsity automatically accelerates dense SIMD hardware

Dynamic channel pruning that alters tensor shapes per batch, because Tensor Cores require dynamic input dimensions
Structured 2:4 sparsity (exactly 2 non-zero values in every contiguous block of 4 elements), because Ampere Tensor Cores include a supported sparse path for that pattern
Activation checkpointing, because recomputing intermediate activations during inference eliminates sparse matrix indexing overhead

The chapter’s example uses compact metadata with 2 bits per retained position, so one 4-element group carries 4 bits of position metadata alongside the retained values. That structure can nearly halve weight traffic and offers up to a \(2\times\) sparse arithmetic-rate improvement, but it is not an end-to-end guarantee once the rest of the execution path is included. Arbitrary unstructured masks do not activate this fixed hardware path.

Hardware implementation alone, because runtime execution scheduling determines disk and RAM consumption

Unstructured magnitude pruning with 90% target sparsity, because arbitrary sparse patterns run fastest on edge memory controllers

LayerNorm operator fusion alone, because LayerNorm compute dominates total parameter storage in large language models

The techniques duplicate each other’s reductions, causing total compression to saturate at the performance of the single strongest method

Applying quantization automatically converts the pruned network into a student model without requiring teacher supervision
Multiplicative gains occur only when the pipeline starts with operator fusion on uncompressed weights

They eliminate the need for engineers to benchmark or validate models on physical target hardware
They automate the insertion and state management of complex compression primitives—such as fake-quantization observers, dynamic range trackers, and sparsity masking hooks—making compression scalable and reproducible across hundreds of models

The practical implication is that compression inside the framework can remain only a logical transformation until the deployment runtime proves that the exported operators, layouts, and kernels really exploit it.

Learning Objective: Identify the additional latency, memory, energy, and calibration measurements needed beyond top-1 accuracy to validate a compressed model
True or False: If an INT8-quantized classifier achieves the exact same top-1 accuracy as its full-precision baseline, its output probability distributions and confidence calibration are guaranteed to be equally reliable for downstream safety thresholds.
Answer: False. Top-1 accuracy counts correct argmax predictions; equal aggregate accuracy does not require the same examples to be correct. Even when every argmax prediction stays unchanged, quantization can alter logit magnitudes and output probabilities, changing confidence calibration. In safety-critical systems, an uncalibrated quantized model may output overconfident or miscalibrated probabilities despite maintaining identical top-1 accuracy.
Learning Objective: Compare top-1 classification accuracy with confidence calibration and probability reliability in quantized models
In PyTorch and TensorFlow quantization toolkits, ____ nodes are temporarily attached to tensor edges during calibration or Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) to collect running statistics (min/max or histograms) and compute scale and zero-point parameters without altering the forward-pass numerical values.
Answer: observer. Observer nodes (or observers / quantization observers / observer nodes) monitor tensor value distributions during calibration passes or QAT epochs, calculating scale (\(S\)) and zero-point (\(Z\)) values before being removed or converted into fixed quantization parameters during final graph freezing.
Learning Objective: Explain the role of observer nodes in collecting activation statistics and computing quantization parameters

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Which statement best captures the chapter’s analysis regarding the interaction between multiple model compression techniques?

Compression techniques compose strictly linearly, so combining a \(2\times\) pruning gain and a \(2\times\) quantization gain always yields a \(4\times\) latency reduction regardless of hardware
Quantization is the only technique that interacts with other methods, while pruning and distillation can always be designed in isolation
Compression techniques interact nonlinearly through shared hardware bottlenecks (cache capacity, memory bandwidth) and competing accuracy budgets; their combined efficacy depends heavily on pipeline sequencing and joint on-target validation
Applying more than one compression technique is never recommended because accuracy degradation is always strictly additive

Answer: The correct answer is C. The chapter emphasizes that compression techniques do not operate in a vacuum: they share physical hardware resources (memory bandwidth, cache capacity, register pressure) and draw from the same underlying model error tolerance. For instance, aggressive pruning reduces the numerical headroom available for subsequent quantization, and uncoalesced sparse memory access can negate quantization bandwidth savings. Therefore, techniques interact nonlinearly and must be evaluated and validated jointly. Claiming linear composition ignores hardware realities, while declaring multi-technique pipelines unviable contradicts proven multiplicative compounding.
Learning Objective: Analyze how compression techniques interact nonlinearly through shared physical resources and joint accuracy budgets
True or False: If a neural network’s parameter count is reduced by \(4\times\) via magnitude pruning, its deployed end-to-end inference latency on a standard mobile CPU is guaranteed to improve by approximately \(4\times\).
Answer: False. A \(4\times\) parameter reduction does not imply a \(4\times\) latency reduction because sparse execution depends on layout, kernel support, tensor shape, and device behavior. On a standard mobile CPU, unstructured sparsity may still incur dense-like traffic or sparse-format overhead, and end-to-end latency also includes work outside the pruned layers.
Learning Objective: Reject the assumption that parameter-count reduction guarantees proportional end-to-end latency improvement
Explain two distinct hidden runtime overheads—such as dynamic dequantization on unsupported hardware and uncoalesced memory access from unstructured sparsity—that can cause a model with an \(8\times\) theoretical compression ratio to exhibit virtually no wall-clock speedup when deployed in production.
Answer: One hidden cost is conversion overhead: if an exported graph crosses unsupported low-precision boundaries, the runtime may insert extra quantize or dequantize work and additional launches, increasing traffic and synchronization instead of reducing them. A fused weight-only path may still save weight traffic, so the real question is what the deployed operator path actually does. A second cost is sparse-execution overhead: unstructured sparsity can require metadata, irregular memory access, and weak cache or SIMD utilization. The practical consequence is that theoretical compression must be validated against the actual exported kernel path, not inferred from bytes or nonzeros alone.
Learning Objective: Analyze how conversion overhead and irregular sparse execution can erase theoretical compression gains in deployment

title: 10 Model Compression
text:
Architecture stack focus for this chapter.
Why do the models that win benchmarks rarely become the models that run in production?
A capable trained model is not automatically a deployable one. Cloud, Edge, Mobile, and TinyML environments each impose physical constraints that research benchmarks ignore, including memory budgets measured in megabytes rather than gigabytes, latency targets measured in milliseconds rather than seconds, and power envelopes measured in milliwatts rather than kilowatts. Research optimizes for accuracy on held-out test sets; production optimizes for accuracy per dollar, accuracy per watt, and accuracy per millisecond. Models that win benchmarks are frequently larger, slower, and more resource-intensive than production envelopes permit. Bridging this gap requires a systematic discipline of compression that trades capabilities the deployment does not need for physical constraints it cannot violate. Because many trained models carry more numerical precision, parameters, or representational capacity than the target workload requires, some of that surplus can be removed while preserving predictive behavior, though a smaller representation is not automatically a faster one. Unless the hardware and runtime software stack exploit the new precision or structure, a nominal size reduction merely moves the bottleneck while latency remains unchanged. Removing half the weights in a tensor leaves execution time and energy untouched if the underlying hardware still fetches, stores, and multiplies every zero. Applied effectively, compression reduces model size by integer factors, transforming a research artifact that runs only on data center accelerators into a production asset capable of executing on a mobile phone, sensor node, or embedded microcontroller. The engineering goal is to make the right model viable within its physical environment, which differs from making a model as small as possible. In D·A·M terms, model compression enacts algorithm-machine co-design directly on the network, reshaping its mathematical structure to satisfy the physical limits of the target hardware.

Learning Objectives

Explain compression as algorithm-machine co-design that trades surplus capacity for memory, latency, and energy constraints
Compare pruning, distillation, and quantization by the resource each relaxes and where each lands on the accuracy-efficiency frontier
Calculate parameter memory, precision, and sparsity reductions to estimate best-case compression gains
Apply post-training, quantization-aware, and weight-only strategies under accuracy and hardware constraints
Select structured pruning and operator choices that map to available accelerator kernels
Design compression pipelines that order pruning, distillation, and quantization and account for why their combined gains do not multiply
Evaluate measured latency, energy, and accuracy on target hardware rather than relying on FLOP counts

title: 10 Model Compression
text:
A trained model arrives with demands on memory capacity, latency, and energy that were set by the server accelerators it trained on, not by the device it must run on. The target device instead enforces a strict deployment budget: the memory, time, and energy it grants to each result the model produces. Memory capacity bounds the bytes of weights and activations that can stay resident, a frame rate or token rate bounds the milliseconds available for each result, and a battery or thermal envelope bounds the joules that each result may consume. Bringing a model’s demands inside that budget, by changing what the model computes, how its values are stored, and how its operations execute, is the work of model compression.



Frontier weights dwarf phone and microcontroller memory; compression bridges the gap.
The gap is easiest to see at its extreme. A 7-billion-parameter language model requires 14 GB merely to store its weights in FP16. A smartphone offers 8 GB of RAM shared across the operating system, background applications, and the user interface, so even if the operating system surrendered its entire memory pool to one process, the weights would not fit. Fitting in memory would only expose a second limit, the token rate. At batch size one, dense autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound because generating each token reads every weight from DRAM, and no other request shares those bytes. Over a flagship phone’s 51.2 GB/s low-power DDR (LPDDR) bus, streaming 14 GB takes about 270 ms per token and about 2 J of DRAM access energy. The memory traffic alone would therefore draw about 8 W, above the phone’s sustained thermal envelope of 3–5 W. A model of this size is the extreme case; the rest of the chapter works with models that come closer to fitting, where the engineering choices are less obvious.
Under the silicon contract (principle \(\ref{pri-silicon-contract}\)), compute throughput, memory bandwidth, memory capacity, and fixed launch overhead determine which physical resource binds first for a given model on a given machine. Training sets those quantities generously. Server-class accelerators supply the aggregate memory and floating-point throughput that wide layers, high numerical precision, and large auxiliary state require, because training must hold gradients, optimizer moment buffers, and activation caches across backward passes. Inference deployment relaxes several of these demands because execution is forward-only, intermediate activation buffers can be reused after their last consumer, and optimizer states disappear, even though residual branches still extend some tensor lifetimes and autoregressive decoding retains KV state across tokens. While mixed-precision methods improve training throughput by selectively adopting FP16 or BF16, deployment can reduce precision further, to INT8, INT4, or specialized microformats, when the target’s execution units support them. Model compression is the systematic process of meeting the silicon contract of a constrained execution context, reducing parameter footprint, memory traffic, or arithmetic operations while preserving task accuracy.


↩︎ Mixed-precision training with FP16 and BF16, including loss scaling and FP32 accumulation, is established in Mixed-precision training.
Across deployment targets, the disparity in weight memory spans about six orders of magnitude, from the 350 GB of FP16 weights in a 175-billion-parameter frontier model to the 512 KB of on-chip SRAM in an embedded microcontroller. The bitter lesson explains why this gap persists. General methods that scale with compute keep winning benchmarks, so the winning models grow with available training compute while a phone’s or microcontroller’s memory and power envelope stays fixed for the life of the device. Compression is the deployment-side counterweight to scale.


↩︎ The bitter lesson, that general methods which scale with compute keep displacing hand-engineered ones, is established in The Bitter Lesson.
Data Selection lowered the cost of producing a trained model by spending training compute only on examples that carry signal, but its savings end where the trained model begins: a model trained on a curated subset has the same parameter count, numerical precision, and memory footprint as one trained on the full corpus, so it can still overflow a phone’s memory or leave inference bound by memory bandwidth. Hardware Acceleration then examines the silicon that executes a model. Compression sits between them because it decides what that silicon is asked to run: how many operations, how many bytes per value, and which kernels.
The record of language models shows how much ground that counterweight can recover. Figure 1 follows the smallest dense model reported to score at least 60 percent on the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark (Hendrycks et al. 2020) at each point in time. That size fell from 280 billion parameters for Gopher at the end of 2021 to 3 billion for Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, a code-specialized model, in 2024, about 93× smaller in under three years (Epoch AI 2026). Better training data, longer training, and distillation from larger models all contributed, so the decline is not compression alone, but it shows that a capability first reached at frontier scale can later fit a far smaller deployment budget.

Hendrycks, Dan, Collin Burns, Steven Basart, Andy Zou, Mantas Mazeika, Dawn Song, and Jacob Steinhardt. 2020. “Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding.” arXiv Preprint.














Figure 1: Smallest Model Reaching a Fixed Score: Parameter counts of dense language models against release date on a logarithmic axis, with models scoring at least 60 percent on the MMLU benchmark in blue and the rest in gray. The red step line tracks the smallest model at or above that score released up to each date. Scores are as reported by each source, and parameter counts come from model names, so the line is a lower envelope of reported results rather than a controlled comparison. Data from Epoch AI (2026).


Epoch AI. 2026. Capabilities and Benchmarking.


Bridging the gap between frontier models and fixed deployment targets requires an engineering framework with predictable physical trade-offs. Every compression technique removes specific structure from the model, whether unnecessary weights, surplus numerical bits, or redundant operator subgraphs. Designing a production deployment requires identifying which resource binds first on the target platform and analyzing how successive approximations compound across the memory hierarchy. The framework this chapter builds works on three tiers: what the model computes (its structure), how many bits represent each value (its precision), and how the result executes on the target processor (its implementation). Benefits compound only when transformations relieve distinct binding bottlenecks and the runtime supports the resulting graph.

Definition 10.1: Model compression
Model compression is a family of techniques that reduce a trained model’s computational cost and memory footprint by eliminating redundant parameters (pruning), reducing numerical precision (quantization), or transferring learned behavior into a smaller architecture (distillation), while preserving as much predictive accuracy as possible.

Significance: In the iron law (principle \(\ref{pri-iron-law}\)), compression targets both the Algorithm factor (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\), and therefore total operations \(\Operations\)) and the Machine factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\), through its physical data-movement and compute terms). INT8 quantization of a 175-billion-parameter LLM leaves \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) unchanged but cuts weight memory from 350 GB (FP16) to 175 GB, a 2× reduction in \(\DataVolume\), while dedicated low-precision matrix units can raise \(\PeakRate\) when kernels and layouts use the supported INT8 path. Unstructured pruning to 50 percent sparsity halves the nonzero parameter count, but executed operations fall only when the runtime can skip those zeros through a supported sparse format or kernel without inflating \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\) via index-traffic stalls.
Distinction: Unlike post-training compression methods such as pruning and quantization, neural architecture search discovers efficient architectures from scratch by exploring a design space. Here, NAS is treated as a related structural optimization technique, because it changes the representation before training rather than compressing a finished model post hoc.
Common pitfall: Compression techniques do not compose without interference. Pruning changes weight distributions and operation patterns; quantization adds calibration and kernel constraints. Their combination can lose accuracy or fail to accelerate without joint validation.



The three tiers form a stack that descends from algorithmic software toward physical silicon, the same direction in which ML Frameworks lowered a computational graph to kernels. At the top sits what operations the model executes, in the middle how many bits encode each operand, and at the bottom how kernels map onto the processor’s compute and memory structures (figure 2).






Figure 2: Three Tiers of Compression: Model optimization progresses from software-level representation (pruning, distillation, NAS) down through numerical precision (quantization) to hardware execution (kernel fusion, sparsity engines). Lowering abstraction moves optimizations closer to physical silicon, where representation decisions dictate achievable execution efficiency.



Each tier removes a different kind of surplus across the two levels of the iron law. The top tier, efficient model representation, removes structure and lowers the Algorithm factor (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\)). Pruning drops weights or whole channels that contribute little to accuracy, knowledge distillation trains a compact student to match a larger teacher, and neural architecture search (NAS) looks for layer shapes that meet an explicit latency or memory bound. The middle and bottom tiers leave \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) unchanged and instead lower the Machine factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)). In the middle tier, efficient numerics representation removes bits. Quantization maps floating-point values to 8-bit or 4-bit integers, which shrinks weight memory and bus traffic (\(\DataVolume\)) by two to four times and lets integer units execute each operation at higher peak rate (\(\PeakRate\)) and lower energy. In the bottom tier, efficient hardware implementation removes wasted execution. Kernel fusion keeps intermediate activations in on-chip memory instead of sending them back to DRAM (shrinking \(\DataVolume\)) and reduces launch overhead (\(\Latency\)). Sparsity pays off only when its zeros follow a pattern the hardware can skip, such as two zeros in every group of four weights, so that cutting \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) does not inflate \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\).
These three tiers are tightly coupled across the compilation and execution boundary. Pruning alters weight distributions and activation profiles, changing the dynamic ranges required for subsequent quantization-range calibration. Quantization reduces data-movement volume across the memory bus, shifting a previously memory-bound workload toward compute-bound execution where kernel fusion and tile scheduling dominate. Achieving compounding performance gains requires co-designing transformations across all three tiers rather than applying them in isolation, a composition strategy that section 10.5.3 develops through a staged pipeline.
Every technique in this chapter answers to the conservation-of-complexity heuristic that opened Part I. Complexity tends to move among the Data, Algorithm, and Machine axes rather than disappear, so engineers must account for where each technique sends cost and risk. It is a heuristic, not a literal conservation law, and removing genuinely avoidable work can reduce total cost. Pruning may reduce parameters while asking the runtime to exploit sparse structure; distillation may reduce inference cost while adding a teacher-student training phase; quantization may reduce data movement while spending numerical precision. The engineer’s task is to move complexity to where the cost is lowest given deployment constraints.
Which tier of the optimization stack yields the highest return depends entirely on the physical machine hosting the workload. A data-center server equipped with several high-bandwidth memory (HBM) accelerators tolerates multi-gigabyte models but demands high token throughput under concurrency. A smartphone or an embedded microcontroller operates under severe physical ceilings on memory capacity, bus bandwidth, and thermal dissipation.


Cloud serving, a phone camera, and an embedded microcontroller each break down on a different term of the deployment budget, so compression begins by asking which term a given model violates and what it costs to stop violating it. Cloud inference centers on throughput (requests per second per dollar), where supported integer quantization paths increase serving density and kernel fusion reduces per-request kernel launch overhead (Choudhary et al. 2020; Dean et al. 2018). Mobile and edge deployments must fit within tight physical memory bounds while meeting deterministic real-time deadlines. A serialized camera pipeline that must finish each frame before the next arrives at 30 frames per second has about 33 ms per frame. A pipelined design that overlaps capture, inference, and display can sustain 30 frames per second even when each frame takes longer than 33 ms end to end, so it must check frame rate and per-frame latency as two separate budgets.

Choudhary, Tejalal, Vipul Mishra, Anurag Goswami, and Jagannathan Sarangapani. 2020. “A Comprehensive Survey on Model Compression and Acceleration.” Artificial Intelligence Review 53 (7): 5113–55. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-020-09816-7.

Dean, Jeff, David Patterson, and Cliff Young. 2018. “A New Golden Age in Computer Architecture: Empowering the Machine-Learning Revolution.” IEEE Micro 38 (2): 21–29. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2018.112130030.

Banbury, Colby R., Vijay Janapa Reddi, Max Lam, William Fu, Amin Fazel, Jeremy Holleman, Xinyuan Huang, et al. 2020. “Benchmarking TinyML Systems: Challenges and Direction.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2003.04821.
TinyML makes physical fit a deployment requirement. A microcontroller with only a few hundred kilobytes of SRAM and limited model storage cannot accommodate a 100 MB model without a compatible placement strategy, regardless of predictive accuracy (Banbury et al. 2020). Persistent weights may reside in flash or other supported storage, while runtime buffers occupy working memory. Without paging, the peak SRAM working set must fit the available SRAM; the model artifact must separately fit its storage budget. Capacity is also a hard bound on mobile and cloud devices, though their placement options differ.


↩︎ The latency, memory, and power envelopes defining cloud, edge, mobile, and TinyML tiers are established in Four Deployment Regimes Across Nine Orders of Magnitude.
Meeting real-time deadlines on commodity mobile hardware depends as much on the hardware-supported precision path as on absolute memory capacity. When execution units provide hardware acceleration exclusively for fixed-point arithmetic, precision selection dictates whether a workload executes on energy-efficient neural processing units or falls back to power-hungry general-purpose cores. That choice decides the chapter’s running case, a camera pipeline that must meet an interactive frame rate within a phone’s thermal budget (Example 10.1).

Example 10.1: The running case: Real-time blur on a phoneScenario: A labeled composite. A camera application deploys a MobileNetV2-based segmentation model for real-time background blur on mid-tier smartphones at 30 FPS.
Diagnosis: An uncompressed FP32 MobileNetV2 model runs on the phone’s CPU at only 8 FPS, about 125 ms per frame against a 33 ms budget, while holding the CPU at a power level the thermal envelope cannot sustain. The phone’s NPU or DSP accelerates integer matrix arithmetic, not FP32, so the uncompressed model cannot use it.
Systems lesson: INT8 quantization cuts raw parameter payload by 4\(\times\), but most of the gain from 8 FPS to 35 FPS comes from what INT8 unlocks, a move from the CPU onto the integer accelerator. The precision change is the enabler; the change of processor supplies most of the speed. The frame rates are illustrative, so speed and power still require device measurement.


The chapter follows that camera pipeline through the structural and hardware tiers of the stack. MobileNetV2 is the book’s compute-bound lighthouse in its efficient regime. Depthwise separable convolutions keep its arithmetic small, and at batch one on a phone its frame time goes to arithmetic and activation traffic rather than to reading weights. The precision tier needs a workload whose time is set by bytes, so it follows GPT-2 XL decoding on the same phone. GPT-2 XL is the book’s bandwidth-bound lighthouse, and every token it generates streams every weight. Two callouts mark the ends of the memory constraint. DLRM (Naumov et al. 2019), the capacity-bound lighthouse, shows precision deciding whether embedding tables fit, and keyword spotting (KWS) (Y. Zhang et al. 2017), the power-bound lighthouse, shows precision deciding whether a model fits a microcontroller’s SRAM and energy budget. ResNet-50, the compute-bound lighthouse, serves twice, as the teacher that distills into MobileNetV2 and as the subject of the closing INT8 deployment profile. Rather than running every technique on all five, the chapter returns to each workload where it exposes the binding resource most clearly.

↩︎ The iron law of ML systems, which splits execution time into data-movement, compute, and fixed-overhead terms, is established in Iron Law of ML Systems.

Table 1 places the cases’ weight bytes and work beside the deployment budget, and two of its rows explain how the chapter divides the work. MobileNetV2’s FP32 weights stream across the phone’s 51.2 GB/s memory bus in about 0.27 ms, roughly 1 percent of the 33 ms frame budget. The frame is therefore spent on its 600 MFLOP of arithmetic and on activation traffic, so the structural and execution tiers are the levers that matter. GPT-2 XL’s FP16 weights fit in the phone’s memory but take about 59 ms to stream for every generated token, so precision, which shrinks the bytes behind each weight, is the lever that matters. Even MobileNetV2 at INT8 exceeds the TinyML envelope by about 6.7×, while the purpose-built depthwise separable convolutional network (DS-CNN) keyword spotter fits it after INT8 quantization.
