These numbers connect directly to the iron law of ML systems. Every cross-device transfer contributes to \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\) at a fraction of on-device bandwidth. Dividing 1 GB by the stated PCIe Gen5 x16 peak gives 15.6 ms, a bandwidth-only lower bound that omits protocol, launch, synchronization, topology, and contention overhead. Transfers can dominate lightweight or small-batch workloads, so deployed latency must be measured rather than inferred from peak bandwidth alone.
Device placement discipline protects the bandwidth hierarchy from accidental PCIe traffic. Every tensor carries a device attribute, and frameworks enforce a strict invariant: operations can only combine tensors on the same device, raising a RuntimeError when cuda:0 and cuda:1 tensors mix so that cross-device transfers remain explicit. Calling .to() on a tensor returns the original tensor when its data type and device already match the request (unless copy=True forces a copy) and otherwise returns a converted copy; in contrast, nn.Module.to() modifies registered parameters and buffers in place and returns the module.
The performance discipline follows directly from this bandwidth gap. Allocate tensors on the target device from the start rather than creating them on the host and transferring them. Reuse GPU memory across iterations rather than reallocating it. Colocate inputs, labels, and model parameters on the same device to eliminate implicit transfers. At 64 GB/s, violating any of these principles inserts PCIe transfers into the critical path that can dominate a training iteration that otherwise runs at 3.35 TB/s on-device.
When transfers are unavoidable, the next optimization is to hide their latency by executing them concurrently with computation. GPUs contain separate hardware units for computation (streaming multiprocessors) and data transfer (copy engines), and the framework exposes them through the CUDA stream, an execution queue whose operations run in order within the stream but concurrently with other streams. When copies and computation share one stream, they execute serially. Placing the next batch’s transfer on one stream while the current batch computes on another can make the steady-state batch interval approach \(\max(\IronLawComputeTime, \BatchTransferTime)\), the larger stage time rather than their sum. Each batch still requires its own transfer to finish before its consumer runs. With sufficient independent work and hardware resources, stream-based overlap can hide much of the \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\) penalty when computation is the longer stage (see listing 13).



Overlap pays the longer stage, not the sum.
The non_blocking=True flag requests a copy that is asynchronous with respect to the host, but real overlap also requires pinned memory. Ordinary host memory is pageable: the operating system may relocate or swap its pages at any time, and a DMA engine, which copies across PCIe without involving CPU cores, cannot handle a page fault. A copy from pageable memory therefore first stages the data synchronously into a temporary pinned buffer. Tensors placed in pinned (page-locked) host memory skip that staging, so their transfers can overlap accelerator computation. In listing 13 the two streams are separate; a complete pipeline must also hand each transferred batch to its consumer only after the copy completes, using the synchronization mechanisms that follow.



Listing 13: Overlapping Computation and Transfer: Separate streams can overlap eligible copies and computation when dependencies are synchronized correctly. Pinned host memory generally enables host-to-device copies to overlap with other device work.


compute_stream = torch.cuda.Stream()
transfer_stream = torch.cuda.Stream()

# Transfer next batch while computing
# current batch
with torch.cuda.stream(transfer_stream):
    next_batch = next_batch_cpu.to("cuda", non_blocking=True)

with torch.cuda.stream(compute_stream):
    output = model(current_batch)
    loss = criterion(output, labels)

# Pinned host memory can enable transfer overlap
x_pinned = torch.randn(1000, 1000).pin_memory()
x_gpu = x_pinned.to("cuda", non_blocking=True)  # Asynchronous

# A pageable source may require staging and
# should not be assumed to overlap
y_regular = torch.randn(1000, 1000)
y_gpu = y_regular.to("cuda", non_blocking=True)



Concurrent execution introduces ordering constraints: when one stream’s output becomes another stream’s input, the system must enforce a happens-before relationship without unnecessarily serializing independent work. Two synchronization mechanisms exist, and their performance consequences differ sharply. Full device synchronization (torch.cuda.synchronize()) blocks all streams and the CPU until every queued operation completes, creating a global serialization point that eliminates overlap. CUDA events provide the alternative: fine-grained synchronization that blocks only the dependent stream, allowing other streams and the CPU to continue execution (see listing 14).



Listing 14: CUDA Events for Synchronization: Events enable fine-grained producer-consumer patterns between streams without blocking the entire device.


# Create streams and event
stream1 = torch.cuda.Stream()
stream2 = torch.cuda.Stream()
event = torch.cuda.Event()

# Stream 1: producer
with torch.cuda.stream(stream1):
    result1 = expensive_computation(data1)
    event.record()  # Mark completion point

# Stream 2: consumer (waits only for stream1's event)
with torch.cuda.stream(stream2):
    event.wait()  # Block stream2 until event is recorded
    result2 = dependent_computation(result1)  # Safe to use result1



Full synchronization after every operation converts a concurrent pipeline into a sequential one, negating the hardware parallelism that streams expose, whereas event-based synchronization enforces only the dependencies that correctness requires. That difference creates a common operational trap: debug code left with torch.cuda.synchronize() in the hot path turns an overlapped pipeline into a serialized one. A timeline profiler shows the resulting gaps between kernels, while the kernel profilers and hardware counters that explain why an individual kernel underperforms belong to the profiling method of Identifying Bottlenecks.



The same placement machinery extends to the one to eight accelerators of a single machine across three alternative placement choices. In data parallelism, each device holds a complete replica of the model and processes a different slice of the batch, summing every replica’s gradients after the backward pass through an AllReduce collective. In pipeline parallelism, devices hold different groups of layers and pass activations between them; in tensor parallelism, individual tensor operations split across devices. Frameworks express device ownership, transfers, and synchronization through named device groups, such as ProcessGroup in PyTorch or Mesh in JAX, while preserving the model’s semantics as the hardware path underneath changes. NVLink delivers 900 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth per H100 inside one node (table 7), while devices joined only by PCIe pay the slower path for every exchange. Parameter state multiplies with each arrangement, because every weight brings a gradient, optimizer moments, and often a second copy at another precision, and each replica or partition must own its share. Which arrangement to choose, and what its communication costs, is developed in Scaling Training Systems; on a single machine, however, even well-placed accelerators sit idle if the host data pipeline cannot feed them fast enough.


↪ The AllReduce collective and its communication cost are developed in Data parallelism.




Streams and events hide transfers behind computation, but scheduling cannot help if input data arrives too slowly in the first place. The data pipeline must sustain the accelerator’s consumption rate. An accelerator processing 1,000 images per second at 224 by 224 resolution needs about 150.5 MB/s of sustained raw uint8 image throughput. Any shortfall idles the accelerator and lowers the effective utilization term in the iron law. The framework’s contribution to this feeding problem is an abstraction that separates what a sample is from how samples reach the device. A Dataset defines access to individual samples, and a DataLoader (Paszke et al. 2019) turns that definition into a pipeline built from parallel worker processes, prefetching, and pinned staging memory.

Paszke, Adam, Sam Gross, Francisco Massa, Adam Lerer, James Bradbury, Gregory Chanan, Trevor Killeen, et al. 2019. “PyTorch: An Imperative Style, High-Performance Deep Learning Library.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 32: 8024–35.

↩︎ The feeding problem, in which data delivery must keep pace with accelerator consumption, is established in The feeding problem.

Worker processes come first. With num_workers > 0, the DataLoader spawns CPU processes that load and preprocess samples independently, distributes sample indices to them through a shared queue, and assembles their completed samples into batches in the main process. Multiple workers overlap I/O wait with decoding and augmentation when one process is too slow to feed the accelerator; once the pipeline meets demand, extra workers add overhead rather than throughput.



Four workers fill eight prefetched batches, which drain through pinned memory to the GPU.
Prefetching sets pipeline depth. The prefetch_factor parameter controls how many batches each worker prepares in advance, so four workers with prefetch_factor=2 keep up to eight batches in flight, at a cost in host memory proportional to the queued data. Prefetching raises the chance that input work overlaps accelerator computation but cannot prevent stalls when storage, decoding, or contention makes production slower than consumption.
Pinned memory completes the path to the device. The pin_memory=True option places batches in the page-locked host memory of section 7.5.2, so their host-to-device copies skip pageable-memory staging and can overlap device work. For a batch of 64 FP32 images at \(224{\times}224{\times}3\) (38.5 MB), dividing by the H100’s PCIe Gen5 x16 peak gives 0.6 ms; this is a bandwidth-only lower bound, not a measured pinned-transfer latency. The realized benefit over pageable memory depends on the platform, batch size, pipeline, and overlap. Pinned pages also reduce pageable system memory.
The DataLoader configuration in listing 15 is useful only when each parameter is tied to a bottleneck: num_workers sets loading parallelism, prefetch_factor sets pipeline depth, and pin_memory enables DMA transfers. Each worker also holds its own copy of the Dataset object and its own Python state, so the worker count trades throughput against host memory. Changes one worker makes to that state do not reach the others or the main process unless the state lives in explicitly shared or memory-mapped storage. PyTorch seeds each worker’s own generator separately, but augmentation code that draws from NumPy or Python’s random module still needs a worker_init_fn such as seed_worker.



Listing 15: DataLoader Throughput Configuration: Four workers with a prefetch depth of two keep up to eight batches in flight through pinned memory, and a per-worker seed function makes NumPy and Python augmentation reproducible.


import random

import numpy as np
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader


def seed_worker(worker_id):
    worker_seed = torch.initial_seed() % 2**32
    np.random.seed(worker_seed)
    random.seed(worker_seed)


loader = DataLoader(
    dataset,
    batch_size=64,
    shuffle=True,
    num_workers=4,  # Parallel worker processes (mechanism 1)
    prefetch_factor=2,  # Batches prepared ahead per worker (mechanism 2)
    pin_memory=True,  # Page-locked memory for DMA (mechanism 3)
    worker_init_fn=seed_worker,  # Reproducible augmentation per worker
)

# Pipeline effect: while GPU processes batch N,
# 4 workers load batches N+1..N+8 into pinned memory,
# ready for DMA transfer when the GPU finishes.





↪ Sizing worker count and prefetch depth against measured throughput and memory is developed in Practical considerations.
The Dataset interface decides how samples can be scheduled. A map-style dataset implements __len__ and __getitem__, so a sampler can shuffle by index, which suits data that fits in memory or supports efficient random access on disk. An iterable-style dataset implements __iter__ and yields samples sequentially from a stream where random access is impractical, so any shuffling must be buffered inside the iterator. Batch collation through the collate_fn parameter then combines samples into a batch. The default stacks tensors along a new batch dimension, which requires identical shapes; variable-length data such as text needs custom collation that pads, sorts by length, or builds attention masks, and those choices change both memory use and throughput.
With input delivered at the rate the accelerator consumes it, the remaining abstraction problem is execution, the translation of each operation into work that runs on the target hardware.



Calling y = torch.matmul(x, w) without selecting a kernel matched to x and w’s device, data type, stride layout, and tile dimensions either fails at runtime or leaves Tensor Cores idle while a generic loop crawls through memory. Bridging that single Python call to thousands of parallel accelerator threads traverses three coordinated functional tiers. From left to right in figure 13, system-level operations (scheduling, memory management, and resource optimization) organize graph execution. Basic numerical operations (GEMM, BLAS, and element-wise kernels) execute algebraic routines. Hardware operations (compute kernel management, memory abstraction, and execution control) bind the workload directly to device streams and physical silicon, starting at the bottom of the stack with the hardware primitives themselves.






Figure 13: Core Operations Stack: Three functional tiers bridge high-level Python code to physical execution. Hardware operations manage low-level kernel dispatch and memory transfers, basic numerical operations execute dense GEMM and element-wise routines, and system-level operations coordinate graph scheduling and memory lifetimes across accelerators.





The hardware abstraction layer isolates framework code from platform-specific details. It solves three concrete problems: selecting the right compute kernel, moving data through the memory hierarchy, and coordinating execution across processing units.
The kernel manager dispatches each supported operation to an implementation for the current backend. For matrix multiplication, this may be a CPU BLAS backend such as Intel oneMKL or OpenBLAS (Intel Corporation 2026; OpenBLAS Project 2026), cuBLAS on NVIDIA GPUs (NVIDIA 2024), or accelerator-specific tensor instructions. Selection depends on dimensions, dtype, layout, backend, and library heuristics. A \(4096{\times}4096\) FP16 GEMM on an H100 may use a Tensor Core path whose published dense peak is 989 TFLOP/s (Choquette 2023; NVIDIA Corporation 2022). If the backend has no implementation for an operator, execution may fall back, be partitioned, or fail, depending on the framework and runtime.

Choquette, Jack. 2023. “NVIDIA Hopper H100 GPU: Scaling Performance.” IEEE Micro 43 (3): 9–17. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2023.3256796.

NVIDIA Corporation. 2022. NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU Architecture. NVIDIA Corporation.
The memory abstraction layer moves tensors among pageable or pinned host memory, device memory, and unified memory, and transforms data layouts to match hardware preferences. Because physical memory is the one-dimensional byte array of section 7.5.1.2, layout formats dictate how 4D image dimensions map to linear addresses: channels-first NCHW places all spatial pixels of one channel contiguously before storing the next channel, whereas channels-last NHWC groups all channel values for a single spatial coordinate consecutively. Accelerator matrix units often prefer NHWC because loading all channels for a pixel aligns with a single, contiguous 128-byte memory transaction (a coalesced access). A framework may therefore execute kernels in NHWC for peak hardware utilization while preserving NCHW for user-facing APIs. Alignment requirements vary from 4 bytes on CPUs to 128 bytes on high-bandwidth accelerators; misaligned or strided accesses split requests across multiple memory transactions and can cut effective bandwidth substantially. The runtime also preserves dependency ordering when multiple execution units access the same tensor, preventing races during concurrent operations.
The execution controller coordinates work across multiple processing units and memory spaces. On a modern GPU, graph runtimes or explicit stream use can overlap independent kernels when dependency analysis proves they are ready and the kernels leave enough resources unused to run concurrently. Eager default-stream execution often serializes this work instead. The controller inserts synchronization barriers where data dependencies require them, tracks event completions to trigger dependent operations, and routes hardware errors (ECC failures, timeout watchdogs) to the framework’s error handling path.



With hardware abstraction managing the platform-specific details, frameworks build a layer of mathematical operations on top. GEMM dominates ML computation. The operation \(\GemmOutputMatrix= \GemmProductScale\ActivationMatrix\WeightMatrix+ \GemmAccumulatorScale\GemmOutputMatrix\) accounts for the vast majority of arithmetic in neural networks: a single ResNet-50 forward pass performs approximately 8.2 GFLOP, nearly all of which reduce to GEMM. General matrix multiply (GEMM) derives how GEMM arithmetic intensity scales with matrix dimension, predicting whether a given layer is compute bound or memory bound before any profiler runs. Frameworks optimize GEMM through cache-aware tiling (splitting matrices into blocks that fit in L1/L2 cache), loop unrolling for instruction-level parallelism, and shape-specific kernels. Fully connected layers use standard dense GEMM, while convolutional layers use im2col transformations that reshape input patches into matrix columns, converting convolution into GEMM.


↪ Tiling on an accelerator, where on-chip storage and the compute array fix the tile size and a dimension one element past a tile boundary can halve utilization, is developed in Tiling.
Beyond GEMM, frameworks implement BLAS operations (AXPY for vector addition, GEMV for matrix-vector products) and element-wise operations (activation functions, normalization). Element-wise operations are individually cheap but collectively expensive, because each one reads and writes its full tensor; they are the fusion targets of section 7.3.2.
Each of these numerical operation families requires separate kernel implementations for every supported precision format. Storing weights and activations in FP32 uses 4 bytes per value, whereas quantizing to INT8 reduces this to 1 byte, cutting memory traffic by 4× and enabling 2–4\(\times\) throughput gains on hardware with INT8 matrix units. Because a single forward pass often mixes narrow-precision GEMMs with higher-precision accumulations and norms, the kernel library must dispatch per-precision routines layer by layer.



Hardware abstraction and numerical operations provide the building blocks; system-level operations orchestrate them. The scheduler orders operations by their graph dependencies and overlaps independent work through the streams and events of section 7.5.2. The memory manager reuses freed blocks through the caching allocator of section 7.4.3.4 and, when a model exceeds device memory, executes the activation-checkpointing policy of section 7.4.2. The resource optimizer ties these decisions to the kernel selection described earlier. Its failures are the ones those mechanisms predict, since a poor schedule leaves resources idle and fragmentation or excessive live state can cause an out-of-memory error even when aggregate device capacity appears sufficient.

Checkpoint 7.3: Hardware abstraction
The abstraction problem is the bridge between portable code and efficient execution.

Two dimensions: can you distinguish data representation (layout, dtype, placement) from execution mapping (kernel selection, scheduling), and explain how they constrain each other?
Kernel dispatch: can you explain why the same high-level operation (for example, GEMM) needs multiple implementations (CPU vector path vs. GPU Tensor Core path) and how shapes/dtypes affect the choice?
Memory abstraction: can you explain why frameworks use caching allocators and layout transforms (NCHW\(\leftrightarrow\)NHWC) rather than calling device allocators on every tensor?
Execution control: can you describe what the runtime is doing when it overlaps independent work (streams) and inserts synchronization only where dependencies require it?



Tensors, streams, and kernel dispatch complete the descent to the hardware, but they operate at the granularity of individual buffers and operations. Model development needs the opposite direction, composing thousands of low-level operations, together with the parameters that automatic differentiation tracks, into reusable, nestable building blocks called modules.

Self-Check: Question

In framework tensor implementations such as PyTorch Tensor or NumPy ndarray, what distinguishes a tensor view from a tensor copy?

A view converts the underlying data from floating-point to integer representation
A view changes only tensor metadata while sharing the same storage, though reshape can do this only when the existing strides permit the requested layout
A view duplicates the tensor into host CPU memory while leaving device memory unchanged
A view guarantees the tensor is stored in contiguous C-order memory

A training loop shows GPU idle time because batches arrive late from the input pipeline. How can pin_memory=True together with tensor.to(device, non_blocking=True) help, and what does it not guarantee by itself?

It automatically quantizes all host tensors to 8-bit precision so the GPU receives less data
It bypasses the data loader by executing preprocessing directly inside GPU kernels
It places batches in page-locked host memory so eligible host-to-device copies can use DMA and potentially overlap with device work, but actual overlap still depends on having independent batches, streams, and correct dependency ordering
It forces every CUDA kernel to run on the default stream so transfer and compute become easier to coordinate

Why can an accidental synchronous CPU-GPU tensor transfer (such as calling .item() or printing a tensor inside a training loop) degrade throughput far more than the raw byte transfer time would suggest?

title: 7 ML Frameworks
text:
Coordinating those same 25.6M ResNet-50 parameters across fifty layers requires registering weights with optimizers, moving buffers across devices, toggling training and evaluation modes, and serializing checkpoints. Managing that state tensor by tensor would drown model development in error-prone bookkeeping. Frameworks resolve this through hierarchical composition, packaging layers into modules that compose into full models.
Every major framework implements this through a module abstraction that binds parameter tensors, forward computation, and lifecycle hooks into a unified interface. PyTorch’s nn.Module23 provides an instructive case study because its design patterns recur across frameworks. Keras uses similar layer abstractions (Chollet 2018), JAX’s Flax employs analogous module structures, and TensorFlow’s functional API shares conceptual parallels. Three enduring design principles recur regardless of syntax or programming paradigm.
23 nn.Module: The pattern recurs across frameworks because the organizational problem is universal. nn.Module automatically registers any assigned submodule or parameter into a hierarchical tree, enabling a single .to('cuda') call to recursively place millions of parameters onto a GPU. Keras layers, JAX Flax modules, and TensorFlow’s tf.Module all implement the same tree-walking pattern. Without it, managing model state would require manual bookkeeping that scales linearly with architectural depth, a cost that grows prohibitive for models with hundreds of layers.
Chollet, François. 2018. Deep Learning with Python. Manning Publications.


Passing each of ResNet-50’s weight and bias tensors to an optimizer by hand would break the moment a layer is added or renamed. Frameworks eliminate that manual wiring through automatic parameter discovery: the system walks the module tree, collecting every parameter tensor so the optimizer can update them in a single call.
This is a tree traversal problem at its core. PyTorch’s Module.__setattr__ registers an assigned nn.Parameter or child nn.Module in the module’s internal mappings. A call to .parameters() recursively traverses registered submodules and yields registered parameters. Other frameworks expose analogous parameter trees or collections, though their mechanisms differ.
Automatic parameter discovery gives the optimizer a complete parameter set or parameter groups, enabling grouped or fused multi-tensor update kernels when the framework and backend support them. The immediate win is correctness and composability: newly attached submodules participate in device moves, serialization, and optimizer construction without a separate manual registry. It also lets optimized update paths operate over parameter collections without per-parameter user code. Listing 16 demonstrates the core mechanism: attribute assignment triggers registration, and .parameters() returns all discovered tensors.
The distinction between parameters and buffers illustrates a subtlety of discovery. Registered parameters appear in .parameters() whether trainable or frozen; requires_grad separately controls whether autograd accumulates a gradient for them. Registered buffers move with the module and can appear in its state dictionary but are excluded from .parameters() and ordinary optimizer discovery. Batch-normalization running statistics are a common buffer use case.



Listing 16: Parameter Registration: Automatic parameter tracking through attribute assignment enables optimizer access to all trainable weights without manual enumeration.


import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class CustomLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, output_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(
            torch.randn(output_size, input_size)
        )
        self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(output_size))
        self.register_buffer("running_mean", torch.zeros(output_size))

    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.matmul(x, self.weight.t()) + self.bias


layer = CustomLayer(10, 20)
# Framework discovers both parameters automatically:
for name, param in layer.named_parameters():
    print(f"{name}: shape {param.shape}")



The other major frameworks draw the same line between trainable parameters and nontrainable state through different accessors (table 8). Regardless of syntax, each API separates tensors that the optimizer should update from persistent buffers that merely ride along in checkpoints and device transfers.



Table 8: Parameter Discovery APIs Across Frameworks: Each framework exposes a different surface for distinguishing trainable parameters from nontrainable buffers, but all four solve the same underlying problem of letting optimizers find weights to update while preserving state (running statistics, frozen tensors) across forward passes. The shared pattern is structured access to parameters and persistent state. Accessor semantics differ: PyTorch also yields frozen registered parameters, so trainability remains a separate property.










Framework
Parameter Access
Nontrainable State




PyTorch
model.parameters()
register_buffer()


Keras
layer.trainable_weights
layer.non_trainable_weights


JAX/Flax
variables["params"] after variables = model.init(key, x)
Separate variable collections (for example, batch_stats)


TensorFlow
module.trainable_variables
module.non_trainable_variables









The same module tree that distinguishes trainable parameters from running-statistic buffers also governs layers whose forward computation changes between training and inference. During training, dropout layers randomly zero elements with probability \(\DropoutProbability= \Pr(\text{drop})\) to regularize the network, while during inference those same layers must perform identity mapping to produce deterministic outputs. Batch normalization uses per-batch statistics during training but switches to accumulated running statistics during inference. If these behavioral changes are left to the programmer, forgetting a single mode switch produces silently incorrect predictions in production.
Frameworks solve this with a state flag that propagates through the module hierarchy. A single call to .eval() on the root module recursively sets self.training = False on every descendant, and each layer queries this flag to select its behavior. This is an instance of a broader systems principle: the same computation graph must produce different execution behavior depending on context. Compilers face the same challenge when the same source code must produce debug builds (with bounds checking and symbol tables) vs. release builds (with aggressive optimization). The flag-propagation pattern ensures correctness by centralizing the mode decision at the root rather than requiring per-layer coordination.
Evaluation mode and gradient recording are separate controls. Calling .eval() changes mode-dependent layer behavior but leaves autograd recording enabled. For inference that needs no gradients, torch.no_grad() disables that recording, avoiding the associated saved backward state while .eval() selects the appropriate layer behavior.
Per-parameter gradient control works alongside torch.no_grad() during transfer learning through parameter freezing. Setting requires_grad=False on a submodule’s parameters prevents autograd from accumulating gradients in those parameters and removes their gradient storage, although gradients may still need to pass through the layer’s operations to reach trainable inputs or earlier parameters. Because both mode propagation and subtree freezing operate on nested modules, they rely on how the framework composes layers into a hierarchy and serializes that hierarchy’s state.



Complex models compose from reusable submodules, creating a tree structure. A ResNet is not implemented as a monolithic block of operations but as a hierarchy: the root module contains a sequence of residual blocks, each block contains convolution layers and normalization layers, and each layer contains parameter tensors. This hierarchical composition must support two operations, made concrete in listing 17: recursive parameter collection for training and state serialization for checkpointing and deployment.



Listing 17: Nested Module Composition: Hierarchical module composition enables recursive parameter collection and a flat state mapping across the module tree.


import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class ResidualBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(channels)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(channels)

    def forward(self, x):
        residual = x
        x = torch.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))
        x = self.bn2(self.conv2(x))
        return torch.relu(x + residual)


class ResNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_blocks, channels=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv_in = nn.Conv2d(3, channels, 7, padding=3)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(
            [ResidualBlock(channels) for _ in range(num_blocks)]
        )
        self.fc = nn.Linear(channels, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv_in(x)
        for block in self.blocks:
            x = block(x)
        x = x.mean(dim=[2, 3])  # Global average pooling
        return self.fc(x)


model = ResNet(num_blocks=4)
total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Total parameters: {total}")
# state_dict() flattens the tree: 'blocks.0.conv1.weight', etc.
print(list(model.state_dict().keys())[:4])



Hierarchical composition mirrors the hardware memory hierarchy in a systems-relevant way: each submodule’s parameters can be loaded independently, enabling placement across devices. When a model is too large for a single GPU, the framework can assign different subtrees of the module hierarchy to different devices, with the tree structure providing natural partition boundaries.
The state_dict() method produces an ordered mapping whose dotted keys (for example, blocks.0.conv1.weight) encode locations in the module hierarchy. A checkpoint for 7 billion FP16 parameters contains approximately 14 GB of weight payload before metadata or additional state, but the file format and storage path determine how those bytes are serialized. Resuming training needs more than the model’s state: optimizers expose their moment buffers and step counts through their own state_dict(), and a training checkpoint saves both so that the run continues with the same optimizer state. load_state_dict() copies matching parameter and buffer values into an already-constructed module and reports missing or unexpected keys according to its strictness setting; it does not reconstruct the module hierarchy. Cross-framework exchange requires a compatible graph and operator representation in addition to weights.
The hierarchical structure also enables module-level traversal for systematic operations. Methods such as .named_modules() iterate the entire tree, supporting bulk transformations such as replacing all BatchNorm layers with GroupNorm or applying Xavier initialization to every Linear layer. These traversal operations depend on the same tree structure that enables parameter discovery, illustrating how a single design decision propagates benefits across multiple use cases.
None of these three principles is specific to PyTorch. Keras layers, Flax modules, and functional approaches address the same problems of parameter management, state tracking, and composition, and differ in how they prioritize among competing solutions rather than in which problems they solve. Two practical patterns show how the principles become system controls: selective parameter freezing reduces unnecessary gradient work for transfer learning (listing 18), and module hooks provide noninvasive inspection (listing 19).



Listing 18: Parameter Freezing: Setting requires_grad=False on a pretrained backbone keeps it fixed while a newly attached head trains, and the optimizer receives only the trainable parameters.


import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision.models import ResNet18_Weights, resnet18

# Freeze all parameters in a pretrained
# model
pretrained_model = resnet18(weights=ResNet18_Weights.DEFAULT)

for param in pretrained_model.parameters():
    param.requires_grad = False

# Replace final layer with trainable parameters
pretrained_model.fc = nn.Linear(512, 10)  # New layer is trainable

# Only fc.parameters() will receive
# gradients during training
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(
    filter(lambda p: p.requires_grad, pretrained_model.parameters()),
    lr=0.001,
)



Module hooks are the inspection counterpart to parameter freezing. They intercept intermediate computations without modifying model code, enabling gradient flow diagnosis and activation monitoring (listing 19).



Listing 19: Module Hooks: Forward hooks capture activations and backward hooks capture gradients during training without modifying the model’s code.


import torch
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 20), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(20, 5))


# Forward hook to inspect activations
def forward_hook(module, input, output):
    print(
        f"Layer: {module.__class__.__name__}, "
        f"Output shape: {output.shape}, "
        f"mean={output.mean():.3f}, "
        f"std={output.std():.3f}"
    )


# Backward hook to inspect gradients
def backward_hook(module, grad_input, grad_output):
    print(f"Gradient norm: {grad_output[0].norm():.3f}")


# Register hooks on specific layer
handle_fwd = model[0].register_forward_hook(forward_hook)
handle_bwd = model[0].register_full_backward_hook(backward_hook)

# Execute forward and backward pass
x = torch.randn(32, 10)
y = model(x)
loss = y.sum()
loss.backward()

# Remove hooks when done
handle_fwd.remove()
handle_bwd.remove()



Parameter discovery, freezing, and hooks are how the module abstraction turns thousands of tensors, each with its own shape, dtype, device, and lifetime, into one object that an optimizer can update, a serializer can save, and a profiler can inspect. With execution, differentiation, and abstraction each examined on its own, the remaining step is to watch them operate together: a single training step exercises every mechanism of this chapter at once.

Self-Check: Question

In framework module abstractions like PyTorch’s nn.Module, what systems mechanism enables optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters()) to find all registered model weights without the developer manually listing every tensor?

Python automatically compiles all local variables into an optimization graph
The GPU driver scans VRAM at runtime to detect all floating-point matrices
The autograd engine injects global hooks into Python’s garbage collector
Overridden attribute assignment registers nn.Parameter objects in the module tree, and parameters() recursively walks that registered structure

Explain why setting model.eval() is necessary for numerically correct inference in models containing BatchNorm or Dropout, and clarify why model.eval() is not a substitute for disabling gradient recording.
In PyTorch’s nn.Module, the dictionary data structure returned by model.____() serializes all learnable parameters and persistent non-parameter buffers (such as BatchNorm running statistics) into named tensor mappings for checkpointing.
What does load_state_dict() fundamentally do in the module serialization pattern described in the section?

It loads parameter and buffer values into an already constructed matching module rather than reconstructing the architecture from scratch
It automatically quantizes all stored tensors before loading them into the model
It discovers the model architecture from weights alone and rebuilds any missing layers
It guarantees cross-framework portability as long as the tensor shapes match

title: 7 ML Frameworks
text:
In every iteration of a training loop, millions of floating-point operations, dynamic memory allocations, and hardware kernel launches must complete within a step that lasts anywhere from microseconds to seconds. For the small network below, as the analysis shows, host dispatch takes most of that time. Execution, differentiation, and hardware abstraction operate simultaneously during model training. In listing 20, a minimal two-layer multilayer perceptron illustrates this convergence across eight executable statements. Tracing each statement through the runtime stack connects the quantitative principles developed in section 7.3.7 to physical execution.
The network is a two-layer version of the MNIST digit classifier from Neural Computation, with 784 inputs, 128 hidden units, and 10 outputs, trained at batch size 32. The example assumes trainable CUDA tensors W1 and W2 with shapes (784, 128) and (128, 10), matching bias vectors b1 and b2, and an optimizer already constructed over these parameters. The listing shows one iteration after that setup.



Listing 20: Training Step Anatomy: One minimal training iteration of a two-layer MLP exercises tensor allocation, kernel dispatch, autograd recording, gradient computation, and parameter updates.


# Single training step for a 2-layer MLP
x = torch.randn(32, 784, device="cuda")  # Input batch
y = torch.randint(0, 10, (32,), device="cuda")  # Labels

# Forward pass
optimizer.zero_grad()
h = torch.relu(x @ W1 + b1)  # Hidden layer
logits = h @ W2 + b2  # Output layer
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y)

# Backward pass
loss.backward()

# Parameter update
optimizer.step()





During the forward pass, executing h = torch.relu(x @ W1 + b1) triggers an eager execution sequence:

Python dispatch: The Python interpreter invokes torch.matmul, which routes through PyTorch’s C++ dispatcher to select the CUDA backend, incurring the Python-dispatch share of the per-operation overhead (about 10 μs in this chapter’s model) before issuing work to the device.
Kernel selection: cuBLAS selects a GEMM kernel configured for dimensions 32 \(\times\) 784 \(\times\) 128, partitioning the computation into thread blocks sized to fit the streaming multiprocessor shared memory and L2 cache tiles.
Kernel launch: The host thread enqueues the launch descriptor into the GPU command stream, consuming driver launch latency while asynchronous execution allows host execution to proceed without blocking on completion.
GPU execution: The streaming multiprocessors stream W1 from HBM24 through L2 cache into registers and the FP32 arithmetic units (Tensor Cores engage only when TF32 or a 16-bit data type is enabled), evaluate the matrix product, and write the output activations back to HBM.
Autograd recording: Concurrently on the host, PyTorch’s autograd engine instantiates an MmBackward node on the dynamic tape, saving references to the device tensors needed for the requested gradients. Here the weight gradient requires x; no input gradient is requested.

24 HBM (high bandwidth memory): Provides 3.35 TB/s on the H100, making it the memory tier that most directly feeds accelerator arithmetic; HBM bandwidth determines whether operations are memory bound or compute bound, and its 80 GB capacity sets the hard ceiling on total live training state. Weights, activations, gradients, optimizer state, and temporary workspace must fit during execution. When they do not, the framework must resort to offloading, selective recomputation, or placement across devices, each adding complexity to what the programmer perceives as a single loss.backward() call.The subsequent bias addition (+ b1) and activation (torch.relu) follow an identical eager path, with each operation dispatching a separate kernel, executing round-trips to HBM, and appending a node to the tape. By the time the forward pass reaches the loss function, the autograd graph holds a complete chain of backward functions and saved activation pointers ready for reverse traversal.



Calling loss.backward() executes reverse-mode automatic differentiation in four stages:

Tape traversal: The autograd engine traverses the recorded computational graph in reverse topological order, starting from the scalar loss node.
Gradient computation: The engine executes the backward kernel registered to each node. Traversing backward, CrossEntropyBackward evaluates \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \text{logits}}\) using the combined softmax-cross-entropy derivative. The MmBackward node for \(\WeightMatrix_2\) computes \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \WeightMatrix_2} = \HiddenActivationMatrix^T \cdot \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \text{logits}}\) and \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \HiddenActivationMatrix}\), where \(\HiddenActivationMatrix\) is the batch of hidden activations (h). The ReluBackward node evaluates the activation mask, zeroing gradients where forward activations satisfy \(\HiddenActivationMatrix \leq 0\). The MmBackward node for \(\WeightMatrix_1\) computes \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \WeightMatrix_1} = \LayerInputMatrix^T \cdot \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \PreactivationMatrix_1}\), where \(\PreactivationMatrix_1 = \LayerInputMatrix\WeightMatrix_1 + \BiasVector_1\) is the pre-activation. Because the input batch \(\LayerInputMatrix\) (x) does not set requires_grad=True, traversal terminates without evaluating \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \LayerInputMatrix}\).
Gradient accumulation: Computed parameter gradients accumulate in-place into the .grad fields of leaf tensors (\(\WeightMatrix_1\), \(\BiasVector_1\), \(\WeightMatrix_2\), \(\BiasVector_2\)).
Saved-state release: As each backward node completes, the framework releases the saved tensor references that it no longer needs. Storage becomes reusable only when no other live reference retains it; in this listing, Python variables such as h can keep tensors alive after backward. The caching allocator can reuse released regions for subsequent operations without returning them immediately to the device.

After backward fills the parameter .grad buffers, optimizer.step() reads those gradients, updates the parameters, and advances any optimizer state. Backward itself computes gradients without applying that update, and the optimizer state the update reads is part of training memory, not of the backward pass.



Knowing which forward and backward kernels run lets us count the arithmetic work and memory traffic of the step to test whether it is bound by compute, HBM bandwidth, or host dispatch. To isolate the core forward and backward operators from section 7.7.1 and section 7.7.2, the count excludes input generation, bias additions and reductions, optimizer updates, and allocator bookkeeping. Within that boundary, each matrix multiplication reads two operands and writes one result, while loss and activation kernels follow the simplified operation-equivalent models stated next.
The traffic model assumes FP32 values occupying 4 bytes each. For x @ W1, it counts one read of the input matrix with shape (32, 784), one read of the weight matrix with shape (784, 128), and one write of the result with shape (32, 128). Multiplying each shape’s dimensions, summing the three element counts, and multiplying by the element width gives the table’s 0.52 MB. The second matrix multiplication uses the same operand rule with its own shapes.
ReLU instead reads and writes each element of its (32, 128) tensor once, so its modeled traffic is twice that tensor’s element count times 4 bytes, yielding 32.8 KB. These counts describe the modeled operator-buffer boundary. They assume full operand reuse within each matrix multiplication and exclude extra layout copies, workspace, and repeated tile loads; cached operands can also reduce actual HBM reads. Saving a reference for backward does not itself copy a tensor. A physical layout conversion, when required, adds its own read and write traffic to these counts.
The backward products use the same read/read/write rule. The weight gradient h.T @ dlogits multiplies (128, 32) by (32, 10); the hidden gradient dlogits @ W2.T multiplies (32, 10) by (10, 128); and x.T @ dz1 multiplies (784, 32) by (32, 128). The first two each cost as much arithmetic as the second forward GEMM, while the third matches the first forward GEMM. No (32, 128) by (128, 784) product is needed because the raw input requests no gradient. The total dense matrix work is therefore 2.013× the forward dense work. This applies the input-gradient exception derived in Derivative calculation process to this two-layer network.
The forward cross-entropy model assigns one operation-equivalent each to exponentiation, accumulation, and normalization per logit, and counts the logit read and saved-score write. For the nonlinear backward work, the ReLU model reads the saved activation and upstream gradient and writes a masked gradient. The simplified combined cross-entropy model reads saved probabilities and integer labels, then subtracts the target and scales by the batch mean to write the logit gradient. Actual loss implementations may split these operations across kernels. The resulting estimates, collected in table 9, make the arithmetic-intensity comparison reproducible without substituting for a measured memory-traffic profile.

The arithmetic-intensity column helps predict each layer’s regime when compared with the target machine’s compute-to-bandwidth ratio. Matrix multiplications reuse operands far more than element-wise operations, but their shapes still determine whether they reach the compute roofline. Conversely, the forward ReLU and cross-entropy estimates perform negligible compute per byte transferred (0.125 FLOP/byte and 0.375 FLOP/byte), making them sensitive to memory bandwidth and, at small sizes, launch latency. In un-fused eager execution, each element-wise operation incurs a separate kernel dispatch and writes intermediate tensors to global-memory buffers between kernels; actual HBM traffic depends on caching.
The analytical model yields ~13.1 MFLOP of arithmetic work and ~1.2 MB of memory traffic for the operations included in the table. Dividing these quantities by peak H100 hardware rates determines the idealized lower bounds:

\(\IronLawComputeTime \approx\) 13.1 MFLOP/67 TFLOP/s FP32 ≈ 0.2 μs
\(\IronLawMemoryTime \approx\) 1.2 MB/3.35 TB/s ≈ 0.4 μs
Under a one-kernel-per-modeled-operator assumption, the 4 selected forward operators and 5 backward operators require 9 driver launches. Python dispatches each of the 4 forward operations individually, whereas backward() enters the C++ autograd engine once and launches all 5 backward kernels without returning to the Python interpreter between them, giving 5 Python entries in total. The illustrative host cost is therefore 5 \(\times\) 10 μs plus 9 \(\times\) 5 μs, or 95 μs.
The excluded optimizer step is not small. An FP32 Adam update reads each parameter, its gradient, and two moments and writes three of them, 28 bytes per parameter, so the 101,770 parameters of this network move about 2.85 MB, more than the whole modeled forward and backward traffic. Counting its launches and the omitted Python calls only raises the host cost above this lower bound.

This dispatch model excludes autograd traversal overhead, allocation, and the operations omitted from the table. A profile must still establish the actual launch count, particularly for loss kernels. Host costs are added without overlap here. In this model, \(\HostSoftwareTime\) exceeds the ideal lower bounds \(\IronLawComputeTime\) and \(\IronLawMemoryTime\) by more than an order of magnitude, so the overhead ratio of equation 4 sits far above 1 and the step is overhead-bound under these assumptions. This is the small multilayer perceptron (MLP) regime of notebook 7.2, now reached from a real training loop. Profiling has a specific job here, which is to confirm that measured kernel times, achieved bandwidth, and host-device overlap match the model before acting on it. When dispatch dominates, three mechanisms attack the launch overhead from different angles. Kernel fusion via torch.compile merges consecutive memory-bound operations into a single kernel, which avoids intermediate round-trips to HBM and collapses launch boundaries. Batch size scaling grows the arithmetic payload linearly while keeping dispatch overhead constant, which amortizes fixed launch latency across more compute work. Graph capture removes repeated Python work in captured regions and allows CUDA Graph replay to submit a captured launch sequence with less host overhead, without requiring the entire step to become one fused kernel.



The timing analysis in section 7.7.3 followed the script’s device="cuda" placement on an H100, but the same eight lines of Python can target a CPU, a TPU, or Apple Silicon by changing the device placement to a supported backend (table 10). Each backend maps common tensor semantics to silicon-specific primitives, so a single loss.backward() invocation routes to different execution pipelines depending on where its tensors live. Because differences in floating-point summation order, reduction trees, and non-deterministic atomic operations introduce numerical variation across backends, equivalence must be validated against explicit numerical tolerances rather than bitwise identity.

Implementation decisions such as device placement, batch size, and compilation mode cascade through execution, differentiation, and abstraction layers simultaneously. Treating the framework as an opaque mathematical interpreter rather than a hardware-aware scheduler hides these interactions until they surface as an idle accelerator or an out-of-memory failure.

Systems Perspective 7.2: The three problems in actionIn D·A·M terms, the single training step exposes how the framework balances algorithm and machine:

Execution: Eager mode preserves imperative line-by-line debugging at the cost of per-kernel launch and dispatch latency.
Differentiation: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation retains intermediate forward activations in HBM to compute exact vector-Jacobian products in reverse topological order.
Abstraction: Unified tensor APIs decouple model code from heterogeneous silicon, dispatching identical operations to cuBLAS, oneMKL, or XLA-compiled HLO programs.

Resolving the friction among these dimensions requires matching operator granularity to hardware rooflines: fusing operations to eliminate memory round-trips, scaling batches to amortize launch latency, and structuring tensors to saturate accelerator execution pipelines.


The step’s costs reduce to a handful of counting rules derived earlier in the chapter and collected in the chapter summary. These rules let a training or inference step be estimated on paper before it is profiled. Count dispatched operations and compare their overhead with device time. Count the passes an unfused elementwise chain makes over memory. Check whether a compiled artifact will run often enough to repay its compilation. Size the activations that backward must keep. Time every host-to-device copy. Applied to the two-layer MLP, the dispatch rule gives the overhead-bound verdict reached above. The elementwise-traffic rule explains why fusing its bias and ReLU kernels removes a round trip. The saved-activation rule bounds what activation checkpointing could save. Every one of these costs exists whichever framework runs the step; frameworks differ in which of them they make easy to see and to reduce. TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX each answer the three framework problems in a different way.

Self-Check: Question

It computes the forward numerical activations on the hardware accelerator and constructs a dynamic autograd tape recording the operations and caching required intermediate tensors for the backward pass
It compiles the entire Python script into a native standalone mobile application

In the chapter’s two-layer MLP training-step analysis, suppose a hypothetical profiler showed many short kernels separated by host-side dispatch gaps. Why could the total eager-mode step time greatly exceed the idealized compute and memory lower bounds even on a very fast GPU?

Because thermal throttling is the main bottleneck for small matrix operations in the scenario
Because the dynamic class hierarchy in the framework leaks memory between layers
Because repeated host-side dispatch and kernel-launch overhead for many small operations can dominate when the device kernels themselves are short

title: 7 ML Frameworks
text:
A team that prototypes quickly but cannot deploy the resulting model, or deploys reliably but cannot debug training failures, has run into a framework design trade-off rather than a missing API call. Each major framework solves all three core problems but emphasizes a different path through them. TensorFlow couples eager development to graph capture and a broad deployment ecosystem. PyTorch begins with eager execution and adds capture, compilation, and export paths. JAX organizes differentiation, vectorization, and compilation as composable function transformations. These are architectural emphases, not exclusive capabilities, and their value depends on the workload and deployment target.


TensorFlow’s architecture spans eager development and graph-based optimization across hardware from cloud TPUs to microcontrollers. TensorFlow 2 executes eagerly by default. Performance-sensitive functions can be captured with tf.function, and deployment formats route captured computation to server, mobile, and browser runtimes. This dual path preserves the production graph capabilities inherited from TensorFlow 1.x without requiring every TensorFlow 2 program to build a complete graph before it runs.
Within a captured tf.function, TensorFlow can apply graph optimizations such as constant folding, kernel fusion, and layout planning. The SavedModel serialization format is the boundary that separates training from deployment (figure 14). Training workflows on the left, including tf.data preprocessing, the Keras modeling API, and distribution strategies across CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs, serialize into one SavedModel artifact. From this central interface, graph definitions pass through supported serving or target-specific conversion paths into deployment runtimes on the right (TensorFlow Serving, TensorFlow Lite, TensorFlow.js, and native language bindings) without retaining Python runtime dependencies.






Figure 14: TensorFlow Training-to-Deployment Pipeline: The SavedModel format provides a boundary between training and deployment by capturing graph structure, weights, and signatures. The right-hand paths include direct serving and target-specific conversion for Lite and JavaScript runtimes. Supported operators and conversion determine whether each path can run without Python in production.



TensorFlow’s answer to the execution problem is therefore two-sided: eager by default for development, with tf.function as the graph-conversion path for performance-sensitive code (TensorFlow Developers 2024). Its strength is the compiled path from a captured graph to many deployment runtimes.

TensorFlow Developers. 2024. Better Performance with tf.function.



Where TensorFlow’s design centers the path from captured graph to deployment runtime, PyTorch centers developer experience. PyTorch was built from the start on dynamic graphs (or “Define-by-Run”). Instead of building a graph before execution, PyTorch builds the computational graph as the code runs, because researchers need immediate feedback when experimenting with novel architectures and a define-then-run cycle slows that loop. Python loops, conditionals, and debuggers work directly inside a model’s forward pass, with no special syntax and no separate compilation step, which matters most while architectures and training objectives are still changing.
PyTorch’s answer to the differentiation problem is tape-based autograd (section 7.4.3.1): flexible and debuggable, but harder to optimize globally because the tape is rebuilt each iteration. Its answer to the abstraction problem is more pragmatic than comprehensive: strong GPU support through cuBLAS and cuDNN, with deployment paths including torch.export, edge-targeted ExecuTorch, ONNX, and specialized runtimes.
The trade-off is therefore a more fragmented deployment path. Because the graph is dynamic, the framework cannot easily perform global optimizations before execution. A model that works perfectly in development may hit performance walls in production when dispatch overhead dominates small operations. To bridge this research-to-production gap, PyTorch added graph-capture and compilation paths (torch.compile and export workflows) that capture a dynamic model and turn it into an optimized representation for deployment. This evolution shows how an eager framework can move toward the production end of the compilation continuum while preserving the interactive experience that motivated the design.



PyTorch’s eager execution and TensorFlow’s graph compilation represent two points on a spectrum, yet both share an imperative programming heritage where computation proceeds as a sequence of stateful operations. JAX takes a different user-facing approach, built on functional programming principles and composable program transformations rather than object-level tapes or user-authored graph APIs (Bradbury et al. 2018). Developed at Google, JAX is especially useful for work requiring custom differentiation, advanced optimization research, and large-scale distributed training.

Bradbury, James, Roy Frostig, Peter Hawkins, Matthew James Johnson, Chris Leary, Dougal Maclaurin, George Necula, et al. 2018. JAX: Composable Transformations of Python+NumPy Programs.
Where PyTorch and TensorFlow track state through objects and expose autograd through dynamic tapes or graph-capture paths, JAX asks users to write pure Python functions and treats differentiation, vectorization, and compilation as composable program transformations (listing 21). The jax.grad function returns a new function that computes gradients, which can then be transformed again when the interfaces are compatible: vmap(grad(f)) computes per-example gradients, and jit(vmap(grad(f))) compiles that batched computation. Transformation order is semantically meaningful rather than arbitrary.



Listing 21: JAX Function Transformations: Wrapping an ordinary loss function in grad, then vmap, then jit yields per-example gradients compiled through XLA.


import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp


def loss_fn(params, x, y):
    pred = jnp.dot(x, params["w"]) + params["b"]
    return jnp.mean((pred - y) ** 2)


# Transform: compute gradients
grad_fn = jax.grad(loss_fn)

# Transform: vectorize over batch dimension
batched_grad = jax.vmap(grad_fn, in_axes=(None, 0, 0))

# Transform: compile to XLA
fast_batched_grad = jax.jit(batched_grad)

# Compose all three: fast, batched gradient computation



This functional approach requires pure functions (no side effects) and immutable data (arrays cannot be modified in place). These constraints are stricter than PyTorch’s mutable object model, and they are what make the transformations safe. Because function outputs depend only on inputs, the compiler can reorder, fuse, and parallelize operations without changing results, and one transformation can be applied to the output of another.
Each transformation does one job. jax.grad returns a gradient function; jax.vmap can vectorize a compatible function over mapped axes; and jax.jit can trace and compile a stable transformed function for a particular argument signature. Unlike an iterative Python loop that issues individual operations sequentially with repeated dispatch overhead, jax.vmap pushes the batch dimension directly into the underlying primitives, allowing compatible per-sample matrix-vector operations to become batched matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMM). The compiled program can contain multiple kernels and library calls. Across devices, JAX shards arrays over a device Mesh and compiles with jax.jit, or maps explicitly with jax.shard_map (the successor to the older jax.pmap); gradient aggregation is expressed with collectives such as lax.psum or lax.pmean. These transformations compose according to their types and semantics, and different orders can compute different quantities.
The same minimalist core delegates neural network abstractions to companion libraries (Flax and Equinox) and optimization to Optax. This separation reflects the functional philosophy: the core provides transformations, while libraries build conventional abstractions on top. The trade-off is that production readiness depends on both the transformation model and the maturity of the surrounding libraries, export paths, and operational tooling for the target environment.
The functional constraints pay off where gradient computation is itself the object of study. Custom differentiation, including higher-order gradients and custom vector-Jacobian product (VJP) and Jacobian-vector product (JVP) rules, composes cleanly because pure functions make differentiation rules predictable, which serves optimization research and scientific computing with AD. Compilation-heavy accelerator workloads gain utilization from XLA when the program fits the functional style. In exchange, JAX demands more upfront investment than PyTorch, with explicit state management, a learning curve for the functional paradigm, and compiled code that is harder to debug than eager execution. It fits teams whose requirements match these strengths rather than serving as a default.



Comparing TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX by asking which framework is fastest in the abstract asks the wrong question, because raw speed changes with model shape, batch size, hardware backend, and compiler configuration. The durable difference among the three designs (graph-first vs. eager-first, stateful vs. functional) is what each one lets the system see and optimize. Table 11 therefore maps TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX back to the three framework problems: execution visibility, differentiation model, and hardware abstraction path.



Table 11: Framework Design Trade-Offs: Each column reflects a distinct answer to the three core problems. TensorFlow makes deployment and graph capture central, PyTorch makes eager execution and debugging central, and JAX makes functional transformation and compiler visibility central. The table is a diagnostic map, not a benchmark ranking.

The comparison therefore tells an engineer which constraint to profile first. In PyTorch, check whether eager dispatch or graph breaks dominate. In TensorFlow, check whether the captured graph covers the operators and deployment target. In JAX, check whether shapes and purity let XLA compile the program actually executed. A framework-level comparison or leaderboard can orient a decision, but it cannot replace profiling the specific workload on the target hardware.
The same simple network exposes how each design philosophy shapes the code. Listing 22 implements one neural network, a single linear layer mapping ten inputs to one output, across all three frameworks.



Listing 22: Hello World in Three Frameworks: One single-layer network is written three ways, in PyTorch (object-oriented), TensorFlow/Keras (declarative), and JAX (functional).


# PyTorch - Dynamic, Pythonic
import torch.nn as nn


class SimpleNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(10, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc(x)


# TensorFlow/Keras - High-level API
import tensorflow as tf

model = tf.keras.Sequential(
    [tf.keras.layers.Dense(1, input_shape=(10,))]
)

# JAX - Functional approach
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import random


def simple_net(params, x):
    return jnp.dot(x, params["w"]) + params["b"]


key = random.PRNGKey(0)
key_w, key_b = random.split(key)
params = {
    "w": random.normal(key_w, (10, 1)),
    "b": random.normal(key_b, (1,)),
}



These three implementations solve the same mathematical problem, yet each reveals where its framework keeps state and when its computation graph comes into existence. PyTorch binds state and computation together through class inheritance (nn.Module) and evaluates eagerly, building the graph as Python runs. Standard debuggers and control flow therefore work naturally, at the cost of hiding the full computation from an optimizer unless a graph-capture pass is invoked. TensorFlow and Keras also execute eagerly by default in TensorFlow 2, whereas structured models can be captured with tf.function and exported to supported deployment runtimes whenever operator coverage and target conversion allow. By contrast, JAX treats the model as a pure function25 over immutable arrays with no internal object state. It turns grad, vmap (automatic vectorization), and jit (just-in-time compilation26) into composable transformations on stateless functions, in exchange for explicit parameter passing.
25 Pure function: Returns outputs determined by its inputs without relying on untracked side effects; JAX transformations are designed for pure functions. Ordinary Python effects may run during tracing but are not represented in the compiled computation, and impure code can fail or behave unexpectedly. Runtime printing or external effects require supported mechanisms such as jax.debug.print or callbacks; random draws require explicitly managed keys.26 Just-in-time (JIT) compilation: Traces a function for an argument signature and lowers it to backend-specific executable code; the first call pays tracing and compilation costs; compatible later calls can reuse the cached executable. New shapes, dtypes, devices, or static arguments may trigger another compilation. Both compilation time and cached-call overhead depend on the program, backend, and hardware.No framework maximizes all three goals simultaneously, and the ten-line program makes the trade visible in source code rather than buried in compiler internals: where state lives, when the graph exists, and what the compiler is allowed to see. Each design trades what the compiler can see against how quickly a person can iterate. Graph capture and ahead-of-time compilation can reduce runtime overhead and intermediate data movement. Eager evaluation shortens the human iteration loop, outside the iron-law runtime equation, at the cost of compiler visibility until a graph-capture path is used. Functional purity gives XLA more freedom to transform a stable traced program. Each philosophy also shapes code syntax, team workflows, debugging practices, and deployment pipelines, so migration costs grow with project-specific integrations and assumptions.



Eager defaults favor iteration; JAX’s traced functions favor the compiler.

Self-Check: Question

Which framework ecosystem in the section is organized around SavedModel as a central boundary between Python-side development and multiple deployment paths such as server serving, mobile conversion, and browser execution?

PyTorch eager execution as originally presented
TensorFlow ecosystem with SavedModel feeding Serving, Lite conversion, and TensorFlow.js paths
Pure NumPy with custom Python socket servers
Scikit-learn with standard pickle deserialization

What core programming-model commitment distinguishes JAX from both PyTorch and TensorFlow in the chapter’s comparison, enabling transformations like jax.grad, jax.vmap, and jax.jit to compose when their contracts align?

Dynamic class inheritance with mutable object references for all layer parameters
Global state mutation across all forward and backward passes
Pure functions over immutable array-like data, with transformations applied to functions rather than hidden mutable objects
Graph capture via AST string parsing of Python source files

Compare the workflow and deployment trade-offs that led PyTorch to dominate academic research while TensorFlow established strong early dominance in enterprise production serving during the late 2010s.
Explain how JAX’s requirement that functions must be pure and free of side effects enables the XLA compiler to generate highly optimized accelerator kernels through jax.jit.

title: 7 ML Frameworks
text:
Those differences in where state lives and what the compiler sees become concrete obligations once a team commits to one framework for a project that must ship to a particular device. Framework selection decides which framework a team develops in, given the model it must express, the team that must maintain it, and the targets it must eventually run on. Development framework and deployment runtime need not be the same system: a model can be developed in PyTorch or TensorFlow and exported to a compact runtime for the device. The choice of that inference runtime is a serving decision, developed in Inference Runtime Selection. The development framework still has to reach it, so the deployment target acts as a filter on which frameworks are viable.
Suppose a team deploys a fixed-shape vision model to a CPU-only embedded Linux device, with a 20 ms p99 (99th-percentile, Latency and tail latency) inference-latency target under a specified load and a 256 MB model-and-runtime memory budget. Assume target-device trials with matching inputs, batch size, precision, and numerical tolerances establish two viable paths. PyTorch development with ONNX Runtime has 18 ms p99 latency and 140 MB peak memory use, while TensorFlow development with TensorFlow Lite has 15 ms p99 latency and 90 MB peak memory use. A path that depends on a GPU-only runtime fails the hardware filter even if its latency elsewhere is lower. These are hypothetical project measurements, not general performance rankings. The selection must now distinguish a feasible path from a worthwhile migration.
The embedded project has already fixed the deployment target, but it leaves two choices open: which development environment the team can maintain and which compatible export path meets its budget. Eager development and compiled deployment can coexist along either path, so the team need not trade away its debugging workflow to obtain a compact inference runtime.

Systems Perspective 7.3: Framework selection constraintsRather than seeking the “best” framework, effective selection first eliminates candidates that cannot satisfy hard constraints: deployment target, required operations, compiler path, and team expertise. Only then should soft preferences such as performance, development speed, and ecosystem rank the survivors.




The two hypothetical measurements establish latency and memory feasibility only for the tested model and inputs. A defensible choice also checks operator semantics, software dependencies, and hardware coverage. The three TensorFlow variants in table 12 make those filters visible within one ecosystem; the same questions apply to the PyTorch-to-ONNX path.



Table 12: TensorFlow Variants Across Deployment Tiers: The rows group what each variant can express (first four), what it requires of the platform (middle three), and what hardware and footprint it targets (last three). Training capability disappears across the tiers while inference and lower-precision tooling survive, which leaves operator coverage as the discriminating capability: broad in TensorFlow, inference-focused in TensorFlow Lite, and reduced to the operators one model selects in TensorFlow Lite Micro. Binary size and memory footprint depend on the build, selected operators, delegates, model, and runtime configuration rather than on the variant alone.
