Across the four eras, engineering effort migrated from handcrafting domain heuristics toward building scalable compute and data pipelines. The bitter lesson explains why this shift recurred.

Self-Check: Question

Which historical transition correctly pairs an AI era with the primary systems bottleneck that limited its scalability and forced the transition to the subsequent paradigm?

Symbolic AI was limited by compute throughput, forcing the transition to expert systems; Deep Learning was limited by human rule maintenance, forcing the transition to statistical learning.
Expert Systems were limited by GPU memory bandwidth, forcing the transition to statistical learning; Statistical Learning was limited by formal logic ambiguity, forcing the transition to deep learning.
Statistical Learning was limited by a complete lack of training labels, forcing the transition to symbolic logic; Symbolic AI was limited by hardware integer arithmetic, forcing the transition to neural networks.
Expert Systems were limited by the knowledge acquisition bottleneck (serial human expert elicitation bandwidth), forcing the transition to statistical learning; Statistical Learning was limited by the feature engineering bottleneck (manual extraction of hand-crafted representations), forcing the transition to deep learning.

Moravec’s paradox observes that tasks humans find easy (such as visual perception, walking, and grasping) require vast computational resources, while tasks humans find hard (such as playing chess or solving algebra) require comparatively little compute. What is the direct implication of this paradox for ML systems hardware?

Symbolic reasoning algorithms require multi-GPU accelerator clusters, whereas computer vision pipelines run efficiently on single-threaded CPUs.
High-level reasoning tasks saturate off-chip memory bandwidth, while low-level perceptual tasks are strictly compute-bound.
Perceptual and physical-world AI tasks demand massive parallelism, high memory bandwidth, and specialized hardware accelerators to process dense, high-dimensional sensor streams in real time.
Robotic perception models can be deployed on microcontrollers without model compression or accuracy degradation.

Place the four historical AI engineering eras in chronological order based on when their primary paradigm dominated, and identify the key bottleneck that constrained each era:


Deep Learning Era
Expert Systems Era
Symbolic AI Era
Statistical Learning Era


Why was AlexNet’s 2012 ImageNet victory considered a breakthrough in systems co-design rather than purely an algorithmic advance?
True or False: The Viola-Jones face detection algorithm achieved real-time execution on early-2000s CPUs by using a cascade of simple rectangular features that evaluated an average of about ten features per candidate region, although the full cascade contained over 6,000 features.

See Answers →

title: Introduction {#sec-introduction}
text:
1.4 The Bitter Lesson
Expert systems invested engineering effort in encoding domain knowledge; deep learning systems invest much of that effort in learning from data at scale. The bitter lesson captures the historical advantage of general methods, especially search and learning, that can make effective use of increasing computation. Richard Sutton16 crystallized this insight in his 2019 essay “The Bitter Lesson” (Sutton 2019). Sutton wrote, “The biggest lesson that can be read from 70 years of AI research is that general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, and by a large margin.”
16 Richard Sutton: A reinforcement learning pioneer whose essay emphasizes search and learning as methods that scale with computation (Sutton 2019). The lesson is “bitter” because carefully encoded human knowledge has repeatedly been overtaken by more general methods. It is a lesson about long-term progress, not a claim that domain knowledge has no engineering value.
Sutton, Richard S. 2019. “The Bitter Lesson.” Incompleteideas.net 43.
Training scale at the frontier is often stated in accelerator-days (GPU-days when the accelerator is a GPU): one reference accelerator running continuously for 24 hours. Table 3 pairs representative benchmark milestones with their hardware. Its final column runs from CPU-based learning to multi-thousand-accelerator clusters, using 2.5 million reference GPU-days as an estimated frontier-training anchor (Patel and Wong 2023).



Table 3: AI Performance Evolution Across Paradigms: Representative systems illustrate the growth in computational scale across eras. GPT-4 training details are estimated reference anchors rather than official disclosures.












Era
Approach
Representative Task
Performance
Computational Resources




Statistical ML (1990s–2000s)
Feature engineering + learning
Handwritten digit recognition
about 98–99% on MNIST-era benchmarks (LeCun et al. 1998)
CPU-era feature pipelines; resources varied by implementation


Deep Learning (2012)
End-to-end neural networks
ImageNet top-5 accuracy
84.7% (AlexNet)
6 days on 2 GPUs


Modern Deep Learning (2020+)
Large-scale transformers (Vaswani et al. 2017)
ImageNet top-1 accuracy
88.55% (ViT-H/14) (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021)
Large-scale Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) pretraining


Modern Deep Learning (2023)
Foundation models
MMLU benchmark
86.4% (GPT-4) (OpenAI et al. 2023)
Estimated ~2.5 million reference GPU-days (on the order of 25,000 reference GPUs run for 100 days) (Patel and Wong 2023)




LeCun, Yann, Léon Bottou, Yoshua Bengio, and Patrick Haffner. 1998. “Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition.” Proceedings of the IEEE 86 (11): 2278–324. https://doi.org/10.1109/5.726791.

Vaswani, Ashish, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, and Illia Polosukhin. 2017. “Attention Is All You Need.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 30: 5998–6008.

Dosovitskiy, Alexey, Lucas Beyer, Alexander Kolesnikov, Dirk Weissenborn, Xiaohua Zhai, Thomas Unterthiner, Mostafa Dehghani, et al. 2021. “An Image Is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Patel, Dylan, and Gerald Wong. 2023. GPT-4 Architecture, Infrastructure, Training Dataset, Costs, Vision, MoE. SemiAnalysis Blog.



Digit recognition, ImageNet classification, and Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) measure different capabilities under separate metrics, so table 3 does not compare methods on one task. It shows instead that each new capability threshold demanded orders of magnitude more hardware, from single-node CPU routines to multi-megawatt accelerator clusters. Testing Sutton’s lesson, whether general methods powered by raw computation surpass hand-engineered representations, requires holding the task fixed and comparing competing approaches within one domain.
Game playing separates the roles of search and learning. In chess, IBM’s Deep Blue17 defeated world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997 by combining custom chess hardware, large-scale search, and chess-specific evaluation knowledge. In Go, DeepMind’s AlphaGo learned from expert games and self-play, using neural networks to guide tree search, but still used some engineered input features (Silver et al. 2016). AlphaGo Zero18 provides the clearer example of Sutton’s lesson: it learned through self-play without human game records or those hand-engineered features (Silver et al. 2017). The advance depended on methods that could turn computation into improved play, not merely on a faster machine.
17 Deep Blue: Its 480 custom chess chips worked alongside general-purpose processors, searching about 100 million positions per second in tactical positions and approaching 200 million in quieter positions (Campbell et al. 2002). The hardware accelerated chess-specific search and evaluation; it did not remove the system’s reliance on encoded chess knowledge.
Campbell, Murray, Jr. Hoane A.Joseph, and Feng-hsiung Hsu. 2002. “Deep Blue.” Artificial Intelligence 134 (1-2): 57–83. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0004-3702(01)00129-1.

Silver, David, Aja Huang, Chris J. Maddison, Arthur Guez, Laurent Sifre, George van den Driessche, Julian Schrittwieser, et al. 2016. “Mastering the Game of Go with Deep Neural Networks and Tree Search.” Nature 529 (7587): 484–89. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature16961.
18 AlphaGo Zero: After three days of self-play training, it defeated AlphaGo Lee, the version that had beaten Lee Sedol, by 100 games to 0 (Silver et al. 2017). Self-play generated the training examples, allowing search and learning to improve play without a dataset of human games.
Silver, David, Julian Schrittwieser, Karen Simonyan, Ioannis Antonoglou, Aja Huang, Arthur Guez, Thomas Hubert, et al. 2017. “Mastering the Game of Go Without Human Knowledge.” Nature 550 (7676): 354–59. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature24270.
The lesson is “bitter” because encoding human expertise can appear to be the most direct path to a solution. Sutton’s examples show how scalable search and learning repeatedly overtook such approaches. More computation does not guarantee better results; the method must use it productively, and the data and objective must support the intended task.
Modern language models such as GPT-4 (OpenAI et al. 2023) and image generation systems such as DALL-E (Ramesh et al. 2021) illustrate the engineering demands of learning at scale. Much of their behavior is learned from large datasets rather than expressed as explicit linguistic or artistic rules. Training GPT-3 alone was estimated to consume roughly 1.3 GWh of energy19 (Patterson et al. 2021), and serving these models to millions of users turns inference into a continuous data-center power, cooling, and capacity-planning problem.

OpenAI, Josh Achiam, Steven Adler, Sandhini Agarwal, Lama Ahmad, Ilge Akkaya, Florencia Leoni Aleman, et al. 2023. “GPT-4 Technical Report.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2303.08774, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2303.08774.

Ramesh, A., M. Pavlov, G. Goh, S. Gray, C. Voss, A. Radford, M. Chen, and I. Sutskever. 2021. “Zero-Shot Text-to-Image Generation.” In Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML 2021, 18-24 July 2021, Virtual Event, edited by Marina Meila and Tong Zhang, vol. 139. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research. PMLR.
19 GPT-3 training energy: Patterson et al. (2021) estimated that GPT-3’s training consumed approximately 1,287 MWh and produced 552 metric tons of CO2-equivalent emissions. The energy estimate corresponds to the annual electricity use of about 120 US households at a baseline of 10.7 MWh/household-year. Emissions also depend on how that electricity is generated.
Patterson, David, Joseph Gonzalez, Quoc Le, Chen Liang, Lluis-Miquel Munguia, Daniel Rothchild, David So, Maud Texier, and Jeff Dean. 2021. “Carbon Emissions and Large Neural Network Training.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2104.10350.
20 Memory bandwidth: The rate at which a memory interface transfers data, measured in bytes per second. A processor must receive the values an operation needs before it can perform the arithmetic. When moving those values takes longer than computing with them, faster arithmetic alone cannot remove the delay; reducing transfers or increasing the available bandwidth addresses the limiting resource.When model capability scales with raw computation, the binding limits shift to physical infrastructure: memory bandwidth,20 interconnect latency, thermal dissipation, and data pipeline throughput. Data movement, arithmetic throughput, and operational reliability must therefore be designed as one problem. Before section 1.9 formalizes the engineering discipline that manages that growth, we first define the boundaries of a machine learning system and the diagnostic axes that govern it.

Self-Check: Question

Why did Richard Sutton describe the fundamental finding of 70 years of AI research as a ‘bitter’ lesson for researchers and engineers?

Human intuition naturally seeks to build intelligence by encoding domain expertise and linguistic rules into models, yet historical progress repeatedly demonstrates that general-purpose search and learning leveraging raw computation outperform hand-crafted human knowledge.
Hardware accelerators have reached physical thermodynamic scaling limits, preventing further increases in neural network parameter counts.
Stochastic gradient descent algorithms produce models whose internal mathematical representations cannot be formally proven correct.
Open-source models consistently match the performance of proprietary industrial foundation models trained at hundred-million-dollar compute budgets.

In comparing IBM’s Deep Blue (1997) and DeepMind’s AlphaGo Zero (2017), how do their designs reflect the progression toward Sutton’s bitter lesson?

Deep Blue relied entirely on deep reinforcement learning, whereas AlphaGo Zero returned to hand-coded expert evaluation tables.
Deep Blue combined custom silicon search (100 to 200 million positions/second) with hand-coded chess heuristics, whereas AlphaGo Zero learned through self-play without human game records or hand-engineered features, using neural networks to guide tree search.
Both systems avoided the use of custom silicon or GPUs, relying strictly on algorithmic elegance over compute scale.
AlphaGo Zero eliminated all tree search mechanisms in favor of pure single-step feedforward classification.

If the bitter lesson states that computation-leveraging methods dominate over time, why does realizing this advantage depend primarily on systems engineering rather than pure algorithmic theory?
True or False: According to the bitter lesson, building domain-specific linguistic or perceptual rules into deep neural network architectures provides a permanent, compounding advantage over general architectures as compute budgets expand.

See Answers →

title: Introduction {#sec-introduction}
text:
1.5 Defining ML Systems
Absorbing computational growth takes a working system, not only a trained model. Return to the email spam filter introduced in section 1.2: in a notebook, it is a classifier that maps message text to a spam probability, but in production it must process global email traffic measured in hundreds of billions of messages per day (Statista Research Department 2024). At that scale, the classifier is only one component inside an end-to-end operational pipeline that must continuously ingest new examples, retrain as attack tactics evolve, and classify incoming mail within strict delivery latency budgets.

Statista Research Department. 2024. Number of Sent and Received e-Mails Per Day Worldwide from 2017 to 2027. Statista.
The challenge begins with data. The filter is trained on labeled examples and needs updated training data and periodic retraining as spam tactics change. It is also an algorithmic problem, because the model must generalize from those examples to messages it has never seen before. Precision measures the fraction of flagged messages that are actually spam; recall measures the fraction of all spam messages that the filter catches. Flagging more messages may catch more spam while also hiding legitimate mail, so the system must evaluate both consequences. Finally, it is an infrastructure problem. Providers must handle incoming traffic, store and update models, and return predictions within their delivery latency budget. The classifier is therefore only one component of an evolving data, software, and hardware system.
When a new phishing template appears, the data layer must capture representative messages, the algorithm must learn to separate attacks from legitimate mail, and the infrastructure must deploy and serve the updated model. Any layer can fail while the others continue working, so the full chain from measurement through learning to execution is the right unit of analysis.

Definition 1.1: Machine learning systems
Machine learning systems combine models that learn from data with the software and hardware needed to train, deploy, and maintain them. Their performance depends jointly on data quality, algorithm choice, and machine capacity.

Significance: Requirements are end to end, so a failure in any layer changes the user-visible result even while the other layers operate correctly.
Distinction: The system includes every path an input travels, not only the model. A feature computed one way in training and another in serving changes what the system predicts even when the model and its weights are identical.
Common pitfall: The model is not the system. Data pipelines, feature transformations, serving infrastructure, monitoring, and feedback loops surround the learned parameters and often dominate the engineering burden (Sculley et al. 2015).




Sculley, D., Gary Holt, Daniel Golovin, Eugene Davydov, Todd Phillips, Dietmar Ebner, Vinay Chaudhary, Michael Young, Jean-François Crespo, and Dan Dennison. 2015. “Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 28: 2503–11.
The definition exposes three diagnostic axes: the data that describes the task, the algorithm that turns examples into behavior, and the machine that executes that behavior within the operating budget. The same user-visible symptom can originate in any of the three. Treating every miss as a model problem risks improving the wrong component. The D·A·M taxonomy separates these causes for diagnosis.
Each explanation calls for different evidence. The data hypothesis sends the engineer to coverage, labels, and distribution shift. The algorithm hypothesis sends the engineer to error slices (errors grouped by input type), model capacity, and the learning objective. The machine hypothesis sends the engineer to latency, throughput, memory, and utilization. These investigations are not interchangeable. Faster hardware cannot supply examples that were never collected, while a larger dataset cannot repair a serving path that misses its deadline because memory is saturated.
The relevant constraint is the one whose relaxation improves the end-to-end result. This idea of a binding constraint, used informally in the history above, prevents teams from optimizing the most visible component instead of the component that governs the outcome. The purpose of D·A·M is therefore operational: it identifies the next hypothesis to test and the class of intervention capable of changing system behavior. The diagnosis is provisional. Once an intervention relaxes one limit, the system must be measured again because a different axis may now bind. D·A·M is a loop, not a one-time label.

Definition 1.2: D·A·M taxonomy
D·A·M taxonomy is a diagnostic framework for examining machine learning system bottlenecks along three axes. Data determines what examples and bytes the system must process, Algorithm determines the model structure and work required to learn or predict, and Machine determines the hardware capacity available to execute that work. The goal is to identify which axis is the binding constraint.

Significance: The diagnostic power is concrete even before detailed hardware arithmetic enters the story. If the spam filter misses a new phishing campaign because the training set never contained that tactic, the binding axis is Data. If the training examples are adequate but the model cannot express the pattern, the binding axis is Algorithm. If both are adequate but the service cannot classify messages quickly enough during a traffic spike, the binding axis is Machine. Quantitative diagnosis begins by asking which axis is limiting the system.
Distinction: The D·A·M taxonomy connects predictive quality to physical execution. Algorithm choice shapes both the data needed to learn useful behavior and the machine resources needed to run it. Those requirements depend on the task and training procedure, so model size alone does not determine either generalization or runtime.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that the three axes are independent. Changing from a simple classifier to a larger model can require more memory, different serving infrastructure, and a broader data distribution. Because changing one of Data, Algorithm, and Machine can change the requirements imposed on the other two, every edge of the triangle in figure 3 points both ways.









Figure 3: The D·A·M Axis Triad: Each vertex is one diagnostic axis, and each double-headed edge is a path along which a relaxed bottleneck can reappear on the neighboring axis.



An operational diagnosis earns confidence only when an intervention validates it, that is, when relaxing the identified constraint improves full-system behavior. Resolving one bottleneck frequently migrates the binding constraint across an adjacent edge of figure 3, so interventions rarely end the optimization process. Upgrading to faster accelerators (Machine) leaves execution units idling if storage I/O cannot stream input batches quickly enough (Data). Conversely, expanding dataset volume (Data) exposes model architectures that lack the expressive capacity to absorb new patterns (Algorithm). Scaling model capacity to close that gap (Algorithm) soon exceeds accelerator memory, triggering out-of-memory faults or expensive paging across the PCIe bus (Machine). Engineering an ML system therefore requires identifying the currently binding constraint while anticipating where the bottleneck will migrate once that constraint is relaxed.
While the triad separates the three axes to simplify initial diagnosis, practical systems operate at their boundaries. Data formats govern memory traffic, model architectures dictate hardware functional unit utilization, and deployment budgets reshape both data representation and algorithmic design. Figure 4 partitions these interfaces into a three-set Venn diagram whose pairwise overlaps each pose one question: what the system can learn from (\(\text{D} \cap \text{A}\)), how information moves (\(\text{D} \cap \text{M}\)), and how computation executes efficiently (\(\text{A} \cap \text{M}\)).






Figure 4: The D·A·M Intersection Landscape: Each circle lists the concerns that belong to one axis, and each pairwise overlap is titled with the question that axis pair must answer jointly. The central region, where all three circles overlap, is labeled ML systems engineering.



At the center, all three questions must be answered together. Data selection and training determine which examples help the model learn useful behavior. Data engineering and hardware acceleration deliver that information to the machine at speed. Frameworks and execution techniques turn the model’s computations into efficient work on that silicon. Pruning a model (Algorithm), which removes parameters that contribute little to its predictions, alters its memory footprint and how much of it stays in fast on-chip memory (Machine). Compressing input features can likewise reduce transfers while adding preparation work (Data). These changes must be evaluated across the interfaces, because a local improvement may leave the end-to-end result unchanged. Even when every component executes without error, a shift on the data axis can still degrade predictions silently.


↪ How pruning shrinks a model’s memory footprint, and why its effect on speed depends on the sparsity pattern the hardware can exploit, is developed in Pruning.

Self-Check: Question

An ML engineering team trains a 70-billion-parameter language model. When profiling the distributed cluster, they notice that accelerator compute engines remain idle for 45% of execution time waiting for batch tensors to be loaded from remote object storage over the network. Along which D·A·M axis does the primary binding constraint lie, and which intersection represents the appropriate optimization space?

Machine axis; \(\text{Algorithm} \cap \text{Machine}\) (mixed precision quantization and kernel fusion)
Algorithm axis; \(\text{Data} \cap \text{Algorithm}\) (curriculum learning and active data selection)
Data axis; \(\text{Data} \cap \text{Machine}\) (I/O pipelining, prefetching, and storage memory hierarchy)
Workload axis; \(\text{Data} \cap \text{Algorithm} \cap \text{Machine}\) (reinforcement learning from human feedback)

Explain what the concept of a ‘binding constraint’ means in the D·A·M framework, and describe the risk of optimizing a non-binding axis.
In the D·A·M intersection landscape, the intersection between Algorithm and Machine (\(\text{A} \cap \text{M}\)) addresses the core question of ‘How to ____’, focusing on how the model’s mathematical work is mapped onto hardware execution and data movement efficiently.

See Answers →

title: Introduction {#sec-introduction}
text:
1.6 When ML Systems Fail Silently
That vulnerability on the data axis governs the first half of the dual mandate: keeping learned behavior trustworthy after deployment. In an automotive driver-assistance system, diagnostic trouble codes and hardware watchdog timers expose hardware or communication faults, yet they do not measure how often a perception model detects pedestrians. When seasonal conditions introduce low-angle winter sunlight, heavy precipitation, or bulky clothing underrepresented in training, pedestrian recall can decline from 95 percent to 85 percent even while the accelerator processes images at full frame rate without raising a hardware fault. Correct execution and predictive quality are separate properties, and an ML system must be engineered and monitored for both.
Crashes, unhandled exceptions, and failed health checks make some software defects directly observable, though conventional software can also produce silent numerical errors or logic bugs. Machine learning adds another route to silent degradation: learned behavior loses predictive quality as the operating population changes, even while the runtime executes instructions without error, memory allocations succeed, and inference servers return predictions well within latency service level agreements (SLAs).



Recall falls while health metrics stay flat.
In this example, the miss rate triples, from 1 in 20 pedestrian frames to 3 in 20. That is a substantial change in detection quality, but it does not imply a tripling of vehicle-level safety risk, because temporal filtering, sensor fusion, and downstream control affect how missed detections influence a driving decision.
Input distributions can drift as environmental conditions, user behavior, or sensor calibrations change (Gama et al. 2014; Quiñonero-Candela et al. 2009). A model may then apply its fixed weights to inputs unlike those on which it was evaluated. The machine can execute every operation correctly while producing predictions whose quality no longer meets the requirement.

Gama, João, Indrė Žliobaitė, Albert Bifet, Mykola Pechenizkiy, and Abdelhamid Bouchachia. 2014. “A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation.” ACM Computing Surveys 46 (4): 1–37. https://doi.org/10.1145/2523813.

Quiñonero-Candela, Joaquin, Masashi Sugiyama, Anton Schwaighofer, and Neil D. Lawrence, eds. 2009. Dataset Shift in Machine Learning. Neural Information Processing Series. The MIT Press.
Outcome measurements establish whether predictive quality has fallen; distribution-divergence signals can prompt investigation before those outcomes arrive. When both are observed, model degradation can be approximated locally as a function of distribution shift. Let \(\InitialAccuracy\) denote the baseline accuracy at deployment, and let \(\StatisticalDivergence\) represent the statistical divergence between current production distribution \(\CurrentDistribution\) and training distribution \(\TrainingDistribution\). Let \(\FittedSensitivity\) denote the locally fitted sensitivity to that shift measure, so that \(\AccuracyAfterDeployment(\DeploymentAge)\) is the accuracy after the model has been deployed for time \(\DeploymentAge\). This relationship, formalized in equation 1, is the degradation equation: \[ \AccuracyAfterDeployment(\DeploymentAge) \approx \InitialAccuracy - \FittedSensitivity \cdot \StatisticalDivergence  \tag{1}\]
This approximation describes a local trend fitted from observed inputs and labeled outcomes; it is not a universal law of accuracy loss. The chapters on deployment return to it as a statistical drift diagnostic. Data drift occurs when \(\CurrentDistribution\) differs from \(\TrainingDistribution\). Such a shift can reduce inference quality even when the model and execution environment remain unchanged, but the shift alone does not establish a quality loss. Large changes may fall outside the range where the fitted relationship holds. The divergence measure \(\DivergenceMeasure(\cdot \lVert \cdot)\) is left general here.


↪ The statistics that measure distribution shift and detect drift in production data are developed in Data drift detection and response.
The equation separates baseline quality from sensitivity to shift. Better data, objectives, and architectures can change both quantities, so an improved baseline does not by itself establish robustness to drift. For the driving example, training on representative winter images may reduce sensitivity to seasonal conditions; evaluating pedestrian recall under those conditions establishes whether it does. Monitoring \(\StatisticalDivergence\) provides a warning that prompts engineers to seek outcome evidence. That evidence determines whether retraining or another intervention is needed. Knowing when to reevaluate is as important as knowing how to train.


↪ How drift signals and labeled outcomes become an operational decision to retrain, made only when the expected benefit exceeds the cost, is developed in Retraining decision framework.
Silent degradation can also originate inside the system through training-serving skew. Training and serving may use separate implementations to transform raw inputs into model features. If those transformations differ, for example by resizing images with a different interpolation method or applying different missing-value defaults, the model receives inputs unlike those used in training. The model can execute cleanly and return predictions on time while accuracy falls. This is a software consistency defect whose consequence is degraded learned behavior.


↪ Keeping transformation code and its fitted parameters identical across training and serving is developed in Training-serving consistency.
Host-health signals such as CPU utilization, memory residency, network I/O, and HTTP status codes remain necessary, but do not measure whether predictions are useful. Machine learning operations must track these infrastructure metrics alongside data quality, feature distributions, and prediction accuracy. Because an ML system can fail silently while infrastructure metrics appear nominal, system design must integrate continuous evaluation from data ingestion through inference serving.
Useful predictions satisfy the first half of the ML systems mandate. The second half requires producing them within the available latency, memory, energy, and cost budgets. Meeting those budgets requires a quantitative account of where execution time goes.

Self-Check: Question

In the degradation equation \(\text{Accuracy}(t) \approx \text{Accuracy}_0 - \lambda \cdot \mathcal{D}(P_t \lVert P_0)\), what do the terms \(\mathcal{D}(P_t \lVert P_0)\) and \(\lambda\) represent, and which engineering lever addresses \(\lambda\)?

\(\mathcal{D}(P_t \lVert P_0)\) is hardware clock jitter, \(\lambda\) is GPU temperature sensitivity, and it is addressed by dynamic voltage and frequency scaling.
\(\mathcal{D}(P_t \lVert P_0)\) is statistical divergence between live production data and training data, \(\lambda\) is model sensitivity to distribution shift, and it is addressed by robust training and domain adaptation to flatten the degradation curve.
\(\mathcal{D}(P_t \lVert P_0)\) is the memory bandwidth ratio, \(\lambda\) is cache miss penalty, and it is addressed by prefetching weights into on-chip memory.
\(\mathcal{D}(P_t \lVert P_0)\) is training loss divergence, \(\lambda\) is the learning rate decay, and it is addressed by tuning the optimization algorithm.

A production fraud detection model begins misclassifying high-risk transactions immediately after deployment. An audit reveals that the training pipeline extracted user account age in integer days, while the live inference microservice computed account age in fractional floating-point seconds. What type of systems failure does this scenario illustrate?

Training-serving skew, where discrepancies in feature computation between training and serving pipelines cause silent model degradation despite bug-free code execution.
Hardware memory corruption caused by unaligned tensor strides in the GPU inference runtime.
Unbounded latency growth where deserialization overhead violates the service-level agreement.
Concept drift caused by macroeconomic shifts in consumer purchasing behavior over multiple years.

Why does the degradation equation indicate that tracking statistical data drift (\(\mathcal{D}(P_t \lVert P_0)\)) alone is necessary but not sufficient to determine whether a deployed model must be retrained?
True or False: Holding drift sensitivity fixed, improving the initial training accuracy (\(\text{Accuracy}_0\)) of an ML model shifts the starting point of the degradation curve upward, but does not change the model’s rate of accuracy decline (\(\lambda\)) with respect to distribution drift over time.

See Answers →

title: Introduction {#sec-introduction}
text:
1.7 Iron Law of ML Systems
Computational scale has a physical cost, and it shows up as two familiar failures. A training job stalls when storage cannot feed an accelerator; an inference path misses its deadline when model state moves too slowly through memory or across the network. Their symptoms differ, but both are governed by how the three D·A·M axes combine to consume wall-clock time. Across Data (D), Algorithm (A), and Machine (M), every ML task completes by processing a set of samples (examples in vision or tabular workloads, tokens in language models) through an algorithm’s operations on hardware. By dimensional cancellation, total execution time \(\Time\) (seconds) is the product of these three factors (equation 2): \[\Time = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Samples}}{\text{Task}}\right)}_{\text{Data}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Sample}}\right)}_{\text{Algorithm}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Seconds}}{\text{FLOP}}\right)}_{\text{Machine}} \tag{2}\]
The same equation governs both training and inference because only the definition of the task and the scale of each factor change. The product of the first two factors sets the total arithmetic work \(\Operations\) (FLOPs), while the third factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) is the realized time the machine takes per operation:

Training: A task is a training run (or an optimization step). Here \(\text{Samples/Task}\) is the corpus token budget \(\DatasetSize\) (billions to trillions of tokens), and \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) spans the forward and backward passes (\(\approx 6\Parameters\) FLOPs per token for a dense transformer, giving \(\Operations \approx 6\Parameters\DatasetSize\)). Because large training batches reuse model weights across thousands of tokens per step, the machine amortizes memory transfers and dispatch overhead, keeping realized \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\) low and near the hardware’s compute ceiling.
Inference: A task is serving a request or generating a response. Here \(\text{Samples/Task}\) shrinks to a small request batch (\(\BatchSize\)) or a stream of generated tokens, and \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) covers only the forward pass (\(\approx 2\Parameters\) FLOPs per token). With far fewer samples per invocation to amortize weight reads and orchestration, realized \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\) rises sharply as memory bandwidth and fixed latency overtake arithmetic.

A real machine does not run at its datasheet peak rate \(1/\PeakRate\) because physical execution requires moving data across memory and interconnect buses, driving arithmetic units at some realized utilization, and paying fixed control overheads. Assuming these three physical costs occur sequentially, the iron law of ML systems unpacks total execution time \(\Time\) (seconds) into their sum (equation 3): \[\Time = \underbrace{\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}}_{\text{Memory Time}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}}_{\text{Compute Time}} + \underbrace{\Latency}_{\text{Latency Overhead}} \tag{3}\]
Together, equation 2 and equation 3 account for the physical-execution half of the dual mandate introduced in section 1.1:

The memory term \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\) represents the physical cost of moving bits. \(\DataVolume\) is the volume of data moved (bytes), and \(\Bandwidth\) is the memory or network bandwidth (bytes/s). Whether loading terabytes from cloud storage or fetching weights from high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) packaged beside an accelerator, performance is often limited by I/O physics. Part I develops this foundation.
The compute term \((\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\) represents the cost of arithmetic. \(\Operations\) is the number of floating-point operations (FLOPs) set by the product of \(\text{Samples/Task}\) and \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\). \(\PeakRate\) is the hardware’s theoretical peak throughput (FLOP/s). \(\EfficiencyHw\) is dimensionless realized compute utilization \((0 \le \EfficiencyHw \le 1)\). Parts II and III develop this term.
The latency term \((\Latency)\) represents orchestration, networking, and serialization overhead (seconds), treated as fixed for the modeled execution. Engineering changes can reduce this overhead, which can dominate small, latency-critical requests where little data moves and little arithmetic runs. Part IV develops this term.

Consider a hypothetical task that spends 2 seconds moving data, 8 seconds computing, and 1 second on overhead. Its total is 11 seconds. Doubling the arithmetic rate reduces computation to 4 seconds, but leaves movement and overhead unchanged. The task now takes 7 seconds, rather than half its original time. A faster component helps only through the portion of the time budget it changes.
Data enters equation 2 and equation 3 in two distinct ways: logical samples versus physical bytes. In equation 2, the Data factor counts how many examples or tokens the task processes (such as the dataset size \(\DatasetSize\) in the \(6 \cdot \Parameters \cdot \DatasetSize\) training estimate), which multiplies \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) to fix total arithmetic work \(\Operations\). In equation 3, by contrast, \(\DataVolume\) counts the physical bytes moved across a memory or interconnect bus, including model weights (\(\Parameters\)), activations, cached sequence state, and gradients alongside the raw inputs. When a language model decodes a single token at batch size one, the logical input is one token (\(\text{Samples/Task} = 1\)), yet \(\DataVolume\) spans gigabytes of model weights streamed from high-bandwidth memory.

Systems Perspective 1.1: The iron law analogyThe name “iron law” follows the processor performance equation of Patterson and Hennessy (2017), \(\text{Time/Program} = (\text{Instructions/Program}) \times (\text{Cycles/Instruction}) \times (\text{Seconds/Cycle})\). Equation 2 is the direct ML counterpart: the Data (\(\text{Samples/Task}\)) and Algorithm (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\)) factors multiply to set total operations \(\Operations\) just as program path length and instruction set determine instruction count. The Machine factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) mirrors cycles per instruction times clock period. Reducing \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) (for example, through unstructured sparsity) can still slow down execution if irregular memory accesses inflate \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\), just as complex CPU instructions that cut instruction count can lose performance by inflating cycles per instruction. Equation 3 then takes the same second step that computer architects take when decomposing processor time into compute cycles, memory-stall cycles, and pipeline overhead.
The additive form assumes sequential execution. When movement and computation overlap, the critical-path lower bound replaces the sum in equation 4: \[\PipelinedExecutionTime\ge \max\left(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}, \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}\right) + \Latency \tag{4}\] This max-based formulation reflects hardware that transfers the next block of data while computing on the current one, so the slower of the two stages hides the faster. Equality requires ideal overlap and assumes that \(\Latency\) remains outside the overlapped phases.
Even as a sum, the iron law identifies which physical constraint dominates before any optimization begins. Amdahl’s law (Amdahl 1967) plays the same role for speedups. Accelerating only part of a task leaves the untouched remainder in place, and that remainder caps the whole task’s speedup however fast the accelerated part becomes. equation 11.1 states that cap quantitatively as a bound on overall speedup. From sum to max presents the refined treatment, including pipelining and overlap techniques that transform the additive model into the max-based formulation used in practice.



Amdahl, Gene M. 1967. “Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities.” Proceedings of the April 18-20, 1967, Spring Joint Computer Conference on - AFIPS ’67 (Spring), AFIPS ’67 (spring), 483–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560.

Hennessy, John L., and David A. Patterson. 2017. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. 6th ed. Morgan Kaufmann.
Diagnosing the limiting term requires comparing the workload with the machine. Arithmetic intensity \((\ArithmeticIntensity = \Operations/\DataVolume)\) counts the operations performed per byte moved. In equation 3, the memory term \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\) and the compute term \((\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\) take equal time when the workload’s operations per byte match the machine’s effective compute rate \((\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\) divided by its memory bandwidth \((\Bandwidth)\), a hardware threshold often stated at peak throughput as \(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\). Below that balance point, each transferred byte supports too few operations to keep the arithmetic units busy for the duration of the transfer, so the workload waits on memory. Above that balance point, arithmetic takes longer than data movement, so the workload waits on computation. Improving the smaller of the two terms yields a limited end-to-end gain, while overhead \((\Latency)\) sits outside this comparison and can dominate small requests. A single-accelerator estimate applies these ideas below.


↪ The roofline model, which bounds attainable throughput by arithmetic intensity and locates the ridge point, is developed in Performance Bounds.

Napkin Math 1.1: Estimating one local executionProblem: A hypothetical workload on one accelerator moves 2 GB at 100 GB/s, performs 1 GFLOP at an effective arithmetic rate of 100 GFLOP/s, and incurs 5 ms of fixed overhead. Movement precedes computation. What execution time does the iron law predict, and which rate should be improved first?
Math: Dividing bytes by bytes/s gives a movement time of 20 ms. Dividing FLOPs by FLOP/s gives a compute time of 10 ms; the supplied effective rate already includes \(\EfficiencyHw\), so it must not be multiplied by efficiency again. Adding these durations and overhead gives 35 ms. Movement is the largest term.
Result: Raising bandwidth to 200 GB/s reduces movement to 10 ms and total sequential time to 25 ms. Arithmetic and overhead remain unchanged, so doubling bandwidth does not halve the total.
Systems insight: If movement and computation could instead overlap ideally, with overhead still outside both phases, the lower bound would be 25 ms before the upgrade and 15 ms afterward. The upgrade balances the two stages; further bandwidth increases alone would leave that ideal bound unchanged. Whether the sum or the bound describes a measured run depends on its execution schedule.


A larger training estimate returns to equation 2 under an explicit compute-dominated assumption. It folds all non-arithmetic delays into an effective end-to-end utilization factor \(\EfficiencyHw\), so that the realized machine factor across \(\AcceleratorCount\) parallel accelerators is \((\AcceleratorCount \cdot \PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)^{-1}\) seconds per FLOP. Its efficiency factor accounts for the losses involved in coordinating many accelerators, beyond the local execution just calculated. A multi-machine cluster of that kind lies outside this book’s single-machine scope; the estimate appears here only to show the scale the compute term can reach.


↪ The training-time form of the iron law, which converts an operation count into days of training at a realized utilization, is developed in Training-Time Law.

Napkin Math 1.2: Training GPT-3Problem: How long would a GPT-3-class model take to train on a hypothetical modern cluster of 1,024 accelerators? This reference cluster uses A100-class accelerators, a generation newer than the V100 GPUs of the original run estimated earlier at roughly 405 V100 GPU-years. The result therefore shows what the same work could cost on newer hardware at the utilization assumed below. The original run achieved lower utilization, so part of the speedup comes from that assumption rather than from the hardware.
Given:

Operations \((\Operations)\): \(\approx 3.14 \times 10^{23}\ \text{FLOPs}\) (the product of the Data factor, 300 billion tokens, and the Algorithm factor, \(6\Parameters\) FLOPs/token for 175 billion parameters)
Peak Rate \((\PeakRate)\): 312 TFLOP/s
Efficiency \((\EfficiencyHw)\): ≈ 45 percent (an assumed planning value for large-scale distributed training, where communication and stalls keep realized throughput well below peak)
Accelerator Count \((\AcceleratorCount)\): 1,024 accelerators

Math:
Assume that the training workload reuses data sufficiently to make arithmetic dominant and overlaps data loading with computation. Under this compute-dominated approximation, the remaining communication and memory stalls are included in the effective end-to-end utilization \(\EfficiencyHw\) across \(\AcceleratorCount\) parallel accelerators, and the training time \(\TrainingTime\) follows:

\(\TrainingTime \approx \frac{\Operations}{\AcceleratorCount \cdot \PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}\) \(\approx \frac{3.14 \times 10^{23}}{1024 \times 312 \times 10^{12} \times 0.45}\) \(\approx 25\ \text{days}\)

Result: 25 days.
Systems insight: If hardware utilization \((\EfficiencyHw)\) improves from 45 percent to 60 percent through better scheduling and more efficient execution, training time drops to 19 days, saving 6 days of expensive compute time.


Each term of the iron law resolves to seconds, making the equation dimensionally consistent, yet execution time is not the only physical constraint. For battery-powered edge devices and warehouse-scale accelerator clusters alike, energy dissipation and thermal limits often bind the system before throughput limits are reached. Moving bits across the memory hierarchy exacts an energy tax that parallels the delay of the memory term.


↪ The term-by-term unit check behind this statement, and its use as a test for any performance equation, are collected for reference in Dimensional analysis.
Let \(\DataVolume\) be the total data volume moved (bytes), \(\EnergyPerByteMoved\) the energy per byte moved, \(\Operations\) the total operation count, and \(\EnergyPerOperation\) the energy per operation. Equation 5 formalizes this relationship, following the hardware-energy observation that data movement can dominate arithmetic energy (Horowitz 2014): \[ \TotalEnergy \approx \underbrace{ \DataVolume \times \EnergyPerByteMoved }_{\text{Movement Term}} + \underbrace{ \Operations \times \EnergyPerOperation }_{\text{Compute Term}}  \tag{5}\]



Moving a byte from DRAM costs about 145 times the energy of a 16-bit floating-point multiply, so data movement, not arithmetic, dominates the energy cost.

Horowitz, Mark. 2014. “1.1 Computing’s Energy Problem (and What We Can Do about It).” 2014 IEEE International Solid-State Circuits Conference Digest of Technical Papers (ISSCC), 10–14. https://doi.org/10.1109/isscc.2014.6757323.
The energy comparison depends on the transfer size and arithmetic operation being counted. Under the energy constants used in this text, moving one byte from off-chip DRAM consumes roughly 145× the energy of a 16-bit floating-point (FP16) multiply and 800× that of an INT8 (8-bit integer) multiply (Horowitz 2014). Whether movement dominates a complete workload also depends on the number and width of transfers relative to its operation count. The physical reason for the per-access gap is that data movement requires charging and discharging wires over longer distances, while arithmetic occurs locally within a processing unit’s circuits. Minimizing avoidable data movement \((\DataVolume)\) can therefore improve both speed and energy efficiency.


↪ The energy ladder from on-chip arithmetic to off-chip memory, and why its gap makes data movement a primary target for accelerator design, are developed in Machine learning hardware specialization.

Checkpoint 1.2: The iron law
Before proceeding, verify that you can manipulate both forms of the iron law (equation 2 and equation 3, where \(\Time = \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency\)):

D·A·M product (equation 2): identify which two factors multiply to set \(\Operations\), and explain the difference between logical samples or tokens (\(\DatasetSize\)) in the Data factor and physical bytes moved (\(\DataVolume\)) in the memory term.
Memory term \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\): identify the physical resource that bounds this term and name one workload regime where it dominates.
Compute term \((\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\): identify the hardware quantity and utilization factor that bound this term.
Latency term \((\Latency)\): identify which costs remain after data movement and arithmetic have been optimized.
Peak throughput: holding the other quantities fixed, if you double \(\PeakRate\), which term improves, and why does total execution time fall by less than half when movement and overhead also contribute?




1.7.1 Lighthouse models put the iron law into practice
Each term of the iron law suggests an engineering intervention. The memory term can be reduced by moving fewer bytes or increasing effective bandwidth. The compute term can be reduced by performing fewer operations or using arithmetic units more effectively. The latency term calls for reducing orchestration and communication overhead. The equation alone does not say which intervention a system needs; that depends on its measured workload and whether the required data fits in memory.
Concrete workloads answer that question. Five recurring lighthouse models serve as diagnostic probes for the iron law throughout this book; later chapters explain the model structures and execution mechanisms behind their constraints. Each is a distinct stress case under the workload conditions stated for it:

Image classification (ResNet-50) (He et al. 2016) probes compute throughput. With sufficient reuse of learned filters across image positions and batched inputs, the arithmetic term (\(\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\)) can dominate execution time.
Text generation (GPT-2/Llama) probes memory bandwidth, with GPT-2 (Radford et al. 2019) anchoring the lighthouse and Llama (Touvron et al. 2023) representing its larger successors. Generating text token by token, the phase called decode, for one request at a time offers little weight reuse per token, so fetching weights from memory (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)) can become the binding constraint.
Recommendation (DLRM), the Deep Learning Recommendation Model (Naumov et al. 2019), probes memory capacity, which determines whether the model can run at all. Embedding tables store numerical vectors for user and item IDs. Large tables can reach about a hundred gigabytes in reference models (Naumov et al. 2019), and terabytes in production (Mudigere et al. 2022), exceeding single-accelerator device memory.
Mobile vision (MobileNetV2) (Sandler et al. 2018) probes compute throughput within a power envelope. Its efficient operators cut arithmetic far enough that a phone-class processor can classify frames in real time while sharing a battery and thermal budget with other applications.
Keyword spotting (KWS) probes the power envelope, because an always-on microcontroller21 must listen continuously for a wake word within a milliwatt budget and kilobytes of memory (Zhang et al. 2017).


He, Kaiming, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun. 2016. “Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition.” 2016 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 770–78. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2016.90.

Radford, Alec, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, and Ilya Sutskever. 2019. Language Models Are Unsupervised Multitask Learners. OpenAI.

Touvron, Hugo, Thibaut Lavril, Gautier Izacard, Xavier Martinet, Marie-Anne Lachaux, Timothée Lacroix, Baptiste Rozière, et al. 2023. “LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2302.13971.

Naumov, Maxim, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Hao-Jun Michael Shi, Jianyu Huang, Narayanan Sundaraman, Jongsoo Park, Xiaodong Wang, et al. 2019. “Deep Learning Recommendation Model for Personalization and Recommendation Systems.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1906.00091.

Mudigere, Dheevatsa, Yuchen Hao, Jianyu Huang, Zhihao Jia, Andrew Tulloch, Srinivas Sridharan, Xing Liu, et al. 2022. “Software-Hardware Co-Design for Fast and Scalable Training of Deep Learning Recommendation Models.” International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), 993–1011. https://doi.org/10.1145/3470496.3533727.

Sandler, Mark, Andrew Howard, Menglong Zhu, Andrey Zhmoginov, and Liang-Chieh Chen. 2018. “MobileNetV2: Inverted Residuals and Linear Bottlenecks.” 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 4510–20. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2018.00474.
21 Microcontrollers: Single-chip computers integrating a processor, memory, and interfaces to sensors or other devices. The keyword-spotting lighthouse has a kilobyte-scale memory budget and a milliwatt-scale power budget. A candidate model must fit those limits as well as meet its prediction-quality requirement.
Zhang, Yundong, Naveen Suda, Liangzhen Lai, and Vikas Chandra. 2017. Hello Edge: Keyword Spotting on Microcontrollers.

Mattson, Peter, Christine Cheng, Cody Coleman, Greg Diamos, Paulius Micikevicius, David Patterson, Hanlin Tang, et al. 2020. “MLPerf Training Benchmark.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys) 2: 336–49.

Gupta, Udit, Carole-Jean Wu, Xiaodong Wang, Maxim Naumov, Brandon Reagen, David Brooks, Bradford Cottel, et al. 2020. “The Architectural Implications of Facebook’s DNN-Based Personalized Recommendation.” 2020 IEEE International Symposium on High Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA), 488–501. https://doi.org/10.1109/HPCA47549.2020.00047.
These five are deliberately not the newest models. Each marks a point where the field turned and isolates one binding constraint in its cleanest form. ResNet-50 made deep convolutional training on accelerators routine and became a reference workload of the MLPerf training benchmark (Mattson et al. 2020). GPT-2 showed that scaling a decoder-only language model changes what it can do. DLRM represents the recommendation models that accounted for most AI inference cycles in Facebook’s data centers when it was introduced (Gupta et al. 2020). Later models grow in scale, but the same terms of the iron law bind them, so the analysis in this book should transfer to models that do not yet exist.
The iron law makes these differences actionable under the stated workload conditions. Raising peak compute \(\PeakRate\) helps convolutions when arithmetic dominates, while increasing memory bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\) helps generation when weight transfers dominate. Batch size, reuse, and serving patterns can change that diagnosis, so the bottleneck belongs to the workload on a particular machine rather than to the model name alone. For that reason, table 4 identifies each lighthouse by the regime it probes.



Same iron law, opposite dominant term, opposite fix.



Table 4: Lighthouse Models as Reference Workloads: Each workload illustrates a resource constraint under the stated conditions, providing a concrete setting for investigating how system constraints affect architectural choices. Each model’s architectural background appears in Network Architectures, and its quantitative specifications in Arithmetic intensity across workloads.

title: Introduction {#sec-introduction}
text:
1.8 Three Dimensions of ML Efficiency
Because training compute grew faster than hardware, every term of the iron law also had to shrink through better algorithms, better utilization, and better data. AlexNet’s 2012 run is where that pressure began. Read through the D·A·M taxonomy, its breakthrough was coordination across all three axes rather than algorithmic novelty in isolation. It combined a convolutional architecture whose parallel matrix operations matched GPU capabilities, the 1.3M labeled images of the 2012 ImageNet challenge training split22 (Deng et al. 2009), and two consumer GPUs running for about six days. A university laboratory could afford that budget. Modern foundation models demand training compute roughly 8 orders of magnitude larger.
22 ImageNet: The full image collection grew from 3.2 million images reported in the initial paper to about 14.2 million across thousands of labeled categories (Deng et al. 2009; Russakovsky et al. 2015). The 2012 challenge used a subset of this collection; AlexNet’s training split contained about 1.3M labeled images. Distinguishing the full collection from a benchmark split matters when comparing dataset sizes and training costs.
Deng, Jia, Wei Dong, Richard Socher, Li-Jia Li, Kai Li, and Li Fei-Fei. 2009. “ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database.” 2009 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 248–55. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2009.5206848.

Russakovsky, Olga, Jia Deng, Hao Su, Jonathan Krause, Sanjeev Satheesh, Sean Ma, Zhiheng Huang, et al. 2015. “ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge.” International Journal of Computer Vision 115 (3): 211–52. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11263-015-0816-y.
Scale drives AI progress, as the bitter lesson (section 1.4) argued, but ever-larger datasets and compute budgets narrow participation to the most resource-rich organizations. Even those organizations eventually meet physical limits in data center power, memory bandwidth, and the diminishing returns of adding more parameters. Using existing compute more efficiently is therefore a complementary path to progress.
Efficiency offers three complementary choices that align with the three factors of equation 2: perform less computation per sample, execute that computation in fewer seconds per FLOP, or choose more informative examples so the task needs fewer samples. Algorithmic efficiency reduces computational requirements (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\)) through model design and training procedures. Compute efficiency lowers realized machine time per operation (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) by raising hardware utilization \(\EfficiencyHw\) and cutting memory and latency stalls, turning more of the machine’s theoretical capacity into useful work. Data selection identifies examples that contribute useful learning signal, reducing \(\text{Samples/Task}\) (and therefore \(\Operations\)) when training processes fewer examples; under a fixed computation budget, it can instead redirect work toward more informative examples.
Choosing among them calls for a bottleneck diagnosis across the interfaces in figure 4. All three must account for information movement: reducing \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) alone has little effect on wall-clock time when the memory term \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\) dominates \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\).
Part III develops these dimensions in the order work flows through a system. Data selection asks which examples merit training computation. Model compression23 asks how much storage and arithmetic a trained model requires. Hardware acceleration explains how the remaining operations map onto memory and compute units. This teaching order does not prescribe an optimization sequence. The measured binding constraint and deployment budget determine where to intervene first, and hardware limits inform data and model choices from the outset.
23 Model compression: A family of techniques that reduces model storage or computation, including quantization (storing values in fewer bits), pruning (removing parameters that contribute little), and distillation (training a smaller model to imitate a larger one). Its size and accuracy effects depend on the model, method, workload, and target hardware.24 Moore’s law: Gordon Moore’s 1965 observation described rapid growth in the number of components that could be economically integrated on a chip (Moore 1998); later industry summaries often expressed the cadence as roughly a two-year doubling.
Moore, G. E. 1998. “Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits.” Proceedings of the IEEE 86 (1): 82–85. https://doi.org/10.1109/jproc.1998.658762.
The historical trajectory of computer vision models isolates the compounding effect of architectural design. Hernandez and Brown (2020) held accuracy fixed at the AlexNet level and asked how much training computation successive architectures needed to reach it. Because they counted operations rather than seconds, hardware speed does not enter the measurement. Between AlexNet in 2012 and EfficientNet in 2019, the required compute fell by 44×, a halving roughly every 15 months between those two endpoints (figure 5). The dashed line in the figure is an exponential fit to those measured points. The reduction measures algorithmic progress at fixed task quality. Comparing it with hardware progress would require a matching measure of useful throughput or energy efficiency; Moore’s law describes transistor integration,24 which alone does not determine either quantity.














Figure 5: Algorithmic Efficiency Trajectory: Each point shows how much less training compute an ImageNet architecture needed than AlexNet to reach AlexNet-level accuracy, so height measures algorithmic progress with hardware speed held out. Most later architectures sit well above AlexNet, although individual points vary; VGG-11 needed more compute than AlexNet. The dashed line is a least-squares exponential fit to the measured points. Data from Hernandez and Brown (2020).


Hernandez, Danny, and Tom B. Brown. 2020. “Measuring the Algorithmic Efficiency of Neural Networks.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2005.04305, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2005.04305.


Architecture-by-architecture gains tell only half the story, because over the same years aggregate training compute in published frontier runs climbed far faster than algorithms could offset. Figure 6 charts that climb on a logarithmic scale, from early deep learning models near \(10^{18}\) FLOPs to frontier systems beyond \(10^{25}\) FLOPs. Sevilla et al. (2022) measured a doubling time of roughly six months across the deep learning era, and a least-squares fit to the runs in the figure gives a similar cadence. An earlier study over 2012 through 2018 found a 3.4-month doubling (Amodei and Hernandez 2018); different windows and sets of runs yield different estimates. Both studies found training compute growing faster than the roughly two-year doubling associated with Moore’s law. This divergence motivates efficiency improvements across algorithms, software runtimes, and hardware architectures, helping keep useful systems within reach as workload demands grow.














Figure 6: The Era of Scale: Each point plots a third-party training-compute estimate (FLOPs) for a notable model against its publication year on a log scale. Runs below \(10^{22}\) FLOPs appear in blue; larger runs appear in red. The dashed line is a least-squares fit to these points and doubles every 5 months. From AlexNet (2012) to GPT-4-class training scale (2023), compute requirements increased by roughly 8 orders of magnitude (about 44.7M times). This endpoint comparison is distinct from training-compute trend studies (Amodei and Hernandez 2018; Sevilla et al. 2022) and is used here to motivate the specialized infrastructure described in this book. Data from Epoch AI’s Notable AI Models database (Epoch AI 2026).


Amodei, Dario, and Danny Hernandez. 2018. “AI and Compute.” OpenAI Blog 6.

Sevilla, Jaime, Lennart Heim, Anson Ho, Tamay Besiroglu, Marius Hobbhahn, and Pablo Villalobos. 2022. “Compute Trends Across Three Eras of Machine Learning.” 2022 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN), 1–8. https://doi.org/10.1109/ijcnn55064.2022.9891914.

Epoch AI. 2026. Notable AI Models.


The two plots show how efficiency gains can coexist with growth in training scale. Figure 5 reports a 44× reduction in compute for a fixed accuracy target, while figure 6 illustrates roughly 8 orders of magnitude of growth in selected training runs. They measure different quantities and include contextual estimates, so they do not by themselves establish an economic cause. Efficiency makes a given capability less expensive; organizations can use the savings to reduce spending, broaden access, or pursue more demanding targets.

Systems Perspective 1.2: The efficiency paradoxJevons paradox (Jevons 1865) describes cases in which more efficient resource use leads to greater total consumption because demand expands. A similar response is possible in AI. If EfficientNet needs 44× less compute than AlexNet to reach the same accuracy, an organization can reinvest the savings in larger models or more experiments. It can also choose a smaller budget or serve more users at the same cost. Reinvestment is a possible consequence of efficiency, not an inevitable one, and the plotted trends alone do not establish it.



Jevons, William Stanley. 1865. The Coal Question: An Inquiry Concerning the Progress of the Nation, and the Probable Exhaustion of Our Coal Mines. Macmillan; Co.
Whether reinvestment pays is an economic question. The same physical terms that determine time and energy also determine cost: every byte moved, operation executed, and millisecond of latency consumes infrastructure budget. The test is whether added compute buys enough model improvement to justify the expenditure.

1.8.1 Return on compute: Weighing accuracy against cost
A model upgrade that raises accuracy by 1 percentage point can still be the wrong choice if it requires a 10\(\times\) increase in \(\Operations\) (total operations) whose cost exceeds the application’s budget or the gain’s value. Return on compute (RoC) measures the incremental accuracy gain per added dollar of infrastructure investment, in accuracy points per dollar: \[ \text{RoC} = \frac{\FiniteChange\text{Accuracy}}{\FiniteChange\text{Compute Cost}}  \tag{6}\]
The RoC test compares that ratio against what each point of accuracy is worth to the application. Each alternative is compared against the same baseline, and the ratio is defined only when the added cost is positive. The GPT-3 estimate above demonstrates a different benefit: assuming scheduling changes preserve model quality, raising \(\EfficiencyHw\) from 45 percent to 60 percent saves 6 days of cluster time for the same training work. This is a cost saving, not an accuracy gain. It can free budget for another experiment, whose incremental accuracy and cost must then be measured. The iron law helps estimate what computation costs; RoC asks whether an additional investment is worthwhile. Efficiency choices must therefore be evaluated against the system’s goals and deployment constraints.

Self-Check: Question

title: Introduction {#sec-introduction}
text:
1.9 AI Engineering as a Discipline
A cloud service may optimize throughput across racks of accelerators, while an edge device must remain within a strict battery and thermal envelope, so the same model can be efficient in one setting and unusable in another. An engineer who must hold predictive quality and resource cost to one specification across such different operating budgets needs to combine the three quantitative tools developed above. The degradation equation judges predictive quality in both settings, the iron law judges execution time and energy, and the efficiency framework judges the cost of improving either. Applying them draws on computer science, electrical engineering, statistics, and established software and systems engineering practice.

Definition 1.3: AI engineering
AI engineering is the discipline of designing, deploying, and maintaining ML systems whose predictive quality and execution meet stated deployment requirements. It integrates decisions about data, algorithms, and machines, using statistical evidence to assess learned behavior and measurements to assess resource use.

Significance: A model improvement must still satisfy the other system requirements. AI engineering jointly considers data quality and governance, prediction quality, execution time, memory, energy, and cost. A model that achieves 95 percent accuracy in research but violates a 100 ms deployment latency requirement does not meet the system specification.
Distinction: A model-level evaluation establishes evidence under a stated dataset and protocol. AI engineering must carry that evidence into a complete system whose latency, throughput, accuracy, cost, fairness, and robustness meet deployment requirements, and reassess it when operating conditions change.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that AI engineering is just “software engineering for ML.” Software correctness remains necessary, but the system specification also includes statistical claims about learned behavior over an operating population. Code tests cannot establish those claims by themselves, making continuing evaluation and monitoring part of the system design.



A requirement can be fixed while the evidence for meeting it remains uncertain. Pedestrian recall of at least 95 percent over a stated population is a fixed target; evaluation estimates recall from sampled outcomes, with uncertainty that must be reported and reassessed as conditions change. Execution requirements also need a defined workload and measurement protocol. Sampled response times support a statistical latency claim; a hard bound requires assumptions and analysis covering the specified execution conditions. Combining these obligations resembles the earlier convergence of computing and electrical engineering in computer engineering.25 In this book’s usage, AI engineering names the discipline and its shared principles, while ML systems engineering names the work of applying them to build and operate a specific system under its deployment constraints.
25 Computer engineering: A discipline spanning digital circuits, processor design, and the software that runs on them. Moving a function from software into specialized hardware can change its speed, power use, and flexibility. ML systems engineering extends this shared design problem to include learned behavior and the data that shapes it.
1.9.1 Engineering across the ML lifecycle
Shipping a trained model to production does not end the engineering work, because the first shift in user behavior or upstream data can force a deployed system back into data collection and training. Putting an algorithmic advance into service requires data ingestion and preprocessing, computation within the available machine budget, reliable serving, and ongoing evidence of real-world performance. These obligations form a recurring lifecycle rather than a linear sequence that ends at deployment. The engineering object is no longer only code but also data, model behavior, deployment context, and monitoring evidence evolving together.
At the project level, six responsibilities organize this work: problem definition, data collection and preparation, model development and training, evaluation and validation, deployment and integration, and monitoring and maintenance. Problem definition sets the task and acceptance requirements before any data is collected, so figure 7 begins after it and splits the data stage into collection and preparation to show where each feedback path re-enters.
The structural difference shows up first in tooling. Version control, continuous integration, and static analysis have long supported code-defined behavior. For learned behavior, these practices must also track dataset and model versions and test predictive quality, because source-code changes alone do not describe changes to the deployed system.


↪ The workflow controls that learned behavior adds to established software practice are developed in ML vs. traditional software.
Feedback must therefore assess learned behavior as well as software execution. In figure 7, a failed evaluation sends work back to data preparation, while degraded production performance sends it back to data collection. Feedback determines which work must be repeated; it does not make every alert a retraining instruction. The six stages and the feedback paths that join them into a loop are developed in The Lifecycle as a Loop.






Figure 7: ML System Lifecycle: Forward arrows carry work from data collection to monitoring, and the two labeled return arrows mark where evidence sends it back. The return arrows end at different stages, so a failed evaluation and a confirmed production problem trigger different amounts of rework.



Each stage of this cycle carries resource demands of its own. Those demands are not uniform, because the binding physical constraints depend on where the system is deployed.


1.9.2 Deployment context shapes the lifecycle
Deployment context determines which lifecycle pressures dominate. The same stages apply across ML systems, but a megawatt-scale data center and a milliwatt-scale embedded device impose different bottlenecks on data collection, model updates, monitoring, and serving. Four deployment paradigms span that range (cloud, edge, mobile, and TinyML), and their envelopes sit orders of magnitude apart.
From cloud to TinyML, the endpoints differ by roughly \(10^{5}\) in memory and \(10^{6}\) in compute. Because a cloud model cannot fit directly on a microcontroller, moving down that scale requires compression, a smaller architecture, or a narrower task. At the upper end, cloud ML systems offer large computing budgets alongside capacity limits, operational complexity, and substantial infrastructure bills. At the lower end, TinyML systems on microcontrollers make memory and energy feasibility an immediate concern, as a sensor may need to detect anomalies on a single battery for years. Between these poles, placement determines where work and resource demands fall. Edge ML systems move computation toward data sources to reduce latency26 and network traffic. Mobile ML systems share memory, thermal headroom, and battery power with foreground applications. Hybrid systems split work across tiers to balance latency, privacy, bandwidth, and update control.
26 Latency at the edge: Every millisecond of delay is distance traveled before a decision takes effect. A vehicle traveling at 30 m/s moves 3 cm during each millisecond of delay. Sensing, communication, computation, and actuation all contribute to the time before braking can begin, so reducing network delay addresses only part of the response budget.
↪ The light barrier, power wall, and memory wall that shape these operating envelopes are developed in Physical Constraints on Deployment.

Tight response deadlines or unreliable connectivity can require local execution, as in vehicle control. Fraud detection, in contrast, can run on cloud infrastructure whenever network and service latency fit the decision budget. Large language-model services rely on centralized clusters to accommodate their memory and compute footprint. In turn, cloud capacity and cost govern how often models are retrained, what historical data is retained, and how inference load is distributed, while edge and mobile limits constrain model size and update frequency.
As computation spreads across tiers, operational complexity grows alongside it. Edge and hybrid deployments must coordinate data collection across sensors with intermittent connectivity, track model versions across thousands of devices, push remote updates with safe rollback, and aggregate monitoring signals from distant endpoints. Data pressures pull in opposite directions at the same time: privacy rules and data sovereignty push computation toward the edge, whereas training high-capacity models pulls data back toward centralized clusters. Production architectures resolve this tension by running inference locally at the edge while routing sampled telemetry to cloud clusters for retraining.
In every deployment context, the model eventually meets inputs its evaluation never sampled. Autonomous driving illustrates this hybrid loop, running perception on the vehicle while cloud clusters train updated weights on logged fleet data. The Waymo Open Dataset shows pronounced domain gaps among San Francisco, Phoenix, and Mountain View (Sun et al. 2020), and models that score well on benchmarks often lose accuracy when deployment inputs shift (Koh et al. 2021). Every remote update must therefore be revalidated against the population it will actually serve. Beyond predictive accuracy and latency, deployed systems must also satisfy fairness, interpretability, and privacy requirements across data, models, and governance. Training sets can encode societal biases. Regulated fields such as healthcare and finance require decisions that auditors and clinicians can interpret. Inference attacks27 can leak sensitive information from trained weights. Meeting these technical, operational, and governance obligations across all four deployment regimes sets the structure of the book that follows.

Sun, Pei, Henrik Kretzschmar, Xerxes Dotiwalla, Aurelien Chouard, Vijaysai Patnaik, Paul Tsui, James Guo, et al. 2020. “Scalability in Perception for Autonomous Driving: Waymo Open Dataset.” Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 2446–54. https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR42600.2020.00252.

Koh, Pang Wei, Shiori Sagawa, Henrik Marklund, Sang Michael Xie, Marvin Zhang, Akshay Balsubramani, Weihua Hu, et al. 2021. “WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts.” In Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML 2021, 18-24 July 2021, Virtual Event, edited by Marina Meila and Tong Zhang, vol. 139. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research. PMLR.
27 Inference attack: An attempt to deduce sensitive information about training data from a model’s outputs. Memorization can expose information, but the risk depends on the data, training procedure, and access available to the attacker. Defensive techniques include adding calibrated noise during training (differential privacy) and restricting the information returned by the system.
