Latin matrices and vectors are set in bold (\(\WeightMatrix\), \(\InputFeatureVector\)); scalars, dimensions, indices, and individual matrix entries stay italic (\(\Glyph{N}\), \(\HiddenDimension\), \(\MatrixRowIndex\), \(\WeightMatrixEntry\)). The generic parameter symbol \(\ModelParameters\) is the one conventional exception and stays italic.
Local matrix algebra follows the same bold rule. Matrix operands are bold (\(\GemmLeftOperand\), \(\GemmRightOperand\), \(\GemmOutputMatrix\)), as in general matrix multiply (GEMM) \(\GemmOutputMatrix=\GemmProductScale \GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand+\GemmAccumulatorScale \GemmOutputMatrix\). The bold form marks a matrix operand and is distinct from the italic scalar batch size \(\BatchSize\), which remains batch size in scalar contexts.
A GEMM’s scalar dimensions are \(\GemmRowDimension\), \(\GemmColumnDimension\), and \(\GemmInnerDimension\) (\(\GemmLeftOperand\) is \(\GemmRowDimension \times \GemmInnerDimension\), \(\GemmRightOperand\) is \(\GemmInnerDimension \times \GemmColumnDimension\)). Asymptotic cost is written \(\mathcal{O}(\cdot)\), which keeps it distinct from the operation count \(\Operations\).



Reusable performance and serving quantities follow the same collision-avoidance rule as the iron law. Rates use \(\Glyph{R}\) or descriptive Greek symbols; request counts use \(\RequestConcurrency\) rather than overloading \(\Glyph{N}\); queue utilization uses a subscripted \(\Glyph{\rho}\) so bare \(\Glyph{\rho}\) remains available for other ratio models.

Physical units: This book uses SI (metric) units throughout, including meters, kilograms, seconds, watts, and °C, consistent with standard engineering and scientific practice. Where source data was originally reported in imperial units, the book converts to SI and notes the original values parenthetically. A space always separates the number from the unit (for example, 100 ms, 2 TB/s).
Data and memory: This book uses decimal SI prefixes only: KB = \(10^3\) bytes, MB = \(10^6\), GB = \(10^9\), TB = \(10^{12}\). Binary-prefixed units do not appear in prose; model sizes, activation footprints, throughputs, and transfer volumes are reported in decimal units (for example, 2 TB/s, 102 MB). Hardware memory capacities retain the vendor’s nameplate figure and label. Calculations requiring an exact byte count use the device’s documented capacity.
Compute: The notation distinguishes operation counts from rates. Total work uses FLOPs (for example, GFLOPs, TFLOPs), while throughput uses FLOP/s with decimal prefixes (for example, GFLOP/s, TFLOP/s).

1 TFLOP = \(10^{12}\) FLOPs
1 TFLOP/s = \(10^{12}\) FLOPs per second
Arithmetic intensity conventionally uses FLOP/byte as a unit ratio (floating-point operations per byte moved). This is a ratio unit, not a total-work symbol or throughput symbol.

Power: Power carries a subscript (\(\AveragePower\), \(\DevicePower\), \(\ClusterPower\)); bare \(\Parameters\) remains parameter count.
Latency percentiles: Written p50, p95, and p99 in upright type, inside math as well as in prose.
Currency: Dollar amounts use the dollar sign ($); unless otherwise noted, dollar-denominated costs are U.S. dollars (USD).
Precision:

FP64: Double precision (8 bytes)
FP32: Single precision (4 bytes)
TF32: TensorFloat-32 (19-bit Tensor Core compute mode; inputs and storage remain FP32)
FP16: Half precision (2 bytes, standard range)
BF16: Brain float (2 bytes, wide dynamic range)
FP8: Quarter precision (1 byte, E4M3 or E5M2 format)
FP4: 4-bit floating-point format
INT8: 8-bit integer (1 byte)
INT4: 4-bit integer; lower integer precisions follow the same uppercase INTn pattern (for example, INT3, INT2)





ML conventions generally take precedence for single letters, while systems quantities use subscripts or descriptive symbols. This preserves familiar ML notation while distinguishing systems quantities across the most common notation collisions in machine learning systems literature:










Symbol
ML Meaning
Systems Meaning
Book Convention




\(\BatchSize\)
Batch Size
Bandwidth
Batch Size. Use \(\Bandwidth\) for bandwidth.


\(\Parameters\)
Parameter Count
Peak FLOP/s
Parameter Count. Use \(\PeakRate\) for peak rate.


\(\DatasetSize\)
Dataset Size
Data Volume
Dataset Size. Use \(\DataVolume\) for bytes moved.


\(\Glyph{L}\)
Loss
Latency
Loss \((\LossFunction)\). Use \(\Latency\) for latency.


\(\LearningRate\)
Learning Rate
Efficiency
Learning Rate. Use \(\EfficiencyHw\) for efficiency.

title: Notation
text:
Across the Data · Algorithm · Machine (D·A·M) axes, execution time factors into the product of workload scale, algorithmic operations per sample, and realized machine time per operation:
\[\Time = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Samples}}{\text{Task}}\right)}_{\text{Data}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Sample}}\right)}_{\text{Algorithm}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Seconds}}{\text{FLOP}}\right)}_{\text{Machine}}\]
where the first two factors multiply to set total floating-point operations \(\Operations\). For serialized execution phases on physical hardware, unpacking how the machine executes those operations gives the three-term iron-law performance decomposition. Each variable is chosen deliberately to avoid collision with standard ML terminology:
\[\Time = \underbrace{\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}}_{\text{Memory Time}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}}_{\text{Compute Time}} + \underbrace{\Latency}_{\text{Latency Overhead}}\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\Time\)
Execution Time
seconds
Total execution time in the iron-law performance decomposition.


\(\DataVolume\)
Data Volume
bytes
Avoids collision with \(\DatasetSize\) (Dataset Size). In scaling laws and the D·A·M product, \(\DatasetSize\) counts logical training samples or tokens. Here we need physical bytes moved through memory. The subscript disambiguates.


\(\Bandwidth\)
Bandwidth
bytes/s
Avoids collision with \(\BatchSize\) (Batch Size). Systems literature often uses \(\Glyph{B}\) for bandwidth, while ML literature often uses \(\BatchSize\) for batch size. The notation preserves the ML convention.


\(\Operations\)
Operations
FLOPs
Total floating-point operations, the product of \(\text{Samples/Task}\) and \(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\). Clean in equations (vs. “\(\text{Ops}\)”).


\(\PeakRate\)
Peak Rate
FLOP/s
Avoids collision with \(\Parameters\) (Parameters). Roofline presentations often use \(\Glyph{P}\) for performance, while ML literature commonly uses \(\Parameters\) for parameter count. The notation preserves the ML convention.


\(\EfficiencyHw\)
Efficiency
—
Hardware utilization \((0 \le \EfficiencyHw \le 1)\). Measures compute-unit utilization in the three-term decomposition, or end-to-end model FLOPs utilization when data movement and overhead are folded into the single-term training law (Model Training). Avoids collision with learning rate \((\LearningRate)\).


\(\Latency\)
Latency
seconds
Avoids collision with \(\LossFunction\) (Loss). Fixed overhead time (kernel launch, network RTT). The subscript distinguishes from the loss function.






Without careful notation, sentences become ambiguous:

“Reducing \(\DatasetSize\) improves performance.”

The sentence has two possible readings:

Reducing dataset size (fewer training samples) can speed training but may reduce accuracy.
Reducing data volume moved (for example, through compression or quantization) can speed inference, with accuracy effects that depend on the technique and calibration.

With our notation, we can write precisely and eliminate this ambiguity so that a statement like “\(\Bandwidth\) limits throughput” has only one reading:

“Reducing \(\DataVolume\) through FP32-to-INT8 quantization cuts parameter memory traffic to one quarter while \(\DatasetSize\) (training data) remains unchanged.”




The root names the quantity, and an upright subscript names which instance of it is meant. The convention distinguishes closely related quantities:

\(\DiskBandwidth\), \(\NetworkBandwidth\), \(\AcceleratorMemoryBandwidth\): bandwidth at three points on the data path
\(\DataVolume\), \(\PeakRate\), \(\Latency\), \(\EfficiencyHw\): iron-law terms, each held clear of a common ML symbol
\(\EnergyPerByteMoved\), \(\EnergyPerOperation\), \(\TotalEnergy\): one energy budget split into components

The subscript identifies where a measurement applies. Disk and accelerator bandwidth differ by orders of magnitude, so a reported bandwidth is meaningful only if readers know where it was measured.

title: Notation
text:
The degradation equation is an approximation fitted to observed outcomes over a limited range. Divergence alone does not determine whether accuracy rises or falls, so estimate \(\FittedSensitivity\) from labeled outcomes. Some symbols below, such as \(\ResponseThreshold\), appear in chapter prose rather than in the equation. \[\AccuracyAfterDeployment(\DeploymentAge) \approx \InitialAccuracy - \FittedSensitivity \cdot \StatisticalDivergence\]










Symbol
Definition
Type or unit
Notes




\(\AccuracyAfterDeployment(\DeploymentAge)\)
Accuracy at Time \(\DeploymentAge\)
Scalar
Model accuracy after the model has been deployed for time \(\DeploymentAge\).


\(\InitialAccuracy\)
Initial Accuracy
Scalar
Model accuracy at deployment time.


\(\FittedSensitivity\)
Fitted Sensitivity
Scalar
Local coefficient estimated from outcomes over a stated range; not a universal constant. (Not wavelength.)


\(\CurrentDistribution\)
Current Distribution
Distribution
The data distribution at time \(\DeploymentAge\). (Not parameters—use \(\Parameters\) for parameter count.)


\(\TrainingDistribution\)
Training Distribution
Distribution
The data distribution at training time.


\(\StatisticalDivergence\)
Statistical Divergence
Scalar \(\ge 0\)
Measures how far \(\CurrentDistribution\) has drifted from \(\TrainingDistribution\). Common choices: KL divergence, total variation, Wasserstein. (Calligraphic to avoid collision with \(\DatasetSize\) = dataset size.)


\(\ResponseThreshold\)
Response Threshold
Scalar \(> 0\)
Operational threshold for investigation; it does not automatically trigger retraining. The same symbol marks a classifier’s decision threshold.


\(\DivergenceMeasure\)
Divergence Measure
Function
Divergence function that measures how far one probability distribution lies from another, with the specific measure left open.


\(\KolmogorovSmirnovStatistic\)
Kolmogorov Smirnov Statistic
Dimensionless
Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, the largest absolute difference between two empirical cumulative distribution functions.


\(\TrainingEmpiricalCdf\)
Training Empirical CDF
Function
Empirical cumulative distribution function of a feature in the training-baseline sample.


\(\MonitoredFeatureLevel\)
Monitored Feature Level
Varies
One value of a monitored feature, the argument at which its distribution or empirical cumulative distribution function is evaluated. The maximization variable of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic.


\(\ServingEmpiricalCdf\)
Serving Empirical CDF
Function
Empirical cumulative distribution function of a feature in the current serving sample.


\(\KolmogorovSmirnovCriticalThreshold\)
Kolmogorov Smirnov Critical Threshold
Dimensionless
Critical threshold that the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic must exceed to reject equal distributions at a given significance level.


\(\DriftTestSampleSize\)
Drift Test Sample Size
Integer
Number of observations in one of the two samples a two-sample drift test compares.


\(\KlDivergence\)
KL Divergence
Function
Kullback-Leibler divergence, the expected extra code length from encoding one distribution with a code built for another.


\(\ShannonEntropy\)
Shannon Entropy
bits or nats
Average uncertainty of a probability distribution, the expected negative log probability of its outcomes. The log base sets the unit: base 2 gives bits, natural log nats.

title: Notation
text:
Effective costs per byte moved and per operation give the following approximation for workload energy. The symbols in the table below separate data-movement energy from arithmetic energy and list the circuit-level quantities that govern dynamic power: \[\TotalEnergy \approx \DataVolume \times \EnergyPerByteMoved + \Operations \times \EnergyPerOperation\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\TotalEnergy\)
Total Energy
joules
Total energy consumed by an ML workload, decomposed into data-movement and compute terms.


\(\EnergyPerByteMoved\)
Energy per Byte Moved
joules/byte
Effective movement cost; total energy also depends on bytes moved and operations executed.


\(\EnergyPerOperation\)
Energy per Operation
joules/FLOP
Energy cost of a single arithmetic operation.


\(\SwitchedCapacitance\)
Switched Capacitance
farads
Capacitance of the wires and gates a circuit charges when it switches.


\(\SupplyVoltage\)
Supply Voltage
volts
Supply voltage that powers a digital circuit, the quantity dynamic voltage and frequency scaling lowers.


\(\ClockFrequency\)
Clock Frequency
hertz
Rate at which a processor’s clock ticks, setting how many switching cycles occur per second.


\(\ClusterPower\)
Cluster Power
watts
Power drawn by a training cluster, including accelerators and hosts. Average power multiplied by training time gives training energy.


\(\DevicePower\)
Device Power
watts
Electrical power one device draws. Integrated over time it gives the device’s energy.


\(\DynamicPower\)
Dynamic Power
watts
Power a chip draws switching its transistors, proportional to switched capacitance, supply voltage squared, and clock frequency.


\(\AveragePower\)
Average Power
watts
Power drawn averaged over a stated period.

title: Notation
text:
This book follows standard deep learning conventions (Goodfellow et al. 2016) with explicit disambiguation for systems variables. Where standard deep learning symbols would collide with hardware or serving quantities, the table below assigns distinct symbols and states the disambiguation rule explicitly.

Goodfellow, Ian, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville. 2016. Deep Learning. MIT Press.










Symbol
Definition
Type or unit
Notes




\(\BatchSize\)
Batch Size
Integer
Number of examples grouped in a training or inference batch. (Never bandwidth.)


\(\Parameters\)
Parameter Count
Integer
The total count of scalar model parameters, including weights and biases. (Never peak FLOP/s.)


\(\DatasetSize\)
Dataset Size
Integer
Number of training samples or tokens. (Never data volume in bytes—use \(\DataVolume\).)


\(\SequenceLength\)
Sequence Length
Integer
Number of tokens or time steps in an input sequence.


\(\HiddenDimension\)
Hidden Dimension
Integer
Size of the hidden state vector of a layer or representation.


\(\LayerInputWidth\)
Layer Input Width
Integer
Number of input features in a layer.


\(\LayerOutputWidth\)
Layer Output Width
Integer
Number of output features in a layer.


\(\AttentionHeadDimension\)
Attention Head Dimension
Integer
Per-head hidden dimension in attention layers.


\(\LayerCount\)
Number of Layers
Integer
Total number of layers in a network.


\(\AttentionHeadCount\)
Number of Attention Heads
Integer
Number of attention heads in a multi-head attention layer.


\(\KvHeadCount\)
Number of Key-Value Heads
Integer
Number of key-value heads in grouped-query or multi-query attention.


\(\LayerIndex\)
Layer Index
Integer
Index for a layer. Use instead of bare \(\Glyph{L}\) when indexing layers, since \(\Glyph{L}\) collides with loss and latency. A numeric subscript marks a norm instead (\(\ell_1\), \(\ell_2\)).


\(\LossFunction\)
Loss Function
Scalar
The objective function minimized during training.


\(\LearningRate\)
Learning Rate
Scalar
Step size for the optimizer. (Never bare for hardware efficiency—use \(\EfficiencyHw\).)


\(\ModelParameters\)
Model Parameters
Vector
All learnable model parameters, treated as a vector.


\(\LossGradient\)
Gradient
Vector
Gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters, \(\nabla_\ModelParameters \LossFunction\); a subscript \(\OptimizerStepIndex\) marks the optimizer step.


\(\InputDistribution\)
Distribution
Probability mass/density
Distribution for a random variable. Use lowercase \(\ProbabilityFunction(\cdot)\) for generic distributions to avoid collision with \(\Parameters\) (parameter count).


\(\ConditionalDistribution\)
Conditional Distribution
Conditional probability/density
Use this form for generic label relationships; reserve \(\TrainingDistribution\) and \(\CurrentDistribution\) for the training/current distributions of drift analysis.


\(\PredictedOutput\)
Predicted Output
Vector
A model’s output for one example, such as class probabilities; \(\LabelVector\) is the label vector.


\(\DistillationTemperature\)
Distillation Temperature
Dimensionless
Softmax temperature in knowledge distillation. It is dimensionless, unlike execution time.


\(\Pr(\Glyph{E})\)
Event Probability
Probability
Probability of an event \(\Glyph{E}\). Use for event statements such as \(\Pr(\text{batch}=0)\); use \(\InputDistribution\) and \(\ConditionalDistribution\) for distributions.


\(\TrainingCompute\)
Training Compute
FLOPs
Total floating-point operations required for model training.


\(\ExampleLabel\)
Example Label
Random variable
The label paired with one input, treated as a random variable.


\(\ModelInput\)
Model Input
Random variable
Input of one example, the data a model receives to produce a prediction.


\(\FiniteChange\)
Finite Change
Operator
Finite change in the quantity it prefixes, between two states, configurations or points in time. Prefix operator, as in the return-on-compute ratio of accuracy change to compute-cost change.


\(\BatchIndex\)
Batch Index
Index
Position of one batch in the sequence delivered by a data loader or runtime.


\(\ProbabilityFunction\)
Probability Function
Function
Probability mass or density function of a random variable, applied to its argument.


\(\ImageHeight\)
Image Height
Integer
Number of pixel rows in an image or its segmentation mask.


\(\ImageWidth\)
Image Width
Integer
Number of pixel columns in an image or its segmentation mask.


\(\ModelWeight\)
Model Weight
Dimensionless
Value of one learnable weight of a model, such as the weight on one input of a neuron.


\(\LayerInputComponent\)
Layer Input Component
Dimensionless
One component, or feature, of a layer’s input vector.


\(\InputFeatureVector\)
Input Feature Vector
Vector
Input feature vector of one example, written as a row vector.


\(\NeuronBias\)
Neuron Bias
Dimensionless
Bias term added to one neuron’s weighted sum. Indexed by neuron: \(\NeuronBias_j\).


\(\NeuronPreactivation\)
Neuron Preactivation
Dimensionless
Preactivation of one neuron, its weighted input sum plus bias before the activation function. At the output layer, \(\NeuronPreactivation_j\) is the logit for one class, the argument of softmax.


\(\ActivationFunction\)
Activation Function
Function
Activation function of a neuron or layer, applied element-wise to the preactivation. A layer superscript names the layer (f^{(l)}); f’ is its derivative.


\(\WeightVector\)
Weight Vector
Vector
Weight vector of one neuron, one weight per input.


\(\PredictedOutputComponent\)
Predicted Output Component
Dimensionless
One entry of a model’s prediction, such as the predicted probability for one class.


\(\WeightMatrix\)
Weight Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of learned weights one layer multiplies its input by, or the kernel tensor of a convolution layer.


\(\ActivationInput\)
Activation Input
Dimensionless
Scalar argument an activation function is applied to in its defining formula.


\(\SigmoidFunction\)
Sigmoid Function
Function
Logistic sigmoid function, one over one plus e to the minus x. Maps any real input to the open interval (0, 1).


\(\ClassCount\)
Class Count
Integer
Number of classes a classifier distinguishes, or vocabulary entries it scores, the length of its softmax output.


\(\PreactivationVector\)
Preactivation Vector
Vector
Preactivation vector of one layer for one example, the logit vector at the output layer.


\(\BiasVector\)
Bias Vector
Vector
Vector of learned biases one layer adds to its weighted sums, one per neuron or output channel. Broadcast across the batch.


\(\LayerWidth\)
Layer Width
Integer
Number of units in the layer at a given position of the network, with \(\LayerWidth_0\) the input width. Indexed by layer position.


\(\ActivationVector\)
Activation Vector
Vector
Activation vector of one layer for one example.


\(\ActivationMatrix\)
Activation Matrix
Matrix
Activation matrix of one layer for a batch, one example per row.


\(\LabelVector\)
Label Vector
Vector
True label of one example written as a vector, such as a one-hot class vector.


\(\ModelPredictor\)
Model Predictor
Function
Trained model viewed as a function that maps an input to its prediction.


\(\PreactivationMatrix\)
Preactivation Matrix
Matrix
Preactivation matrix of one layer for a batch, one example per row.


\(\LayerInputMatrix\)
Layer Input Matrix
Matrix
Input to a layer in matrix form, one row per example or token, or a single-channel image.


\(\ClassIndex\)
Class Index
Index
Index of an output class.


\(\InputChannelCount\)
Input Channel Count
Integer
Number of channels in the feature map a convolution layer reads.


\(\KernelSize\)
Kernel Size
Integer
Side length, in input positions, of a square convolution kernel.


\(\HiddenActivation\)
Hidden Activation
Vector
Activation vector a hidden layer outputs and passes to the next layer.


\(\OutputChannelCount\)
Output Channel Count
Integer
Number of channels, one per filter, in the feature map a convolution layer produces.


\(\LayerFunction\)
Layer Function
Function
Function computed by a layer, operator, or recurrent cell, mapping inputs to outputs.


\(\LayerInputVector\)
Layer Input Vector
Vector
Vector of activations one layer receives as input.


\(\FeatureMapHeight\)
Feature Map Height
Integer
Height, in pixels, of the image or feature map a convolution layer reads.


\(\FeatureMapWidth\)
Feature Map Width
Integer
Width, in pixels, of the image or feature map a convolution layer reads.


\(\OutputFeatureMapHeight\)
Output Feature Map Height
Integer
Number of output rows a convolution produces.


\(\OutputFeatureMapWidth\)
Output Feature Map Width
Integer
Number of output columns a convolution produces.


\(\AttentionQueryMatrix\)
Attention Query Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of query vectors, one row per token, in an attention layer.


\(\AttentionKeyMatrix\)
Attention Key Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of key vectors, one row per token, in an attention layer.


\(\AttentionValuesMatrix\)
Attention Values Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of value vectors, one row per token, that attention weights combine into the output.


\(\AttentionWeightMatrix\)
Attention Weight Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of attention weights, the row-wise softmax of scaled query-key scores.


\(\IdentityMatrix\)
Identity Matrix
Matrix
Square matrix with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Size follows from context.


\(\MiniBatchSet\)
Mini Batch Set
Set
Set of examples processed together as one mini-batch.


\(\NormalizationScale\)
Normalization Scale
Dimensionless
Learned factor a normalization layer multiplies each normalized activation by.


\(\NormalizationScaleVector\)
Normalization Scale Vector
Vector
Vector of learned per-channel or per-feature factors a normalization layer multiplies its normalized output by.


\(\NormalizationShiftVector\)
Normalization Shift Vector
Vector
Vector of learned per-channel or per-feature offsets a normalization layer adds to its scaled output.


\(\TraceIntermediateVariable\)
Trace Intermediate Variable
Dimensionless
Intermediate variable in the evaluation trace of a differentiated program, its primal value.


\(\TraceIntermediateAdjoint\)
Trace Intermediate Adjoint
Dimensionless
Reverse-mode adjoint of an intermediate variable, the derivative of the output with respect to it.


\(\FunctionInputVector\)
Function Input Vector
Vector
Vector a layer or differentiated function takes as input.


\(\FunctionInputDimension\)
Function Input Dimension
Integer
Number of inputs of a differentiated function, the column count of its Jacobian.


\(\FunctionInputElement\)
Function Input Element
Dimensionless
One element of the input vector of a layer or elementwise function.


\(\MatrixRowIndex\)
Matrix Row Index
Index
Position of a row within a matrix.


\(\MatrixColumnIndex\)
Matrix Column Index
Index
Column index of a matrix entry.


\(\AttentionScoreMatrix\)
Attention Score Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of attention scores, the scaled dot products of every query with every key before the softmax.


\(\SoftmaxInputVector\)
Softmax Input Vector
Vector
Vector of scores an online softmax normalizes block by block.


\(\SoftmaxRunningMaximum\)
Softmax Running Maximum
Dimensionless
Largest score seen so far in a block of the online softmax, subtracted before exponentiation. Superscripts (1), (2), new mark the block it covers.


\(\SoftmaxNormalizer\)
Softmax Normalizer
Dimensionless
Sum of the max-shifted exponentials of a softmax row or block, the softmax denominator, kept as a running sum by online softmax. Not the class logit z of the data appendix.


\(\AttentionHeadOutput\)
Attention Head Output
Matrix
Output of one attention head before the output projection, the attention weights applied to the value matrix. Distinct from the output-projection result of a whole attention layer.


\(\DataScalingExponent\)
Data Scaling Exponent
Dimensionless
Fitted power-law exponent at which loss falls as the training dataset or token count grows.


\(\DerivativeOperator\)
Derivative Operator
Operator
Differential operator d used in an ordinary derivative.


\(\OptimizerStepIndex\)
Optimizer Step Index
Index
Position of one optimizer update in the sequence of training steps.


\(\EpochCount\)
Epoch Count
Integer
Number of full passes a training run makes over its dataset. Training work scales with it times dataset size.


\(\OutputLogit\)
Output Logit
Dimensionless
Raw score a model outputs for one class before the softmax.


\(\InputResolution\)
Input Resolution
Integer
Input image resolution of a convolutional model. Subscript 0 marks the base model in compound scaling.


\(\QuantizationScale\)
Quantization Scale
Varies
Real-valued step between adjacent integer levels of a uniform quantizer.


\(\QuantizedIntegerCode\)
Quantized Integer Code
Integer
Integer code a quantizer assigns to one real value.


\(\LayerWeightEntry\)
Layer Weight Entry
Dimensionless
One scalar entry of a layer’s weight matrix, picked out by a layer superscript and row and column subscripts.


\(\WeightMatrixEntry\)
Weight Matrix Entry
Dimensionless
One entry of a weight matrix at a given row and column; italic because it is a scalar.


\(\FusedConvolutionWeight\)
Fused Convolution Weight
Dimensionless
Convolution weights after the following batch normalization is folded into them, so inference runs one layer instead of two.


\(\QuantizerInput\)
Quantizer Input
Varies
Full-precision real value, a weight or activation, that a quantizer maps to an integer code. Unit: units of the quantized tensor.


\(\ClippingRangeLowerBound\)
Clipping Range Lower Bound
Varies
Lower end of the real-valued range a quantizer represents, below which values are clipped. Calibration estimates it.


\(\ClippingRangeUpperBound\)
Clipping Range Upper Bound
Varies
Upper end of the real-valued range a quantizer represents, above which values are clipped.


\(\QuantizationBitWidth\)
Quantization Bit Width
Integer
Number of bits in each integer code a quantizer produces.


\(\BatchNormRunningStandardDeviation\)
Batch Norm Running Standard Deviation
Vector
Per-channel square root of the running variance plus the numerical stabilizer that batch normalization uses at inference.


\(\StructuredSparsityNonzeroCount\)
Structured Sparsity Nonzero Count
Integer
Number of values kept nonzero in each group of an N:M structured-sparsity pattern.


\(\StructuredSparsityGroupSize\)
Structured Sparsity Group Size
Integer
Number of consecutive values in one group of an N:M structured-sparsity pattern.


\(\KernelHeight\)
Kernel Height
Integer
Height of a convolution kernel, in input positions.


\(\KernelWidth\)
Kernel Width
Integer
Width of a convolution kernel, in input positions.


\(\TopClassCount\)
Top Class Count
Integer
Number of highest-scoring classes a top-k prediction returns or checks for the correct label.


\(\ServiceRate\)
Service Rate
items/s
Rate at which one server, such as a worker, consumer, or model endpoint, completes items or calls.


\(\ModelPrediction\)
Model Prediction
Dimensionless
Prediction a model outputs for one example, compared with its label by the loss.


\(\LayerOutputMatrix\)
Layer Output Matrix
Matrix
Output matrix of a layer’s matrix multiplication of the input matrix by the weight matrix, one row per example. Shape batch size by layer output width; before any bias or activation function.


\(\SoftmaxRowMaximum\)
Softmax Row Maximum
Dimensionless
Largest score in a softmax row or block, subtracted before exponentiation to prevent overflow.


\(\SoftmaxInputScore\)
Softmax Input Score
Dimensionless
One entry of the score vector the online softmax normalizes. Written with an index and a block superscript, \(\SoftmaxInputScore_j^{(1)}\).


\(\SymmetricClippingThreshold\)
Symmetric Clipping Threshold
Varies
Largest magnitude a symmetric quantizer represents, so values are clipped to plus or minus this bound.




Latin matrices and vectors are set in bold (\(\WeightMatrix\), \(\InputFeatureVector\)); scalars, dimensions, indices, and individual matrix entries stay italic (\(\Glyph{N}\), \(\HiddenDimension\), \(\MatrixRowIndex\), \(\WeightMatrixEntry\)). The generic parameter symbol \(\ModelParameters\) is the one conventional exception and stays italic.
Local matrix algebra follows the same bold rule. Matrix operands are bold (\(\GemmLeftOperand\), \(\GemmRightOperand\), \(\GemmOutputMatrix\)), as in general matrix multiply (GEMM) \(\GemmOutputMatrix=\GemmProductScale \GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand+\GemmAccumulatorScale \GemmOutputMatrix\). The bold form marks a matrix operand and is distinct from the italic scalar batch size \(\BatchSize\), which remains batch size in scalar contexts.
A GEMM’s scalar dimensions are \(\GemmRowDimension\), \(\GemmColumnDimension\), and \(\GemmInnerDimension\) (\(\GemmLeftOperand\) is \(\GemmRowDimension \times \GemmInnerDimension\), \(\GemmRightOperand\) is \(\GemmInnerDimension \times \GemmColumnDimension\)). Asymptotic cost is written \(\mathcal{O}(\cdot)\), which keeps it distinct from the operation count \(\Operations\).

title: Notation
text:
Reusable performance and serving quantities follow the same collision-avoidance rule as the iron law. Rates use \(\Glyph{R}\) or descriptive Greek symbols; request counts use \(\RequestConcurrency\) rather than overloading \(\Glyph{N}\); queue utilization uses a subscripted \(\Glyph{\rho}\) so bare \(\Glyph{\rho}\) remains available for other ratio models.










Symbol
Definition
Type or unit
Notes




\(\ArithmeticIntensity\)
Arithmetic Intensity
FLOP/byte
Workload FLOPs per byte moved. The Roofline Model uses \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) as the independent variable.


\(\RooflineRidgePoint\)
Roofline Ridge Point
FLOP/byte
\(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate/\Bandwidth\). Prefer this explicit form over starred shorthand so the meaning remains clear in prose.


\(\AttainableComputeRate\)
Attainable Compute Rate
FLOP/s
Roofline bound: \(\AttainableComputeRate \leq \min(\PeakRate, \ArithmeticIntensity \times \Bandwidth)\). Uses \(\Glyph{R}\), not \(\Time\), because this quantity is a rate.


\(\ModelFlopsUtilization\)
Model FLOPs Utilization
Dimensionless
Useful model FLOP/s divided by available peak FLOP/s. Text acronym avoids overloading \(\LearningRate\).


\(\RequestConcurrency\)
Request Concurrency
requests
Average in-flight requests in a stable serving system (\(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem\) via Little’s Law). Avoids overloading \(\Glyph{N}\), which counts devices, elements, or samples elsewhere.


\(\ArrivalRate\)
Arrival Rate
requests/s
Request arrival rate. The subscript keeps bare \(\FittedSensitivity\) free for fitted sensitivities.


\(\IronLawMemoryTime\)
Iron-Law Memory Time
seconds
Data-movement term \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\) in the iron law.


\(\IronLawComputeTime\)
Iron-Law Compute Time
seconds
Compute term \(\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\) in the iron law.


\(\AcceleratorCount\)
Accelerator Count
Integer
Number of accelerators in one job.


\(\RequestTimeInSystem\)
Request Time in System
seconds
Average time a request spends queueing and being served, as used in Little’s law. Distinct from \(\Latency\), the fixed-latency term in the iron law.


\(\EndToEndRequestLatency\)
End-to-End Request Latency
seconds
Request-path latency budget, \(\NetworkLatency + \PreprocessingLatency + \InferenceLatency + \PostprocessingLatency + \QueueingLatency\). \(\RequestTimeInSystem\) covers only the time inside the serving system.


\(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\)
Batch Service Time
seconds
Time to serve a batch of size \(\BatchSize\).


\(\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize)\)
Effective Service Rate
requests/s
Batched service rate, typically \(\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) = \BatchSize/\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\). The unbatched service rate is \(\ServiceRate = \EffectiveServiceRate(1)\).


\(\ServingUtilization\)
Serving Utilization
Dimensionless
Queue/server utilization. The subscript keeps bare \(\Glyph{\rho}\) free for other ratio models.


\(\TotalMemoryFootprint\)
Total Memory Footprint
bytes
Sum of explicit memory components; avoids bare \(\Glyph{M}\) ambiguity.


\(\WeightMemory\)
Weight Memory
bytes
Memory occupied by model weights (\(\Parameters \times \text{bytes-per-parameter}\)).


\(\GradientMemory\)
Gradient Memory
bytes
Memory occupied by stored gradients.


\(\OptimizerStateMemory\)
Optimizer-State Memory
bytes
Momentum, variance, master weights, and related optimizer buffers.


\(\ActivationMemory\)
Activation Memory
bytes
Retained activations for the backward pass or serving intermediates.


\(\KvCacheMemory\)
KV-Cache Memory
bytes
Memory occupied by the key-value cache during autoregressive inference.


\(\ElementStorageSize\)
Element Storage Size
bytes/element
Bytes per stored tensor element.


\(\SampleStorageSize\)
Sample Storage Size
bytes/sample
Bytes per stored training or serving sample.


\(\LossScaleFactor\)
Loss-Scale Factor
Dimensionless
Multiplier applied to the loss in reduced-precision training so small gradients stay representable.


\(\PipelinedExecutionTime\)
Pipelined Execution Time
seconds
Ideal steady-state execution time when data movement and computation overlap, approximated by the slower stage plus fixed latency.


\(\AcceleratedFractionSpeedup\)
Accelerated Fraction Speedup
Dimensionless
Speedup factor applied to the accelerated fraction of a workload in Amdahl’s law, whether it comes from faster hardware or from more workers.


\(\TrainingTime\)
Training Time
seconds
Wall-clock time to complete one training run.


\(\IoTransferTime\)
I/O Transfer Time
seconds
Time to move a workload’s data over a storage or network link, the input/output stage of a pipelined step. Overlaps with compute in the pipelined iron law; the step is I/O bound when it is the largest stage.


\(\NetworkBandwidth\)
Network Bandwidth
bytes/s
Sustained rate at which a network path delivers bytes between machines.


\(\NetworkLatency\)
Network Latency
seconds
Time a request and its response spend crossing the network, including propagation, routing, and protocol handling.


\(\DeviceMemoryCapacity\)
Device Memory Capacity
bytes
Total memory a device provides for a model’s weights and activations.


\(\AcceleratorGain\)
Accelerator Gain
Dimensionless
Speedup an optimization or accelerator gives the fraction of execution it applies to, in Amdahl’s law.


\(\FirstFloatingPointAddend\)
First Floating Point Addend
Dimensionless
First of three floating-point numbers added in either grouping to show that floating-point addition is not associative.


\(\SecondFloatingPointAddend\)
Second Floating Point Addend
Dimensionless
Second of three floating-point numbers added in either grouping to show that floating-point addition is not associative.


\(\ThirdFloatingPointAddend\)
Third Floating Point Addend
Dimensionless
Third of three floating-point numbers added in either grouping to show that floating-point addition is not associative.


\(\StorageBandwidth\)
Storage Bandwidth
bytes/s
Sustained rate at which the storage system delivers bytes to the input pipeline.


\(\TrainingStepTime\)
Training Step Time
seconds
Wall-clock time of one training step, bounded below by the slower of compute and input I/O.


\(\SquareGemmDimension\)
Square GEMM Dimension
Integer
Side length of the square matrices in a matrix multiply, the shared row, column, and inner dimension.


\(\GemmRowDimension\)
GEMM Row Dimension
Integer
Number of rows of the left operand and of the output in a matrix multiply.


\(\GemmInnerDimension\)
GEMM Inner Dimension
Integer
Shared inner dimension of a general matrix multiply, the number of products summed per output element.


\(\GemmColumnDimension\)
GEMM Column Dimension
Integer
Number of columns of the right operand and of the output in a matrix multiply.


\(\MicroUnitPrefix\)
Micro Unit Prefix
Operator
SI unit prefix micro, one millionth, written before a unit such as seconds.


\(\TensorElementCount\)
Tensor Element Count
Integer
Number of elements in one tensor.


\(\ChainedOperationCount\)
Chained Operation Count
Integer
Number of consecutive operations that read and write the same intermediate tensor and can be combined through kernel fusion.


\(\BatchTransferTime\)
Batch Transfer Time
seconds
Time to copy one batch of input data from host memory to the device that consumes it.


\(\GemmOutputMatrix\)
GEMM Output Matrix
Matrix
Output matrix of a general matrix multiply, of size M by N, which the operation updates in place.


\(\GemmProductScale\)
GEMM Product Scale
Dimensionless
Scalar multiplier applied to the matrix product in a general matrix multiply.


\(\GemmAccumulatorScale\)
GEMM Accumulator Scale
Dimensionless
Scalar multiplier applied to the existing output matrix before the product is added in a general matrix multiply.


\(\GemmLeftOperand\)
GEMM Left Operand
Matrix
Left input matrix of a general matrix multiply, of size M by K.


\(\GemmRightOperand\)
GEMM Right Operand
Matrix
Right input matrix of a general matrix multiply, of size K by N.


\(\DiskBandwidth\)
Disk Bandwidth
bytes/s
Sustained rate at which a storage disk delivers bytes.


\(\SustainedComputeRate\)
Sustained Compute Rate
FLOP/s
Operation rate an accelerator or system actually sustains on a workload.


\(\HostPreparationTime\)
Host Preparation Time
seconds
Time the host takes to prepare one batch for the accelerator, from read through batching.


\(\AcceleratorMemoryBandwidth\)
Accelerator Memory Bandwidth
bytes/s
Sustained rate at which bytes move between an accelerator’s own memory, such as HBM, and its compute units.


\(\TimeInstant\)
Time Instant
seconds
A point in continuous wall-clock time, the variable over which time-varying quantities are integrated.


\(\InferenceLatency\)
Inference Latency
seconds
Time the model takes to compute a request’s output.


\(\IntermediateTensorSize\)
Intermediate Tensor Size
bytes
Bytes in the intermediate tensor that a sequence of operations passes between its steps.


\(\NonzeroCount\)
Nonzero Count
Integer
Number of nonzero values a sparse matrix format stores.


\(\SparseMatrixRowCount\)
Sparse Matrix Row Count
Integer
Number of rows in a sparse matrix. Compressed sparse row (CSR) storage uses one more row pointer than the number of rows.


\(\DecodeTokenTimeFloor\)
Decode Token Time Floor
seconds
Lower bound on the time to generate one token at batch one, bytes streamed per step divided by memory bandwidth.


\(\QueueingLatency\)
Queueing Latency
seconds
Time a request waits in queues before it is served.


\(\PreprocessingLatency\)
Preprocessing Latency
seconds
Time spent preparing a request’s input before inference.


\(\PostprocessingLatency\)
Postprocessing Latency
seconds
Time spent turning a model’s output into the response.


\(\NumericBitWidth\)
Numeric Bit Width
Integer
Number of bits used to represent one numeric value, such as an arithmetic operand or a quantized weight or activation.


\(\DatasetTransferTime\)
Dataset Transfer Time
seconds
Ideal line-rate time to move a dataset over a network or storage path: data volume divided by bandwidth.


\(\AcceleratorBatchTime\)
Accelerator Batch Time
seconds
Time the accelerator takes to run one training step on one batch, excluding input preparation.

title: Notation
text:
Statistical thresholds, workload fractions, and system constraints follow standard statistical and operational conventions. Each symbol in the table below carries an explicit domain and unit so that hypothesis tests, queueing bounds, and fairness metrics can be combined without ambiguity:










Symbol
Definition
Type or unit
Notes




\(\InterAnnotatorAgreement\)
Cohen’s Kappa
Dimensionless
Inter-annotator agreement coefficient \(\InterAnnotatorAgreement \in [-1, 1]\).


\(\CompletionDeadline\)
Deadline
seconds
Latency deadline for query completion or batch execution.


\(\OperationalOverheadFraction\)
Operational Overhead Fraction
Dimensionless
Fraction of wall time spent outside productive step execution (\(\OperationalOverheadFraction\)).


\(\ParallelFraction\)
Parallel Fraction
Dimensionless
Fraction of workload execution that can be parallelized in Amdahl’s Law (\(0 \le \ParallelFraction \le 1\)).


\(\SignificanceLevel\)
Significance Level
Dimensionless
Statistical significance threshold \(\SignificanceLevel\) for hypothesis tests.


\(\NumericalStabilityConstant\)
Numerical Stability Constant
Scalar
Small numerical constant \(\NumericalStabilityConstant > 0\) for numerical stability.


\(\WorkerCount\)
Worker Count
Integer
Number of parallel worker threads, processes, or devices.


\(\ObservationTimestamp\)
Observation Timestamp
seconds
Time at which a labeled observation, such as a churn event, occurred. Upper bound on the feature timestamps an as-of join may use.


\(\ErroneousPredictionCost\)
Erroneous Prediction Cost
dollars
Average business cost incurred by one erroneous prediction. Multiplies the skew rate and query volume in the training-serving skew cost.


\(\StorageAccessFactor\)
Storage Access Factor
Dimensionless
Fraction of peak storage throughput a workload’s access pattern achieves.


\(\SubgroupIndex\)
Subgroup Index
Index
Label of one population subgroup whose outcomes are compared against a reference group.


\(\FeedbackIntervalCount\)
Feedback Interval Count
Integer
Number of fixed feedback intervals, such as retraining cycles, elapsed since the disparity was first measured.


\(\BiasFeedbackFactor\)
Bias Feedback Factor
Dimensionless
Factor by which a group’s disparity is multiplied over one feedback interval, fitted from observed disparities. Above 1 the feedback loop is self-reinforcing; at or below 1 it is stable or damped.


\(\GroupDisparity\)
Group Disparity
Dimensionless
Size of the performance gap between one group and a reference group; the feedback analysis tracks how it grows from one feedback interval to the next.


\(\AnonymitySetSize\)
Anonymity Set Size
Integer
Smallest number of records that share every quasi-identifier value in a k-anonymous release.


\(\DeploymentDistribution\)
Deployment Distribution
Distribution
Joint distribution of inputs and labels a deployed model must serve, the population a verification guarantee is stated over.


\(\TaskDistance\)
Task Distance
Function
Task-specific distance between a model’s prediction and the correct label, the error measure a verification guarantee bounds.


\(\TaskErrorTolerance\)
Task Error Tolerance
Dimensionless
Largest task distance between a prediction and its label that still counts as an acceptable output.


\(\ToleratedFailureProbability\)
Tolerated Failure Probability
Dimensionless
Maximum allowed probability that a deployed model exceeds its task error tolerance. The confidence level used to estimate this probability is specified separately.


\(\TrainingServingSkew\)
Training Serving Skew
Dimensionless
Expected absolute difference between the serving-path and training-path model scores on the same inputs, over a stated comparison-input distribution. Measurable without labels; a risk signal, not an accuracy-loss equation.


\(\ServingPathPredictor\)
Serving Path Predictor
Function
Serving code path viewed as a function from a raw input to the model’s output, including its preprocessing and runtime.


\(\TrainingPathPredictor\)
Training Path Predictor
Function
Training code path viewed as a function from a raw input to the model’s output, as offline validation evaluates it.


\(\TargetCompletionQuantile\)
Target Completion Quantile
Dimensionless
Required probability that a request completes within its latency deadline, the completion quantile a service level states.

title: Notation
text:
Physical units: This book uses SI (metric) units throughout, including meters, kilograms, seconds, watts, and °C, consistent with standard engineering and scientific practice. Where source data was originally reported in imperial units, the book converts to SI and notes the original values parenthetically. A space always separates the number from the unit (for example, 100 ms, 2 TB/s).
Data and memory: This book uses decimal SI prefixes only: KB = \(10^3\) bytes, MB = \(10^6\), GB = \(10^9\), TB = \(10^{12}\). Binary-prefixed units do not appear in prose; model sizes, activation footprints, throughputs, and transfer volumes are reported in decimal units (for example, 2 TB/s, 102 MB). Hardware memory capacities retain the vendor’s nameplate figure and label. Calculations requiring an exact byte count use the device’s documented capacity.
Compute: The notation distinguishes operation counts from rates. Total work uses FLOPs (for example, GFLOPs, TFLOPs), while throughput uses FLOP/s with decimal prefixes (for example, GFLOP/s, TFLOP/s).

1 TFLOP = \(10^{12}\) FLOPs
1 TFLOP/s = \(10^{12}\) FLOPs per second
Arithmetic intensity conventionally uses FLOP/byte as a unit ratio (floating-point operations per byte moved). This is a ratio unit, not a total-work symbol or throughput symbol.

Power: Power carries a subscript (\(\AveragePower\), \(\DevicePower\), \(\ClusterPower\)); bare \(\Parameters\) remains parameter count.
Latency percentiles: Written p50, p95, and p99 in upright type, inside math as well as in prose.
Currency: Dollar amounts use the dollar sign ($); unless otherwise noted, dollar-denominated costs are U.S. dollars (USD).
Precision:

FP64: Double precision (8 bytes)
FP32: Single precision (4 bytes)
TF32: TensorFloat-32 (19-bit Tensor Core compute mode; inputs and storage remain FP32)
FP16: Half precision (2 bytes, standard range)
BF16: Brain float (2 bytes, wide dynamic range)
FP8: Quarter precision (1 byte, E4M3 or E5M2 format)
FP4: 4-bit floating-point format
INT8: 8-bit integer (1 byte)
INT4: 4-bit integer; lower integer precisions follow the same uppercase INTn pattern (for example, INT3, INT2)

title: Acknowledgments
text:
This book owes its existence to a single conversation. During a sabbatical at Google, Pete Warden invited me to work on what seemed like an impossible moonshot for TinyML: running a small speech model on a microcontroller. That collaboration on TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers revealed something fundamental. The constraints that govern a device with 16 KB to 256 KB of memory are the same constraints that govern an accelerator in a data center, even when the scale is entirely different. Bandwidth, latency, energy, and memory obey the same physics across both settings. That insight became the seed of this book.
The TinyML work led to an online course on HarvardX, co-taught with Laurence Moroney, that grew to over 100,000 students worldwide. Brian Plancher helped build the TinyML curriculum. Marcelo Rovai, a professor who first encountered the material through the TinyML course, went on to develop the hands-on labs and kits that accompany this book. Zach Shelby opened the Edge Impulse platform for student use. Massimo Banzi and the Arduino team, along with Eric Pan and Seeed Studio, collaborated with us in developing and providing the hardware kits that made hands-on instruction possible. Marco Zennaro brought the material to developing countries through ICTP and planted the idea that these principles deserved a proper textbook. Teaching at that scale, without one, made the need undeniable.
That need turned into a book through CS249r at Harvard University. In 2023, the semester-long class project was to write the class notes: each student group took ownership of a topic, researched it, and worked with me to develop it into a chapter. That work seeded every chapter in this book. The premise was that writing forces you to think more deeply than reading alone. We then opened it all on GitHub, and what began as rough class notes has been rewritten and refined with every semester since.
Reflecting that same collaborative history, a gallery of GitHub contributors follows. Contribution guidelines are available at mlsysbook.ai/git.

Beyond the class and GitHub community, my earlier collaborations shaped the book’s intellectual foundations. My time at Google informed much of the systems thinking in these pages. That period began with performance modeling for the first Pixel system on chip (SoC), drawing on my background in computer architecture. A collaboration with Mark Hill on roofline-style analytical modeling for heterogeneous SoCs taught me to reason about hardware from first principles, the kind of quantitative thinking that runs through every chapter. That emphasis on quantitative evaluation carried into my work on MLPerf. MLPerf involved many contributors across MLCommons, but I worked most closely with Peter Mattson, David Kanter, Carole-Jean Wu, Christine Cheng, Guenther Schmuelling, Cody Coleman, and Cliff Young. That collaboration shaped how I think about rigorous measurement of ML systems.
Boris Murmann and Song Han convinced me in the early stages that this project was worth pursuing. As I wrote, I sought feedback from colleagues in industry and academia alike. Practitioners at Arm, Google, Intel, Meta, Microsoft, Qualcomm, STMicroelectronics, and other organizations offered perspectives grounded in production systems, while academic reviewers at universities across Europe, Asia, and the Americas stress-tested the material against their own research and teaching. Their combined feedback sharpened every chapter. Evgeni Gousev at Qualcomm and Pete Bernard at the Edge AI Foundation supported the project’s outreach and helped build the community around it.
That feedback loop extended to classrooms around the world, where instructors put the material to the test when it was still rough. Sophia Shao at UC Berkeley, Xiaofan (Fred) Jiang at Columbia, Tushar Krishna and Divya Mahajan at Georgia Tech, and Wenkai Guan at the University of Minnesota Morris were among the first, and instructors at IIT Bombay, NUST Pakistan, De La Salle University in the Philippines, and universities across Europe, Latin America, and Africa have since adopted the book for their own courses. Their willingness to teach from an unfinished textbook provided invaluable feedback and confirmed that the need for this material was not limited to any one institution or any one country.



Closer to home, my students in the Edge Computing Lab at Harvard shaped this book in ways I cannot fully trace. Some did foundational work that helped establish TinyML as a field; their research and the ideas that emerged from years of collaboration informed the book’s technical content. This cohort helped set the field in motion and then helped me write about it: Andy Cheng, Arya Tschand, Brian Plancher, Colby Banbury, Elizabeth Suitor, Emma Chen, Ikechukwu Uchendu, Jason Jabbour, Jason Yik, Jeffrey Ma, Jessica Quaye, Mark Mazumder, Matthew Stewart, Maximilian Lam, Radhika Ghosal, Shvetank Prakash, Srivatsan Krishnan, Yu-Shun Hsiao, and Zishen Wan. Kai Kleinbard, then at the Harvard Extension School, built the online generative AI SocratiQ tutor bot. Naeem Khoshnevis, from the Harvard Kempner Institute, established essential infrastructure including GitHub Actions and documentation standards. Željko Hrček produced the TikZ diagrams and contributed to the PDF layout, page composition, and final visual formatting of the book.
I am also grateful to the researchers whose work this book builds on and to the open-source contributors worldwide who helped refine the manuscript, whether by fixing a single typo or by rewriting entire sections. The book improved because people who owed it nothing chose to make it better. What kept me going, aside from stubbornness, was that community: every GitHub star was a signal that someone out there cared, that someone was learning, that the work mattered. I am grateful to every one of them.



This work also depended on support from the Harvard Data Science Initiative, Harvard Extension School, and the National Science Foundation, as well as from the Edge AI Foundation and ICTP for educational outreach and scholarships. Arduino, Edge Impulse, Google, and Seeed Studio provided hardware, tooling, and infrastructure that enabled the practical labs.
At MIT Press, Susan Hartman believed in this project and guided it from an open-source experiment to a published textbook. Her support, editorial judgment, and friendship made this book real in a way that GitHub alone could not. I am equally grateful to MIT Press for agreeing to keep this book available as open access. A textbook about a discipline shaped by the open-source community should be accessible to everyone in it. That MIT Press shared this conviction made all the difference.
Finally, I thank my wife, Kari, and my daughters, Nora and Maya. This book was written in the hours that belonged to them: late nights that started at ten and ended at two or three in the morning, weekends that disappeared into revisions, years of mornings when I was present but not quite there. The cost was real, and they paid it with patience I did not always deserve.

title: Author’s Note
text:
Author’s Note

The world is rushing to build AI systems; it is not yet engineering them. That sentence is the reason this book exists. A model that wins on a benchmark is not yet a system, and the distance between the two is not a detail of implementation. It is engineering: the work of making something hold up under constraints that do not negotiate. A demo answers to no one. A system answers to latency budgets, memory limits, power envelopes, and the cost of being wrong in front of real users.
What makes this its own discipline is an unusual coupling. A processor answers to the physics of the machine, to clock cycles, cache lines, and the heat it can shed. A statistical model answers to the mathematics of learning, to bias, variance, and how generalization changes with data and model capacity. A machine learning system must answer to both at once, in the same decision, and the two do not always agree. A change that pleases the hardware can starve the model of the precision or throughput it needs to converge; a change that helps the model can ask the silicon for more memory or bandwidth than it can give. Hold that tension in view and the field stops looking like a pile of tools and starts looking like a structure you can reason about.
This book hands you that structure. Not the framework that is fashionable this year or the accelerator that is fastest this quarter, but the way of thinking that outlasts them. Frameworks change, hardware turns over every few years, and the benchmarks reset; the forces underneath stay the same. If the book works, you will finish it able to look at any machine learning system, from a sensor sipping microwatts to a server farm drawing megawatts, and see the same small set of forces deciding what is possible.
The textbooks that changed me when I was a student did not hand me facts. They handed me a way of seeing, and the facts arranged themselves around it. That is what I have tried to do here.
— Vijay Janapa Reddi
Cambridge, Massachusetts
2026

title: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems
text:
Machine learning has evolved from a research discipline into an engineering practice. Building systems that learn from data requires more than understanding algorithms; it demands expertise spanning data pipelines, model development, deployment constraints, accelerator behavior, and operational practice. The book treats AI capability as the result of designing data, algorithms, and machines together under statistical and computational constraints. This book introduces AI engineering as the discipline of building intelligent systems that operate in the real world, then develops its ML systems foundation on a single compute node. The treatment progresses through four parts: foundations (deployment paradigms, the ML lifecycle, and data engineering), development (neural computation, model architectures, execution frameworks, and training), optimization (data selection, model compression, hardware acceleration, and benchmarking), and deployment (model serving, operations, and responsible engineering). Throughout, the emphasis is on quantitative trade-offs across data, algorithms, and machines.
  

  
    
    Introduction to Machine Learning Systems
    Publisher: The MIT Press (2026)
  


What You Will Learn

The book progresses through four stages:

  Part I: Foundations. What is being built, under which physical constraints, across which lifecycle stages, and from what engineered data pipelines.
  Part II: Development. How mathematical models reach hardware execution, through neural computation, model architectures, frameworks, and single-node training loops.
  Part III: Optimization. How data selection, model compression, and hardware acceleration reduce system cost, and how benchmarking verifies each claimed speedup.
  Part IV: Deployment. How the system serves live requests under strict latency budgets, how monitoring catches silent drift and skew in production, and how responsible engineering controls are enforced.


Prerequisites

This book assumes:

  Programming proficiency in Python with familiarity in NumPy
  Mathematics foundations in linear algebra, calculus, and probability at the undergraduate level
  Prior ML experience is helpful but not required; neural computation provides essential background


Learn by Doing

Beyond the chapters, this volume is the reading spine for a broader AI engineering curriculum. Pair the chapters with Labs to test predictions, TinyTorch to build framework internals, MLSys·im to model hardware constraints, and Hardware Kits to deploy on real devices. Instructors can adopt the full sequence through Instructor Hub.

title: Foreword
text:
David A. Patterson Pardee Professor of Computer Science Emeritus University of California, Berkeley Distinguished Engineer, Google ACM A.M. Turing Award Laureate Berkeley, California

My career has been dedicated to understanding and improving the very foundations upon which computing operates – from the instruction set architectures that define processors to the storage systems that hold our data. I’ve seen firsthand how profound advancements are rarely about a single brilliant idea in isolation, but rather about the holistic integration of many ideas into a robust, efficient, and reliable system.
Today, we stand at another pivotal moment. Machine learning (ML) has transcended scientific curiosity to become a force reshaping industries, driving innovation, and transforming our daily lives. The intellectual power of the algorithms, the gains in accuracy, and the seemingly magical capabilities they unlock have rightly captured the world’s imagination.
One concern is that much of this progress has been achieved by a community that, through no fault of its own, was never taught to think in systems terms about what it was building. Engineers who can call model.fit() but cannot explain why training is slow. Researchers who tune hyperparameters without understanding the memory bandwidth constraints that make certain choices impractical. Practitioners who deploy models into production without a framework for reasoning about latency, throughput, or failure modes.
A brilliant algorithm, without a well-engineered system to support it, is like a powerful engine without a chassis and brakes. It won’t get you far, and it certainly won’t get you there reliably.
This gap is not a talent deficit. It is a curriculum deficit. The field has simply not had the textbooks it deserves. This book, Introduction to Machine Learning Systems, arrives precisely at the right time to illuminate this critical, often overlooked, dimension of the ML revolution.


My career has leveraged the power of systems thinking. Identify the bottlenecks, understand the interactions between components, and design for performance, reliability, cost-effectiveness, and ease of use across the entire stack. You could not reach the conclusion from first principles alone. You had to think about the system.
ML systems demand exactly the same discipline. A neural network is not a mathematical abstraction floating free of physical constraints. It is a computation that must execute on silicon with finite memory bandwidth, finite power budgets, and finite communication capacity. Arithmetic intensity, the Roofline Model, and memory hierarchy effects are not advanced topics to be addressed after students learn the basics. They are the basics.



The purpose of a textbook is not just to catalog the current frontier. It is to provide the conceptual scaffolding that allows students to understand the frontier, and to advance it themselves. The neural network architectures covered in these pages will evolve. The hardware accelerators described will be superseded. But some fundamentals will not change. We will still have memory hierarchies and arithmetic intensity will still be a critical measure. The principles of pipelining, of latency versus throughput trade-offs, of quantization and precision reflect physical and mathematical realities that do not go out of date. Anyone who genuinely understands them will be able to reason about whatever new system the field produces next year or ten years from now.
I am also struck by the scope of what this book attempts. It is not enough to explain how training works; one must also address data engineering, model optimization, hardware acceleration, deployment, benchmarking, responsible AI, and sustainability. These are not separate topics bolted together for completeness. They are interconnected aspects of a single engineering discipline. A decision made at the data layer has implications for model behavior, which has implications for inference latency, which has implications for deployment cost, which has implications for the communities that can and cannot access the resulting system. The book correctly treats this integration as a first-class concern.
I am particularly pleased to see the quantitative methodology that runs through every chapter. Claims are backed by measurements. Trade-offs are expressed numerically. Students are taught to estimate, measure, and verify rather than to rely on their gut. The difference between an engineer and a dilettante is precisely this capacity for rigorous, measurement-grounded reasoning.



I applaud the decision to make this invaluable resource freely available.
When I co-wrote Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach with John Hennessy, we debated how to make the material as accessible as possible. We lobbied our publisher to keep the price down and even came out with a low cost international student edition for sales outside North America. Those concerns have only grown more urgent as ML has become infrastructure—as consequential to the modern world as the electrical grid or the internet.
The decision to publish this book as a freely available educational resource is not a compromise. It is a statement of values. ML systems are being deployed in every sector of every economy on every continent. The engineers who build and maintain them will come from everywhere. If the foundational education required to do this work responsibly is available only to students at well-resourced institutions, we will contribute to an expertise gap that mirrors the societal concerns of who benefits from AI and who bears its costs.
What impresses me further is that this project has gone well beyond open access to a static text. The accompanying ecosystem—interactive laboratories, a build-from-scratch framework in TinyTorch, hardware deployment kits, instructor materials, a global network of adopting universities—reflects a familiar educational maxim: “I hear and I forget. I see and I remember. I do and I understand.”
The open-source model also makes the curriculum itself better. Errors get corrected. Examples get sharpened. New chapters emerge in response to what the field actually needs. As we found with Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach, a community of contributors that forms around a book can offer a form of quality assurance that no single author team, however expert, can match alone.



The field of computer architecture has a tradition I am proud of: we build things, measure them honestly, share what we learn, and revise our philosophies when the measurements demand it. We do not hide behind the complexity of our systems to avoid accountability for whether they actually work. We do not conflate novelty with progress. We debate, rigorously, about what matters and why.
Hopefully, ML systems engineering will follow this tradition. It needs the habits of mind that come from taking systems seriously: thinking about interactions, measuring at the right level of abstraction, being honest about trade-offs, and holding oneself accountable to real-world performance rather than benchmark folklore. This book embodies those habits.
Introduction to Machine Learning Systems is more than just a textbook; it is a clarion call for systems thinking in the age of AI, a guide for building robust ML applications, and a testament to the power of open education.
We are at an extraordinary moment. Over my career there has been a major breakthrough every decade: the microprocessor in the 1970s, the personal computer in the 1980s, the Internet in the 1990s, the smartphone in the 2000s, and AI in the 2010s. The first four changed business and society, yet AI looks likely to have the largest impact of them all.
The systems being built today will shape how intelligence is deployed, who benefits from it, and what it costs—in money, in energy, and in carbon footprint. We need the engineers who build those systems to have the best possible systems skills.
This book is a significant step toward making it possible for anyone to learn them.

David A. Patterson
