Convolutional layers typically use small spatial kernels (\(3{\times}3\) or \(5{\times}5\)) to maintain compact parameter footprints while stacking layers to widen the effective receptive field. Each output activation depends on one small window of the input. In figure 4, a \(3{\times}3\) receptive field in a \(7{\times}7\) input produces one value of the \(5{\times}5\) output map, and sliding the same filter to every position fills in the rest. Sharing the filter across positions encodes translation equivariance: the same edge detector works at any image location.



Applying a CNN to \(28{\times}28\) MNIST images demonstrates the difference in state representation. Rather than flattening the image into a 784-element vector that destroys spatial adjacency, each convolutional layer applies a bank of filters (for example, 32 filters of size \(3{\times}3\)) directly to the 2D grid. The stride is how many positions the filter moves between evaluations, and padding adds a border of zeros so that a filter centered on an edge pixel still has a full window. With unit stride and padding to preserve border dimensions, the layer outputs a \(28{\times}28{\times}32\) activation tensor preserving the spatial grid. Each coordinate holds 32 distinct feature measurements extracted from its immediate neighborhood. Between groups of convolutional layers, a pooling layer summarizes each small window, typically \(2{\times}2\), by its maximum or average. This shrinks the grid by a factor of four in area while keeping the channels, so later layers see a coarser map that covers more of the image at a quarter of the activation memory.
Preserving spatial topology changes how execution units access memory. Instead of loading an unshared weight matrix once per sample as in an MLP, a convolutional layer streams input feature maps through hardware registers while keeping compact filter weights pinned in fast on-chip SRAM or register files. This arithmetic pattern drives the memory-hierarchy optimizations of AI accelerators, where loop tiling (splitting the loops into blocks whose data fits on chip, developed under data movement below) and parallel channel reduction relieve high-bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic.
Weight sharing is what guarantees this reuse. Because the same filter applies at every coordinate, the computational schedule and memory access geometry are identical across spatial positions. The same sharing gives the layer a mathematical property, translation equivariance: translating the input produces an identical spatial translation in the output feature map.
Equivariance and invariance govern how an architecture responds to spatial transformations. An operator \(\LayerFunction\) is equivariant to a transformation \(\SpatialTransformation\) if transforming the input transforms the output by the same operator (equation 4): \[
\LayerFunction(\SpatialTransformation(\LayerInputVector)) = \SpatialTransformation(\LayerFunction(\LayerInputVector))
\tag{4}\]
For a stride-1 convolutional layer without boundary padding effects, translating the input by vector \(\TranslationVector= (\TranslationComponent_1, \TranslationComponent_2)\) shifts the resulting feature maps by exactly \(\TranslationVector\). Spatial coordinate information propagates deterministically through the layer. By contrast, an operator is invariant to \(\SpatialTransformation\) if transforming the input leaves the output unchanged (equation 5): \[
\LayerFunction(\SpatialTransformation(\LayerInputVector)) = \LayerFunction(\LayerInputVector)
\tag{5}\]
A global average pooling layer over an entire feature map is translation-invariant: shifting the input alters the spatial locations of activations, but averaging across all spatial positions collapses coordinates into a scalar that is identical regardless of where the features appeared. This mathematical distinction dictates where equivariance must be maintained and where invariance should be introduced across the network hierarchy. Tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation require equivariance through the final layer: bounding-box coordinates and per-pixel masks must track object coordinates precisely. Classification tasks, by contrast, require equivariance in intermediate feature extractors to preserve relative spatial relations (“eyes above nose”), while the final layers introduce translation invariance via pooling to collapse spatial coordinates into a class probability vector.
Re-indexing the convolution sum under a shift confirms that stride-1 convolution is translation equivariant up to boundary conditions. An equivariant convolutional layer preserves coordinate information, whereas an invariant pooling layer discards spatial coordinates entirely. Example 6.3 verifies this tracking through explicit matrix operations.

\end{bmatrix}
\]

\SpatialTransformation_2 \LayerInputVector= \begin{bmatrix}

0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\

Parameter efficiency is the most immediate systems consequence of the weight sharing that produces translation equivariance, because sharing decouples parameter capacity from the input resolution. For example, processing a \(224{\times}224\) RGB image with an MLP requires each hidden neuron to connect to all 150,528 input pixels. A CNN with a \(3{\times}3\) filter requires only 27 parameters per filter, reused across all \(224{\times}224\) spatial positions. A compact parameter footprint lets the weights stay resident in accelerator SRAM or L2 cache rather than streaming from external DRAM on every use.
Equivariance also increases sample efficiency, reducing training pipeline overhead. When a network updates a filter to recognize a feature at one coordinate, parameter sharing ensures that the feature is recognized across all spatial coordinates simultaneously. The model does not require separate training examples to learn the same feature at different pixel offsets, functioning as structural data augmentation. This sample efficiency reduces the total training iterations, dataset storage, and host-to-device I/O bandwidth required to reach target accuracy.
Convolution’s translation equivariance is one instance of a general principle: data symmetries can be embedded as equivariances in the architecture. Group-equivariant CNNs (Cohen and Welling 2016) extend the construction to rotations and reflections for satellite and medical imagery, where orientation does not determine meaning. For systems engineering, stronger symmetry constraints often produce smaller models, but specialized equivariances may require custom operations, such as rotation convolutions, that need either hardware support or efficient software implementations.

A single equivariant stencil sees only its \(\KernelSize{\times}\KernelSize\) window, so CNNs build the edge-to-object hierarchy of figure 3 by stacking layers (Bengio et al. 2013; Zeiler and Fergus 2014). With fixed \(\KernelSize{\times}\KernelSize\) kernels and unit stride, each added layer widens the effective receptive-field side length by \(\KernelSize-1\) pixels, while receptive-field area grows quadratically until later layers span the entire input. How efficiently accelerators execute this expanding stack depends on how sliding-window stencils map onto parallel execution pipelines.



A framework expresses a whole convolutional layer as one call (listing 3). Behind that call, the underlying runtime must schedule memory traffic across cache hierarchies and lower sliding-window stencils onto matrix execution hardware.



Listing 3: Convolutional Layer Abstraction: Framework-level convolution operations hide the complexity of sliding window computations, typically dispatching to cuDNN or MKL which internally handle im2col transformations or direct convolution algorithms.


def conv_layer_spatial(input, kernel, bias):
    """Framework-level convolution.

    Single call dispatches to optimized kernel (often via im2col + GEMM).
    """
    # Convolution applies shared weights across all positions
    # For a 3x3 kernel on 28x28 input (padded): 9 MACs per position x 784 positions
    output = convolution(input, kernel) + bias
    return activation(output)



To expose the mechanics that the framework abstraction conceals, listing 4 details the canonical seven-deep loop nest required to evaluate a direct 2D convolution. These loops partition into three structural tiers: batch iteration across samples, spatial traversal over feature map coordinates \((\FeatureMapRowCoordinate, \FeatureMapColumnCoordinate)\), and channel accumulation over input and output dimensions \((\InputChannelCount, \OutputChannelCount)\) coupled with kernel offsets \((\KernelVerticalLoopOffset, \KernelHorizontalLoopOffset)\). Traversing spatial coordinates and output channels defines the grid of independent output activations. The listing uses unit stride and no padding, with channels stored contiguously at each spatial position (NHWC: batch, height, width, channels). Each output window stays within the input, so the output height and width are the corresponding input dimensions minus the kernel dimensions plus one.



Listing 4: Logical Convolution Computation: Seven nested loops expose \(\mathcal{O}(\BatchSize \times \FeatureMapHeight \times \FeatureMapWidth \times \OutputChannelCount \times \KernelSize \times \KernelSize \times \InputChannelCount)\) complexity. The spatial dimensions here count output positions. The scalar order exposes overlapping input reads; tiled implementations exploit this reuse directly or through matrix multiplication.


def conv_layer_compute(input, kernel, bias):
    # NHWC input; kernel axes: height, width, input, output channels.
    # Unit stride, no padding; activation follows the convolution.
    batch_size, in_h, in_w, in_channels = input.shape
    kernel_h, kernel_w, _, out_channels = kernel.shape
    out_h, out_w = in_h - kernel_h + 1, in_w - kernel_w + 1
    output = zeros((batch_size, out_h, out_w, out_channels))
    for image in range(batch_size):
        for y in range(out_h):
            for x in range(out_w):
                for out in range(out_channels):
                    result = bias[out]
                    for ky in range(kernel_h):
                        for kx in range(kernel_w):
                            for ch in range(in_channels):
                                result += (input[image, y + ky, x + kx, ch]
                                           * kernel[ky, kx, ch, out])
                    output[image, y, x, out] = result
    return activation(output)



The inner three loops execute the kernel dot product at each spatial site. For a \(3{\times}3\) filter, each output activation accumulates contributions from a local input patch across all input channels. Advancing x by one makes the next output read a patch overlapping the previous one, while changing out reuses the same patch with a different filter. These repeated accesses offer reuse, but the scalar schedule does not explicitly keep tiles in fast memory or distribute work across execution lanes. Their actual cost depends on which reads the cache serves and how the implementation maps iterations to hardware.
To expose these patches to optimized matrix engines, convolution implementations can use the im2col (image-to-column) transformation.15 By unfolding each receptive-field patch into a contiguous row of an input matrix and stacking filter weights into columns (figure 5 lays this out for two input channels), im2col recasts the entire convolution as a dense general matrix multiply (GEMM) that runs on mature, vendor-tuned libraries. To see how the lowering rearranges data in memory, consider a miniature single-channel image (\(\InputChannelCount= 1\)) of size \(3 \times 3\) convolved with a \(2 \times 2\) filter (\(\KernelSize= 2\)) with valid padding: \[
\LayerInputMatrix= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 9 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \WeightMatrix= \begin{bmatrix} \FilterWeight_1 & \FilterWeight_2 \\ \FilterWeight_3 & \FilterWeight_4 \end{bmatrix}
\] The window visits four overlapping \(2 \times 2\) receptive fields. To evaluate all four in one matrix multiplication, im2col flattens each patch into a row vector of length \(\KernelSize^2 = 4\) and stacks the rows into an unfolded matrix \(\UnfoldedPatchMatrix\): \[
\UnfoldedPatchMatrix= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 5 & 6 \\ 4 & 5 & 7 & 8 \\ 5 & 6 & 8 & 9 \end{bmatrix}
\] Flattening the filter weights into a column vector \(\FlattenedFilterWeights= [\FilterWeight_1, \FilterWeight_2, \FilterWeight_3, \FilterWeight_4]^T\), the entire convolution collapses into a single standard matrix product: \(\UnfoldedConvolutionOutput= \UnfoldedPatchMatrix\FlattenedFilterWeights\). For batched multi-channel inputs, the unfolded matrix has shape \([(\BatchSize \cdot \OutputFeatureMapHeight \cdot \OutputFeatureMapWidth) \times (\KernelSize^2 \cdot \InputChannelCount)]\) and the filters reshape to \([(\KernelSize^2 \cdot \InputChannelCount) \times \OutputChannelCount]\). In \(\UnfoldedPatchMatrix\), input element 5 appears in all four rows, and the miniature input expands from nine elements to sixteen, a storage ratio of \(16/9\). For large stride-1 inputs, fully materialized unfolding approaches the kernel area as its expansion factor. The smaller ratio here reflects the borders of a valid convolution. Materializing the buffer trades this additional storage and traffic for access to wide matrix engines optimized for GEMM throughput. Implicit GEMM, described next, avoids allocating the duplicated buffer.
15 im2col (image to column): Rather than being a new learning algorithm, im2col-style lowering is an implementation technique used by CNN frameworks and libraries such as Caffe and cuDNN (Chellapilla et al. 2006; Jia et al. 2014; Chetlur et al. 2014): it converts convolutions into standard GEMM calls by unfolding overlapping patches into matrix columns. The trade-off is memory: in a simple fully materialized stride-1 \(\KernelSize{\times}\KernelSize\) transform, interior input elements can appear in up to \(\KernelSize^2\) columns (9 times for \(3{\times}3\) filters), though borders, stride, padding, tiling, and direct-convolution algorithms reduce the realized expansion. This memory-for-simplicity exchange explains why mobile frameworks (TFLite, NNAPI) prefer direct convolution, while data center GPUs with abundant HBM may use GEMM-oriented lowering when it improves throughput.

Implicit GEMM techniques run the same matrix multiplication without building the unfolded matrix. They compute each patch element’s address on the fly, inside the processor’s registers, so the duplicated buffer is never materialized. With \(3{\times}3\) filters and 32 output channels, each output coordinate requires only 9 MAC operations per input channel, whereas each output neuron of the reference MLP layer requires 784. The window overlap creates reuse that the memory system must be scheduled to exploit.



Weight sharing flips the hardware bottleneck of a neural network. Compact convolutional filters fit in on-chip cache and are reused across thousands of pixel positions, which pushes arithmetic intensity into the compute-bound regime. The intermediate feature maps they write out, however, dominate off-chip memory capacity and bandwidth. Whether a deep CNN stalls on memory or saturates the matrix units depends on layer depth, how long activations stay live for the backward pass, and whether feature-map tiles remain in on-chip SRAM or spill to external HBM.


On a \(224{\times}224\) ImageNet input, a convolutional layer with 64 filters of size \(3{\times}3\) needs only 576 weights per input channel, or 36,864 weights (147.5 KB in FP32) across 64 input channels. These weights fit comfortably in on-chip L1 or L2 cache, yet the layer produces 3.2M output activation values (about 12.8 MB in FP32 per sample in the batch). Memory consumption in convolutional layers splits sharply between these compact, static filter weights and large, transient feature maps. During training, those feature maps must stay live in memory until backpropagation computes the layer’s gradients, making activation memory, not weight capacity, the binding memory constraint for deep CNNs on accelerators.
Accelerators exploit this footprint disparity through hierarchical caching. CPUs retain compact filter weights in L2/L3 caches while streaming activation tensors. GPUs stage filter weights and input tiles in on-chip scratchpad SRAM (shared memory) and register files, reusing loaded weights across thousands of spatial coordinates and eliminating redundant round-trips to off-chip HBM.


↪ The memory hierarchy of register files, on-chip SRAM, and HBM that these caching patterns exploit is developed in Memory hierarchy.



Evaluating a convolutional layer requires repeatedly evaluating local dot products across spatial positions. For an ImageNet input with \(3{\times}3\) filters and 64 output channels, computing a single spatial position requires 576 multiply-accumulate operations per input channel. Summed over 64 input channels and repeated at all 50,176 spatial positions, one such layer performs about 1.85 billion multiply-accumulates. The general count follows the same steps: a layer with \(\FeatureMapHeight{\times}\FeatureMapWidth\) output positions performs \(\FeatureMapHeight \FeatureMapWidth \KernelSize^2 \InputChannelCount \OutputChannelCount\) multiply-accumulates, one \(\KernelSize^2 \InputChannelCount\) dot product for every output position and every filter. Although each spatial stencil touches fewer parameters than a dense layer, spatial repetition multiplies the total floating-point operation count.
This computational regularity provides rich opportunities for hardware parallelization. Because each spatial coordinate is independent, processors parallelize work along multiple axes simultaneously: across the batch dimension, across spatial coordinates \((\FeatureMapColumnCoordinate, \FeatureMapRowCoordinate)\), and across output channels. CPUs execute vectorized SIMD instructions16 to evaluate multiple spatial outputs per clock cycle, while GPUs dispatch thread warps across thousands of concurrent execution lanes.
16 SIMD (single instruction, multiple data): CPU instructions that apply the same operation to multiple data elements simultaneously; AVX-512 can process 16 single-precision values per vector instruction; realized speedup over scalar code also depends on instruction throughput, vectorization, and memory access. For CNN inference on edge CPUs without GPU access, SIMD utilization can affect whether a model meets real-time latency targets. Frameworks like TFLite and Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) Runtime use vectorized convolution kernels to exploit this parallelism. 


Data movement in a convolutional layer has an arithmetic intensity profile different from that of an MLP. In a fully connected layer at batch size one, each loaded weight is used exactly once, yielding an arithmetic intensity bounded below 1 FLOP/byte. In a 2D convolution, each \(3{\times}3\) filter weight is reused across all 50,176 positions of the \(224{\times}224\) feature map. This weight reuse increases operational intensity, shifting computation from the memory-bandwidth-bound regime toward the compute-bound ceiling.
The systems challenge shifts from loading weights to staging activations. Because adjacent spatial receptive fields overlap, a naive memory access pattern would re-fetch each input pixel from memory up to \(\KernelSize^2 = 9\) times. Runtimes avoid this redundant memory traffic by tiling computation into 2D spatial blocks sized to fit inside accelerator SRAM, the technique that Tiling develops for the accelerator’s memory hierarchy. Once an input tile is loaded into shared memory, all overlapping filter dot products for that tile execute in place, amortizing the DRAM/HBM transfer and maximizing the 50,176 reuses of each filter weight. Reuse also moves the energy. Each filter weight fetched from off-chip memory feeds tens of thousands of multiply-accumulates. Once filters and input tiles stay on chip, a convolutional layer spends its energy on arithmetic and on-chip SRAM rather than on DRAM reads, the reverse of the batch-one dense layer.

CNNs succeed because they match the structure of image data. Verify you understand how:

Parameter sharing: how does using the same filter across the image reduce parameter count by orders of magnitude compared to MLPs?
Translation equivariance: why does shifting the input image result in a corresponding shift in the feature map?
Compute-bound convolution: how does filter reuse raise arithmetic intensity, and how would comparing that intensity with the target machine’s roofline balance establish whether the layer is compute bound?



These memory, compute, and data-movement patterns converge in ResNet-50 (He et al. 2016a), which anchors the chapter’s compute-intensive vision lighthouse. The Residual Network (ResNet) addressed the degradation problem in deep plain networks: adding layers could increase training error despite sufficient capacity. By introducing skip connections, shortcut paths that add a block’s input directly to its output and so give gradients a route around each block (developed in section 6.4), it enabled networks of 50, 100, or even 1,000 layers. The ResNet architecture won the ImageNet 2015 competition (with 152-layer models), and ResNet-50 has become a widely used backbone and benchmark workload for computer vision.

Lighthouse 6.1: ResNet-50 (vision lighthouse)
Why it matters: ResNet-50 is a reference point for regular, convolution-heavy vision workloads. Its architecture consists almost entirely of dense convolutional layers, making it highly regular and efficient on GPUs. Under batched execution with good data reuse, ResNet-50 performance is typically limited by floating-point throughput (FLOP/s), making it a useful lighthouse for explaining data parallelism, quantization, and batching strategies. Table 2 summarizes the quantitative properties and their system consequences:

Under batched convolutional reuse, ResNet-50 has high effective arithmetic intensity and is typically compute-bound, so peak FP throughput on Tensor Cores often sets the ceiling before memory bandwidth does.

ResNet-50’s compute-bound profile assumes abundant hardware resources, yet most inference runs on devices with power budgets three orders of magnitude smaller than a data center accelerator. Standard convolutions scale as \(\mathcal{O}(\SpatialPositionCount\times \KernelSize^2 \times \InputChannelCount\times \OutputChannelCount)\), a compute volume that exceeds the strict energy budgets of always-on edge devices. To bridge this gap, efficient architectures like depthwise separable CNNs (DS-CNN) decompose the standard convolution into two distinct operations. This factorization, introduced by Sifre in the context of feature extraction (Sifre and Mallat 2014) and popularized by MobileNet (Howard et al. 2017), decouples spatial filtering from cross-channel combination. The depthwise convolution applies filters to each input channel independently (\(\KernelSize\times \KernelSize\times \InputChannelCount\) parameters), while the pointwise convolution uses a \(1{\times}1\) convolution to project channels to the output dimension (\(1 \times 1 \times \InputChannelCount\times \OutputChannelCount\) parameters). Per output position, a standard layer performs \(\KernelSize^2 \InputChannelCount \OutputChannelCount\) multiply-accumulates, while the factorized pair performs \(\KernelSize^2 \InputChannelCount+ \InputChannelCount \OutputChannelCount\). Dividing the two shows that the decomposition reduces parameter count and FLOPs to roughly \(\frac{1}{\OutputChannelCount} + \frac{1}{\KernelSize^2}\) of standard convolution, a reduction factor approaching \(\KernelSize^2\), or about 8–9\(\times\) for \(3{\times}3\) filters with large \(\OutputChannelCount\). That reduction makes real-time execution feasible on resource-constrained microcontrollers.

Sifre, Laurent, and Stéphane Mallat. 2014. “Rigid-Motion Scattering for Image Classification.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1403.1687, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1403.1687.
The channel paths in figure 6 show where the arithmetic reduction comes from. The depthwise stage produces one intermediate value per input channel at each output position, and the pointwise stage combines those values across channels.






Figure 6: Spatial Filtering and Channel Mixing: At one output position, the standard layer combines spatial and channel sums separately for each output filter. The factorized layer first filters each input channel, then mixes the intermediate values into the same output shape. The lower panel uses one spatial filter per input channel, or depth multiplier one.



The shared spatial filter within each input channel restricts the functions the factorized layer can represent. Matching input and output shapes therefore does not make the pair an algebraically equivalent replacement for an arbitrary trained standard convolution. An implementation may also materialize the intermediate activations, adding a memory cost that the MAC count alone does not reveal.
MobileNet (Howard et al. 2017) made this factorization the basis of a model family, challenging the trend toward ever-larger networks by designing for the battery and latency budgets of smartphones and embedded devices. MobileNetV2 anchors the chapter’s edge-efficiency lighthouse, reaching competitive accuracy at a fraction of ResNet-50’s arithmetic, and its small compute footprint made it a natural target for compression and lower-precision deployment, which stores and computes with fewer bits per value.

Howard, Andrew G., Menglong Zhu, Bo Chen, Dmitry Kalenichenko, Weijun Wang, Tobias Weyand, Marco Andreetto, and Hartwig Adam. 2017. “MobileNets: Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks for Mobile Vision Applications.” CoRR abs/1704.04861.

↪ Compression and lower-precision deployment techniques for compact models such as MobileNet are developed in Model Compression.


Lighthouse 6.2: MobileNetV2 (efficiency lighthouse)
Why it matters: MobileNetV2 represents edge workloads that must meet a latency budget within a power envelope. Its depthwise separable convolutions trade channel-mixing capacity for fewer operations, making it a useful baseline for mobile apps, embedded vision, and neural architecture search (NAS), automated search over model designs. Set side by side, the ResNet-50 and MobileNetV2 profiles show that a model with 13.7× fewer FLOPs does not automatically run 13.7× faster. Whether operational reduction translates into wall-clock speedup depends on arithmetic intensity, operator dispatch overhead, and the hardware’s roofline balance. A standard convolution reuses each loaded input patch across all output filters in a single matrix multiplication. Splitting that pass into depthwise and pointwise stages removes cross-channel reuse from the spatial step. Each depthwise filter operates on one channel in isolation, which cannot form a wide matrix product to fill GPU Tensor Cores, and the split writes and re-reads an extra intermediate feature map while performing roughly eight to nine times less arithmetic on those bytes. On data center GPUs engineered for high arithmetic intensity, MobileNetV2 therefore achieves only a modest speedup. Architectural efficiency techniques like depthwise separable convolutions and pruning (removing redundant weights or channels) alter this hardware mapping balance, and Perspective 6.1 addresses the central fallacy linking FLOP counts directly to execution latency.

Systems Perspective 6.1: Misconception: FLOPs equal speedFallacy: “MobileNetV2 has 13.7× fewer FLOPs than ResNet-50, so it must run 13.7× faster.”
Resolution: On high-end GPUs at small batch, MobileNetV2 gains far less than its FLOP advantage suggests, and in some framework configurations runs no faster than ResNet-50. MobileNetV2’s depthwise separable convolutions have low arithmetic intensity: they move more data relative to computation. GPUs optimized for dense matrix operations may use their compute units poorly on these kernels. FLOPs measure work; throughput depends on how well that work maps to hardware.


KWS (Warden 2018) pushes the same factorization to the microcontroller end of the spectrum and anchors the always-on TinyML lighthouse. A continuous audio stream is first converted by a short-time Fourier transform into a 2D time-frequency spectrogram (or Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients), so 2D convolutional filters can slide across time and frequency bins to detect acoustic phoneme signatures. Models that listen for “Hey Siri” or “Ok Google” run on always-on microcontrollers with kilobyte-scale memory and milliwatt power budgets (Warden and Situnayake 2020; C. R. Banbury et al. 2021; C. Banbury et al. 2021), so their designers count every byte and cycle.

Warden, Pete. 2018. “Speech Commands: A Dataset for Limited-Vocabulary Speech Recognition.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1804.03209, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1804.03209.

Warden, Pete, and Daniel Situnayake. 2020. TinyML: Machine Learning with TensorFlow Lite on Arduino and Ultra-Low-Power Microcontrollers. O’Reilly Media.

Banbury, Colby R, Chuteng Zhou, Igor Fedorov, Ramon Matas, Urmish Thakker, Dibakar Gope, Vijay Janapa Reddi, Matthew Mattina, and Paul N Whatmough. 2021. “MicroNets: Neural Network Architectures for Deploying TinyML Applications on Commodity Microcontrollers.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 3: 517–32.

Banbury, Colby, Vijay Janapa Reddi, Peter Torelli, Jeremy Holleman, Nat Jeffries, Csaba Kiraly, Pietro Montino, et al. 2021. “MLPerf Tiny Benchmark.” arXiv Preprint.

Lighthouse 6.3: KWS (TinyML lighthouse)Why it matters: Keyword spotting models (like DS-CNN) represent the power-constrained end of the spectrum. Used in always-on applications like smart doorbells that wake a larger vision pipeline only after an audio trigger, these models must run on microcontrollers with milliwatt power budgets.
At 200K parameters, a DS-CNN keyword spotter’s 800 KB of FP32 weights already exceeds the few hundred kilobytes of memory a typical microcontroller can devote to a model, so the model fits only after 8-bit quantization cuts it fourfold. KWS is therefore the lighthouse for extreme quantization (INT8/INT4) and specialized architectural primitives (depthwise separable convolutions) that trade theoretical representational power for maximum efficiency per watt.


From ResNet-50’s compute-heavy standard convolutions through MobileNet’s depthwise separable variants to KWS’s micro-power deployment, CNNs demonstrate how architectural constraints transform data structure into hardware efficiency. Local connectivity and weight sharing reduce parameter storage and expose reuse. Depth is what lets those stacks compose edges into objects, and ResNet-50’s fifty layers depend on two building blocks that make depth trainable at all.

title: 6 Network Architectures
text:
When plain convolutional networks are stacked beyond roughly 20 layers, adding more layers can make training error worse rather than better: gradients vanish or explode on the way back through the stack, and the scale of intermediate activations drifts on the way forward. Convolution made deep vision networks affordable in parameter count, and two building blocks made them trainable. Skip connections keep gradients alive through dozens of layers, and normalization keeps the activations those layers produce within a stable numerical range. Both arrived with deep CNNs, both carry their own memory and bandwidth costs, and both reappear in the deep families that follow, most visibly the transformer.


Why gradients vanish or explode across depth, and why additive identity shortcuts (skip connections) resolve that barrier, follows directly from the chain rule, whose layer-by-layer Jacobian form appears in Error signal propagation. For a deep network with layers \(\LayerFunction_1, \LayerFunction_2, \ldots, \FinalLayerFunction\), the gradient of the loss \(\LossFunction\) with respect to the weights in layer 1 is: \[
\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \WeightMatrix^{(1)}} = \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \ActivationVector^{(\LayerCount)}} \cdot \frac{\partial \ActivationVector^{(\LayerCount)}}{\partial \PreactivationVector^{(\LayerCount)}} \cdot \frac{\partial \PreactivationVector^{(\LayerCount)}}{\partial \ActivationVector^{(\LayerCount-1)}} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{\partial \PreactivationVector^{(2)}}{\partial \ActivationVector^{(1)}} \cdot \frac{\partial \ActivationVector^{(1)}}{\partial \PreactivationVector^{(1)}} \cdot \frac{\partial \PreactivationVector^{(1)}}{\partial \WeightMatrix^{(1)}}
\] where \(\PreactivationVector^{(\LayerIndex)}\) represents the preactivation and \(\ActivationVector^{(\LayerIndex)} = \SigmoidFunction(\PreactivationVector^{(\LayerIndex)})\) the postactivation output of layer \(\LayerIndex\). Each layer contributes both a weight transformation and an activation derivative \(\SigmoidFunction'(\PreactivationVector^{(\LayerIndex)})\). With sigmoid activations, whose derivative peaks at 0.25 (Sigmoid), the activation-derivative factors alone contribute at most \((0.25)^{\LayerCount}\) along a path. The full gradient also depends on the intervening weight matrices; when their transformations do not offset this attenuation, early layers receive negligible updates. Exploding gradients are the destabilizing counterpart. If each layer Jacobian expands a shared direction by about 1.5, that component grows exponentially, producing overflow, NaN (not-a-number) values, and training divergence rather than a silent stall.
ReLU removes the activation’s share of this decay, since its derivative is one on active paths (ReLU), and that change made networks of 10–20 layers trainable. It does not remove the problem. Inactive units pass zero gradient, and a poorly initialized weight or a large update can leave a unit permanently dead. More fundamentally, ReLU does nothing to regulate the singular values of the weight matrices, which continue to attenuate or amplify gradients across depth. The original ResNet study showed the consequence on CIFAR-10: a 56-layer plain network had higher training and test error than a 20-layer plain network throughout training (He et al. 2016a). Because the deeper network was worse on the training set, the failure was an optimization barrier, not overfitting.
A residual block gives the gradient a direct path back through its input. Equation 6 adds the identity path \(\LayerInputVector\) to the residual mapping \(\ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector)\): \[
\ResidualBlockOutput= \ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector) + \LayerInputVector \tag{6}\] where \(\ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector)\) represents the residual function (typically two convolutional layers with batch normalization and ReLU) and \(\LayerInputVector\) is the identity skip connection. The original post-activation ResNet block (figure 7) routes an identity shortcut around two weight layers and the ReLU between them, adds it back at a junction, and then applies the final activation.






Figure 7: Residual Connection Block (Original Post-Activation Form): The original ResNet block (He et al. 2016a) implements \(\ResidualBlockOutput = \text{ReLU}(\ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector) + \LayerInputVector)\), where an identity shortcut bypasses the weight layers before a final ReLU activation. In later pre-activation variants (He et al. 2016b) and modern transformer blocks, the nonlinearity moves inside \(\ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector)\), making the addition a completely clean identity shortcut \(\ResidualBlockOutput = \ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector) + \LayerInputVector\) that matches the unobstructed gradient flow in equation 6.



During backpropagation, the gradient flows through this addition, and applying the chain rule gives: \[
\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \LayerInputVector} =
\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \ResidualBlockOutput} \cdot
\left(\frac{\partial \ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector)}{\partial \LayerInputVector} + \IdentityMatrix\right)
= \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \ResidualBlockOutput} \cdot
\ResidualFunction'(\LayerInputVector) +
\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \ResidualBlockOutput}
\]
Here \(\IdentityMatrix\) is the identity matrix, and the gradient decomposes into two additive terms. Even if the residual term \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \ResidualBlockOutput}\ResidualFunction'(\LayerInputVector)\) attenuates, the identity term passes \(\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \ResidualBlockOutput}\) directly to the earlier layer. While the residual branch can partially interfere with the identity signal, keeping \(\|\ResidualFunction'(\LayerInputVector)\|\) small keeps the block Jacobian close to identity and bounds its condition number. Through \(\LayerCount\) residual blocks, the gradient becomes: \[
\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \LayerInputVector^{(0)}} =
\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \LayerInputVector^{(\LayerCount)}} \cdot
\prod_{\LayerIndex=1}^{\LayerCount}
\left(\ResidualFunction'_\LayerIndex(\LayerInputVector^{(\LayerIndex-1)}) + \IdentityMatrix\right)
\]
Each factor \((\ResidualFunction'_\ell + \IdentityMatrix)\) contains the identity term, keeping the factor near identity when the residual-branch Jacobian is small. A plain network instead multiplies arbitrary layer Jacobians, and if their average gain is even slightly below one the product vanishes exponentially (\(0.9^{50} \approx 0.005\)). ResNets multiply near-identity factors. The deviations can still compound, and the additive path does not guarantee exact unit gain across arbitrary depth, but this structure improves conditioning enough to make networks with 100+ layers trainable. The CIFAR-10 experiments confirm it: a 56-layer residual network reached about 7.0 percent test error against 8.8 percent for its 20-layer residual counterpart, reversing the degradation seen in plain networks (He et al. 2016a). There is no single depth at which skip connections suddenly become mandatory; trainability also depends on initialization, normalization, optimizer dynamics, and block architecture (He et al. 2016b).

He, Kaiming, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun. 2016a. “Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition.” 2016 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 770–78. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2016.90.

He, Kaiming, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun. 2016b. “Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks.” Computer Vision – ECCV 2016, 630–45. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-46493-0_38.
The shortcuts carry a concrete hardware cost that every deep network pays. Evaluating \(\ResidualBlockOutput= \ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector) + \LayerInputVector\) requires the input tensor \(\LayerInputVector\) to remain resident in memory throughout the execution of every operation in the branch \(\ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector)\). This extended liveness window increases peak activation memory in accelerator HBM during the forward pass and preserves \(\LayerInputVector\) for backpropagation unless activation checkpointing is used (Activation checkpointing). The elementwise addition is also memory-bandwidth bound. It performs one addition per two loaded operands and one stored result, about 0.08 FLOP/byte in FP32 (one FLOP per 12 bytes), so un-fused residual merges become memory stalls.
Residual connections stabilize the backward gradient path, but they do not constrain the forward scale of intermediate activations. Unbounded variance across depth can still destabilize layer inputs, which calls for a complementary block: normalization.



Without normalization, small weight updates in early layers compound across depth, shifting and amplifying intermediate activations until later nonlinearities saturate or overflow and training requires tiny learning rates. Skip connections protect the backward pass, and normalization steadies the forward pass by re-centering and re-scaling those intermediate activations at each block. Batch normalization in CNNs17 (Ioffe and Szegedy 2015), layer normalization for sequence models, and RMSNorm18 for large language models illustrate different choices of reduction axes and statistics.
17 Batch normalization (BatchNorm): The original normalization layer (Ioffe and Szegedy 2015), which re-scales activations using per-mini-batch statistics. In one ImageNet experiment, it reached the target accuracy with 14\(\times\) fewer training steps. Its batch-size dependency and training-serving skew (switching from batch statistics to running averages at inference) are systems limitations that motivated alternatives: LayerNorm removed batch dependency for transformers, and RMSNorm removed mean centering.
Ioffe, Sergey, and Christian Szegedy. 2015. “Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift.” Proceedings of the 32nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 37: 448–56.
18 RMSNorm (root mean square normalization): Introduced by Zhang and Sennrich (2019) at NeurIPS, RMSNorm simplifies LayerNorm by normalizing with the root mean square alone, dropping the mean-centering step. Across the paper’s tested models and implementations, RMSNorm reduced overall running time by 7–64 percent relative to LayerNorm. LLaMA-family and Mixtral-style transformer reports use RMSNorm (Touvron, Lavril, et al. 2023; Touvron, Martin, et al. 2023; Jiang et al. 2024), illustrating why a simpler normalization kernel matters at large language model scale. 
Zhang, Biao, and Rico Sennrich. 2019. “Root Mean Square Layer Normalization.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS).

Touvron, Hugo, Thibaut Lavril, Gautier Izacard, Xavier Martinet, Marie-Anne Lachaux, Timothée Lacroix, Baptiste Rozière, et al. 2023. “LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2302.13971.

Touvron, Hugo, Louis Martin, Kevin Stone, Peter Albert, Amjad Almahairi, Yasmine Babaei, Nikolay Bashlykov, et al. 2023. “Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2307.09288.

Jiang, A. Q., A. Sablayrolles, A. Roux, A. Mensch, B. Savary, C. Bamford, D. S. Chaplot, et al. 2024. “Mixtral of Experts.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2401.04088.
Batch normalization standardizes activations using statistics computed across the mini-batch for each feature or channel during training. For fully connected activations, the reduction axis is the batch dimension. For convolutional activations, implementations compute per-channel statistics over both the batch and spatial positions (\(\BatchSize \times \FeatureMapHeight\times \FeatureMapWidth\)). For a mini-batch \(\MiniBatchSet= \{\MiniBatchActivation_1, \ldots, \FinalMiniBatchActivation\}\) of activations at a particular layer, the transformation proceeds in two stages, starting with the mini-batch mean and variance: \[
\BatchNormMean= \frac{1}{\BatchSize}\sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \MiniBatchActivation_i \qquad \BatchNormStandardDeviation^2 = \frac{1}{\BatchSize}\sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} (\MiniBatchActivation_i - \BatchNormMean)^2
\]
The second stage normalizes each activation over the batch and applies a learned scale and shift. The normalization step in equation 7 centers and scales activations, while equation 8 lets the network learn a useful output scale and offset: \[
\NormalizedActivation_i = \frac{\MiniBatchActivation_i - \BatchNormMean}{\sqrt{\BatchNormStandardDeviation^2 + \NumericalStabilityConstant}}
\tag{7}\] \[
\BatchNormOutput_i = \NormalizationScale\NormalizedActivation_i + \NormalizationShift \tag{8}\]
The parameters \(\NormalizationScale\) (scale) and \(\NormalizationShift\) (shift) are learned during training, while \(\NumericalStabilityConstant\) (typically \(10^{-5}\)) prevents division by zero. The affine transform restores learned scale and shift flexibility, but fixed \(\NormalizationScale\) and \(\NormalizationShift\) cannot exactly invert varying statistics for every batch. Normalization permits larger learning rates by preventing intermediate activations from exploding into saturating non-linear regimes, accelerating convergence relative to unnormalized networks.
While batch normalization enabled training of much deeper CNNs, it needs batch-wide statistics, which constrains distributed and sequence workloads. When a mini-batch is split across several accelerators, computing true mini-batch statistics requires an all-reduce, a collective that sums every accelerator’s partial statistics and returns the total to all of them, adding communication latency to every normalized layer. If instead computed locally on small per-accelerator batches, noisy empirical statistics destabilize optimization. Furthermore, batch normalization cannot handle variable-length sequences or text generation, which produces one token at a time, without complex padding masks and training-serving skew. Layer normalization resolves these limitations by normalizing across the feature dimension rather than across the batch (Ba et al. 2016).

Ba, Jimmy Lei, Jamie Ryan Kiros, and Geoffrey E. Hinton. 2016. “Layer Normalization.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1607.06450.

↪ The AllReduce collective and its communication cost are developed in Data parallelism.

For an input vector \(\LayerInputVector\in \mathbb{R}^{\HiddenDimension}\) with \(\HiddenDimension\) features, layer normalization first computes the mean and variance across those \(\HiddenDimension\) components: \[
\LayerNormMean= \frac{1}{\HiddenDimension}\sum_{i=1}^{\HiddenDimension} \LayerInputComponent_i \qquad \LayerNormStandardDeviation^2 = \frac{1}{\HiddenDimension}\sum_{i=1}^{\HiddenDimension} (\LayerInputComponent_i - \LayerNormMean)^2
\]
With those per-token statistics in hand, equation 9 defines the complete layer normalization operation, where \(\odot\) denotes element-wise multiplication: \[
\text{LayerNorm}(\LayerInputVector) = \frac{\LayerInputVector- \LayerNormMean}{\sqrt{\LayerNormStandardDeviation^2 + \NumericalStabilityConstant}} \odot \NormalizationScaleVector+ \NormalizationShiftVector \tag{9}\]
Because each token or sample is normalized independently, the computation stays within an accelerator’s on-chip SRAM and registers, with no cross-sample or cross-device communication. That independence makes layer normalization the standard choice for transformers, where sequences vary in length and text generation evaluates a single token at a time. Table 4 contrasts the three variants along the machine and operational dimensions that decide between them.



Table 4: Normalization Variant Comparison: Different normalization techniques trade off between computational efficiency, batch size sensitivity, and architectural compatibility. RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich 2019), used in LLaMA-family and other efficient transformer architectures (Touvron, Lavril, et al. 2023; Touvron, Martin, et al. 2023), omits mean centering: \(\text{RMSNorm}(\LayerInputVector) = \LayerInputVector/ \sqrt{\frac{1}{\HiddenDimension}\sum_i \LayerInputComponent_i^2 + \NumericalStabilityConstant} \odot \NormalizationScaleVector\).

The computational profile of normalization is defined by its arithmetic intensity. Because normalization applies elementwise operations to large activation tensors, execution is memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. A straightforward LayerNorm kernel makes two reductions across the hidden dimension \(\HiddenDimension\), one for the mean \(\LayerNormMean\) and one for the variance \(\LayerNormStandardDeviation^2\), although Welford’s algorithm can compute both in a single pass. RMSNorm drops the mean-centering reduction, leaving a single sum of squares, which simplifies the kernel and eases fusion with neighboring operations; its authors report 7–64 percent lower running time across the models they tested.


↪ Kernel fusion, which collapses memory-bound normalization and activation chains into single kernels whose intermediates stay on chip, is developed in The memory wall and kernel fusion.
The table’s last row is an operational cost. BatchNorm keeps nonlearned running mean and variance buffers and switches from mini-batch statistics in training to those running statistics at inference, so a mismatch between the buffers and deployment data is a frequent source of training-serving skew. LayerNorm and RMSNorm compute identically in both modes and carry no running state. With skip connections and normalization in place, depth stops being an optimization barrier.

Checkpoint 6.2: Making depth trainable

Gradient path: can you explain why the identity term in a residual block keeps gradients from vanishing across many layers?
Liveness cost: why does a skip connection raise peak activation memory, and why is an unfused residual addition memory-bandwidth bound?
Normalization choice: why does layer normalization suit sequence models and token-by-token generation better than batch normalization?



Depth extends how far a network’s view reaches across its input, but a convolutional stack still sees only its receptive field, whether that field spans pixels or the time bins of a spectrogram. A streaming system that must carry information across variable time spans within a fixed state budget motivates a different trade-off: updating a compact recurrent state as each observation arrives.

Self-Check: Question

In a residual block implementing \(\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}\), how does the additive identity shortcut mathematically improve gradient conditioning through the layer Jacobian \(\mathbf{J} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\) during backpropagation in very deep networks?

The shortcut forces the residual function \(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})\) to have zero weights, turning the network into an immutable linear identity operator.
The Jacobian takes the form \(\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{I} + \frac{\partial \mathcal{F}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\), so when residual-branch derivatives are small the block stays near identity and gradients have a direct additive path, improving conditioning without guaranteeing exact unit gain at arbitrary depth.
The shortcut doubles the singular values of the weight matrix at every layer, ensuring gradients explode exponentially rather than vanish.
The shortcut eliminates the backpropagation chain rule by replacing gradient updates with forward-only finite differences.

Compare Batch Normalization (BatchNorm) and Layer Normalization (LayerNorm) along two critical systems dimensions: (a) sensitivity to mini-batch size during training, and (b) operational differences between training and inference (including training-serving skew).

title: 6 Network Architectures
text:
An MLP requires a fixed-width input vector and a CNN sees only a bounded spatial window, so neither can process a continuous audio stream or a sentence of arbitrary length without padding, truncating, or stacking layers until activation memory overflows. Where convolutional networks exploit spatial structure, many real-world signals carry temporal structure, in which sequential order and prior context determine meaning. Recurrent networks process these variable-length streams within a fixed memory budget by carrying and updating a persistent state vector from one time step to the next.

Definition 6.4: Recurrent neural networks
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are sequence-processing architectures that maintain a hidden state \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t = \LayerFunction(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}, \LayerInputVector_t)\) updated at each time step, encoding the assumption that the current output depends on all prior inputs through this fixed-size state vector.

Significance: The fixed-size state provides \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) inference state memory regardless of sequence length (processing a 10,000-token sequence requires the same state memory as a 10-token sequence), but the sequential update rule forces all \(\SequenceLength\) recurrent transitions to execute in order. Separate per-step kernels (compiled accelerator routines, a different sense of the word from a convolution kernel) add launch overhead \((\Latency)\); fusion can reduce those launches while preserving the serial dependency chain.
Distinction: Unlike MLPs, which require a fixed-dimensional input vector, or CNNs, which restrict context to a fixed spatial window, RNNs compress an unbounded history into a fixed-size bottleneck state, so they accept sequences of any length without widening the input layer. Gradient signals pass back through the recurrent steps, where repeated Jacobian products can attenuate or amplify them (derived below).
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that RNNs are obsolete. For streaming inference on resource-constrained hardware, such as keyword spotting on a microcontroller, a model that must keep every past input to see the whole stream needs memory that grows with stream length, which can be prohibitive. An RNN’s \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) state size makes it a candidate when a fixed state budget is required.






RNNs hold state memory fixed, but latency grows with sequence length.

Elman, Jeffrey L. 1990. “Finding Structure in Time.” Cognitive Science 14 (2): 179–211. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1402_1.
Recurrent architectures, from simple recurrent networks to gated variants such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks (Elman 1990; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997), encode a temporal inductive bias in which execution order follows causal time and history compresses into that recurring state. Rather than scaling parameter count or activation storage with dilated or deeply stacked windows when relevant tokens sit far apart, the network reuses one transition operator at every step. That choice trades parallelism for bounded state: it provides variable-length temporal context within a fixed memory footprint, but it introduces loop-carried data dependencies that serialize execution on parallel accelerator hardware.


A word like “bank” cannot be disambiguated on its own: “river bank” refers to a shoreline, whereas “investment bank” refers to a financial institution. Only the preceding words resolve which meaning applies. Acoustic waveforms and sensor telemetry behave the same way: a single audio sample or temperature reading is ambiguous without the history that came before it.
Data with this sequential structure imposes three requirements on a model:

Variable-length inputs: Sequences arrive with different lengths \(\SequenceLength\), ruling out a single fixed-width input layer.
Long-range memory: The model must carry relevant signals across many time steps without requiring a fixed window size.
Continuous state updates: Internal representations must update as each new token arrives, folding in new evidence while dropping stale history.

Meeting all three streaming requirements without growing the model alongside the input length requires turning the feedforward graph into a state machine whose output at step \(\TimeStepIndex-1\) feeds step \(\TimeStepIndex\).



To meet the requirements of section 6.5.1, recurrent neural networks introduce directed cycles in their computational graph. Rather than mapping inputs directly to outputs through feedforward layers, an RNN maintains a persistent vector, the hidden state, that updates iteratively at each time step. The hidden state is a running summary of the past.
The fundamental state transition in equation 10 computes the current hidden state \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\) by combining the incoming token vector \(\LayerInputVector_t\) with the preceding state \(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}\): \[
\RecurrentHiddenState_t = \LayerNonlinearity(\RecurrentStateWeights\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1} + \RecurrentInputWeights\LayerInputVector_t + \RecurrentHiddenBias)
\tag{10}\] where \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\) denotes the hidden state at time \(\TimeStepIndex\), \(\LayerInputVector_t\) denotes the input at time \(\TimeStepIndex\), \(\RecurrentStateWeights\) contains the recurrent weights, \(\RecurrentInputWeights\) contains the input weights, \(\RecurrentHiddenBias\) is the hidden-state bias vector, and \(\LayerNonlinearity\) is the activation function. The equation uses column vectors; the later listings use row-major batched tensors, so their weight multiplications appear on the right. Unrolled across time (figure 8, right), the loop becomes a chain of transitions \(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1} \to \RecurrentHiddenState_t \to \RecurrentHiddenState_{t+1}\) in which every link reuses the same recurrent weight matrix \(\RecurrentStateWeights\), so no step can begin until the one before it has finished.






Figure 8: Recurrent Neural Network Unfolding: The compact recurrent loop (left) unfolds into one copy of the cell per time step (right). Three weight matrices are shared across all steps: \(\RecurrentInputWeights\) (input-to-hidden), \(\RecurrentStateWeights\) (hidden-to-hidden), and \(\RecurrentOutputWeights\) (hidden-to-output). These matrices are reused at every step, so the parameter count is independent of sequence length. For a 128-dimensional hidden state and a 100-dimensional input, each time step requires 16,384 MACs for recurrent connections plus 12,800 for input projection.



Unfolding the recurrent loop across \(\SequenceLength\) steps reveals the algorithmic properties of recurrence. Parameter count remains independent of sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) because the weight matrices \(\RecurrentStateWeights\) and \(\RecurrentInputWeights\) are shared across all time steps. However, sharing weights across time establishes a loop-carried dependency: step \(\TimeStepIndex\) cannot evaluate \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\) until step \(\TimeStepIndex-1\) finishes producing \(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}\). This dependency forms a critical path of length \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) serial operations that prevents hardware accelerators from parallelizing across the sequence dimension.
This sequential structure produces different memory characteristics in inference and in training. During streaming inference, an RNN evaluates one step at a time, discarding prior raw inputs and retaining only the current hidden state. State memory overhead remains strictly \(\mathcal{O}(\HiddenDimension)\) in the hidden dimension \(\HiddenDimension\), regardless of whether the sequence spans 10 or 10,000 steps. In contrast, training via backpropagation through time (BPTT) (Werbos 1990) unrolls the graph across the entire sequence of length \(\SequenceLength\). Computing gradients via the chain rule requires evaluating the Jacobian product across all intermediate transitions: \[
\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \RecurrentHiddenState_0} = \frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \FinalRecurrentHiddenState} \prod_{t=1}^{\SequenceLength} \frac{\partial \RecurrentHiddenState_t}{\partial \RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}}
\] Ordinary BPTT retains the intermediate activations \(\RecurrentHiddenState_1, \RecurrentHiddenState_2, \dots, \FinalRecurrentHiddenState\) for these Jacobian products. This retained-state scheme converts an \(\mathcal{O}(\HiddenDimension)\) runtime state into an \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength \cdot \HiddenDimension)\) training footprint; recomputing saved intermediates trades additional work for memory. Because every factor in the product combines activation derivatives with \(\RecurrentStateWeights\), the backpropagated signal attenuates or amplifies exponentially over long horizons, preventing a plain RNN from learning dependencies across more than a few dozen time steps unless the recurrence gives the state a selective bypass around \(\RecurrentStateWeights\).

Werbos, Paul J. 1990. “Backpropagation Through Time: What It Does and How to Do It.” Proceedings of the IEEE 78 (10): 1550–60. https://doi.org/10.1109/5.58337.



Gated recurrent architectures prevent long-horizon gradients from vanishing by replacing the unconditional state overwrite of equation 10 with learned gates, elementwise valves that decide at each step how much of the stored state to keep, overwrite, or expose. Each gate applies a sigmoid to a learned projection of the current input and previous state, producing values between zero and one that multiply the quantity it controls: a value near one passes that quantity through, and a value near zero blocks it. LSTMs19 (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997) maintain a separate cell state beside the hidden state and govern it with input, forget, and output gates plus a candidate update. When the forget gate stays near one, the cell state passes from step to step almost unchanged, giving gradients a path across long horizons without being multiplied by \(\RecurrentStateWeights\) at every transition. GRUs20 (Cho et al. 2014) merge the same mechanism into two gates. For the machine, an LSTM step computes four affine transformations of the input and previous state instead of one, so it holds four times the recurrent weights, performs four times the multiply-accumulates per step, and carries twice the state (hidden and cell). Runtimes fuse the four projections into one matrix multiply four times as wide, which raises its arithmetic intensity without shortening the serial chain of steps.
19 LSTM (long short-term memory): Invented by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997, LSTMs introduced a “Constant Error Carousel,” a gated cell state that protects error signals from exponential decay during backpropagation through time. The systems cost is that a standard LSTM computes input, forget, and output gates plus a candidate cell update, giving roughly four affine transformations per time step vs. one in a vanilla RNN. Transformers replaced LSTMs in many large-scale language workloads not because attention costs less arithmetic, since it costs more, but because it parallelizes across sequence positions where a recurrence cannot. 
Hochreiter, Sepp, and Jürgen Schmidhuber. 1997. “Long Short-Term Memory.” Neural Computation 9 (8): 1735–80. https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1997.9.8.1735.
20 GRU (gated recurrent unit): Cho et al. (2014) describes a gated hidden unit for encoder-decoder translation that uses reset and update gates to control how the hidden state is updated. Relative to an LSTM’s input, forget, and output gates plus candidate cell update, this gives a simpler gated recurrence. The broader systems lesson: architectural simplification can reduce state and matrix operations when it preserves task performance, a principle that recurs in efficiency-oriented designs from MobileNet to distilled transformers. 
Cho, Kyunghyun, Bart van Merrienboer, Dzmitry Bahdanau, and Yoshua Bengio. 2014. “On the Properties of Neural Machine Translation: Encoder-Decoder Approaches.” Proceedings of SSST-8, Eighth Workshop on Syntax, Semantics and Structure in Statistical Translation, 103–11. https://doi.org/10.3115/v1/w14-4012.



In hardware, a recurrent step is two matrix products followed by an elementwise update. Convolution reuses each weight across a grid of positions available all at once (section 6.3.4.3); a recurrent step reuses its weights only across time, and each step must wait for the state the previous step produces.
Listing 5 demonstrates the single-time-step mechanism using framework-level matrix operations: combine the previous hidden state with the current input, add the bias, and apply the activation to produce the next hidden state. The code is intentionally local to one step because the systems cost is not the step itself, but the dependency chain that prevents parallel execution across time.



Listing 5: RNN Layer Abstraction: Framework-level implementation combining two matrix multiplications, \(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}\RecurrentStateWeights\) and \(\LayerInputVector_t\RecurrentInputWeights\), per time step. For 128-dimensional hidden state and 100-dimensional input, each step requires 16,384 + 12,800 = 29,184 MACs, but sequential dependencies prevent parallelization across time.


def rnn_layer_step(x_t, h_prev, W_hh, W_hx, b):
    # x_t: input at time t (batch_size × input_dim)
    # h_prev: previous hidden state (batch_size × hidden_dim)
    # W_hh: recurrent weights (hidden_dim × hidden_dim)
    # W_hx: input weights (input_dim × hidden_dim)
    h_t = activation(matmul(h_prev, W_hh) + matmul(x_t, W_hx) + b)
    return h_t



At the framework level, rnn_layer_step hides the underlying loop structure and memory traffic behind high-level matrix multiplications (matmul). In hardware, evaluating this step requires moving weights and activations through the memory hierarchy. To see where execution serializes and where parallelism remains, listing 6 expands the matrix operations into explicit loop nests down to scalar multiply-accumulate operations.



Listing 6: RNN Layer Computation: Nested loops expose the sequential dependency structure. Loop 1 enables batch parallelism, but Loops 2-3 must complete before Loop 4’s activation; because each time step depends on the previous step’s output, the resulting \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) sequential depth prevents GPU parallelization across the time dimension.


def rnn_layer_compute(x_t, h_prev, W_hh, W_hx, b):
    # Initialize next hidden state
    h_t = np.zeros_like(h_prev)

    # Loop 1: Process each sequence in the batch
    for batch in range(batch_size):
        # Loop 2: Compute recurrent contribution (h_prev × W_hh)
        for i in range(hidden_dim):
            for j in range(hidden_dim):
                h_t[batch, i] += h_prev[batch, j] * W_hh[j, i]

        # Loop 3: Compute input contribution (x_t × W_hx)
        for i in range(hidden_dim):
            for j in range(input_dim):
                h_t[batch, i] += x_t[batch, j] * W_hx[j, i]

        # Loop 4: Add bias and apply activation
        for i in range(hidden_dim):
            h_t[batch, i] = activation(h_t[batch, i] + b[i])

    return h_t



The loop structure exposes the concurrency boundaries of recurrent execution. Batch instances in Loop 1 are independent, so sequences within a batch parallelize across accelerator cores without cross-talk. Within each batch instance, Loops 2 and 3 execute the recurrent transformation (\(\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1}\RecurrentStateWeights\)) and input projection (\(\LayerInputVector_t\RecurrentInputWeights\)). Both reductions must accumulate fully before Loop 4 can apply the elementwise bias addition and activation function to produce \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\).
For an input dimension of 100 and a hidden state dimension of 128, each step executes two matrix multiplications: a \(100{\times}128\) input projection and a \(128{\times}128\) recurrent transformation. When batch size is large (\(\BatchSize\gg 1\)), these operations execute as general matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMM) that reuse each loaded weight across all \(\BatchSize\) samples. When batch size is small (\(\BatchSize=1\), typical of real-time streaming inference), they collapse into the same weight-streaming matrix-vector products as the batch-one dense layer of equation 2, which starve accelerator compute units.



The hard physical constraint that recurrent architectures impose is sequential dependency. In the update \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t = \tanh(\RecurrentStateWeights\RecurrentHiddenState_{t-1} + \RecurrentInputWeights\LayerInputVector_t)\), the recurrent transformation at time step \(\TimeStepIndex\) needs the state produced by step \(\TimeStepIndex-1\). An input sequence of length \(\SequenceLength= 1{,}000\) therefore requires \(1{,}000\) ordered state updates, even when a fused kernel executes several or all updates within one launch. Hardware can parallelize across batch instances and within each matrix operation; input projections can also be computed across time when the inputs are available. Faster arithmetic or memory shortens individual steps, while the recurrent dependency chain remains.
During inference, recurrent networks need little state memory. Because the recurrent state compresses history into a fixed-size vector \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\), inference state memory scales as \(\mathcal{O}(\HiddenDimension)\) (for example, 2 KB for a 512-dimensional FP32 state), remaining completely flat whether sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) is 10 or 10,000 tokens. This constant memory footprint contrasts sharply with attention mechanisms (section 6.6), whose stored context grows with every token generated, an \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength\cdot \HiddenDimension)\) store that the transformer section sizes. For streaming deployments on memory-constrained edge hardware, such as microcontrollers, an RNN’s \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) runtime state avoids the growing context store that limits attention-based models.
Recurrent execution splits the memory hierarchy between two behaviors: high temporal locality for parameters, and low operational intensity under standard framework dispatch. Weight matrices \(\RecurrentStateWeights\) and \(\RecurrentInputWeights\) are reused at every time step, residing comfortably in SRAM or L2 cache if the model fits on-chip. However, naively launching separate kernels for input projection, recurrent projection, bias addition, and activation at each time step incurs severe kernel-launch overhead and forces intermediate tensors back and forth across HBM. To mitigate this memory-bandwidth bottleneck, production recurrent runtimes fuse the projections, bias addition, and activation into a single monolithic kernel that maintains \(\RecurrentHiddenState_t\) within GPU registers and shared memory throughout the sequence execution. At batch one, each recurrent step is the dense layer’s matrix-vector product again, with the same energy profile. Unless the recurrent weights stay on chip from step to step, every step pays DRAM energy for every weight, about 139× the energy of its arithmetic, which is a second reason streaming runtimes keep those weights resident.


↪ What a fused kernel that holds its state in registers and shared memory costs in on-chip capacity and occupancy is developed in Kernel fusion on the accelerator.

Checkpoint 6.3: Recurrent state and the serial chain
Recurrence trades parallelism for a fixed memory budget. Check your understanding:

Serial chain: why can a faster accelerator not remove the 1,000 ordered updates of a 1,000-step sequence, and which parts of the work can still run in parallel?
Fixed state: why does an RNN’s inference memory stay flat as a stream grows, while training through time stores state for every step?
Gates: what does an LSTM step cost the machine compared with a plain recurrent step, and what does fusing its four projections change?



This architectural tension between fixed-capacity state and serialized execution defined sequence processing before transformers. While recurrent networks maintain constant memory overhead regardless of sequence length, the sequential dependency prevents hardware from parallelizing across time steps. The fixed-capacity state also becomes an information bottleneck in which early inputs fade over long spans, and gradients through long chains of recurrent steps vanish or explode (the vanishing gradient problem) (Bengio et al. 1994). State-space models such as Mamba (Gu and Dao 2023) later revived recurrence for exactly its systems strength, a fixed-size state at decode time where an attention model’s stored context grows, while training with a parallel scan instead of a step-by-step loop. Overcoming the serial chain and the fading state in general, however, required an architecture capable of establishing direct, content-addressable links across arbitrary sequence positions without intervening recurrent steps: the attention mechanism (section 6.6).

Bengio, Yoshua, Patrice Simard, and Paolo Frasconi. 1994. “Learning Long-Term Dependencies with Gradient Descent Is Difficult.” IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks 5 (2): 157–66. https://doi.org/10.1109/72.279181.

Gu, Albert, and Tri Dao. 2023. “Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2312.00752.

Self-Check: Question

An RNN processes a sequence of length \(S = 1{,}000\) tokens with hidden state dimension \(d_{\text{hidden}} = 128\). Which statement correctly describes the scaling of its inference state memory versus its training activation memory?

Inference state memory is \(\mathcal{O}(d_{\text{hidden}})\) (constant \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) with respect to sequence length \(S\)), whereas training with backpropagation through time (BPTT) requires storing activations across all steps, scaling as \(\mathcal{O}(S \cdot d_{\text{hidden}})\) under ordinary retained-state BPTT.
Both inference state memory and training activation memory scale quadratically as \(\mathcal{O}(S^2)\) due to recurrent hidden-to-hidden weight matrices.
Inference state memory scales linearly as \(\mathcal{O}(S \cdot d_{\text{hidden}})\), while training memory is constant because weights are shared across all time steps.
Inference requires zero memory because recurrent states are discarded immediately after computing output probabilities.

Explain why upgrading an accelerator from 10 TFLOP/s to 100 TFLOP/s can reduce the elapsed time per recurrent step in an RNN processing a single long sequence, but cannot reduce the number of ordered state updates on the critical dependency chain. Contrast this with the parallel sequence processing capability of a transformer.
Because transformers offer superior parallelization and representational capacity for long-range dependencies, recurrent neural networks are entirely obsolete and have no valid deployment use cases in modern ML systems.
Order the mathematical and dataflow operations executed during a single time-step forward pass of a standard Elman RNN cell:


Multiply the previous hidden state vector \(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}\) by the recurrent weight matrix \(\mathbf{W}_{\text{hh}}\)
Multiply the current input vector \(\mathbf{x}_t\) by the input weight matrix \(\mathbf{W}_{\text{hx}}\)
Sum the recurrent contribution, input contribution, and hidden bias vector \(\mathbf{b}_h\)
Apply the nonlinear activation function (e.g., \(\tanh\)) to generate the new hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_t\)
Multiply the new hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_t\) by the output weight matrix \(\mathbf{W}_{\text{yh}}\) to produce output \(\mathbf{y}_t\)


During backpropagation through time (BPTT) over \(S\) time steps, the gradient of the loss with respect to the initial hidden state satisfies \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_0} \propto \prod_{t=1}^S \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_t}{\partial \mathbf{h}_{t-1}}\). Explain the mathematical mechanism that causes gradients to vanish or explode as \(S\) grows large.
In a standard RNN layer with input dimension \(d_{\text{in}} = 100\) and hidden state dimension \(d_{\text{hidden}} = 128\), how many total multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations are performed per sequence step to compute the unactivated hidden state?

12,800 MACs, because only the input projection performs matrix multiplication.
29,184 MACs, consisting of \(128 \times 128 = 16{,}384\text{ MACs}\) for the recurrent projection plus \(100 \times 128 = 12{,}800\text{ MACs}\) for the input projection.
1,280,000 MACs, because recurrence multiplies all hidden states across all past time steps simultaneously.
256 MACs, because an RNN updates only a single vector addition per step.
