Key Takeaways: Why training costs millions

Training cost is an iron-law budget: \(\TrainingTime= \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \times \EfficiencyHw}\) makes every optimization accountable: reduce work, raise effective throughput, or improve utilization. A change that misses the dominant term only moves cost around the training loop.
Memory determines whether a step fits: Standard mixed-precision Adam holds 16 bytes per parameter, 8× the FP16 inference weights, before activations. Optimizer state and batch-dependent activations, not weights alone, determine whether training fits.
Profiles choose the remedy: Profile, diagnose, fix, and re-profile. Compute-bound jobs need better arithmetic or algorithms; memory-bound jobs need less state or traffic; data- and communication-bound jobs need pipeline or parallelism changes.
Precision and IO-aware kernels shift bottlenecks: FP16 with FP32 accumulation can improve throughput and shrink activation memory (the static state is unchanged), while FlashAttention avoids materializing the full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) matrix in HBM; realized gains depend on workload and hardware.
Checkpointing trades recomputation for memory: The segment schedule counts retained boundaries and one live reconstructed segment, reducing GPT-2 XL’s batch-32 activations from 85.6 GB to 11.5 GB for about one-third more arithmetic. Use it when memory, not compute, binds.
Composed optimizations can postpone scale-out: Mixed precision, FlashAttention, and gradient accumulation turn GPT-2 XL’s 598 GB batch-32 step into a modeled 66.8 GB that fits one H100, for a run of about 35 days. Use relevant local levers before accepting distributed communication and operational overhead.



Training is where the iron law becomes a daily instrument. A profile read against the law names the dominant term, and the engineering task is to apply the least costly intervention that changes it before reaching for more hardware. The analysis took the model and training corpus as given, while changing how the system executed their work, including the extra arithmetic needed for recomputation. A further lever is which examples enter that workload in the first place.

What’s Next: From training to data selectionTraining produces learned parameters by spending compute on every example. Once the training loop is efficient, the next question is whether every example earns that cost. Repeated or low-information samples consume the same forward pass, backward pass, optimizer update, and communication as examples that add coverage or correct a weakness.
Data Selection therefore turns upstream from execution to workload composition, and in doing so opens the book’s optimization sequence, which asks whether work is necessary before asking how to simplify or accelerate it. It starts from a supply imbalance. Accelerator fleets can grow usable compute faster than the stock of high-quality data, so extracting more learning from each example begins to matter more than collecting more examples. Its measure is the information-compute ratio, the learning an example returns per unit of training compute, and redundancy, representativeness, uncertainty, and class coverage all enter through it. A useful subset must reduce work without erasing rare cases or shifting the effective training distribution. When that balance holds, a carefully selected subset can approach full-dataset accuracy while lowering the cost of every epoch and making additional experiments affordable. The optimization target is no longer only how efficiently the system processes an example, but which examples the system should process at all.

title: 8 Model Training
text:
Self-Check: Answer

A 7-billion-parameter model uses 14 GB of FP16 weights for inference and fits comfortably on a single 40 GB accelerator. Switching the same model to standard mixed-precision Adam training causes immediate out-of-memory failures even before activations are accounted for. Using the mixed-precision Adam accounting that the section previews, which factor is most directly responsible?

Adam internally re-runs the forward and backward passes, so the same weights must be stored several extra times during each step.
Adam adds 14 GB of FP16 gradients, 28 GB of FP32 master weights, and 56 GB of FP32 first- and second-moment state, pushing the static training state to about 112 GB before activations.
Adam requires the full training corpus to be cached in accelerator memory so batches can be reused across optimizer steps.
Adam forces all model tensors into FP64 during backpropagation, which multiplies the weight footprint beyond device capacity.

Answer: The correct answer is B. In the section’s standard mixed-precision Adam recipe, training state includes 14 GB of FP16 weights, 14 GB of FP16 gradients, 28 GB of FP32 master weights, and 56 GB of FP32 moment state, for about 112 GB before activations. The idea that Adam re-runs model passes confuses optimizer state with the forward/backward computation, and dataset caching is part of the input pipeline rather than resident model-training state on the accelerator.
Learning Objective: Calculate the static mixed-precision Adam training-state footprint from weights, gradients, master weights, and optimizer state.
True or False: Sudden NaN loss spikes during mixed-precision training are usually the same failure mode as an out-of-memory error, because both come from the GPU running out of memory during backpropagation.
Answer: False. An out-of-memory failure is a capacity problem that triggers an allocation error, while NaNs indicate numerical instability somewhere in the training computation. Mixed precision can contribute to numerical issues, but a NaN spike is not the same diagnosis as memory exhaustion.
Learning Objective: Distinguish memory-capacity failures from numerical-instability failures in mixed-precision training.
In machine learning frameworks, the technique of discarding selected intermediate forward activations and recomputing them on demand during the backward pass to reduce peak memory is known as activation ____.
Answer: The correct answer is checkpointing (also called gradient checkpointing or activation recomputation). Activation checkpointing allows training systems to trade additional computation for a substantially reduced activation memory footprint.
Learning Objective: Identify the systems term for trading backward recomputation against forward activation storage.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A training run has confirmed that input delivery and communication are off the critical path. The model FLOP count and the peak-throughput convention are being held fixed, yet profiling still reports only 38 percent effective end-to-end utilization relative to the stated peak. Under the training-time law \(T_{\text{train}} = \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \times \eta_{\text{hw}}}\), which lever is the most direct target for the next round of profiling?

Hardware utilization \(\eta_{\text{hw}}\), because with \(O\) and the relevant \(R_{\text{peak}}\) convention fixed, the remaining gap points to how efficiently kernels are being executed end to end.
Peak throughput \(R_{\text{peak}}\), because low effective end-to-end utilization relative to the stated peak automatically means the hardware peak specification is too small for the workload.
Total operations \(O\), because once data and communication are hidden, utilization is no longer relevant to training time.
Dataset size, because shrinking the number of tokens directly raises effective end-to-end utilization relative to the stated peak even when execution efficiency is unchanged.

Answer: The correct answer is A. In the current equation, \(O\) and the chosen \(R_{\text{peak}}\) convention are fixed, so 38 percent effective end-to-end utilization relative to the stated peak points to the effective utilization term \(\eta_{\text{hw}}\). That does not prove one unique cause, but it does justify profiling device execution for stalls, inefficient kernels, launch overhead, or other losses inside the end-to-end throughput term. Reducing \(O\) may shorten total training time, but it answers a different question than why this execution reaches only 38 percent of the chosen peak.
Learning Objective: Apply the training-time law to identify utilization as the immediate profiling target when workload size and peak-throughput convention are fixed.
When a team transitions a model from FP32 training to mixed-precision (FP16/BF16) on Tensor Core accelerators without changing the model architecture, batch size, or dataset, which term of the training-time law (\(T_{\text{train}} = \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \times \eta_{\text{hw}}}\)) is most directly improved?

Total operations \(O\), because lower numerical precision halves the number of multiplications required in each matrix multiplication.
Hardware utilization \(\eta_{\text{hw}}\), because mixed precision automatically eliminates all GPU pipeline bubbles and CPU data stalls.
Peak throughput \(R_{\text{peak}}\), because Tensor Cores provide a substantially higher theoretical FLOP/s ceiling for reduced-precision matrix operations compared to standard FP32 execution units.
Data volume \(D_{\text{tokens}}\), because lower precision requires fewer training tokens for the loss to converge.

Answer: The correct answer is C. The chapter’s optimization matching table assigns mixed precision (FP16/BF16) to peak throughput (\(R_{\text{peak}}\)). Tensor Cores execute reduced-precision matrix multiplications at several times the theoretical FLOP/s ceiling of FP32 ALUs. The claim regarding total operations \(O\) is incorrect because the algorithmic graph and number of multiply-accumulate operations remain identical. The utilization claim is incorrect because \(\eta_{\text{hw}}\) measures efficiency relative to the available peak, and precision changes do not inherently eliminate data loader bubbles. The data volume claim is false because precision does not reduce sample requirements.
Learning Objective: Classify mixed-precision training by its direct target term (\(R_{\text{peak}}\)) in the training-time law.
Explain the scope conditions under which the simplified training-time law \(T_{\text{train}} = \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \times \eta_{\text{hw}}}\) is useful, and identify why the formula alone cannot diagnose a slow small-batch debugging run.
Answer: The equation is useful as an accounting identity: it relates total work, a chosen peak-throughput reference, and effective achieved throughput into one training-time estimate. But because the end-to-end utilization term can already include stalls from launches, transfers, synchronization, and underfilled kernels, the formula alone does not reveal which mechanism caused a slow run. In a small-batch debug session, the problem is not that the law becomes invalid; it is that a low measured utilization could come from many overheads, so diagnosis still requires profiling rather than reading the formula by itself.
Learning Objective: Explain what the simplified training-time law captures and why it does not by itself localize the cause of low-throughput execution.
True or False: All large deep learning models are primarily compute-bound, so training speed is always governed mainly by Tensor Core TFLOP/s.
Answer: False. Dense transformer training often spends much of its work in matrix multiplications, but other workloads can be limited by memory capacity or bandwidth instead. The section’s DLRM example is dominated by large embedding tables, where fitting and moving the state can matter more than raw dense-math throughput.
Learning Objective: Distinguish compute-bound dense training from regimes where memory capacity or bandwidth is the binding constraint.
Place the following milestones in chronological order, reflecting how training-system constraints evolved: (1) Transformers shift sequence modeling toward high-throughput dense matrix multiplication and large activation footprints. (2) Backpropagation is popularized for multilayer neural networks. (3) Large-scale foundation models such as GPT-3 make utilization and multi-accelerator scaling central engineering concerns. (4) AlexNet demonstrates that deep neural network training maps effectively to GPUs. (5) IO-aware FlashAttention appears as a response to attention memory-bandwidth limits.
Answer: The correct order is: (2) Backpropagation is popularized for multilayer neural networks, (4) AlexNet demonstrates that deep neural network training maps effectively to GPUs, (1) Transformers shift sequence modeling toward high-throughput dense matrix multiplication and large activation footprints, (3) Large-scale foundation models such as GPT-3 make utilization and multi-accelerator scaling central engineering concerns, (5) IO-aware FlashAttention appears as a response to attention memory-bandwidth limits. This sequence matters because each later systems response addresses a constraint exposed by the earlier stage: GPU acceleration follows practical deep learning, transformers amplify activation and attention costs, frontier-scale models make utilization and scaling decisive, and FlashAttention targets the resulting IO bottleneck in attention.
Learning Objective: Trace the historical sequence linking major training-system milestones to the constraints they exposed.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why do batched matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMM, BLAS Level 3) usually achieve much higher accelerator utilization in neural network training than matrix-vector operations (GEMV, BLAS Level 2)?

Matrix-matrix operations avoid gradient computation during backpropagation, so they save both memory traffic and arithmetic work.
Under the ideal traffic model in the section, GEMM reuses loaded operands across many outputs, so arithmetic intensity can grow with matrix size, whereas GEMV offers much less reuse and tends to stay near constant arithmetic intensity.
Matrix-vector operations cannot run efficiently on GPUs because every layer result must be synchronized back to the CPU before the next layer starts.
Batched matrix-matrix operations reduce the model’s parameter count, which is why they keep more of the network in HBM.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Under the section’s idealized traffic analysis, GEMM performs many more FLOPs per byte moved because tiles of weights and activations are reused across multiple outputs, so its arithmetic intensity can scale upward with problem size. GEMV offers far less reuse, so moving bytes can dominate execution. The claim that GEMM avoids gradients is wrong because training uses matrix multiplies heavily in backward as well as forward, and the CPU-synchronization explanation confuses low arithmetic intensity with an unsupported execution model.
Learning Objective: Compare GEMM and GEMV using arithmetic intensity and operand reuse in the accelerator memory hierarchy.
A team trains a 7-billion-parameter model on accelerators with 80 GB of HBM each. Weights, gradients, activations, and common workspaces already occupy 64 GB per accelerator, and this total already includes any FP32 master weights if the recipe uses them. The model is unsharded per device. Using the section’s optimizer-memory accounting, explain the systems trade-off between choosing plain SGD and Adam for this run.
Answer: Adam adds two FP32 moment tensors, or 8 bytes per parameter, so a 7B-parameter model needs about 56 GB more optimizer state. That pushes the per-device total from 64 GB to about 120 GB, which exceeds an 80 GB accelerator before any sharding decision is considered, whereas plain SGD adds no auxiliary optimizer state and still fits at 64 GB. The practical consequence is that this choice is first a capacity question; once a feasible optimizer is chosen, the team should then measure time to target quality rather than assume one optimizer will always converge faster.
Learning Objective: Calculate whether SGD or Adam fits within a fixed HBM budget when common training state is already accounted for.
The point on a roofline model curve where the memory-bandwidth-bound diagonal ceiling intersects the flat peak-compute ceiling, defined mathematically as \(\text{Peak FLOP/s} / \text{Memory Bandwidth}\), is known as the ____ point.
Answer: The correct answer is ridge (or roofline ridge). The ridge point represents the minimum arithmetic intensity required for an operation to reach the accelerator’s maximum computational throughput.
Learning Objective: Identify the definition and significance of the ridge point in roofline model analysis.
**Order the following events in a standard backpropagation training step to reflect their strict causal and data dependencies:


Compute scalar objective loss by evaluating predictions against ground-truth labels.
Update model parameters using gradient-based optimization rules (such as Adam or SGD).
Execute forward propagation through successive layers while caching intermediate activations.
Evaluate the chain rule backward from the loss through layers to compute parameter and activation gradients.
Fetch and preprocess the training mini-batch on the host and transfer it to device memory.**

Answer: The correct answer is 5, 3, 1, 4, 2: (5) Fetch and preprocess the training mini-batch on the host and transfer it to device memory. (3) Execute forward propagation through successive layers while caching intermediate activations. (1) Compute scalar objective loss by evaluating predictions against ground-truth labels. (4) Evaluate the chain rule backward from the loss through layers to compute parameter and activation gradients. (2) Update model parameters using gradient-based optimization rules.
Learning Objective: Order the operations of a training iteration based on their mathematical and data dependencies.

For a transformer with hidden dimension \(d_{\text{model}} = 768\) and 12 heads (\(d_{\text{head}} = 64\)), the section’s restricted accounting gives the materialized attention-score computation an arithmetic intensity of about \(d_{\text{head}}/2 = 32\text{ FLOP/byte}\). If the target accelerator is the reference H100, whose ridge point is about \(295\text{ FLOP/byte}\), what does that imply and what optimization direction best matches the section?

The kernel is compute-bound, so increasing peak TFLOP/s is the main expected lever under this model.
The kernel is latency-bound, so shrinking the batch is the main way to move it onto the compute roof.
The kernel is network-bound, so the right first response is a faster inter-node AllReduce fabric.
The kernel falls on the memory-bandwidth side of the roofline under this accounting, so reducing materialized score traffic through IO-aware tiling is the appropriate optimization direction.

Answer: The correct answer is D. With an estimated intensity of \(32\text{ FLOP/byte}\) against the H100’s ridge point of about \(295\text{ FLOP/byte}\), the roofline classifies this implementation as memory-bandwidth-limited under the stated traffic model. That does not prove a measured kernel already saturates bandwidth or that hardware upgrades can never help, but it does indicate that reducing score-matrix traffic is the matching optimization direction. The network answer is irrelevant because this is a local attention-kernel analysis, and shrinking batch size does not address the materialized-attention IO term the section highlights.
Learning Objective: Use ridge-point comparison to classify an attention implementation and select the matching traffic-reduction optimization direction.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Which set of subsystems defines the chapter’s high-level training system architecture, and what systems engineering advantage does this decomposition provide?

Storage controller, compiler intermediate representation, and runtime execution engine; this separates hardware target code generation from storage layout.
Data pipeline, training loop, and evaluation pipeline; this separates distinct resource profiles (CPU/storage I/O, accelerator compute/memory, and periodic validation) so bottlenecks can be isolated at subsystem interfaces.
Tokenizer, hyperparameter optimizer, and model registry; this organizes the model deployment lifecycle around developer interfaces.
Gradient aggregator, parameter server, and checkpoint restorer; this decomposes cloud service microservices.

Answer: The correct answer is B. The training architecture decomposes the system into three interconnected subsystems: the data pipeline (ingestion, transformation, batching), the training loop (forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimizer update), and the evaluation pipeline (validation metrics on held-out data). This separation enables engineers to diagnose bottlenecks by subsystem resource demands (host CPU/disk for data, accelerator compute/HBM for training loop, and periodic synchronization pauses for evaluation). The storage controller and compiler option describes compiler infrastructure rather than runtime training systems. The tokenizer and registry option describes MLOps lifecycle tools. The gradient aggregator option lists distributed implementation components rather than end-to-end training subsystems.
Learning Objective: Identify the three major subsystems of a training pipeline architecture and explain the systems rationale for this decomposition.
In a profiled training pipeline, CPU data preprocessing sustains \(4\text{ GB/s}\) on the same logical batch representation that host-to-device transfer and GPU consumption are being compared against. Host-to-device PCIe transfer sustains \(32\text{ GB/s}\), and GPU compute consumes data at an equivalent rate of \(12\text{ GB/s}\). Under the section’s ideal-overlap pipeline model, what determines end-to-end throughput, and what is the best first engineering action?

The average of the three rates, so the effective throughput is \(16\text{ GB/s}\) and all stages should be tuned evenly.
The PCIe transfer rate, because every batch must cross the bus before any compute can happen.
The minimum rate, \(4\text{ GB/s}\) from preprocessing, so the first action is to reduce the input-side bottleneck before tuning faster stages.
The GPU compute rate, because training pipelines are ultimately limited by accelerator execution speed rather than host stages.

Answer: The correct answer is C. In the section’s pipeline model, comparable stage rates are combined through a minimum: the slowest stage caps throughput even if transfer and compute are faster. Here preprocessing at \(4\text{ GB/s}\) is the binding constraint, so the first goal is to raise input-side service rate and remove that bottleneck. An answer based on averaging ignores how pipelines work, and upgrading a non-binding PCIe or compute stage does not change a system still waiting on preprocessing.
Learning Objective: Apply the pipeline bottleneck model to identify the slowest comparable stage as the limit on end-to-end throughput.
Explain why CPU-side tokenization and data augmentation can severely bottleneck GPU training even when the resulting tensor transfer across PCIe takes less than one millisecond.
Answer: A fast PCIe copy only shows that the transfer stage is short once a batch already exists; it says nothing about how long the CPU needed to create that batch. If CPU preprocessing takes 65 ms and GPU compute takes 80 ms, then with proper overlap the next batch can still be ready in time, but without overlap or with an unstable host service interval the GPU can see bubbles despite the sub-millisecond transfer. The practical consequence is that busy-time fractions alone are not peak arithmetic efficiency and do not prove a specific worker count; what matters is whether preprocessing can consistently supply the next batch before compute needs it.
Learning Objective: Analyze why preprocessing latency can dominate input delivery even when the PCIe transfer itself is short.
True or False: Scaling the training batch size by \(8\times\) while keeping the learning rate and schedule unchanged guarantees the same model quality in less wall-clock time.
Answer: False. A larger batch changes both the number of updates per epoch and the gradient statistics seen by the optimizer, so the old learning-rate schedule may no longer be appropriate. The section says validation is needed after a large batch-size change, and retuning may be needed rather than guaranteed.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why changing batch size can alter optimization behavior even when hardware throughput improves.
To enable fast, asynchronous Direct Memory Access (DMA) transfers from host RAM to GPU memory without intermediate CPU staging copies, host memory buffers must be allocated as page-locked or ____ memory.
Answer: The correct answer is pinned (or page-locked). Pinned memory prevents the operating system from paging memory to disk, enabling the GPU DMA controller to read tensors asynchronously concurrently with compute.
Learning Objective: Identify the systems mechanism (pinned memory) used for asynchronous host-to-device transfers.
In the chapter’s staged system pipeline framework, what constitutes an “accelerator bubble” and what is the primary diagnostic step to resolve it?

An intentional synchronization barrier inserted by automatic differentiation to ensure memory coherence across gradient passes; resolved by disabling graph checks.
An on-chip SRAM cache eviction event caused by large transformer sequence lengths; resolved by switching to smaller embedding tables.
A loss of arithmetic intensity when batch sizes fall below the hardware ridge point; resolved by forcing FP64 accumulation.
Silicon idleness where accelerator ALUs wait for data loading, host-to-device PCIe transfer, or parameter synchronization; resolved by profiling the four pipeline stages to identify and overlap the slowest stage.

Answer: The correct answer is D. An accelerator bubble is defined as idle or underutilized accelerator time resulting from a throughput mismatch across the four pipeline stages (Data Loading & Preprocessing, Host-to-Device Transfer, Forward/Backward Compute, and Parameter Synchronization). Resolving bubbles requires profiling each stage to locate the binding constraint and applying overlapping techniques such as asynchronous prefetching. The assertion of intentional synchronization misinterprets a performance inefficiency as a design feature. The SRAM cache eviction option confuses low-level cache misses with macro pipeline stalls. The ridge-point loss option misapplies roofline terminology to pipeline-level time allocation.
Learning Objective: Explain the systems definition of accelerator bubbles across the four pipeline stages and identify the diagnostic procedure to eliminate them.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why is Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) a more reliable metric than raw GPU busy percentage (reported by tools like nvidia-smi) when evaluating training systems efficiency?

MFU is measured directly from host CPU clock cycles, eliminating GPU driver instrumentation overhead.
MFU is mathematically fixed to 100% on any healthy accelerator cluster regardless of software overhead.
MFU counts only the theoretical forward and backward FLOPs required by the model architecture divided by the product of peak hardware throughput and measured step time, whereas raw GPU busy percentage also counts time spent on recomputation, padding, and memory stalls outside that model-FLOP numerator.
MFU measures training loss convergence speed per dollar rather than floating-point operations.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Raw GPU utilization measures the percentage of time GPU execution units or kernels are active. A GPU can show 95% utilization while spending half its time stalling on memory bandwidth or recomputing activations during gradient checkpointing. In contrast, MFU (\(\text{MFU} = \frac{O_{\text{model}}}{R_{\text{peak}} \times T_{\text{step}}}\)) includes only the useful forward and backward model FLOPs in the numerator, explicitly penalizing recomputation, padding FLOPs, memory stalls, and pipeline bubbles. MFU is an accelerator metric, not a CPU metric. MFU is not fixed to 100%; reported values depend on workload, hardware, precision, and the FLOP-counting convention. MFU measures hardware efficiency, not loss convergence per dollar.
Learning Objective: Differentiate Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) from raw GPU busy utilization and explain which overheads MFU exposes.
An engineer profiles two training workloads. Workload A shows 92 percent GPU busy time, near-saturated HBM bandwidth, low CPU activity, and continuous kernel timelines. Workload B shows 20 percent GPU busy time with regular 50 ms idle gaps, low HBM bandwidth, and 100 percent CPU utilization. Apply the D·A·M taxonomy to classify each workload’s likely bottleneck and state the next optimization category for each.
Answer: Workload A supports a bandwidth-bound hypothesis on the Machine side: kernels are running continuously and HBM is heavily used, so the next step is to confirm that critical kernels are limited by memory traffic and then target traffic reduction or fusion. Workload B is consistent with a Data-side bottleneck only if the GPU gaps correlate with batch preparation rather than host dispatch or synchronization, so the next step is stage correlation and then input-pipeline optimization if starvation is confirmed. The practical consequence is that D·A·M categories are diagnostic guides, not exclusive labels you can assign from one metric alone.
Learning Objective: Apply D·A·M reasoning to profile signatures while distinguishing likely bottlenecks from confirmed diagnoses.
**Order the steps of the systematic training optimization workflow recommended in the chapter:


Classify the primary performance constraint (Data-, Memory-, or Compute-bound) using the D·A·M taxonomy.
Run a representative training run with framework and system profilers enabled to capture CPU, PCIe, and GPU timeline traces.
Re-profile the system to evaluate MFU improvement and identify whether the bottleneck has shifted to a new pipeline stage.
Apply a targeted optimization technique specifically addressing the identified binding constraint.**

Answer: The correct answer is 2, 1, 4, 3: (2) Run a representative training run with framework and system profilers enabled to capture CPU, PCIe, and GPU timeline traces. (1) Classify the primary performance constraint (Data-, Memory-, or Compute-bound) using the D·A·M taxonomy. (4) Apply a targeted optimization technique specifically addressing the identified binding constraint. (3) Re-profile the system to evaluate MFU improvement and identify whether the bottleneck has shifted to a new pipeline stage.
Learning Objective: Order the systematic profile-diagnose-fix-reprofile optimization cycle.

An engineering team suspects that an individual custom LayerNorm kernel has poor arithmetic intensity and low register occupancy, while another team suspects their DataLoader is causing host-to-device PCIe transfer stalls. Which combination of profiling tool classes from the chapter is best suited to investigate each respective issue?

A kernel-level GPU profiler with per-kernel counters for the arithmetic intensity and occupancy analysis; a framework-level or system-level timeline profiler for the DataLoader and PCIe transfers.
nvidia-smi for kernel-level arithmetic intensity; TensorBoard loss curves for DataLoader PCIe transfer stalls.
NVIDIA Nsight Compute for cluster-wide inter-node network bandwidth; PyTorch Profiler for register allocation analysis.
Linux top command for GPU kernel instruction analysis; NVIDIA Nsight Systems for CPU register spill tracking.

Answer: The correct answer is A. The chapter distinguishes two classes of profilers. Kernel-level GPU profilers record per-kernel counters such as achieved memory throughput and arithmetic-unit occupancy, making them right for the custom LayerNorm kernel. Framework-level and system-level timeline profilers (for example PyTorch Profiler or NVIDIA Nsight Systems) record timeline traces capturing CPU thread execution, CUDA API dispatches, PCIe memory copies, and GPU stream synchronization, making them ideal for diagnosing DataLoader and PCIe stalls. nvidia-smi provides coarse device-wide polling rather than kernel-level roofline analysis. Linux top monitors host OS processes, not GPU internal instruction pipelines.
Learning Objective: Select the appropriate class of profiler (kernel-level counters versus timeline traces) based on the granularity of the performance investigation.
A team’s profiler shows the GPU at 18 percent utilization with periodic drops to zero, while one CPU core is pinned near 100 percent and the PCIe link is mostly idle. Using the section’s staged-pipeline framework, explain how to diagnose the bubble’s source and what fix should be targeted.
Answer: This pattern suggests the input side of the staged pipeline may be starving the accelerator, because the GPU has bubbles while host work is active and PCIe is not the limiting stage. To confirm the source, correlate the GPU idle gaps with batch-preparation time versus host dispatch or synchronization delays; if the gaps line up with preprocessing, then the right fix is input-pipeline work such as additional workers or prefetching. The practical implication is that high CPU usage alone is not enough to blame tokenization or the GIL with certainty—the stage correlation must come first.
Learning Objective: Analyze staged-pipeline signals to distinguish likely input starvation from other host-side causes of accelerator bubbles.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

For each batch, a training step has three dependent stages in a serial baseline: data preprocessing (\(T_{\text{prep}} = 30\text{ ms}\)), host-to-device transfer (\(T_{\text{xfer}} = 10\text{ ms}\)), and GPU compute (\(T_{\text{comp}} = 50\text{ ms}\)). Different batches can occupy independent resources and overlap with correct handoff. If the team implements steady-state overlapping with prefetching and double buffering, what iteration interval is theoretically possible after fill and before drain?

\(40\text{ ms}\), because preprocessing and transfer replace compute once overlap is enabled.
\(50\text{ ms}\), because in ideal steady state the interval is bounded by the slowest overlapped stage rather than the serial sum.
\(10\text{ ms}\), because all stages run concurrently and the fastest one sets the pace.
\(90\text{ ms}\), because DMA transfers cannot overlap useful GPU computation.

Answer: The correct answer is B. The serial baseline takes \(30 + 10 + 50 = 90\text{ ms}\) per batch, but ideal steady-state overlap changes the limiting interval to \(\max(30, 10, 50) = 50\text{ ms}\). That is a throughput improvement to \(90/50 = 1.8\times\), not a promise that the latency of one isolated batch falls to 50 ms from startup. The \(10\text{ ms}\) answer uses the fastest stage instead of the slowest, and the no-overlap answer ignores the purpose of prefetching and copy/compute concurrency.
Learning Objective: Calculate the steady-state throughput interval of an overlapped training pipeline from its stage times.
Explain how FlashAttention computes exact self-attention with substantially lower memory footprint than standard attention, and describe what its backward pass does instead of reading a full stored score matrix from HBM.
Answer: FlashAttention keeps the same attention mathematics, with possible floating-point rounding differences, but changes where intermediate work lives: it processes query, key, and value tiles in on-chip SRAM and maintains the softmax statistics online instead of materializing the full \(S \times S\) score matrix in HBM. That cuts saved activation storage and reduces off-chip traffic tied to those score blocks rather than implying a linear law for all HBM IO. In backward, it recomputes the needed tiled score and probability blocks from saved inputs and normalization statistics rather than loading a full stored score matrix, so the systems gain comes from less HBM traffic, not from changing the attention mathematics.
Learning Objective: Explain how IO-aware tiling and backward recomputation reduce attention memory traffic without changing attention mathematics.
Why does the chapter’s conventional FP16 mixed-precision recipe keep FP32 master weights and perform selected reductions in FP32 instead of forcing every part of training into 16-bit precision?

Tensor Cores cannot execute backpropagation unless gradients are stored in FP64.
FP16 allocations can lock the accelerator memory bus unless the master weights are moved to host RAM.
Automatic differentiation requires symbolic derivatives to be represented only in FP32.
Very small parameter updates can be rounded away when applied directly to FP16 weights, and selected reductions benefit from the wider range or precision of FP32 accumulation.

Answer: The correct answer is D. The section’s FP16 recipe keeps FP32 master weights because an update can be too small to change a stored FP16 weight after rounding even when the update itself is representable; preserving the update in FP32 avoids losing it across many steps. The same section also notes that selected reductions are often kept in FP32 because wider accumulation improves numerical behavior, though it does not guarantee stability everywhere. The FP64 and host-RAM claims invent hardware requirements the chapter does not make, and autodiff does not require a purely FP32 graph representation.
Learning Objective: Justify FP32 master weights and selected FP32 reductions in the conventional FP16 mixed-precision training recipe.
Gradient accumulation increases the memory footprint on the accelerator linearly with the accumulation factor \(K\) because all \(K\) micro-batches’ intermediate activations must remain in GPU memory simultaneously until the optimizer step.
Answer: False. Gradient accumulation executes forward and backward passes sequentially across \(K\) micro-batches, accumulating (summing) only the parameter gradients in a single fixed-size gradient buffer. Saved backward tensors for each micro-batch can be released after its backward pass when the graph is not retained; other references or cached tensors may extend storage lifetime. Consequently, activation memory is bounded by the size of a single micro-batch (\(B_{\text{micro}}\)), allowing systems to emulate an effective batch size of \(K \times B_{\text{micro}}\) without increasing activation memory.
Learning Objective: Analyze the memory behavior of gradient accumulation across multiple micro-batches.
In FP16 mixed-precision training, the loss is multiplied before backpropagation so the resulting gradients are shifted into a safer numeric range, then divided back down before the optimizer update. This technique is known as loss ____.
Answer: scaling. Loss scaling multiplies the loss before backward so the resulting gradients are less likely to underflow in FP16, then unscales them before the optimizer step.
Learning Objective: Identify loss scaling as the technique used to reduce FP16 gradient underflow risk.
A team enables mixed precision on a transformer model and observes compute time drop by 45 percent, but total step time decreases by only 10 percent because the GPU now shows large idle gaps. Explain what likely happened in the system pipeline and what the team should do next.
Answer: The compute optimization removed part of the old critical path, but the new timeline shows that another stage is now exposed because the GPU is spending meaningful time idle. Those gaps are not proof of a data-loader problem by themselves: they could come from input waits, dispatch overhead, synchronization, or another serial stage. The right next step is to re-profile and correlate the gaps with pipeline stages so the next optimization targets the newly binding bottleneck rather than assuming mixed precision failed.
Learning Objective: Explain why speeding up compute can expose a different bottleneck and why re-profiling is required before choosing the next optimization.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A team trains a 1.5-billion-parameter model that already fits on one 80 GB GPU with batch size 16 and its Adam training state, but one epoch still takes 12 days. The team has an 8-GPU node available. Which strategy is the best first baseline, and why?

Tensor parallelism, because splitting every weight matrix across the 8 GPUs is always the fastest way to improve training throughput.
Pipeline parallelism, because dividing layers across devices is the default first step whenever a model is a transformer.
Data parallelism such as DDP, because the model already fits per device and replication avoids unnecessary pipeline bubbles or intra-layer communication as the initial throughput baseline.
Full parameter sharding first, because any multi-GPU run should avoid keeping complete replicas even when memory is sufficient.

Answer: The correct answer is C. When the full model and training state already fit on one device, data parallelism is the natural first baseline because each GPU can run the local forward and backward pass without introducing the extra sequential dependencies of pipeline parallelism or the frequent collectives of tensor partitioning. An answer based on splitting layers or tensors solves a memory problem the scenario does not currently have. Sharding may still become useful later, but it is not the first throughput baseline when replication already fits.
Learning Objective: Select data parallelism as the first multi-GPU baseline when memory already fits on each device and the main goal is throughput.
In distributed data parallel training with \(N\) GPUs and a model with \(P\) parameters whose gradients use \(B_{\text{bytes}}\) bytes each, what is the number of bytes sent by each GPU during a Ring AllReduce?

\(2 \times \frac{N-1}{N} \times P \times B_{\text{bytes}}\), which approaches \(2 P B_{\text{bytes}}\) as \(N\) grows.
\(N \times P \times B_{\text{bytes}}\), because each GPU must broadcast the full gradient to every other GPU.
\(\frac{P \times B_{\text{bytes}}}{N^2}\), because the ring divides both the model and the communication quadratically.
Zero, because GPU replicas synchronize through shared CPU memory rather than explicit data movement.

Answer: The correct answer is A. In a ring AllReduce, each GPU participates in a scatter-reduce phase and an all-gather phase, and the bytes sent per GPU total \(2 \times \frac{N-1}{N} \times P \times B_{\text{bytes}}\). That expression tends toward \(2 P B_{\text{bytes}}\) as \(N\) becomes large, so the per-GPU sent volume stays bounded rather than growing linearly with the cluster size. The broadcast-style answer describes a different and less efficient mental model of synchronization.
Learning Objective: Calculate the per-GPU bytes sent in Ring AllReduce and interpret its scaling with device count.
Explain what communication overhead is in distributed training, and analyze why adding more GPUs can lead to diminishing throughput returns.
Answer: Communication overhead is the time spent synchronizing gradients or exchanging partitioned activations and tensors instead of doing local model computation. As more GPUs are added, ideal compute work per device can fall, but communication latency, transfer volume, and incomplete overlap do not disappear, so synchronization becomes a larger fraction of each step. The practical consequence is that scaling efficiency drops once communication and coordination consume enough of the step that extra devices save less compute time than they add in communication cost.
Learning Objective: Analyze how communication overhead limits scaling efficiency as distributed training spans more accelerators.
In pipeline model parallelism, partitioning a network linearly across \(K\) stages without micro-batching (naive pipeline parallelism) achieves 100 percent GPU utilization because downstream devices can compute backward gradients while upstream devices run forward passes.
Answer: False. In naive pipeline parallelism without micro-batching, downstream devices must wait idle until upstream devices complete their forward passes, and upstream devices must wait idle until downstream devices compute backward loss gradients. This introduces massive idle pipeline bubbles where device utilization collapses to \(\approx 1/K\). Practical pipeline parallelism systems (like GPipe and 1F1B in PipeDream) mitigate this by splitting batches into multiple small micro-batches and interleaving forward and backward passes to fill the pipeline.
Learning Objective: Identify the pipeline bubble pathology of naive pipeline parallelism and explain how micro-batch schedules mitigate it.
Arrange the following engineering steps in the chapter’s preferred order for deciding whether to scale beyond one device, assuming the initial bounds do not already prove that single-device training is infeasible: (1) Re-evaluate whether memory or time limits still justify scaling. (2) Add distributed parallelism or sharding if the remaining limit still requires it. (3) Establish a single-device baseline and quantify the current bottleneck. (4) Apply relevant local optimizations such as mixed precision, prefetching, checkpointing, or accumulation.
Answer: The correct order is: (3) Establish a single-device baseline and quantify the current bottleneck, (4) Apply relevant local optimizations such as mixed precision, prefetching, checkpointing, or accumulation, (1) Re-evaluate whether memory or time limits still justify scaling, (2) Add distributed parallelism or sharding if the remaining limit still requires it. This order matters because the chapter’s scaling discipline uses baseline measurement first, then local fixes targeted to the observed constraint, then a new decision about whether a hard limit remains. Jumping straight to distributed scaling can add communication and operational complexity before the single-device bottleneck is even understood.
Learning Objective: Sequence the chapter’s single-machine-first process for deciding when distributed scaling is actually justified.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A team scales a dense model from 7 billion to 20 billion parameters while keeping the same training-token budget, precision recipe, and optimizer structure. Under the chapter’s fallacies discussion, what is the most defensible conclusion?

Validation accuracy must improve in proportion to parameter count because the larger model can represent more functions.
The run will necessarily move to CPU execution because 20B parameters cannot be trained on accelerators.
The larger model guarantees worse accuracy because fixed-token training always causes catastrophic interference at higher parameter counts.
The training-state and compute budgets rise substantially under the same dense-model accounting, but model quality is not guaranteed to improve because it still depends on data, optimization, and evaluation.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Under the chapter’s dense-model accounting with fixed precision and optimizer assumptions, a larger parameter count clearly raises memory and leading FLOP requirements, so systems cost goes up in a predictable direction. But the scientific outcome is not guaranteed: keeping the same token budget does not prove either improvement or collapse in validation quality. The “must improve” answer mistakes model size for a universal quality guarantee, while the CPU answer invents a hardware consequence the chapter does not state.
Learning Objective: Distinguish the predictable systems costs of scaling parameter count from the uncertain effect on final model quality.
Explain why directly transferring hyperparameters such as learning rate and weight decay from a batch-size 512 baseline to a batch-size 4,096 distributed run can cause training to underperform, even when raw GPU busy time stays above 90 percent.
Answer: An eightfold batch increase means eight times fewer parameter updates per fixed epoch, and it also changes the gradient statistics seen by the optimizer, so the old hyperparameters no longer operate in the same regime. High GPU busy time only shows that hardware is active; it does not prove that the optimizer is making equally effective progress per unit data. The practical response is to validate the learning-rate schedule, warmup, and target quality metric on the larger-batch run instead of assuming the small-batch recipe transfers unchanged.
Learning Objective: Explain why batch-size scaling can invalidate a previously successful optimization recipe even when hardware utilization looks strong.
Which engineering mistake exemplifies the input-pipeline pitfall described in the chapter’s fallacies and pitfalls?

Using BF16 mixed precision instead of FP16 on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs.
Spending weeks hand-tuning custom CUDA attention kernels to achieve 95% peak arithmetic throughput, only to discover in production that the GPU sits idle 50% of the time waiting for single-threaded Python CPU tokenization.
Setting pin_memory=True and num_workers=8 in a PyTorch DataLoader.
Checkpointing activations every \(\sqrt{N_L}\) layers to reduce peak memory.

Answer: The correct answer is B. The chapter’s pitfall of optimizing kernels before profiling the input pipeline occurs when engineers focus exclusively on accelerator-side compute optimizations (such as custom CUDA kernels, mixed precision, or Tensor Core utilization) while neglecting end-to-end profiling. If the upstream data pipeline (CPU tokenization, disk I/O, or augmentation) is bottlenecked, the GPU will starve, rendering kernel-level speedups useless at the system level. BF16, DataLoader worker and pinned-memory settings, and checkpointing are candidate interventions whose value depends on the diagnosed constraint and validation results.
Learning Objective: Recognize optimizing kernels before profiling the input pipeline as a major operational pitfall in training optimization.
A team proposes moving a single-GPU training job to a 16-GPU cluster to achieve a \(16\times\) reduction in development cycle time. Explain two reasons why distributed training rarely delivers a linear \(16\times\) improvement in developer velocity.
Answer: First, distributed execution adds communication and synchronization overhead, so throughput rarely scales linearly with GPU count even when the code is correct. Second, developer velocity depends on more than throughput: distributed jobs bring extra debugging, launch, checkpointing, and failure-handling overhead that can delay iteration even if step time improves. The practical consequence is that cluster scaling should be justified by measured end-to-end iteration gains, not by hardware count alone.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why communication overhead and operational complexity both limit the developer-velocity gains of distributed training.

← Back to Questions

title: 9 Data Selection
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Architecture stack focus for this chapter.
How can a carefully selected subset retain most of the value of a much larger dataset?
Training pays to acquire, label, score, move, and process examples even though their learning value differs. Large datasets contain redundant, noisy, or target-misaligned samples, while scarce regions may lack the cases a model needs, such as the rare conditions under which a deployed system is most likely to fail. Training on every example treats a near-duplicate and a rare failure case as equally worth paying for, and at scale much of the compute budget can go to relearning what the model already knows. That heterogeneity turns the choice of examples into a systems optimization rather than a data-cleaning chore. The objective is therefore not the smallest dataset but the lowest end-to-end cost of reaching target quality without losing rare cases, underrepresented groups, or deployment-relevant coverage. Every strategy adds its own overhead: examples must be scored, generated, shuffled, stored, or validated, and those costs can erase the savings they promise. That judgment must be made end to end, because gains in labeling or training can be erased by selection latency, storage access, or distributed coordination. A method is worth applying only when the learning it preserves or creates exceeds the work required to apply it. This distinction matters across repeated experiments, where useful reductions compound, and across adaptation, where the value of an example changes with the model and target distribution. In D·A·M terms, it is data-algorithm co-design: shape the training signal so each unit of machine work yields more useful learning.

Learning Objectives

Explain data selection as data-algorithm co-design that controls sample value, training work, and labeling cost
Calculate the information-compute ratio and apply the compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter check to diagnose a data-starved run
Apply the selection inequality to test whether selection overhead beats full-dataset training cost
Compare deduplication, coreset selection, and quality pruning for reducing redundant pretraining data
Design curriculum, active learning, synthetic-data, or label-free strategies for changing data value during training
Evaluate whether a selection pipeline keeps the accelerator fed under storage locality, data echoing, and multi-accelerator consistency constraints
Select data-selection investments using return on investment, break-even, and amortization analysis



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



Every example a training run processes costs the same forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer update, whether it teaches the model something new or repeats what the model already knows. A duplicated image, a mislabeled record, and a rare boundary case cost the same arithmetic while contributing very different learning signals. Model Training made each of those steps as cheap as one machine allows and accounted for a whole run as roughly \(6\Parameters\DatasetSize\) floating-point operations for \(\Parameters\) parameters and \(\DatasetSize\) tokens. Once each step is cheap, the next saving lies upstream, in choosing which examples deserve a step at all. This waste becomes acute at the data wall, the point at which the compute available for training grows faster than the supply of novel, high-quality examples to spend it on.1
1 Data wall: Unlike compute (which scales with capital expenditure) or algorithms (which improve through research), the stock of high-quality human-generated text grows slowly; Epoch AI’s updated projections estimated that, under the paper’s modeled consumption assumptions, models could use datasets roughly equal in size to the stock of public human-generated text between 2026 and 2032 (Villalobos et al. 2024). The point for systems design is not a fixed calendar deadline; it is that data can become a supply constraint rather than merely an economic one. The wall does not change how many operations \((\Operations)\) a run performs. It lowers the learning each of those operations yields, because once quality data runs short, additional compute spent on repeated or weaker data yields diminishing accuracy regardless of hardware throughput.
Villalobos, Pablo, Anson Ho, Jaime Sevilla, Tamay Besiroglu, Lennart Heim, and Marius Hobbhahn. 2024. “Position: Will We Run Out of Data? Limits of LLM Scaling Based on Human-Generated Data.” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 235: 49523–44.


Compute outruns high-quality data supply; the widening gap is the data wall.
2 Scaling laws: Jared Kaplan and colleagues at Johns Hopkins and OpenAI empirically demonstrated in 2020 that language model loss follows power-law relationships with model size, dataset size, and compute budget over the regimes they studied (Kaplan et al. 2020). Their fitted data exponent was approximately \(\Glyph{\alpha} = 0.095\) in \(\LossFunction \propto \DataScalingLossFactor\). The value is not universal, but the diminishing-return shape makes it possible to reason about when selection becomes more cost-effective than collection.
Kaplan, Jared, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, and Dario Amodei. 2020. “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.” ArXiv Preprint abs/2001.08361.

Scaling laws2 (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022) quantify how model performance improves with dataset size, and teams have responded by collecting ever larger corpora, yet accelerator capacity expands faster than human-generated text and expert annotations. Much of the accessible public web has already been incorporated into large training sets, and specialist labeling grows slowly. Data Engineering measured the growth of training corpora, and Training Data Approaching the Stock of Public Text sets the largest of them against the estimated stock of public text, between \(10^{14}\) and \(10^{15}\) tokens, which they reach late this decade at the fitted rate. That is the wall at frontier scale, on fleets far larger than one machine, and it shifts engineering effort from collecting everything available to extracting more learning signal from each stored and processed sample.


↩︎ GPT-2, the bandwidth-bound lighthouse for decoder-only language models, is established in Autoregressive decoding.

Radford, Alec, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, and Ilya Sutskever. 2019. Language Models Are Unsupervised Multitask Learners. OpenAI.
The full GPT-2 XL run that Model Training costed on one H100 shows the same wall on a single machine. WebText, GPT-2’s training corpus (Radford et al. 2019), holds 40 GB of text, about 10 billion tokens at roughly 4 bytes per token. The compute-optimal balance fitted by the Chinchilla study, about 20 training tokens per parameter (developed in section 9.2.3), asks for 30 billion unique tokens for GPT-2’s 1.5 billion parameters, 3× what WebText holds. The original run spent about 1.5 × 10²¹ FLOPs, which at six FLOPs per parameter per token processed about 167 billion tokens, so the model saw its corpus roughly 17 times. One machine with 8 H100 accelerators running at 50 percent model FLOPs utilization (MFU), the fraction of peak arithmetic a training run actually delivers (definition \(\ref{dfn-training-model-flops-utilization-mfu}\)), completes that budget in about 4.4 days and 590 kWh of accelerator energy. Less than a week of one machine’s compute therefore passes over the whole corpus many times. An engineering team in that position can repeat epochs over the same text, where gradient updates on familiar tokens yield diminishing loss reductions, or it can lower quality thresholds to admit uncurated web text, where noisy and misaligned tokens degrade downstream evaluation. Instead of accepting either penalty, the team can invest in data selection (refining quality filters, constructing difficulty curricula, and synthesizing missing edge cases) to raise the learning return per FLOP.
When compute is abundant and quality data is scarce, the optimization priority inverts. Selection, not faster kernels, then extracts more learning per dollar, and for teams whose accelerator budget exceeds their curated corpus, the bottleneck shifts from accelerator access to the quality, legality, and diversity of the training data.
The bitter lesson applies here in data terms. A filter written from human intuition about which examples matter is the hand-built expertise the lesson warns against, whereas selection that uses the model’s own signals, such as loss, gradient norms, or embedding similarity, scales with compute. Either way, improved rankings must be established against downstream quality and coverage.


↩︎ The bitter lesson, that general methods using more computation outperform encoded human expertise, is established in The Bitter Lesson.
Data engineering makes data correct; data selection asks which correct examples are worth training on. When selection removes processing at matched quality, it shrinks the Data factor (\(\text{Samples/Task}\)) and therefore the total operations \((\Operations)\) term in the iron law (principle \(\ref{pri-iron-law}\)). Selection therefore needs sample value stated relative to compute cost, and the information-compute ratio of section 9.2.1 measures that value as learning signal gained per unit of training compute.

Definition 9.1: Data selection
Data selection is the process of retaining, prioritizing, or generating training examples to minimize the end-to-end cost of reaching target quality while preserving required coverage.

Significance: Each excluded example removes a forward pass, a backward pass, and an optimizer update, so selection reduces \(\text{Samples/Task}\) and therefore total operations \((\Operations)\) directly.
Distinction: A dataset can pass every data engineering check and still contain many examples that teach the model nothing new; selection judges informativeness and diversity, not correctness.
Common pitfall: Minimizing dataset size instead of end-to-end cost. Scoring, labeling, and lost coverage can erase the savings of a smaller set.



Holding epoch count, batch size, and per-sample work fixed, a 50 percent reduction in dataset size directly halves the required forward passes, backward passes, and gradient updates. For the GPT-2 run above, it would halve both the 4.4 days on one eight-H100 machine and the 590 kWh of accelerator energy, provided the training schedule does not compensate by adding optimization steps. When data selection is combined with model compression and hardware acceleration, those reductions compound across all three axes of the iron law.

Systems Perspective 9.1: Data selection and the iron lawIn the multiplicative D·A·M form of the iron law of ML systems (equation 1.2, where \(\Time = (\text{Samples/Task}) \times (\text{FLOPs/Sample}) \times (\text{Seconds/FLOP})\)), data selection reduces the first factor (\(\text{Samples/Task}\)). Model-level optimizations reduce the second (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\)). Machine-level optimizations reduce the third (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\), by increasing \(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw\) and cutting memory and latency stalls). Selection removes work before those downstream optimizations execute it.
Because the three D·A·M factors multiply, their speedups compound. A 2× reduction in dataset size with 2× fewer operations per sample and 2× higher effective machine throughput yields an 8× reduction in run time because each axis divides the work or time the next axis sees. The machine factor unpacks into the three physical terms of equation 1.3 (\(\Time = \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency\)), which state the condition for realizing that full product. Halving the number of training steps cuts all three terms in half. The algorithmic and hardware speedups, however, achieve their full multiplier only when the dominant physical bottleneck falls in step, whether that bottleneck is compute, data movement \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\), or fixed overhead \((\Latency)\).


These compute savings propagate throughout the hardware hierarchy. By decreasing total data volume (\(\DataVolume\)), deduplication and coreset selection alleviate storage bandwidth demands, network fabric ingress, and host-to-accelerator PCIe transfers that otherwise leave the accelerator’s arithmetic units waiting on input. Upstream, active learning curbs annotation budgets by directing human labeling to samples chosen for uncertainty, diversity, or other task-relevant query criteria.
Yet selection is not free. Every selection strategy incurs its own runtime overhead to score, filter, shuffle, or coordinate samples. An online selection algorithm that executes additional forward passes to rank sample difficulty can consume more accelerator cycles than it saves if its selection overhead exceeds the subsequent reduction in training time. A pipeline claiming a training-time saving must make filtering plus subset training faster than full-data training at the same target quality, the selection inequality of section 9.2.6. Labeling savings and reusable representations require the broader cost accounting of section 9.8.
A learning-theory view of this problem counts the samples needed to reach a test error and treats each sample as free. The systems view counts the FLOPs, bytes, labels, seconds, and joules needed to reach the same quality, including the cost of choosing the samples. In the D·A·M taxonomy, data selection works on the data axis, deciding whether an example warrants processing at all before the algorithm fixes the operations each example costs and the machine fixes how fast those operations run. Removing an example therefore lightens both adjacent boundaries, the storage and input traffic between data and machine and the learning return between data and algorithm.


↩︎ The D·A·M taxonomy and its three diagnostic axes are established in Defining ML Systems.
The engineering toolkit for intelligent data selection follows a deliberate optimization ordering, first asking whether a sample is worth processing and only then how to process the remaining workload efficiently. Static pruning acts first by fixing the retained subset before target-model training begins, even when its scoring step uses a smaller proxy model. Because a sample’s usefulness changes as the model learns, dynamic selection then adapts which examples the training loop sees and which receive human labels during training through curriculum learning and active learning. Where real data still falls short after pruning and reordering, synthetic generation creates missing high-value samples on demand through augmentation, simulation, or examples labeled by a larger trained model (a teacher). Learning from unlabeled data complements these three levers by redefining what counts as a supervision signal. Rather than selecting among labeled examples, semi-supervised and self-supervised methods derive learning targets from the structure of unannotated data. Which levers to use, and in what order, depends on the workload (figure 1).






Figure 1: An Example Data Selection Pipeline: One possible combination of interventions for increasing data value. The three intervention points are Static Pruning before target training, Dynamic Selection during training, and Synthetic Generation on demand. The sequence is illustrative rather than required: synthetic data can enter independently and can itself be pruned or dynamically selected. The final evaluation determines whether the quality gain justifies the compute cost through the Information-Compute Ratio (ICR).



Two lighthouses carry the chapter, each in its own role. GPT-2 XL, bandwidth-bound when it decodes one token at a time but compute-bound when it trains on long batches (Model Training), carries the wall itself, the compute-optimal diagnosis of whether a run is data-starved, and token-level deduplication. ResNet-50 on ImageNet, the book’s compute-bound lighthouse, carries coresets, labels, augmentation, the input pipeline that must feed it, and the decision of which lever to fund. Its training crosses into an input-bound regime whenever the host cannot decode images as fast as the accelerator consumes them (Pipeline stages and accelerator bubbles), and that crossing returns when selection runs on the machine. The measures of value in the next section use both, and both run on the book’s reference machine, the H100, so every saving can be stated in accelerator seconds and joules. The recommendation lighthouse (DLRM), MobileNetV2, and keyword spotting return only in the closing comparison of section 9.8, where each turns out to be bound by a different resource.
Every lever in the chapter removes work at one stage of the machine and adds work of its own, so each must pass a test before it is accepted (table 1). Each test in the right-hand column depends on measuring what an example is worth, which is the subject of the next section.

Self-Check: Question

In an ML infrastructure scaling scenario where available GPU compute grows by approximately \(10\times\) every 3 years while high-quality web data grows by only \(2\times\) every 5 years, what primary systems regime emerges, and what is the appropriate systems response?

A compute-rich, data-constrained data wall regime where intelligent data selection and curation must maximize the learning signal extracted per token
A memory bandwidth-bound regime where model parallel sharding must replace data parallelism across all training clusters
An I/O ingestion bottleneck where disk read bandwidth must be quadrupled to keep GPUs saturated
A compute-starved regime where synthetic data generation should be eliminated to avoid wasting accelerator cycles

A ResNet-50 trained on an aggressively filtered ImageNet subset can hold its aggregate accuracy while failing on rare classes that the filter discarded as low-density noise. A GPT-2 run on a filtered corpus can cost less per epoch while needing more epochs to reach the same loss. A measurement framework is therefore needed to show what a reduction actually saves. Every data selection technique claims to improve efficiency, but only measurement separates genuine training savings from work that has merely moved to another pipeline stage, or from degradation on safety-critical tail distributions. The measures build from the information-compute ratio through a diagnostic of whether a run is data-limited, metrics that tie sample reduction to accuracy, and checks that a reduced set still covers the cases deployment needs, to the selection inequality that every training-time claim must satisfy.


Both failure modes bound a Pareto frontier (principle \(\ref{pri-pareto-frontier}\)) between accuracy and cost, the set of operating points where retaining every example spends FLOPs on redundant signal and pruning further sacrifices rare-slice recall. Locating a run on that frontier requires measuring how much learning signal each sample yields per unit of hardware work. Data engineering already measured task-relevant signal against one cost, the data gravity of moving bytes, in the data selection gain of equation 4.3. Selection puts training compute in the denominator instead, because a sample that is cheap to move still costs a full forward and backward pass. That ratio is the information-compute ratio (ICR).


↪ Locating a model’s operating point on the accuracy-efficiency frontier, and moving along it with compression, is developed in The accuracy-efficiency frontier.
Let \(\FiniteChange\DataInformationContent\) be the learning signal a sample or batch adds and \(\FiniteChange\Operations\) the training operations spent processing it. In practice \(\FiniteChange\DataInformationContent\) is measured as the gain in a fixed evaluation metric, such as percentage points of validation accuracy, so ICR carries units of metric gain per FLOP. The ratio relates the two: \[\text{ICR} = \frac{\FiniteChange\DataInformationContent}{\FiniteChange\Operations}\]
A higher ICR indicates that each FLOP of training yields more measured learning signal over the stated interval. Validation gain and training FLOPs can be observed for a specified experiment with a fixed evaluation protocol; the causal contribution of an individual example generally cannot. Uncertainty and gradient-based scores instead rank candidate examples before their downstream benefit is known. Those rankings require validation against measured quality, compute cost, and deployment-critical slice coverage. The core metrics in section 9.2.4 supply complementary evidence for that evaluation rather than interchangeable measurements of per-example information, and they also track how ICR decays as the dataset grows.



As a training run adds more examples from the same source, a growing share of those examples repeat patterns the model has already seen, and the information-compute ratio falls. The ICR frontier is the dataset size beyond which the marginal ICR, the learning returned by the next FLOP spent on more data, drops below what that FLOP could return elsewhere: a larger model, a different data source, or an earlier stop.
To illustrate diminishing returns, let \(\DataInformationContent(\DatasetSize)\) be the information content of a dataset of size \(\DatasetSize\) and assume \(\DataInformationContent(\DatasetSize) \propto \log \DatasetSize\). This is a simplified analytical model rather than a universal law. If compute cost scales linearly with the per-sample operation count \(\OperationsPerSample\), then total operations are \(\Operations = \OperationsPerSample \cdot \DatasetSize\), and the resulting marginal ICR follows equation 1: \[\text{ICR}(\DatasetSize) = \frac{\DerivativeOperator\DataInformationContent/d\DatasetSize}{d\Operations/d\DatasetSize} \approx \frac{1/\DatasetSize}{\OperationsPerSample} = \frac{1}{\OperationsPerSample\cdot \DatasetSize} \tag{1}\]
The derivative ratio in equation 1 describes the return on an infinitesimal increase in dataset size, whereas for two controlled finite allocations the corresponding incremental ratio divides the additional evaluation gain by the additional training FLOPs under the same evaluation metric and protocol. Under this illustrative model, marginal ICR falls as \(1/(\OperationsPerSample \cdot \DatasetSize)\), so doubling the dataset halves the learning each additional FLOP yields. Inverted, the compute spent per unit of learning grows linearly with \(\DatasetSize\). ICR never reaches zero in this model and the curve has no knee of its own, so the frontier is located by comparing marginal ICR with the threshold the engineer sets, not read off the curve. That saturation is distinct from the data wall (a limit on how much new, high-quality data exists), but the two compound. When new data is scarce and marginal data is weak, selection becomes the main lever. Beyond the frontier, additional data still adds compute but returns less learning than the threshold demands. In this regime additional data inflates the \(\Operations\) term of the iron law without a commensurate gain in ICR. Measured in dollars rather than FLOPs, the same excess lowers the return on compute (RoC) of equation 1.6, the accuracy gained per added dollar of infrastructure.


↩︎ Return on compute, the economic lens that measures accuracy gains against infrastructure spending, is established in Return on compute: Weighing accuracy against cost.
Data selection turns the total operations \((\Operations)\) term in the iron law from a fixed constant into a variable. A 2\(\times\) improvement in measured ICR halves the FLOPs required to reach the same measured gain. It produces the same ideal time reduction as a 2\(\times\) throughput increase only when the workload is compute-bound and the saved work lies on the critical path. ICR focuses specifically on compute; the cost model of section 9.8.1 extends the same reasoning to acquisition, labeling, and storage costs.
The ratio becomes concrete on a coreset, a deliberately selected subset intended to preserve the full dataset’s learning signal. Computing ICR for an ImageNet coreset used to train the ResNet-50 lighthouse shows how large the efficiency gap could become once dataset size, per-sample model cost, and selection strategy meet concrete FLOP budgets. The comparison averages gain over one epoch of each dataset rather than measuring the incremental return on the next data slice, and it uses assumed accuracy gains to illustrate the arithmetic rather than a reported result for the scoring method (EL2N) that section 9.3.4 develops.

Napkin Math 9.1: Computing ICR: CoresetsProblem: Training the ResNet-50 lighthouse model on ImageNet for one epoch costs 3.2 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs. Under the scenario’s assumed accuracy gains, how would retaining 50 percent of the data change the information-compute ratio? The calculation holds the per-sample work fixed and does not include selection overhead.
Setup:

Dataset: ImageNet (1.28M)
Model: ResNet-50 lighthouse (~8.2 GFLOP per forward pass, roughly 24.6 GFLOP for a forward plus backward training step, depending on implementation)
One epoch: 1.28M \(\times\) 24.6 GFLOP = 3.2 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs
Assumed accuracy improvement per epoch (early training): 5 percentage points

Random selection (baseline):

Process all 1.28M samples uniformly
Accuracy gain: 5 percentage points
\(\text{ICR}_{\text{random}}\) = 5 percentage points / (3.2 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs) = \(1.6 \times 10^{-16}\) per FLOP

Difficulty-scored coreset (EL2N, a training-dynamics score defined in section 9.3.4; 50 percent of data):

Process 640.6K selected samples
Assumed accuracy gain: 4.5 percentage points (90 percent of the full-data gain)
Compute: 640.6K \(\times\) 24.6 GFLOP = 1.6 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs
\(\text{ICR}_{\text{coreset}}\) = 4.5 percentage points / (1.6 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs) = \(2.9 \times 10^{-16}\) per FLOP

Systems insight: Under these assumptions, the selected subset achieves 1.8× higher ICR with a 0.5 percentage points smaller accuracy gain. The comparison is learning per FLOP over one epoch of each dataset. It does not show that the coreset reaches the full-data run’s final accuracy, which must be checked separately at equal quality, and a real decision also requires measured gains, selection overhead, and coverage checks.

The goal is to improve ICR subject to target quality and required coverage, then verify that the resulting pipeline reduces the cost it is intended to address.
