Key Takeaways: Curate, do not accumulate

Selection optimizes system cost: The objective is minimizing total cost across compute, storage, labeling, and energy rather than reducing sample counts alone. The information-compute ratio measures learning gained per FLOP spent; total-cost accounting and pipeline measurements establish whether that gain serves the system objective.
Start with deduplication: Exact deduplication is often the lowest-risk first technique because it removes repeated bytes without a learned scoring pass. Apply near-duplicate and semantic deduplication only after validating thresholds against downstream quality metrics.
Training-time savings must exceed selection overhead: At matched quality, \(\SelectionTime+ \TrainingTime(\SubsetDatasetSize) < \TrainingTime(\FullDatasetSize)\). Lightweight proxy models and cached embeddings keep \(\SelectionTime\) low, whereas unoptimized selection algorithms can consume all the compute they save.
Dynamic selection adapts the training mix: Curriculum learning changes presentation order, while active learning changes which samples receive labels. Either improves efficiency when its scoring rule, coverage, and refresh overhead are validated.
Self-supervised pretraining can amortize adaptation cost: Pretraining once and fine-tuning many times spreads pretraining cost across downstream tasks. The worked scenario assumes a 100× label reduction and a 20× marginal-compute reduction; realized savings depend on transfer quality and reuse.
Synthetic data is a supplement, not a replacement: Synthetic samples augment scarce tail cases effectively, but cannot substitute entirely for empirical data. Unanchored synthetic training introduces domain-gap degradation, and recursive synthetic loops trigger catastrophic model collapse.
Validated workload reduction compounds downstream: When selection safely eliminates examples or tokens without adding compensating steps, that work never reaches later model or machine optimizations. Dynamic scoring and synthesis add their own costs, so the combined saving must be measured rather than assumed.



Examples differ greatly in how much they teach per byte transferred and per FLOP executed, and selection spends compute on the ones that teach most. Within the D·A·M taxonomy, selection operates at the head of the system: every redundant sample or uninformative token safely eliminated directly reduces operation count (\(\Operations\)) in the iron law of ML systems (principle \(\ref{pri-iron-law}\)) and can avoid downstream training reads. Scoring may still read the entire pool, and shard streaming may read discarded records, so reductions in data volume (\(\DataVolume\)) must count scoring and shard-read traffic separately. When selection overhead satisfies the inequality at matched quality, the reduction removes work before downstream compression or hardware acceleration sees it. Model-based scoring offers a way to invest additional compute in selection, consistent with the bitter lesson, but a stronger scorer justifies that investment only if its improved rankings save more downstream work than it costs. The Pareto frontier (principle \(\ref{pri-pareto-frontier}\)) applies upstream of the model as well. Each retained fraction is an operating point that trades coverage and rare-slice accuracy against compute, and no single fraction is optimal for every workload.

What’s Next: From data to algorithmsData selection changes what the system learns from. Model Compression turns to how the model represents what it has learned. It starts from the deployment envelope the model must fit and adjusts three things to fit it: the model’s structure through pruning and distillation, its numerical precision through quantization, and the way the remaining operations map onto the hardware that executes them.

title: 9 Data Selection
text:
Self-Check: Answer

In an ML infrastructure scaling scenario where available GPU compute grows by approximately \(10\times\) every 3 years while high-quality web data grows by only \(2\times\) every 5 years, what primary systems regime emerges, and what is the appropriate systems response?

A compute-rich, data-constrained data wall regime where intelligent data selection and curation must maximize the learning signal extracted per token
A memory bandwidth-bound regime where model parallel sharding must replace data parallelism across all training clusters
An I/O ingestion bottleneck where disk read bandwidth must be quadrupled to keep GPUs saturated
A compute-starved regime where synthetic data generation should be eliminated to avoid wasting accelerator cycles

Answer: The correct answer is A. Compute throughput growing faster than accessible high-quality human data creates a compute-to-data imbalance known as the data wall. In this regime, additional raw compute yields diminishing returns on uncurated corpora, making data selection essential to maximize the Information-Compute Ratio (ICR). Shifting model parallelism addresses parameter memory limits rather than data scarcity, scaling disk bandwidth solves I/O stalls rather than token information quality, and eliminating synthetic generation ignores a key strategy for expanding scarce data pools.
Learning Objective: Analyze the systems implications of the compute-to-data scaling asymmetry and diagnose the data wall regime.
True or False: Doubling the amount of raw, deduplicated web data will always double the total information learned by the model.
Answer: False. The section argues for diminishing returns, not a universal doubling law: additional data can add much less marginal signal than its extra compute cost. That is why teams must evaluate learning curves and target quality empirically instead of assuming linear gains from corpus size.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the misconception that information value scales linearly with raw corpus volume.
Order the following stages as they are presented in this chapter’s conceptual map of the data-selection pipeline: (1) Dynamic Selection, (2) Static Pruning, (3) Synthetic Data Generation.
Answer: The correct order is: (2) Static Pruning, (1) Dynamic Selection, (3) Synthetic Data Generation. This is the chapter’s presentation order: prune low-value data before target training, adapt sample usage during training, then create missing coverage when needed. The sequence is a conceptual map rather than a mandatory runtime chronology, because synthetic data can also be created earlier and then pruned or selected before final training.
Learning Objective: Identify the chapter’s conceptual ordering of the three main data-selection intervention points.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Under the illustrative analytical model where dataset information content scales as \(\mathcal{I}(D) \propto \log D\) and training compute scales linearly as \(O = O_{\text{sample}} \cdot D\), how does the marginal Information-Compute Ratio \(\mathrm{ICR}(D)\) scale with dataset size \(D\)?

It remains constant at \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) because additional compute scales proportionally with dataset size
It decays as \(\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{1}{O_{\text{sample}}D}\right)\), so under this illustrative model additional data eventually adds compute faster than marginal information
It grows logarithmically as \(\mathcal{O}(\log D / O_{\text{sample}})\) due to power-law parameter scaling
It decays exponentially as \(\mathcal{O}(\exp(-D))\) once the training corpus exceeds accelerator memory capacity

Answer: The correct answer is B. Under the chapter’s illustrative model, \(d\mathcal{I}/dD \propto 1/D\) and \(dO/dD = O_{\text{sample}}\), so their ratio is \(\mathrm{ICR}(D) \approx 1/(O_{\text{sample}}D)\). This captures diminishing marginal learning signal under the stated log-information and linear-compute assumptions. A constant or growing answer ignores the derivative of \(\log D\), while the exponential-decay choice introduces a memory-capacity mechanism that is not part of this model.
Learning Objective: Calculate the scaling behavior of the Information-Compute Ratio under the section’s illustrative logarithmic-information model.
Explain why a dataset where \(100\%\) of the sample labels are verifiably correct can still exhibit a very low Information-Compute Ratio (ICR).
Answer: Label correctness measures ground-truth accuracy, whereas ICR measures evaluation gain per unit of training compute over a stated interval. A dataset of completely correct examples will have near-zero ICR if the samples are redundant, easily classified by the current model state, or already mastered, because processing them consumes forward and backward FLOPs without producing a corresponding evaluation gain; parameter updates alone do not establish learning value.
Learning Objective: Compare data correctness with data value in the Information-Compute Ratio framework.
An ML systems diagnostic plot maps normalized training compute on the horizontal axis against model performance on the vertical axis. A 10M-parameter run sits well below a fitted frontier under a fixed evaluation protocol and fixed total budget. A controlled sweep then shows that reallocating the same budget toward a larger model improves performance. What is the most defensible diagnosis of the original operating point?

Data-starved regime
I/O bandwidth-saturated regime
The model/data allocation was suboptimal under the tested budget
Over-echoing regime

Answer: The correct answer is C. Under the chapter’s measurement framework, a point below a fitted frontier does not identify a unique cause by itself. What the controlled sweep supports is that the original allocation of budget across model size and data was suboptimal for the tested regime. Calling it purely data-starved or purely capacity-limited would overclaim from one observation, and the other choices describe different bottlenecks entirely.
Learning Objective: Interpret a controlled compute-optimal-frontier sweep without over-inferring a unique bottleneck from a single operating point.
A team wants one metric for how much smaller a selected dataset is at a target accuracy, and another for how much learning is gained per sample over a measured interval. Which pair of chapter metrics matches that need?

Data Curation Rate and Accuracy Reduction Ratio
Data Compression Ratio and Performance-Per-Data
Dynamic Checkpoint Rate and Active Retention Rate
Data Convergence Ratio and Amortized Risk Ratio

Answer: The correct answer is B. Data Compression Ratio (DCR) asks how much the dataset can be reduced while still reaching a target accuracy, and Performance-Per-Data (PPD) measures accuracy gain per sample over a stated interval. The other choices introduce names the chapter does not use. AULC is another valid core metric, but it summarizes performance across dataset sizes rather than serving as the per-sample interval metric in the question.
Learning Objective: Match the chapter’s core metrics to the measurement goals they are designed to answer.
Why is Area Under the Learning Curve (AULC) a more informative metric than single-point final validation accuracy when comparing data selection methods across dataset sizes?
Answer: AULC integrates performance over dataset size \(n\), so it rewards methods that achieve stronger accuracy earlier in the data-allocation range rather than judging them only at one endpoint. Under the same evaluation protocol and integration limits, a higher AULC means better aggregate performance over that same dataset-size range. The practical caveat is that this does not automatically imply the method is better at every dataset size, nor does it guarantee lower total FLOPs if per-sample cost differs across methods.
Learning Objective: Justify AULC as a data-efficiency metric by relating it to performance across dataset sizes rather than a single endpoint.
A training team reduces a dataset from \(1{,}000{,}000\) to \(100{,}000\) images. Full-data training takes 10 hours, subset training takes 1 hour, and scoring the full pool with the production model takes 12 hours. Which conclusion and next step best fit the selection inequality?

Yes, the inequality is satisfied because a \(90\%\) dataset reduction guarantees positive ROI
Yes, because the 9 hours saved in training outweigh the scoring cost; the team only needs more GPUs
No, because \(12+1=13\) hours exceeds the 10-hour baseline; a plausible fix is proxy scoring or cached embeddings, but the team must verify that scoring drops below 9 hours while target quality holds
No, because coreset training always increases memory-bandwidth consumption; the team should switch from NVMe SSDs to HDDs

Answer: The correct answer is C. The chapter’s time-saving test is \(T_{\text{selection}}+T_{\text{train}}(D_{\text{subset}})<T_{\text{train}}(D_{\text{total}})\). Here, \(12+1=13\) hours, which is worse than the 10-hour baseline. Proxy models or cached embeddings are sensible candidate fixes, but they only restore training-time saving if measured scoring time falls below the 9-hour savings window and the selected subset still preserves target quality. A large reduction ratio alone does not prove success, and slower storage would move in the wrong direction.
Learning Objective: Apply the selection inequality to diagnose when scoring overhead erases subset-training savings and identify what must be re-measured after a proposed fix.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A team wants to score a dataset cheaply before training a large production model. They plan to train a small proxy for a few epochs and rank examples by prediction error, knowing that confidently wrong predictions can still score highly. Which method best matches that plan and its trade-off?

\(k\)-Center clustering on raw pixel inputs, because it guarantees zero-cost label-aware boundary identification
Forgetting Events scoring on the full production model, because it requires no proxy architecture and computes in \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) time
EL2N (Error L2-Norm) scoring with a briefly trained proxy model, accepting that high error can reflect hard examples or noise
Herding on Gaussian-distributed features, because it completely avoids computing feature representations

Answer: The correct answer is C. EL2N ranks samples by early prediction error \(\lVert \hat{\mathbf{y}}-\mathbf{y} \rVert_2\), so a cheap proxy can score examples without a full target-model run. The section also warns that high EL2N can include noisy samples and that transfer from proxy to target is useful but not guaranteed. Geometry-based \(k\)-Center is not label-aware boundary scoring, Forgetting Events is much more expensive, and Herding still depends on feature representations.
Learning Objective: Compare proxy-based EL2N scoring with other coreset methods in terms of cost, signal, and validation needs.
Why is Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) with MinHash preferred over exhaustive pairwise Jaccard similarity comparison for large-scale text deduplication?

MinHash LSH guarantees \(100\%\) precision in detecting semantic paraphrases across different natural languages
MinHash eliminates the need to tokenize or shingle input documents before hashing
Exhaustive pairwise Jaccard comparison requires training a deep neural network, whereas LSH is purely rule-based
Exhaustive pairwise comparison requires \(\mathcal{O}(D^2)\) document comparisons, whereas MinHash LSH hashes compact signatures into sublinear candidate collision buckets

Answer: The correct answer is D. Comparing all pairs in a dataset of \(D\) documents requires \(\mathcal{O}(D^2)\) comparisons, which is computationally intractable for web-scale datasets (\(D \ge 10^7\)). MinHash compresses documents into fixed-size sketches where collision probability equals Jaccard similarity, and LSH bands these sketches into hash buckets so only candidate pairs colliding in a bucket are compared. MinHash LSH does not detect cross-lingual semantic paraphrases, still requires shingling/tokenization, and pairwise Jaccard comparison is an exact set operation rather than a deep learning method.
Learning Objective: Analyze the computational scaling benefits of MinHash and Locality-Sensitive Hashing for web-scale deduplication.
True or False: Removing near-duplicate documents with MinHash LSH always improves model accuracy because duplicate data has zero statistical value in all training regimes.
Answer: False. While deduplication reduces redundant computation and memorization risk, in some domains duplicate frequency reflects natural empirical data distributions or intentional weighting. Aggressive deduplication with miscalibrated thresholds can prune legitimate variations or distort class priors, necessitating empirical validation on downstream accuracy.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the systems and statistical trade-offs of aggressive near-duplicate filtering.
The training-dynamics coreset metric that measures the Euclidean norm of the difference between predicted class probabilities and the one-hot target vector early in training is known as ____.
Answer: EL2N. It measures \(\lVert p(x)-y \rVert_2\) early in training as an error-based difficulty score. The chapter notes that proxy-model rankings can transfer usefully to larger targets, but that transfer must be validated rather than assumed universal.
Learning Objective: Identify EL2N from its mathematical definition and explain why proxy-based use still requires validation.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

In curriculum learning, an engineer implements an easy-to-hard pacing schedule that controls the fraction of the sorted training pool available at each stage. What is the primary objective of this pacing strategy?

To guide early optimization with more stable examples before gradually introducing harder ones
To eliminate the need for backward passes during the first half of training
To maximize GPU memory bandwidth utilization by sorting tensors strictly by length in bytes
To replace human labelers with an automated oracle during the late stages of training

Answer: The correct answer is A. The chapter presents curriculum learning as a way to shape the optimization trajectory: easier examples can provide steadier early gradients, while harder examples are introduced later as the model matures. That is not a guarantee against divergence on every task, and ‘easy’ depends on the scoring rule, but it is the pacing mechanism this section teaches. The other choices confuse curriculum with memory-layout tricks or active-learning workflows.
Learning Objective: Analyze how curriculum pacing can stabilize early learning by controlling when harder examples appear.
An active learning pipeline chooses unlabeled examples for costly radiologist annotation. The team notices that simple uncertainty sampling repeatedly selects images from a single ambiguous artifact class, starving other disease categories. Which query strategy should they adopt to resolve this pathology?

Least-confidence sampling, because it strictly selects the lowest top-1 probability prediction
Diversity sampling or hybrid uncertainty-diversity sampling (such as BADGE), which balances uncertainty near decision boundaries with feature-space coverage
Random undersampling of the entire unlabeled pool to reduce dataset size before scoring
Uniform zero-shot pseudo-labeling without confidence thresholds

Answer: The correct answer is B. Pure uncertainty sampling often suffers from sampling bias by selecting clustered points near a single ambiguous boundary region. Diversity sampling (or hybrid strategies like BADGE that incorporate gradient embeddings) ensures that selected queries span diverse clusters across the feature space while still targeting model uncertainty. Least-confidence sampling exacerbates the clustering issue, random undersampling discards informative candidates arbitrarily, and unthresholded pseudo-labeling introduces catastrophic label noise.
Learning Objective: Compare active learning query strategies to mitigate sampling bias and redundancy.
Order the steps in an active learning closed-loop iteration: (1) Select top query samples via query strategy, (2) Acquire expert annotations from the oracle, (3) Score unlabeled pool using current model, (4) Retrain or update model on expanded dataset, (5) Add newly labeled samples to the training set.
Answer: The correct order is: (3) Score unlabeled pool using current model, (1) Select top query samples via query strategy, (2) Acquire expert annotations from the oracle, (5) Add newly labeled samples to the training set, (4) Retrain or update model on expanded dataset. The cycle begins with proxy or model scoring over the candidate pool, selecting candidate queries, querying the human oracle, incorporating verified labels into the dataset, and updating the model.
Learning Objective: Design the closed-loop workflow of an iterative active learning system.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

What causes the phenomenon of ‘model collapse’ when generative models are trained recursively on synthetic data generated by earlier model iterations?

GPU memory fragmentation caused by variable-length synthetic sequences during distributed training
Overfitting to floating-point rounding errors during fp16 mixed-precision matrix multiplication
A failure of the I/O storage subsystem to deliver synthetic batches at line rate
Systematic underrepresentation and erosion of tail patterns across generations, so recursive retraining compounds missing or distorted rare cases

Answer: The correct answer is D. The section’s model-collapse mechanism is recursive tail erosion: generated data underrepresents rare but important patterns, and retraining on later synthetic generations compounds those omissions and errors. High-probability modes dominating the sample stream is part of that story, but it does not prove universal collapse under every sampling regime. The other choices are execution problems, not the chapter’s statistical mechanism.
Learning Objective: Analyze how recursive synthetic training can degrade tail coverage and diversity over generations.
A team distills a ResNet-50 student on ImageNet and chooses offline distillation, precomputing the teacher’s FP32 logits for every training image instead of keeping the teacher in accelerator memory. Which cost does this choice move onto the data path?

Every epoch must read per-class logit vectors in place of single integer labels, multiplying the label bytes the storage tier and input pipeline must deliver
Every training step must run a teacher forward pass beside the student, restricting the student’s per-accelerator batch size
The student must be trained with a lower learning rate, because soft targets produce larger gradients than one-hot labels
The teacher must be retrained once per student epoch, so preparation cost grows linearly with the number of epochs

Answer: The correct answer is A. Offline distillation stores one logit per class for every sample, so the per-sample label grows from a single integer index to four bytes per class, an expansion of more than three orders of magnitude for ImageNet’s thousand classes, and every epoch reads it back through the input pipeline. Teacher residency and the reduced student batch size are the costs of online distillation, which this choice avoids. Soft targets do not force a lower learning rate, and the teacher pass runs once during precomputation rather than once per epoch.
Learning Objective: Analyze knowledge distillation as a data-synthesis lever by locating its storage and input-pipeline cost.
Why is training exclusively on \(100\%\) synthetic data from a simulation engine often suboptimal for real-world deployment, and how does synthetic-to-real data mixing bridge this gap?
Answer: Simulation engines have an inherent domain gap (\(\mathcal{D}_{\text{synth}} \ne \mathcal{D}_{\text{real}}\)) caused by simplified physics, missing sensor artifacts, and unmodeled environmental noise. Mixing synthetic data with a curated set of real-world examples anchors the model to real feature distributions while using synthetic samples to expand volume, cover edge cases, and balance rare classes.
Learning Objective: Analyze domain gap challenges and justify synthetic-to-real mixing ratios.
True or False: Using a high-capacity diffusion model or state-of-the-art LLM to generate synthetic training data guarantees that the resulting training set will be completely free of distribution shift relative to the real deployment environment.
Answer: False. Generator quality does not eliminate domain gap. Synthetic generators can amplify subtle distribution shifts, introduce generator-specific artifacts, and omit edge cases present in real-world deployment environments, requiring domain validation against real ground truth.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the misconception that advanced generative models eliminate domain shift.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Explain the mechanism of confirmation bias in semi-supervised pseudo-labeling, and specify how confidence thresholding mitigates it.
Answer: Confirmation bias arises when the model trains on its own wrong pseudo-labels and reinforces those mistakes in later rounds. A high confidence threshold filters out low-confidence predictions, but confidently wrong pseudo-labels can still survive, so thresholding is only a partial defense. The practical check is to compare the model’s confidence against held-out labeled validation evidence before trusting the expanded training set.
Learning Objective: Explain confirmation bias in pseudo-labeling and evaluate what confidence thresholding can and cannot fix.
True or False: Consistency regularization methods such as FixMatch assume that label-preserving perturbations of an input should not change the model’s predicted class distribution much.
Answer: True. The method relies on a task-valid smoothness assumption: if the augmentation preserves the label, predictions across the two views should stay consistent. The key caveat is that closeness in raw input space alone is not enough—rotations, crops, or other perturbations can change the true label on some tasks.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the task-dependent assumption behind consistency regularization.
In the economics of foundation models, an organization invests \(C_{\text{pretrain}} = 10{,}000\) GPU-hours in self-supervised pretraining. Each downstream task fine-tuning costs \(C_{\text{finetune}} = 50\) GPU-hours. Training each task from scratch would cost \(C_{\text{scratch}} = 1{,}000\) GPU-hours. What is the minimum number of downstream tasks \(N^*\) required to break even on the pretraining investment?

\(N^* = 5\) downstream tasks
\(N^* = 8\) downstream tasks
\(N^* = 11\) downstream tasks (\(10{,}000 + 11 \times 50 = 10{,}550 < 11 \times 1{,}000 = 11{,}000\))
\(N^* = 50\) downstream tasks

Answer: The correct answer is C. The break-even condition is \(C_{\text{pretrain}} + N \cdot C_{\text{finetune}} \le N \cdot C_{\text{scratch}}\), which gives \(10{,}000 + 50N \le 1000N\), or \(950N \ge 10{,}000\). Solving for \(N\) yields \(N \ge 10{,}000 / 950 \approx 10.53\). Thus, at least 11 downstream tasks are required for the foundation model approach to use fewer total GPU-hours under these assumptions. This is a compute-only crossover at matched target quality; a dollar comparison must also price labels, accelerator hours, and other differing costs. At 10 tasks, scratch training costs \(10{,}000\) hours while the foundation model costs \(10{,}500\) hours. At 11 tasks, scratch training costs \(11{,}000\) hours while the foundation model costs \(10{,}550\) hours.
Learning Objective: Calculate the break-even threshold for amortizing self-supervised pretraining across downstream tasks.
How does the MoCo (Momentum Contrast) framework reduce the hardware and memory constraints of contrastive self-supervised learning compared to naive SimCLR?

By replacing convolutional backbones with rule-based lookup tables to avoid backpropagation
By requiring fully supervised class labels to filter out false negative pairs
By using a dynamic queue of negative keys and a slowly updating momentum encoder, decoupling negative dictionary size from mini-batch size
By computing exact pairwise Jaccard similarities on raw byte sequences rather than latent embeddings

Answer: The correct answer is C. Contrastive learning requires large sets of negative examples for effective representation learning. While SimCLR scales the mini-batch size (batches of up to 8,192 examples, paid for in activation memory and all-gather traffic), MoCo decouples the dictionary size from the mini-batch size by maintaining a memory queue of negative keys updated with a momentum-averaged teacher encoder. MoCo still uses neural backbones and backpropagation, operates in an unsupervised manner without human labels, and computes cosine similarities in latent space rather than raw byte Jaccard comparisons.
Learning Objective: Compare contrastive self-supervised learning architectures and their memory-compute scaling trade-offs.
What is the systems-level ‘homogenization risk’ (or blast radius) of pretraining a shared foundation model on an uncurated dataset?
Answer: A shared base model can propagate the same upstream defect into many downstream tasks, so a bad pretraining-data choice has a much larger blast radius than in train-from-scratch workflows. For example, a memorized private pattern or systematic bias in the base model may affect many adaptations built on top of it. The actual impact is not universal, because downstream fine-tuning and validation can reduce or expose some defects.
Learning Objective: Analyze why pretraining-data defects in a shared foundation model can affect many downstream adaptations.
True or False: Because self-supervised pretraining learns general representations from unlabeled data, it completely eliminates the need for data selection or quality filtering during the pretraining stage.
Answer: False. Self-supervised pretraining at web scale remains highly sensitive to pretraining data quality; uncurated corpora containing boilerplate, corrupted text, toxic samples, or pervasive duplicates degrade representation quality and inflate training FLOPs without improving downstream transfer.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the misconception that self-supervised learning eliminates data curation requirements.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why do naive random sample lookups across non-contiguous indices in large un-sharded dataset files severely degrade I/O throughput on storage hardware, and how do shuffle buffers mitigate this?

Random lookups bypass host CPU caches, forcing floating-point registers to re-encode all labels
Random lookups violate PCIe parity checks, causing GPU kernel timeouts during backward passes
Random lookups trigger hash collisions in the Python garbage collector, halting dataloading threads
Random 4 KB reads fall below peak sequential storage bandwidth due to IOPS limits, by hundreds of times on HDDs, whereas shuffle buffers read large sequential chunks and randomize locally in memory

Answer: The correct answer is D. Storage devices (HDDs, SATA SSDs, NVMe SSDs, and cloud object stores) provide peak throughput under large, contiguous sequential reads. Non-contiguous random 4 KB reads cut realized bandwidth (about 375\(\times\) on HDDs, about 14\(\times\) on SATA SSDs, and under 2\(\times\) on NVMe SSDs). Shuffle buffers co-design data loading by reading large sequential shards into host RAM and performing pseudo-random shuffling locally within memory, preserving peak sequential disk bandwidth. The other choices describe fictitious hardware or software failures.
Learning Objective: Analyze the hardware empathy principles governing storage I/O and shuffle buffer design.
Contrast upstream data echoing (echoing before data augmentation) with downstream data echoing (echoing after augmentation) in terms of computational overhead and sample diversity.
Answer: Upstream echoing amortizes work before augmentation and lets repeated passes receive fresh random augmentations, so it can preserve more view diversity while still reducing some repeated upstream overhead. Downstream echoing amortizes earlier work through augmentation, but repeats the same already-augmented tensors rather than creating new views. The practical implication is to place the echo point after the bottleneck stage whose work you want to amortize, then check whether the repeated data still preserves target quality.
Learning Objective: Compare upstream and downstream echoing by how much pipeline work they amortize and how much sample diversity they preserve.
True or False: If the GPU training step takes 20 ms and the CPU data loading/augmentation pipeline takes 10 ms (\(R = T_{\text{pipeline}} / T_{\text{GPU}} = 0.5\)), applying a data echoing factor of \(e = 2\) will double the end-to-end training throughput.
Answer: False. When \(R < 1\), the training job is accelerator-bound (the data pipeline is already faster than the GPU), so the GPU is never starved for data. Applying data echoing in this regime provides zero throughput gain and merely feeds duplicate or stale data to the accelerator.
Learning Objective: Evaluate pipeline balance conditions under which data echoing provides zero throughput improvement.
On one host with two to eight accelerator workers, how can centralized coreset selection become a bottleneck, and what trade-off does hierarchical selection introduce?

Centralized selection requires all workers to share a single GPU; hierarchical selection distributes weights across SSDs
Centralized selection fails because sharding prevents network cards from transmitting floating-point values
Centralized selection can bottleneck host memory and coordinator dispatch; hierarchical selection prunes locally per shard, risking loss of globally rare samples across shards
Centralized selection eliminates gradient synchronization; hierarchical selection disables local backpropagation

Answer: The correct answer is C. Centralized selection gathers candidate scores or embeddings at a coordinator process on the same host. Its memory demand and CPU dispatch can compete with decoding and batch preparation, so adding accelerator workers does not necessarily accelerate selection. Hierarchical selection distributes selection by having workers select local coresets on their shards before merging at the coordinator; however, this shard-local pruning can introduce distribution skew if rare classes or boundary cases are unevenly distributed across shards. The other choices state incorrect hardware, communication, or backpropagation limitations.
Learning Objective: Compare centralized, shard-local, and hierarchical architectures for distributed coreset selection.
In distributed active learning, Worker A scores candidate samples using checkpoint step \(t\), while Worker B has already advanced the shared model to step \(t+100\). What consistency challenge arises, and what is the best response?

Worker A encounters deadlock in CUDA streams; disable autograd during scoring
Worker B overwrites Worker A’s local storage; mount the dataset read-only
Worker A’s GPU runs out of memory; reduce batch size to 1
Worker A may produce stale rankings that differ from fresher ones; version checkpoints and choose the score-refresh interval from measured ranking agreement

Answer: The correct answer is D. The issue is ranking staleness: uncertainty scores from an older checkpoint can differ from those produced by a newer model. The chapter’s remedy is not to assume such rankings are automatically invalid, but to make them reproducible with checkpoint versioning and to set refresh frequency from measured agreement decay. The other choices confuse the problem with autograd deadlock, storage overwrites, or memory exhaustion.
Learning Objective: Analyze score staleness in distributed active learning and choose a reproducible refresh strategy based on measured rank agreement.
Explain why performing independent, shard-local coreset pruning on an unstratified, partitioned dataset can cause minority class collapse during distributed training.
Answer: When a dataset is sharded across workers without stratification, rare minority classes may appear in very few shards. If each worker independently selects its top-\(k\) coreset based on local metrics, workers with only a few minority samples may discard them as outliers, systematically erasing the minority class from the global training corpus.
Learning Objective: Explain how unstratified data sharding leads to minority class loss during distributed pruning.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A company invests \(\$30{,}000\) to compute a high-quality coreset. Training on the full dataset costs \(\$10{,}000\) per run, whereas training on the coreset costs \(\$4{,}000\) per run. What is the break-even number of training runs, and what is the ROI after 10 runs?

Break-even is 5 runs, and ROI after 10 runs is \(100\%\)
Break-even is 3 runs, and ROI after 10 runs is \(300\%\)
Break-even is 8 runs, and ROI after 10 runs is \(50\%\)
Break-even is 10 runs, and ROI after 10 runs is \(0\%\)

Answer: The correct answer is A. Each run saves \(\$10{,}000-\$4{,}000=\$6{,}000\), so break-even is \(\$30{,}000/\$6{,}000=5\) runs. After 10 runs, gross savings are \(10\times\$6{,}000=\$60{,}000\), net savings are \(\$60{,}000-\$30{,}000=\$30{,}000\), and ROI is \(\$30{,}000/\$30{,}000=1.0\), or \(100\%\). The other answers use the wrong per-run savings or the wrong ROI arithmetic.
Learning Objective: Calculate break-even run count and ROI for a one-time static-selection investment.
Using the chapter’s cost model \(C_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{acquire}} + C_{\text{label}} + C_{\text{store}} + C_{\text{process}}\), which scenario best justifies an upstream filtering investment?

Skip filtering so that maximum raw volume reaches training, regardless of downstream processing and labeling cost
Spend \(\$5{,}000\) on automated filtering only if measured avoided labeling, storage, and processing costs exceed that amount while task coverage and target quality still hold
Double human labeling effort to manually review every raw sample before filtering, because filtering cost is always worse than labeling cost
Cut evaluation entirely to offset the cost of training on unfiltered data

Answer: The correct answer is B. The chapter’s four-term cost model says filtering earns its place only when the costs it avoids downstream exceed the filtering investment at matched quality. That means measuring reductions in later labeling, storage, or processing costs rather than assuming that filtering a large fraction of samples automatically saves money. Sending everything downstream ignores preventable cost, the full-manual-review claim is wrong because it asserts filtering is always worse than labeling without the measurements needed to support that universal comparison, and eliminating evaluation removes the evidence needed to claim target-quality preservation.
Learning Objective: Analyze when an upstream filtering cost is justified under the chapter’s four-term total-cost model.
Explain why calculating Return on Investment (ROI) for data selection requires tracking engineering implementation and pipeline maintenance costs in addition to raw accelerator compute hours.
Answer: A data selection method that saves GPU training hours may require custom storage infrastructure, indexing services, proxy model scoring pipelines, and human maintenance. If these engineering overheads exceed the cloud compute savings, the net systems ROI is negative despite apparent model FLOP reductions.
Learning Objective: Evaluate non-compute engineering overheads in the data selection ROI equation.
According to the chapter’s decision framework, if an ML team has an abundant pool of unlabeled domain data, very limited annotation budget, and access to human domain experts for selective queries, which technique branch is recommended?

Pure transformation-based data augmentation without labeling
Active learning (human-in-the-loop selective query) or semi-supervised learning
Generative self-instruct synthesis to replace all human annotators entirely
Exhaustive pairwise Jaccard deduplication across all unlabeled samples

Answer: The correct answer is B. When the primary bottleneck is labeling cost, the decision framework routes based on oracle availability: if a human oracle is available, active learning queries the most informative samples; when combined with unlabeled data, semi-supervised learning leverages structural priors. Pure augmentation does not provide ground truth for novel concepts, generative self-instruct cannot replace domain experts where ground-truth verification is required, and pairwise deduplication is a pruning step rather than a labeling strategy.
Learning Objective: Apply the data selection decision framework to match operational constraints with appropriate selection paradigms.
When deciding between static coreset pruning and dynamic online active selection for a production pipeline, what role does the expected number of training runs (\(N\)) play in the architectural choice?
Answer: The expected run count determines how much upfront static-selection cost can be amortized. If the same curated subset will support many retrains, sweeps, or ablations, a static investment can pay off quickly; if there is only one run, that same cost may still be worth it, but only if its measured quality and savings beat the one-run baseline. Dynamic selection is not automatically cheaper, because it can add repeated scoring cost during training instead of paying once upfront.
Learning Objective: Compare static and dynamic selection choices using amortization, reuse, and measured cost-quality trade-offs.
In recommendation systems like DLRM where embedding tables consume terabytes of memory, how does interaction deduplication differ in systems impact from cold embedding pruning?
Answer: Interaction deduplication removes repeated user-item examples, so under a fixed epoch count and fixed per-sample work it means fewer examples are actually processed, reducing total traffic and total training work. Cold-ID pruning or reindexing reduces allocated embedding capacity only when IDs disappear from the table design, but that alone does not guarantee lower realized memory traffic or bandwidth cost. A useful deployment check is whether removing rare IDs hurts recommendation quality on sparse users or items.
Learning Objective: Compare how interaction deduplication and cold-ID pruning affect training work, embedding capacity, and quality risk in recommendation systems.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

In an idealized compute-bound training scenario with fixed target quality and negligible new overheads, a team halves the number of processed examples, halves the operations per processed example on the same compute-critical path, and doubles realized arithmetic throughput. What total speedup follows from the chapter’s multiplicative D·A·M reasoning?

An \(8\times\) speedup, because halving workload, halving per-sample work, and doubling throughput multiply on the same critical path
A \(6\times\) speedup, because the factors add across layers
A \(2\times\) speedup, because only the hardware improvement matters once arithmetic throughput doubles
A \(4\times\) speedup, because reducing training examples and reducing per-sample work are the same effect

Answer: The correct answer is A. Under the chapter’s ideal multiplicative setup, halving examples gives a \(2\times\) workload reduction, halving compute on the same path gives another \(2\times\), and doubling realized throughput gives a final \(2\times\), for \(2\times2\times2=8\times\). This reasoning assumes fixed target quality, fixed effective batch/schedule assumptions, negligible new overheads, and that the saved work lies on the compute-critical path. Measured end-to-end speedup can be smaller once other bottlenecks appear.
Learning Objective: Calculate ideal multiplicative speedup across data, algorithm, and machine levers under the chapter’s fixed-assumption scenario.
Why are upstream data selection and downstream model compression complementary rather than interchangeable?

Model compression can only be applied to computer vision models, whereas data selection is restricted to NLP
Data selection eliminates backward passes entirely, whereas model compression eliminates forward passes
Data selection optimizes only inference latency on edge devices, whereas model compression only affects training time
Data selection reduces how many examples are processed, whereas model compression reduces the artifact size and can lower execution cost per example on compatible hardware

Answer: The correct answer is D. The chapter separates two different levers: data selection changes how much workload is processed during training, while model compression changes properties of the trained model artifact and can reduce execution cost per example when the deployment hardware and software stack can exploit it. Post-training compression can help serving, but it does not retroactively remove past training work. The two are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable, and their gains are not guaranteed to multiply cleanly in every pipeline.
Learning Objective: Compare how workload reduction and model compression target different cost terms in the optimization stack.
A team curates its training corpus to half its original size and reports that the resulting model will be cheaper to deploy. What does the reduction actually change, and what evidence would support the deployment claim?
Answer: Halving the corpus halves the forward and backward passes of training, but the trained model keeps the same architecture and parameter count, so its serving cost is unchanged by the reduction itself. A curated corpus may yield more compact representations that later compression can exploit, but that is a hypothesis to verify, not a property of every selected dataset. Supporting the deployment claim requires compressing the model and measuring serving latency and task accuracy on the target hardware, rather than inferring deployment savings from the upstream dataset reduction.
Learning Objective: Distinguish the training-work reduction that data selection delivers from the deployment savings that require model compression and measurement.
Explain how an aggressive data filter that discards rare but critical edge cases can raise costs in the compression and deployment stages of the optimization stack.
Answer: Each downstream stage inherits both the computational savings and any representational deficits created upstream. If the filter removes rare edge cases, the trained model may already sit close to its accuracy threshold on those cases, leaving little headroom for compression. Engineers may then have to train longer or abandon aggressive quantization to preserve task accuracy, which gives back part of the saving. The practical implication is that a selection policy must be evaluated on the deployed model’s accuracy and latency, not only on training FLOPs saved.
Learning Objective: Explain how representational deficits introduced by data selection propagate into compression and deployment costs.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A research paper reports that an EL2N coreset selection method successfully pruned \(50\%\) of CIFAR-10 with \(0\%\) loss in accuracy. A medical imaging team applies the exact same \(50\%\) pruning ratio to a rare tumor detection dataset and suffers a disastrous \(28\%\) drop in recall. What fallacy explains this failure?

The team failed to use GPU acceleration during the inference pass
The team used float32 precision instead of bfloat16 mixed precision
CIFAR-10 contains more total classes than medical imaging datasets
Assuming that benchmark coreset pruning ratios transfer directly to specialized, highly imbalanced production domains with rare failure modes

Answer: The correct answer is D. Pruning ratios calibrated on balanced, homogeneous academic benchmarks like CIFAR-10 rarely transfer to specialized production domains like medical imaging. In domains with extreme class imbalance or subtle pathological features, a \(50\%\) global prune disproportionately discards rare minority samples and critical edge cases, causing severe domain-specific performance drops. Hardware precision and class counts are irrelevant to this transfer fallacy.
Learning Objective: Analyze why benchmark data pruning ratios fail to transfer to specialized production domains.
A team implements an elaborate multi-stage active learning pipeline that reduces training dataset size by \(40\%\). However, the continuous clustering, proxy scoring, and cross-worker all-gather synchronization take 3 times longer than the GPU time saved during training. Which pitfall does this represent?

Violating the Selection Inequality by incurring selection overheads that exceed downstream training savings (\(T_{\text{selection}} > \Delta T_{\text{train}}\))
Encountering model collapse due to recursive generator loops
Failing to implement 4 KB small-read alignment on host NVMe storage
Violating the smoothness assumption in semi-supervised consistency regularization

Answer: The correct answer is A. This is the canonical violation of the Selection Inequality: an engineering team designs a selection algorithm that successfully reduces sample count, but the computational and synchronization overhead of scoring and filtering (\(T_{\text{selection}}\)) exceeds the training time saved on the reduced subset, leading to a net increase in total wall-clock time. Model collapse relates to recursive generative training, NVMe alignment relates to I/O access patterns, and the smoothness assumption belongs to semi-supervised learning.
Learning Objective: Analyze violations of the Selection Inequality in complex data selection architectures.
Why is evaluating a data selection strategy solely on aggregate validation accuracy a dangerous pitfall when dealing with imbalanced datasets?
Answer: In imbalanced datasets, aggregate accuracy is heavily dominated by majority classes. A data pruning algorithm could discard \(90\%\) of rare minority or safety-critical examples to optimize overall compute while aggregate accuracy appears unchanged, completely compromising model performance on rare real-world failure modes.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the pitfall of aggregate metric optimization under severe class imbalance.
True or False: Because modern high-capacity generative models produce photorealistic images and fluent text, a model trained on recursively generated synthetic data will never suffer performance degradation.
Answer: False. The chapter warns that recursive synthetic training can cause model collapse by progressively eroding rare patterns and compounding earlier errors. High generator quality can reduce the risk in some settings, but it does not make degradation impossible.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the misconception that high synthetic fidelity rules out recursive-training failure modes.

← Back to Questions

title: 11 Hardware Acceleration
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter: Part 1 · Part 2












Architecture stack focus for this chapter.
Why does moving data cost more than computing it?
Arithmetic is inexpensive relative to data movement. In the time required to fetch a single scalar operand from off-chip DRAM, modern arithmetic units can execute dozens to hundreds of floating-point operations, and that DRAM access consumes on the order of a hundred times more energy than the computation itself. This imbalance, the memory wall, means specialized accelerators are not merely faster arithmetic engines. Rather, their microarchitectures are designed to stage, amortize, and hide data movement through wide spatial interconnects, deep on-chip memory hierarchies, and specialized execution pipelines. When general-purpose processor scaling faltered, hardware specialization enabled machine learning models to continue scaling by turning transistor budgets into high-throughput tensor datapaths. Delivered performance, however, depends on whether a model’s tensor access patterns match the data paths of the underlying silicon. Hardware selection cannot be reduced to comparing peak FLOP/s: two accelerators with identical theoretical compute ratings often deliver radically different throughput on real workloads because one saturates its functional units while the other starves for data. A recommendation model dominated by sparse embedding lookups stresses memory bandwidth and interconnect latency, demanding a different memory architecture than a dense transformer training run bounded by matrix multiply-accumulate throughput. If an operation is bandwidth bound, reducing theoretical operation count yields zero speedup because arithmetic is not the binding constraint. Matching workload characteristics to architectural dataflows determines whether an accelerator operates near its hardware ceiling or languishes at a fraction of its advertised peak. In D·A·M terms, the accelerator makes the machine constraint concrete, governing which algorithms and model architectures remain practical in production.

Learning Objectives

Explain hardware acceleration as tensor-workload specialization and why Amdahl’s law bounds its end-to-end speedup
Compare Tensor Cores, systolic arrays, SIMD/SIMT units, and sparse execution for ML compute primitives
Diagnose memory-wall bottlenecks using bandwidth, cache hierarchy, host-device transfer, and energy-movement costs
Calculate arithmetic intensity and execution-path roofline ceilings, then use profiling to diagnose compute or memory limits
Select dataflow, tiling, and mapping strategies that maximize reuse under memory-capacity constraints
Analyze compiler and runtime optimizations that fuse kernels, plan memory, and schedule accelerators
Evaluate accelerator choices across throughput, latency, power, cost, and deployment-context constraints



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗






Hardware acceleration turns on the machine axis.
Model Compression closed on a deployment profile for ResNet-50 quantized to INT8 (ResNet-50 INT8 Deployment Profile on the Reference H100): a model four times smaller whose large-batch throughput rises severalfold on the reference H100 while its batch-one latency barely moves. Data selection reduced the iron law’s Data factor (\(\text{Samples/Task}\)) and compression reduced the Algorithm factor (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\)) and byte traffic (\(\DataVolume\)), but whether either saving reaches the wall clock is decided by the Machine factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)). This chapter supplies the machine side of that profile. It explains why the same INT8 weights run faster on one execution path than on another, and why the hardware, not the model, determines how much of every compression saving survives execution. The explanation starts with the memory wall: arithmetic is cheap relative to data movement, so specialized hardware matters less because it raises compute throughput than because it organizes memory, dataflow, and parallelism so that its arithmetic units stay fed.
One workload runs through the chapter. ResNet-50 quantized to INT8 carries the book’s compute-bound regime (Lighthouse Models as Reference Workloads): its convolutions reuse each weight across many image positions, so on a data-center accelerator most of its time can go to arithmetic rather than to moving bytes. It reappears at every level of the machine, from the matrix units that execute its convolutions to the compiler that lowers its graph, and each time the question is what the INT8 path changes. GPT-2 XL decoding one token at a time supplies the single contrast. It carries the bandwidth-bound regime: every generated token streams all of the model’s weights from memory for about two operations per parameter, so the machine that keeps ResNet-50 busy spends most of a decode step waiting for bytes. MobileNetV2, whose depthwise layers trade arithmetic for a small parameter footprint, and keyword spotting (KWS), the power-bound lighthouse, return where the chapter reaches phone-class and embedded chips. DLRM appears where its embedding lookups, the capacity-bound regime, break the regular access patterns that accelerators assume. The reference machine is the NVIDIA H100, the data-center accelerator this book uses for training and serving examples; its numbers are one generation’s instance of limits that every generation obeys.

Definition 11.1: Hardware acceleration
Hardware acceleration is the practice of mapping work from general-purpose execution onto specialized processors or functional units optimized for a narrower operation class. For ML workloads, that specialization commonly trades some programmability for the compute density \((\PeakRate)\) and performance-per-watt gains that regular tensor operations can exploit.

Significance: An H100 GPU delivers 989 TFLOP/s for dense FP16/BF16 matrix multiplication; against this chapter’s illustrative 1–2 TFLOP/s reference-CPU baseline, this is a 490–990× gap. Its 80 billion transistors devote far more silicon to parallel arithmetic than to branch prediction, out-of-order scheduling, and large caches (Choquette 2023).
Distinction: A general-purpose CPU is designed for flexible execution, low-latency control, and varied workloads. An accelerator instead concentrates resources on a narrower operation class, so it achieves its gains only when the workload exposes the supported operations and enough parallel work to keep its arithmetic units busy.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that an accelerator’s advertised peak throughput is the throughput a workload receives. Delivered performance is bounded above by the lower of the compute ceiling and what memory bandwidth can feed (the roofline constraint, developed later in this chapter). A low-arithmetic-intensity kernel can therefore sit at a small fraction of peak FLOP/s no matter how fast the silicon is rated, because it starves for data rather than for arithmetic.



The anatomy of an accelerator is the arrangement of parts that every machine learning accelerator shares: arithmetic units built for tensor operations, on-chip memory that holds operands next to those units, a wide path to off-chip memory, and a host interface through which work arrives. Every inference and every training step on such a machine is a stream of operand movements that ends in multiply-accumulate operations, and the anatomy decides how far each operand travels before it is used. A matrix unit that can retire thousands of multiply-accumulates per cycle sits idle whenever its next operands are still in flight, and an off-chip access can take many processor cycles and cost orders of magnitude more energy than the low-precision operation it feeds. The arithmetic units are the easy part of the design; the rest of the anatomy exists to keep them fed.
The definition becomes concrete in the generic chip of figure 1, which serves as this chapter’s map. External high-bandwidth memory (HBM) feeds shared on-chip storage (an L2 cache), which distributes operands into rows of processing elements, each equipped with a private scratchpad or cache, a matrix unit, a vector unit, and a special function unit. A host interface connects the chip to the CPU that issues its work.






Figure 1: Anatomy of a Modern AI Accelerator: This generic schematic combines common components rather than depicting one product. A host interface connects the accelerator to a CPU, a high-bandwidth device-memory interface feeds shared on-chip storage, and processing elements contain matrix, vector, and special-function units with local memory. Real accelerators differ in which units they provide and whether storage is hardware-managed cache or software-managed scratchpad.



Within each processing element, specialized units partition execution across distinct mathematical primitives: dedicated matrix units (Tensor Cores) execute dense matrix multiplication, vector units evaluate element-wise arithmetic, and special function units (SFUs) approximate transcendental operations such as activations and exponentials. Their number, grouping, and names vary by vendor; some designs arrange them into an explicit 2D systolic grid, and others distribute matrix engines among wide parallel cores.
The memory hierarchy amortizes the cost of data transport across tiers. High-bandwidth memory provides off-chip capacity and throughput, while shared on-chip storage and per-element caches or scratchpads cut off-chip traffic. Because moving a tensor tile across the package boundary costs orders of magnitude more energy than keeping it on chip, compilers and kernels must coordinate tile capacity, reuse, and prefetching to keep operands staged locally. More HBM bandwidth raises the off-chip ceiling, but without local reuse the execution units still stall. The system assumptions appendix (System Assumptions) collects reference specifications for the accelerators this book uses, including the H100.
The host interface links the accelerator to the host CPU, which coordinates execution graphs, asynchronous I/O, and fallback operations while the accelerator executes dispatched kernels. Direct-memory-access engines can overlap host-device transfers with execution, but an operator unsupported by the accelerator backend may require a CPU round-trip. An operator outside the matrix-unit instruction set may instead use vector or other device kernels. These execution boundaries help set the effective speedup envelope. Kernel execution time matters little if transfers, launches, and synchronization dominate end-to-end latency. The three parts of the figure (the processing elements, the memory tiers, and the host link) are the parts this chapter takes apart in turn.
The anatomy embodies the chapter’s central engineering trade-off. General-purpose processors allocate silicon area to complex control logic, speculative execution, branch prediction, and multi-level cache hierarchies to handle arbitrary control flow. An accelerator redirects that transistor budget toward dense arithmetic arrays, dedicated register files, and high-bandwidth memory paths tailored to a narrower workload class. When the software path exposes sufficient tensor parallelism, this specialization yields order-of-magnitude improvements in energy efficiency and throughput per watt. Silicon built for a narrow class of dense tensor operations pays off only because, as the bitter lesson predicts, the general methods that win by exploiting computation keep reducing to those same operations at ever larger scale. The dependence also runs the other way, because scale keeps winning only while accelerators keep lowering the time and energy of each additional operation, so the hardware this chapter studies is part of what sustains the bitter lesson itself.


↩︎ The bitter lesson, the observation that general methods exploiting computation win as computation grows, is established in The Bitter Lesson.
Hardware alone cannot achieve these gains. Algorithms must structure operations to expose data reuse and regular memory access, while silicon architectures must allocate physical units to the mathematical primitives and numeric precisions that algorithms actually execute. That mutual dependence motivates a complementary principle: hardware-software co-design.

Definition 11.2: Hardware-software co-design
Hardware-Software Co-design is an ML accelerator development method that crosses conventional abstraction boundaries, allowing algorithm constraints to inform silicon design and hardware capabilities to shape algorithm formulation.

Significance: On a supported tensor-core path, 8-bit integer (INT8) quantization can deliver multi-fold throughput gains because hardware executes lower-precision operations more densely and moves fewer bytes than an FP32 path; the exact gain depends on the architecture and workload (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a; Dally et al. 2021; Dally 2023).
Distinction: Unlike layered abstraction (where software calls a hardware API without knowing the silicon details), co-design exposes hardware constraints directly to algorithm and compiler authors: data alignment requirements, precision formats, and memory access patterns all become visible inputs to global cross-layer optimization.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that co-design is a one-time hardware design choice. In practice, the supported features continue to evolve: NVIDIA Tensor Cores began with FP16 matrix multiplication, later generations added TF32 and broader integer support, and Ampere added acceleration for 2:4 structured sparsity (NVIDIA 2017; NVIDIA Corporation 2020a).



Co-design explains why model compression techniques deliver real speedups. Quantization shows why converting FP32 to INT8 accelerates execution on supported hardware: reduced precision cuts memory traffic, while specialized arithmetic units execute more low-precision operations per cycle than FP32 equivalents (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). Structured pruning improves performance when it produces smaller dense shapes or a sparsity pattern recognized by silicon, whereas arbitrary unstructured sparsity incurs metadata handling and non-coalesced memory accesses that often erase theoretical gains. Evaluating accelerator performance requires tracing this path from workload to silicon: compute primitives, memory hierarchies, roofline diagnosis, mapping and dataflow, and compiler scheduling. The recurring question is why algorithmic improvements frequently fail to deliver proportional end-to-end speedups. Amdahl’s law (principle \(\ref{pri-amdahl}\)) already answered it for model-side optimizations, since whatever an optimization leaves untouched caps the overall gain. The same bound governs hardware. The theorem below applies the principle to an accelerator, and the only new quantity is the gain, which becomes the accelerator’s path gain \(\AcceleratorGain\).


↩︎ Quantization and its effect on weight payload, memory traffic, and compute cost are established in Numerical Precision: Changing How Values Are Stored.

Theorem 11.1: The fundamental limit of acceleration (Amdahl's law)Hardware acceleration does not speed up the entire system; it speeds only the baseline-time fraction using the accelerated path. For that fraction \(\ParallelFraction\) and path gain \(\AcceleratorGain\), Amdahl’s law (Amdahl 1967) gives the bound in equation 1. \[ \text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1 - \ParallelFraction) + \frac{\ParallelFraction}{\AcceleratorGain}}  \tag{1}\]

Accelerated fraction (\(\ParallelFraction\)): Share of baseline time receiving the stated gain, often in matrix multiplication or another supported kernel.
Accelerator gain (\(\AcceleratorGain\)): The raw speed advantage of the GPU or Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) over the CPU for the accelerated portion of the workload.
Unaccelerated fraction (\(1-\ParallelFraction\)): Work outside the chosen path, such as data loading, host overhead, unsupported operators, and kernel launch latency.

Pitfall: Unaccelerated work caps total speedup. If 10 percent of baseline time is unaffected (\(\ParallelFraction=0.9\)), even infinite path gain (\(\AcceleratorGain=\infty\)) yields at most 10\(\times\) overall. Once the accelerated component is fast enough, unaffected work dominates.



Amdahl, Gene M. 1967. “Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities.” Proceedings of the April 18-20, 1967, Spring Joint Computer Conference on - AFIPS ’67 (Spring), AFIPS ’67 (spring), 483–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560.
1 Amdahl’s law: Maps onto the iron law only after the proposed change is specified. If a faster tensor unit reduces the computation term \((\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\) but leaves data transfer and fixed latency unchanged, those unaffected terms bound total speedup. A different accelerator or memory system may improve bandwidth as well. The unaccelerated fraction is therefore defined by the intervention, not by a permanent classification of each term as serial.Hardware acceleration targets specific terms in the iron law of ML systems, which decomposes end-to-end time into data movement \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\), computation \((\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\), and fixed latency \((\Latency)\). Data selection reduced the number of samples processed (\(\text{Samples/Task}\), shrinking both \(\Operations\) and input traffic \(\DataVolume\)), and model compression reduced the operations and bytes per sample (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) and weight traffic \(\DataVolume\)). Hardware acceleration instead reduces the realized time per operation (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) by improving \(\PeakRate\), \(\EfficiencyHw\), and \(\Bandwidth\). Which of these physical terms an upgrade actually improves determines its accelerated fraction under Amdahl’s law.1

This dynamic explains why hardware upgrades frequently fail to produce proportional end-to-end speedups. Where the unaccelerated fraction \(1-\ParallelFraction\) remains substantial, the white contour curves flatten horizontally into the unaccelerated-bound regime, bounding total speedup at the \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) asymptote regardless of how far \(\AcceleratorGain\) scales along the horizontal axis. Because \(\ParallelFraction\) differs substantially across workload archetypes running on identical hardware, a workload’s vertical position on this map determines whether an accelerator investment pays off or stalls on non-matrix operations.

The serial bottleneck becomes concrete on real hardware, where the same accelerator that nears its parallel ceiling on one workload can stall on another. The comparison below uses the INT8 (8-bit integer) path, whose advantage over FP32 or FP16 has two sources. Each operand occupies a half or a quarter of the bytes, and an 8-bit multiplier occupies far less silicon area than a floating-point one, so the same die holds more multiply-accumulate (MAC) units. Two workloads on an NVIDIA H100 with different unaccelerated fractions show how that fraction governs whether this peak INT8 advantage becomes realized speedup. Lighthouse 11.1: An illustrative Amdahl budget on H100Illustrative ResNet-50 inference on NVIDIA H100:

Assume H100 provides \(\AcceleratorGain\) = 247× on matrix multiplication relative to a server CPU without matrix extensions (1979 TOPS INT8 vs. ~8 TOPS) (Choquette 2023). The CPU’s INT8 rate is a scenario assumption for this budget, not the FP32 peak of the reference CPU used elsewhere in the chapter.
Assume \(\ParallelFraction\) = 0.95: 95 percent of baseline time receives that gain, while 5 percent remains in data loading, preprocessing, postprocessing, and other work. \[
\text{$\text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1-0.95) + \frac{0.95}{247}} = \frac{1}{0.05 + 0.0038} \approx 18.6\times$}
\] The 247× path gain produces only 18.6× end-to-end speedup because the 5 percent unaffected fraction sets the ceiling.

Contrast with GPT-2 (autoregressive):

For GPT-2 token generation, assume \(\ParallelFraction\) = 0.80; the remaining 20 percent includes host overhead, sampling, and decoding work outside the accelerated matrix path. \[
\text{$\text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1-0.80) + \frac{0.80}{247}} = \frac{1}{0.20 + 0.0032} \approx 4.9\times$}
\] Less token-generation time receives the assumed gain, so even an infinite path gain yields at most \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) = 5×.

This calculation still overstates the decode path gain. Decode is bandwidth bound, so its accelerated path runs at the rate weights stream from memory rather than at the INT8 TOPS rate. The relevant ratio is the H100’s memory bandwidth over the reference CPU socket’s, 67× (a different path from the host-DRAM link used below). INT8 helps decode on either machine by halving the bytes each weight occupies relative to FP16, not by multiplying faster. With that gain the bound falls from 4.9× to 4.7×, barely moving, because the unaccelerated fraction already dominates. Two distinct limits are at work. Bandwidth-boundedness shrinks \(\AcceleratorGain\), whereas the unaccelerated fraction caps what any \(\AcceleratorGain\) can deliver. Serving optimizations attack both. Batching raises the work done per weight byte fetched. Speculative decoding, developed in Model Serving, lets a small draft model propose several tokens that the full model then verifies in one step, reducing the number of sequential full-model steps.


Whether an operation is limited by compute rate or by data movement dictates both hardware selection and software optimization. Under the arithmetic intensity law (principle \(\ref{pri-arithmetic-intensity}\)), upgrading to an accelerator with \(10\times\) higher peak compute yields negligible speedup if data delivery is the binding bottleneck. The roofline model, previewed in Matching workloads to hardware, makes this diagnosis (Williams et al. 2009). It compares an operation’s arithmetic intensity, the ratio of operations to bytes of memory traffic (FLOP/byte), with the hardware’s ridge point. An operation below the ridge is bandwidth bound, the regime the roofline literature calls memory bound; an operation above it is compute bound. GPT-2 decode and ResNet-50 sit on opposite sides of that line, a difference the Amdahl budget above already registered in the decode path gain. Section 11.6 turns the classification into numbers once the compute units and memory systems that set the two ceilings have been examined.

Compute primitives and compute units supply the arithmetic side of the anatomy, ending with the INT8 and sparse paths that ResNet-50’s profile depends on, and memory systems supply the other side, from registers to host memory. Performance bounds then combine the two into the roofline’s ceilings and show which ResNet-50 layers clear the H100’s ridge at FP16 and which fall below it at INT8; this is the chapter’s midpoint, marked by a checkpoint. The second half asks how software reaches those ceilings, through hardware mapping and then the compilers and runtimes that make its choices automatically. Three shorter sections widen the view to work beyond one accelerator, heterogeneous systems-on-chip, and the choice of an accelerator for a workload and a budget.

General-purpose processors dedicate substantial silicon area and power to instruction fetch, branch prediction, out-of-order scheduling, and cache coherence, machinery built for arbitrary control flow that yields poor arithmetic density on regular, dense linear algebra. When Google deployed its first Tensor Processing Unit (TPU v1) into production data centers alongside contemporary CPUs and NVIDIA K80 GPUs, stripping away that general-purpose control machinery in favor of a dedicated matrix array produced an immediate efficiency jump (example 11.1). Whenever an algorithmic pattern becomes sufficiently dominant and structured, specialized hardware outperforms general-purpose platforms by replacing dynamic control hardware with dense arithmetic arrays and software-managed data movement.

Example 11.1: The TPU v1 vs. K80 efficiency gapScenario: In 2015, Google deployed its first Tensor Processing Unit (TPU v1) into production data centers, comparing its throughput and energy efficiency against general-purpose NVIDIA K80 GPUs (Jouppi et al. 2017).
Diagnosis: The K80 was a programmable GPU designed to support a broader mix of graphics and compute workloads. The TPU v1 domain-specific architecture (DSA) made a narrower, inference-focused design choice, pairing a large 8-bit systolic matrix unit with software-managed memory and simpler control.
Systems lesson: On the six Google inference workloads and contemporary CPU/GPU baselines evaluated in the TPU paper, tailoring silicon to the dominant matrix operations delivered 15–30\(\times\) higher throughput and 30–80\(\times\) better performance per watt (Jouppi et al. 2017). Those ratios describe the evaluated systems, not every workload.


2 TPU (tensor processing unit): The first TPU made a deliberately narrow design choice, centering the design on a single \(256{\times}256\) systolic array for 8-bit matrix multiplication and avoiding much of the control machinery required by a general-purpose core (Jouppi et al. 2017). That trade buys high compute density on dense matrix multiplication at the cost of flexibility. Irregular or branch-heavy code remains a poor fit, and compiler tiling, padding, and layer dimensions determine how fully the array is used.
