In D·A·M terms, this efficiency gain stems from tailoring machine resources to algorithmic structure. The TPU2 replaced hardware caches with software-managed buffers and routed data directly between neighboring arithmetic units, raising data reuse and cutting off-chip traffic. The cost is rigidity. Irregular memory access, dynamic control flow, or an unsupported numeric precision stalls a fixed-function data path and leaves expensive silicon idle. Every modern ML accelerator, from DianNao-class designs (Chen et al. 2014) to GPUs with Tensor Cores, strikes its own balance between specialization and flexibility, following a pattern that began decades before deep learning.


On a late-1970s microprocessor without floating-point hardware, a single 32-bit floating-point multiply required a software routine of dozens of integer shift-and-add instructions, turning scientific and signal-processing loops into an instruction-fetch bottleneck. Hardware specialization emerges whenever one computational pattern becomes a bottleneck that general-purpose processors cannot scale past. The Intel 8087 coprocessor (1980) executed floating-point operations directly in hardware (Palmer 1980), and the Intel 486DX (1989) later moved the floating-point unit onto the CPU die itself (Hennessy and Patterson 2017). That cycle—specializing silicon to relieve an acute bottleneck and integrating it once the capability proves universal—recurs in every later era, and so does its limit. Dedicated silicon removes the instruction overhead around a dominant operation, but the overall gain is bounded by how much of the run time that operation occupies.

Lyons, Richard G. 2011. Understanding Digital Signal Processing. 3rd ed. Prentice Hall.
Graphics supplied the second lesson, throughput over latency. A CPU spends most of its silicon on control logic, branch prediction, and caches that minimize the latency of a single instruction stream, which buys nothing when identical arithmetic must be applied to millions of independent pixels. GPUs reallocated that silicon to dense arrays of arithmetic units, and when unified shader architectures (2006) replaced separate vertex and pixel pipelines with arrays of identical programmable cores, the GPU became a general-purpose parallel processor (Owens et al. 2008). Digital signal processors such as Texas Instruments’ TMS32010 (1983) contributed the memory organization. To meet hard real-time deadlines, they replaced caches, whose misses introduce variable latency, with software-managed scratchpads feeding dedicated MAC data paths (Lyons 2011). ML accelerators inherit both lessons.
The payoff arrived in 2012, when AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al. 2012) won the ImageNet competition after training on two consumer GPUs, the co-design result examined in The deep learning era and the infrastructure bottleneck. Its dense 2D convolutions mapped directly onto thousands of GPU arithmetic lanes. In D·A·M terms, the machine constraint had dictated which algorithms were feasible, and aligning the algorithm’s parallel structure with throughput-oriented hardware lifted it.
Across five eras from the 1980s to the 2020s (figure 3), specialization moved from discrete coprocessors such as the Intel 8087 FPU and TMS32010 DSP through graphics engines and dedicated media codecs to deep-learning tensor arrays and wafer-scale hardware. Each era’s specialized unit targets a different bottleneck, yet the principles modern accelerators depend on (dedicating silicon to the dominant operation, staging operands in local memory, and minimizing off-chip data movement) were all in place before deep learning arrived.






Figure 3: Hardware Specialization Timeline: Computing architectures evolve through recurring cycles of specialization and integration across five eras. Each era introduces domain-specific hardware to resolve an important memory or arithmetic bottleneck, from off-chip FPUs to GPUs, codecs, and TPU/Tensor Core array units. Many of these capabilities later appear alongside CPUs in broader systems, even when the specialized units remain distinct.






A general-purpose CPU core spends most of its energy on instruction fetch and decode, branch prediction, speculative execution, and cache coherence rather than arithmetic: executing one scalar instruction can burn hundreds of picojoules of control overhead just to perform a floating-point operation that costs a few picojoules. For decades, Moore’s law3 (Moore 1998) and Dennard scaling (Dennard et al. 1974) hid that overhead by letting operating voltage fall as transistors shrank, so clock frequencies rose at constant power density. When leakage current halted voltage scaling in the mid-2000s, frequencies stalled against the power wall of Physical Constraints on Deployment. Adding more general-purpose cores then ran into Amdahl’s law and dark silicon, the thermal limit under which only a fraction of a chip’s transistors can switch at full speed simultaneously (Esmaeilzadeh et al. 2011). As Hennessy and Patterson (2019) argued in their Turing Lecture, the way past this wall is domain-specific architectures (DSAs),4 hardware that gives up general-purpose control machinery to spend its power budget directly on the operations a target domain performs.

A DSA wins by specializing every layer of the machine around the workload’s invariants. Its data path is custom-built. Matrix units in AI accelerators are often systolic arrays, grid-like networks of processing elements that compute and forward data directly to neighboring units. A value fetched once from on-chip memory is therefore reused across an entire row or column of multiply-accumulate operations instead of returning to a register file after each use. Its memory hierarchy follows the workload’s reuse pattern, with software-managed scratchpads and prefetching replacing hardware-managed caches for deterministic tensor streams. Its instruction set encodes coarse tensor operations, so one macro-instruction configures thousands of arithmetic units. The same recipe produced smartphone video codecs, genomics aligners, and cryptographic application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) wherever a kernel stabilized (Sullivan et al. 2012; Turakhia et al. 2018; Bedford Taylor 2017).
The pressure to specialize has grown because model demand has outrun single-device hardware scaling. The measured trend is the historical training-compute curve charted in Introduction, whose fitted doubling time runs from 3.4 to about 6 months depending on the window, far faster than the roughly two-year doubling of transistor density (Amodei and Hernandez 2018; Epoch AI 2024). No single chip closes a gap that compounds at that rate; parallelism and co-design must close the rest.

That compounding gap between model demand and transistor scaling turned into an operational crisis at Google in 2013, when an internal projection showed that three minutes of daily voice search per user would require doubling the company’s global CPU fleet just to serve neural-network inference (example 11.2), the projection that launched the TPU v1 program introduced at the start of this section. Many important neural-network workloads concentrate their arithmetic in regular tensor operations, such as dense matrix multiplications and convolutions, with substantial data parallelism, predictable reuse, and tolerance for reduced precision. Other ML operations remain irregular, bandwidth bound, or too small to fill a wide engine, so an accelerator need not speed up every part of a model. Hardware built to exploit the regular portion forms the class of ML accelerators.

Example 11.2: The TPU capacity cliffScenario: Google projected in 2013 that user adoption of voice-search speech recognition (3 minutes/day/user) would require doubling global data center capacity to run CPU-based neural network inference (Jouppi et al. 2017).
Diagnosis: General-purpose CPU server capacity was economically unable to absorb the exponential growth in inference FLOPs, threatening a capital infrastructure bottleneck.
Systems lesson: Custom hardware acceleration becomes a candidate when workload volume makes the existing fleet uneconomical. Workload reuse, supported operations, development cost, and server total cost of ownership determine whether a custom ASIC is preferable to software changes or other hardware.


The fleet projection exposed how little of a CPU’s rated throughput survives on dense tensor layers. Take the chapter’s reference CPU, the low end of the 1–2 TFLOP/s baseline used in the definition of hardware acceleration, and assume it sustains 5 percent–10 percent of its peak on a neural network workload. The upper endpoint then delivers approximately 100 GFLOP/s (billions of floating-point operations per second). CPUs optimize for single-thread performance and irregular memory access, whereas neural networks require extensive parallelism and predictable data streams, and a single layer that touches gigabytes of parameters overwhelms cache hierarchies designed for smaller working sets.
The deeper mismatch is energy. Per event, accessing a 32-bit value from DRAM costs about 640 pJ in the 45 nm estimates of Horowitz (2014), roughly 173× the 3.7 pJ of one FP32 multiply, the same ratio Energy Cost of Moving vs. Computing on a 32-Bit Value reported for the data pipeline. The roughly 145-fold gap quoted with the iron law in Iron Law of ML Systems comes from the same table but compared one DRAM byte, a quarter of this 32-bit access, with one FP16 operation. Exact values vary by technology node and design, but a gap of two orders of magnitude, the energy-movement principle (\(\ref{pri-energy-movement}\)), makes data movement a primary optimization target (Sze et al. 2017). Purpose-built accelerators such as TPUs sustain high utilization on dense kernels because systolic arrays and similar structures maximize data reuse while minimizing movement.
5 Von Neumann bottleneck: Separating storage from compute requires instructions and data to cross interfaces rather than remain in local registers. The exact cost of each crossing changes with technology and operation, but locality remains a first-order design concern.Data access can dominate the energy budget of a memory-intensive kernel.5 On a logarithmic scale, representative 45 nm operation energies span more than four orders of magnitude, from an INT8 addition (\(0.03\text{ pJ}\)) and an FP32 multiply (\(3.7\text{ pJ}\)) to an off-chip DRAM fetch (\(640\text{ pJ}\)) (figure 4). This ladder is the chapter’s single reference for what moving a value costs; later sections cite it rather than restate it.

An off-chip DRAM access costs about 173\(\times\) an FP32 multiply and about 128\(\times\) a read from an 8 KB SRAM array in this model; a small, register-adjacent L1 access (about 0.5 pJ in the registry used elsewhere in this chapter) is cheaper still. The values are not universal device specifications; they illustrate why reuse in registers and SRAM can matter more than reducing arithmetic count alone.



Training and inference load an accelerator differently. Training computes gradients, typically in mixed precision with lower-precision tensor operations and higher-precision accumulation (Micikevicius et al. 2018), and backpropagation retains or recomputes activations, raising memory demand. Inference requires only the forward path and may use INT8 or INT4 when the model and kernels support it. The service objective, whether tail latency, throughput, cost, or energy, then decides which accelerator fits.

Definition 11.3: ML accelerator
Machine Learning Accelerators are processors or specialized units designed primarily for common neural-network tensor operations and dataflows. They pursue high \(\PeakRate\) and data reuse on matching workloads by devoting more resources to arithmetic and local data movement than a general-purpose execution path can.

Significance: An ML accelerator’s defining feature is not raw arithmetic alone but a balanced path that supplies operands and retains reusable values nearby. The H100 provides 3.35 TB/s of device-memory bandwidth, about 16.8× the illustrative 200 GB/s host-DRAM path used here (Choquette 2023). This is a ceiling comparison, not a guarantee: sufficient arithmetic intensity, concurrency, and reuse are still required to approach its 989 TFLOP/s dense FP16/BF16 peak.
Distinction: The gains are conditional on operation support, parallel work, regular data access, and a software stack that selects the intended path. An ML accelerator can be orders of magnitude faster than a reference CPU on large dense matrix multiplication, yet lose much of that advantage on small, irregular, synchronization-heavy, or control-heavy workloads. Transfers and unsupported operators can dominate even when the accelerated kernel itself is fast.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that ML accelerators always accelerate ML. Approaching peak throughput requires a compatible precision, operation shape, layout, and enough parallel work to keep the relevant units busy, and memory and interconnect paths must sustain that work. A batch-1 autoregressive request may therefore use only a small fraction of a large training accelerator’s arithmetic capacity even though the same device performs well on batched prefill or training.



Deployment context decides which constraint binds. In data centers it is often time-to-result for training large models. An NVIDIA H100 trades hundreds of watts of power for high throughput (Choquette 2023), and Google’s TPU v4 makes a similar trade through systolic arrays and high-bandwidth memory (Jouppi et al. 2023); whether either lowers total cost depends on utilization, rental price, workload scaling, and the electricity rate.
At the edge, the priority shifts toward energy per inference and hard latency or power limits. A smartphone camera or always-on audio path inside a few-watt budget cannot adopt a data center memory system, so edge architectures reduce movement through local scratchpads, tight integration, and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. Because the binding constraint differs by setting, no single architecture dominates, yet the memory wall governs both. Data center chips buy capacity and bandwidth with HBM, while edge chips depend on proximity and reuse.

Packing thousands of multiply-accumulate units onto a die buys nothing if those units spend most cycles stalled waiting for operands to cross the memory hierarchy. Once specialized arrays make arithmetic cheap and abundant (Palmer 1980; Sze et al. 2017; Jouppi et al. 2017), the dominant hardware difficulty shifts from computing products to feeding the units that compute them. This integration bottleneck is the memory wall seen from inside the accelerator: transporting operands and results through the memory hierarchy quickly and efficiently enough to keep thousands of parallel compute units busy. Specialized silicon delivers its performance-per-watt advantage only when the workload’s demand concentrates into regular operations that align with the hardware’s data paths.
6 Scratchpad memory: When a compiler can determine a tensor kernel’s access pattern, it can explicitly stage tiles in fast, software-controlled local memory. This avoids some tag, replacement, and coherence machinery, but transfers, synchronization, banking, and capacity must be scheduled correctly. Scratchpads complement rather than universally replace caches because irregular or shared data may still benefit from hardware management. Google’s TPU v1, for example, used a 24 MB software-managed Unified Buffer for intermediate activations, while weights and instructions used other paths (Jouppi et al. 2017).
Jouppi, Norman P., Cliff Young, Nishant Patil, David Patterson, Gaurav Agrawal, Raminder Bajwa, Sarah Bates, et al. 2017. “In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit.” Proceedings of the 44th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, ISCA ’17, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1145/3079856.3080246.
Neural-network kernels make this integration bottleneck tractable because their arithmetic, dataflow, and numerical requirements reinforce one another. Large matrix multiplications and convolutions expose abundant data parallelism that dense processing-element arrays can execute concurrently. Because static or compiled tensor graphs move those operands along predictable paths, compilers can tile and stage transfers into local scratchpads6 instead of relying exclusively on hardware-managed caches. Those staged operands also tolerate reduced precision, allowing supported 8-bit or 4-bit paths to pack more values into each scratchpad and multiply them more densely (Dally et al. 2021; Dally 2023). Workloads dominated by dynamic control flow, large embedding tables, small tensors, variable shapes, or strict precision requirements break these assumptions and remain bound by memory latency and irregular access.
Because off-chip DRAM transfers carry that 173× energy penalty over an FP32 multiply, accelerator architects allocate silicon area and thermal budgets to stacked HBM, wide on-chip SRAM, and software-managed scratchpads rather than packing in additional floating-point logic.7 Those are the memory tiers drawn in figure 1, and they occupy as much of the design as the arithmetic units they feed.
7 HBM: The A100 and H100 generations provide 2.0–3.4 TB/s of device-memory bandwidth through stacked memory and wide interfaces, compared with 760 GB/s for the GDDR6X reference used here (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a; Choquette 2023). Raising the bandwidth ceiling can move some kernels toward the compute-bound side of the roofline, but only if their access pattern and arithmetic intensity can use it. HBM also increases packaging and system cost, so its value depends on the workload’s bandwidth demand.The specialization evident in processing elements, vector pipelines, and tiered scratchpads reflects the computational profile of neural networks, which repeatedly invoke a compact set of linear-algebraic and element-wise primitives. Within the D·A·M framework, an algorithmic change produces a wall-clock speedup only when its computational structure and memory access pattern map onto these primitives; one that cuts theoretical operations without aligning with the hardware’s data paths leaves compute units starved. The next section identifies those primitives, beginning with the multiply-accumulate that carries nearly all of ResNet-50’s arithmetic.

A single forward pass through a neural network layer can issue millions or billions of MAC operations, and executing them one scalar instruction at a time would swamp the processor in instruction-fetch and register-access overhead. Across fully connected, convolutional, and attention layers, learned linear transformations reduce to these repeated MACs, whose regular tensor structure exposes the parallel work and operand reuse that hardware specialization requires. MACs do not dominate every model or phase (normalization, routing, indexing, communication, and element-wise operations can become limiting), but they account for much of the peak arithmetic capacity in modern ML accelerators. Whether they dominate elapsed time still depends on tensor shape, data movement, and the surrounding operators.
The hardware units that exploit these patterns are AI compute primitives: specialized functional blocks, each optimized for a particular class of operation. Three primitives are especially common in accelerators, each targeting a distinct computational pattern found in neural networks; at the framework level, a single declarative statement encapsulates thousands of their arithmetic operations (listing 1).



Listing 1: Dense Layer Abstraction: High-level framework APIs encapsulate 131,072 MACs (256 inputs times 512 outputs) in a single function call, hiding the computational complexity from developers while enabling automatic hardware optimization.


# Framework abstracts compute-intensive operations
dense = Dense(512)(input_tensor)  # 256x512 MACs per sample



Beneath this API call, an autograd or compilation engine lowers the layer into a computational graph. Listing 2 exposes a bulk matrix multiplication and bias broadcast, followed by an optional element-wise activation; the activation is a separate stage rather than an implicit part of the shown Dense call.



Listing 2: Matrix Operation Expansion: Each dense layer decomposes into matrix multiplication and element-wise operations, exposing the dominant compute pattern that many neural-network kernels are built around.


# Linear transformation work scales with input_dim x output_dim x
# batch.
output = (
    matmul(input, weights) + bias
)  # Matrix multiply dominates cost
output = activation(
    output
)  # Element-wise: proportional to output_dim x batch



While graph representations group these steps into coarse tensor operators, execution on physical hardware requires scheduling individual scalar operations. Lowering the matrix multiplication to loop nests (listing 3) makes the execution structure explicit: three nested iterations traverse the batch, output feature, and reduction dimensions, establishing \(\mathcal{O}(\BatchSize\times \LayerInputWidth \times \LayerOutputWidth)\) arithmetic complexity.



Listing 3: Processor-Level Execution: Nested loops reveal the \(\mathcal{O}(\BatchSize \times \LayerInputWidth \times \LayerOutputWidth)\) multiply-accumulate operations that accelerators must execute, with 4.2M MACs for \(\BatchSize\)=32, \(\LayerInputWidth\)=256, \(\LayerOutputWidth\)=512 configurations.


# Total operations: batch_size × output_size × input_size MACs
for n in range(batch_size):  # Batch dimension: parallelizable
    for m in range(output_size):  # Output neurons: parallelizable
        sum = bias[m]  # Initialize accumulator
        for k in range(input_size):  # Reduction dimension: sequential
            sum += input[n, k] * weights[k, m]  # MAC operation
        output[n, m] = activation(sum)  # Nonlinear transformation
# Example work scales as batch_size × output_size ×
# input_size multiply-accumulate operations



These nested loops expose three recurring computational patterns: element-wise operations along vectors, matrix-level multiply-accumulate reductions, and nonlinear transformations. Their ubiquity justifies dedicated hardware execution paths: vector pipelines stream independent elements and reductions, matrix engines organize multiply-accumulate grids across spatial tiles, and special-function units approximate nonlinear math. The boundaries between these units are architectural rather than mathematical; an optimizing compiler frequently fuses operations across all three paths within a single kernel invocation to eliminate intermediate memory traffic.


In the scalar loop nest of listing 3, evaluating a batch of 32 samples through a 256-to-512 dense layer requires 4.2M MACs. A scalar processor must fetch and decode separate instructions to load each input-weight pair, multiply-accumulate them, and advance the loop counters. Vector architectures eliminate this per-element control overhead by packing multiple data elements into wide register files (typically 128 to 512 bits) and applying a single decoded instruction across parallel execution lanes simultaneously.
RISC-V,8 an open instruction-set architecture (ISA) with a standardized vector extension (Waterman et al. 2013), provides a concrete vehicle for this execution model. The contiguous loads in listing 4 assume that the selected weight column has been packed into a contiguous vector; the row-major weights[k, m] access in the scalar example is otherwise strided. In RISC-V vector assembly, code does not depend on a fixed hardware width. The instruction vsetvli queries the hardware to determine how many elements fit into available registers, the code processes that chunk, and the loop repeats until all features are exhausted.
8 RISC-V (reduced instruction set computer V): The open ISA allows hardware teams to add custom ML instructions, including vector dot products, activation functions, and sparse tensor operations, without changing the base ISA. The trade-off is software ecosystem maturity: custom extensions require corresponding compiler, library, and runtime support, which can limit portability and increase integration work.
Waterman, Andrew, Yunsup Lee, Rimas Avizienis, Henry Cook, David Patterson, and Krste Asanovic. 2013. “The RISC-V Instruction Set.” 2013 IEEE Hot Chips 25 Symposium (HCS), 1–1. https://doi.org/10.1109/hotchips.2013.7478332.



Listing 4: Vectorized Dot-Product Loop: This illustrative loop processes several element pairs per iteration and reduces them into one scalar dot product.


fmv.w.x fa0, zero          # Scalar dot-product accumulator
fmv.w.x ft1, zero          # Zero seed for vector reduction
loop_feature:
    vsetvli t0, feature_cnt, e32, m1, ta, ma
    vle32.v v1, (in_ptr)
    vle32.v v2, (wt_ptr)
    vfmul.vv v3, v1, v2
    vfmv.v.f v0, ft1
    vfredusum.vs v4, v3, v0
    vfmv.f.s ft0, v4
    fadd.s fa0, fa0, ft0
    slli t1, t0, 2         # Four bytes per FP32 element
    add in_ptr, in_ptr, t1
    add wt_ptr, wt_ptr, t1
    sub feature_cnt, feature_cnt, t0
    bnez feature_cnt, loop_feature



Each pass of the loop in listing 4 asks the hardware how many 32-bit elements fit in its vector registers (vsetvli) and loads that many input and weight elements with two wide loads (vle32.v). It then multiplies them lane by lane (vfmul.vv), reduces the products into a partial sum (vfredusum.vs), and advances the pointers until no elements remain. One decoded instruction thus does the work of a whole chunk of scalar instructions.
Across iterations, the vector multiply instruction processes multiple data elements concurrently while wide loads amortize instruction decode and memory-request overhead. Because the runtime vector length dynamically adapts to the implementation’s hardware width (VLEN), the identical binary executes correctly on both narrow embedded vector units and wide data-center pipelines. For this 256-feature workload, an 8-lane implementation breaks the reduction into approximately 524,288 vector chunks across the batch.

The benefit extends beyond instruction count. Contiguous vector loads can use memory interfaces efficiently, and control overhead is amortized across several data elements. Gather, scatter, masking, and short tails may use fewer lanes or require extra memory transactions, so vector width alone does not guarantee proportional speedup. The architectural pattern is not new. The Cray-19 used vector registers and pipelined functional units for scientific computing in the 1970s (Jordan 1982); modern ML processors apply related principles at much larger commercial scale. In ResNet-50 the vector path carries the ReLU after every convolution and the residual addition that closes every bottleneck block. Each touches every activation element once and performs about one operation per element, so on its own it is limited by how fast the activations stream past, not by lane count.
9 Cray-1 vector legacy: The Cray-1 (1975) used 64-element vector registers with pipelined functional units, allowing a stream of elements to advance through arithmetic operations without issuing one scalar instruction per element. Modern accelerators extend the same principles of wide registers, pipelined execution, and data reuse to vector and matrix tiles.

Vector operations excel at element-wise transformations such as activation functions, where each output depends only on its corresponding input. Neural networks, however, also require structured computations where each output depends on all inputs, the weighted sums that define layer transformations. These many-to-many operations naturally express themselves as matrix multiplications, the second compute primitive.



Evaluating a dense layer one vector dot product at a time wastes reuse: each weight row is loaded for one sample and discarded before the next sample in the batch arrives, and each input vector is re-read for every output neuron. Matrix multiplication eliminates this redundant traffic by organizing work across two-dimensional tiles of weights, activations, and gradients, accounting for much of the arithmetic in dense neural networks (Goodfellow et al. 2016). Hardware and libraries tile those dimensions so blocks of weights and activations are reused across an entire tile while partial sums accumulate locally, though small or irregular matrices can still leave tile capacity unused.


Neural network computations decompose into hierarchical matrix operations. Listing 5 captures this hierarchy through a linear layer that transforms input features into output neurons over a batch. Its expanded mathematics uses a column-batch convention and adds an optional ReLU; this illustrates the arithmetic rather than the framework API’s internal tensor layout or an activation implicit in nn.Linear.



Listing 5: Linear-Layer Operation Hierarchy: The example expands a linear layer into a matrix multiply and bias broadcast, then applies element-wise ReLU, separating the matrix and vector work that hardware must execute.


layer = nn.Linear(256, 512)  # Layer transforms 256 inputs to 512 outputs
output = layer(input_batch)  # Process a batch of 32 samples

# Framework Internal: Core operations (column-batch convention)
Z = matmul(weights, input)  # Matrix: transforms [256×32]
# input to [512×32] output
Z = Z + bias  # Vector: adds bias to each
# output independently
output = relu(Z)  # Vector: applies activation to
# each element independently



The scale of this matrix work follows from the layer dimensions. Each output neuron (512 total) must process all input features (256 total) for every sample in the batch (32 samples). The weight matrix alone contains 256 \(\times\) 512 = 131,072 parameters that define these transformations, illustrating why efficient matrix multiplication dominates performance considerations.
Neural networks employ matrix operations across architectural patterns beyond simple linear layers. Convolution operations transform into matrix multiplications through the im2col technique,10 enabling efficient execution on matrix-optimized hardware. Listing 6 illustrates these applications.
10 Im2col (image-to-column): The im2col lowering of Computational mapping turns convolution into a matrix multiplication by unfolding each receptive-field patch into one row or column of a dense matrix. An explicit materialization can duplicate overlapping values and expand storage by up to roughly the kernel area before edge, stride, and channel effects are considered. Production libraries often use implicit-GEMM or direct-convolution kernels to obtain matrix-friendly execution without materializing the full expanded matrix.


Listing 6: Matrix Patterns Across Architectures: Linear layers, attention mechanisms, and convolutions all reduce key work to matrix multiplications, making matrix hardware the shared primitive across modern neural architectures.


hidden = matmul(weights, inputs)
# weights: [out_dim x in_dim], inputs: [in_dim x tokens]
# Result combines all inputs for each output

# Attention Mechanisms - Multiple matrix operations
Q = matmul(Wq, inputs)
# Project inputs to query space [query_dim x tokens]
K = matmul(Wk, inputs)
# Project inputs to key space [key_dim x tokens]
attention = matmul(Q.T, K)
# Compare all query tokens with all key tokens [tokens x tokens]

# Convolutions - Matrix multiply after reshaping
patches = im2col(input)
# Convert [H x W x C] image to matrix of patches
output = matmul(kernel, patches)
# Apply kernels to all patches simultaneously



These examples differ in tensor shape and reuse pattern, which determines how efficiently each multiplication occupies a matrix unit. Linear layers reuse one weight matrix across a batch; attention forms projections and then a token-to-token score matrix; convolution reuses each kernel across many image patches. Expressing all three as matrix multiplication exposes a common interface to hardware, but it does not make their execution costs identical. Batch size, sequence length, channel count, and tiling determine whether operands are reused locally or repeatedly fetched from memory. For ResNet-50 the lowering is nearly total: every convolution and the final fully connected layer become matrix multiplications, so almost all of its operations run on whatever matrix hardware the accelerator provides. The INT8 profile of Model Compression is in effect a statement about that hardware.



Accelerators therefore need units that handle whole tiles. Listing 7 demonstrates a representative dedicated matrix unit that processes an entire \(16{\times}16\) block at once, illustrating why matrix instructions and Tensor Cores can deliver much higher throughput than scalar or vector-only execution paths (NVIDIA 2017; Intel Corporation 2021a).



Listing 7: Illustrative Matrix-Unit Operation: Representative load, matrix-multiply-accumulate, and store instructions operate on matrix blocks rather than individual scalar elements.


mload mr1, (weight_ptr)     # Load e.g., 16x16 block of
                            # weight matrix
mload mr2, (input_ptr)      # Load corresponding input block
matmul.mm mr3, mr1, mr2     # Multiply and accumulate entire
                            # blocks at once
mstore (output_ptr), mr3    # Store computed output block



The illustrative unit operates on matrix tiles rather than individual elements. A full \(16{\times}16{\times}16\) tile product contains \(16^3=4{,}096\) multiply-accumulate operations, but the cycles required depend on the actual instruction and architecture. Sustained throughput also depends on the number of matrix units, operand precision, issue rate, pipeline behavior, and whether memory can keep the units fed. Matrix units complement vector execution by accelerating structured many-to-many transformations.
Much like vector processing, matrix acceleration has deep historical roots; digital signal processors (DSPs) and graphics processors optimized matrix computations in the 1980s–1990s for image processing, scientific computing, and 3D rendering (Owens et al. 2008; Hwu 2011). Neural networks have made matrix multiplication commercially dominant, driving the integration of two-dimensional systolic arrays and matrix execution engines (such as NVIDIA Tensor Cores and Google TPUs) directly into processor datapaths.

While piecewise-linear functions such as ReLU map to simple vector comparison instructions, transcendental computations (such as exponentials in softmax and GELU, or reciprocal square roots in normalization) cannot be computed directly on multiply-accumulate datapaths without incurring severe cycle penalties. Standard multiply-accumulate hardware evaluates an exponential in softmax, a hyperbolic tangent in GELU, or a reciprocal square root in layer normalization only through a multi-instruction polynomial approximation, which can stall the pipeline between fast matrix kernels. Special Function Units (SFUs) and specialized instruction paths remove this bottleneck, completing the chapter’s trio of processing primitives. The need is not new: floating-point coprocessors addressed scalar arithmetic bottlenecks (Palmer 1980), and digital signal processors added specialized arithmetic for signal-processing workloads (Smith 1997). An implementation may use a standalone unit, vector approximation instructions, or a library sequence, trading accuracy, latency, and throughput. In neural networks, activation, normalization, and softmax operations can become the limiting stage between matrix kernels when repeated memory passes or transcendental functions cap throughput.

Listing 8: Linear–Nonlinear Layer Sequence: A linear layer, ReLU, and BatchNorm combine matrix, element-wise, and normalization work in one common layer sequence.


layer = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(256, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.BatchNorm1d(512)

Listing 9 expands this sequence into its arithmetic primitives, isolating the element-wise thresholding of ReLU from the cross-batch reductions and reciprocal square root required by batch normalization. Here rows are samples and columns are features; weights has input features by output features, while bias, gamma, and beta contain one value per output feature. Keeping the reduced batch dimension permits those per-feature statistics to broadcast across samples.



Listing 9: Nonlinear Operation Expansion: Expanding the layer sequence exposes ReLU comparison, BatchNorm reductions, variance computation, and square-root normalization around the matrix multiply.


Z = matmul(input, weights) + bias  # Linear transformation
H = max(0, Z)  # ReLU activation
mean = reduce_mean(H, axis=0, keepdims=True)  # BatchNorm statistics
var = reduce_mean((H - mean) ** 2, axis=0, keepdims=True)  # Variance computation
output = gamma * (H - mean) / sqrt(var + eps) + beta  # Normalization






Translating these mathematical functions to silicon exposes sharp differences in memory traffic, instruction count, and pipeline utilization. For instance, batch normalization (Ioffe and Szegedy 2015) demands multi-pass statistics gathering across memory, variance accumulation, and a reciprocal square root, while softmax requires computing exponentials across an entire normalization dimension. While a rectified linear unit (ReLU) is mathematically simple, a naive scalar implementation incurs branch overhead or redundant memory round-trips unless fused into adjacent kernels. Listing 10 contrasts the memory and dependency overheads of pointwise activation against multi-pass normalization in an unfused loop model.

The label nonlinear hides three different execution patterns. Pointwise functions such as ReLU leave elements independent and therefore map naturally to vector lanes or parallel threads. Reductions such as the mean and variance in batch normalization introduce cross-element dependencies: partial results must be combined before later stages can proceed. Transcendental functions such as exponential, logarithm, and reciprocal square root add a numerical trade-off because their implementations balance latency, precision, and valid input range. The dependency pattern, not the mathematical label alone, determines whether vector arithmetic, a reduction tree, or a specialized approximation path is appropriate. A faster special-function path accelerates only the operation it implements; it does not remove surrounding tensor traffic or synchronization.
Listing 10 is intentionally dependency-explicit rather than a model of an optimized kernel. The loops expose three state lifetimes: per-element activations, per-feature accumulators, and the final normalized outputs. The normalization parameters cannot be applied until the required statistics are available, so implementations must either retain intermediate activations or recompute them. Training derives those statistics from the current batch, whereas inference can use stored statistics and reduce normalization to an element-wise affine transform. Compilers may fuse legal stages, but the data dependencies determine which transformations preserve the computation. Reading the listing as a dependency graph therefore reveals the durable hardware questions: how often each tensor crosses a memory interface, which intermediates remain local, and where reductions impose synchronization.



Listing 10: ReLU and BatchNorm Operations: Neural networks process input data through element-wise selections and multiple normalization passes, highlighting efficiency challenges in naive implementations.


for batch in range(32):
    for feature in range(512):
        # ReLU: Naive scalar compare/select; optimized kernels
        # usually implement this branchlessly.
        z = matmul_output[batch, feature]
        h = max(0.0, z)  # Conditional operation

        # BatchNorm: Multiple passes over data
        mean_sum[feature] += h  # First pass for mean
        var_sum[feature] += h * h  # Additional pass for variance

        temp[batch, feature] = h  # Extra memory storage needed

# Normalization requires complex arithmetic
for feature in range(512):
    mean = mean_sum[feature] / batch_size
    var = (var_sum[feature] / batch_size) - mean * mean

    # Square root computation: Multiple iterations
    scale = gamma[feature] / sqrt(var + eps)  # Iterative
    # approximation
    shift = beta[feature] - mean * scale

    # Additional pass over data for final computation
    for batch in range(32):
        output[batch, feature] = temp[batch, feature] * scale + shift



The dependency structure in listing 10 exposes two costs of naive execution. The pointwise ReLU and normalization scale-and-shift perform little arithmetic per accessed byte, so materializing each pass can place a low bandwidth ceiling on throughput. In this unfused loop model, temp is stored and reread after batch statistics are finalized; its physical traffic depends on cache residency and the chosen memory interface. Computing \(1/\sqrt{\text{var} + \NumericalStabilityConstant}\) also adds a dependent arithmetic path. The listing illustrates an iterative approximation, but actual kernels may use a reciprocal-square-root instruction and refinement, with device- and accuracy-dependent latency. Specialized function paths address this arithmetic cost, while legal fusion and local buffering reduce intermediate traffic. Neither removes the need to complete the reductions before normalization.



SFUs address arithmetic bottlenecks by implementing nonlinear and transcendental operations in specialized functional units rather than multi-instruction software routines. Accelerators deploy dedicated datapath circuits, such as quadratic polynomial interpolators and small lookup tables (LUTs), that evaluate functions like exponential, reciprocal square root, and logarithm within a few pipeline stages. Listing 11 illustrates how an instruction set exposes these operations alongside vector memory accesses.

The two lighthouses use this path differently. ResNet-50 barely touches it: its only activation is ReLU, a comparison, and its only exponentials are the thousand in its final softmax. GPT-2 XL leans on it at every step, because each attention head applies softmax across the whole context and each feed-forward block applies GELU, so its special-function work grows with sequence length while ResNet-50’s stays fixed.
Vector operations, matrix operations, and special-function paths establish the foundational arithmetic primitives of ML accelerators, but functional units alone do not dictate sustained throughput. These primitives govern what the silicon computes; the execution model and memory hierarchy govern how data feeds the datapath. A matrix unit rated for hundreds of teraFLOP/s will idle if memory bandwidth cannot sustain operand delivery, if tile dimensions mismatch register blocking, or if thread synchronization serializes execution. Peak assumes operands are always ready; the execution model decides how much of it a real workload achieves.

Applying ReLU to a 512-element vector shows why execution models matter. The operation is simple, but throughput depends on whether the hardware treats those 512 comparisons as scalar instructions, as lanes of a single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) unit, as GPU threads, or as tensor-program fragments. Modern AI processors package the three compute primitives into distinct execution units: vector units for vector work, matrix units such as Tensor Cores and systolic arrays for matrix work, and special function units for nonlinear functions. They then group those units into processing elements. That organization defines how computations are structured and exposed to programmers, and it explains why theoretical capability and delivered throughput diverge.
The packaging follows reuse per operand. For the reference low-precision operations, reading an operand from a register file and moving it across on-chip wires can cost more energy than the arithmetic itself, so each primitive goes to the unit whose dataflow supplies the reuse it offers. In D·A·M terms, this partition binds algorithmic primitives to machine execution paths. Routing dense matrix multiplications through vector pipelines saturates register-file read ports and collapses throughput to a small fraction of peak, while routing low-intensity elementwise work through matrix arrays leaves their lanes idle.


Even a wide CPU vector unit stalls when streaming through gigabytes of tensor data: cache misses freeze the pipeline for hundreds of cycles waiting on main memory, the instruction reorder buffer fills, and the SIMD lanes sit empty. The vector path of section 11.3.1 follows Flynn’s SIMD execution model, which amortizes instruction fetch and decode by issuing a single decoded instruction across multiple data elements packed into wide vector registers (Flynn 1966). A 512-bit SIMD register processes sixteen 32-bit floating-point values per instruction. The same idea appears in fixed-width CPU vector extensions, Arm’s length-agnostic Scalable Vector Extension (SVE) (Stephens et al. 2017), and two-dimensional tile extensions such as Intel’s Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) (Intel Corporation 2021a). Even so, those wide registers still live inside a CPU core built around branch predictors, out-of-order execution logic, and deep cache hierarchies for a few sequential threads. Conditional branching within a vector also requires evaluating divergent paths under bitmasks, further cutting useful lane utilization.

11 SM (streaming multiprocessor): The physical hardware engine that implements the SIMT model by using warp schedulers to coordinate many parallel threads. Maintaining enough active warps can help hide instruction and memory latency, but occupancy alone does not identify the bottleneck. Low occupancy may result from register use, shared-memory use, block dimensions, or insufficient parallel work, while a memory-bound kernel can still have high occupancy.Architectures built on single instruction, multiple threads (SIMT) execution resolve these bottlenecks by decoupling the logical programming abstraction from physical hardware execution (Lindholm et al. 2008; Nickolls et al. 2008). Instead of requiring the programmer to pack data into explicit vector registers, SIMT exposes an execution model of independent scalar threads. In GPU architectures, each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)11 coordinates thousands of concurrent threads. Hardware warp schedulers group these threads into warps, the 32-thread scheduling groups (wavefronts in AMD architectures) whose granularity already set lane utilization in training kernels. Every thread in a warp executes a common instruction in lockstep across parallel ALUs. This lockstep execution introduces a constraint known as warp divergence. When threads within a single warp take different paths through a conditional branch, the hardware must execute both required paths sequentially, masking off the inactive lanes during each path. This serialization reduces useful lane utilization and increases execution time, which is why performance-critical ML kernels avoid divergent branching in favor of uniform or predicated control flow.


↩︎ Warps as the 32-thread unit in which GPUs schedule tensor kernels are established in Compute operations.
Rather than relying on large caches to reduce memory latency, GPUs hide latency through extensive thread-level concurrency. An SM statically partitions an on-chip register file across all active threads, eliminating context-saving overhead. When one warp stalls waiting hundreds of cycles for an off-chip memory fetch, the warp scheduler selects and issues instructions from another ready warp on the very next cycle. The baseline matrix multiplication kernel in listing 12 illustrates how this scalar thread model maps onto hardware. CUDA organizes a grid of threads into blocks: blockIdx locates a block in the grid, blockDim gives the block dimensions, and threadIdx locates a thread within that block. Multiplying a block coordinate by its dimension and adding the within-block coordinate gives the global row or column used by the listing.



Listing 12: SIMT Execution: Each thread processes a unique output element in parallel, demonstrating how SIMT enables efficient matrix multiplication on GPUs.


__global__ void matrix_multiply(float* C, float* A, float*
                                B, int N) {  // CUDA kernel
    // Each thread processes one output element
    int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
    int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;

    float sum = 0.0f;
    for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
        // Threads in a warp execute in parallel
        sum += A[row * N + k] * B[k * N + col];
    }
    C[row * N + col] = sum;
}



In listing 12, the CUDA12 kernel assigns one output element C[row * N + col] to each thread. Adjacent threads in a warp share the same row index while having consecutive column indices (threadIdx.x). When threads fetch B[k * N + col], their memory requests target contiguous 4-byte floating-point addresses. The memory controller merges these 32 individual 4-byte loads into a single 128-byte coalesced memory transaction, maximizing DRAM bus efficiency. Concurrently, all threads in the warp read the identical element A[row * N + k], allowing the hardware to broadcast that single fetched value across all 32 lanes. However, this naive kernel runs into the arithmetic intensity law (principle \(\ref{pri-arithmetic-intensity}\)). Because each inner-loop iteration performs only two floating-point operations while reloading operands from global memory without on-chip SRAM staging, the kernel remains severely memory bound. Furthermore, executing dense matrix multiplication on scalar SIMT ALUs requires one instruction fetch, decode, and issue cycle for every multiply-accumulate, saturating register file read ports. Overcoming this machine bottleneck requires moving beyond vector-of-scalars execution to specialized two-dimensional matrix units.
12 CUDA (compute unified device architecture): Released by NVIDIA in 2006, CUDA eliminated the need to disguise general-purpose computations as graphics operations, opening GPUs to scientific and ML workloads through a C-like programming model. The ecosystem it created (cuBLAS, cuDNN, TensorRT) constitutes a software ecosystem whose switching cost can lock the ML training stack to NVIDIA hardware: migrating away requires rewriting or replacing thousands of GPU-optimized kernels, a cost that often exceeds the hardware savings of competing platforms. This software lock-in, not raw silicon performance alone, helps explain why many large ML training stacks remain CUDA-centered.


For a single transformer attention head over a 2,048-token sequence with 64-dimensional embeddings, the \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\times \AttentionKeyMatrix^T\) product multiplies a \(2048{\times}64\) matrix by a \(64{\times}2048\) matrix. That is roughly 268.4M MACs, or 536.9 MFLOP when the multiply and add are counted separately. On a scalar processor executing one FLOP per cycle at 2 GHz, that single attention head would take 268.4 ms. Even on GPU SIMT lanes, issuing a separate scalar fused multiply-add for every element pair saturates instruction-issue bandwidth and register-file read ports. Dedicated matrix engines remove both bottlenecks by organizing work around multidimensional tiles and reusing fetched operands across many multiply-accumulate operations on chip. NVIDIA GPUs expose Tensor Cores, the reduced-precision matrix units13 that mixed-precision training was built to exploit, whereas Google TPUs use matrix units built around systolic arrays. Both execute tiled matrix multiplication and accumulation.14

Assume, for illustration, that the Tensor Cores of a single streaming multiprocessor complete that 2,048-token attention head in 0.5 ms, an implied rate of about 1.1 TFLOP/s and a small slice of a full GPU’s tensor peak. The tiled path is then roughly 536.9× faster than the scalar baseline, and that speedup comes not from a higher clock frequency but from hardwiring tile-level data reuse into the execution datapath. Whether a workload reaches that rate depends on tile reuse, matrix shape, numeric precision, and memory delivery.
In NVIDIA Parallel Thread Execution (PTX), Tensor Core operations are invoked through warp-synchronous matrix instructions (mma.sync).15 The mnemonic encodes the tile geometry and data types: .m16n8k16 gives the tile dimensions (\(\GemmRowDimension=16, \GemmColumnDimension=8, \GemmInnerDimension=16\)), and the trailing types (.f32.f16.f16.f32) declare FP16 inputs accumulated into an FP32 destination. In listing 13, all 32 threads in a warp execute this single instruction collectively to compute the tile product \(\MatrixMultiplyDestination= \GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand+ \GemmOutputMatrix\).
15 Tensor Core: A single Tensor Core instruction executes a complete matrix-multiply-accumulate operation on a small tile of data using a dedicated hardware block (NVIDIA 2017; NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). This approach bypasses the overhead of fetching and scheduling dozens of individual arithmetic instructions on general-purpose CUDA cores. Because these blocks constitute a large fraction of a modern accelerator’s advertised tensor throughput, failing to use them can leave most of the chip’s theoretical peak unavailable to the workload.

Listing 13: Tensor Core Operation: Matrix multiplications are performed in parallel across entire matrix blocks, optimizing computational efficiency for neural network training.



Tensor Core Operation (example GPU PTX):
mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k16.row.col.f32.f16.f16.f32
  {d0,d1,d2,d3},     // Destination registers
  {a0,a1,a2,a3},     // Source matrix A
  {b0,b1},           // Source matrix B
  {c0,c1,c2,c3};     // Accumulator



Here inputs \(\GemmLeftOperand\) (\(16{\times}16\)) and \(\GemmRightOperand\) (\(16{\times}8\)) are FP16, while accumulator \(\GemmOutputMatrix\) and destination \(\MatrixMultiplyDestination\) (\(16{\times}8\)) are FP32. The register operands in listing 13 represent the per-thread fragment held by each of the 32 threads in the warp rather than the entire matrix tile. Because each 32-bit GPU register packs two 16-bit FP16 values, a single thread’s four source registers {a0,a1,a2,a3} hold 8 FP16 elements of \(\GemmLeftOperand\), so all 32 threads together supply the \(32 \times 8 = 256\) elements of the \(16{\times}16\) tile. Similarly, {b0,b1} holds 4 FP16 elements per thread (\(32 \times 4 = 128\) elements for the \(16{\times}8\) tile \(\GemmRightOperand\)), and {c0,c1,c2,c3} holds four 32-bit FP32 accumulator elements per thread (\(32 \times 4 = 128\) elements for the \(16{\times}8\) tile \(\GemmOutputMatrix\)). A single warp instruction evaluates all \(16 \times 8 \times 16 = 2{,}048\) multiply-accumulate operations that would otherwise require 64 separate scalar fused multiply-add (fma) instructions per thread. This tile-level execution relieves two bottlenecks of conventional SIMT pipelines: instruction-issue bandwidth and register-file read-port contention. In scalar SIMT execution, every fma reads its source operands fresh from the register file, whereas the Tensor Core reads each thread’s register fragment once and reuses every fetched element across multiple inner-product steps inside the matrix datapath.
Design priorities determine how matrix engines appear in different processor families. GPU Tensor Cores preserve programmability while accelerating general-purpose deep learning kernels. TPU-style designs use large-scale matrix units arranged in systolic arrays to maximize sustained training throughput on dense tensor kernels. Mobile NPUs16 shrink the same idea into low-power inference blocks, while server CPUs add matrix instruction extensions (AMX-class tiles) for inference and mixed workloads. Each version keeps a different amount of flexibility in exchange for removing a different amount of data movement.
16 NPU (neural processing unit): Mobile NPUs achieve low-power inference by implementing common tensor operations in fixed-function or narrowly programmable hardware rather than as fully general GPU kernels. This architectural commitment can deliver large energy-efficiency gains for supported kernels, but it makes deployment dependent on operator coverage: unsupported functions must fall back to a CPU or GPU path that may be far less efficient for that workload (Sze et al. 2017).

Tensor Cores also changed how each accelerator generation states its peak. Successive generations combined more matrix units with narrower formats (FP16, then INT8, FP8, and FP4) and, from Ampere onward, a structured-sparsity path. As a result, the headline rating rose by more than three orders of magnitude between 2012 and 2024 while measuring a different precision at almost every step (NVIDIA Corporation 2017, 2020a, 2024; Choquette 2023). A peak quoted without its precision and sparsity assumption therefore says little about a given workload. The generation-by-generation ratings, with their precision-specific peaks, bandwidths, and power limits, are collected with the other dated specifications in Master accelerator matrix. Whatever the format, a Tensor Core retires a tile per instruction only when its operands are already nearby, so accelerators never deploy matrix units on their own. The next level of the execution hierarchy exists to supply that proximity.



High-throughput matrix units cannot be fed directly from global memory: off-chip DRAM and even on-package HBM lack the bandwidth and low latency required to stream fresh operands into dense arithmetic arrays on every cycle. Accelerators resolve this bandwidth deficit by grouping Tensor Cores, vector units, and special function units alongside high-bandwidth register files and scratchpad SRAM inside modular processing elements (PEs). Staging operands inside the PE keeps data adjacent to the functional units, amortizing the latency and energy cost of external memory accesses across repeated arithmetic reuse. The term is used at two scales in this chapter. Here a PE is a tile or core that bundles several units with local memory, the role a streaming multiprocessor plays in a GPU and a core plays in a TPU. Inside a systolic array (section 11.4.4), a PE is a single multiply-accumulate cell in the grid.
Processing element design varies because each architecture chooses a different balance between compute density, local memory capacity, and interconnect distance. Graphcore’s Intelligence Processing Unit (IPU), for example, distributes computation across tiles backed by dedicated local SRAM (Graphcore 2020). Retaining an operand in one tile saves external traffic, but a consumer on another tile still requires an interconnect transfer. Local storage therefore shifts the mapping problem toward keeping repeated consumers close to their operands.

Graphcore. 2020. The Colossus MK2 IPU Processor.
Across these designs, the binding physical constraint is compute density versus data locality: silicon area dedicated to arithmetic units cannot simultaneously house SRAM storage or routing wires. Packing more execution units raises peak theoretical FLOP/s, but those units idle if memory bandwidth and routing channels cannot deliver operands. A processing element’s delivered efficiency therefore depends as much on its local memory hierarchy and interconnect strategy as on its raw arithmetic capability. Systolic arrays push this locality principle to its limit: rather than staging operands in a processing element’s local memory and fetching them again for each operation, they pass operands directly from one processing element to its neighbor.



Even when operands sit in local SRAM or registers, reading two inputs and writing a partial sum back to a central register file on every multiply-accumulate burns wire energy and port bandwidth that limit how many arithmetic cells a chip can pack. While Tensor Cores amortize register access across instruction-driven micro-tiles, systolic arrays remove intermediate register-file round-trips altogether by wiring hundreds or thousands of processing elements into two-dimensional spatial grids. In a classic 2D systolic array, data streams rhythmically through adjacent cells on regular clock cycles: inputs march horizontally, partial sums accumulate vertically, and stationary weights remain anchored in place. Because every value passed from one processing element to its immediate neighbor participates in an arithmetic operation without returning to a register file or SRAM buffer, nearest-neighbor wires replace memory reads. An operand loaded once at the array edge contributes to \(\SquareGemmDimension\) sequential multiply-accumulate steps across an \(\SquareGemmDimension \times \SquareGemmDimension\) grid, driving memory traffic down by an order of magnitude. Counting DRAM accesses per multiply-accumulate with and without neighbor-to-neighbor passing makes the saving concrete.

Napkin Math 11.1: The energy advantage of pulsing data
Scenario: The systolic architecture improves energy efficiency by keeping operands local as work pulses through the array; the “Systolic” (heartbeat) metaphor reflects this benefit of reusing operands locally. This worked model compares systolic dataflow with a naive implementation that streams every operand through DRAM:

DRAM-streaming baseline: Loads \(\GemmLeftOperand\), \(\GemmRightOperand\), and the running \(\GemmOutputMatrix\), computes \(\GemmLeftOperand\times \GemmRightOperand+ \GemmOutputMatrix\), and writes \(\GemmOutputMatrix\) back without cache or register reuse.

Data movement: 3 loads + 1 write = 4 DRAM accesses (per operation).
Energy: ≈ 4 \(\times\) 640 pJ + 1 pJ (compute) = 2561 pJ/op.

Systolic array (128 \(\times\) 128): Loads \(\GemmLeftOperand\) and \(\GemmRightOperand\) once at the edges. Data “pulses” through 128 processing elements.

Data movement: 2 loads per 128 operations = 0.016 DRAM accesses (per operation).
Energy: ≈ 0.016 \(\times\) 640 pJ + 1 pJ (compute) ≈ 11 pJ/op.


Systems insight: Under this deliberately naive DRAM-streaming baseline, the worked model gives the systolic array a 232.8× energy advantage. The ratio measures locality, not an inherent gap between vector and systolic arithmetic.

Concretely, a \(128{\times}128\) array can sustain 16,384 MACs/cycle with a large energy saving by pulsing data through processing elements instead of repeatedly loading it from DRAM (Horowitz 2014; Jouppi et al. 2023).
This locality lets dense arrays sustain many simultaneous MAC operations without paying a DRAM access for every operation.
Limitation: The comparison assumes no effective reuse in the baseline and full reuse across the array. Caches, register blocking, array underutilization, and other dataflows change the ratio substantially.



17 Systolic array: Kung and Leiserson used the term for arrays in which data advances through neighboring processing elements on a regular schedule (Kung and Leiserson 1979). Pipeline fill permits concurrent wavefronts and local reuse. The benefit depends on the stationary operand, tile, buffers, and utilization; it does not guarantee fixed DRAM savings. Irregular workloads and poorly aligned shapes remain a weaker fit because fill, drain, and idle elements consume capacity.

Kung and Leiserson17 (Kung and Leiserson 1979) first introduced systolic arrays, formalizing their use in parallel computing architectures for efficient matrix operations (Kung 1982). Unlike general-purpose execution units, systolic arrays exploit spatial and temporal locality by reusing operands as they propagate through the grid. Google’s TPU exemplifies this architectural approach: in the TPU v4, a \(128{\times}128\) systolic array of multiply-accumulate units processes matrix operations by streaming data through the array in a pipelined manner (Jouppi et al. 2023). Figure 5 traces this 2D pipelined dataflow: a control unit stages operands into input FIFO buffers that stream activation data horizontally across the processing grid, while partial sums accumulate vertically down columns into the bottom adder-accumulator chain. Each processing element performs one multiply-accumulate per cycle and passes its operands to its neighbors, so a value loaded once is reused across an entire row or column rather than refetched from memory.






Figure 5: Systolic Array Dataflow Architecture: A pipelined grid of processing elements (PEs) passes operands and partial results between neighbors. The illustrated movement is one possible matrix-multiplication dataflow; designs choose which operand or partial sum remains stationary to match reuse, buffers, and tensor shape. Utilization depends on mapping and dimensions.



A 128 \(\times\) 128 systolic array capable of 16,384 operations per cycle requires a continuous operand stream to maintain utilization. On-chip buffers feed activations and weights to the array edges and are replenished from off-chip memory as needed; reuse within the array avoids fetching every operand from HBM each cycle. The TPU v4’s 1,200 GB/s HBM2 bandwidth helps sustain this stream, but off-chip bandwidth can still limit models whose working sets and reuse patterns exceed on-chip capacity.

Systems Perspective 11.1: Matching architecture to workloadChallenge: Systolic arrays must choose which operand to keep stationary in processing-element registers (weights, inputs, or partial sums), and that choice hard-codes the hardware’s preference for certain model types. Section 11.7.3 develops the three options as a general mapping decision.
No single accelerator architecture suits every workload. A chip optimized for weight-stationary dataflow (like early TPUs) excels at convolutional neural networks (CNNs), where filter weights are small and reused across many image patches. That same architecture stalls on large language model (LLM) autoregressive inference at batch size 1, where the entire weight matrix must be read from off-chip memory once per generated token with zero batch reuse. No choice of stationary operand recovers reuse that does not exist; the levers are batching, lower-precision weights, and memory bandwidth.





Storing weights in INT8 or pruning half of them to zero shrinks a checkpoint on disk. If the accelerator lacks a datapath that multiplies narrow integers or skips zero weights in silicon, however, the runtime must unpack those weights back to dense floating point and executes no faster than the baseline. Number formats and structured sparsity patterns were defined in Model Compression; what turns them into wall-clock speedups—including the ResNet-50 INT8 profile—is the hardware datapath that executes them. Systolic arrays and Tensor Cores often provision higher multiply-accumulate capacity for narrower formats such as FP16, BF16, INT8, and FP8, while halving or quartering the bytes moved per value relative to FP32. That speedup is not automatic: it requires a supported kernel, matching input and accumulation formats, and enough parallel work to keep the narrower datapath full without hitting another bottleneck.


Lower precision is not free, for the range-and-precision reasons that forced loss scaling in mixed-precision training and that Numerical formats compared format by format. FP16 trades dynamic range for significand bits, BF16 keeps FP32’s exponent range at the cost of precision, and INT8 has no exponent at all, so its usable range depends on scale, zero-point, and clipping choices. For the hardware designer, those numerical properties set the silicon cost of each datapath. A narrower format needs a smaller multiplier and moves fewer bytes, but accumulation usually stays wider, as the FP32 accumulator of the Tensor Core instruction in listing 13 shows, so part of the area saved in the multipliers is spent keeping sums accurate.

Precision support is integrated into execution units and memory paths. SIMD and SIMT lanes may support several scalar formats, while Tensor Cores (section 11.4.2) and systolic units (section 11.4.4) expose architecture-specific input and accumulation combinations. Changing storage alone may reduce bytes without producing the advertised arithmetic speedup, because the model must select a kernel that uses the efficient path. Converting FP32 weights to INT8 cuts weight traffic by 4\(\times\). Whether that moves a kernel from bandwidth bound to compute bound depends on the operation’s original arithmetic intensity, the ridge point of the accelerator’s INT8 path, and the overhead of quantization and dequantization (equation 10.4). Tiling and dataflow, not precision itself, determine reuse, while conversion, scaling, or fallback overhead can offset part of the gain. A format is useful only when the kernel and numerical policy can employ it safely.



Modern AI accelerators support mixed-precision execution, in which different stages of one computation use different numerical formats. The training recipe (FP16 or BF16 multiplications with FP32 accumulation) (Micikevicius et al. 2018; Mellempudi et al. 2019) is developed in Mixed-precision training, and the inference recipe (INT8 or INT4 weights with selected activations kept wider) in Numerical Precision: Changing How Values Are Stored. The hardware’s part is to execute several formats side by side, with an accumulator wide enough for each.

The shift toward precision diversity is evident in the evolution of AI hardware. Early architectures such as NVIDIA Volta provided Tensor Core support only for FP16, whereas later architectures, including Turing and Ampere, added integer formats and then TF32, a hybrid between FP32 and FP16, alongside BF16 (NVIDIA 2020b; NVIDIA Corporation 2017, 2018, 2020a). The generation-by-generation list of supported formats belongs with the other dated specifications in System Assumptions; the durable observation is the direction of the trend, toward more formats, each narrower than the last.
The precision format used in hardware design has cascading implications across the entire system. Reducing an operand from FP32 to FP16 halves its value bytes. When those values dominate traffic, the reduction can substantially lower movement energy; the full energy budget still includes access counts, arithmetic, and other device activity (Horowitz 2014). Simultaneously, Tensor Cores and systolic arrays can pack more lower-precision multiply-accumulate units into the same silicon area, raising peak throughput (Dally et al. 2021; Dally 2023). Lower-precision integer arithmetic also consumes less energy than FP32 in representative technology studies (Horowitz 2014), and the inference-focused TPU v1 was built around 8-bit multiply units (Jouppi et al. 2017). Reduced precision can therefore cut value traffic and raise the supported compute ceiling at the same time.

Each narrower format raises the arithmetic ceiling again. The H100 advertises 989 TFLOP/s on its dense FP16 tensor path and 1,979 TFLOP/s on its FP8 path, an 8-bit floating-point format introduced for training and inference (Choquette 2023; Kuzmin et al. 2022; Micikevicius et al. 2022). NVIDIA’s Blackwell (B200) architecture extends this trajectory with an FP4 tensor datapath (a 4-bit floating-point format that, unlike INT4, spends some of its four bits on an exponent and so trades uniform spacing for range). The datapath is rated at up to 9 PFLOP/s dense or 18 PFLOP/s sparse peak throughput per chip (NVIDIA Corporation 2024). Reaching those theoretical ceilings requires numerical representations, kernel implementations, and sparsity patterns that align exactly with the specialized hardware paths. Narrower numerical formats expand the available design space, but numerical stability and dynamic range requirements dictate whether a workload can safely use FP4.



The sparse rating in that comparison depends on one more datapath feature, one that skips zeros only when they follow a fixed pattern. While unstructured pruning reduces model parameter counts, it rarely translates to hardware speedup because arbitrary nonzero placements destroy memory locality. Hardware accelerators resolve this with N:M structured sparsity,18 the pruning constraint from model compression that keeps exactly \(\StructuredSparsityNonzeroCount\) of every \(\StructuredSparsityGroupSize\) contiguous values along the reduction dimension nonzero, so memory access stays uniform and indexing predictable across parallel execution units.

At 2:4, the metadata overhead is compact enough to store alongside the weights without overwhelming the memory-traffic savings, which is the constraint that makes the advertised 2\(\times\) tensor-math throughput path plausible when kernels and model weights satisfy the pattern.

Parallel hardware needs this regularity because of how sparse matrices are encoded. Classical formats such as Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) and Block Compressed Sparse Row (BSR) rely on auxiliary index arrays to locate nonzero entries, and the corresponding activation gathers can touch scattered addresses, reducing useful bytes per memory transaction. Varying numbers of nonzeros across rows also create load imbalance and divergent execution. Block sparsity groups retained values into larger dense tiles to restore regularity, at the cost of a more restrictive pruning pattern. In the block formats, a short list of nonzero block indices tells the hardware which tiles to fetch, so zero blocks are never read. Whether an indexed format saves bytes or time at a given sparsity, its break-even point, is derived in Storage and execution break-even. The datapath question here is how regular the retained values must be for parallel hardware to use them.

NVIDIA’s Sparse Tensor Cores implement the 2:4 instance of the N:M pattern (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a; NVIDIA 2020a). Their input is the compressed 2:4 encoding, the two retained values of each group plus a 4-bit metadata tag (2 bits per value) recording their original positions. During execution, the memory hierarchy transfers only the compressed weights and their metadata, halving the weight-value payload while adding metadata traffic; total transferred bytes therefore fall by less than half before other overheads. Inside the Sparse Tensor Core datapath, the 4-bit metadata steers an internal multiplexer network that selects the matching two values from an uncompressed four-element activation vector. These selected activations and the two nonzero weights are then routed into a half-sized dot-product multiplier tree. Because the hardware computes only on the nonzeros while streaming compressed weights, this design doubles the peak arithmetic instruction throughput. The result is an advertised 2\(\times\) tensor-math speedup over dense operations when weights are fine-tuned to satisfy the pattern (figure 6).

The 2:4 pattern saves about half of the weight bytes and half of the multiplies, minus the metadata, so the reduced weight payload can lower traffic across HBM and on-chip SRAM. A roofline comparison must use consistent accounting: useful dense-equivalent operations can stay fixed while bytes decrease, whereas the count of physically executed sparse operations also decreases. Metadata and activation traffic remain in either traffic budget. Narrower values and skipped zeros therefore help when they reduce the bytes moved and keep the matrix engines fed. The ResNet-50 INT8 profile collects that benefit only on an execution path that supports both its format and its shapes. How fast such a path can possibly run follows from one division.
Dividing a model’s total operation count by peak arithmetic throughput produces an idealized lower bound on execution time, not a realistic inference latency. On the H100’s INT8 tensor path, dividing ResNet-50’s 8.2 GFLOP per inference by the 1,979 TOPS peak yields a floor of about 4 μs, against 8 μs at the FP16 peak. Real single-image ResNet-50 inference takes far longer than either floor. Part of that gap is kernel launch, synchronization, and host overhead that no roofline captures; part is memory traffic in low-intensity layers, because bandwidth has improved more slowly than tensor arithmetic throughput. That imbalance decides whether the advertised INT8 peak delivers high sustained utilization or sits largely idle on a given workload (Horowitz 2014; Gholami et al. 2024). Closing the gap requires the other half of the anatomy, the memory hierarchy that supplies the compute units.
