Evaluating these trade-offs requires navigating an unconstrained search space governed by three structural decisions: loop execution order, spatial parallelization across processing elements, and memory placement across the hierarchy. Counting each dimension on its own shows why exhaustive search is impractical.
Machine learning workloads are expressed as nested loops over tensor dimensions, and the loop execution order dictates which tensor elements remain resident in registers or SRAM between iterations. Ignoring dependences and equivalent orderings, the number of ways to arrange \(\LoopNestDepth\) loops has the toy upper bound: \[
\LoopOrderCount= \LoopNestDepth!
\] A convolutional layer with seven loop dimensions already has \(7! = 5{,}040\) possible execution orders. If each memory level could choose an ordering independently, the toy upper bound would expand as: \[
(\LoopNestDepth!)^{\MemoryHierarchyLevelCount}
\] where \(\MemoryHierarchyLevelCount\) is the number of memory hierarchy levels. A suboptimal ordering evicts values prematurely and multiplies DRAM traffic, whereas an optimized ordering maximizes reuse in local SRAM and caches (Sze et al. 2017).
Parallelization multiplies the count again. Parallelizing outer independent loops (such as batch or output feature channels) lets each core execute without interconnect traffic, whereas parallelizing an inner reduction loop requires cross-core synchronization and collective communication. Before legality and capacity constraints are applied, the number of ordered ways to select loops for parallel execution has the upper bound: \[
\LoopParallelizationChoiceCount= \frac{\LoopNestDepth!}{(\LoopNestDepth-\ParallelLoopCount)!}
\] where \(\ParallelLoopCount\) is the number of loops selected for parallel execution; three of six loops already give \(6!/3! = 120\) candidates, each with different demands on synchronization, interconnect bandwidth, and PE utilization. Memory placement is the third dimension, and physical capacity bounds it. In a toy model where five tensor structures can each be assigned to one of four storage handling choices at a single hierarchy level, a single level already yields \(4^5 = 1{,}024\) placement combinations, and choosing independently across three memory levels expands the unconstrained count to \((4^5)^3 = 4^{15}\) placements. Because an off-chip DRAM fetch costs roughly 128\(\times\) more energy than a read from an 8 KB SRAM array (figure 4), where each tensor resides directly dictates the achieved arithmetic intensity. Yet an operand tile can remain in on-chip SRAM only if its working set fits the allocated buffer. Larger resident tiles raise reuse but consume scarce capacity and register pressure, potentially reducing thread concurrency or forcing spills to slower tiers.



Per memory level, from the section’s separate toy examples: \(4^5 = 1{,}024\) placements, \(7! = 5{,}040\) orders, \(6!/3! = 120\) parallelizations. The product is raised to the number of levels, so three levels give \(4^{15}\) placements alone.
These structural choices (loop ordering, spatial parallelization across processing elements, tile sizing, and memory placement) are deeply coupled. Choosing an output-stationary schedule, for example, pins accumulators in local registers and dictates which loops can be mapped spatially across processing elements without requiring inter-core reduction networks. Conversely, parallelizing across more execution units reduces the per-core SRAM budget available for operand staging, forcing smaller tile dimensions and increasing off-chip memory traffic.
While the unconstrained Cartesian product of these decisions suggests a very large combinatorial space, hardware capacity limits, data dependencies, and symmetry prune the vast majority of candidates as either physically illegal or strictly dominated. Exhaustive search across arbitrary loop permutations and placement choices is therefore both unnecessary and intractable. Production compilers and kernel developers manage this complexity by structuring their search around a small family of canonical dataflow patterns, spatial and temporal schedules engineered to exploit the specific reuse properties of neural network operators.




Those canonical patterns exist because two mathematically identical loop schedules for the same convolution can differ by more than an order of magnitude in off-chip weight reads (example 11.4), and every avoided read that would have reached DRAM saves the most expensive access on the energy ladder. While spatial and temporal mapping establish where operations execute and where operands reside, dataflow optimization governs the exact trajectories and schedules of data moving through processing elements and the memory hierarchy to maximize operand reuse. In a systolic array or tiled vector unit, the temporal schedule and spatial routing of weights, inputs, and partial sums dictate how frequently operands must be fetched from energy-expensive DRAM rather than reused from local registers or scratchpads. By controlling off-chip traffic, the dataflow establishes the effective operational intensity of the kernel, determining whether execution achieves the compute-bound plateau or stalls in the bandwidth-bound regime of the roofline model. Optimizing compilers (section 11.8) and runtime systems (section 11.8.3) therefore tailor dataflow patterns to match the reuse characteristics of each layer to the hardware constraints of the target accelerator.
Three recurring architectural decisions structure this design space, providing a compact vocabulary for navigating dataflow choices without exhaustive search across billions of candidate schedules:

Locality: Stationary operand selection (weight-stationary, output-stationary, or input-stationary) dictates which tensor remains pinned in local registers or processing-element scratchpads, trading off memory traffic against register pressure.
Organization: Physical tensor layouts (such as channels-last NHWC versus channels-first NCHW) govern whether memory accesses match hardware memory controller burst sizes and SIMD vector widths, preventing uncoalesced memory transactions.
Combination: Kernel fusion and loop tiling partition iteration spaces and merge adjacent operations to eliminate round-trips to off-chip memory for intermediate tensors.




The first lever, locality, begins with the reuse already present in the inner loops of a tensor operator. Because fetching an operand from DRAM costs orders of magnitude more energy than the arithmetic operation that consumes it (figure 4) (Chen et al. 2016), a data movement strategy must hold reused values in local registers or scratchpads rather than refetching them across the memory bus. Listing 14 shows the canonical three-loop matrix multiplication, exposing the three distinct reuse streams across weights, inputs, and partial sums that a stationary schedule can pin on chip.



Listing 14: Naïve Matrix-Multiplication Dataflow: The loop nest revisits weight rows, input columns, and output accumulators, exposing the reuse that a mapping must capture in local memory.


# Matrix multiplication where:
# weights: [512x256] - model parameters
# input:   [256x32]  - batch of activations
# Z:       [512x32]  - output activations

# Computing each output element Z[i,j]:
for i in range(512):
    for j in range(32):
        for k in range(256):
            Z[i, j] += weights[i, k] * input[k, j]



Every operand in this loop nest is reused, but along a different loop. Each weight weights[i, k] is used once for each of the 32 output columns, each input input[k, j] is used once for each of the 512 output rows, and each output Z[i, j] accumulates 256 products before it is final. A processing element’s local storage holds only a small tile at a time, so the mapping cannot capture all three reuses at once. Fetching from DRAM whichever operand is not held locally, on every use, is what turns a compute-bound kernel into a memory-bound one (Han et al. 2016).

Han, Song, Xingyu Liu, Huizi Mao, Jing Pu, Ardavan Pedram, Mark A. Horowitz, and William J. Dally. 2016. “EIE: Efficient Inference Engine on Compressed Deep Neural Network.” 2016 ACM/IEEE 43rd Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), 243–54. https://doi.org/10.1109/isca.2016.30.
The central dataflow decision is therefore which operand to keep local. The loop order answers it: whatever the innermost loops touch repeatedly without changing stays resident, and everything else streams. Listing 15 reorders the same computation three ways, and the three orders are the three classic stationary dataflows.



Listing 15: Three Stationary Dataflows: The same matrix multiplication as the naïve loop, reordered three ways; the operand held fixed across the innermost loop is the one fetched once and reused from local storage, while the other two stream.


# Weight stationary: hold one weight, stream inputs and partial sums past it
for i in range(512):
    for k in range(256):
        w = weights[i, k]  # fetched once, reused 32 times
        for j in range(32):
            Z[i, j] += w * input[k, j]

# Output stationary: hold one partial sum, stream weights and inputs past it
for i in range(512):
    for j in range(32):
        acc = 0  # stays in a local accumulator
        for k in range(256):
            acc += weights[i, k] * input[k, j]
        Z[i, j] = acc  # written once

# Input stationary: hold one input, stream weights and partial sums past it
for k in range(256):
    for j in range(32):
        x = input[k, j]  # fetched once, reused 512 times
        for i in range(512):
            Z[i, j] += weights[i, k] * x



A weight-stationary dataflow keeps parameters on chip, so each weight crosses the expensive memory boundary once no matter how many inputs it touches. That pays off wherever one filter or weight tile is applied to many inputs, as in convolutions and batched matrix multiplication, and it is the canonical TPU dataflow traced cycle by cycle in section 11.7.5. The saved traffic reappears on the other operands: inputs must arrive fast enough to keep the resident weights busy, and partial sums must move between processing elements as they accumulate. The resident tile is also bounded by on-chip capacity, so a layer whose weights far exceed it must cycle weight tiles through, reloading the inputs for each one.
An output-stationary dataflow keeps each running sum in a local accumulator until all of its contributions have arrived, so every output is written to memory exactly once (Chen et al. 2016). It suits layers with wide fan-in, such as fully connected layers and attention projections, where writing a partial sum out after every step would cost far more than the reads it avoids. The cost is two operand streams at once, since both weights and inputs must now be delivered from memory. The naïve loop in listing 14 already has this order, because its innermost loop runs over \(\GemmReductionIndex\) while \(\MatrixRowIndex\) and \(\MatrixColumnIndex\) stay fixed.
An input-stationary dataflow keeps an activation tile local while weights stream past it. It pays off when one activation feeds several computations before eviction, as when a transformer token’s activation feeds the query, key, and value projections. Its costs mirror weight stationary’s, with weights now streaming from memory and partial sums still moving as they accumulate.

Example 11.4: Loop ordering in a small convolutionConsider a convolution applying 16 filters of size \(3{\times}3\) to an \(8{\times}8\) single-channel input. The computation can be expressed as five nested loops iterating over output rows (\(\OutputFeatureMapHeight\)), output columns (\(\OutputFeatureMapWidth\)), filter count (\(\LayerOutputWidth\)), filter height (\(\KernelHeight\)), and filter width (\(\KernelWidth\)). The \(5! = 120\) permutations are an unconstrained upper bound: legal orderings preserve the mathematical result, although floating-point reduction order can change rounding, and they generate different memory traffic.
Ordering A (weight-stationary): Place the filter loops (\(\LayerOutputWidth\), \(\KernelHeight\), \(\KernelWidth\)) outermost and the spatial loops (\(\OutputFeatureMapHeight\), \(\OutputFeatureMapWidth\)) innermost. Each \(3{\times}3\) filter is loaded into registers once and then applied across all 36 output positions before the next filter is loaded. Total weight loads: \(16 \times 9 = 144\) values, each loaded exactly once.
Ordering B (output-stationary, filters spilled): Place the spatial loops outermost and the filter loops innermost. For every output position, all 16 filters must be loaded, applied, and their partial sums accumulated before advancing to the next position. If the register file cannot hold all 16 filters simultaneously, filters are repeatedly fetched from cache or DRAM. In the worst case, each of the 36 output positions reloads all 144 filter weights, producing \(36 \times 144 = 5{,}184\) weight reads.
Systems insight: Under these two limiting assumptions, Ordering A reduces modeled weight reads by 36\(\times\) relative to the worst case for Ordering B. Real kernels also account for activation and partial-sum traffic, register capacity, cache behavior, and vectorization. The example nevertheless shows why two mathematically equivalent loop orders can place widely different demands on the memory system.


The three strategies form a decision framework rather than a quality ranking. The right choice is the operand with the highest reuse relative to the on-chip storage it would occupy, which depends on layer dimensions and batch size, so compilers select among them per layer. Convolution-specific designs add a fourth label, row-stationary. The Eyeriss accelerator maps one-dimensional rows of filter weights and input activations to processing-element registers and accumulates rows of partial sums locally, a hybrid that captures more of a convolution’s multidimensional reuse than fixing any single operand (Chen et al. 2016).

Chen, Yu-Hsin, Joel S. Emer, and Vivienne Sze. 2016. “Eyeriss: A Spatial Architecture for Energy-Efficient Dataflow for Convolutional Neural Networks.” 2016 ACM/IEEE 43rd Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), 367–79. https://doi.org/10.1109/ISCA.2016.40.



A stationary dataflow decides which operand stays local; tiling decides how large a block of it local storage can hold. A mismatch exists between the computational graph (which sees a single 4,096 \(\times\) 4,096 matrix multiplication) and the physical silicon (which possesses a fixed 128 \(\times\) 128 systolic array). Bridging this gap requires tiling, which partitions a large tensor operation into tiles that fit exactly into the hardware’s fast local memory (SRAM or scratchpad memory), so that each tile is reused many times before it is evicted.


↩︎ Tiling in its software form, the cache-aware blocking a framework applies to matrix multiplication, is established in Basic numerical operations.
To process the 4,096-wide worked-example layer on a 128-wide systolic array, the compiler decomposes the result into 1,024 output tiles. Each output tile accumulates across 32 reduction-dimension tiles, so the complete matrix multiplication executes 32,768 \(\GemmLeftOperand\)-tile-by-\(\GemmRightOperand\)-tile products. This decomposition is a physical requirement imposed by memory hierarchy limits: operand tiles are fetched from high-capacity, high-latency HBM, staged in fast SRAM, and pulsed through the systolic array.



Exceeding the tile width along a single dimension tips utilization along that axis off a cliff.
Tile dimensions balance on-chip capacity against arithmetic intensity. A larger tile reuses each loaded byte across more multiply-accumulate operations, raising operational intensity toward the compute-bound regime of the roofline model. The capacity ceiling is how much of \(\GemmLeftOperand\), \(\GemmRightOperand\), and \(\GemmOutputMatrix\) fits simultaneously in fast on-chip memory. Tiling sustains high hardware efficiency \((\EfficiencyHw)\) by ensuring that for every byte loaded from main memory, the data is reused 128× within the systolic grid. When a layer dimension is not an exact multiple of the hardware tile size, the accelerator pays a fringe penalty in idle silicon. Consider a layer where only one output dimension expands from 128 to 129 while the other dimensions remain perfectly aligned to the 128-element tile. Processing that single extra column requires scheduling a second 128-wide tile across the systolic array, leaving 127 execution units idle during the fringe pass. Two tiles execute where one nearly sufficed, so the utilization factor along that dimension falls to \(129/256\), or approximately 50 percent, creating the efficiency cliff illustrated in the margin figure. When multiple dimensions misalign simultaneously, these padding losses multiply across the tiled axes: a \(129 \times 129\) output block partitioned into four \(128 \times 128\) physical tiles yields a useful-area efficiency of \((129/256)^2\), or barely 25 percent. Algorithm 1 formalizes the resulting loop nest emitted by the compiler to orchestrate this on-chip staging and accumulation.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Tiled (blocked) matrix multiply}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{M\times K}$, $\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{K\times N}$; tile sizes $M_{\text{tile}}, N_{\text{tile}}, K_{\text{tile}}$
\Ensure $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$
\For{each row tile $i_0$ (size $M_{\text{tile}}$)}
    \For{each column tile $j_0$ (size $N_{\text{tile}}$)}
        \State initialize the $\mathbf{C}$-tile accumulator to zero on chip
        \For{each $k_0$ over $K$ in steps of $K_{\text{tile}}$}
            \State load $\mathbf{A}$-tile $[i_0,k_0]$ and $\mathbf{B}$-tile $[k_0,j_0]$ on chip
            \State accumulate the tile product on chip \Comment{reuse $N_{\text{tile}}$/$M_{\text{tile}}$ per byte}
        \EndFor
        \State write the $\mathbf{C}$-tile back to memory
    \EndFor
\EndFor
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{M\times K}\)

Once operand tiles reside in fast local SRAM, the hardware executes the tile product without further off-chip memory traffic. Systolic arrays achieve computational efficiency by routing operands through a structured 2D grid of processing elements (PEs) that communicate directly with adjacent neighbors across dedicated registers, bypassing shared-memory bus contention. In a weight-stationary design, the canonical TPU arrangement of figure 5, weights from the \(\GemmRightOperand\)-tile are preloaded into local PE registers and held stationary. Input activations from the \(\GemmLeftOperand\)-tile stream horizontally across rows from left to right, while partial sums accumulate vertically down columns. On each clock cycle, every active PE multiplies its incoming activation by its stationary weight, adds the result to the incoming partial sum from above, and passes the activation rightward to its adjacent neighbor for the next cycle.
Because operands propagate one hop per cycle, synchronized execution requires an intentional time skew. Consider a minimal \(2{\times}2\) tile product where output element \(\GemmOutputElement_{ij} = \GemmLeftOperandElement_{i0}\GemmRightOperandElement_{0j} + \GemmLeftOperandElement_{i1}\GemmRightOperandElement_{1j}\) requires two products and one accumulation. The weight matrix \(\GemmRightOperand\) is held stationary across four PEs: \(\text{PE}_{00}\) stores \(\GemmRightOperandElement_{00}\), \(\text{PE}_{01}\) stores \(\GemmRightOperandElement_{01}\), \(\text{PE}_{10}\) stores \(\GemmRightOperandElement_{10}\), and \(\text{PE}_{11}\) stores \(\GemmRightOperandElement_{11}\). Activation \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{i0}\) enters the top row and \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{i1}\) the second row, because each row holds the weights for one reduction index. If \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{00}\) enters the top row at \(\text{PE}_{00}\) in cycle 0, its partial product \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{00}\GemmRightOperandElement_{00}\) moves down to \(\text{PE}_{10}\) in cycle 1. That PE holds \(\GemmRightOperandElement_{10}\), so the activation it needs is \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{01}\), which must therefore enter the second row at \(\text{PE}_{10}\) one cycle later than \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{00}\) entered the first. In cycle 1, \(\text{PE}_{10}\) adds \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{01}\GemmRightOperandElement_{10}\) to the arriving partial sum and emits \(\GemmOutputElement_{00}\). Meanwhile \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{00}\) has moved right to \(\text{PE}_{01}\), and its product \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{00}\GemmRightOperandElement_{01}\) reaches \(\text{PE}_{11}\) in cycle 2, just as \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{01}\) arrives there from \(\text{PE}_{10}\). As a result, \(\GemmOutputElement_{01}\) emerges one cycle after \(\GemmOutputElement_{00}\). Inputs along each successive row and column are staggered in the same way, so operands meeting at any physical coordinate represent identical reduction indices. Local reuse amortizes the initial fill and drain overhead: each loaded activation is reused across an entire row of \(\GemmTileColumnDimension\) processing elements, while each stationary weight serves an entire sequence of input vectors before eviction. Sustained throughput, however, remains bounded by off-chip memory bandwidth whenever operand replenishment cannot keep pace with array retirement (section 11.5.1).


The systolic array is one instance of a general hierarchy rule. The same blocking that fits a graph-level matrix onto a fixed array, together with its fringe penalty and the loop structure of algorithm 1, recurs across registers, L1/shared memory, and L2 caches (Lam et al. 1991). At every tier of the memory hierarchy, tiling22 bounds the active working set so that each block is reused locally before eviction rather than refetched from a slower tier.
22 Tiling (loop blocking): This restructuring partitions a computation into blocks sized for a fast local tier. A naive loop makes repeated references to the same elements; caches may capture some, while blocking deliberately concentrates reuse before eviction (Lam et al. 1991). This reduction in lower-tier traffic is a primary source of the gap between naive matrix multiplication and optimized GEMM routines.

The naïve loop nest of listing 14 shows the cost of leaving reuse to chance. Written as \(\GemmOutputMatrix= \GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand\), with the weights as \(\GemmLeftOperand\) and the input batch as \(\GemmRightOperand\), it references the same elements of both operands again and again. Without tiling, those repeated accesses consume unnecessary bandwidth. Some references can hit in cache, but large matrices and an unfavorable traversal order can still cause excessive lower-tier traffic. Tiling partitions this multiplication across its three principal dimensions (\(\GemmRowDimension\), \(\GemmInnerDimension\), and \(\GemmColumnDimension\)) (figure 13). Each highlighted region represents the working set staged in fast memory at one moment. An \(\GemmTileRowDimension{\times}\GemmTileInnerDimension\) block of \(\GemmLeftOperand\) (within the green row band) multiplies a \(\GemmTileInnerDimension{\times}\GemmTileColumnDimension\) block of \(\GemmRightOperand\) (within the pink column band) to accumulate one \(\GemmTileRowDimension{\times}\GemmTileColumnDimension\) output tile (\(\text{Block}_{\TileRowIndex,n}\), shaded blue) of \(\GemmOutputMatrix\). Processing all inner-product operations for an active tile before evicting it amortizes off-chip DRAM latency across \(\GemmTileRowDimension\cdot \GemmTileColumnDimension\cdot \GemmTileInnerDimension\) arithmetic operations.






Figure 13: Matrix Tiling Mechanics: Partitioning large matrix multiplication (\(\GemmOutputMatrix=\GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand\)) into \(\GemmTileRowDimension\times \GemmTileInnerDimension\) and \(\GemmTileInnerDimension\times \GemmTileColumnDimension\) blocks aligns memory footprints with fast on-chip SRAM/registers. Maximizing register reuse within each tile amortizes slow off-chip DRAM accesses and keeps compute engines operating at peak throughput.





In the untiled loop of listing 14, each inner-loop step fetches \(\GemmLeftOperandElement_{ik}\) and \(\GemmRightOperandElement_{kj}\) across an entire row of \(\GemmLeftOperand\) and column of \(\GemmRightOperand\) to update \(\GemmOutputElement_{ij}\) before advancing to the next column or row. Once \(\SquareGemmDimension\) grows large enough that a full row or column evicts earlier entries from local storage, the processor reloads values it touched moments earlier and pays the lower-tier latency and energy penalty on every miss (Horowitz 2014; Sze et al. 2017).

Splitting the three loops into outer tile-stepping loops and inner within-tile loops confines the working set to three TILE_SIZE \(\times\) TILE_SIZE submatrices at a time. Listing 16 shows this loop-blocking transformation in Python: the outer loops step in increments of TILE_SIZE, while the inner loops complete all \(\text{TILE\_SIZE}^3\) multiply-accumulates for the active block before advancing.



Listing 16: Cache-Blocked Matrix Multiplication: This high-level loop blocking approach divides matrices into smaller index ranges so hardware caches can reuse data within each tile, improving computational efficiency without explicit scratchpad loads.


TILE_SIZE = 32  # Choose a tile size based on hardware constraints

# Cache blocking: partition data via loop bounds.
# Loads are implicit through the hardware cache hierarchy.
for i in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):
    for j in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):
        for k in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):
            # Each tile computed independently
            for ii in range(i, min(i + TILE_SIZE, N)):
                for jj in range(j, min(j + TILE_SIZE, N)):
                    for kk in range(k, min(k + TILE_SIZE, N)):
                        C[ii, jj] += A[ii, kk] * B[kk, jj]



The restructuring produces a chain of effects. A small tile is revisited while it is still likely to be cached, so most operand references hit in L1/L2 or shared memory instead of DRAM. DRAM traffic falls as a result, and the processing units spend less time waiting for operands. When an untiled access pattern repeatedly fetches operands from lower memory tiers, that traffic can impose a bandwidth ceiling below the arithmetic ceiling.



Tiling implementations differ along one axis, which is whether the hardware or the program decides what stays in fast memory. The two ends are implicit (cache) blocking and explicit (scratchpad) staging, and practical kernels often combine them.
Implicit (cache) blocking restructures only the loop bounds. The tiled matrix multiplication in listing 16 issues no explicit loads; its tile-shaped access pattern lets hardware caches reuse nearby values before they are evicted. It suits CPUs and GPUs with capable caches and large tensors that exceed fast-memory capacity.
Explicit (scratchpad) staging copies each tile into shared memory, a scratchpad, or registers and reorganizes the computation around the staged copy. It is the only option on accelerators whose fast memory is software managed, and it guarantees reuse that a cache might lose to eviction. Convolution is the classic case, because staging a filter once lets it serve many input regions without being refetched. Listing 17 loads blocks of \(\GemmLeftOperand\) and \(\GemmRightOperand\) into temporary fast storage and reuses them across the inner loops. It includes shortened boundary tiles when \(\SquareGemmDimension\) is not divisible by TILE_SIZE, the software counterpart of the fringe penalty that a fixed-size array pays in idle processing elements.



Listing 17: Explicit Tile Staging Pseudocode: A backend maps the temporary tile objects to fast storage and reuses them across inner-loop operations.


# Explicit tile staging: load data into fast
# temporary storage before the inner loops.
for i in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):
    for j in range(0, N, TILE_SIZE):

            # Pseudocode: map these tile objects to fast memory
            A_tile = A[i : i + TILE_SIZE, k : k + TILE_SIZE]
            B_tile = B[k : k + TILE_SIZE, j : j + TILE_SIZE]

            # Reuse loaded tiles for all inner iterations
            for ii in range(A_tile.shape[0]):
                for jj in range(B_tile.shape[1]):
                    for kk in range(A_tile.shape[1]):

Tiling improves performance only when the tile matches the locality budget of the hardware. If the tile is too small, memory fetches still dominate execution time because reuse is too limited. If the tile is too large, it exceeds fast memory and causes cache thrashing or scratchpad spills. Selecting the right tile size therefore directly determines computational efficiency and memory bandwidth usage.
The capacity test counts every buffer that is live at the same time. For the tile dimensions in algorithm 1, the operand blocks contain \(\GemmTileRowDimension \GemmTileInnerDimension\) and \(\GemmTileInnerDimension \GemmTileColumnDimension\) elements, while the output accumulator contains \(\GemmTileRowDimension \GemmTileColumnDimension\) elements. Suppose a hypothetical accelerator retains all three in one software-managed local store, uses FP16 operands and an FP32 accumulator, and loads only the current operand pair. Element storage size \(\ElementStorageSize\) is then 2 bytes for each operand and 4 bytes for each accumulator entry. After reserving space for other live state, the tile must satisfy \[
(2\text{ bytes})\GemmTileRowDimension \GemmTileInnerDimension+ (2\text{ bytes})\GemmTileInnerDimension \GemmTileColumnDimension+ (4\text{ bytes})\GemmTileRowDimension \GemmTileColumnDimension\le \text{available local bytes}.
\tag{6}\] Keeping the output dimensions fixed while doubling the reduction tile doubles both operand buffers without changing the accumulator. Reject that larger candidate if the revised left-hand side of equation 6 exceeds the available capacity, even if its longer reduction amortizes accumulator handling over more products. Double buffering has the same operand-capacity effect at fixed tile dimensions: retaining the next \(\GemmLeftOperand\) and \(\GemmRightOperand\) tiles while computing the current pair requires a second copy of each operand buffer, while the running accumulator remains single buffered.
Actual storage tiers must be budgeted separately. A GPU kernel may stage operand tiles in shared memory while keeping output accumulators in thread registers; unused register capacity cannot make an oversized shared-memory allocation fit. Its shared-memory test counts the staged operand copies and any other shared state, while its register test counts accumulators, operand fragments, and temporary values across the participating threads. Passing both tests establishes capacity feasibility. It does not establish speed: alignment, bank conflicts, occupancy, synchronization, and measured traffic still determine whether the tile improves execution.
The tile choice also controls load balance. In architectures such as GPUs and TPUs, computations execute in parallel across thousands of processing units. If tiles are not evenly distributed, some units remain idle while others are overloaded, leading to suboptimal utilization of computational resources. Effective tile scheduling keeps parallel execution balanced and efficient.
Data movement remains a cost after tiling, even when another resource becomes the throughput limit. Although tiling reduces the number of slow memory accesses, transferring tiles between hierarchy levels still incurs latency and energy cost, especially when data falls from cache or scratchpad back to DRAM. Efficient memory prefetching and scheduling strategies minimize this residual movement and ensure that data is available when needed.
Hybrid tiling combines implicit blocking and explicit staging when neither alone captures the workload’s reuse, for example relying on caches for an outer tier while staging convolution weights explicitly in a scratchpad. Register blocking, double buffering, and hierarchical tiling extend the same locality principle at smaller and larger memory tiers. AI compilers and runtime systems such as TensorFlow XLA, TVM, and MLIR automatically select these tiling strategies based on hardware constraints, enabling fine-tuned performance optimization without manual intervention. Stationary dataflows (section 11.7.4) and tiling determine which operands stay close to compute units and in what blocks; tensor layouts determine whether those operands can be accessed efficiently once they arrive. A well-chosen weight-stationary schedule still stalls if weights are laid out in a format that produces strided, non-coalesced memory fetches. Tensor layout is a kernel requirement. The physical ordering of multidimensional data in linear memory must match the memory access stride expected by the accelerator’s execution units, or the processor pays in memory stalls, cache underutilization, and redundant bus transactions.
Hardware accelerators fetch data from device memory in fixed-size transactions, typically 32 to 128 bytes per transaction. When compute units request non-contiguous addresses, each transaction delivers only a fraction of useful payload, degrading effective memory bandwidth. Aligning tensor layout with the execution model lets concurrent threads or SIMD lanes access nearby aligned locations in fewer transactions; the count depends on access width and device granularity (NVIDIA Corporation 2021).
Machine learning frameworks and compilers often manage this layout selection automatically. Optimization tools such as cuDNN for NVIDIA GPUs, XLA for TensorFlow and JAX, and MLIR-based compiler stacks transform tensor layouts as they lower operations to backend-specific kernels (NVIDIA Corporation 2021; Google 2025; Lattner et al. 2020). In high-level frameworks, layout transformations are typically applied transparently, but developers authoring custom kernels or targeting low-level APIs such as CUDA, Metal, or OpenCL must manage tensor formats directly.
In PyTorch, for example, view operations such as tensor.permute() adjust tensor strides without moving data in memory, requiring an explicit tensor.contiguous() call to materialize a packed buffer when a downstream kernel requires contiguous storage (PyTorch Contributors 2026). Conversely, TensorFlow defaults to channels-last (NHWC) for convolutional models on NVIDIA GPUs, warning that NCHW inputs introduce automatic transpose overhead when lowered to GPU kernels (TensorFlow Developers 2024). Hardware-optimized libraries such as cuDNN on GPUs and oneDNN on CPUs implement tailored memory formats to maximize cache line utilization and SIMD throughput. The governing principle is to treat memory layout as an intrinsic property of the backend execution path: the fastest tensor format is the one that minimizes layout conversion overhead and makes memory accesses contiguous across hardware execution units.

PyTorch Contributors. 2026. Tensor Views.

TensorFlow Developers. 2024. Optimize TensorFlow Performance Using the Profiler.


In an NHWC channels-last layout, the channel index varies fastest in a contiguous tensor, placing the channel values for each spatial coordinate adjacent in memory. The label names the order in which dimensions are laid out in memory, from slowest-varying to fastest-varying, so NCHW and NHWC hold the same values in different linear orders.
Consider an RGB image tensor of shape \((\text{Height}, \text{Width}, \text{Channels}) = (3, 3, 3)\). The elements \(\ImageTensorElement(\ImageRowIndex,\ImageColumnIndex,\ImageChannelIndex)\) are laid out in linear memory as follows: \[\begin{gather*}
X(0,0,0), X(0,0,1), X(0,0,2), X(0,1,0), X(0,1,1), \\
X(0,1,2), X(0,2,0), X(0,2,1), X(0,2,2), \ldots
\end{gather*}\]
All channel values for a given pixel are adjacent, and memory addresses advance across width before advancing down height. This layout supports vectorized execution when a compute kernel processes multiple channels simultaneously: CPU SIMD registers and GPU Tensor Cores can load contiguous channel vectors directly without intra-register shuffling.
The advantage of channels-last storage depends on the target operator and hardware unit. TensorFlow uses NHWC by default, whereas PyTorch provides a dedicated channels-last memory format that decouples logical dimension ordering from physical storage. Modern Tensor Core kernels in cuDNN favor NHWC because matrix-multiply units pack channel dimensions directly into accumulator tiles. When kernels require channel-contiguous inputs, passing an incompatible format forces the framework runtime to insert an explicit memory transpose, incurring a memory bandwidth penalty before computation begins.



In a contiguous NCHW channels-first layout, the spatial width index varies fastest, and all spatial values across an entire channel are stored contiguously before the next channel begins. Accelerators process data in parallel across thread warps or SIMD lanes; when consecutive threads in a warp access consecutive memory addresses, the memory controller coalesces those requests into fewer memory transactions (memory coalescing).23
23 Memory coalescing: The GPU hardware mechanism that combines memory requests from threads in a warp into transactions according to address locality, alignment, access width, and device granularity. Tensor layout therefore decides how many transactions a warp’s loads become, and whether a given layout helps depends on how the kernel assigns threads to tensor dimensions.Consider the same RGB image tensor with dimensions reordered in channels-first order as \((\text{Channels}, \text{Height}, \text{Width}) = (3, 3, 3)\). Retaining \(\ImageTensorElement(\ImageRowIndex,\ImageColumnIndex,\ImageChannelIndex)\) as semantic coordinate notation, the data are stored in channels-first order as follows: \[\begin{gather*}
X(0,0,0), X(0,1,0), X(0,2,0), X(1,0,0), X(1,1,0), X(1,2,0), \ldots, \\
X(0,0,1), X(0,1,1), X(0,2,1), \ldots, X(0,0,2), X(0,1,2), X(0,2,2), \ldots
\end{gather*}\]
In this format, all red channel values for the entire image are stored first, followed by all green values, and then all blue values. This arrangement allows kernels that parallelize across spatial coordinates \((\ImageHeight, \ImageWidth)\) to issue coalesced reads along image rows, which suited earlier GPU convolution algorithms and SIMD execution pipelines (Chetlur et al. 2014).

24 NHWC vs. NCHW: NHWC lists dimensions as batch, height, width, channel; NCHW lists batch, channel, height, width. Physical memory format determines whether adjacent threads read adjacent addresses, so the performance effect is backend-specific. Layout-to-hardware mismatch is not a micro-optimization; it can create multi-fold performance gaps, especially when a conversion prevents Tensor Core convolution or fusion paths from being used.The relative advantage of NCHW versus NHWC depends on how the underlying kernel maps computation to hardware threads. Convolutional layers evaluate filters across spatial and channel dimensions simultaneously. In classic direct or FFT-based convolutions, channels-first ordering enabled efficient spatial sliding without stride jumps. However, modern GEMM-lowered convolutions and Tensor Core pipelines map channel reduction directly to matrix multiply accumulators, favoring channels-last structures. When a model operates in NCHW but invokes a Tensor Core-optimized backend, the runtime must either run an unoptimized fallback kernel or dynamically transpose the tensor into NHWC, burning memory bandwidth in both cases.24



Both channels-last (NHWC) and channels-first (NCHW) layouts address specific hardware access patterns, with their efficiency determined by whether a kernel parallelizes over spatial coordinates or vectorizes across channel dimensions. Layout choice directly governs cache line utilization, memory bus transaction count, and compute unit occupancy. While compilers such as XLA, TensorRT, and PyTorch Inductor automate layout propagation and insert layout conversions when beneficial, format conversions are not free. Transposing a tensor requires reading every element from memory and writing it back in a different order, which consumes memory bandwidth without executing useful arithmetic. In production deployments, matching the model’s memory layout to the accelerator’s native kernel format eliminates these layout transformations entirely. Even when tensor layout is perfectly aligned with the hardware, however, executing operations as isolated kernels introduces a separate bottleneck: intermediate values must be exposed through global-memory buffers between operations, even when caches absorb some physical traffic. Resolving that bottleneck requires changing how operations are scheduled rather than how tensors are laid out.




At 2.0 FLOP/byte, the standalone LayerNorm kernel of notebook 11.8 can reach at most 6.7 TFLOP/s, about 0.7 percent of the H100’s tensor peak, no matter how its internal arithmetic or tensor layout is scheduled. Kernel fusion25 removes that bottleneck by combining successive operations into a single kernel so intermediate tensors stay in registers or on-chip SRAM instead of making round-trips through device memory. On an accelerator, the two engineering questions are which intermediate transfers fusion eliminates from the memory bus and what the combined kernel costs in register pressure and thread occupancy.
25 Kernel fusion: Separate GPU kernels expose intermediate results through device memory, although caches can absorb some traffic. A fused kernel can keep intermediates in registers or local storage and avoid corresponding external write/read cycles. The resulting speedup depends on cache behavior, occupancy, launch overhead, and whether memory traffic was the bottleneck; it is not necessarily proportional to the byte reduction.
↩︎ Kernel fusion (also called operator fusion), with its LayerNorm, dropout, and ReLU example and the traffic count for unfused versus fused chains, is established in The memory wall and kernel fusion.

The case for fusion rests on a traffic count. Run as separate kernels, a chain of three elementwise operations writes each intermediate result to device memory and reads it back for the next operation. In contrast, a fused kernel reads the input once, keeps the intermediates in registers or on-chip SRAM, and writes only the final output, which cuts idealized external traffic by roughly 3\(\times\). On an accelerator the saving matters most for elementwise operators, whose arithmetic intensity sits far below one FLOP per byte, so moving each intermediate across the memory bus takes longer than computing it (Jia et al. 2019). Fused execution also shortens the lifetime of intermediate buffers, although an optimizing runtime can often reuse those buffers anyway. What fusion guarantees is the removed write and read for each eliminated intermediate, and how much of that removed traffic would have reached DRAM depends on cache behavior.


Because high-bandwidth memory is the scarce resource on GPUs and TPUs, eliminating redundant memory transactions translates directly into higher compute utilization (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). Not all operations can be fused arbitrarily, however. Element-wise operations and frozen inference normalization are strong candidates because their computations do not require batch-wide reductions, whereas training-mode batch normalization computes batch statistics and is not purely element-wise. Matrix multiplications and convolutions constrain fusion further because they involve reductions and large data movement; compilers routinely fuse them with element-wise epilogues such as bias or activation, yet cannot freely merge them with unrelated global operations.
Even when two operators are algebraically compatible, register pressure bounds how aggressively they should be fused. Keeping intermediate values in registers eliminates redundant memory writes, but if a fused kernel exceeds the available registers per thread, the compiler spills excess values to per-thread local memory backed by device DRAM, adding latency that can negate the benefits of fusion. On GPUs, where thread occupancy (the number of threads active in parallel) is bounded by the register file, excessive fusion can also starve parallelism. Different accelerators and compilers therefore strike different balances. NVIDIA GPUs favor warp-level parallelism where element-wise epilogue fusion is straightforward (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). TPUs prioritize systolic-array execution coupled to vector post-processing (Jouppi et al. 2017). Compiler stacks such as TVM, XLA, TensorRT, and MLIR use graph rewrites and engine-building heuristics to weigh memory savings against register and occupancy limits (Chen et al. 2018; Google 2025; NVIDIA 2024b; Lattner et al. 2020). When debugging performance regressions or modifying models frequently, frameworks also allow developers to disable fusion selectively so that memory savings, register usage, and hardware execution constraints can be evaluated independently.

Checkpoint 11.4: Data movement and kernel fusion
The dataflow building blocks are now in place: data locality, tensor layout, and kernel fusion. These fusion decisions are ultimately about data locality, which ties together the chapter’s core data movement strategies:

Locality choice: given weight-stationary, output-stationary, and input-stationary dataflows, which tensor does each hold near the compute units, and how does that choice shift where the memory traffic lands?
Layout match: a kernel runs on a backend expecting NHWC but receives an NCHW tensor. Predict what happens to its memory access pattern and to delivered throughput.
Fusion eligibility: for a Conv2D, a BatchNorm, and a ReLU executed in sequence, decide which pairs are worth fusing and what determines whether fusing them pays off.
Remaining gap: an operation still repeatedly fetches operands because its active blocks exceed fast-memory capacity. How could tiling from section 11.7.5 change this access pattern, and what capacity and reuse evidence would justify that choice?







Convolutional networks, transformers, and multilayer perceptrons stress the memory hierarchy in different places (section 11.5.5), so each model family requires a different combination of stationary dataflow, tiling, tensor layout, and kernel fusion. Mapping is a systematic search over loop permutations, tiling factors, and stationarity policies that maximizes data reuse under hard SRAM and register constraints. Because each family presents a distinct ratio of weights to activations and differing opportunities for temporal locality, optimal mapping policies diverge across workloads. Convolutional networks exploit 2D spatial weight reuse across receptive fields. Transformers split between compute-bound matrix multiplications during prefill and bandwidth-bound KV-cache streaming during autoregressive decoding. Dense MLPs demand blocked GEMM execution across batch dimensions. Table 14 consolidates how dataflow, memory layout, kernel fusion, and tiling align with these three architectural archetypes.


For ResNet-50 and similar CNNs, a key mapping opportunity is spatial weight reuse. A small filter is applied across many spatial locations, so its weights participate in many multiply-accumulate operations. Weight-stationary mappings can capture that reuse by retaining filter tiles locally, while row-stationary or output-stationary mappings may better balance activation and partial-sum traffic on other architectures. Favorable convolution shapes can achieve high arithmetic intensity, which makes them well suited to matrix and systolic execution paths. The model family does not determine one universal dataflow: layer shape, batch size, local-storage capacity, and the target’s supported kernels decide which reuse pattern is worth retaining.

This spatial regularity also enables aggressive fusion and tiling. For inference with frozen BatchNorm statistics, compilers can fold or fuse convolution, normalization, and activation to avoid unnecessary intermediate writes. Training-mode BatchNorm requires reductions over batch statistics and does not have the same element-wise structure that permits fusion. Spatial tiling partitions the feature map into subregions sized to fit within on-chip SRAM, so the fused kernel processes each tile from fast memory before moving to the next.



Transformer mapping depends on execution phase. During training and prefill, attention creates large intermediate matrices unless a tiled implementation avoids materializing them; during autoregressive decoding, attention reads the growing key-value (KV) cache. Each new query vector must access the stored key and value pairs across the preceding sequence. As sequences grow, the full KV cache usually lives in HBM or device DRAM, while attention kernels tile active blocks through SRAM, registers, or shared memory. This access pattern motivates staging active K/V tiles in SRAM so attention consumes them from fast local storage. During training and prefill, the memory traffic created by standard attention implementations similarly explains why fused attention kernels, such as FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022), can deliver large performance gains. They tile the query-key product, softmax, and value summation through on-chip SRAM so the full attention matrix never reaches HBM. The \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) computation is preserved (FlashAttention: IO-aware attention optimization develops the algorithm).



MLPs present the most straightforward mapping problem because their computation reduces largely to dense GEMM.26 Each fully connected layer multiplies an activation matrix by a weight matrix. The weight matrix is fixed across samples, so batching reuses each loaded weight across more activations and raises arithmetic intensity. A batch size of one provides little cross-sample weight reuse and often leaves wide matrix engines underused, while larger batches can move execution toward the compute-bound regime.
26 GEMM: The operation \(\GemmOutputMatrix= \GemmProductScale\GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand+ \GemmAccumulatorScale\GemmOutputMatrix\), with scalars \(\GemmProductScale\) and \(\GemmAccumulatorScale\), is the dense linear-algebra primitive that many deep-learning layers lower to. Optimized GEMM libraries such as cuBLAS and oneDNN use register blocking, vectorization, and hierarchical tiling to approach hardware limits on favorable shapes (NVIDIA 2024a; Intel Corporation 2021b). Modern AI accelerators are heavily specialized for GEMM-like tiles: Tensor Cores, systolic arrays, and matrix extensions all exist to accelerate this primitive, which is why GEMM performance is an important predictor of end-to-end throughput across architectures.

Because MLP layers are typically followed by activation functions and bias additions, GEMM fusion combines these steps into a single kernel, avoiding intermediate memory writes. Blocked tiling partitions the large matrix multiplications into sub-blocks sized for the accelerator’s shared memory, ensuring high cache utilization throughout computation. The simplicity of the MLP mapping, dominated by a single primitive with predictable access patterns, is precisely why hardware vendors optimize GEMM libraries so aggressively: gains in GEMM performance translate directly to MLP throughput. DLRM is not purely an MLP workload, however. Its large sparse embedding tables and feature-interaction stage can dominate capacity and memory traffic, so the dense mapping described here applies to its bottom and top MLP towers rather than to the entire model (Naumov et al. 2019).




Production models rarely consist of a single layer type. A vision transformer, for example, combines a convolutional patch-embedding stage, self-attention layers, and dense MLP blocks within a single forward pass (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021). Those layers create different reuse patterns: the embedding stage can benefit from weight-stationary mapping, attention emphasizes activation movement and tiling, and MLP blocks demand blocked GEMM tiling and fusion. Because no single dataflow strategy is optimal across all three stages, hardware mapping in practice is hybrid and layer-specific.

Dosovitskiy, Alexey, Lucas Beyer, Alexander Kolesnikov, Dirk Weissenborn, Xiaohua Zhai, Thomas Unterthiner, Mostafa Dehghani, et al. 2021. “An Image Is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
Hybrid mapping addresses this heterogeneity by allowing the accelerator to switch strategies at layer boundaries. Each layer presents a different balance of compute intensity, data reuse, and memory access pattern, and the optimal mapping must shift accordingly (Sze et al. 2017). Rather than committing to one dataflow for the entire model, hybrid approaches consider weight stationary execution when weights can be reused locally, input-stationary execution when activation reuse justifies its storage, and output stationary execution when partial-sum traffic is costly. Layer dimensions and available local memory determine which candidate pays off.
TPU-style systolic arrays, NVIDIA GPUs, and tile-based accelerator designs expose different combinations of local memory, tensor layouts, fusion, and scheduling controls. Compilers and runtimes can therefore choose layer-specific strategies rather than one global dataflow for the whole model (Jouppi et al. 2023; NVIDIA Corporation 2020a; Chen et al. 2018). These implementations depend on programmable memory hierarchies, efficient interconnects, and specialized execution pipelines. However, hybrid mapping remains a design-time optimization: in production workloads, execution conditions change dynamically due to varying input sizes, memory contention, and hardware resource availability. Machine learning compilers and runtime systems extend these static mapping choices by introducing dynamic scheduling, memory optimizations, and automatic tuning, ensuring that deep learning workloads operate efficiently across diverse accelerators and deployment environments.

The roofline gives each ResNet-50 layer a ceiling, and hardware mapping showed which schedules can approach it, but neither reaches the silicon by itself. Every layer needs a tiling, a stationary operand, a tensor layout, a precision for the activations it reads and writes, and a fusion boundary. The resulting plan must then run on a device whose input shapes, free memory, and clock rate change while it serves. Across a whole model these choices number in the thousands, which is why compilers and runtimes, not engineers, make them. Graph capture and dispatch overhead, which decide how a model reaches a compiler, belong to ML Frameworks, and the choice of a deployment runtime for a service belongs to Inference Runtime Selection. What remains here is lowering, the path from a captured graph to the accelerator’s units, and the runtime that executes the result. The decode floors this chapter quotes for GPT-2 XL assume that the step is launched as a captured graph (Graph capture and JIT compilation); executed one eager kernel at a time, launch overhead rather than memory bandwidth would set the floor.
A single convolution can be implemented with dozens of valid tiling strategies, kernel variants, and memory layouts, most of which perform poorly on a given target. Machine learning compilers navigate this space by translating high-level dataflow representations into target-specific executable code, making the mapping and dataflow decisions of the preceding sections automatically. Compiling ResNet-50 for GPU inference illustrates the core compiler stages:

Graph optimization fuses repeated Conv2D-BatchNorm-ReLU patterns into single compound kernels, eliminating intermediate round-trips to HBM.
Kernel selection chooses specialized Tensor Core implementations for compatible matrix multiplications, exploiting the high arithmetic intensity of dense convolutions.
Memory planning determines activation lifetimes to safely overlap and reuse intermediate buffer allocations.
Computation scheduling pipelines memory copies with execution across independent hardware queues to hide data transfer latencies.



↩︎ Graph compilation, kernel fusion, and framework dispatch overhead are established in Execution: From Graphs to Kernels.
On the reference H100, the modeled batch-one forward pass falls from 3.53 ms in an eager framework to 0.33 ms as a compiled FP16 engine, a 10.6× improvement without altering the model’s mathematical output. The arithmetic per image is unchanged. The gain comes from fusing the network’s 174 framework kernels into 56 and launching them as one graph instead of one Python dispatch at a time, which removes the fixed cost that dominates a single image. That answers the question the chapter opened with. The INT8 arithmetic for one image takes about 4 μs on the H100 (8 μs at FP16), so even the compiled pass spends almost all of its time on launch and overhead. Batch-one latency sits on the overhead floor rather than on either roofline ceiling, which is why halving the arithmetic barely moves it. The latencies are modeled rather than measured, and Inference Runtime Selection separates the same gap into the contribution of each runtime, but the mechanism is general. Graph rewrites, kernel selection, memory planning, and scheduling systematically apply kernel fusion (section 11.7.7) and memory-efficient tiling (section 11.7.5.1) to convert theoretical hardware FLOP/s into delivered throughput (Chen et al. 2018; NVIDIA 2024b).


A conventional C++ compiler such as gcc or clang cannot collapse ResNet-50’s 174 framework dispatches into 56 fused kernels on its own, because by the time operators lower to scalar loops and pointer arithmetic, the high-level tensor algebra is gone. Machine learning compilers preserve that domain structure by operating on tensor graphs and operator libraries before lowering to machine code. Whereas general-purpose compilers optimize scalar control flow, vector instructions, register allocation, and cache locality, ML compiler stacks optimize graph topology, tensor memory layouts, shape specialization, accelerator kernel dispatch, and inter-device execution planning (Li et al. 2021). Table 15 contrasts the emphasis of these two compiler layers. The boundary is complementary rather than disjoint: an ML compiler stack lowers high-level tensor operations into intermediate representations that feed into an LLVM, GPU, or vendor-specific backend.

The distinction in table 15 explains why compiler configuration dictates delivered performance even when the underlying neural network code remains unmodified. ML compilers manage the translation layer between high-level tensor operations and hardware execution units; when this mapping fails to expose reuse or efficient access, execution can be limited by memory traffic, latency, or insufficient parallel work.



Bridging those two compiler layers requires a staged ML compilation pipeline that progressively lowers a framework’s dataflow graph into executable code for CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, or custom ASICs (Chen et al. 2018; Google 2025; Lattner et al. 2020). A full production pipeline adds a fifth stage, code generation, to the four stages previewed on ResNet-50 (graph optimization, kernel selection, memory planning, and computation scheduling), emitting target-specific machine instructions, assembly, or interpreted bytecode. Across these five stages, the compiler applies the dataflow strategies developed in section 11.7.3: kernel fusion, memory tiling, and compute placement. Hardware acceleration delivers its theoretical throughput only when these compiler-driven transformations expose sufficient arithmetic intensity and align memory access with the hardware hierarchy.


Machine learning frameworks represent models as high-level computation graphs, where nodes represent mathematical operators (such as convolutions, matrix multiplications, and activations) and directed edges represent tensor data dependencies. Executing each operator as a separate kernel can incur intermediate-buffer traffic and repeated launches. An edge denotes a dependency, not necessarily a new allocation or an off-chip transfer, and asynchronous dependencies need not synchronize the host. When intermediate materialization and dispatch dominate execution, graph transformations can remove substantial overhead.
Graph optimization transforms this computation graph into an efficient execution plan before hardware code generation (Chen et al. 2018; Jia et al. 2019). Working primarily at a target-independent intermediate representation (IR) level before lowering (section 11.8.2.5), graph passes apply four core transformations. Kernel fusion merges adjacent operations into a single compound kernel to eliminate off-chip memory round-trips and launch overheads. In convolutional networks, fusing Conv2D, batch normalization with frozen inference statistics, and ReLU keeps activations in local registers or shared SRAM throughout the sequence (section 11.7.7). In transformers, pattern matchers replace multi-operator self-attention subgraphs (score matrix multiplication, scaling, masking, softmax, and multiplication by the value matrix) with IO-aware attention kernels that keep active tiles and running reduction statistics in fast on-chip memory (Dao et al. 2022). Redundant computation elimination and constant folding remove work that need not happen at runtime at all. A typical case is folding frozen normalization parameters into the weights and biases of the preceding linear or convolutional layer (Compression-specific fusion). These passes also prune dead subgraphs and merge identical parallel paths through common subexpression elimination.

The remaining two passes reduce data movement and live memory footprint without changing the operator set. Algebraic simplification and layout adjustments reorder mathematically equivalent operations to avoid runtime reshape traffic, for example by pushing transpositions through elementwise ops or canceling them against inverse permutations. Memory-aware node reordering evaluates topological sorts of the dependency graph. It schedules independent operations so intermediate activations are consumed and deallocated promptly before memory pressure forces spills to host DRAM. Production compilers execute these rewrites through pattern-matching rules, producing a coarse-grained execution graph aligned with the accelerator’s bandwidth constraints before binding each node to a concrete hardware routine.



Kernel selection binds each node in the optimized graph to a concrete hardware implementation. Accelerators provide dozens of valid kernel implementations for a single tensor operation, each parameterized by tile dimensions, thread block configurations, memory staging patterns, and target precision. Choosing the optimal kernel determines whether the execution engine achieves high compute utilization or stalls on uncoalesced memory accesses and pipeline bubbles (Chen et al. 2018; Zheng et al. 2020).
In most production pipelines, compilers draw from vendor-optimized kernel libraries (NVIDIA’s cuDNN and cuBLAS for GPUs, Intel’s oneDNN for x86) rather than synthesizing kernels from scratch. These libraries encode microarchitectural details such as register file capacity, cache latency, and vector lane width, so the compiler can invoke pre-tuned implementations.
AI compilers trade compilation time against execution speed across three strategies when choosing among candidate kernels, with numerical precision constraining all three. Rule-based selection is the fastest at compile time. It relies on static heuristics over tensor shapes, alignment, data types, and target support to pick implementations such as a Tensor Core GEMM without benchmarking a large candidate set, at the risk of missing faster configurations on irregular shapes. Cost-model selection refines that choice without running hardware benchmarks by estimating kernel latency, register pressure, cache hit rates, and arithmetic intensity with analytical models that prune unpromising candidates (Lattner et al. 2020). When compilation budgets allow hardware measurement, profile-guided selection benchmarks candidates directly on the target device. Autotuners such as TVM’s AutoTVM and Ansor search over tile sizes, unrolling factors, and thread configurations to converge on the fastest implementation (Chen et al. 2018; Zheng et al. 2020), and TensorRT similarly times candidate tactics against the target batch sizes. Across all three strategies, precision-aware constraints govern which candidates are legal: inference can use lower-precision paths after quality validation, but selecting INT8 without appropriate range handling degrades accuracy, whereas selecting a wider path unnecessarily forgoes available throughput.

Memory planning assigns physical storage locations, buffer offsets, and tensor lifetimes across the accelerator’s memory hierarchy (Roesch et al. 2018; Chen et al. 2018). High-performance execution plans fail if memory management introduces uncoalesced memory transactions, bank conflicts, or unnecessary memory allocations that exhaust accelerator memory, so the compiler coordinates three core memory management mechanisms.

Google. 2025. XLA: Optimizing Compiler for Machine Learning.
Tensor layout optimization chooses the physical arrangement of tensor dimensions that each kernel needs for coalesced access and vectorization, such as channels-last NHWC for Tensor Core convolutions (section 11.7.6) (NVIDIA Corporation 2021; Google 2025). Compilers perform layout assignment globally across the graph to prevent back-to-back layout transformation kernels that consume memory bandwidth.
Liveness analysis and buffer reuse prevent out-of-memory errors by sharing physical memory across non-overlapping tensors. Deep neural networks generate dozens of intermediate activation tensors during forward propagation. Allocating a unique memory buffer for every tensor would quickly exceed the capacity of device memory (such as 16 to 80 GB on typical accelerator GPUs). The compiler analyzes the graph to compute the liveness interval of each tensor, from its generation to the completion of its last consumer. By modeling memory allocation as an interval graph coloring or 2D bin-packing problem, the compiler assigns multiple non-overlapping intermediate tensors to the same physical memory offsets (Roesch et al. 2018). This static reuse reduces peak device memory requirements to the working set size of concurrently active tensors, avoiding runtime allocation overhead and fragmentation.

Memory hierarchy placement optimizes the staging of data between external memory (HBM or GDDR) and on-chip scratchpad memories (SRAM or shared memory). External memory bandwidth is a scarce resource; moving intermediate tiles back and forth across the memory bus creates memory-bound stalls. Compilers synthesize tiling parameters that guarantee intermediate blocks remain resident in on-chip SRAM until all local compute operations complete, minimizing round-trip traffic across the memory bus. With memory layouts fixed and buffer addresses assigned, the compiler schedules operation execution across hardware compute resources.



Computation scheduling determines the execution timeline and hardware resource binding for operations in the compiled graph (Zheng et al. 2020). Modern accelerators feature deep hardware pipelines, multiple independent compute engines, and dedicated DMA copy engines. Effective scheduling coordinates these resources across three distinct architectural dimensions to maximize hardware occupancy, preserve data dependencies, and prevent pipeline stalls (Chen et al. 2018).

Task partitioning maps computational subgraphs onto the target’s physical execution units. On GPUs, computations are partitioned into grids of thread blocks dispatched across Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs). On TPUs, matrix multiplications are partitioned into tile sequences matched to the physical dimensions of systolic arrays (e.g., \(128 \times 128\) or \(256 \times 256\) processing elements) (Norrie et al. 2021). On CPUs, tasks are split into thread pools matching physical cores and vectorized to fill SIMD registers.
Execution ordering resolves dependencies while minimizing live memory pressure. Operations that depend on prior results must wait for producer kernels to complete, but independent branches (such as multi-head attention projections or parallel residual paths) can execute concurrently or interleave to maintain uniform compute utilization. Compilers analyze the dependency graph to schedule operations in an order that keeps compute pipelines full while keeping activation lifetimes short, preventing buffer bloat.
Asynchronous overlap hides memory latency by executing data transfers concurrently with compute kernels. Accelerators feature dedicated DMA engines that operate independently of arithmetic pipelines. Compilers exploit this architectural separation by scheduling memory transfers (such as host-to-device weights or inter-accelerator halo exchanges) in separate hardware queues or CUDA streams, overlapping transfer latency behind long-running compute operations (Chen et al. 2018; NVIDIA 2024b). When compute and transfer overlap completely, data movement costs are hidden behind arithmetic execution. Poor scheduling instead introduces execution bubbles where arithmetic units sit idle waiting for kernel dispatches or serialized data copies, so synchronizing kernels via explicit compiler-generated events and stream schedules ensures the hardware sustains continuous execution without CPU driver intervention (NVIDIA 2024b; Zheng et al. 2020).

With scheduling complete, the final compilation stage translates the scheduled execution plan into target-specific machine instructions. Code generation applies traditional backend compiler passes (instruction selection, register allocation, instruction scheduling, and peephole optimization) tailored to accelerator architectures.
Instruction selection for ML targets must emit instructions that directly engage specialized matrix ISA extensions. On NVIDIA GPUs, code generators emit PTX instructions such as mma.sync.aligned to invoke Tensor Cores directly, as shown in listing 13. On Intel CPUs with Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX), the backend targets tile-multiply instructions operating on 2D register tiles. On Arm architectures with the Scalable Matrix Extension (SME), the target is outer-product accumulation across scalable vector tiles. A backend that emits generic floating-point vector instructions instead of these matrix extensions leaves the primary compute engines idle, reducing effective throughput by an order of magnitude. For CPUs and GPUs, compilers emit machine code or optimized assembly; for TPUs, field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs),27 and proprietary NPUs, the output is often an optimized bytecode or binary execution package executed by a specialized hardware runtime.

FPGAs can improve performance for latency-sensitive data center services by implementing custom pipelines matched to a particular workload (Putnam et al. 2014). This reconfigurability makes FPGAs attractive for rapidly evolving ML architectures where committing to an ASIC risks obsolescence, but the requirement for hardware description languages (Verilog/VHDL) and compilation times measured in hours creates a productivity barrier that limits adoption to deployments where the efficiency benefit justifies the engineering cost.

A compiler transforms a high-level model into an execution plan tailored to target hardware, but that plan embeds static assumptions about runtime conditions: tensor shapes, workspace allocation limits, device capabilities, and execution concurrency. Ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation optimizes graph structures, fusion boundaries, and memory layouts for fixed shapes and known hardware configurations. While just-in-time (JIT) compilation can compile specialized variants dynamically as new shapes arrive, each compiled kernel still executes a fixed execution plan. Production serving breaks those assumptions: request arrival rates fluctuate, batch sizes vary, several inference workloads compete for shared accelerator memory, and thermal throttling can pull clock frequencies below their rated values. Request batching and admission control belong to the serving layer (Model Serving); the concern here is how the accelerator runtime dispatches compiled execution plans once a batch reaches the hardware.
An AI runtime bridges static graph compilation and the dynamic realities of accelerator execution. Compilers optimize and lower computational graphs under fixed structural assumptions, but production systems encounter variable batch sizes, fluctuating sequence lengths, and constrained memory budgets. The runtime executes compiled engines while managing input-dependent tensor shapes, device-memory buffers and workspace, asynchronous hardware streams, and precompiled execution profiles. In production inference stacks such as NVIDIA TensorRT, the offline builder optimizes the network and benchmarks candidate tactics to construct an execution engine, while the runtime engine binds input buffers, selects valid optimization profiles, and dispatches kernels to the accelerator (NVIDIA Corporation 2026a, 2026b).

Second, it manages device memory through arena allocators and static buffer reuse, reducing repeated allocation and associated host-device synchronization overhead. While serving schedulers oversee request batching and admission control across clusters, the accelerator runtime governs local execution on the device.


General-purpose runtimes manage threads, preemptive tasks, heap allocations, and asynchronous I/O across arbitrary control-flow paths. Tensor memory management represents a primary architectural divergence. In traditional systems, general-purpose allocators manage variable-sized heap objects using runtime metadata. Traditional device allocation calls such as cudaMalloc can introduce costly driver work and synchronization. AI runtimes reduce repeated allocation overhead by combining lifetime analysis with pooled or arena allocation. For fixed-shape graphs, the compiler computes static memory offsets, mapping non-overlapping intermediate tensors to shared physical buffers. For variable-shape tensors, the runtime can carve device-memory buffers from preallocated pools, avoiding repeated driver allocation calls within the reserved capacity.
Production environments introduce physical constraints that differ from offline benchmarks. For example, an NVIDIA A100 SXM accelerator operates with a maximum TDP of 400 W, whereas the A100 PCIe variant is constrained to a 300 W TDP envelope. Because sustained clock frequencies scale with available power and thermal dissipation, a compiled kernel tuned for an SXM module may experience thermal throttling or fail to meet latency bounds on a PCIe card. The runtime cannot re-synthesize loop structures or change thread-block dimensions dynamically in response to thermal constraints; it must execute within precompiled profiles while the serving system handles request batching and admission control.



While static compilation generates high-performance machine code for fixed shapes, production inference requires executing requests with dynamic dimensions. In language models, input sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) and batch size \(\BatchSize\) vary across requests. Recompiling an execution plan for each unexpected shape can violate a request deadline: exploring loop unrolling, shared-memory tiling, and register allocation requires seconds or minutes, while serving deadlines operate on millisecond timescales.


↪ How serving runtimes form batches of varying size under latency deadlines is developed in Static vs. dynamic batching.
Profile-based inference stacks address this mismatch with precompiled shape ranges. The engine is built for a declared range of each dynamic dimension (the minimum, typical, and maximum shapes), with device-memory workspace reserved for that range. A request inside the range binds its tensors to preallocated buffers and launches precompiled kernels without compilation overhead. A request outside it must be padded, split, or routed to a slower general-purpose kernel, because the runtime cannot synthesize new tiling strategies on the fly. TensorRT’s optimization profiles are the common example, and choosing and configuring such a runtime for a service is developed in Inference Runtime Selection.
Variable requests also keep the host link busy, and the runtime hides those transfers with the asynchronous streams and double buffering of section 11.5.4.2, copying batch \(\BatchIndex{+}1\) while batch \(\BatchIndex\) executes. The overlap holds only while compute duration exceeds transfer duration.



An operation may have multiple kernel implementations, termed tactics in TensorRT. The builder selects tactics while constructing an engine; other stacks may retain variants for runtime dispatch. The available choice depends on tensor dimensions, the compiled plan, and permitted device-memory workspace.
Operational batch size changes the available reuse and parallelism. At \(\BatchSize=1\) in weight-streaming autoregressive decoding, GEMV kernels often target memory throughput. Larger prompt-processing batches can favor GEMM kernels using Tensor Core paths, register tiles, and shared memory. The transition depends on dimensions, precision, traffic, and hardware balance; no fixed batch threshold establishes compute-bound execution.
Device-memory workspace availability further constrains tactic selection. In a standard output-tiled GEMM, each thread block computes one \((\GemmRowDimension, \GemmColumnDimension)\) output tile and loops sequentially over the entire inner reduction dimension \(\GemmInnerDimension\), accumulating partial sums in on-chip registers before writing the final output tile once. When the output matrix is small but the reduction dimension \(\GemmInnerDimension\) is long, the output grid spawns too few thread blocks to occupy every streaming multiprocessor. A split-\(\GemmInnerDimension\) tactic exposes extra parallelism by partitioning the \(\GemmInnerDimension\) reduction loop across multiple thread blocks running on different multiprocessors. Because separate multiprocessors do not share registers or local scratchpad memory, each split-\(\GemmInnerDimension\) block must write its partial tile sum to a temporary buffer in global device memory so a subsequent reduction step can sum the slices into the final result. A runtime execution plan built under a tight workspace memory limit may therefore disallow split-\(\GemmInnerDimension\) tactics and accept lower multiprocessor occupancy instead.
Runtime selection remains strictly bounded by the numerical formats established during compilation. In mixed-precision training and inference systems such as Megatron-LM, executing matrix multiplications in FP16 or BF16 on Tensor Cores with FP32 accumulation is a numerical requirement of the chosen recipe, validated prior to deployment (Shoeybi et al. 2019). The runtime does not monitor loss values or dynamically alter precision; it only chooses among the validated tactics that implement the specified numerical precision.
