Kernel dispatch represents the final stage of runtime execution, coordinating host-side task queues with device-side execution. The software runtime manages host-side command queues (such as CUDA streams or TPU command rings) and records hardware events or semaphores to enforce dataflow dependencies asynchronously. When independent operations (such as parallel multi-head attention projections) have no mutual data dependencies, the runtime dispatches them onto separate streams to enable concurrent execution on the accelerator. Once submitted to the device queue, however, execution control transfers entirely to hardware schedulers. On a GPU, the hardware warp scheduler and work distribution engine assign thread blocks to SMs based on register file availability, shared memory capacity, and maximum warp occupancy. The software runtime cannot schedule individual threads or dictate L1/L2 cache replacement policies. Similarly, TPU runtimes submit macro-instructions to on-chip command queues, while hardware sequencers feed systolic matrix units and vector units (Jouppi et al. 2017).
A low achieved rate alone cannot distinguish runtime gaps from a memory bottleneck. Consider three supplied illustrative profiles of low-intensity kernels, not measurements from a particular device. In the first, the timeline shows continuous kernel execution and HBM traffic close to the sustainable bandwidth ceiling. Reducing transferred bytes or increasing reuse addresses that observed limit. In the second, kernels remain active but dependent loads produce long stalls while HBM traffic stays well below its ceiling. More bandwidth alone need not help: independent requests or a different access schedule must expose enough concurrency to hide the latency. In the third, short kernels alternate with device-idle gaps while the host submits work. Reducing dispatch and synchronization overhead addresses those gaps; changing the arithmetic instruction rate does not.
The discriminating evidence is the timeline together with traffic and stall observations. If added independent requests raise bandwidth and shorten load stalls, they support the latency hypothesis; if bandwidth is already sustained near its ceiling, traffic reduction is the more direct lever. The roofline bounds the resource opportunity, while the profile identifies which mechanism leaves the kernel below it. Even with aggressive kernel fusion, optimal tactic selection, and zero-allocation memory reuse, the execution capacity of a single accelerator is physically bounded by its silicon area, thermal dissipation limit, and high-bandwidth memory capacity. Scaling beyond these physical boundaries therefore requires distributing computation across multiple accelerators.

A single accelerator holds the chapter’s ResNet-50 workload and GPT-2 XL decoding comfortably in on-package memory, but larger workloads outgrow one device either because their arithmetic would take too long on it or because their weights and runtime state do not fit in its HBM. Multi-chip scaling still depends on an efficient per-device dataflow, since each accelerator must feed its own execution units, but communication adds further boundaries to the memory hierarchy. Moving data through on-chip storage, HBM, an intra-node link, and a network fabric generally increases latency and energy at each step, so scaling is not merely a question of adding chips.
Each step outward moves the communication boundary and changes the dominant trade-off. Inside the package, chiplet-based architectures partition a large design into smaller dies joined at relatively low latency, bypassing the manufacturing limits of a monolithic chip. Wafer-scale integration takes the opposite approach and keeps more computation on one device. At the node, a multi-accelerator server joins several chips, each with its own memory, through board- or server-level interconnects such as NVLink. A workload then splits through data parallelism (each accelerator processes different batches) or model parallelism (different accelerators hold different layers, or individual matrix multiplications are sliced across devices). When a model’s weights and runtime state exceed one device’s HBM, that split becomes a placement requirement rather than a speed choice. How training uses the accelerators of one machine, including how they synchronize gradients, is developed in Single-node multi-GPU training. Within a server, the engineering test compares the computation or device-memory capacity that partitioning saves with the communication it exposes, accounting for overlap and the actual directional link bandwidth.
Beyond the node, the network interface card links each machine to the others over Ethernet or InfiniBand. It is the narrowest, highest-latency step of the bandwidth taper measured in section 11.5.4.1, and traffic that must cross it leaves single-node reasoning behind. Work that spans several machines lies beyond this book’s one-machine scope. Scaling out across identical data-center accelerators is one way a system combines multiple engines; at the opposite end of the power spectrum, mobile and embedded systems integrate several different engines onto a single silicon die.

Edge, mobile, and automotive deployments operate under strict physical constraints: sealed enclosures without active fans limit thermal dissipation to a few watts, while battery capacity caps total energy consumption. To deliver machine learning capabilities within these boundaries, heterogeneous system-on-chip (SoC) architectures integrate general-purpose CPU cores, GPU shader arrays, digital signal processors (DSPs), and specialized neural processing units (NPUs) onto a single silicon die sharing a unified memory subsystem. The workload mapping problem introduced for discrete accelerators persists, but it expands to include hardware operator coverage, cross-engine transfer overheads, real-time deadlines, and dynamic thermal throttling. Two of the book’s lighthouses take over from ResNet-50 here. MobileNetV2, compute-bound in its efficient regime and built for phone cameras, runs its convolutions on a phone’s NPU within a few watts. KWS, the power-bound lighthouse, listens continuously on a DSP or microcontroller within milliwatts. Both run on silicon that shares one memory system among every engine on the chip.


That single-die integration evolved as mobile workloads outgrew what a CPU and graphics pipeline could sustain within a battery budget. Mobile system-on-chip architectures implement heterogeneous computing by connecting each specialized block, namely CPU clusters, wide SIMD GPU shaders, fixed-point DSPs, and dedicated neural processing units (NPUs), over an on-chip network to shared low-power DRAM (LPDDR) so sensory and perceptual tasks can run on the engine best aligned with their arithmetic structure. Continuous audio feature extraction and keyword spotting run on low-power DSPs, dense convolution and matrix-multiplication layers execute on systolic or tensor-array NPUs, parallel graphics and image postprocessing map to GPUs, and sequential control flow runs on the CPU. Meeting real-time frame deadlines without triggering aggressive thermal throttling requires scheduling execution across these engines while respecting their differing power profiles.

Example 11.5: Heterogeneous microcontrollersScenario: An embedded smart doorbell must run periodic person detection within a tight memory, energy, and latency budget.
Diagnosis: On a supported deployment, a general-purpose Cortex-M path misses the measured energy or latency target. A micro-NPU such as Arm Ethos-U can offload compatible convolution operators, while the CPU retains control flow and unsupported operations.
Systems lesson: Micro-NPU specialization can improve the energy and latency of supported operators, but feasibility must be measured for the whole pipeline, including fallbacks and sensor processing.


Modern mobile SoCs use unified memory architectures where all processing units share a common physical address space in LPDDR. Unlike discrete accelerator architectures that incur explicit PCIe transfer latencies, unified memory allows zero-copy buffer passing between the image signal processor (ISP), CPU, GPU, and NPU. Sharing physical DRAM does not guarantee zero software overhead, however. Non-coherent engines need explicit cache maintenance (section 11.10.4), and specialized NPUs often require hardware-specific tensor layouts (such as channels-last (NHWC) with 16- or 32-byte channel alignment to feed vector register lanes), forcing memory-bound transpositions when interfacing with CPU layers structured in channels-first (NCHW) formats.
SoC architects customize these compute blocks according to domain-specific physical constraints. High-end smartphone SoCs emphasize peak burst performance and low idle leakage for interactive tasks such as real-time computational photography and on-device text generation. In contrast, embedded and automotive SoCs prioritize deterministic memory access, hardware fault detection, and bounded worst-case latency to satisfy real-time control constraints.



Consider a real-time object detection pipeline executing on a mobile SoC with an integrated CPU, GPU, and NPU. The pipeline comprises three consecutive stages: a MobileNetV2 backbone for feature extraction, nonmaximum suppression (NMS) for postprocessing candidate bounding boxes, and a display overlay to render final detections onto a camera feed. Partitioning neural network workloads across those heterogeneous cores requires matching the arithmetic intensity and memory regularity of each stage to the microarchitecture built for it. The convolutional backbone has regular, deterministic memory access and dense arithmetic suited to the NPU’s fixed-function tensor engine, even though depthwise separable layers have lower arithmetic intensity than standard convolutions. NMS, by contrast, relies on score-based sorting and conditional intersection-over-union loops evaluated across variable-length candidate lists. This irregular, branch-heavy control flow maps poorly to an NPU’s spatial array but executes efficiently on out-of-order CPU cores with branch prediction and hardware caching. Finally, the display overlay requires per-pixel rasterization and alpha blending across a high-resolution frame (an embarrassingly parallel, memory-bandwidth-bound task that maps directly to the GPU’s rasterizers and texture units). Splitting the pipeline across the three engines, with the NPU for feature extraction, the CPU for NMS, and the GPU for display compositing, is a candidate mapping. Its compute savings must exceed transfer, layout, and synchronization costs before it improves end-to-end latency or energy over a single-engine implementation.
This pipeline partitioning reflects the broader relationship between algorithmic structures and machine architectures. Regular matrix contractions and convolutions map cleanly to systolic or vectorized NPU datapaths, whereas data-dependent control flow maps to CPU execution resources. Transformer attention layers span both paradigms: the projection GEMMs (\(\AttentionQueryMatrix, \AttentionKeyMatrix, \AttentionValuesMatrix, \AttentionOutputMatrix\)) and attention score contractions (\(\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T\), and the product of the attention weights with \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\)) execute efficiently on NPU matrix units. Intermediate softmax reductions, causal masking, and layer normalizations, however, involve elementwise operations. If the NPU runtime cannot fuse these elementwise operations into on-chip SRAM scratchpads, intermediate tensors must spill to LPDDR, eroding the accelerator’s throughput advantage.
Optimal processor assignment is dynamic rather than static. As device thermal conditions deteriorate or battery reserves drop, the runtime must adapt its scheduling policy. However, migrating an executing model across processor backends carries non-trivial overhead: weights must be re-bound in memory, intermediate buffers may require layout reformatting, and device drivers incur kernel dispatch latency. If the overhead of synchronizing state across processors exceeds the compute savings of offloading, retaining execution on a single suboptimal engine can yield lower total latency and energy than continuous cross-engine migration.
Shared memory subsystems introduce cross-engine interference during simultaneous execution. Because the CPU, GPU, NPU, camera ISP, and display engine share a single LPDDR memory bus, the SoC memory controller enforces Quality of Service (QoS) priorities to satisfy real-time hardware deadlines. The display engine and camera ISP must receive guaranteed memory bandwidth and bounded latency to prevent display flicker and sensor FIFO overflow; the memory controller consequently prioritizes display and camera transactions over NPU and GPU traffic. During memory-intensive phases (such as autoregressive language model decoding where model weights must be read from DRAM for every generated token) high-priority ISP or display traffic reduces effective NPU memory bandwidth, increasing token generation latency.
Automotive computing platforms expose a stricter form of the same interference. A perception pipeline with a hard deadline may share the SoC and memory system with a cabin assistant or infotainment model. If the convenience workload streams weights from DRAM without a bandwidth limit, it can delay the perception pipeline even when the two use different compute engines. Such deployments require resource isolation and validation under concurrent load; average inference throughput alone cannot establish deadline compliance. The hardware lesson is the interference boundary: assigning work to separate engines does not isolate workloads that still share memory bandwidth.



Fanless mobile devices operate within strict continuous power budgets and thermal envelopes, typically dissipating no more than 3 to 5 watts sustained across the entire chassis before touch temperatures exceed safety thresholds. Although transient bursts can draw 10 to 15 watts, continuous inference rapidly saturates the thermal capacitance of the device, heating the silicon junction and requiring active power management across the SoC.
Heterogeneous SoCs manage power across distinct silicon partitions using dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), which exploits the cubic dependence of dynamic power on frequency behind the power wall (equation 2.2). Total power in complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) digital circuits is the sum of dynamic switching power and static leakage power: \[\TotalChipPower= \DynamicPower+ \LeakagePower= \SwitchingActivityFactor \SwitchedCapacitance \SupplyVoltage^2 \ClockFrequency+ \LeakageCurrent \SupplyVoltage\] where \(\SwitchingActivityFactor\) is the gate switching activity factor, \(\SwitchedCapacitance\) is physical load capacitance, \(\SupplyVoltage\) is supply voltage, \(\ClockFrequency\) is clock frequency, and \(\LeakageCurrent\) is temperature-dependent leakage current. Over an operating range where increasing clock frequency \(\ClockFrequency\) requires supply voltage \(\SupplyVoltage\) to rise approximately proportionally, fixed activity and capacitance give the cubic approximation for dynamic power dissipation: \[\DynamicPower\propto \ClockFrequency^3\] Under that approximation, doubling clock frequency can incur an eightfold penalty in dynamic power (Le Sueur and Heiser 2010). The same relation run in reverse is what DVFS exploits: dropping the clock lets the core voltage fall, and dynamic power falls faster than throughput. The cubic penalty also explains why ML accelerators favor large parallel arrays of simple execution units clocked at moderate frequencies over narrow pipelines clocked at extreme frequencies.

Le Sueur, Etienne, and Gernot Heiser. 2010. “Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling: The Laws of Diminishing Returns.” Proceedings of the 2010 International Conference on Power Aware Computing and Systems, 1–8.
On a heterogeneous SoC, CPU clusters, GPU shader cores, and NPU engines occupy separate power and voltage domains. Increasing the voltage and frequency of the NPU to meet a tight latency deadline consumes electrical current and thermal headroom that would otherwise be available to the CPU or GPU. System power governors continuously adjust these operating points based on workload queues, temperature sensor readings, and frame deadline targets.
When sustained computation exceeds the chassis dissipation rate, the platform initiates thermal throttling. Because specialized NPUs achieve higher energy efficiency (TOPS/W) for tensor math than general-purpose cores, offloading matrix workloads to a CPU or GPU during a thermal event often increases total energy dissipation, exacerbating thermal accumulation. Instead, runtimes manage thermal limits by capping clock frequencies, reducing inference duty cycles (such as throttling a perception model from 30 frames per second to 15 frames per second), or dynamically switching to a smaller, pruned model checkpoint. Task migration is applied selectively to move non-tensor preprocessing away from localized silicon hot spots on the die. Battery state further shapes runtime scheduling. When battery charge drops below critical thresholds or the device enters a low-power mode, the system scheduler trades inferencing fidelity for battery life. It does so by selecting prevalidated lower-precision or sparse model variants, or by batching asynchronous inference requests to maximize the time cores spend in deep low-power sleep states.



When a model deployed on an SoC contains even a single operator unsupported by the NPU delegate (such as a custom activation, dynamic tensor shape, or non-standard reduction), the inference runtime must split the computation graph into subgraphs and insert fallback paths to the CPU or GPU. Each boundary crossing requires synchronizing execution and translating data representations, transforming a single algorithmic graph into a fragmented sequence of hardware dispatches. Standard programming models like OpenCL and Vulkan provide portable low-level execution abstractions across compute devices, but they do not eliminate this delegation overhead or the need for microarchitecture-specific kernel tuning.
Shared memory subsystems require explicit cache and memory management across non-coherent execution domains. While CPUs maintain cache coherence across their own cores via hardware snooping protocols, mobile NPUs and DSPs frequently interface with system memory as non-coherent DMA bus masters. When the CPU writes input tensors to cached DRAM and hands control to an NPU, software must explicitly flush the CPU’s dirty cache lines to DRAM before NPU execution begins. Similarly, upon NPU completion, the CPU must invalidate its own cache lines over the destination memory range to prevent reading stale cached data. If unsupported operators cause an inference graph to ping-pong repeatedly between CPU and NPU, the latency of cache maintenance and intermediate DRAM round-trips can exceed the execution time of the operators themselves.
Runtimes navigate this scheduling complexity using ahead-of-time compilation, empirical profile databases, and dynamic dispatch heuristics. Device telemetry (monitoring frame completion times, core temperatures, and battery drain) informs runtime decisions to throttle clock frequencies or swap execution delegates. However, dynamic adaptation cannot replace deterministic graph lowering for latency-sensitive applications; deployment requires validating the compiled, lowered partition on physical target silicon under worst-case thermal and memory contention.
On an SoC, speed comes from keeping work and data on the right engine, not from how many engines the chip has. In the D·A·M taxonomy, an SoC represents a composite Machine layer whose components have different memory hierarchies, arithmetic strengths, and thermal envelopes. The iron law’s data term and the energy-movement principle (\(\ref{pri-energy-movement}\)) together make data movement the governor of both runtime and energy. When software coordination fails to maintain tensor locality or induces frequent cross-engine fallbacks, energy dissipation is dominated by interconnect and DRAM traffic rather than arithmetic. Maximizing performance on heterogeneous SoCs requires minimizing data movement across domain boundaries while matching each algorithmic operation to the specialized datapath architected to accelerate it. From the microcontroller that runs keyword spotting to the data-center accelerator that serves GPT-2 XL, that matching ends in a choice of machine, which the next section makes explicit.

The table turns the chapter’s diagnosis into a selection rule. ResNet-50 rewards arithmetic throughput on a supported INT8 path, GPT-2 XL decode rewards memory bandwidth, DLRM rewards memory capacity, and MobileNetV2 and KWS reward energy per inference on chips that never see a data center. The rest of the section applies that rule at three levels: the configurations accelerator families adopt for their target deployments, the cost of delivered throughput, and the energy each request consumes.


Across data-center, server-CPU, and mobile targets, architects assemble SIMD lanes, Tensor Cores, and systolic arrays into markedly different full-chip organizations depending on which resource binds first. Training-optimized accelerators such as the NVIDIA A100 pack 108 Streaming Multiprocessors with wide SIMD units and FP16 Tensor Cores because training throughput scales with aggregate multiply-accumulate capacity across general kernels (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). Google’s TPU v4, by contrast, concentrates each chip into two cores built around large \(128{\times}128\) BF16 systolic arrays, trading per-thread flexibility for area and energy efficiency on dense matrix multiplications (Jouppi et al. 2023). Inference and edge targets shift the balance again. Intel’s Sapphire Rapids dedicates Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) tile engines to INT8 and BF16 because server inference models tolerate reduced precision (Intel Corporation 2021a), while mobile neural engines shrink those matrix datapaths into low-power SoC blocks that prioritize energy per operation over peak throughput. The pattern across these configurations reveals a consistent engineering principle: each design sacrifices generality to optimize for its target workload’s dominant operation and precision. Training chips invest silicon in wide floating-point datapaths; inference chips trade precision for throughput; mobile chips trade throughput for energy efficiency. No single design dominates across all workloads, which is precisely why hardware selection depends on workload analysis rather than headline specifications.



Consider an engineering team choosing between deploying a larger cluster of older accelerators or a smaller cluster of newer units. Architectural specifications define computational potential, but procurement decisions require cost-performance analysis grounded in delivered throughput rather than datasheet peaks. Because memory access costs dominate computation (section 11.2.3), accelerators achieve only a fraction of their advertised FLOP/s on memory-bound kernels while sustaining high utilization on dense matrix multiplications that amortize each fetch across many operations.
Peak FLOP/s figures therefore mislead whenever dominant kernels are memory-bandwidth or communication bound. In a large model pipeline, dense feed-forward and attention projection layers may remain compute bound, whereas embedding lookups, layer normalization, residual additions, and small-batch autoregressive decoding often have low arithmetic intensity. Their measured bottlenecks can include memory bandwidth, dependent access latency, reductions, and launch overhead; the operator name alone does not identify the limiting resource. The decisive metric is delivered workload throughput per dollar under realistic cluster utilization, memory capacity constraints, available memory bandwidth, and scale-out interconnect efficiency.
These architectural and economic constraints explain the rapid industry adoption of newer accelerators despite substantial increases in nominal unit price. For bandwidth-bound workloads, generational improvements in memory bandwidth and compiler code generation dominate end-to-end execution time. Cloud deployments introduce additional trade-offs: hourly rental rates, dynamic instance utilization, and infrastructure overhead continuously shift the economic break-even point between purchasing on-premises hardware and leasing cloud capacity.
Price-per-peak worksheets for named products age quickly. List prices vary with vendor, region, contract terms, and procurement volume, and each product’s headline peak uses a different precision, so the ratio of price to peak is meaningful for one device but not as a comparison across devices. A dated worksheet for several accelerator generations is kept with the other specifications in System Assumptions. The durable rule is the one the lighthouse table states: divide cost by the throughput the workload delivers on its binding resource, not by the advertised peak.
No worksheet reduces accelerator selection to a single headline specification. A bandwidth-bound kernel benefits more from the H100’s 3,350 GB/s memory subsystem than from an incremental gain in peak arithmetic, whereas a compute-bound GEMM shows the opposite sensitivity. Device memory capacity dictates whether working sets fit on-chip without spilling or partitioning, while compiler and driver maturity determines whether the application can actually reach the advertised datapath.



At fleet scale, energy per useful inference becomes an important hardware-selection criterion. Operational emissions depend on workload throughput, measured system power, utilization, cooling overhead, and the electricity mix; embodied emissions add another lifecycle cost. Peak performance per watt is therefore a screening metric, not a substitute for end-to-end energy per request. The following scenario shows how useful throughput and a common power boundary determine the fleet needed for the same inference service.

Napkin Math 11.11: An illustrative operational-energy comparisonProblem: An inference service must complete 1 billion requests per day. Which of two hypothetical server platforms uses less operational energy for that service?
Supplied observations: For the same model, input distribution, accuracy, and latency target, a CPU server sustains 100 requests/s, and an NPU-equipped server sustains 1,000 requests/s. Their whole-server wall powers are 100 W and 200 W, respectively, including hosts and attached accelerators. These are hypothetical observations for this exercise, not product benchmarks. Assume requests arrive steadily through the day. Both fleets operate at no more than 80 percent of the supplied throughput to reserve capacity for arrival-rate variation. Assume the listed wall power throughout the 24 h day, including spare capacity. Facility cooling and embodied emissions are outside this operational boundary.
Calculation:

Size the fleets from useful work. Multiplying useful throughput by the operating fraction and the day length gives 6,912,000 requests per CPU server per day and 69,120,000 per NPU-equipped server. Divide the daily target by each capacity and round up to whole servers. The service requires 145 CPU servers or 15 NPU-equipped servers.
Account for the provisioned fleet. Server count multiplied by wall power and day length yields 348 kWh per day for CPUs and 72 kWh for NPUs. Dividing each fleet’s energy by the same completed-request target gives 1.2528 J per request and 0.2592 J per request. These values include capacity headroom and integer fleet rounding.
Translate the energy difference. At a common grid factor of 0.429 kg/kWh, the NPU-equipped fleet avoids approximately 43.2 t of operational CO2 emissions per year at the stated system boundary.

Decision: Choose the NPU-equipped fleet if the objective is to minimize operational energy under these supplied conditions. Each server draws more power, but its greater useful throughput reduces the required fleet enough to lower joules per completed request. This conclusion depends on meeting the same quality and latency targets; a faster peak arithmetic rate alone would not establish the advantage. A procurement decision must additionally compare acquisition costs, software support, and embodied emissions.


Energy per request completes the selection rule that the lighthouse table began. Hardware selection is not determined by peak speed alone. Energy per useful result, carbon intensity, embodied impact, and total cost of ownership belong beside latency, throughput, and memory capacity, and each is measured against the resource the workload actually exhausts. The misconceptions that follow are the ways teams skip that measurement and choose the wrong hardware path.

Hardware acceleration often defies intuition because headline specifications mask workload-specific bottlenecks. The fallacies and pitfalls here capture selection, scaling, and optimization errors that leave expensive compute resources underused. Sound system evaluation follows one diagnostic habit instead: characterize the workload arithmetic intensity, identify the physical bottleneck metric, match execution to the appropriate datapath, and account for interconnect, scaling, and portability costs.

Fallacy: More specialized hardware always provides better performance than general-purpose alternatives.
Specialized accelerators achieve high efficiency only when workload access patterns match underlying execution datapaths: the core tenet of algorithm-machine co-design. On the roofline (section 11.6), the A100 reference tensor path has a ridge point of 153 FLOP/byte; below that ridge, increasing its 312 TFLOP/s arithmetic peak does not raise the modeled bandwidth ceiling. A transformer attention softmax with \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) = 2 FLOP/byte–5 FLOP/byte is capped at 4.1 TFLOP/s–10.2 TFLOP/s (3.3 percent of tensor peak) on an A100. On a CPU, whose ridge point sits around 10 FLOP/byte–20 FLOP/byte, the same traffic model places the kernel below the reference ridge, and its bandwidth ceiling represents 10 percent–50 percent of the CPU’s compute capacity. These fractions are modeled bandwidth bounds, not measured utilization. When workloads have irregular memory access, tiny batch sizes, or dynamic control flow, highly parallel execution pipelines stall on memory latency and thread divergence. General-purpose CPUs with large cache hierarchies, out-of-order execution, and branch predictors often deliver superior latency and resource efficiency under these conditions. Hardware selection requires matching workload arithmetic intensity and dataflow regularity to architectural ridge points rather than assuming specialization guarantees speed.


Pitfall: Ignoring memory bandwidth limitations when selecting acceleration strategies.
Procurement decisions frequently target peak arithmetic throughput while overlooking memory interface constraints. Off-chip data movement imposes severe performance and energy penalties: fetching an operand from DRAM consumes roughly 640 pJ compared to 0.5 pJ for a small, register-adjacent L1 SRAM access, the cheapest tier noted in the caption of figure 4. Consider an accelerator providing 300 TFLOP/s of compute alongside 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth, setting a ridge point of 150 FLOP/byte. A normalization kernel such as LayerNorm with an arithmetic intensity of 1.5 FLOP/byte has a bandwidth ceiling of 3 TFLOP/s (1 percent of compute peak). Under the stated HBM streaming assumption, memory bandwidth supplies this upper bound, and adding compute units alone does not raise it.


Fallacy: Hardware acceleration benefits scale linearly with additional accelerators.
Distributed training need not deliver \(8\times\) throughput on eight accelerators because exposed inter-chip communication can reduce parallel efficiency. Synchronizing gradients across ranks via ring AllReduce makes each rank send and receive about twice the gradient payload (equation 8.12), or 1.75× payloads across eight devices. With an interconnect such as NVLink providing 600 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth (half that per direction), transmitting a 1 GB gradient payload consumes 5.83 ms. For a model with a 50 ms compute step, this data exchange adds 11.7 percent communication overhead before counting software collective latency. Without compute-communication pipelining, an eight-accelerator node reaches only 7.2× speedup (89.6 percent parallel efficiency). Stragglers, barrier synchronizations, and collective protocol overhead widen the gap between linear expectations and physical cluster scaling.


Pitfall: Planning accelerator capacity from peak FLOP/s specifications.
Peak FLOP/s measures arithmetic unit capacity under ideal instruction mixes and continuous operand availability, not delivered application throughput. Realized performance depends on kernel arithmetic intensity, matrix dimensions, memory coalescing, and runtime launch overhead. The roofline model (section 11.6) bounds the gap between peak compute and bandwidth-limited execution. On an A100 GPU with a 312 TFLOP/s peak, an illustrative dense-transformer scenario supplies a sustained range of 120 TFLOP/s–180 TFLOP/s (40 percent–60 percent model FLOPs utilization). This supplied range is illustrative, not a measurement or a prediction for every model. Sizing cluster capacity from peak FLOP/s creates severe under-provisioning; capacity planning must rely on measured sustained throughput or roofline-bounded kernel projections.


Fallacy: One peak FLOP/s rating describes a workload at every precision.
Accelerators have separate datapaths for different precisions, and the peak throughput varies dramatically across them. An H100 delivers roughly 989 TFLOP/s in FP16 tensor operations but only about 67 TFLOP/s in FP32 CUDA-core operations: a roughly 15× gap within the same chip (Choquette 2023). Dividing achieved BF16 model FLOP/s by the smaller FP32 peak inflates the reported utilization, while using that FP32 peak to estimate ideal training time overestimates the time. Matching against the wrong roofline misclassifies kernels as compute-bound when they are memory-bound (or vice versa). Useful model FLOP utilization divides the model’s useful operations per elapsed second by the matching supported precision and execution-path peak. Hardware busy time is a different metric: an active device can spend time on transfers, redundant work, or fallback execution. Quote the denominator and precision explicitly.


Pitfall: Deploying small-batch inference workloads on high-compute accelerators.
Small-batch dense inference can use only a small fraction of arithmetic peak because single-sample execution lacks cross-sample parameter reuse. For a dense linear projection with widths \(\LayerInputWidth=\LayerOutputWidth=2048\), a single request (\(\BatchSize=1\)) is modeled as streaming the entire weight tensor from device memory to execute a matrix-vector product, yielding an arithmetic intensity of only 1 FLOP/byte. At batch size \(\BatchSize=256\), weight reuse amortizes memory transfers across tokens, elevating arithmetic intensity to 204.8 FLOP/byte. At \(\BatchSize=1\), memory bandwidth bounds performance at 2.04 TFLOP/s on an A100 and 0.32 TFLOP/s on a T4. Although the T4 provides a lower peak of 65 TFLOP/s with a ridge point of 203.1 FLOP/byte, the two batch-1 ceilings differ by 6.4×, which is exactly their memory-bandwidth ratio. The A100’s 4.8× advantage in peak compute contributes nothing. The A100 costs 6× as much as the T4, so their modeled batch-1 throughput ceilings per dollar are nearly the same. Actual procurement requires measured latency, throughput, memory fit, and the intended request mix.


Fallacy: Vendor-specific optimizations have no long-term portability cost.
Optimizing exclusively for a single vendor runtime captures immediate kernel efficiency but introduces severe architectural lock-in (section 11.8). Codebases saturated with proprietary device intrinsics, vendor-specific assembly, and non-standard memory layouts require months of engineering labor to port when newer, more cost-effective accelerators emerge. This technical debt delays hardware transitions and prevents multi-vendor procurement. To preserve flexibility, systems must isolate vendor-tuned micro-kernels behind hardware abstraction layers or target intermediate compiler representations (such as Triton or MLIR).

Key Takeaways: Moving data costs more than computing it

The roofline model bounds attainable performance: Compare a kernel’s arithmetic intensity with the ridge for its memory interface and supported execution path (295.2 FLOP/byte for the H100’s dense FP16 tensor path and 590.7 FLOP/byte for its INT8 path). Below it, bandwidth supplies the tighter modeled ceiling; above it, compute does. Profiling establishes whether the kernel approaches that ceiling or is limited by dependencies, dispatch, or another execution resource.
Memory bandwidth constrains performance: GPU compute capacity has grown faster than memory bandwidth. Many inference phases are memory bound, especially low-batch decoding and embedding lookup, while large-batch GEMMs can remain compute bound.
Hardware-software co-design compounds performance: Matching algorithm patterns to architectural capabilities, such as dense GEMM on systolic or tensor units and supported sparsity on sparse paths, can produce large improvements.
Tensor Cores require a compatible path: Precision, dimensions, layouts, and library support must match the architecture. Batch and shape affect reuse and utilization, but no single batch threshold guarantees peak performance.
End-to-end speedup stops at the next bottleneck: Accelerating one kernel leaves launch, transfer, synchronization, communication, and unsupported work unchanged. Use Amdahl’s law (principle \(\ref{pri-amdahl}\)) and profiling to decide whether further silicon, better mapping, or less movement will improve the complete workload.



An accelerator is not a uniformly faster computer. It provides efficient paths for particular operations and dataflows, and each of those paths is a way of moving fewer bytes per useful operation. Tiling, fusion, stationary dataflows, and systolic execution pay off only when the workload, numerical format, and software path can use them. The diagnostic habit the chapter leaves is therefore an ordering. Place the kernel on the relevant roofline to bound its performance, bound the end-to-end gain with Amdahl’s law, and only then choose among more silicon, a better mapping, or less movement. Each step is a prediction that measurement must confirm. The same habit is what keeps the bitter lesson affordable. Scale keeps winning only while each additional operation gets cheaper in time and energy, and on modern accelerators the operation is rarely the expensive part. The bytes that feed it are.

What’s Next: From optimization to validationData selection, model compression, and hardware acceleration each end with a favorable local number. Data selection reaches target accuracy on fewer examples, compression produces a smaller artifact, and the roofline places a kernel below a ceiling that the vendor’s peak overstates. Each number is a prediction made for one stage in isolation, and the stages interact once they run together on a real device under real load. Benchmarking takes up that test, beginning with this chapter’s ResNet-50 workload, whose predicted roofline position becomes the first claim a measurement must confirm. It asks which local gains survive deployment-representative conditions, and it supplies the measurement scope, standardized suites, and statistical protocols that let different systems be compared on the same terms.

Explain how the \(\text{im2col}\) (image-to-column) transformation allows standard 2D convolution operations to execute on high-throughput matrix multiplication hardware (GEMM engines), and describe the primary memory overhead associated with this approach.

What is the primary numerical difference between FP16 and BF16 as presented in this section?

FP16 uses fewer total bits than BF16, so it always transfers less data

Answer: The correct answer is D. HBM achieves ultra-high bandwidth by vertically stacking DRAM dies with Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) and interfacing with the accelerator through a silicon interposer with extremely wide memory buses (1024 bits per stack vs. 32/64 bits for standard GDDR channels). Because physical wire distances over the silicon interposer are short and the bus is wide, HBM can run at lower pin clock frequencies, significantly reducing energy per bit (\(pJ/\text{bit}\)) compared to driving high-frequency GDDR signals over long PCB traces. For example, a partitioning that is acceptable within one node may become communication-heavy once activations or gradients must repeatedly cross the internode boundary. However, it does not make the entire wafer a uniform zero-cost machine: distance, routing capacity, thermal limits, fault tolerance, and manufacturing constraints still shape which communication patterns remain efficient. Answer: The correct answer is B. Treating a \(2\times\) increase in peak TFLOP/s as an automatic \(2\times\) workload speedup ignores memory-bandwidth limits, host and launch overheads, unsupported operators, and other bottlenecks that often dominate real execution. The higher-bandwidth statement is a conditional architectural fact rather than a fallacy, and the fusion and warp-divergence statements describe real mechanisms discussed in the chapter.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why peak TFLOP/s alone cannot predict end-to-end workload speedup.

title: 11 Hardware Acceleration
text:
Architecture stack focus for this chapter.
Why does moving data cost more than computing it?
Arithmetic is inexpensive relative to data movement. In the time required to fetch a single scalar operand from off-chip DRAM, modern arithmetic units can execute dozens to hundreds of floating-point operations, and that DRAM access consumes on the order of a hundred times more energy than the computation itself. This imbalance, the memory wall, means specialized accelerators are not merely faster arithmetic engines. Rather, their microarchitectures are designed to stage, amortize, and hide data movement through wide spatial interconnects, deep on-chip memory hierarchies, and specialized execution pipelines. When general-purpose processor scaling faltered, hardware specialization enabled machine learning models to continue scaling by turning transistor budgets into high-throughput tensor datapaths. Delivered performance, however, depends on whether a model’s tensor access patterns match the data paths of the underlying silicon. Hardware selection cannot be reduced to comparing peak FLOP/s: two accelerators with identical theoretical compute ratings often deliver radically different throughput on real workloads because one saturates its functional units while the other starves for data. A recommendation model dominated by sparse embedding lookups stresses memory bandwidth and interconnect latency, demanding a different memory architecture than a dense transformer training run bounded by matrix multiply-accumulate throughput. If an operation is bandwidth bound, reducing theoretical operation count yields zero speedup because arithmetic is not the binding constraint. Matching workload characteristics to architectural dataflows determines whether an accelerator operates near its hardware ceiling or languishes at a fraction of its advertised peak. In D·A·M terms, the accelerator makes the machine constraint concrete, governing which algorithms and model architectures remain practical in production.

Learning Objectives

Explain hardware acceleration as tensor-workload specialization and why Amdahl’s law bounds its end-to-end speedup
Compare Tensor Cores, systolic arrays, SIMD/SIMT units, and sparse execution for ML compute primitives
Diagnose memory-wall bottlenecks using bandwidth, cache hierarchy, host-device transfer, and energy-movement costs
Calculate arithmetic intensity and execution-path roofline ceilings, then use profiling to diagnose compute or memory limits
Select dataflow, tiling, and mapping strategies that maximize reuse under memory-capacity constraints
Analyze compiler and runtime optimizations that fuse kernels, plan memory, and schedule accelerators
Evaluate accelerator choices across throughput, latency, power, cost, and deployment-context constraints

title: 11 Hardware Acceleration
text:
Hardware acceleration turns on the machine axis.
Model Compression closed on a deployment profile for ResNet-50 quantized to INT8 (ResNet-50 INT8 Deployment Profile on the Reference H100): a model four times smaller whose large-batch throughput rises severalfold on the reference H100 while its batch-one latency barely moves. Data selection reduced the iron law’s Data factor (\(\text{Samples/Task}\)) and compression reduced the Algorithm factor (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\)) and byte traffic (\(\DataVolume\)), but whether either saving reaches the wall clock is decided by the Machine factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)). This chapter supplies the machine side of that profile. It explains why the same INT8 weights run faster on one execution path than on another, and why the hardware, not the model, determines how much of every compression saving survives execution. The explanation starts with the memory wall: arithmetic is cheap relative to data movement, so specialized hardware matters less because it raises compute throughput than because it organizes memory, dataflow, and parallelism so that its arithmetic units stay fed.
One workload runs through the chapter. ResNet-50 quantized to INT8 carries the book’s compute-bound regime (Lighthouse Models as Reference Workloads): its convolutions reuse each weight across many image positions, so on a data-center accelerator most of its time can go to arithmetic rather than to moving bytes. It reappears at every level of the machine, from the matrix units that execute its convolutions to the compiler that lowers its graph, and each time the question is what the INT8 path changes. GPT-2 XL decoding one token at a time supplies the single contrast. It carries the bandwidth-bound regime: every generated token streams all of the model’s weights from memory for about two operations per parameter, so the machine that keeps ResNet-50 busy spends most of a decode step waiting for bytes. MobileNetV2, whose depthwise layers trade arithmetic for a small parameter footprint, and keyword spotting (KWS), the power-bound lighthouse, return where the chapter reaches phone-class and embedded chips. DLRM appears where its embedding lookups, the capacity-bound regime, break the regular access patterns that accelerators assume. The reference machine is the NVIDIA H100, the data-center accelerator this book uses for training and serving examples; its numbers are one generation’s instance of limits that every generation obeys.

Definition 11.1: Hardware acceleration
Hardware acceleration is the practice of mapping work from general-purpose execution onto specialized processors or functional units optimized for a narrower operation class. For ML workloads, that specialization commonly trades some programmability for the compute density \((\PeakRate)\) and performance-per-watt gains that regular tensor operations can exploit.

Significance: An H100 GPU delivers 989 TFLOP/s for dense FP16/BF16 matrix multiplication; against this chapter’s illustrative 1–2 TFLOP/s reference-CPU baseline, this is a 490–990× gap. Its 80 billion transistors devote far more silicon to parallel arithmetic than to branch prediction, out-of-order scheduling, and large caches (Choquette 2023).
Distinction: A general-purpose CPU is designed for flexible execution, low-latency control, and varied workloads. An accelerator instead concentrates resources on a narrower operation class, so it achieves its gains only when the workload exposes the supported operations and enough parallel work to keep its arithmetic units busy.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that an accelerator’s advertised peak throughput is the throughput a workload receives. Delivered performance is bounded above by the lower of the compute ceiling and what memory bandwidth can feed (the roofline constraint, developed later in this chapter). A low-arithmetic-intensity kernel can therefore sit at a small fraction of peak FLOP/s no matter how fast the silicon is rated, because it starves for data rather than for arithmetic.



The anatomy of an accelerator is the arrangement of parts that every machine learning accelerator shares: arithmetic units built for tensor operations, on-chip memory that holds operands next to those units, a wide path to off-chip memory, and a host interface through which work arrives. Every inference and every training step on such a machine is a stream of operand movements that ends in multiply-accumulate operations, and the anatomy decides how far each operand travels before it is used. A matrix unit that can retire thousands of multiply-accumulates per cycle sits idle whenever its next operands are still in flight, and an off-chip access can take many processor cycles and cost orders of magnitude more energy than the low-precision operation it feeds. The arithmetic units are the easy part of the design; the rest of the anatomy exists to keep them fed.
The definition becomes concrete in the generic chip of figure 1, which serves as this chapter’s map. External high-bandwidth memory (HBM) feeds shared on-chip storage (an L2 cache), which distributes operands into rows of processing elements, each equipped with a private scratchpad or cache, a matrix unit, a vector unit, and a special function unit. A host interface connects the chip to the CPU that issues its work.






Figure 1: Anatomy of a Modern AI Accelerator: This generic schematic combines common components rather than depicting one product. A host interface connects the accelerator to a CPU, a high-bandwidth device-memory interface feeds shared on-chip storage, and processing elements contain matrix, vector, and special-function units with local memory. Real accelerators differ in which units they provide and whether storage is hardware-managed cache or software-managed scratchpad.



Within each processing element, specialized units partition execution across distinct mathematical primitives: dedicated matrix units (Tensor Cores) execute dense matrix multiplication, vector units evaluate element-wise arithmetic, and special function units (SFUs) approximate transcendental operations such as activations and exponentials. Their number, grouping, and names vary by vendor; some designs arrange them into an explicit 2D systolic grid, and others distribute matrix engines among wide parallel cores.
The memory hierarchy amortizes the cost of data transport across tiers. High-bandwidth memory provides off-chip capacity and throughput, while shared on-chip storage and per-element caches or scratchpads cut off-chip traffic. Because moving a tensor tile across the package boundary costs orders of magnitude more energy than keeping it on chip, compilers and kernels must coordinate tile capacity, reuse, and prefetching to keep operands staged locally. More HBM bandwidth raises the off-chip ceiling, but without local reuse the execution units still stall. The system assumptions appendix (System Assumptions) collects reference specifications for the accelerators this book uses, including the H100.
The host interface links the accelerator to the host CPU, which coordinates execution graphs, asynchronous I/O, and fallback operations while the accelerator executes dispatched kernels. Direct-memory-access engines can overlap host-device transfers with execution, but an operator unsupported by the accelerator backend may require a CPU round-trip. An operator outside the matrix-unit instruction set may instead use vector or other device kernels. These execution boundaries help set the effective speedup envelope. Kernel execution time matters little if transfers, launches, and synchronization dominate end-to-end latency. The three parts of the figure (the processing elements, the memory tiers, and the host link) are the parts this chapter takes apart in turn.
The anatomy embodies the chapter’s central engineering trade-off. General-purpose processors allocate silicon area to complex control logic, speculative execution, branch prediction, and multi-level cache hierarchies to handle arbitrary control flow. An accelerator redirects that transistor budget toward dense arithmetic arrays, dedicated register files, and high-bandwidth memory paths tailored to a narrower workload class. When the software path exposes sufficient tensor parallelism, this specialization yields order-of-magnitude improvements in energy efficiency and throughput per watt. Silicon built for a narrow class of dense tensor operations pays off only because, as the bitter lesson predicts, the general methods that win by exploiting computation keep reducing to those same operations at ever larger scale. The dependence also runs the other way, because scale keeps winning only while accelerators keep lowering the time and energy of each additional operation, so the hardware this chapter studies is part of what sustains the bitter lesson itself.


↩︎ The bitter lesson, the observation that general methods exploiting computation win as computation grows, is established in The Bitter Lesson.
Hardware alone cannot achieve these gains. Algorithms must structure operations to expose data reuse and regular memory access, while silicon architectures must allocate physical units to the mathematical primitives and numeric precisions that algorithms actually execute. That mutual dependence motivates a complementary principle: hardware-software co-design.

Definition 11.2: Hardware-software co-design
Hardware-Software Co-design is an ML accelerator development method that crosses conventional abstraction boundaries, allowing algorithm constraints to inform silicon design and hardware capabilities to shape algorithm formulation.

Significance: On a supported tensor-core path, 8-bit integer (INT8) quantization can deliver multi-fold throughput gains because hardware executes lower-precision operations more densely and moves fewer bytes than an FP32 path; the exact gain depends on the architecture and workload (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a; Dally et al. 2021; Dally 2023).
Distinction: Unlike layered abstraction (where software calls a hardware API without knowing the silicon details), co-design exposes hardware constraints directly to algorithm and compiler authors: data alignment requirements, precision formats, and memory access patterns all become visible inputs to global cross-layer optimization.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that co-design is a one-time hardware design choice. In practice, the supported features continue to evolve: NVIDIA Tensor Cores began with FP16 matrix multiplication, later generations added TF32 and broader integer support, and Ampere added acceleration for 2:4 structured sparsity (NVIDIA 2017; NVIDIA Corporation 2020a).



Co-design explains why model compression techniques deliver real speedups. Quantization shows why converting FP32 to INT8 accelerates execution on supported hardware: reduced precision cuts memory traffic, while specialized arithmetic units execute more low-precision operations per cycle than FP32 equivalents (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). Structured pruning improves performance when it produces smaller dense shapes or a sparsity pattern recognized by silicon, whereas arbitrary unstructured sparsity incurs metadata handling and non-coalesced memory accesses that often erase theoretical gains. Evaluating accelerator performance requires tracing this path from workload to silicon: compute primitives, memory hierarchies, roofline diagnosis, mapping and dataflow, and compiler scheduling. The recurring question is why algorithmic improvements frequently fail to deliver proportional end-to-end speedups. Amdahl’s law (principle \(\ref{pri-amdahl}\)) already answered it for model-side optimizations, since whatever an optimization leaves untouched caps the overall gain. The same bound governs hardware. The theorem below applies the principle to an accelerator, and the only new quantity is the gain, which becomes the accelerator’s path gain \(\AcceleratorGain\).


↩︎ Quantization and its effect on weight payload, memory traffic, and compute cost are established in Numerical Precision: Changing How Values Are Stored.

Theorem 11.1: The fundamental limit of acceleration (Amdahl's law)Hardware acceleration does not speed up the entire system; it speeds only the baseline-time fraction using the accelerated path. For that fraction \(\ParallelFraction\) and path gain \(\AcceleratorGain\), Amdahl’s law (Amdahl 1967) gives the bound in equation 1. \[ \text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1 - \ParallelFraction) + \frac{\ParallelFraction}{\AcceleratorGain}}  \tag{1}\]

Accelerated fraction (\(\ParallelFraction\)): Share of baseline time receiving the stated gain, often in matrix multiplication or another supported kernel.
Accelerator gain (\(\AcceleratorGain\)): The raw speed advantage of the GPU or Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) over the CPU for the accelerated portion of the workload.
Unaccelerated fraction (\(1-\ParallelFraction\)): Work outside the chosen path, such as data loading, host overhead, unsupported operators, and kernel launch latency.

Pitfall: Unaccelerated work caps total speedup. If 10 percent of baseline time is unaffected (\(\ParallelFraction=0.9\)), even infinite path gain (\(\AcceleratorGain=\infty\)) yields at most 10\(\times\) overall. Once the accelerated component is fast enough, unaffected work dominates.



Amdahl, Gene M. 1967. “Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities.” Proceedings of the April 18-20, 1967, Spring Joint Computer Conference on - AFIPS ’67 (Spring), AFIPS ’67 (spring), 483–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560.
1 Amdahl’s law: Maps onto the iron law only after the proposed change is specified. If a faster tensor unit reduces the computation term \((\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\) but leaves data transfer and fixed latency unchanged, those unaffected terms bound total speedup. A different accelerator or memory system may improve bandwidth as well. The unaccelerated fraction is therefore defined by the intervention, not by a permanent classification of each term as serial.Hardware acceleration targets specific terms in the iron law of ML systems, which decomposes end-to-end time into data movement \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\), computation \((\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\), and fixed latency \((\Latency)\). Data selection reduced the number of samples processed (\(\text{Samples/Task}\), shrinking both \(\Operations\) and input traffic \(\DataVolume\)), and model compression reduced the operations and bytes per sample (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) and weight traffic \(\DataVolume\)). Hardware acceleration instead reduces the realized time per operation (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) by improving \(\PeakRate\), \(\EfficiencyHw\), and \(\Bandwidth\). Which of these physical terms an upgrade actually improves determines its accelerated fraction under Amdahl’s law.1


↩︎ The decomposition of execution time into data, compute, and latency terms is established in Iron Law of ML Systems.
This dynamic explains why hardware upgrades frequently fail to produce proportional end-to-end speedups. Figure 2 maps system speedup across accelerator gain (\(\AcceleratorGain\)) and accelerated fraction (\(\ParallelFraction\)), charting where those returns diminish. Where the unaccelerated fraction \(1-\ParallelFraction\) remains substantial, the white contour curves flatten horizontally into the unaccelerated-bound regime, bounding total speedup at the \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) asymptote regardless of how far \(\AcceleratorGain\) scales along the horizontal axis. Because \(\ParallelFraction\) differs substantially across workload archetypes running on identical hardware, a workload’s vertical position on this map determines whether an accelerator investment pays off or stalls on non-matrix operations.














Figure 2: The Iron Law Heatmap: Total system speedup as a function of accelerator gain (\(\AcceleratorGain\)) and accelerated fraction (\(\ParallelFraction\)). High speedup appears only near the top-right corner, where both accelerator gain and accelerated fraction are high. At \(\ParallelFraction=0.9\), for example, even an infinite gain on the accelerated path cannot exceed 10\(\times\) end-to-end speedup. Contours span roughly 1\(\times\)–200\(\times\) speedup.




Checkpoint 11.1: The parallelism gate
These checks turn Amdahl’s bound into a hardware-selection test.
Amdahl’s reality

Serial bottlenecks: use Amdahl’s bound to explain why a 1,000\(\times\) faster GPU may only speed up training by 5\(\times\) when data loading is slow.
Speedup ceiling: for \(\ParallelFraction=0.95\) and \(\AcceleratorGain=100\), estimate total speedup and compare it with the infinite-accelerator ceiling.
Workload variation: what baseline profiling would establish the ResNet-50 and MobileNet accelerated fractions for a proposed hardware change? Explain how those fractions would determine which benefits more.



The serial bottleneck becomes concrete on real hardware, where the same accelerator that nears its parallel ceiling on one workload can stall on another. The comparison below uses the INT8 (8-bit integer) path, whose advantage over FP32 or FP16 has two sources. Each operand occupies a half or a quarter of the bytes, and an 8-bit multiplier occupies far less silicon area than a floating-point one, so the same die holds more multiply-accumulate (MAC) units. Two workloads on an NVIDIA H100 with different unaccelerated fractions show how that fraction governs whether this peak INT8 advantage becomes realized speedup. A second look at the decode case then separates that limit from a different one, bandwidth-boundedness.


↪ Order-of-magnitude throughput, bandwidth, and capacity for each accelerator class are collected for reference in Accelerator classes.

Lighthouse 11.1: An illustrative Amdahl budget on H100Illustrative ResNet-50 inference on NVIDIA H100:

Assume H100 provides \(\AcceleratorGain\) = 247× on matrix multiplication relative to a server CPU without matrix extensions (1979 TOPS INT8 vs. ~8 TOPS) (Choquette 2023). The CPU’s INT8 rate is a scenario assumption for this budget, not the FP32 peak of the reference CPU used elsewhere in the chapter.
Assume \(\ParallelFraction\) = 0.95: 95 percent of baseline time receives that gain, while 5 percent remains in data loading, preprocessing, postprocessing, and other work. \[
\text{$\text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1-0.95) + \frac{0.95}{247}} = \frac{1}{0.05 + 0.0038} \approx 18.6\times$}
\] The 247× path gain produces only 18.6× end-to-end speedup because the 5 percent unaffected fraction sets the ceiling.

Contrast with GPT-2 (autoregressive):

For GPT-2 token generation, assume \(\ParallelFraction\) = 0.80; the remaining 20 percent includes host overhead, sampling, and decoding work outside the accelerated matrix path. \[
\text{$\text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1-0.80) + \frac{0.80}{247}} = \frac{1}{0.20 + 0.0032} \approx 4.9\times$}
\] Less token-generation time receives the assumed gain, so even an infinite path gain yields at most \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) = 5×.

This calculation still overstates the decode path gain. Decode is bandwidth bound, so its accelerated path runs at the rate weights stream from memory rather than at the INT8 TOPS rate. The relevant ratio is the H100’s memory bandwidth over the reference CPU socket’s, 67× (a different path from the host-DRAM link used below). INT8 helps decode on either machine by halving the bytes each weight occupies relative to FP16, not by multiplying faster. With that gain the bound falls from 4.9× to 4.7×, barely moving, because the unaccelerated fraction already dominates. Two distinct limits are at work. Bandwidth-boundedness shrinks \(\AcceleratorGain\), whereas the unaccelerated fraction caps what any \(\AcceleratorGain\) can deliver. Serving optimizations attack both. Batching raises the work done per weight byte fetched. Speculative decoding, developed in Model Serving, lets a small draft model propose several tokens that the full model then verifies in one step, reducing the number of sequential full-model steps.


Whether an operation is limited by compute rate or by data movement dictates both hardware selection and software optimization. Under the arithmetic intensity law (principle \(\ref{pri-arithmetic-intensity}\)), upgrading to an accelerator with \(10\times\) higher peak compute yields negligible speedup if data delivery is the binding bottleneck. The roofline model, previewed in Matching workloads to hardware, makes this diagnosis (Williams et al. 2009). It compares an operation’s arithmetic intensity, the ratio of operations to bytes of memory traffic (FLOP/byte), with the hardware’s ridge point. An operation below the ridge is bandwidth bound, the regime the roofline literature calls memory bound; an operation above it is compute bound. GPT-2 decode and ResNet-50 sit on opposite sides of that line, a difference the Amdahl budget above already registered in the decode path gain. Section 11.6 turns the classification into numbers once the compute units and memory systems that set the two ceilings have been examined.


↩︎ The arithmetic-intensity spectrum that separates the workload signatures of the major architectures is established in Arithmetic intensity across workloads.
The chapter builds the machine from the bottom up (table 1). Compute primitives and compute units supply the arithmetic side of the anatomy, ending with the INT8 and sparse paths that ResNet-50’s profile depends on, and memory systems supply the other side, from registers to host memory. Performance bounds then combine the two into the roofline’s ceilings and show which ResNet-50 layers clear the H100’s ridge at FP16 and which fall below it at INT8; this is the chapter’s midpoint, marked by a checkpoint. The second half asks how software reaches those ceilings, through hardware mapping and then the compilers and runtimes that make its choices automatically. Three shorter sections widen the view to work beyond one accelerator, heterogeneous systems-on-chip, and the choice of an accelerator for a workload and a budget.



Table 1: Chapter Map: Each section supplies one part of the accelerator’s anatomy and follows the chapter’s INT8 ResNet-50 workload into it; the first five sections build the machine and its ceilings, and the remaining sections ask how software and system choices reach them.

The first stage of the accelerator’s anatomy begins with a simpler question: why build specialized silicon for tensor math at all, rather than running those operations on general-purpose processors?

Self-Check: Question

An ML engineer upgrades a training cluster from baseline CPUs to NVIDIA H100 GPUs, providing an accelerator compute gain of \(G_{\text{accel}} = 250\times\) on matrix operations. If data preprocessing, serialization, and CPU-GPU transfers constitute \(10\%\) of the baseline execution time (\(p = 0.90\)), what is the maximum achievable end-to-end speedup according to Amdahl’s Law?

Approximately \(25\times\) (bounded by the memory bandwidth ratio)
Approximately \(125\times\) (half of the matrix unit throughput multiplier)

The metric defined as the ratio of floating-point operations performed to bytes of memory traffic transferred across a specific memory hierarchy interface is called ____.
