A recurring systems question is why accelerators cannot bypass on-chip SRAM entirely and stream all operands directly from high-capacity off-chip DRAM. A dependent DRAM request exposes the full access latency. Many independent requests can hide that latency, but their sustained operand supply remains limited by off-chip bandwidth; on-chip staging also enables reuse.

Napkin Math 11.2: Why HBM cannot feed the array directlyProblem: Why is on-chip SRAM necessary instead of fetching all data from HBM?
Math:

Clock cycle: At 2 GHz, \(1/(2\text{ GHz}) = 500\text{ ps}\).
DRAM access: Off-chip HBM sits millimeters away on the package, but row activation, DRAM-array latency, serialization, protocol traversal, and queuing add up to 100+ cycles per access.
Distance, for comparison: On an H100-class 814 mm² die, signals travel ~20 mm; at \(\approx 0.5\VacuumLightSpeed\), \(20\text{ mm}/(0.5\VacuumLightSpeed) \approx 130\text{ ps}\), less than one cycle.

Systems insight: The propagation estimate alone does not explain the DRAM access cost, and it omits real interconnect delay from wiring and routing. Independent requests can overlap the 100-plus-cycle access path; a dependent request cannot. Registers and SRAM supply operands at the rate the array needs while reusing values that would otherwise cross HBM repeatedly. Transformer tiling addresses both operand supply and reuse, whereas streaming a growing KV cache can still limit inference when its required traffic exceeds the available bandwidth.




The on-chip memory subsystem integrates registers, Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM) caches, and software-managed scratchpads directly on the accelerator die. Register files provide the immediate operand and accumulator storage needed by execution pipelines. Modern accelerators provision substantial register capacity in aggregate across the chip, but partition this pool dynamically among concurrent threads or warps. Increasing per-thread register allocation allows individual threads to retain larger matrix tiles, but limits the total number of concurrently scheduled warps, reducing the hardware’s ability to hide memory latency. Conversely, underallocating registers forces the compiler to spill values to off-chip memory, converting single-cycle register accesses into multi-cycle stalls. Efficient kernel design balances register allocation to maintain maximum occupancy while keeping hot operands resident.
Hardware-managed L1 and L2 caches provide fast buffering for frequently referenced data using automatic tag checking and hardware eviction policies. However, automatic caches are poorly suited for streaming multi-gigabyte tensor operations: scanning through large activation tensors can evict reusable weight tiles before arithmetic units can reuse them. Furthermore, specialized execution pipelines impose strict layout and data-type constraints that general caches cannot satisfy automatically. As illustrated in example 11.3, hardware matrix engines require specific alignments and memory layouts; a mismatch may require padding, conversion, or a different kernel whose efficiency must be checked.

Example 11.3: Tensor Cores that never engageScenario: An engineering team migrates a transformer workload to NVIDIA A100 GPUs expecting automatic Tensor Core acceleration, but profiling reveals Tensor Cores remain idle (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a).
Diagnosis: The workload used shapes and data types that selected less efficient kernels rather than the intended Tensor Core path.
Systems lesson: Specialized paths have operator, precision, layout, and shape requirements. Libraries can often handle nonaligned dimensions through padding or alternative kernels, but reaching high utilization requires verifying which path was actually selected.


To avoid the eviction overhead and unpredictability of automatic caches, AI accelerators incorporate scratchpad memory. Unlike hardware caches, scratchpads are software-managed SRAM structures mapped directly into the core’s address space without tag directories or hardware replacement logic. The compiler or programmer explicitly controls when tensor tiles are loaded from external DRAM, how long they reside on-chip, and when updated values are written back. In convolutional models, scratchpads retain input feature maps and weight kernels across sliding receptive windows, eliminating redundant DRAM reads (Chen et al. 2017). On NVIDIA GPUs, scratchpad memory is exposed as shared memory: a fast, programmer-controlled SRAM bank shared across all threads within a thread block. Custom kernels written in CUDA or Triton manage shared memory explicitly. FlashAttention demonstrates the power of this mechanism. Rather than materializing the full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) attention score matrix in off-chip HBM, the kernel tiles queries, keys, and values through shared memory and updates softmax statistics online (Dao et al. 2022). The speedup stems entirely from eliminating high-latency HBM round trips rather than reducing arithmetic operations; in fact, the algorithm recomputes intermediate attention values during the backward pass to avoid storing them to off-chip memory.


↩︎ FlashAttention as an IO-aware attention kernel for training is established in FlashAttention: IO-aware attention optimization.



When tensor working sets exceed on-chip SRAM capacity, operands and parameters reside in device-local DRAM. Rather than sequential hierarchy levels, HBM, Graphics DDR (GDDR), and Low-Power DDR (LPDDR) represent alternative memory architectures engineered for distinct cost, bandwidth, and power envelopes. High-performance accelerators use HBM, which stacks DRAM dies vertically using through-silicon vias (TSVs) and interfaces with the accelerator die across a wide silicon interposer (e.g., 1,024 to 8,192 bits). This wide bus delivers multi-terabyte-per-second bandwidth at lower clock frequencies and lower energy per bit than conventional DRAM, but requires complex 2.5D packaging. Where silicon interposers are cost-prohibitive, accelerators adopt GDDR, which uses narrower buses (e.g., 256 to 384 bits) driven at high pin speeds across standard circuit boards. Mobile and embedded accelerators use LPDDR, trading raw bandwidth for low operating voltage and reduced standby power.
When parameter and activation footprints exceed device-local DRAM capacity, the system must offload state to host DRAM (typically standard DDR). Accessing host memory requires crossing an I/O interconnect such as PCIe or a coherent fabric like NVLink or Compute Express Link (CXL). Because PCIe bandwidth (tens of gigabytes per second) is one to two orders of magnitude lower than accelerator DRAM bandwidth, unmanaged offloading stalls arithmetic execution. Efficient runtimes mitigate this penalty by overlapping asynchronous direct memory access (DMA) copies with kernel execution, prefetching upcoming layer parameters while current layers compute.
At the base of the hierarchy, nonvolatile flash storage and solid-state drives (SSDs) provide persistent, multi-terabyte capacity for datasets and training checkpoints (Narayanan et al. 2021). With read latencies measured in tens of microseconds and bus bandwidths capped at single-digit gigabytes per second, flash devices cannot participate directly in kernel execution. Checkpointing and data-loading pipelines treat flash storage as an asynchronous streaming source, staging batches through host DRAM into accelerator memory before computation begins.

Narayanan, Deepak, Mohammad Shoeybi, Jared Casper, Patrick LeGresley, Mostofa Patwary, Vijay Korthikanti, Dmitri Vainbrand, et al. 2021. “Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM.” Proceedings of the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis, 1–15. https://doi.org/10.1145/3458817.3476209.
The physical tiers of the memory hierarchy establish the latency floors and capacity ceilings of the accelerator, but advertised memory bandwidth is only a ceiling within them. Achievable bandwidth depends on access pattern, batching, locality, and the host interface that feeds the accelerator. Peak figures assume continuous, stride-1 coalesced access across all memory channels. Real neural network workloads deviate substantially from this ideal: transformer attention, convolution, and fully connected layers realize distinct fractions of peak bandwidth because their memory access strides, tiling dimensions, and operational reuse differ. A sufficiently large, coalesced weight stream can approach peak bandwidth even at small batch size. Batching instead reuses each loaded weight across more samples, raising arithmetic intensity as analyzed under the roofline model in section 11.6. Small or irregular kernels may lack enough concurrent accesses to approach the bandwidth ceiling, making memory latency and available parallelism part of the diagnosis.




An accelerator rated for hundreds of teraflops sits idle if its input tensors are still crawling across a host PCIe bus an order of magnitude slower than its on-package HBM. In discrete accelerator systems, the host CPU and the accelerator operate as separate computational domains joined by a peripheral bus. The host manages storage I/O, network streams, and runtime orchestration in system DRAM, while the accelerator executes dense mathematical kernels over device memory (HBM or GDDR). Because those two memories occupy separate physical address spaces, computation cannot begin until tensors cross the host-accelerator interconnect, making peripheral bus bandwidth and launch latency a hard gate on end-to-end speedup.
Figure 9 sequences the four-stage execution trace across host and device lifelines. Step 1 copies input data across PCIe to device memory via DMA. Step 2 dispatches kernel instructions from the CPU. Step 3 executes parallel core compute with local writeback. Step 4 copies results back to host memory. In a naive synchronous execution model, every transfer step sits directly on the critical path, stalling either the host or the accelerator until each memory transaction finishes.






Figure 9: Host-Accelerator Data Transfer Sequence: Four-step execution flow between CPU host and GPU device: (1) copying input data over PCIe, (2) issuing kernel instructions, (3) GPU compute, and (4) transferring results back to host memory. Low PCIe bandwidth and host dispatch latencies can easily dominate runtime unless kernel compute time exceeds data transfer overhead.



The end-to-end latency of a kernel launch decomposes into transfer time, queue dispatch overhead, and arithmetic execution time. When tensor transfers are small or frequent, the fixed overhead of driver submission and bus round trips dominates runtime. When transfers are large, the low bandwidth of PCIe relative to on-package HBM creates a sustained I/O bottleneck. In D·A·M terms, the Machine boundary between host and accelerator forces the Algorithm to maximize arithmetic reuse on the device once tensors arrive.


Within a single machine, how bits move between GPUs and the CPU sets the next ceiling. In the 1–8 GPU regime, scaling is achieved through high-speed intra-node interconnects such as NVLink and host-to-device PCIe transfers that mitigate the memory wall. These links form a bandwidth taper: data-movement speed falls at each step away from the compute units, from on-package HBM through the GPU-to-GPU NVLink bridge down to the host PCIe link. The PCIe step is much slower than the accelerator-local memory and inter-GPU fabric, so any data path that touches the CPU can become a performance hazard. Keeping accelerator-to-accelerator traffic off that link is the reason NVLink exists (NVIDIA Corporation 2020b). A typical AI server is therefore not a flat mesh of connected devices, and optimizing data movement starts from its physical topology.


Bandwidth tapers steeply as data moves farther from the accelerator.

Within a multi-accelerator server node, two interconnect tiers define this bandwidth taper below device memory:

Device-device interconnect (NVLink/Infinity Fabric): Modern multi-GPU nodes use specialized high-speed bridges like NVLink20 to connect accelerators directly, bypassing the host CPU. Bandwidth ranges from 600 GB/s to 900 GB/s per GPU (NVIDIA Corporation 2020b; Choquette 2023). This link matters whenever tensors must move between accelerators within one server, including model partitioning, activation exchange, and gradient synchronization during training. The architectural principle is the boundary: traffic that stays on the accelerator fabric is far cheaper than traffic that falls back through the host.
Host-device interconnect (PCIe): The link between the CPU and the accelerator. Bandwidth ranges from 32 to 64 GB/s (PCIe Gen4/Gen5). Host-staged training data can bottleneck here, although resident data, direct storage or network I/O, and coherent accelerator links can use other paths. Multi-GPU servers may also provide multiple PCIe links rather than a single shared 64 GB/s path.

20 NVLink (NVIDIA Link): This direct GPU-to-GPU interconnect exists to keep accelerator-to-accelerator traffic off PCIe when tensors must move inside a server. Its 600–900 GB/s aggregate bidirectional bandwidth is roughly 300–450 GB/s per direction under balanced full-duplex traffic, several times the directional bandwidth of a standard PCIe link, so workloads with frequent cross-device tensor movement can remain in the fast part of the bandwidth taper (NVIDIA Corporation 2020b; Choquette 2023). Training algorithms determine how much tensor traffic must cross this link; the hardware fact needed here is the bandwidth gap. 
NVIDIA Corporation. 2020b. “NVLink: Scalable High-Performance Interconnect.” NVIDIA Technical Report 2020.

Choquette, Jack. 2023. “NVIDIA Hopper H100 GPU: Scaling Performance.” IEEE Micro 43 (3): 9–17. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2023.3256796.
A third tier, the network link from one server to others, continues the taper beyond the node (section 11.9). Together the levels produce a characteristic bandwidth taper:
\[\begin{aligned} \text{HBM (3350 GB/s)} &\gg \text{NVLink (900 GB/s)} \\ &\gg \text{PCIe (64 GB/s)} > \text{Network (50 GB/s)} \end{aligned}\]
System efficiency depends on keeping tensors on the highest-bandwidth links available. Because PCIe and network links offer orders of magnitude less bandwidth and higher latency than on-package memory, placement and scheduling must minimize crossings across these boundaries.



The standard remedy for transfer overhead is the asynchronous pipeline of Devices and memory. Batches staged in pinned (page-locked) host memory are copied by dedicated DMA engines while the accelerator computes on the previous batch. This double buffering conceals transfer latency behind arithmetic runtime whenever computation time exceeds transfer time (\(\IronLawComputeTime \ge \BatchTransferTime\)). When compute duration is too short to amortize the transfer, execution remains bus bound and the compute units stall.


↩︎ The feeding problem, in which data delivery fails to keep pace with compute throughput, is established in The feeding problem.
Unified Memory takes the opposite approach, presenting a single virtual address space that spans host DRAM and device HBM while the driver migrates pages on demand whenever either processor touches an address. On-demand migration removes staging code at the cost of predictability, because each page fault stalls execution and scattered accesses can thrash pages across the PCIe bus. High-throughput production workloads therefore rely on explicit, pipelined DMA transfers and reserve Unified Memory for prototyping or for applications where programmer productivity outweighs sustained hardware utilization. Once tensors reside on the accelerator, the model’s own architecture determines whether weights, activations, or lookup tables dominate the device memory hierarchy.




An optimization that relieves memory pressure for one model family can leave another untouched: caching weights helps nothing when ResNet-50’s early convolutions spill large activation maps to DRAM, and spatial activation tiling helps nothing when GPT-2 decode streams gigabytes of weights for a single token. Model architecture determines which memory term binds. The architectural reasons each family stresses memory as it does were traced in Arithmetic intensity across workloads; the hardware consequence differs by family, and the lighthouse models of Lighthouse Models as Reference Workloads cover the cases.
Dense layers, the multilayer perceptron (MLP) blocks that every family contains, are bound by weight traffic at small batch. At batch size \(\BatchSize= 1\), each parameter loaded from off-chip memory serves a single multiply-accumulate operation (often \(\le 1\text{ FLOP/byte}\)), so execution sits on the bandwidth slope; batching reuses each loaded weight across \(\BatchSize\) inputs and moves the layer toward the compute ceiling. Dense weight matrices regularly exceed the tens of megabytes of on-chip SRAM, so parameters reside in HBM and stream through tiles that the accelerator double-buffers into SRAM (Chen et al. 2017). The host link enters the critical path only when inputs stream from the host or when the model exceeds device memory.

Chen, Yu-Hsin, Joel Emer, and Vivienne Sze. 2017. “Using Dataflow to Optimize Energy Efficiency of Deep Neural Network Accelerators.” IEEE Micro 37 (3): 12–21. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2017.54.
Convolutional layers, the core of ResNet-50, place their memory pressure on activations rather than weights. Small filters sliding across feature maps supply three forms of reuse: neighboring windows share input activations, each filter is applied at every spatial position, and each input channel feeds every output filter. Early layers therefore carry compact parameter tensors but large activation maps that exceed on-chip SRAM, and unoptimized layer-by-layer execution spills those maps to device DRAM. Spatial tiling keeps activation tiles, with their overlapping boundary pixels, in on-chip buffers so adjacent convolutions consume them without refetching (Chen et al. 2017).
Transformers such as GPT-2 stress both capacity and bandwidth, differently in each phase. During training and prefill, standard attention materializes an \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) score matrix for sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) and moves \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) bytes through HBM; IO-aware kernels such as FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022) keep those tiles in on-chip SRAM instead (FlashAttention: IO-aware attention optimization). During autoregressive decode, each generated token reads the weights and the accumulated key-value (KV) cache from HBM for a vector-matrix product, which binds generation speed to memory bandwidth.

↩︎ How much memory one request’s KV cache claims as its sequence grows is established in Autoregressive decoding.

Two other lighthouses stress memory in other ways. DLRM’s sparse embedding lookups stress random-access bandwidth rather than dense compute, and MobileNetV2’s depthwise convolutions trade arithmetic intensity for a smaller parameter footprint, so both reappear as memory-bound rows in the roofline operations table (table 7). Accelerators answer these divergent demands with the tiered hierarchy. On-chip SRAM captures high-reuse activations and tiled matrix blocks at tens of terabytes per second, HBM stages large weight tensors and sequence state, and NVLink-class links carry tensors between accelerators when a model exceeds one device, avoiding the narrower host PCIe bus. Table 14 later pairs each family’s memory profile with the mapping that answers it. A reference off-chip DRAM access costs far more energy per event than arithmetic (figure 4), so reducing repeated external accesses improves efficiency. Deciding whether a given kernel is limited by compute throughput or by memory bandwidth, however, requires an analytical boundary. The roofline model supplies that boundary by comparing operational intensity against hardware performance limits, so that optimization effort targets the resource that actually binds.

Self-Check: Question

When training a \(7\)-billion-parameter model using a hypothetical mixed-precision Adam recipe stated for this question—\(2\) bytes for weights, \(2\) for gradients, \(4\) for FP32 master weights, \(4\) for the first moment, and \(4\) for the second moment per parameter—calculate the model-state memory for weights, gradients, and optimizer states, and explain why optimizer-related state dominates this footprint.
Arrange the following levels of a modern GPU memory hierarchy in order of access latency, from lowest latency (fastest) to highest latency (slowest):


High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM3)
Register File

Shared Memory / L1 Cache
On-Chip L2 Cache


Why does High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) achieve significantly higher bandwidth (e.g., \(>2\text{ TB/s}\)) than traditional GDDR6X memory (e.g., \(\approx 760\text{ GB/s}\)) while maintaining comparable or lower power per bit?

HBM operates at a \(10\times\) higher clock frequency than GDDR6X on standard PCB traces
HBM uses optical photonic signaling to transmit data across the motherboard
HBM eliminates all error correction codes and row buffer precharge cycles
HBM vertically stacks DRAM dies using Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) and connects to the GPU via a wide 1024-bit per stack silicon interposer bus at lower clock speeds

Memory allocated on the host CPU that is locked into physical RAM and prevents operating system paging, enabling direct DMA transfers over PCIe to the GPU, is called ____ host memory.
True or False: The AI Memory Wall refers solely to the limited physical capacity (GBs) of GPU DRAM, meaning that if an accelerator has sufficient gigabytes to store model weights, memory bandwidth will never bottleneck execution.

title: 11 Hardware Acceleration
text:
Low arithmetic intensity places the modeled throughput ceiling on the bandwidth slope.
The compute units fix how fast an accelerator can calculate, and the memory system fixes how fast it can be fed. A kernel’s performance is bounded by whichever of the two runs out first. Putting numbers on that statement takes three pieces: the roofline’s ceilings for each precision path, the ridge point at which they meet, and the hardware balance that moves the ridge from one generation to the next. The ResNet-50 INT8 workload meets its sharpest lesson in these bounds. The INT8 path doubles the H100’s arithmetic ceiling without moving its bandwidth ceiling, so a layer that cleared the ridge at FP16 can fall below it at INT8.


Quoting an accelerator’s peak FLOP/s cannot explain why one kernel runs near the hardware ceiling while another stalls below 1 percent of peak on the same chip, because peak compute measures only what execution units can retire when operands are already in registers. With the compute units and memory systems that set the arithmetic and bandwidth ceilings now in place, the roofline model21 (Williams et al. 2009), which sorted training kernels in Arithmetic intensity, combines both limits on a single plot. It graphs attainable performance against arithmetic intensity and identifies the lower modeled ceiling, compute or memory bandwidth, for the chosen execution path before profiling establishes which physical resource limits execution.
21 Roofline model: Introduced by Williams et al. (2009) at UC Berkeley, building on earlier I/O complexity work from the 1980s. Their specific contribution was making the compute vs. bandwidth trade-off visual and actionable: the characteristic roofline plot immediately reveals whether a kernel is compute bound (hitting the flat ceiling) or memory bound (hitting the sloped bandwidth line) and quantifies the gap to hardware limits. A kernel operating at only 50 percent of its ceiling has 2\(\times\) theoretical headroom, but instruction mix, latency, and occupancy may prevent it from closing that gap.
Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
Performance is bounded by two ceilings, as equation 2 formalizes; it writes the bound of the arithmetic intensity law (principle \(\ref{pri-arithmetic-intensity}\)) as an idealized equality that ignores launch and synchronization overheads. Here, attainable performance \(\AttainableComputeRate\) and peak compute \(\PeakRate\) are in FLOP/s (often reported as TFLOP/s), peak bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\) is in bytes/s (often TB/s), and arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) is in FLOP/byte: \[\AttainableComputeRate = \min(\PeakRate, \Bandwidth \times \ArithmeticIntensity) \tag{2}\]
Arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity = \Operations/\DataVolume\) is the ratio of operations to bytes moved across the memory interface being modeled (definition \(\ref{dfn-nn-computation-arithmetic-intensity}\)), and it depends on the implementation as well as the operation. Under the stated traffic models, a large well-tiled 1024 \(\times\) 1024 multiply reaches about 341.3 FLOP/byte, while standalone ReLU is about 0.125 FLOP/byte, so the two meet different ceilings on the same hardware.
The roofline visualization shows performance (TFLOP/s) on the vertical axis and arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte) on the horizontal axis. At low arithmetic intensity, the upper bound increases linearly along the memory bandwidth slope (\(\Bandwidth \times \ArithmeticIntensity\)). Above the ridge point, the upper bound is peak compute (\(\PeakRate\)). A kernel approaching the slope is bandwidth limited, while one approaching the flat roof is compute limited on the specified path. Merely lying below either line does not establish the cause; profiling explains that remaining gap. Acting on the binding term maps each regime to the optimizations that pay off and the ones that waste effort, so classifying a kernel tells the engineer whether more bandwidth, less traffic, or more arithmetic throughput is the investment to test first.



A kernel with 200 FLOP/byte that was comfortably compute bound on a V100 or A100 falls below the compute ceiling when migrated unchanged to an H100, because different devices place the compute-bandwidth boundary at different intensities. The ridge point, the balance point between a machine’s memory and compute limits previewed alongside the iron law, is a property of the device. Computer architects call the same ratio the hardware balance \((\RooflineRidgePoint)\), peak arithmetic throughput divided by peak memory bandwidth, the intensity at which the roofline’s compute and bandwidth ceilings intersect: \[ \RooflineRidgePoint = \frac{\PeakRate}{\Bandwidth} \]
The ratio sets a device-specific boundary. Depending on the chosen precision, the H100 requires about 295.2 FLOP/byte on its dense FP16 path (989 TFLOP/s over 3.35 TB/s) to reach its arithmetic ceiling, and twice that on its INT8 path, whereas a microcontroller may have a much lower ridge point. The same kernel can therefore be bandwidth bound on a compute-dense accelerator and compute bound on an edge processor. Hardware balance does not label either device as universally efficient; it identifies how much reuse a workload needs on that device.
Peak computational capability has expanded faster than memory bus performance across accelerator generations, and the size of that mismatch is what sets how much data reuse a kernel needs to stay fed. Across 2017–2024, NVIDIA’s data center generations multiplied dense FP16 compute by 18× and memory bandwidth by only 8.9×, a 2.0× rise in the reuse a kernel needs on B200 relative to V100.
That ratio measures how far the hardware ridge point, the threshold a kernel must clear to become compute bound, has risen since the V100. Figure 10 plots it generation by generation, leaving out the H200 exception. The doubling of the gap appears directly as the ridge point roughly doubling from V100 (139 FLOP/byte) to H100 (295 FLOP/byte) and then holding near that level on B200 (281 FLOP/byte). A kernel that cleared the V100 ridge comfortably can fall below the H100 ridge without any change to its code, so newer hardware demands more operational reuse before execution reaches peak throughput.














Figure 10: The Rising Ridge: Hardware arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte) over time computed as each chip’s dense FP16 tensor peak divided by its memory bandwidth: 125 TFLOP/s over 0.9 TB/s for V100, 312 TFLOP/s over 2.04 TB/s for A100, and 989 TFLOP/s over 3.35 TB/s for H100. This is the arithmetic intensity a kernel must reach before compute rather than bandwidth limits it. As compute capability grows faster than memory bandwidth, the ridge point rises from V100 through H100 and remains high on B200. This trend explains why architectures with high data reuse flourish while low-reuse workloads face a growing performance penalty.



The generations in figure 10 come from one vendor, but the divergence is industry-wide. Figure 11 tracks the best memory bandwidth and the best dense FP16/BF16 tensor throughput among 52 accelerators from every major vendor released since 2017 (Epoch AI 2026). Measured from TPU v2, the best compute rate grew about 55× while the best bandwidth grew about 13×, so the ridge point of the leading devices rose several-fold. The ratio is larger than the NVIDIA-only one above because TPU v2’s 16-bit baseline was low. Since early 2025 the best bandwidth has held near 8 TB/s, and the best dense FP16 rate has leveled as well, because new devices put their added arithmetic into FP8 and FP4 paths rather than 16-bit ones. For a kernel whose reuse stays fixed, this rising ridge shows up as a ceiling on achievable utilization that falls with each generation.














Figure 11: Compute and Bandwidth Across Vendors: Dense FP16/BF16 tensor throughput and memory bandwidth of machine learning accelerators from all major vendors with at least 16 GB of off-chip memory, each relative to TPU v2 (2017) on a logarithmic axis. Points are individual devices; step lines track the best device released to date. Compute pulls away from bandwidth, and both best-device envelopes level off in 2025 and 2026 as added arithmetic moves into lower-precision formats. Data from Epoch AI (2026).


Epoch AI. 2026. Machine Learning Hardware.



Napkin Math 11.3: The utilization gapProblem: Why is it harder to get 100 percent utilization on an H100 than a V100?
Metric: The ridge point \(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate / \Bandwidth\) (FLOP/byte), the number of operations the hardware must perform for every byte loaded to keep its compute units busy.
Result: The intensity needed to reach the tensor peak has increased. Under this simple HBM roofline, a kernel with \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) = 200 FLOP/byte lies above the A100 ridge but below the H100 ridge. If its intensity and implementation remain unchanged, its idealized gain is about 2.1×, between the 1.6× bandwidth ratio and the 3.2× peak-compute ratio, because the kernel moves from the compute roof on the A100 to the bandwidth slope on the H100.
Systems insight: Fusion is valuable for low-intensity chains because it can remove intermediate round-trips; it is not automatically the best optimization for every kernel.


Operations such as depthwise convolution, embedding lookup, LayerNorm, and softmax serve as low-intensity reference points that commonly fall below the HBM ridge on compute-dense accelerators under the stated traffic models. Table 7 maps common neural network operations to their representative roofline regimes and to the lighthouse workload that exercises each. Classification depends on the implementation, memory interface, and target path; profiling distinguishes a bandwidth ceiling from latency, limited parallelism, or other execution constraints.



Table 7: Operations on the Roofline: Neural network layers span a wide range of arithmetic intensities. Large, well-tiled convolutions and batched GEMMs can be compute-bound, while MobileNet depthwise layers, attention softmax, normalization, and DLRM embeddings are often memory-bound. To see how these intensity values translate into real performance predictions, a transformer layer provides a complete arithmetic-intensity calculation across its major sub-operations.

Napkin Math 11.4: Transformer layer analysisFor one GPT-2 XL layer during prefill, with hidden dimension \(\HiddenDimension\) = 1600, batch size \(\BatchSize\) = 8, sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) = 1024, and \(\AttentionHeadCount\) = 25 attention heads:
Attention QKV projection:

FLOPs: 2 \(\times\) 3 \(\times\) 8 \(\times\) 1024 \(\times\) 1600 \(\times\) 1600 = 125.8 GFLOP
Bytes: (input + weights + output) = (8 \(\times\) 1024 \(\times\) 1600 + 3 \(\times\) 1600 \(\times\) 1600 + 8 \(\times\) 1024 \(\times\) 1600 \(\times\) 3) \(\times\) 2 ≈ 120.2 MB
\(\ArithmeticIntensity\) = 125.8 GFLOP / 120.2 MB = 1046.7 FLOP/byte, which is compute bound on the H100 (above the 295.2 FLOP/byte ridge point)

Softmax:

FLOPs: 8 \(\times\) 25 \(\times\) 1024 \(\times\) 1024 \(\times\) 3 ≈ 629.1 MFLOP (exp, sum, div)
Bytes: 8 \(\times\) 25 \(\times\) 1024 \(\times\) 1024 \(\times 2 \times 2\) = 838.9 MB
\(\ArithmeticIntensity\) = 629.1 MFLOP / 838.9 MB = 0.75 FLOP/byte under this simple operation count, placing it below the reference tensor-path HBM ridge. Counting exponentials and division as multiple operations raises the numerical intensity, but those instructions use different execution units. The relevant vector, reduction, and special-function ceilings, together with profiling, determine whether bandwidth actually binds.

Systems insight: This analysis explains why FlashAttention focuses on reducing memory traffic in attention rather than reducing FLOPs.


The roofline supplies an initial resource bound; profiling determines which physical subsystem limits the kernel. When a kernel approaches its relevant off-chip bandwidth ceiling, optimization should focus on conserving memory traffic. Fusing adjacent operators keeps intermediate activations in on-chip registers or shared memory (SRAM). Lower-precision numeric formats reduce the physical byte count of memory transfers. Algorithmic refactorings like FlashAttention restructure access patterns to compute within SRAM tiles. When a kernel approaches the compute ceiling of its actual execution path, high data reuse keeps execution units supplied and off-chip bandwidth is no longer the binding resource. Performance here depends on saturating arithmetic execution pipelines: structuring matrix tiles to sustain Tensor Core throughput, hiding instruction latencies through software pipelining, and scaling batch sizes to distribute work across all available streaming multiprocessors.


↪ How a benchmark determines where a workload actually sits against its roofline ceiling is developed in System benchmarks.



When a kernel’s arithmetic intensity falls below the ridge point, adding more Tensor Cores cannot speed it up because off-chip memory bandwidth cannot deliver operands fast enough to sustain the target compute rate \(\TargetComputeRate\) (FLOP/s). For a workload with arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) (FLOP/byte), keeping the compute units fed at rate \(\TargetComputeRate\) requires the memory subsystem to transfer data at the rate defined by equation 3: \[\RequiredMemoryBandwidth = \frac{\TargetComputeRate}{\ArithmeticIntensity} \text{ bytes/s} \tag{3}\]
When this required bandwidth exceeds the hardware’s peak memory bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\), memory transfers cap attainable throughput according to equation 4: \[\AttainableComputeRate = \Bandwidth \times \ArithmeticIntensity \tag{4}\]
Evaluating an operation against its execution path’s ridge point identifies the lower modeled ceiling. Extensive data reuse can raise arithmetic intensity above that ridge, making compute the tighter bound; profiling must establish whether execution approaches it. ResNet-50’s stage-3 \(3{\times}3\) convolution demonstrates this behavior.

Napkin Math 11.5: Convolutional layer analysisConsider the \(3{\times}3\) convolution in a stage-3 bottleneck block of ResNet-50, with input shape (batch = 32, channels = 128, height = 28, width = 28) and 128 output channels, on an H100 at FP16:
Computational requirements:

Output size: \(32 \times 128 \times 28 \times 28\) = 3.2M elements
FLOPs per output: \(128 \times 3 \times 3 \times 2\) = 2,304 (multiply-add)
Total FLOPs: 3.2M \(\times\) 2,304 = 7.4 GFLOP

Memory traffic analysis:

Input: \(32 \times 128 \times 28 \times 28 \times 2\) = 6.4 MB (FP16)
Weights: \(128 \times 128 \times 3 \times 3 \times 2\) ≈ 0.3 MB (FP16)
Output: \(32 \times 128 \times 28 \times 28 \times 2\) = 6.4 MB (FP16)
Total: 13.1 MB

Arithmetic intensity: \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) = 7.4 GFLOP / 13.1 MB = 563.1 FLOP/byte
Systems insight: This is well above the H100’s FP16 ridge point of 295.2 FLOP/byte, so the simple roofline model places the operation in the compute-limited region. The dense FP16 tensor peak of ~989 TFLOP/s is therefore the ceiling, but realized performance still depends on tiling, occupancy, instruction mix, and library efficiency.


The convolutional layer’s high arithmetic intensity arises from spatial weight reuse: the same \(3{\times}3\) kernel is applied across every spatial location in the feature map, amortizing the cost of loading weights from off-chip memory across millions of multiply-accumulate operations. Keeping active tiles in registers and shared memory reduces repeated off-chip transfers, making high arithmetic throughput possible. Whether a particular kernel then saturates the Tensor Cores depends on tiling, occupancy, and instruction mix, which the roofline does not model. Moreover, the FP16 analysis is only half of the chapter’s workload, because the profile Model Compression ended on runs ResNet-50 in INT8. Quantization changes both sides of the roofline at once, and the two changes need not cancel.

Napkin Math 11.6: When INT8 moves a layer below the ridgeProblem: The H100’s INT8 tensor path offers about 2× the operations per second of its FP16 path from the same 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth. Which ResNet-50 layers stay compute bound when the model moves from FP16 to INT8?
The two ridges: The ridge rises from 295.2 FLOP/byte at FP16 to 590.7 FLOP/byte at INT8. A layer keeps its position relative to the ridge only if every byte it moves halves along with the operand width.
Three layers at batch 32 (operations per byte, one read of input and weights and one write of the output):

Stage-3 \(3{\times}3\) convolution (the layer of notebook 11.5): 563 at FP16, above the FP16 ridge. With INT8 activations it reaches 1,126, above the INT8 ridge. If its activations stay FP16 between layers, as when the kernel reads and writes 16-bit tensors for FP16 neighbors, its intensity rises only to 569, well below the INT8 ridge. At batch 32, the input and output activation tensors together account for roughly 12.8 MB of traffic while the shared \(3{\times}3\) weight tensor is only about 0.3 MB in FP16, so halving weight bytes alone barely changes total memory traffic.
Stage-2 \(3{\times}3\) convolution (\(56{\times}56\) positions, 64 channels in and out): 287 at FP16 and 574 at INT8, just below the ridge in both precisions.
Stage-2 \(1{\times}1\) expansion (\(56{\times}56\) positions, 64 channels in and 256 out): 51 at FP16 and 102 at INT8, far below the ridge in both.

Systems insight: INT8 raises the arithmetic ceiling but leaves the bandwidth ceiling where it was, so the layers that were already bandwidth bound gain only the halved bytes, and a compute-bound layer whose activations stay wide crosses below the new ridge. The INT8 speedup of Model Compression’s profile therefore depends on whether activations travel at INT8 between layers, a decision made by the compiler and runtime (section 11.8), not by the quantized weights alone.


Not all neural network layers reuse data so heavily. Fully connected (dense) layers, such as ResNet-50’s classification head, feed-forward networks, and linear projections in transformer attention blocks, lack spatial dimensions. When evaluated at small batch sizes, their arithmetic intensity drops substantially, shifting execution into the bandwidth-bound regime:

Napkin Math 11.7: Dense layer analysisConsider ResNet-50’s final fully connected layer, which maps 2,048 pooled features to 1,000 class scores for a batch of 32 images on the same H100:
Computational requirements:

Matrix multiply: \((32 \times 2048) \times (2048 \times 1000)\)
Total FLOPs: \(2 \times 32 \times 2048 \times 1000\) = 131.1 MFLOP

Memory traffic analysis:

Input: \(32 \times 2048 \times 2\) = 131.1 KB (FP16)
Weights: \(2048 \times 1000 \times 2\) = 4.1 MB (FP16)
Output: \(32 \times 1000 \times 2\) = 64 KB (FP16)
Total: 4.3 MB

Arithmetic intensity: \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) = 131.1 MFLOP / 4.3 MB = 30.5 FLOP/byte
This intensity sits below the H100’s ridge point of 295.2 FLOP/byte, making this operation memory bound under the stated traffic model. Attainable performance: \(\AttainableComputeRate\) = 3,350 GB/s \(\times\) 30.5 FLOP/byte = 102.3 TFLOP/s
Systems insight: Attainable throughput is only 10.3 percent of peak compute capability, so at batch 32 the memory wall caps this layer long before the Tensor Cores do.


The dense layer’s lower arithmetic intensity stems from limited parameter reuse. While a convolutional kernel is reused across every spatial location in an activation map, a dense weight matrix is reused only across the batch dimension. At a batch size of 32, each fetched weight contributes to 32 sample products in this operation. When the weights stream from HBM on each invocation, as modeled, the bandwidth ceiling caps throughput at 10.3 percent of peak compute capacity. The fraction is a bound rather than a measured stall count, and a layer whose weights stay cached between invocations would do better. The same arithmetic explains why transformer inference at low batch sizes is governed by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic capability, a regime the throughput-ceiling notebook below quantifies for GPT-2.
While small-batch matrix multiplications suffer from restricted parameter reuse, elementwise and reduction operators represent an even more acute memory bottleneck. Operations such as layer normalization, activation functions, and residual additions perform only a few arithmetic operations per element loaded from memory, driving arithmetic intensity to its physical floor:

Napkin Math 11.8: LayerNorm analysisLayerNorm over one GPT-2 XL layer’s activations, with input shape (batch = 8, sequence = 1024, hidden = 1600):
Computational requirements:

Elements: \(8 \times 1024 \times 1600\) = 13.1M
Approximate operations per element: mean reduction (1 ADD), variance (2 ADD, 1 MUL), normalization and affine transform (2 ADD, 2 MUL) ≈ 8; reciprocal-square-root overhead is amortized across each hidden vector
Total FLOPs: 13.1M \(\times\) 8 = 104.9 MFLOP

Memory traffic:

Input: 13.1M \(\times\) 2 = 26.2 MB
Parameters (scale, bias): \(1600 \times 2 \times 2\) = 6.4 KB (negligible)
Output: 13.1M \(\times\) 2 = 26.2 MB
Total: 52.4 MB

Arithmetic intensity: \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) = 104.9 MFLOP / 52.4 MB = 2.0 FLOP/byte
This arithmetic intensity sits severely below the H100 ridge point (148× below). The HBM performance upper bound is: \(\AttainableComputeRate\) = 3,350 GB/s \(\times\) 2.0 FLOP/byte = 6.7 TFLOP/s
Systems insight: The simple HBM roofline bounds this standalone LayerNorm at about 0.7 percent of the H100’s tensor peak. That tensor peak is a reference, not the throughput available to LayerNorm’s vector and reduction instructions. Actual latency also depends on their execution ceilings, fusion, launch overhead, and which memory level supplies the data.


Standalone normalization performs minimal arithmetic relative to the memory traffic it generates, as the LayerNorm analysis demonstrates. Under the modeled unfused HBM read/write boundary, the implementation performs approximately 2 FLOP/byte, giving a low bandwidth ceiling relative to the tensor peak. Reaching that ceiling still requires enough parallel work and an efficient reduction. Cache residency changes the physical HBM byte count and can shift the relevant bound to another memory interface. In the D·A·M framework, when the machine constraint is a memory bandwidth wall, the algorithmic response is kernel fusion, which collapses adjacent projections, bias additions, normalization, and activations into one kernel so that intermediate values stay in registers or SRAM. Fusion pays off when the grouping preserves numerical behavior and fits the local register and SRAM budget, and profiling confirms that the saved traffic outweighs any loss of occupancy.



Tuning thread-block occupancy on a bandwidth-bound LayerNorm kernel wastes engineering effort for zero speedup, just as fusing two already compute-bound matrix multiplications cannot raise throughput past the Tensor Core ceiling. The roofline’s intensity regimes (table 8) match each bottleneck to the lever that can move it.



Table 8: Optimization by Arithmetic Intensity Regime: Position relative to the target execution path’s ridge guides compute and traffic optimization. Profiling confirms the bottleneck; fusion removes intermediate round-trips when dependencies and local storage permit it.












Intensity regime
Typical operations
Optimization priority
Common techniques
Expected impact




Above the target path’s ridge
Large convolutions
Maximize compute utilization.
Tensor Cores, thread-block tuning, and high occupancy.
Raises sustained compute utilization when the kernel already clears the ridge.


Near the target path’s ridge
Medium-sized dense layers
Balance compute and memory optimization.
Larger batches, register tiling, and fusion with adjacent operations.
Can move the binding bottleneck between memory and compute.


Below the target path’s ridge

Reduce memory traffic.

Low-intensity operator chains

Eliminate memory round-trips.

For low-intensity operations, kernel fusion is often the decisive optimization: LayerNorm combined with the Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU), for example, can become a single fused kernel. One of the most accessible levers for moving an operation up and right on the roofline is batching.

Napkin Math 11.9: Batch size and arithmetic intensityIncreasing batch size improves arithmetic intensity for matrix operations by amortizing weight loading. Equation 5 formalizes this relationship for an idealized FP16/BF16 dense layer \((\BatchSize{\times}\LayerInputWidth){\times}(\LayerInputWidth{\times}\LayerOutputWidth)\), counting one read each of the input and weights and one write of the output, where \(\BatchSize\) is batch size and \(\LayerInputWidth\) and \(\LayerOutputWidth\) are the layer’s input and output widths: \[\ArithmeticIntensity = \frac{2\BatchSize\LayerInputWidth\LayerOutputWidth}{2\BatchSize\LayerInputWidth + 2\LayerInputWidth\LayerOutputWidth + 2\BatchSize\LayerOutputWidth} \approx \frac{2\BatchSize\LayerInputWidth\LayerOutputWidth}{2\LayerInputWidth\LayerOutputWidth} = \BatchSize\quad (\text{when } 2\LayerInputWidth\LayerOutputWidth \gg 2\BatchSize(\LayerInputWidth+\LayerOutputWidth)) \tag{5}\]
Example: Dense layer with \(\LayerInputWidth = \LayerOutputWidth\) = 2048 (FP16)

Batch = 1: \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) ≈ 1 FLOP/byte (memory bound)
Batch = 32: \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) ≈ 31 FLOP/byte (memory bound)
Batch = 512: \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) ≈ 341.3 FLOP/byte (compute bound on the H100)

Systems insight: This explains why batching can produce large throughput improvements in production inference systems, as MLPerf Inference, the standardized benchmark suite, demonstrates by separating bulk-throughput runs from latency-constrained serving runs (Reddi et al. 2019).



Reddi, Vijay Janapa, Christine Cheng, David Kanter, Peter Mattson, Guenther Schmuelling, Carole-Jean Wu, Brian Anderson, et al. 2019. “MLPerf Inference Benchmark.” 2020 ACM/IEEE 47th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), 446–59. https://doi.org/10.1109/isca45697.2020.00045.

↪ The MLPerf Inference execution scenarios that separate throughput runs from latency-constrained runs are developed in MLPerf execution scenarios.

The batch size analysis reveals why inference serving systems are designed around batching: it changes the arithmetic intensity regime of bandwidth-bound workloads. However, batching introduces latency trade-offs, since requests must wait in a queue until a batch forms. This tension between throughput (favoring large batches) and latency (favoring small batches) is a central challenge in ML serving systems, explored in depth in Dynamic batching latency-throughput trade-offs. When service latency limits batching, batch-1 or small-batch LLM decode often retains low weight reuse and low arithmetic intensity, and the next worked model quantifies that particular regime rather than treating all LLM inference as identical.

Napkin Math 11.10: The throughput ceilingProblem: A batch-1 GPT-2 calculation makes this bandwidth ceiling concrete: what is the maximum possible utilization of an NVIDIA H100 when running GPT-2 inference (batch size 1)?
The hardware constraints (the denominators)

Peak compute: 989 TFLOP/s (FP16 Tensor Core).
Peak bandwidth: 3.35 TB/s (HBM3).
Ridge point \((\PeakRate/\Bandwidth)\): 989 TFLOP/s / 3.35 TB/s = 295.2 FLOP/byte (for FP16 Tensor Core).
Interpretation: Saturating this chip at FP16 precision requires 295.2 FLOP/byte operations for every byte loaded. The ridge point varies by precision: FP32 operations (67 TFLOP/s peak) have a ridge point of only ~20 FLOP/byte.

The workload characteristics (the numerator)

Model: GPT-2 XL (1.5 billion parameters).
Operation: Autoregressive generation (1 token at a time).
Data movement: Must load all weights (3 GB @ FP16) for every token.
Compute: Vector-Matrix multiplication. Two FLOPs per parameter, \(2\Parameters\) ≈ 3 GFLOP.
Arithmetic intensity: 3 GFLOP / 3 GB = 1 FLOP/byte

The prediction (iron law)
Since the modeled intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) (1) \(\ll\) the ridge point \(\RooflineRidgePoint\) (295.2 FLOP/byte), batch-1 decode is bandwidth bound.

Maximum throughput: 1 FLOP/byte \(\times\) 3.35 TB/s = 3.4 TFLOP/s.
Utilization ceiling: 3.4 TFLOP/s (Bound) / 989 TFLOP/s (Peak) ≈ \(0.3\%\)

Systems insight: Without batching, a ~$25,000 accelerator cannot exceed 0.3 percent of its compute peak in this weight-streaming decode scenario. Batching and weight quantization address that gap; key-value caching instead avoids recomputing prior attention states. The ceiling also assumes that the decode step is launched as a captured graph (Graph capture and JIT compilation); executed one eager kernel at a time, launch overhead rather than weight streaming would set the floor.


Placed on one roofline, the layers and the decode step analyzed above fall on either side of two ridges, and only the stage-3 \(3{\times}3\) convolution reaches a flat ceiling (figure 12). Through this derivation, the roofline model provides a diagnostic framework for identifying whether operations are compute bound or memory bound. Knowing that batch-1 decode is bandwidth bound at a ceiling of 0.3 percent of peak is only the first step; the next challenge is translating this diagnosis into efficient execution plans that exploit accelerator architectures.














Figure 12: ResNet-50 and GPT-2 XL on the H100 Roofline: Attainable throughput against arithmetic intensity on log-log axes, with the dense FP16 ceiling and the INT8 ceiling sharing one bandwidth slope. INT8 raises the ridge from 295.2 FLOP/byte to 590.7 FLOP/byte. Arrows connect each layer’s FP16 point to its INT8 point. ResNet-50’s stage-3 convolution clears the ridge in both precisions when its activations move at the format’s width, but falls below the INT8 ridge when its activations stay FP16; its stage-2 expansion and classifier sit far below either ridge, and GPT-2 XL decode sits more than an order of magnitude further left.

title: 11 Hardware Acceleration
text:
Consider one of ResNet-50’s \(3{\times}3\) convolutions running on an accelerator tile. The mathematical operation is fixed, but the execution plan is not. One schedule can keep a filter in local registers while many output pixels stream past it; another can advance pixel by pixel and reload the same filter values repeatedly from a slower memory tier. Both schedules compute the same tensor. Only one turns the reuse in the convolution into real bandwidth savings.

Definition 11.4: Mapping in AI acceleration
Mapping in AI acceleration is the accelerator-compiler process of binding the logical computation graph to the physical hardware topology by deciding which operations execute on which processing elements, which data resides in which memory tier, and in what temporal order.

Significance: Within the D·A·M taxonomy, mapping is a machine-axis decision that helps determine how closely an operation approaches the roofline bound \(\min(\PeakRate,\; \Bandwidth \times \ArithmeticIntensity)\). A poor tiling choice that forces unnecessary DRAM accesses can reduce effective arithmetic intensity enough to move a nominally compute-bound operation into the bandwidth-bound regime.
Distinction: Traditional compilation often emphasizes instruction selection, register allocation, and scheduling for general-purpose processors. Accelerator mapping gives equal prominence to spatial placement and explicit data movement across a dataflow architecture. The reason is physical: as quantified by the storage-tier energy ladder in figure 4, an off-chip DRAM access costs about 173× the energy of an FP32 multiply, making operand placement as critical to efficiency as the execution unit that evaluates it.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that mapping is automatically handled by frameworks. For general GPU workloads, compilers such as Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA) can find strong mappings for common kernels. For specialized accelerators (systolic arrays, custom ASICs), compiler-generated mappings may still lag hand-tuned schedules because the compiler’s search space is limited by the time budget at compilation.



The convolution example exposes the three decisions that recur throughout accelerator compilation. Placement assigns the multiply-accumulate work to processing elements so parallelism does not turn into idle time or interconnect congestion. Allocation keeps weights, activations, and partial sums in the memory tier where their next use will occur, rather than letting reuse spill back to DRAM. Scheduling orders loops and kernels so the chosen placement and allocation remain valid over time. A poor choice in any one dimension can collapse a high-arithmetic-intensity operation back into a bandwidth-bound execution. In practice, these choices are too coupled for developers to manage by hand at model scale. Systems such as XLA, TVM, and TensorRT therefore lower high-level models and search or select execution plans within their compile-time and hardware budgets. Section 11.8 examines that compiler support in detail.


Spatial and storage mapping decisions pull against each other across the chip. Computation placement spreads operations across processing elements to expose parallelism, but placing producer and consumer operations on distant units increases the interconnect bandwidth required to shuttle intermediate tensors between them. Memory allocation stages operands in fast on-chip buffers to cut access latency, but the small capacity of registers and SRAM limits how many processing elements can hold their working sets concurrently. Getting either side wrong leaves thousands of execution units idle or starved for data.


The scale of modern hardware magnifies any spatial imbalance: the NVIDIA H100 contains more than 16,000 CUDA cores and more than 500 Tensor Cores (Choquette 2023), TPUs organize thousands of multiply-accumulate units into systolic arrays (Jouppi et al. 2017), and wafer-scale processors such as Cerebras’ CS-2 integrate more than 850,000 cores (Systems 2021). Across arrays of that size, even a small fraction of idle processing elements or redundant cross-chip transfers wastes substantial time and energy.
The difficulty of placement depends on workload regularity. Convolutional networks and dense transformer operations possess regular access patterns that tile predictably, though transformer architectures mix operations with distinct tensor shapes and reuse profiles. Graph neural networks (GNNs) present greater difficulty: sparse, input-dependent neighborhood aggregations introduce load imbalance and non-uniform communication across processing elements. Static spatial mappings suffice for regular dense operations whose shapes and loop bounds are known ahead of time. Workloads with dynamic shapes, sparsity, or mixture-of-experts routing instead require runtime scheduling to balance execution across processing elements. Yet even an optimal computation placement stalls if the required operands are not staged in time: compute units can execute only as fast as operands arrive from the memory hierarchy.



While computation placement determines where operations execute, memory allocation defines where data resides and how it flows through the hierarchy. The goal is to keep reused data near the processing elements without exceeding faster-tier capacity. GPUs expose global memory, shared memory, caches, and registers that kernels coordinate through tiling (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). TPUs use on-chip SRAM buffers to stage the activations that flow horizontally through the 2D systolic-array dataflow (Jouppi et al. 2017) of figure 5, with partial sums flowing vertically, while wafer-scale processors partition memory and computation to control interconnect traffic (Systems 2021). General-purpose processors and accelerators both use memory hierarchies, but many accelerators expose more placement decisions to compilers and kernels. When allocation fails to exploit locality, processing elements stall waiting for operands, driving down utilization and dissipating energy across the memory bus.

The severity of these penalties varies by workload. Convolutional networks rely on structured, localized access patterns and benefit from well-defined memory layouts that support predictable reuse (Chen et al. 2016). Transformers require access to large parameter sets and intermediate activations, making them sensitive to capacity and bandwidth. Graph neural networks add irregular sparse structures that complicate allocation and prefetching.
Capacity is only the first allocation test. A tensor can fit in accelerator memory yet still dominate execution if each kernel rereads it from a distant tier; conversely, tiling can keep a larger working set efficient by preserving reuse locally. The allocation diagnostic is therefore traffic, not capacity alone: compilers must track how frequently values cross each memory boundary and keep high-reuse tensors in the fastest feasible tier. Systems combine static memory plans for known shapes with dynamic buffer management when shapes vary, while device capacity limits which models fit without partitioning or offload. The convolution that opened this section illustrates why hardware mapping becomes a combinatorial search problem. Keeping a filter resident in local storage improves reuse only if the assigned processing elements have sufficient storage and if the loop schedule revisits that filter before eviction. Similarly, parallelizing across more processing elements improves throughput only until synchronization overhead and interconnect contention erode the benefit. Because changing one decision alters the feasible and efficient choices for the others, compilers must evaluate placement, allocation, and scheduling jointly rather than independently.
