Approximately \(1.10\times\) overall speedup; according to Amdahl’s Law, the unaccelerated 90% serial preprocessing fraction strictly caps end-to-end speedup to \(\text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{0.90 + \frac{0.10}{10}} = \frac{1}{0.91} \approx 1.10\times\). Amdahl’s Law (principle 8) governs end-to-end ML pipelines. When 90% of execution time remains unaccelerated on the host CPU (e.g., JPEG decoding, tokenization, or database feature lookups), even an infinite (\(S = \infty\)) speedup on the GPU inference kernel would yield at most \(\frac{1}{0.90} \approx 1.11\times\) overall system speedup. Optimizing without profiling where time actually goes is guessing, and Amdahl’s Law severely penalizes optimizations that target the non-dominant term. The other options violate Amdahl’s Law arithmetic.
Learning Objective: Apply Amdahl’s Law to calculate end-to-end speedup when optimizing isolated pipeline stages and identify when unaccelerated preprocessing bounds system throughput.
A team selects Model Alpha over Model Beta because Alpha achieves 94.8% top-1 accuracy on a static benchmark versus Beta’s 93.2%. When deployed, Model Alpha violates the 100 ms P99 serving latency SLO by taking 420 ms, consumes \(4\times\) more memory, and exhibits a 16% error rate on an underrepresented user demographic. Which systems concept explains why single-metric evaluation led to this production failure?

The Pareto Frontier; production ML systems operate across a multi-dimensional objective space (accuracy, tail latency, memory, energy, cost, and subgroup fairness), where optimizing aggregate accuracy in isolation can select an infeasible, costly, or discriminatory operating point.
The Silicon Contract; models with higher accuracy automatically violate hardware execution contracts.
Data Gravity; higher accuracy models physically pull network packets away from edge caches.
Amdahl’s Law; aggregate accuracy scales inversely with the number of parallel workers.

Answer: The correct answer is A. The Pareto Frontier; production ML systems operate across a multi-dimensional objective space (accuracy, tail latency, memory, energy, cost, and subgroup fairness), where optimizing aggregate accuracy in isolation can select an infeasible, costly, or discriminatory operating point. Evaluating models solely along a single accuracy dimension inhabits a one-dimensional fantasy. In production, models must satisfy multi-objective constraints along the Pareto Frontier (principle 5): meeting P99 latency budgets (principle 12), fitting hardware memory capacity, respecting energy/cost limits, and ensuring equitable error rates across demographic subgroups (principle 13). A model with 1.6% higher aggregate accuracy that violates latency SLOs and exhibits extreme subgroup disparity is an engineering failure. The other options misapply unrelated systems concepts.
Learning Objective: Critique single-metric accuracy evaluation and apply the Pareto Frontier to assess production models across latency, memory, energy, and subgroup fairness.
True or False: High-level software frameworks, AutoML tools, and compiler abstractions eliminate underlying physical ML systems constraints (such as memory bandwidth bottlenecks, thermal dissipation limits, and Amdahl’s Law ceilings), allowing software engineers to ignore low-level hardware characteristics.
Answer: False. Tools and abstractions hide and manage complexity; they do not eliminate physical constraints. A framework that abstracts memory management still transfers bytes across physical buses and consumes memory capacity; an AutoML engine tuning hyperparameters still operates on the Pareto frontier; and a compiler optimizing GPU kernels remains strictly bounded by Amdahl’s Law and memory wall physics. Engineers who assume tools eliminate physical constraints are routinely surprised when those constraints resurface at scale as mysterious OOM errors, tail latency spikes, or thermal throttling.
Learning Objective: Analyze why software abstractions manage complexity rather than eliminating physical hardware constraints.
A production drift alarm fires due to seasonal changes in user shopping patterns. Explain why triggering an automated rollback to a model checkpoint trained three months earlier is an operational pitfall, and state the appropriate remediation.
Answer: Automated rollback is effective for software bugs or bad releases, but external real-world distribution drift cannot be repaired by restoring an older model trained on an even staler distribution. Restoring the older checkpoint will perform just as poorly or worse. The appropriate remediation is a diagnosed response: alerting the team, temporarily routing traffic to fallback heuristics or reducing traffic, collecting fresh ground-truth labels from the new distribution, and retraining/adapting the model.
Learning Objective: Differentiate between release regressions and external distribution drift to select appropriate operational remediations.
Looking across all seven fallacies and pitfalls detailed in the chapter (tools hiding complexity, untraced displaced costs, component-only mastery, untraced data-scaling costs, single-metric accuracy evaluation, unconditional rollbacks, and unprofiled stage optimization), identify the shared intellectual root cause that unites them and state the corrective systems engineering posture.
Answer: The shared root cause is the reductionist temptation to treat an ML system as decomposable into independent, isolated parts—optimizing one dimension, one metric, one pipeline stage, or one moment in time as if the surrounding system were static. The corrective systems engineering posture is holistic boundary reasoning: measuring the end-to-end request path, profiling where time and bytes actually go before optimizing, tracing how decisions in one layer displace costs to other layers (conservation-of-complexity heuristic), and evaluating performance across the full multi-dimensional Pareto surface under real-world operational constraints.
Learning Objective: Synthesize the shared systems misconception (reductionism and isolated optimization) underlying common ML systems failures.

← Back to Questions

title: The D·A·M Taxonomy
text:
A system that runs slowly rarely announces why. An idle accelerator can stem from a starved input pipeline (Data), an algorithm with too little arithmetic intensity (Algorithm), or a saturated memory bus (Machine). This appendix maps profiler symptoms and measurements to the axis that binds execution, before optimization begins. Readers should arrive with the three axes from the opening chapters and the iron law that quantifies them.


Use the D·A·M taxonomy when a system misses a performance, cost, or quality target and the cause is not yet clear. Work through the framework in four passes:

State the symptom and operating budget: Record the missed end-to-end target, workload, and deployment context.
Localize the candidate axis or boundary: Use table 2 for a first pass and table 3 when the evidence crosses axes.
Test the hypothesis: Map the evidence to the iron law and arithmetic intensity, then gather confirming measurements with table 5 and table 6.
Intervene and remeasure: Choose a lever from table 7, repeat the end-to-end measurement, and score the result with table 8. If the target does not improve, revise the hypothesis.

Table 1 maps each common need to the section that answers it. In every case the axis label is a hypothesis, not a verdict. The axes overlap, and a useful diagnosis may name both a dominant axis and a boundary effect.



Table 1: Need-to-Section Lookup: Each row names a diagnostic need and the section of this appendix that answers it. Start from the need that matches the observed symptom.

When a training step stalls or a serving call misses its latency budget, the cause can sit in JPEG decoding on the host, quadratic attention work in the model, or a saturated memory bus on the accelerator. The taxonomy separates those causes along the three axes of the iron law of ML systems (Iron Law of ML Systems). Data is what the model learns from and what the pipeline must deliver, Algorithm is the computation the model performs, and Machine is the hardware that executes that computation. Table 2 summarizes the role, primary physical constraint, and core optimization pathway for each axis.



Table 2: D·A·M Axis Reference: Each axis maps to a constraint class and optimization strategy. Form a hypothesis, confirm it with measurements, then follow the chapter pointer.











Axis
Role
Physical Constraint
High-Leverage Optimization




Data (D)
What the model learns from
Volume, quality, arrival rate

Algorithm (A)

Operations and dependencies

Machine (M)
The hardware that executes it
Compute, memory, I/O
Hardware Acceleration (Hardware Acceleration)






This first-pass separation is useful, but production systems rarely suffer from a single axis-centered bottleneck. More often, the problem sits at the boundary between two axes, as when a data format choice determines whether the accelerator can be saturated or a pruning strategy changes the memory access pattern. Handling these cases requires mapping the intersections.



Pruning weights to cut Algorithm FLOPs can fragment Machine memory access, and changing a Data storage format can saturate host CPUs while trying to feed the accelerator. Because an intervention on one axis shifts pressure onto the other two, the conceptual Venn overlaps in The D·A·M Intersection Landscape become an operational diagnostic triad of Data, Algorithm, and Machine joined by bidirectional coupling (figure 1). To diagnose a production bottleneck, an engineer first identifies which axis currently binds the workload, then traces its two incident edges to predict how a candidate fix will alter memory, compute, or I/O demand across the system.






Figure 1: The D·A·M Axis Triad: A compact diagnostic view of Data, Algorithm, and Machine as three interdependent axes. The bidirectional links emphasize that an intervention on one axis changes the constraints on the other two.



With the first-pass axis identified, the pairwise and three-way intersections expand into concrete engineering techniques and the chapters that teach them (table 3).

In the D·A·M acronym, Data, Algorithm, and Machine name the three diagnostic axes rather than single-letter algebraic variables; formal quantities follow the notation chapter, where \(\DatasetSize\) denotes logical dataset size (samples or tokens) and \(\DataVolume\) denotes physical data volume moved (bytes). The axis-centered zones contain concepts that belong primarily to one axis: storage formats and distributions emphasize Data, loss functions and gradients emphasize Algorithm, and silicon physics and peak FLOP/s emphasize Machine. Single-domain expertise can introduce them, but deployed behavior may still depend on the other axes.
The pairwise intersections are where systems thinking begins. At \(\DataTaxonomyAxis\cap \AlgorithmTaxonomyAxis\) (What to Learn From), data selection, curriculum learning, active learning, and scaling laws (section 1.8.1) couple information content to algorithmic capacity. Information content and algorithmic capacity are coupled because adding data that the model cannot absorb wastes compute, while choosing architectures that outstrip available data wastes engineering time. That boundary governs statistical efficiency. At \(\DataTaxonomyAxis\cap \MachineTaxonomyAxis\) (How to Move Information), the concern is physical delivery through I/O bandwidth, prefetching strategies, data formats, and the energy-movement invariant. Here data gravity manifests, because the cost of moving bytes through the memory hierarchy decides whether the machine stays fed. Once data reaches the device, \(\AlgorithmTaxonomyAxis\cap \MachineTaxonomyAxis\) (How to Execute Efficiently) links mathematical structure to hardware execution across quantization, pruning, kernel fusion, mixed precision, and computational graph optimization. It explains why a pruning scheme that cuts FLOPs while fragmenting memory access can still run slower on silicon.
The center, \(\DataTaxonomyAxis\cap \AlgorithmTaxonomyAxis\cap \MachineTaxonomyAxis\), is where all three axes converge. The iron law, the roofline model, end-to-end training loops, serving pipelines, and holistic benchmarking all require simultaneous reasoning about data flow, algorithmic complexity, and hardware utilization. The intersections classify where a technique operates. Isolating which axis actively throttles a workload requires translating these relationships into wall-clock execution time, which is the role of the iron law.



Placing quantization at the Algorithm/Machine intersection does not by itself tell an engineer how many milliseconds a 4-bit weight format will save, because the wall-clock gain depends on whether byte transfers, arithmetic, or kernel launches dominate the step. For any workload, the iron law turns the D·A·M axes into execution time \(\Time\) (seconds) in two steps. First, at the workload level (equation 1.2), time factors multiplicatively across the three axes: \[ \Time = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Samples}}{\text{Task}}\right)}_{\text{Data}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Sample}}\right)}_{\text{Algorithm}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Seconds}}{\text{FLOP}}\right)}_{\text{Machine}} \] where the product of the Data and Algorithm factors sets the total arithmetic work \(\Operations = (\text{Samples/Task}) \times (\text{FLOPs/Sample})\) in FLOPs. Second, for serialized execution phases (equation 1.3), unpacking how the machine executes those operations maps work across the D·A·M interfaces into three physical time terms. In these terms, \(\DataVolume\) is bytes moved, \(\Bandwidth\) is bytes per second, \(\PeakRate\) is peak throughput in FLOP/s, \(\EfficiencyHw\) is dimensionless hardware efficiency, and \(\Latency\) is fixed overhead in seconds: \[ \Time= \underbrace{ \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} }_{\text{Data/Machine}} + \underbrace{ \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} }_{\text{Algorithm/Machine}} + \underbrace{ \Latency }_{\text{Cross-axis overhead}} \]
Dividing this serialized decomposition by \(\Operations\) (and substituting arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity = \Operations/\DataVolume\)) expresses the realized Machine factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) directly in terms of the three physical bottlenecks: \[ \frac{\text{Seconds}}{\text{FLOP}} = \frac{\Time}{\Operations} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\ArithmeticIntensity \cdot \Bandwidth}}_{\text{Memory time per FLOP}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}}_{\text{Compute time per FLOP}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Latency}{\Operations}}_{\text{Overhead per FLOP}} \]
Algorithm and Machine share the compute term, separated by which variable the engineer controls. Reducing the total operations (\(\Operations\)) is a Data or Algorithm lever, while reducing the realized time per operation (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) by raising peak throughput (\(\PeakRate\)), utilization (\(\EfficiencyHw\)), or bandwidth (\(\Bandwidth\)) is a Machine lever. This per-FLOP expression also shows why training and inference occupy different regimes under the same law. In large-batch training, high arithmetic intensity (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\)) and large operation counts (\(\Operations\)) shrink the first and third terms so \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\) approaches the compute term (Training-Time Law). In small-batch or single-token inference, low \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) and small \(\Operations\) per request inflate the memory and overhead terms (Model Serving).
The dominant measured cost appears in one of these terms. A slow system may move too much data (\(\DataVolume\)), lack bandwidth (\(\Bandwidth\)), execute too many operations (\(\Operations\)), fail to use the hardware’s peak capability (\(\EfficiencyHw\)), or pay cross-axis overhead (\(\Latency\)). A workload whose time is dominated by \(\Latency\) is overhead-bound: kernel launches, dispatch, and synchronization, not bytes or arithmetic, set its pace.


Once profiling isolates the largest time term, each axis offers a distinct set of engineering levers that shrink its numerator or raise its denominator:

Data lever: Reducing the samples processed per task (\(\text{Samples/Task}\), which shrinks \(\Operations\)) or the moved bytes (\(\DataVolume\)) through deduplication and selection, or increasing I/O bandwidth (\(\Bandwidth\)).
Algorithm lever: Reducing operations per sample (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\), and thus \(\Operations\)) through pruning, distillation, or architectural refinement, or reducing the bytes each weight and activation occupies through lower-precision representation. Quantization is an Algorithm choice that shrinks the Data/Machine term \(\DataVolume\) and may raise hardware throughput \(\PeakRate\), lowering \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\) without reducing operation count.
Machine lever: Lowering \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\) by increasing peak throughput (\(\PeakRate\)), memory bandwidth (\(\Bandwidth\)), or the utilization factor (\(\EfficiencyHw\)) via kernel fusion and scheduling.

Shrinking individual terms is the first lever; hiding one term behind another is the second.



When a training step waits for each batch to finish copying across PCIe before launching the forward pass, data-transfer time and compute time add directly; prefetching the next batch while the accelerator computes the current one hides the shorter stage behind the longer one. The additive iron law represents this unpipelined, sequential execution. Let \(\SequentialExecutionTime\) denote time without overlap and \(\PipelinedExecutionTime\) denote measured time with overlap. Overlap can move the sum toward a max, but dependencies, contention, and incomplete overlap keep the measured time above this ideal lower bound: \[ \SequentialExecutionTime= \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency \quad \xrightarrow{\text{overlap}} \quad \PipelinedExecutionTime\geq \max\left(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}, \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}\right) + \Latency \]
Compute should overlap with data movement wherever dependencies allow. Table 4 summarizes key D·A·M coordination techniques that overlap work across axes.



Table 4: D·A·M Overlap Techniques: Each technique overlaps work across axes, moving sequentially added Data/Machine and Algorithm/Machine time toward their ideal lower bound: the larger of the two terms. Dependencies and contention limit realized overlap.










Technique
D·A·M Axes Overlapped
Implementation

DataLoader with prefetch_factor, pin_memory=True

Separate streams for H2D transfer and compute

D overlaps M
Fill buffer N+1 while computing on buffer N






Overlaps provide the greatest relative speedup when the D·A·M time terms are reasonably balanced. If one term dominates (for example, a severely bandwidth-bound kernel), overlapping the smaller term with the larger yields negligible gain, because the max is still set by the same bottleneck. This balance occurs near \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth \approx \Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\). The overhead term is treated separately below.

Systems Perspective 1.1: The overhead that cannot hideThe unhidden latency term \(\Latency\) (kernel launch, synchronization barriers, Python dispatch) contains serialization points that cannot be fully overlapped. Kernel fusion can reduce this term by combining operations, but it does not eliminate all launch, scheduling, or synchronization overhead.


The iron law separates data-movement time from compute time, but it does not by itself say which of the two sets the hardware ceiling for a given kernel.




Doubling an accelerator’s peak FLOP/s leaves a kernel no faster if the arithmetic units spend most of each cycle waiting for bytes from memory. Which side of that ceiling a kernel sits on is decided by its arithmetic intensity1 (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\)), the operations performed per byte moved between memory and compute. A kernel whose intensity falls below the hardware’s ridge point \(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\) is bandwidth-bound, the regime the roofline literature calls memory-bound. This book keeps the bandwidth name so the regime is not confused with running out of memory capacity. A kernel above the ridge point is compute-bound.
1 Arithmetic intensity: This book uses the term for floating-point operations per byte transferred. Williams et al. (2009) calls the measured DRAM quantity operational intensity in the Roofline Model. Comparing the workload ratio with the hardware ridge point (\(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\)) gives an upper-bound diagnosis of bandwidth- versus compute-bound execution.
Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
The reference accelerator places the boundary concretely. An H100’s dense FP16 ridge point is about 295 FLOP/byte. GPT-2 XL decoding one token at batch one reads all 3 GB of its FP16 weights and reaches an arithmetic intensity of only about 1 FLOP/byte, more than two orders of magnitude below the ridge. With kernel launches captured into a replayable graph (Graph capture and JIT compilation), the weight read takes about 0.9 ms while the arithmetic needs about 3 μs, so a faster arithmetic unit would leave the per-token time unchanged. Performance Bounds develops the ridge point, hardware balance, and the regimes on either side of it. The Roofline model carries the worked roofline template. The decode floor turns the weight read into the decode floor a serving system plans around.
The roofline gives an upper performance bound when traffic and achieved rates are measured consistently. During a production incident, screening heuristics point to the measurements to collect first, which is where diagnosis begins.



When a benchmark or production service misses its target, diagnosis narrows the search in four passes. Fast screening heuristics come first, followed by confirming hardware counters and profiler traces, targeted interventions on the binding term, and a stopping scorecard that decides when to stop optimizing.


Under incident pressure there is rarely time to solve the full iron law. Quantitative heuristics narrow the search space quickly. The thresholds below are screening signals to check against profiler traces and hardware counters, not conclusions.

Low accelerator utilization (< 80 percent): Screen for data, CPU, or launch starvation. Confirm with input-pipeline wait, host CPU saturation, memory-bandwidth counters, and trace gaps.
High accelerator utilization (> 95 percent): Treat this as machine bound only if compute units are busy and memory bandwidth is not saturated. If memory bandwidth is saturated, the bottleneck is still on the Data/Machine boundary.
Batch size of one: Treat this as a warning that launch or dispatch overhead may dominate; confirm with traces before labeling the algorithm itself the bottleneck.
Low arithmetic intensity (below ridge point): The workload is likely bandwidth-bound (Data/Machine boundary). The precise boundary is \(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\) and depends on hardware and precision.
Development-production mismatch: Treat data drift as one hypothesis alongside configuration, load, dependency, and runtime differences.

Common industry labels cross the axes. Bandwidth-bound execution sits on the Data/Machine boundary because both bytes moved and available bandwidth matter. Compute-bound execution couples Algorithm work with Machine throughput. Overhead-bound execution may reflect algorithmic serial depth, runtime dispatch, synchronization, or queueing. A screened candidate becomes a diagnosis only when a measurement confirms it.



Once a screening heuristic flags a suspect axis, the next step is to collect the hardware counter or profiler trace that can confirm or falsify it. Table 5 maps common production failure modes to candidate axes and the measurements that validate them.

Once those counters confirm which term binds, an intervention that speeds up any other term leaves end-to-end performance flat: adding peak FLOP/s to bandwidth-bound token decoding or adding memory bandwidth to compute-bound dense training does not move wall-clock time. Table 7 covers the four regimes the book’s lighthouse workloads occupy, plus the overhead-bound regime that any of them enters when the fixed latency term dominates. The compute, bandwidth, and overhead rows are named by terms of the iron law. Capacity-bound and power-bound workloads are limited by preconditions the time equation assumes are already met, that the working set fits in memory and that the energy budget can pay for the run. Either can therefore decide feasibility before any time term is evaluated (Workload archetypes). For each regime, the table contrasts the interventions that yield end-to-end gains against those that waste engineering effort.



Table 7: What Works vs. What Is Wasted: Optimizing a nonbinding term yields little or no end-to-end improvement. A bandwidth-bound language model will not benefit from additional peak FLOP/s alone, though an accelerator with more memory bandwidth may help. Capacity and power limits act before time does, so they are checked first.

The lighthouse column names each regime’s home workload, and a workload can cross regimes. GPT-2’s decode is bandwidth-bound, yet its training is compute-bound (section 1.7.3), and ResNet-50, compute-bound in its kernels, becomes input-bound when the data pipeline cannot keep pace (section 1.7.1). Dispatch overhead in eager execution develops the dispatch overhead behind the overhead-bound row, and Power and thermal management develops the power envelope behind the last. A repaired system still needs a verdict on whether it is good enough, which is what the scorecard supplies.



Raw profiler metrics (utilization percentages, FLOP counts, bandwidth measurements) mean little until compared with the workload’s targets. The efficiency indicators of the D·A·M scorecard in table 8 set those targets and show whether a repaired system can stop or must keep investigating. They are screening signals, not universal grades. Model FLOPs utilization (MFU)2 is especially useful for large-model training.
2 MFU: The ratio of achieved model FLOP/s to the hardware’s theoretical peak FLOP/s, introduced in the PaLM paper (Chowdhery et al. 2022). Unlike raw accelerator utilization (which counts any work the accelerator performs), MFU measures model computation rate relative to peak hardware throughput, so non-model work and system overhead are not counted as achieved model FLOPs. Identifying Bottlenecks develops MFU as a training diagnostic.
Chowdhery, Aakanksha, Sharan Narang, Jacob Devlin, Maarten Bosma, Gaurav Mishra, Adam Roberts, Paul Barham, et al. 2022. “PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2204.02311.

The four steps work only when they are followed in order. In practice, teams under deadline pressure skip the confirming step and optimize the wrong axis with confidence, and these failure modes are common enough to deserve their own names.




Before committing to complex kernel optimizations, watch for these common traps that waste engineering cycles. Each anti-pattern arises when a team applies an expensive engineering lever to an axis that does not bind end-to-end execution:

The hardware crutch: Buying faster accelerators (Machine) to fix a slow Python data loader (Data). The new hardware will idle faster.
The model twiddle: Changing neural architectures (Algorithm) when the bottleneck is actually network bandwidth or disk I/O.
The premature optimizer: Writing custom CUDA kernels (Machine) before verifying if the Algorithm is doing too many unnecessary operations.

Each anti-pattern follows the same root cause: acting before diagnosing. The case studies that follow show proper diagnosis on the reference accelerator, starting from a confusing symptom and narrowing to the binding term, and the first of them puts a number on the hardware crutch.



The three cases below run the four-step workflow on an H100, the book’s reference accelerator. Each uses a lighthouse workload in a regime the chapters develop: ResNet-50 starved by its input pipeline, DLRM paying launch overhead at batch one, and GPT-2 XL training against the compute term. In each scenario, an initial utilization reading could easily point to the wrong axis until a second measurement isolates the true bottleneck.


A team moves ResNet-50 training from an A100 to an H100 and sees no change in epoch time. A well-tuned A100 sustains about 3,200 images/s. At the same fraction of its higher peak the H100 would train about 10,100 images/s, yet nvidia-smi on the new machine shows utilization oscillating far below that. Screening flags low utilization, and the trace confirms the hypothesis, showing the accelerator idle in gaps while every loader process is saturated decoding JPEGs. With 9 workers each decoding and augmenting about 375 images/s, the pipeline delivers 3,375 images/s regardless of the accelerator, a rate that kept the A100 fully busy while leaving the H100 busy only about 33 percent of the time. Because the upgrade was the hardware crutch, the useful intervention lies upstream of the model. Balancing the H100 requires about 28 workers’ worth of decode throughput, supplied by adding loader parallelism where host cores allow and by moving decode onto the accelerator, as the supply-and-demand pipeline model in Data pipeline develops.



A recommendation service on an H100 must rank 200 candidate items per request within a 10 ms p99 budget. It misses badly while accelerator utilization stays low, because the serving code scores each candidate with its own DLRM call at batch one. Screening flags the batch size, and a trace confirms an overhead-bound regime. Each call issues about 40 kernels at about 15 μs of dispatch and launch apiece, costing 0.6 ms before any device work happens. By contrast, reading 51.2 KB of embeddings takes only about 15.3 ns at high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth, and the multilayer perceptron (MLP) needs only about 2.1 ns of arithmetic. Because the \(\Latency\) term exceeds the other two by more than four orders of magnitude, scoring candidates one at a time multiplies that fixed tax to about 120 ms. A faster accelerator or wider memory bus would shrink only the nanosecond terms. Instead, batching all candidates into one call pays the overhead once to bring the request to about 0.6 ms, while capturing the call as a graph shortens what remains. The cliff runs the other way too: with large tables the same model becomes capacity-bound, the embedding reads grow, and the measurements must be repeated. Why batching helps develops why batching amortizes this fixed cost and where the latency budget stops it.



A team trains GPT-2 XL on one H100 in TF32. Accelerator utilization is pinned near its maximum, memory-bandwidth counters are unsaturated, and the profiler reports MFU near 50 percent, the strong-signal end of the scorecard. Because the data path keeps the accelerator fed and the trace shows no dispatch gaps, the compute term binds. GPT-2’s home regime in serving is bandwidth-bound decode, but training at batch reuses every weight across many tokens and crosses the ridge. The run needs about 1.5 ZFLOP of arithmetic, which at this efficiency takes about 70 days, so only levers on the compute term help while adding loader workers or memory bandwidth changes nothing. Lowering precision from TF32 to BF16 where numerically safe raises the H100’s Tensor Core peak by about 2× (Choquette 2023), cutting the run to about 35 days. Data parallelism across the 8 accelerators of one node then brings it to about 4 days before communication losses. Running cases: GPT-2 XL and ResNet-50 develops this workload as the training running example, including the memory limits that decide what batch fits.

Choquette, Jack. 2023. “NVIDIA Hopper H100 GPU: Scaling Performance.” IEEE Micro 43 (3): 9–17. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2023.3256796.
Taken together, the three cases show why the same utilization number can imply different next steps. Low utilization meant a starved pipeline in the first case and dispatch overhead in the second, while high utilization in the third meant the run was already doing useful work and only the compute term could shrink. The same discipline applies when the question is not how fast the system runs but how much better the model can get.




The case studies diagnosed wall-clock bottlenecks, where the target is step time or serving latency. When a training run already executes at high hardware efficiency yet held-out loss flattens despite more GPUs and longer runs, the diagnostic question shifts from throughput ceilings to learning ceilings: whether the stall reflects the normal diminishing returns of scale or a data-quality floor that added compute cannot move.


A team that doubles its training compute budget must decide whether to spend those extra FLOPs on more parameters or on more training tokens. Scaling laws3 guide that split with empirical power laws that predict how held-out loss changes as resources increase within the fitted regime. Two landmark results are Kaplan scaling (Kaplan et al. 2020), which studied loss against parameter count (\(\Parameters\)), data (\(\DatasetSize\)), and total operations (\(\Operations\)), and Chinchilla scaling (Hoffmann et al. 2022). Chinchilla estimated a compute-optimal balance for the dense autoregressive language-model regime studied, often summarized as roughly 20 training tokens per parameter (\(\DatasetSize\approx 20\Parameters\)). Compute-optimal scaling laws derives that balance from a parametric loss surface, so a reader can see where the tokens-per-parameter ratio comes from and which fitted exponents it depends on.
3 Scaling laws: Empirical relationships, typically power laws with a fitted negative exponent, that predict model loss as a function of dataset size, parameter count, or compute budget. Kaplan et al. (2020) studied these relationships for neural language models at OpenAI; Hoffmann et al. (2022) later estimated the compute-optimal training trade-off for its studied dense language-model regime. The compute-optimal frontier develops the compute-optimal frontier and its data-starvation diagnostic in detail.
Kaplan, Jared, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, and Dario Amodei. 2020. “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.” ArXiv Preprint abs/2001.08361.

Hoffmann, Jordan, Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch, Elena Buchatskaya, Trevor Cai, Eliza Rutherford, Diego de Las Casas, et al. 2022. “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 30016–30. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-2176.
As planning tools, these fits estimate how held-out loss changes with compute inside the observed regime. They do not guarantee a task error-rate reduction or extrapolate unchanged across architectures and data distributions.



When held-out loss flattens below the fitted scaling trend while tokens, parameters, and compute keep growing, adding accelerators or parameters buys no further accuracy. The information roofline names this limit that data quality places on what a model can learn, the counterpart to the ceiling the roofline model places on how fast it computes. Because it is a diagnostic label rather than a quantitative law, that flattening pattern tells the team to examine the data before buying more hardware. Four checks separate the causes. Deduplicating the training set and remeasuring tests whether repeated examples inflated the apparent data volume. Auditing a sample of labels estimates label noise. Comparing per-slice validation loss exposes coverage gaps. Comparing the training and validation distributions detects shift. If loss resumes falling after cleaning or reweighting the data at fixed compute, data quality was binding. If it does not, the cause lies in optimization, model capacity, or evaluation noise, and the scaling-law fit itself should be rechecked.
For classification under a fixed data distribution and loss, the Bayes error rate4 is an irreducible error floor, not a ceiling. Noise, label ambiguity, coverage gaps, and distribution shift can create data-quality limits above that floor, but they do not define one universal slope or breakpoint.
4 Bayes error rate: The lowest achievable error rate under 0–1 loss for any classifier on a given data distribution, determined by class priors and the overlap between class-conditional distributions (Goodfellow et al. 2016). No amount of data, parameters, or compute can reduce error below this theoretical floor.
Goodfellow, Ian, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville. 2016. Deep Learning. MIT Press.
Adding accelerators or parameters is futile only after measurements establish that data quality is binding. Whether debugging a training step, evaluating hardware utilization, or planning a scaling campaign, measure which axis is binding before choosing a lever.

Checkpoint 1.1: D·A·M diagnosis check

A training job shows 95 percent accelerator utilization but loss has plateaued for two epochs. Which D·A·M axes could be responsible, and why is utilization alone insufficient to distinguish them?
Your colleague suggests adding more data loader workers to a job where nvidia-smi shows 98 percent GPU utilization. What trace evidence is needed before deciding whether this will help?
An inference server meets its latency SLO at batch size 1 but fails at batch size 16. Which iron-law terms and queueing effects may have changed, and which measurements identify the binding regime?







D·A·M localizes candidate causes across Data, Algorithm, and Machine. The iron law and arithmetic intensity translate those causes into time, operations, and bytes. The four-step workflow screens, confirms, acts on, and scores them across the four lighthouse regimes (compute-bound, bandwidth-bound, capacity-bound, and power-bound) and the overhead-bound regime that a deployment choice such as batch-one serving can create. The anti-patterns and the H100 case studies show what skipping or following that workflow costs. Scaling laws and the information roofline then separate observed improvement trajectories from data-quality limits. Use the framework as a loop rather than as a label.

Key Takeaways: Where to look first

Begin with cross-axis hypotheses; a symptom rarely identifies its cause.
Translate each hypothesis into the relevant iron-law term, or the capacity or power precondition, and a measurement that could falsify it.
Use arithmetic intensity and the scorecard to identify the binding constraint, not to assign universal grades.
Apply the corresponding lever and remeasure end to end; a local gain that leaves the binding term unchanged is not a system improvement.

When a training step stalls or a serving call misses its latency budget, the cause can sit in JPEG decoding on the host, quadratic attention work in the model, or a saturated memory bus on the accelerator. The taxonomy separates those causes along the three axes of the iron law of ML systems (Iron Law of ML Systems). Data is what the model learns from and what the pipeline must deliver, Algorithm is the computation the model performs, and Machine is the hardware that executes that computation. Table 2 summarizes the role, primary physical constraint, and core optimization pathway for each axis.

This first-pass separation is useful, but production systems rarely suffer from a single axis-centered bottleneck. More often, the problem sits at the boundary between two axes, as when a data format choice determines whether the accelerator can be saturated or a pruning strategy changes the memory access pattern. Handling these cases requires mapping the intersections.

Because an intervention on one axis shifts pressure onto the other two, the conceptual Venn overlaps in The D·A·M Intersection Landscape become an operational diagnostic triad of Data, Algorithm, and Machine joined by bidirectional coupling (figure 1). To diagnose a production bottleneck, an engineer first identifies which axis currently binds the workload, then traces its two incident edges to predict how a candidate fix will alter memory, compute, or I/O demand across the system.

In the D·A·M acronym, Data, Algorithm, and Machine name the three diagnostic axes rather than single-letter algebraic variables; formal quantities follow the notation chapter, where \(\DatasetSize\) denotes logical dataset size (samples or tokens) and \(\DataVolume\) denotes physical data volume moved (bytes). The axis-centered zones contain concepts that belong primarily to one axis: storage formats and distributions emphasize Data, loss functions and gradients emphasize Algorithm, and silicon physics and peak FLOP/s emphasize Machine. Single-domain expertise can introduce them, but deployed behavior may still depend on the other axes.
The pairwise intersections are where systems thinking begins. At \(\DataTaxonomyAxis\cap \AlgorithmTaxonomyAxis\) (What to Learn From), data selection, curriculum learning, active learning, and scaling laws (section 1.8.1) couple information content to algorithmic capacity. Information content and algorithmic capacity are coupled because adding data that the model cannot absorb wastes compute, while choosing architectures that outstrip available data wastes engineering time. That boundary governs statistical efficiency. At \(\DataTaxonomyAxis\cap \MachineTaxonomyAxis\) (How to Move Information), the concern is physical delivery through I/O bandwidth, prefetching strategies, data formats, and the energy-movement invariant. Here data gravity manifests, because the cost of moving bytes through the memory hierarchy decides whether the machine stays fed. Once data reaches the device, \(\AlgorithmTaxonomyAxis\cap \MachineTaxonomyAxis\) (How to Execute Efficiently) links mathematical structure to hardware execution across quantization, pruning, kernel fusion, mixed precision, and computational graph optimization. It explains why a pruning scheme that cuts FLOPs while fragmenting memory access can still run slower on silicon.
The center, \(\DataTaxonomyAxis\cap \AlgorithmTaxonomyAxis\cap \MachineTaxonomyAxis\), is where all three axes converge. The iron law, the roofline model, end-to-end training loops, serving pipelines, and holistic benchmarking all require simultaneous reasoning about data flow, algorithmic complexity, and hardware utilization. The intersections classify where a technique operates. Isolating which axis actively throttles a workload requires translating these relationships into wall-clock execution time, which is the role of the iron law.

title: The D·A·M Taxonomy
text:
Placing quantization at the Algorithm/Machine intersection does not by itself tell an engineer how many milliseconds a 4-bit weight format will save, because the wall-clock gain depends on whether byte transfers, arithmetic, or kernel launches dominate the step. For any workload, the iron law turns the D·A·M axes into execution time \(\Time\) (seconds) in two steps. First, at the workload level (equation 1.2), time factors multiplicatively across the three axes: \[ \Time = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Samples}}{\text{Task}}\right)}_{\text{Data}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Sample}}\right)}_{\text{Algorithm}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Seconds}}{\text{FLOP}}\right)}_{\text{Machine}} \] where the product of the Data and Algorithm factors sets the total arithmetic work \(\Operations = (\text{Samples/Task}) \times (\text{FLOPs/Sample})\) in FLOPs. Second, for serialized execution phases (equation 1.3), unpacking how the machine executes those operations maps work across the D·A·M interfaces into three physical time terms. In these terms, \(\DataVolume\) is bytes moved, \(\Bandwidth\) is bytes per second, \(\PeakRate\) is peak throughput in FLOP/s, \(\EfficiencyHw\) is dimensionless hardware efficiency, and \(\Latency\) is fixed overhead in seconds: \[ \Time= \underbrace{ \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} }_{\text{Data/Machine}} + \underbrace{ \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} }_{\text{Algorithm/Machine}} + \underbrace{ \Latency }_{\text{Cross-axis overhead}} \]
Dividing this serialized decomposition by \(\Operations\) (and substituting arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity = \Operations/\DataVolume\)) expresses the realized Machine factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) directly in terms of the three physical bottlenecks: \[ \frac{\text{Seconds}}{\text{FLOP}} = \frac{\Time}{\Operations} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\ArithmeticIntensity \cdot \Bandwidth}}_{\text{Memory time per FLOP}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}}_{\text{Compute time per FLOP}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Latency}{\Operations}}_{\text{Overhead per FLOP}} \]
Algorithm and Machine share the compute term, separated by which variable the engineer controls. Reducing the total operations (\(\Operations\)) is a Data or Algorithm lever, while reducing the realized time per operation (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) by raising peak throughput (\(\PeakRate\)), utilization (\(\EfficiencyHw\)), or bandwidth (\(\Bandwidth\)) is a Machine lever. This per-FLOP expression also shows why training and inference occupy different regimes under the same law. In large-batch training, high arithmetic intensity (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\)) and large operation counts (\(\Operations\)) shrink the first and third terms so \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\) approaches the compute term (Training-Time Law). In small-batch or single-token inference, low \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) and small \(\Operations\) per request inflate the memory and overhead terms (Model Serving).
The dominant measured cost appears in one of these terms. A slow system may move too much data (\(\DataVolume\)), lack bandwidth (\(\Bandwidth\)), execute too many operations (\(\Operations\)), fail to use the hardware’s peak capability (\(\EfficiencyHw\)), or pay cross-axis overhead (\(\Latency\)). A workload whose time is dominated by \(\Latency\) is overhead-bound: kernel launches, dispatch, and synchronization, not bytes or arithmetic, set its pace.


Once profiling isolates the largest time term, each axis offers a distinct set of engineering levers that shrink its numerator or raise its denominator:

Data lever: Reducing the samples processed per task (\(\text{Samples/Task}\), which shrinks \(\Operations\)) or the moved bytes (\(\DataVolume\)) through deduplication and selection, or increasing I/O bandwidth (\(\Bandwidth\)).
Algorithm lever: Reducing operations per sample (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\), and thus \(\Operations\)) through pruning, distillation, or architectural refinement, or reducing the bytes each weight and activation occupies through lower-precision representation. Quantization is an Algorithm choice that shrinks the Data/Machine term \(\DataVolume\) and may raise hardware throughput \(\PeakRate\), lowering \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\) without reducing operation count.
Machine lever: Lowering \(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\) by increasing peak throughput (\(\PeakRate\)), memory bandwidth (\(\Bandwidth\)), or the utilization factor (\(\EfficiencyHw\)) via kernel fusion and scheduling.

Shrinking individual terms is the first lever; hiding one term behind another is the second.



When a training step waits for each batch to finish copying across PCIe before launching the forward pass, data-transfer time and compute time add directly; prefetching the next batch while the accelerator computes the current one hides the shorter stage behind the longer one. The additive iron law represents this unpipelined, sequential execution. Let \(\SequentialExecutionTime\) denote time without overlap and \(\PipelinedExecutionTime\) denote measured time with overlap. Overlap can move the sum toward a max, but dependencies, contention, and incomplete overlap keep the measured time above this ideal lower bound: \[ \SequentialExecutionTime= \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency \quad \xrightarrow{\text{overlap}} \quad \PipelinedExecutionTime\geq \max\left(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}, \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}\right) + \Latency \]
Compute should overlap with data movement wherever dependencies allow. Table 4 summarizes key D·A·M coordination techniques that overlap work across axes.

Overlaps provide the greatest relative speedup when the D·A·M time terms are reasonably balanced. If one term dominates (for example, a severely bandwidth-bound kernel), overlapping the smaller term with the larger yields negligible gain, because the max is still set by the same bottleneck. This balance occurs near \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth \approx \Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\). The overhead term is treated separately below.

Systems Perspective 1.1: The overhead that cannot hideThe unhidden latency term \(\Latency\) (kernel launch, synchronization barriers, Python dispatch) contains serialization points that cannot be fully overlapped. Kernel fusion can reduce this term by combining operations, but it does not eliminate all launch, scheduling, or synchronization overhead.


The iron law separates data-movement time from compute time, but it does not by itself say which of the two sets the hardware ceiling for a given kernel.

title: The D·A·M Taxonomy
text:
Doubling an accelerator’s peak FLOP/s leaves a kernel no faster if the arithmetic units spend most of each cycle waiting for bytes from memory. Which side of that ceiling a kernel sits on is decided by its arithmetic intensity1 (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\)), the operations performed per byte moved between memory and compute. A kernel whose intensity falls below the hardware’s ridge point \(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\) is bandwidth-bound, the regime the roofline literature calls memory-bound. This book keeps the bandwidth name so the regime is not confused with running out of memory capacity. A kernel above the ridge point is compute-bound.
1 Arithmetic intensity: This book uses the term for floating-point operations per byte transferred. Williams et al. (2009) calls the measured DRAM quantity operational intensity in the Roofline Model. Comparing the workload ratio with the hardware ridge point (\(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\)) gives an upper-bound diagnosis of bandwidth- versus compute-bound execution.
Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
The reference accelerator places the boundary concretely. An H100’s dense FP16 ridge point is about 295 FLOP/byte. GPT-2 XL decoding one token at batch one reads all 3 GB of its FP16 weights and reaches an arithmetic intensity of only about 1 FLOP/byte, more than two orders of magnitude below the ridge. With kernel launches captured into a replayable graph (Graph capture and JIT compilation), the weight read takes about 0.9 ms while the arithmetic needs about 3 μs, so a faster arithmetic unit would leave the per-token time unchanged. Performance Bounds develops the ridge point, hardware balance, and the regimes on either side of it. The Roofline model carries the worked roofline template. The decode floor turns the weight read into the decode floor a serving system plans around.
The roofline gives an upper performance bound when traffic and achieved rates are measured consistently. During a production incident, screening heuristics point to the measurements to collect first, which is where diagnosis begins.

title: The D·A·M Taxonomy
text:
When a benchmark or production service misses its target, diagnosis narrows the search in four passes. Fast screening heuristics come first, followed by confirming hardware counters and profiler traces, targeted interventions on the binding term, and a stopping scorecard that decides when to stop optimizing.


Under incident pressure there is rarely time to solve the full iron law. Quantitative heuristics narrow the search space quickly. The thresholds below are screening signals to check against profiler traces and hardware counters, not conclusions.

Low accelerator utilization (< 80 percent): Screen for data, CPU, or launch starvation. Confirm with input-pipeline wait, host CPU saturation, memory-bandwidth counters, and trace gaps.
High accelerator utilization (> 95 percent): Treat this as machine bound only if compute units are busy and memory bandwidth is not saturated. If memory bandwidth is saturated, the bottleneck is still on the Data/Machine boundary.
Batch size of one: Treat this as a warning that launch or dispatch overhead may dominate; confirm with traces before labeling the algorithm itself the bottleneck.
Low arithmetic intensity (below ridge point): The workload is likely bandwidth-bound (Data/Machine boundary). The precise boundary is \(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\) and depends on hardware and precision.
Development-production mismatch: Treat data drift as one hypothesis alongside configuration, load, dependency, and runtime differences.

Common industry labels cross the axes. Bandwidth-bound execution sits on the Data/Machine boundary because both bytes moved and available bandwidth matter. Compute-bound execution couples Algorithm work with Machine throughput. Overhead-bound execution may reflect algorithmic serial depth, runtime dispatch, synchronization, or queueing. A screened candidate becomes a diagnosis only when a measurement confirms it.

The lighthouse column names each regime’s home workload, and a workload can cross regimes. GPT-2’s decode is bandwidth-bound, yet its training is compute-bound (section 1.7.3), and ResNet-50, compute-bound in its kernels, becomes input-bound when the data pipeline cannot keep pace (section 1.7.1). Dispatch overhead in eager execution develops the dispatch overhead behind the overhead-bound row, and Power and thermal management develops the power envelope behind the last. A repaired system still needs a verdict on whether it is good enough, which is what the scorecard supplies.



Raw profiler metrics (utilization percentages, FLOP counts, bandwidth measurements) mean little until compared with the workload’s targets. The efficiency indicators of the D·A·M scorecard in table 8 set those targets and show whether a repaired system can stop or must keep investigating. They are screening signals, not universal grades. Model FLOPs utilization (MFU)2 is especially useful for large-model training.
2 MFU: The ratio of achieved model FLOP/s to the hardware’s theoretical peak FLOP/s, introduced in the PaLM paper (Chowdhery et al. 2022). Unlike raw accelerator utilization (which counts any work the accelerator performs), MFU measures model computation rate relative to peak hardware throughput, so non-model work and system overhead are not counted as achieved model FLOPs. Identifying Bottlenecks develops MFU as a training diagnostic.
Chowdhery, Aakanksha, Sharan Narang, Jacob Devlin, Maarten Bosma, Gaurav Mishra, Adam Roberts, Paul Barham, et al. 2022. “PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2204.02311.

The four steps work only when they are followed in order. In practice, teams under deadline pressure skip the confirming step and optimize the wrong axis with confidence, and these failure modes are common enough to deserve their own names.

title: The D·A·M Taxonomy
text:
Before committing to complex kernel optimizations, watch for these common traps that waste engineering cycles. Each anti-pattern arises when a team applies an expensive engineering lever to an axis that does not bind end-to-end execution:

The hardware crutch: Buying faster accelerators (Machine) to fix a slow Python data loader (Data). The new hardware will idle faster.
The model twiddle: Changing neural architectures (Algorithm) when the bottleneck is actually network bandwidth or disk I/O.
The premature optimizer: Writing custom CUDA kernels (Machine) before verifying if the Algorithm is doing too many unnecessary operations.

Each anti-pattern follows the same root cause: acting before diagnosing. The case studies that follow show proper diagnosis on the reference accelerator, starting from a confusing symptom and narrowing to the binding term, and the first of them puts a number on the hardware crutch.

title: The D·A·M Taxonomy
text:
The three cases below run the four-step workflow on an H100, the book’s reference accelerator. Each uses a lighthouse workload in a regime the chapters develop: ResNet-50 starved by its input pipeline, DLRM paying launch overhead at batch one, and GPT-2 XL training against the compute term. In each scenario, an initial utilization reading could easily point to the wrong axis until a second measurement isolates the true bottleneck.


A team moves ResNet-50 training from an A100 to an H100 and sees no change in epoch time. A well-tuned A100 sustains about 3,200 images/s. At the same fraction of its higher peak the H100 would train about 10,100 images/s, yet nvidia-smi on the new machine shows utilization oscillating far below that. Screening flags low utilization, and the trace confirms the hypothesis, showing the accelerator idle in gaps while every loader process is saturated decoding JPEGs. With 9 workers each decoding and augmenting about 375 images/s, the pipeline delivers 3,375 images/s regardless of the accelerator, a rate that kept the A100 fully busy while leaving the H100 busy only about 33 percent of the time. Because the upgrade was the hardware crutch, the useful intervention lies upstream of the model. Balancing the H100 requires about 28 workers’ worth of decode throughput, supplied by adding loader parallelism where host cores allow and by moving decode onto the accelerator, as the supply-and-demand pipeline model in Data pipeline develops.



A recommendation service on an H100 must rank 200 candidate items per request within a 10 ms p99 budget. It misses badly while accelerator utilization stays low, because the serving code scores each candidate with its own DLRM call at batch one. Screening flags the batch size, and a trace confirms an overhead-bound regime. Each call issues about 40 kernels at about 15 μs of dispatch and launch apiece, costing 0.6 ms before any device work happens. By contrast, reading 51.2 KB of embeddings takes only about 15.3 ns at high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth, and the multilayer perceptron (MLP) needs only about 2.1 ns of arithmetic. Because the \(\Latency\) term exceeds the other two by more than four orders of magnitude, scoring candidates one at a time multiplies that fixed tax to about 120 ms. A faster accelerator or wider memory bus would shrink only the nanosecond terms. Instead, batching all candidates into one call pays the overhead once to bring the request to about 0.6 ms, while capturing the call as a graph shortens what remains. The cliff runs the other way too: with large tables the same model becomes capacity-bound, the embedding reads grow, and the measurements must be repeated. Why batching helps develops why batching amortizes this fixed cost and where the latency budget stops it.



A team trains GPT-2 XL on one H100 in TF32. Accelerator utilization is pinned near its maximum, memory-bandwidth counters are unsaturated, and the profiler reports MFU near 50 percent, the strong-signal end of the scorecard. Because the data path keeps the accelerator fed and the trace shows no dispatch gaps, the compute term binds. GPT-2’s home regime in serving is bandwidth-bound decode, but training at batch reuses every weight across many tokens and crosses the ridge. The run needs about 1.5 ZFLOP of arithmetic, which at this efficiency takes about 70 days, so only levers on the compute term help while adding loader workers or memory bandwidth changes nothing. Lowering precision from TF32 to BF16 where numerically safe raises the H100’s Tensor Core peak by about 2× (Choquette 2023), cutting the run to about 35 days. Data parallelism across the 8 accelerators of one node then brings it to about 4 days before communication losses. Running cases: GPT-2 XL and ResNet-50 develops this workload as the training running example, including the memory limits that decide what batch fits.

Choquette, Jack. 2023. “NVIDIA Hopper H100 GPU: Scaling Performance.” IEEE Micro 43 (3): 9–17. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2023.3256796.
Taken together, the three cases show why the same utilization number can imply different next steps. Low utilization meant a starved pipeline in the first case and dispatch overhead in the second, while high utilization in the third meant the run was already doing useful work and only the compute term could shrink. The same discipline applies when the question is not how fast the system runs but how much better the model can get.

title: The D·A·M Taxonomy
text:
The case studies diagnosed wall-clock bottlenecks, where the target is step time or serving latency. When a training run already executes at high hardware efficiency yet held-out loss flattens despite more GPUs and longer runs, the diagnostic question shifts from throughput ceilings to learning ceilings: whether the stall reflects the normal diminishing returns of scale or a data-quality floor that added compute cannot move.


A team that doubles its training compute budget must decide whether to spend those extra FLOPs on more parameters or on more training tokens. Scaling laws3 guide that split with empirical power laws that predict how held-out loss changes as resources increase within the fitted regime. Two landmark results are Kaplan scaling (Kaplan et al. 2020), which studied loss against parameter count (\(\Parameters\)), data (\(\DatasetSize\)), and total operations (\(\Operations\)), and Chinchilla scaling (Hoffmann et al. 2022). Chinchilla estimated a compute-optimal balance for the dense autoregressive language-model regime studied, often summarized as roughly 20 training tokens per parameter (\(\DatasetSize\approx 20\Parameters\)). Compute-optimal scaling laws derives that balance from a parametric loss surface, so a reader can see where the tokens-per-parameter ratio comes from and which fitted exponents it depends on.
3 Scaling laws: Empirical relationships, typically power laws with a fitted negative exponent, that predict model loss as a function of dataset size, parameter count, or compute budget. Kaplan et al. (2020) studied these relationships for neural language models at OpenAI; Hoffmann et al. (2022) later estimated the compute-optimal training trade-off for its studied dense language-model regime. The compute-optimal frontier develops the compute-optimal frontier and its data-starvation diagnostic in detail.
Kaplan, Jared, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, and Dario Amodei. 2020. “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.” ArXiv Preprint abs/2001.08361.

Hoffmann, Jordan, Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch, Elena Buchatskaya, Trevor Cai, Eliza Rutherford, Diego de Las Casas, et al. 2022. “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 30016–30. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-2176.
As planning tools, these fits estimate how held-out loss changes with compute inside the observed regime. They do not guarantee a task error-rate reduction or extrapolate unchanged across architectures and data distributions.



When held-out loss flattens below the fitted scaling trend while tokens, parameters, and compute keep growing, adding accelerators or parameters buys no further accuracy. The information roofline names this limit that data quality places on what a model can learn, the counterpart to the ceiling the roofline model places on how fast it computes. Because it is a diagnostic label rather than a quantitative law, that flattening pattern tells the team to examine the data before buying more hardware. Four checks separate the causes. Deduplicating the training set and remeasuring tests whether repeated examples inflated the apparent data volume. Auditing a sample of labels estimates label noise. Comparing per-slice validation loss exposes coverage gaps. Comparing the training and validation distributions detects shift. If loss resumes falling after cleaning or reweighting the data at fixed compute, data quality was binding. If it does not, the cause lies in optimization, model capacity, or evaluation noise, and the scaling-law fit itself should be rechecked.
For classification under a fixed data distribution and loss, the Bayes error rate4 is an irreducible error floor, not a ceiling. Noise, label ambiguity, coverage gaps, and distribution shift can create data-quality limits above that floor, but they do not define one universal slope or breakpoint.
4 Bayes error rate: The lowest achievable error rate under 0–1 loss for any classifier on a given data distribution, determined by class priors and the overlap between class-conditional distributions (Goodfellow et al. 2016). No amount of data, parameters, or compute can reduce error below this theoretical floor.
Goodfellow, Ian, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville. 2016. Deep Learning. MIT Press.
Adding accelerators or parameters is futile only after measurements establish that data quality is binding. Whether debugging a training step, evaluating hardware utilization, or planning a scaling campaign, measure which axis is binding before choosing a lever.

Checkpoint 1.1: D·A·M diagnosis check

A training job shows 95 percent accelerator utilization but loss has plateaued for two epochs. Which D·A·M axes could be responsible, and why is utilization alone insufficient to distinguish them?
Your colleague suggests adding more data loader workers to a job where nvidia-smi shows 98 percent GPU utilization. What trace evidence is needed before deciding whether this will help?
An inference server meets its latency SLO at batch size 1 but fails at batch size 16. Which iron-law terms and queueing effects may have changed, and which measurements identify the binding regime?

title: The D·A·M Taxonomy
text:
D·A·M localizes candidate causes across Data, Algorithm, and Machine. The iron law and arithmetic intensity translate those causes into time, operations, and bytes. The four-step workflow screens, confirms, acts on, and scores them across the four lighthouse regimes (compute-bound, bandwidth-bound, capacity-bound, and power-bound) and the overhead-bound regime that a deployment choice such as batch-one serving can create. The anti-patterns and the H100 case studies show what skipping or following that workflow costs. Scaling laws and the information roofline then separate observed improvement trajectories from data-quality limits. Use the framework as a loop rather than as a label.

Key Takeaways: Where to look first

Begin with cross-axis hypotheses; a symptom rarely identifies its cause.
Translate each hypothesis into the relevant iron-law term, or the capacity or power precondition, and a measurement that could falsify it.
Use arithmetic intensity and the scorecard to identify the binding constraint, not to assign universal grades.
Apply the corresponding lever and remeasure end to end; a local gain that leaves the binding term unchanged is not a system improvement.

title: Algorithm Foundations
text:
A profile showing low utilization is often misdiagnosed as a hardware limit when the cause is algorithmic: a matrix multiply shape that underfills matrix arithmetic units, a layout that breaks contiguity, or activation memory held for backpropagation. This appendix collects the computational complexity models, memory footprint derivations, numerical-stability rules, and proofs that the book’s performance chapters lean on. With them, readers can evaluate algorithmic trade-offs before committing code to accelerators. It assumes familiarity with linear algebra and with the iron law introduced early in the book.


This appendix is designed as a reference. Reach for it when translating a profiler symptom (“slow matmul,” “shape mismatch,” “OOM during training”) into a concrete computational or memory cause. Each symptom or need maps to one section (table 1), and conventions throughout follow the book-wide notation (for example, \(\BatchSize\) is reserved for batch size and \(\Bandwidth\) denotes bandwidth). Every section names the chapter that teaches its concept in context; the chapter carries the argument, and this appendix carries the derivation or the reference formula.



Table 1: Where to Look: Each row pairs a profiler symptom or a design question with the section that carries its derivation or reference formula.

section 1.2.1

section 1.2.2

section 1.3.2

section 1.3.3

Neural networks turn linear algebra into learned behavior. Matrices transform activations, tensor layouts determine how data move through memory, and backpropagation carries error signals through the resulting computation. These foundations support the deep learning treatment in Neural Computation, the framework internals in ML Frameworks, and the training strategies in Model Training.



Frameworks such as PyTorch hide raw linear algebra behind single function calls, yet changing a layer’s width or a serving request’s batch size can shift the underlying matrix operations from compute-bound execution to a bandwidth-bound stall without altering a line of model logic. While Numerical Representations establishes how individual numbers are represented in bits, the primitives below govern how those numbers are combined into contractions, inner products, and dense or sparse matrix multiplies.

Systems Perspective 1.1: Why this mattersMany dense neural networks, especially transformers and large convolutional neural networks, spend most of their compute in matrix multiplication or GEMM-like kernels. A self-attention block executes query, key, value, and output projection GEMMs alongside two attention-matrix products for scores and weighted values, and the layer’s feed-forward block adds two or three more. Because those kernels dominate execution, GEMM performance characteristics explain why batch size governs throughput, why aligned layer dimensions run faster than unaligned ones, and whether a dense workload will be compute bound or bandwidth bound before any profiler trace runs.




Tensor operations in deep learning contract across batch, head, sequence, and hidden dimensions at once. Einstein summation1 notation writes those contractions as a single index string rather than a chain of nested loops and transposes (implemented as torch.einsum in PyTorch and np.einsum in NumPy). Matrix multiplication \(\GemmOutputMatrix= \GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand\) becomes: \[ \GemmOutputEntry = \sum_k \GemmLeftOperandEntry \GemmRightOperandEntry \]
1 Einstein summation convention: Repeated indices in a product are implicitly summed over, eliminating explicit summation signs. ML frameworks adopted the convention because it concisely expresses arbitrary tensor contractions in a single string.In einsum notation, this is ik,kj->ij. The same notation handles batched multi-head attention, bhid,bhjd->bhij (batch \(\BatchAxisLabel\), head \(\HeadAxisLabel\), query sequence \(\QueryAxisLabel\), key sequence \(\KeyAxisLabel\), and head dimension \(\HeadDimensionAxisLabel\)). The head dimension \(\HeadDimensionAxisLabel\) appears in both inputs but not in the output, so it is the index that is summed.



Summing over that shared head dimension \(\HeadDimensionAxisLabel\) for a single query vector and a single key vector is a dot product, the primitive that scores how closely two token embeddings or feature vectors align. The sum \(\InnerProductLeftVector\cdot \InnerProductRightVector= \sum \InnerProductLeftComponent_i \InnerProductRightComponent_i\) grows when the vectors point in the same direction and vanishes when they are orthogonal because it equals \(\|\InnerProductLeftVector\| \|\InnerProductRightVector\| \cos \VectorAngle\). For nonzero vectors, its sign distinguishes acute, right, and obtuse angles, while its magnitude scales with both vector norms.
In attention mechanisms, query (\(\AttentionQueryMatrix\)) and key (\(\AttentionKeyMatrix\)) vectors are dot-produced to compute a similarity score that determines how much each token attends to every other token. The resulting attention weights are then used to form a weighted combination of value (\(\AttentionValuesMatrix\)) vectors, so every token can draw on every other token. Attention: Dynamic Processing develops attention itself, including the cost of computing one score for every query-key pair.



Evaluating those dot products across every query-key pair at once, or projecting a batch of activations through a dense layer, packs individual inner products into a general matrix multiply (GEMM).2 Whether that GEMM saturates an accelerator’s Tensor Cores or stalls on memory bandwidth depends on its three dimensions: for matrices of size \(\GemmRowDimension{\times}\GemmInnerDimension\) and \(\GemmInnerDimension{\times}\GemmColumnDimension\), a GEMM performs \(2\GemmRowDimension \GemmColumnDimension \GemmInnerDimension\) floating-point operations (counting multiply-accumulate as two operations).
2 General matrix multiply (GEMM): The BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) family began with vector routines standardized in 1979 (Lawson et al. 1979); GEMM was standardized later as a Level 3 routine (Dongarra et al. 1988). The “GE” prefix stands for “general,” as opposed to symmetric or triangular forms. GEMM computes \(\GemmOutputMatrix= \GemmProductScale\GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand+ \GemmAccumulatorScale\GemmOutputMatrix\) and is a performance-critical routine in deep learning. Matrix operations explains how GEMM shapes determine training throughput.
Lawson, Charles L., Richard J. Hanson, David R. Kincaid, and Fred T. Krogh. 1979. “Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms for Fortran Usage.” ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software 5 (3): 308–23. https://doi.org/10.1145/355841.355847.

Dongarra, Jack J., Jeremy Du Croz, Sven Hammarling, and Richard J. Hanson. 1988. “An Extended Set of FORTRAN Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms.” ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software 14 (1): 1–17. https://doi.org/10.1145/42288.42291.
The arithmetic intensity of GEMM scales linearly with matrix dimension. For square \(\SquareGemmDimension{\times}\SquareGemmDimension\) matrices in FP16 (2 bytes/element), the ideal \(\GemmAccumulatorScale=0\) bound reads \(\GemmLeftOperand\) and \(\GemmRightOperand\) once and writes \(\GemmOutputMatrix\) once: \[\text{Intensity} = \frac{\Operations}{\DataVolume} = \frac{2\SquareGemmDimension^3}{3\SquareGemmDimension^2 \times 2} = \frac{\SquareGemmDimension}{3}\text{ FLOP/byte}\]
Reading the old \(\GemmOutputMatrix\) when \(\GemmAccumulatorScale\ne 0\) changes the intensity to \(\SquareGemmDimension/4\) FLOP/byte. Three consequences follow for GEMM execution:

Larger batches can improve efficiency: Batching increases effective matrix dimensions when it forms larger GEMMs or enables reuse; merely queuing independent small GEMMs does not raise intensity.
Aligned dimensions help: Hardware Tensor Cores are optimized for precision- and architecture-specific tile multiples. Dimensions that align with these multiples avoid padding overhead and improve kernel efficiency, but they do not need to be powers of two.
Small matrices are inefficient: A square GEMM with \(\SquareGemmDimension =\) 64 has intensity 64/3 ≈ 21.3 FLOP/byte, well below the ridge point of the book’s reference accelerator, the H100 (295.2 FLOP/byte). Its roofline cap is ~7.2 percent of peak; launch and tiling overhead can lower realized throughput. Performance Bounds derives the ridge point and the compute-bound and bandwidth-bound regimes on either side of it, which is the comparison each of these consequences relies on.




Dense GEMM assumes every weight or feature entry carries signal, yet recommendation tables and heavily pruned weight matrices can be 90 to 99 percent zeros, where a dense tensor wastes gigabytes of memory and bandwidth storing and reading values that contribute nothing to the output. Specialized sparse storage formats avoid storing those zeros and let kernels skip them. The compressed sparse row (CSR) format represents a sparse matrix with three arrays:

Values: The nonzero elements, stored in row order
Col_Idx: The column index of each nonzero element
Row_Ptr: The starting position in Values for each row (length = num_rows + 1)

CSR is useful for sparse feature matrices in recommendation pipelines and for pruned model weights. For a matrix with \(\SparseMatrixEntryCount\) elements, \(\SparseMatrixRowCount\) rows, and \(\NonzeroCount\) nonzeros, CSR uses \(\mathcal{O}(\NonzeroCount+ \SparseMatrixRowCount)\) storage instead of \(\mathcal{O}(\SparseMatrixEntryCount)\); when \(\NonzeroCount\) is large relative to \(\SparseMatrixRowCount\), this is often summarized as \(\mathcal{O}(\NonzeroCount)\).
To see the trade-off concretely, consider a vocabulary embedding matrix with 100,000 rows and 10,000 columns (1B parameters):

Dense (FP32): 1B parameters \(\times\) 4 bytes each = 4 GB.
Sparse (1 percent density): CSR stores roughly 10M entries \(\times\) (4-byte value + 4-byte column index), plus one row pointer per row and a final pointer, totaling ≈ 80.4 MB.
Result: A 50× reduction in memory footprint, fitting a model that would otherwise trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) error.

The saving holds only at low density. Each stored nonzero carries its index, so at high density CSR occupies more memory than the dense tensor it replaces. Storage and execution break-even finds that break-even density for pruned weights, and N:M structured sparsity mechanics shows the fixed pattern of two nonzeros in every four that an accelerator datapath decodes without a general index.



Each common layer type reduces to the GEMMs and elementwise operations above, so its parameter count and forward-pass FLOPs follow from its shapes (table 2). Given layer dimensions and input shapes, the formulas give first-order estimates of model size and compute before hardware is provisioned. The attention row is the one to watch. Sequence length contributes an \(\SequenceLength^2\) term, while hidden dimension contributes \(\HiddenDimension^2\) projection work, so long-context models can shift the dominant cost without changing the parameter count.



Table 2: Deep Learning Tensor Primitives: Summary of shapes, parameters, and FLOP counts. Note: \(\BatchSize\) is batch size, \(\SequenceLength\) is sequence length, and \(\KernelSize\) is kernel size. The attention FLOPs include QKV projections and score interactions. The \(\SequenceLength^2\) term applies to full-sequence training and prefill, while KV-cached generation is linear per token in cached context; \(\HiddenDimension^2\) projection work dominates at large hidden dimensions.
