title: System Assumptions
text:
Sizing a training cluster or a serving fleet requires a single set of per-chip ceilings so that estimates across chapters compare the workload rather than shifting hardware baselines. These accelerator assumptions supply the peak throughput, memory bandwidth, memory capacity, and thermal design power (TDP) for each generation the chapters cite. Values are vendor datasheet peaks, which serve as ceilings for napkin math rather than as sustained utilization. They are drawn from NVIDIA product documentation and IEEE Micro architecture articles (NVIDIA Corporation 2017, 2020b, 2020a, 2021, 2018, 2024; Choquette et al. 2021; Choquette 2023), AMD MI300X documentation (AMD 2023), Google Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) publications (Jouppi et al. 2020; Jouppi et al. 2023), and Google Cloud’s current TPU v6e specification page (Google Cloud 2026). Capacity rows keep the vendor’s labeled capacity. The master matrix compares the generations on one page, and the sections after it give the per-chip values and three dated comparisons on precision support, advertised peaks, and price per unit of peak throughput. Performance Bounds develops the roofline analysis that turns these values into a regime for a given workload.

Jouppi, Norman P., Doe Hyun Yoon, George Kurian, Sheng Li, Nishant Patil, James Laudon, Cliff Young, and David Patterson. 2020. “A Domain-Specific Supercomputer for Training Deep Neural Networks.” Communications of the ACM 63 (7): 67–78. https://doi.org/10.1145/3360307.


Side by side, the accelerators the book cites span more than an order of magnitude in peak rate, memory capacity, and power, yet most place their FP16 ridge point within a band of a few hundred FLOP per byte (table 3). The ridge point divides peak FP16 throughput by memory bandwidth (The Roofline model develops the model). A workload whose arithmetic intensity falls below a chip’s ridge is bandwidth bound on that chip and gains nothing from a faster datapath. Two chips sit far outside that band, at opposite ends. The first TPU paired an INT8-only datapath with DDR3 memory, which places its ridge point far above the band, and the wafer-scale engine keeps its weights in on-wafer SRAM, which places its ridge point far below it.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Hardware ceilings only become bottlenecks when paired with a workload’s parameter count, operation budget, and working-set footprint: the same H100 that is compute-bound on a 256-image ResNet-50 training step becomes bandwidth-bound on single-sequence language-model decode and capacity-bound on a 100 GB recommendation table. Pairing the book’s recurring models with the hardware baselines of section 1.2 fixes both the operational regime of each lighthouse workload and the parameter counts, inference FLOPs, and training-scale anchors that the chapters plug into their estimates.


Five lighthouse workloads recur through the book, each introduced in the regime it typifies (Lighthouse models put the iron law into practice; Workload archetypes). A regime belongs to a workload on a machine rather than to a model name. Each row of table 14 is therefore keyed by model, phase, and batch, with the second GPT-2 XL row recording a crossing out of the model’s home regime. Across those rows, four regimes appear. Compute-bound and bandwidth-bound workloads are separated by the roofline’s ridge point. Capacity-bound and power-bound workloads are constrained before either time term applies, because the working set must fit in memory and the energy budget must cover the run. For the compute- and bandwidth-bound rows, the last column compares the time a step spends on arithmetic at peak FP16 throughput with the time it spends reading the weights once at peak HBM bandwidth on one H100. Whichever time is larger names the regime. A fifth regime, overhead-bound, arises when the iron law’s fixed latency term dominates, and it belongs to a deployment choice such as batch-one serving rather than to a lighthouse (Case 2: The latency cliff (cross-axis)).

title: System Assumptions
text:
Multiplying a model’s parameter count by 2 bytes sizes its BF16 weights for inference, but a full training run must also hold gradients, an FP32 master copy of the weights, and optimizer state in accelerator memory before a single activation is allocated. Training-memory napkin math across the book therefore uses the mixed-precision Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) storage model: BF16 weights, BF16 gradients, and FP32 master weights plus Adam first- and second-moment buffers (16 bytes per parameter in total). This is a book convention, not a measured hardware constant. The BF16 data path uses standard BF16 mixed-precision training (Kalamkar et al. 2019), the FP32 master copy of the weights follows earlier FP16 work (Micikevicius et al. 2018; NVIDIA 2017), and Adam’s first- and second-moment buffers follow (Kingma and Ba 2015). Multiplying the bytes per parameter by the parameter count gives the nonactivation training-state footprint, and table 16 lists the per-component byte widths. Training memory derives each component and the activation memory that adds to it, and Optimizers and their memory applies the convention to the book’s training runs.

title: System Assumptions

Peak throughput and byte widths bound how fast a chip can run and how much state it holds, whereas energy assumptions determine whether that execution is thermally and economically viable at the level of individual operations and memory accesses. Horowitz’s 45 nm arithmetic and 32-bit DRAM estimates (Horowitz 2014), together with illustrative book anchors for register and SRAM access, MobileNetV2 inference, and 5G transfer, underpin the book’s efficiency comparisons but are not process-independent. Access energy rises from registers through DRAM, and the arithmetic energy of an add and a multiply falls with operand width (table 17). The access hierarchy quantifies why data reuse dominates kernel design, and The memory hierarchy explains the physics behind it as ratios that hold across process nodes.

The arithmetic rows carry two orderings that hold at every process node. A multiply costs several times an add at the same precision, because multiplier area grows roughly with the square of the operand bit width \(\NumericBitWidth\) while an adder grows linearly in it, and both fall as the operand narrows (Horowitz 2014; Dally et al. 2021). Newer nodes lower every absolute value in the table, so the 45 nm figures are upper anchors for current silicon, and the orderings, not the absolute values, are what precision and reuse arguments depend on.

title: System Assumptions
text:
A table of peak rates, byte widths, and utility prices does not by itself tell an engineer whether a kernel is bandwidth bound, whether a fine-tuning job fits on one GPU, or what a training run’s electricity bill covers. Three worked templates combine the reference tables of this appendix to answer those performance, capacity, and cost questions in sequence, and each names the section that develops its method so a reader can rerun the calculation with substituted values.
On a single accelerator, the first question is whether arithmetic throughput or memory bandwidth limits execution. Applying the roofline method of The Roofline model to the H100 constants in table 4 separates compute-bound matrix multiplies from bandwidth-bound token generation.

Napkin Math 1.1: Classify a roofline regimeProblem: For the stated H100 and workload intensities, which operations are compute bound and which are bandwidth bound?
Variables: For an H100 at FP16/BF16 peak, use 989 TFLOP/s peak compute and 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth.
Math: Divide peak FLOP/s by memory bandwidth to get the roofline ridge point: 989 TFLOP/s/3.35 TB/s \(\approx\) 295.2 FLOP/byte. A large general matrix multiply (GEMM) with \(\SquareGemmDimension=\) 4096 has intensity \(\SquareGemmDimension/3 \approx\) 1,365.3 FLOP/byte.
Result: Operations above 295.2 FLOP/byte are compute bound; operations below it are bandwidth bound. The GEMM example is compute bound, while a single-token autoregressive decode at FP16, with intensity of about 1 FLOP/byte, is deeply bandwidth bound.
Systems insight: The same accelerator can be compute rich and memory constrained. Arithmetic intensity determines which resource the workload actually consumes.


Before a workload can reach either roofline ceiling, its working state must fit in device memory. Combining the Llama 3 8B parameter count (table 15) with the mixed-precision Adam layout (table 16) tests whether full fine-tuning fits on a single H100; Training memory derives the state components, and Fine-tuning memory on one accelerator shows how parameter-efficient fine-tuning brings the same model onto one accelerator.

Napkin Math 1.2: Estimate training-state memoryProblem: How much model-state memory is required to fully fine-tune Llama 3 8B with mixed-precision Adam?
Variables: Mixed-precision Adam stores BF16 weights, gradients, FP32 master weights, momentum, and variance. The model-state budget is 16 bytes per parameter.
Math: For 8.03B parameters, model state is 8.03B \(\times\) 16 bytes = 128.5 GB.
Result: An H100 has 80 GB of HBM, so the model state alone exceeds a single accelerator before accounting for activations.
Systems insight: Optimizer state, not weights alone, sets the floor for training memory. Capacity planning that starts from parameter bytes underestimates the real requirement.


When a training job scales beyond one accelerator to a multi-week cluster run, thermal design power and duration turn hardware utilization into megawatt-hours and utility cost. Multiplying the V100 power envelope (table 5), the reconstructed GPT-3 cluster duration (table 15), and the cloud electricity rate (table 20) estimates the accelerator-only electricity bill; Dimensional analysis verifies that the units of such a product reduce to energy, and Accounting for cost and carbon extends the accounting to total cost and carbon at deployment scale.

Napkin Math 1.3: Estimate accelerator electricity costProblem: What is the accelerator-only electricity cost of the GPT-3 training run?
Variables: Use 10,000 V100s, 300 W per accelerator, ~14.8 days wall-clock, and $0.12/kWh electricity (Patterson et al. 2021).
Math: The run requires roughly \(3.14 \times 10^{23}\) FLOPs. The accelerator-only electricity-cost estimate is ~14.8 days wall-clock \(\times\) 10,000 V100s \(\times\) 24 h/day \(\times\) 0.3 kW \(\times\) $0.12/kWh = ~$127,872.
Result: The accelerator-only electricity cost is roughly $128,000. This TDP-only estimate excludes host CPUs, networking, storage, cooling, and facility overhead. The 1,066 MWh of accelerator energy behind it covers about 83 percent of the 1,287 MWh reported for the run, which also counts host power and data center overhead. The GPU count and duration are a published reconstruction from measured per-GPU throughput, so only their product is firm (Patterson et al. 2021).
Systems insight: Energy follows directly from power and time, while the dollar figure depends on the electricity rate assumed.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Those three calculations mix an H100 vendor datasheet ceiling, a book convention for Adam training state, a published reconstruction of the GPT-3 training run, and an illustrative utility rate, and treating all four as interchangeable measurements would misstate what an estimate proves. Each quantitative input in this appendix therefore carries a provenance record that places it in an explicit evidence class alongside its primary references (table 22). Vendor specifications and standards define published limits, peer-reviewed measurements provide empirical anchors, and explicitly marked editorial scenarios supply illustrative values where no durable universal constant exists. Every value is read from the book’s hardware, model, systems, and infrastructure registries, which record the same provenance per entry. Checking the evidence class before trusting a number keeps vendor ceilings distinct from empirical anchors and scenario placeholders.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Back-of-envelope estimates stay comparable across chapters only when they share a single set of unit conventions and dated hardware, model, energy, interconnect, and economic inputs. Because those values come from vendor datasheet peaks, published empirical measurements, interface standards, and editorial scenarios, they carry different evidentiary weight and age at different rates.
Use these tables as starting inputs, not universal constants. For each estimate, record the table row, unit convention, and provenance. Replace time-sensitive peaks, prices, and rates with local values. Distinguish a physical ceiling from a measured operating point and a scenario assumption. Report which assumptions dominate the result. This keeps napkin math reproducible and makes clear which input controls the conclusion.
